one_paragraph_summary: China's protest of the newly enacted Maritime Zones Act (RA 12064) and the Archipelagic Sea Lanes Act (RA 12065) is, in CJ Panganiban's framing, neither surprising nor warranted: the laws 'merely preserve and buttress our sovereign rights' under UNCLOS and the July 12, 2016 Arbitral Award issued by the Hague Permanent Court of Arbitration as registrar. RA 12064 defines the Philippine exclusive economic zone and continental shelf; RA 12065 designates the sea lanes and air routes foreign military and civilian aircraft/vessels may use within those zones. They clarify Article I of the 1987 Constitution's National Territory provision -- but by adopting UNCLOS-consistent boundaries, the Philippines voluntarily cedes some claims under the 1898 Treaty of Paris, the 1900 US-Spain supplement, and the controversial 1930 US-UK North Borneo treaty. CJ canvasses Unclos compliance asymmetry: 168 signatories; nine of ten ASEAN members signatories (Cambodia signed but did not ratify); China ratified in 1996 'with reservations' but 'has steadfastly claimed sovereignty over all the islands and islets, and maritime rights over almost the entire SCS under its nebulous nine-dash line theory (lately amended to 10-dash line) that had been invalidated by the Arbitral Award' -- enforced by 'more powerful and more numerous coast guard ships' patrolling 'with impunity' through 'laser guns, water cannons, ship boardings, and other gray zones tactics' under 'the old, old theory of discovery and conquest, a mode of acquiring title that has been overtaken by Unclos.' Why did China join Unclos in the first place? Because during the 1973-1982 negotiations the post-1971-UN-recognized PRC (vis-à-vis the Kuomintang-led Taiwan driven there 'by the hordes of Mao Tse Tung') identified itself with Third-World states needing treaty protection -- but today, as the world's number-two economy, it 'no longer needs the protection of treaties' and reportedly considers withdrawing. Why is the US not a member? Because the US Senate has refused ratification 'and will probably never ratify it' since the US prefers its actions 'governed only by its national interest, not by treaties' -- yet it enforces freedom of navigation under Unclos anyway. And why can't ASEAN unite against China? Four structural facts: ASEAN is not a NATO-style military alliance; Cambodia is not an Unclos member and aligns with China; Malaysia, the Philippines, and Vietnam have overlapping EEZ/CS claims among themselves; and ASEAN operates by consensus, not majority vote. Past dispute-settlement paths include diplomacy (PH-Indonesia) and the ICJ (Indonesia-Malaysia-Singapore). CJ's recommended way forward: bring the Malaysia-Philippines-Vietnam overlap to arbitration under Unclos itself -- 'in my humble opinion, this is the best way forward under the rule of law.'

one_paragraph_summary: Sen. Robinhood C. Padilla, the 2022 senatorial topnotcher, personally signed under oath and filed on August 5 a petition -- 'by his lonesome -- without being represented or assisted by lawyers' -- asking the Supreme Court for a binding opinion on how Congress should vote in revising or amending the Constitution. He quoted Article XVII: Section 1 (amendments/revisions proposed by Congress 'upon a vote of three-fourths of all its Members') and Section 3 ('two-thirds of all its Members' to call a concon; 'majority vote' to submit concon-calling to the electorate). As chair of the Senate committee on constitutional amendment and revision of codes, the 54-year-old 'champion of federalism' has called public hearings, but invited legal experts could not agree on the meaning of 'vote of three-fourths.' One camp argues joint voting (sum senators + congressmen, extract 3/4); another argues separate voting (as in ordinary legislation). 'Most senators insist on separate voting; otherwise, they would drown in the sea of the much more numerous representatives, who, understandably, want joint voting.' Padilla frames the irreconcilable differences as 'actual controversy' or 'gloomy atmosphere' and pleads transcendental national interest. He concedes he is asking for 'declaratory relief' (Rule 63 Section 1) which 'should be filed in the Regional Trial Courts (RTCs)' but asks for an exception due to 'transcendental importance.' CJ deeply admires Padilla's patriotic intentions but identifies -- IMHO -- three difficult remedial-law problems. FIRST, declaratory-relief jurisdiction is initially vested in RTCs with SC review only on appeal; though SC has granted exceptions for 'transcendental importance' in rare cases, it could dismiss the petition on short shrift. SECOND, the petition includes no opposing party with adverse interest, but 'our judicial system is essentially adversarial in nature. Justices and judges are passive participants in conducting trials in the lower courts and in reviewing the records when they pass upon appeals.' THIRD -- flowing from the second -- Padilla is asking for an 'advisory opinion' which 'our Constitution does not allow the judiciary to promulgate' (unlike the International Court of Justice and some foreign tribunals). CJ recommends: the Court should NOT simply dismiss given the transcendental issue. Because Padilla already furnished copies to OSG, Senate President, and Speaker, the Court should let them intervene voluntarily or be directed to file comments -- to comply with 'the constitutional edicts of due process' -- and then 'promulgate a full decision and thereby avoid issuing an advisory opinion.' CJ closes: 'Should Padilla win this case on its merits despite its seemingly insurmountable procedural mountain peaks, he could be admitted to the Philippine Bar and become a full-fledged lawyer as an exception to the Rules of Court's requirement to pass a four-year basic law degree and the stringent bar exam.'

one_paragraph_summary: CJ reports that his July 29 column 'Scotus legalizes bribery' drew 'a record number of applauses (and some applesauce)' via emails, texts, and calls from the Philippines and abroad -- even rating a full column from Manila Overseas Press Club prexy Tony Lopez ('The decline of Scotus,' Philippine Star, 6/18/24). An anonymous NYC reader sent a screenshot of Google top news in the US on July 29 at 10:30 AM NYC time showing CJ's column and portrait alongside The Guardian and the Chicago Tribune's 'Ex-AT&T boss accused of bribing Michael Madigan,' 'catapulting the Inquirer among the most respected British and US dailies.' Another US reader emailed a July 30 Gallup report -- 'Approval of US Supreme Court Stalled Near Historic Low' -- tracing Scotus approval from a high of 62% (2000, 2001) to below 50% from 2011-2017, back to majority approval 2018-2020 during Trump's three appointments, then below 50% since the 2023-2024 term. CJ quotes retired PH SC colleagues. J Antonio T. Carpio: 'This Scotus decision is utterly shameful and morally bankrupt. What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. Those Scotus justices are announcing publicly that they expect to collect gratuities after they retire. All US government officials can also expect the same gratuities.' J Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez, who heads the PH SC's Judicial Integrity Board (which investigates judicial misconduct in all courts except the SC, which has its own ethics committee): 'Chief, I am also flabbergasted and shocked. This is not the Court we knew. Sadly, the sterling Justices we visited and admired have retired.' To be fair, CJ quotes 'the lone Scotus defender,' Yale alumnus J Vicente V. Mendoza: 'The real question or gravamen of the crime here may not really be whether payment was given before or after the subject of the crime. The Court held that those given before are inherently bribes but those amounting to 5,000 dollars or more which are given after may only be tokens [of] appreciation and do not per se show a corrupt state of mind. In the case in question, the transaction was worth 1.1 million dollars but the payment to the mayor was only 13,000 dollars [that] may not really show corrupt intent.' Cross-sector reactions follow: Dean Nilo Divina -- 'I concur with nary a dissent, CJ'; former PCCI president Edgardo Lacson -- 'shocking indeed to know the Scotus distinguished bribery and gratuity by a timeline... politically silly and kindergarten decision... the BEST JUSTICES MONEY CAN BUY'; Dr. Jose Acuin in Taglish -- 'Hindi ka pwedeng sumuntok pag may nakatago sa kilikili mo' (you can't throw a punch when you have something hidden in your armpit). CJ then recites President Biden's July 29 three measures: (1) a constitutional amendment ensuring no immunity for in-office presidential crimes; (2) Scotus term limits with the President appointing a Justice every two years to serve 18 years in active service; (3) a binding Code of Conduct requiring gift disclosure, prohibiting public political activity, and mandating recusal for financial or spousal conflicts. Whether 'lame-duck' US Congress will follow remains uncertain. CJ closes: 'I wrote my three columns not to degrade the Scotus further into the abyss but to entice it to levitate itself. I merely stated the facts and the truth, for the truth shall set the Scotus free to climb anew to its former Olympian heights that I used to look up to. At bottom, I firmly believe that justice is blind and that justices must be beyond reproach. My prayer is for the Scotus to rise like the Phoenix and become again the indisputable cradle of the rule of law and the unblemished judicial standard for all freedom-loving countries.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with the 'dizzying political turmoil' in the US -- Biden's July 12 press conference 'miserably confused Russian Vladimir Putin to be the president of Ukraine, and Donald Trump to be the US veep'; his July 21 withdrawal-and-Harris-endorsement after contracting COVID; Harris's record '$150 million in campaign contributions in 24 hours.' The contest is now 'between a relatively young incumbent lady vice president, former US senator, and federal prosecutor with Asian descent versus a former president, Caucasian blabbermouth, and the oldest felon to seek the presidency of the most powerful country in the planet.' But as a lawyer and retired jurist, CJ is 'more befuddled by' the recent decision in Snyder v. United States (June 26, 2024) that 'practically legalized bribery.' The facts: James Snyder, mayor of Portage, Indiana, presided over the city's 2013 purchase of five trash trucks from Great Lakes Peterbilt Co. for about $1.1M; in 2014, Peterbilt 'cut a check for $13,000 to Snyder.' A federal jury convicted him of 'accepting an illegal gratuity in violation of Section 666 of the US Code,' rejecting his 'consulting services' defense; the district court sentenced him to 1 year and 9 months; the US Court of Appeals affirmed. Section 666(a)(1)(B) penalizes any agent of an organization or state/local/tribal government who 'corruptly solicits or demands... or accepts, or agrees to accept, anything of value... intending to be influenced or rewarded in connection with any business, transaction... involving any thing of value of $5,000 or more.' The Scotus, 6-3 (six conservatives appointed by Republican presidents -- three by Trump -- against three liberals appointed by Democratic presidents), acquitted by distinguishing bribes (given BEFORE an official act, 'inherently corrupt and unlawful') from gratuities (given AFTER as 'reward or token of appreciation,' which 'might be innocuous' or might 'raise ethical and appearance concerns,' with 'Federal, state, and local governments... drawn different lines'). Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh's 16-page majority held that Section 666 is a 'bribery statute' requiring a 'corrupt state of mind,' not proven in Snyder's case -- and left the issue as a state, not federal, matter. With a 'veiled swipe at the majority,' the 22-page dissent of 'neophyte Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson' sneered, 'Snyder's absurd and atextual reading of the statute is one [that] only today's Court could love.' Like Justice Jackson, CJ's 'simple mind cannot grasp and accept the Scotus distinction between money or gift given BEFORE and AFTER an official act is performed. In both, the purpose of the gift is the same -- to influence the public official into performing an official act according to the giver's direction. To me, it does not matter whether the reward or token of appreciation was given before or after the act; or a part was given before and the balance after. The act is a simple, plain, and shameful crime against the people.' CJ 'cannot imagine our Supreme Court proudly posing a linguistic distinction that does not make a substantive difference.' But perhaps he should not be shocked: his June 17 column was already 'utterly dismayed' at Scotus practices -- 'their unabashed acceptance of enormous sums as royalties, speaking fees, expensive gifts, paid vacations in exclusive hotels with private yachts and private planes, hobnobbing with the rich and famous in private clubs and, lately, partisan political bias' -- 'unethical, if not illegal.' Closing escalation: 'Now, I am no longer dismayed. I am flabbergasted! The great chief justice John Marshall must be rolling in his grave.'

one_paragraph_summary: Not until the Philippines won the 501-page unanimous Arbitral Award of July 12, 2016 did the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) become a household name in the Philippines, Asia, and the world -- yet it is the oldest existing international dispute-settlement body, celebrating its 125th birth anniversary on July 29, older than both the International Court of Justice and the United Nations (both October 24, 1945) and the League of Nations (January 10, 1920). It owes its birth to the Conventions for the Pacific Settlement of International Disputes of 1899 and 1907. The ICJ, judicial organ of the UN, is composed of 15 judges elected with staggered 15-year terms by the UN General Assembly and Security Council 'simultaneously but separately'; only states qualify as parties; the court sits en banc and renders binding decisions, with enforcement entrusted to the UN Security Council. In contrast, the PCA has no permanent judges with fixed terms -- parties choose arbitrators for each controversy; parties may be states, private organizations, or even individuals; and the PCA itself does not render awards but 'merely functions as a Registry' that, somewhat like the Office of the Clerk of Court in the PH Supreme Court, provides administrative services: transmitting communications between parties and the arbitral tribunal, maintaining the archive, arranging arbitrator fees, holding arbitration funds and paying expenses, providing hearing rooms in the Peace Palace in The Hague (or elsewhere), and any other tasks entrusted by parties or tribunal. Arbitral tribunals -- whether under PCA, ICC, or ICSID auspices -- are 'ad hoc by nature and are disbanded after settling the dispute referred to them,' though their proceedings and awards are binding on parties and PCA member states. The 2016 PH vs China arbitration illustrates this. The full title of the award preserved verbatim: 'AN ARBITRAL TRIBUNAL CONSTITUTED UNDER ANNEX VII TO THE 1982 UNITED NATIONS CONVENTION ON THE LAW OF THE SEA' (Caps in original) -- it did NOT call itself the PCA. Under UNCLOS Article 287(1), a signatory state may choose: (1) ITLOS based in Hamburg; (2) ICJ in The Hague; (3) ad hoc arbitration per Annex VII; or (4) special tribunal per Annex VIII. The PH vs China tribunal fell under (3) and was constituted June 21, 2013 with five members: German Judge Rudiger Wolfrum (PH-chosen); after China opted not to participate, the ITLOS president appointed Polish Judge Stanislaw Pawlak, then named Frenchman Judge Jean-Pierre Cot, Dutchman Professor Alfred H. A. Soons, and Ghanaian Judge Thomas A. Mensah as presiding arbitrator. After constitution, the tribunal issued Administrative Directive No. 1 appointing the PCA as its Registry. The PCA itself is composed of four arbitrators from each of its 122 member-states. Current PH members: Ambassador Eduardo Malaya, Dean Antonio La Viña, Dean Sedfrey Candelaria, and retired International Criminal Court judge Raul Pangalangan (who replaced CJ as chair of the PH group of four when CJ's six-year term expired in August last year). PCA members are also empowered to nominate ICJ members and Nobel Peace Prize candidates. At the 208th meeting of PCA member states on December 12, 2022, Malaya was elected president of the PCA Administrative Council for the 2023-2024 term, successfully supervising the Congress of Members held in The Hague June 12-14 (attended by 'amiable Solicitor General Menardo I. Guevarra' as PH government representative). Malaya will also oversee the worldwide 125th anniversary celebration. 'Mabuhay po kayo, Amba Ed!'

one_paragraph_summary: After reviewing the significant 2023 SC decisions, CJ shares seven 'little-known ones' affecting both lawyers and ordinary people. FIRST, under Ko v. Republic (April 12, 2023), Family-Code children conceived or born during a marriage are presumed legitimate even when conceived/born during parental separation and biologically the offspring of the wife and a man other than her legal husband. The Court distinguished legitimacy ('the civil status established for a person born during the subsistence of a marriage') from filiation ('the state of being someone's offspring as determined by biology and biotechnology'). The biological father cannot petition to tag the offspring as his 'natural child' because that would deprive the child of legitimacy rights including inheritance from the legal father. Only the child (and in some instances the legal father or his heirs) can challenge directly -- not collaterally -- because the presumption is for the child's benefit, and 'Even the mother is prohibited by law from declaring against the child's legitimacy.' SECOND, under Republic v. Pryce (March 8, 2023), the 20% senior discount 'necessarily include interment services, such as diggings for the deceased person's grave, its concreting, and other services being done during the actual burial.' THIRD, under Ong v. Senate (March 28, 2023), congressional legislative-investigation power has four limitations: (1) inquiry 'in aid of legislation,' (2) per chamber's published rules, (3) rights of appearing persons respected, (4) contempt-based detention only until termination of inquiry. The Senate (in the Pharmally case) met the first two but failed the third by citing petitioners in contempt and ordering arrest 'without giving them the opportunity to be heard'; only detention -- not criminal/civil liability -- was decided. FOURTH, under Soliman v. People (April 25, 2023), the Cybercrime Law penalty for online libel is one degree higher than RPC traditional libel (prision correcional minimum-medium OR fine P40,000-P1,200,000, or both); for online libel, courts 'may impose the alternative penalty of fine instead of imprisonment.' FIFTH, under 4E Steel Builders v. Maybank Philippines (March 13, 2023), foreign banks may foreclose and acquire mortgaged real property under three conditions: 5-year maximum possession; title not transferred to the foreign bank; required transfer to a qualified Philippine national within the 5-year period. SIXTH, under ACT Teachers v. Duterte (January 24, 2023), livestream video and photographs demonstrating absence of a House quorum cannot prevail over the Congressional Journal because 'no less than the Constitution itself grants the Congressional Journal its imprimatur.' CJ adds his 'humble opinion' that the principle of separation of powers grants the three branches autonomy on internal processes -- SC respects Congressional Journal entries; Congress respects internal SC deliberations and votes; both respect Executive Branch's internal Cabinet processes. SEVENTH, under People v. Almayda (June 14, 2023), in warrantless seizures of illegal drugs the physical inventory and photo-taking 'must, as a rule, be done in the place of seizure.' The exception -- at the nearest police station or apprehending officer's office -- applies only when 'clear, consistent, and sensible affidavits' show (1) impracticability of place-of-seizure inventory or (2) seized items threatened by 'immediate or extreme danger' at the place of seizure.

one_paragraph_summary: CJ is 'totally amazed' at the emails, calls, and texts on his prior June 17 column 'From awe to dismay at the Scotus' -- samples: 'Disgusting, the Scotus is no longer the highest court we admire'; 'No different from politicians'; 'I hope Amb. MaryKay Carlson reported this to her superiors to stop the self-destruct of the Scotus.' It even rated a full column from Manila Overseas Press Club prexy Tony Lopez ('The decline of Scotus,' Philippine Star, 6/18/24). Two reader questions need response: (1) Why equate CJ Sereno's removal with the two unidentified erring justices? (2) Did you forget the dismaying decisions involving Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, Juan Ponce Enrile, and Jinggoy Estrada? CJ clarifies: he did NOT equate those three decisions -- he cited Sereno only because they 'exemplify how our Supreme Court disciplines its own members, while the Supreme Court of the United States (Scotus) has yet to do so.' He restates his prior position: the 8-6 decision ousting Sereno was (1) 'plainly unconstitutional' because -- IMHO -- Supreme Court justices may be removed 'only via impeachment expressly canalized by our Constitution and only for the grounds provided therein, not via quo warranto'; and (2) 'unduly harsh' because expressly made immediately executory -- 'on the very day it was issued, the embarrassed and belittled erstwhile chief justice had to leave the Supreme Court premises carrying all her personal belongings. Decisions convicting even the most hardened criminals are not immediately executory. They could still file motions for reconsideration that would stay immediate execution.' Rule-of-law discipline: 'Though I disagreed with the decision, I must follow it and cite it as a valid judgment.' Same for the Arroyo/Enrile/Estrada decisions: 'I must respect and obey them. That is the rule of law. As I always say, we can disagree without being disagreeable and we can differ without being difficult.' Justices must render full-time service and shed political, business, and professional connections -- 'No side incomes.' CJ's own example: he 'dissolved my law firm when I ascended to the Court in 1995 to heed the Constitution's call for proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence' -- dissolution was not legally required (only resignation), but he chose to adhere to the ideal of being 'like Caesar's wife, beyond suspicion.' The Gesmundo Court has not been tested by 'nation-shaking cases comparable to those of the Concepcion Court on the ratification of the 1973 Constitution, or of the Davide Court on stopping the House of Representatives from impeaching the chief justice, or of the Panganiban Court on rejecting the people's initiative to change our presidential system to the parliamentary' -- but CJ is 'still impressed by its solid effort to implement the Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations 2022-2027.' Then the personal transition: amazing comments also came on his June 3 and 10 columns about master's-degree scholarships granted to his three talented grandkids by top US universities 'without their applying.' This proud Lolo just learned that a fourth 'apo,' Katrina P. Hannett, was offered bioethics-master's scholarships. CJ recounts: Katrina was gifted from kindergarten -- taught a fellow 5-year-old cursive script when he didn't yet write in print; in first grade she was given fourth-grade-level work to keep her busy; 'She did her homework lying upside down on a sofa, feet up on a wall, and hair cascading down the chair to the floor. Still, she got top grades and was elected student body president (like her Lolo).' Her compassion-and-humility traits stand out: when her sibling was scolded for pushing her around, she was 'the first to hug her crying offender'; as an eighth-grade dancer landing prima donna roles, she pulled back to avoid 'dramas' among beat dancers; now as a young adult she does medical-volunteer marathon work helping save cardiac-arrest runners. She aspires to be a 'compassionate doctor' and chose a pre-med master's in bioethics -- 'the study of ethical, social, and legal issues that arise in medicine.' Scholarships offered by Johns Hopkins, NYU, and Penn. She hasn't made her final choice -- 'maybe still pondering real-world human issues?' -- but 'she will crack her mega-class dilemma soon.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban traces a personal arc from lifelong awe at the US Supreme Court -- whose justices he regarded as 'deities in the legendary Mount Olympus,' quoting Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., Benjamin Cardozo, and Felix Frankfurter, and admiring Hugo Black, William Brennan, and Thurgood Marshall -- to dismay at current ethical practices. He recalls pilgrimages to the SCOTUS office (visits to Sandra Day O'Connor, Anthony Kennedy, and the deceased Antonin Scalia, and homage at John Marshall's bronze statue), then itemizes the recent financial disclosures: royalties of $340,000 (Brett Kavanaugh), $250,000 (Neil Gorsuch), $87,000 (Sonia Sotomayor), and even new Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson's $900,000 book advance, four Beyoncé tickets worth about $3,700, and $12,500 for chamber artwork, all on top of the 2023 salaries of $285,400 (justices) and $298,500 (chief justice) per www.uscourts.gov. Senior Justice Clarence Thomas only belatedly disclosed Republican mega-donor Harlan Crow's 2019 hospitality in Bali and Monte Rio as 'inadvertently omitted,' explaining that ethics officials advised that 'personal hospitality' from friends need not be disclosed. Worse, Justice Samuel Alito allegedly took a private-jet Alaska vacation with a hedge-fund billionaire with interests before the Court -- undisclosed thanks to a 90-day filing extension. The New York Times photographed an upside-down US flag at Alito's home -- a signal the US Code permits only for 'dire distress or extreme danger,' but in January 2021 widely tied to the stolen-2020-election narrative and the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. Alito blamed his wife Martha Ann's altercation with a neighbor, but neighbor Emily Baden told CNN's Erin Burnett that Alito was 'at best mistaken, but at worst, he's just lying,' since the altercation occurred in mid-February (police call Feb. 15, 2021) while the upside-down flag photograph dates to Jan. 17, 2021. A second NYT photo showed an 'Appeal to Heaven' flag -- a Revolutionary War banner re-adopted by Trump supporters -- at Alito's New Jersey home. Both Thomas and Alito refused to recuse from pending Jan. 6 and Trump-immunity cases ('My wife is fond of flying flags. I am not.'). The Scotus code of ethics promulgated late last year has 'no enforcement mechanism' -- like international law. By contrast, CJ recalls, the Philippine Supreme Court penalizes unethical conduct: two justices fined and disqualified from law practice (one for not reporting a filial relationship with a bar examinee, the other as source of a premature draft-decision leak), and a chief justice ousted 8-6 for failing to file SALN as a law professor before joining the Court.

CJ then sets out the Rome Statute architecture: July 17, 1998; 124 member-states (non-members include the US, Russia, China, and Israel); four principal organs (Presidency, Judicial Divisions, Office of the Prosecutor, Registry); and a four-element jurisdictional rule -- RS-listed crimes, committed in a member-state's territory or by its national, while membership is active, and only absent 'complementarity' (the state being 'unwilling or unable to prosecute'). To bridge the membership gap, Khan convened a Panel of Experts in International Law in January 2024; its nine-page Report dated May 20, 2024 concluded that the ICC has jurisdiction and that Palestine including Gaza is a State for ICC purposes -- but CJ flags that the Report 'made no mention of Israel's non-membership' and 'omitted the requirement for complementarity,' even though Israel has 'functioning prosecutorial offices' and a judiciary CJ has personally observed (during his May 2000 visit) to be 'active, competent, and independent.' He recalls inviting Israeli CJ Dorit Beinisch -- then not yet CJ -- to the PH SC's 2001 Centenary Celebrations to speak on 'Protecting Civil Liberties in a State of Continuing Emergency,' and quotes her letter from his book 'Reforming the Judiciary' (pp. 178-179). He admits he does not know enough about Hamas to assess the Panel's allusion to it as 'part of the Palestinian state,' noting that countries that have designated Hamas a terrorist organization may treat ICC action as irrelevant because they can 'deal with Hamas more effectively than the ICC.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban refutes the headline impression that the Supreme Court is hostile to doctors. In Nuñez v. Daz (Jan. 29, 2024, Third Division, ponente Justice Maria Filomena D. Singh -- a well-written 15-page signed ponencia), the Court upheld Dr. Henry Daz's acquittal of reckless imprudence and reversed even the RTC Baguio's civil award of P200,000 moral damages, P300,000 exemplary damages, and P25,000 actual damages tied to the death of two-year-old John Ray Nuñez. The boy was treated for hypothermia with a hot water bag on his legs; the bag allegedly burst and scalded him, requiring burn surgery that delayed chemotherapy for a prior brain tumor; the tumor recurred and the boy died during a second surgery. The Court agreed with the RTC that the prosecution failed to prove Daz's negligence in the bursting -- indeed, 'failed to offer any evidence that a hot water bag broke' -- and asked rhetorically, 'How can a doctor be responsible for the usability of an instrument that can be safely assumed to be that of the hospital's?' Applying a natural-and-continuous-chain test of causation, the Court held that the first event did not set the subsequent operations in motion such that the death could be deemed the natural and probable result of the bag incident. CJ contrasts this with the 2021 Agbayani v. People case -- an Unsigned Extended Resolution (UER), which does not create precedent -- where the late Dr. Benigno Agbayani Jr. was convicted by the MeTC (July 29, 2013) and lost on appeal at every level because his counsel missed the 15-day reglementary period for the appeal memorandum at the RTC despite an extension, then 'failed to append' the witnesses' affidavits, prosecution evidence, and lower-court pleadings required by the Rules of Court at the CA, then failed again at the SC. Documentary attachments 'should not be perfunctorily ignored or violated' and the 'heavy workload' excuse 'does not persuade.' The lesson, CJ concludes, is that the two cases differ not in judicial attitude toward doctors but in counsel quality -- and he wonders 'why the well-known physician did not replace his lawyer in the wake of his series of convictions due to his counsel's palpable negligence.'

one_paragraph_summary: The Supreme Court issued the writ of amparo in Deduro v. Vinoya (July 4, 2023, released only May 8, 2024) to protect petitioner Siegfred Deduro after he was Red-tagged by the government. Panganiban hails the unanimous 39-page ponencia of Justice Rodil V. Zalameda as a 'well-written treatise' on the writ's (1) purpose, (2) coverage, (3) parties, and (4) process. He recalls retired Justice Adolfo S. Azcuna's 1991 bar question on the writ -- very few examinees answered correctly -- and his personal interview with Azcuna, who traces the writ's origins to Mexico and Prof. Héctor Fix-Zamudio. As a delegate to the 1971 Constitutional Convention Azcuna proposed its inclusion 'but failed because only a few understood it then'; as a member of the 1986 Constitutional Commission he tried again to place it in the Bill of Rights, but the late CJ Roberto Concepcion convinced him to incorporate it under SC powers, where it now lives. For his 'untiring spade work,' CJ bestows on him the title 'Father of the Writ of Amparo in the Philippines.' He then distinguishes the writ of amparo from the privilege of the writ: the writ is issued when, 'on its face,' the petition and affidavits show prima facie violation of the right to life, liberty, or security; the privilege follows only after 'summary proceedings' requiring 'substantial evidence' -- analogous (but not identical) to a preliminary vs permanent injunction in civil cases (with proof scales of prima facie, substantial, preponderance, and beyond reasonable doubt). So Deduro's writ is 'a good start' but to complete his victory he must produce substantial evidence to earn the privilege. Coverage extends to extralegal killings (per UN instruments, killings without due process regardless of motive, by state or non-state actors), enforced disappearances (per RA 10353), and threats thereof -- and SND v. Manalo (Oct. 7, 2008) recognizes the right to security as 'freedom from fear,' independent of any liberty deprivation. Red-tagging as a 'communist' or 'terrorist' is actionable harassment because it exposes the target to vigilantes, paramilitary groups, or state agents -- and creates justifiable fear of killing or abduction. For lack of space, CJ leaves parties and process to lawyers and law students reading the Zalameda treatise -- which 'could erupt in another bar exam.'

one_paragraph_summary: The Supreme Court, in a unanimous decision penned by Justice Jose Midas P. Marquez, struck down the Comelec en banc's Nov. 29, 2023 resolution disqualifying Smartmatic TIM Corp. from any public bidding (especially for the 2025 automated election system), holding that the agency committed grave abuse of discretion by disqualifying Smartmatic without due process and in violation of the Government Procurement Reform Act (RA 9184) and Comelec's own IRR -- Comelec had acted on information from the US Department of Justice about an ongoing investigation of alleged irregularities in the 2016 AES procurement under former Comelec chair Andres D. Bautista. Yet the Court did not invalidate the bidding already won by the joint venture led by Miru Systems for 2025. The reason is the doctrine of operative fact: acts done in good faith before a determination of unconstitutionality produce consequences that cannot always be erased -- the void act is set aside but its effects sustained where a higher public good (here, the strict 2025-election timeline) so requires. Smartmatic's victory is not Pyrrhic -- it may participate in future biddings (such as the 2028 presidential elections) unless properly disqualified after due process, the GPRA, and the Comelec IRR are faithfully observed. CJ thinks any Comelec motion for reconsideration would be 'a waste of time and resources' and, while taking no position on Smartmatic substantively, anchors his view in the rule of law: 'I may not agree with what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it.' The column then pivots to a tribute to the late Rene A.V. Saguisag -- 'profound, tenacious, honest, and humble' -- who 'opted to be poor, to serve the poor, and to remain poor until his death.' CJ recalls offering in 1961 to help RAVS get elected NUS president; RAVS declined and asked CJ to nominate Raul S. Roco. After RAVS's Ledesma Law Office stint, CJ invited him to be a partner; RAVS preferred solo practice and later collaborated with CJ and Dean Antonio H. Abad Jr. on pro bono cases. Viewed as a 'leftist' by many, RAVS was no political creature -- initially reluctant to run for the Senate and firmly refusing reelection despite favorable surveys. CJ last saw him alive on April 9, when he was acclaimed as one of 13 'Haligi' of the Bantayog ng mga Bayani Foundation at the UP-University Hotel; though wheelchair-bound and 'numbed by illness,' RAVS 'manfully raised his clenched fist' for each honoree and stretched his weakened right arm for 'Bayan Ko.' 'Compadre Rene (the baptism ninong of my daughter Celine), rest in Heaven with my Leni in the peace and love of the Lord.'

one_paragraph_summary: The Supreme Court plans to require all Philippine lawyers to render at least 60 hours of pro bono legal aid services to the poor every three years throughout their professional career under its new Unified Legal Aid Services (ULAS) program. A Technical Working Group chaired by Justice Alfredo Benjamin S. Caguioa, with Justice Rodil V. Zalameda as vice chair, drafted the ULAS Rules, and the Court has launched a four-leg Regional Consultation series keynoted by Chief Justice Alexander G. Gesmundo: Baguio (April 12), Cagayan de Oro (April 18), Makati (May 17), and Iloilo (TBA). The new Rules will replace earlier initiatives that limited creditable legal aid to litigation work; they will credit 'any service involving the application of law' across non-litigation practice areas, allowing lawyers in their respective fields to serve 'qualified beneficiaries': (a) indigents (per Revised Rules of Court or by Affidavit of Indigency), (b) marginalized-sector members with respect to their public-interest cases -- farmer-peasant, artisanal fisherfolk, formal and informal-sector workers, migrant workers, indigenous peoples and cultural communities, women, differently abled persons, senior citizens, victims of calamities and disasters, youth and students, children, and urban poor -- and (c) NGOs and nonprofits whose work benefits (a) and (b). Creditable pro bono services include court and quasi-judicial representation (with mediation and ADR); legal counseling and contract negotiation/drafting; developmental legal assistance (rights awareness, capacity building, training in human rights, documentation, affidavit-making); participation in Accredited Legal Outreach Programs and Missions including mentorship under the Law Student Practice Rule; and other services as the SC may define. 'Public-interest cases' cover civil rights and liberties, women's rights, children and youth services, workers' rights, employment law, public benefits, gender and sexuality issues, environmental law, prisoners' rights, criminal law, and the death penalty. Enforcement starts January 1, 2025 and will be 'earth-shaking' -- reaching even 'abogados de campanilla' who charge up to $1,000 per hour (research and travel included), making 60 pro bono hours worth $60,000 in foregone billings. The Court justifies the rule on the constitutional ground that the practice of law is 'imbued with public interest' and that 'membership in the Bar is a special privilege burdened with conditions' -- including the duty to make legal services readily accessible to the public. CJ closes: 'God bless the Supreme Court and the lawyers. May they never tire of aiding the poor.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban welcomes 'to my delight' the recently released 404-page Supreme Court Stylebook, which replaces the old 'Manual for Judicial Writing' under the leadership of Senior Associate Justice Marvic M.V.F. Leonen and his team, with a 'Message' by CJ Alexander G. Gesmundo stating it 'was impelled by the need for greater clarity, consistency, and uniformity so that litigants and the public in general will clearly understand court decisions.' He traces his lifelong advocacy for simplicity and clarity through three career stages: as a young lawyer winning Ermita-Malate Hotel v. City Mayor (July 31, 1967, per J -- later CJ -- Fernando, en banc) with co-counsel Antonio H. Abad Jr. (candidly admitting he 'did not immediately catch the rather complicated structure of' that landmark verdict); as Inquirer part-time president in 1991-1992 encouraging publisher Isagani Yambot and Cristina Pantoja-Hidalgo to produce the Inquirer Stylebook; and as a magistrate authoring Velarde v. Social Justice Society (April 28, 2004), which the new SC Stylebook repeatedly cites as the touchstone for replacing the 'archaic ... WHEREFORE' with the plain 'ACCORDINGLY' or 'FOR THESE REASONS.' He walks readers through SAJ Leonen's eloquent Foreword ('Words do have power. Used in the wrong ways, they can destroy and bury an entire segment of society. Used correctly, they can liberate and, sometimes, even heal'), the 'Make every word count' rule with its 'Before/After' example, the proper use of 'e.g.' and 'i.e.' as interrupters with commas before and after, and the capitalization rules for titles directly preceding vs following proper names. He notes that the Inquirer Stylebook differs by capitalizing only current titleholders ('President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and president Rodrigo Duterte') -- drawing the moral lesson that stylebooks of different institutions may differ but should be used 'in their proper milieu.' Chapter 11 dives into SC decision structure (case title, introduction, body, parties' arguments, issues, discussion, dispositive portion), Chapters 12-14 handle citations of jurisprudence (here and abroad), statutes, ordinances, court issuances, legislative journals, law reviews, articles, and even simple letters, and the final chapter provides templates. He closes by hailing the Court and Leonen team for a 'truly commendable work to demystify the judiciary and keep it relevant in this age of artificial intelligence and the Swifties.'

one_paragraph_summary: Following his March 11 column (A78) on Scotus's narrow Trump ruling, Panganiban offers four cases that exemplify the PH Supreme Court's 'courage and grit' in jumping into 'the vortex of political whirlpools' -- in stark contrast to Frankfurter's 'political thicket' avoidance practiced by the US Scotus. First, Santiago v. Comelec (March 19, 1997, per J -- later CJ -- Davide, en banc) shut down the People's Initiative to shift to a parliamentary system that would have let FVR continue as prime minister, ruling the PI implementing law 'insufficient and inadequate.' Second, Lambino v. Comelec (Oct. 25, 2006, per J Carpio, en banc) scuttled GMA's parliamentary-extension PI as a 'grand deception' and 'gigantic fraud.' Third -- and 'worse,' because the justices entered politics 'of their own volition without waiting for a complaint or petition' -- Estrada v. Desierto (March 2, 2001, per J -- later CJ -- Puno, en banc) legitimized the GMA-Erap transition via Edsa People Power 2 by a 13-0 vote (CJ Davide and CJ Panganiban inhibited). 'But even more courageous, if not more heroic,' was CJ Davide's unilateral Jan. 20, 2001 announcement to swear in GMA at noon -- triggered by CJ Panganiban's own suggestion to administer the oath as 'acting president' after the Cabinet, AFP, and PNP withdrew support from Estrada and 'the country was left with no leader!' -- which the Court unanimously approved in an emergency session 'after a lot of hemming and hawing'; at noon at Edsa Shrine, Davide skipped 'acting' and swore in GMA as 'president' amid chants of 'Davide, Davide, Davide,' 'gallantly owning sole responsibility,' with the Court on Jan. 22, 2001 unanimously passing a resolution 'to confirm the authority' of the CJ. Fourth, Francisco v. House (Nov. 10, 2003, per J Carpio Morales, en banc) barred the House from entertaining the second impeachment of CJ Davide within the constitutional one-year period; the House 'reluctantly obeyed' after several days. CJ closes with the IMHO doctrinal point that even when the Constitution grants exclusive powers (like the House's exclusive power to initiate impeachment), the judiciary may pass on whether constitutionally imposed conditions, limitations, or restrictions have been observed -- and the first-person witness warrant: 'As a member of the Court when these four cases were decided, I can vouch for the courage and grit displayed by the justices in tiptoeing the political minefields to uphold the rule of law and to save the nation from chaos and civil strife.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the Scotus's March 4, 2024 'unanimous unsigned resolution' overturning the Colorado Supreme Court's December 2023 4-3 ruling that had barred Donald Trump from the state's ballot under Section 3 of the 14th Amendment for his alleged 'insurrection or rebellion' role in the Jan. 6, 2021 Capitol assault. Trump's victory -- among approximately 100 civil, criminal, and other cases pending against him -- turned on 'what laypersons call a technicality': the Scotus held that only Congress (not state courts) may enforce the constitutional ban, and pointedly 'skirted the main issue of whether Trump is an insurrectionist or a rebel.' Five of nine justices in separate opinions argued the ban must be contained in a law, but passing such legislation before November 2024 is 'almost impossible' given the chasm between the Democratic-controlled Senate and the Republican-controlled House -- reminiscent of similarly stalled PH Charter-change attempts. The Scotus also left open what constitutes an 'insurrection,' acknowledged state-court jurisdiction over state-office (not federal-office) candidates, and used an unsigned resolution that does not bear the kind of constitutional certification PH SC decisions must carry under our 1987 Constitution. CJ frames this as Scotus's 'rule narrowly' approach -- avoiding what 'the late conservative Justice Felix Frankfurter described as the political thicket' -- and contrasts it sharply with the PH SC, where 'this typical judicial shyness is, however, taboo' because our Constitution mandates 'the duty, not just the power, to determine whether or not there has been a grave abuse of discretion,' placing the PH SC repeatedly 'in the vortex of political whirlpools' (foreshadowing A77 the following week). Whether by coincidence or design (?), the Scotus ruling was released on the eve of Super Tuesday, when Trump 'triumphantly waived' it as implied endorsement and handily won 14 of 15 states (Vermont excepted), forcing Nikki Haley to withdraw without the traditional endorsement -- instead warning MAGA Republicans that 'chaos and personal grievance always follow Trump.' CJ closes with the forward-projection: worth watching whether the Scotus will 'rule narrowly again and bury its head in the political sand' on Trump's presidential-immunity defense in pending federal cases -- including the New York court's $454 million fraud fine.

one_paragraph_summary: Engaging reluctantly with the ongoing Charter-change 'noise' -- at friends' request, despite his sense that President Marcos had 'already settled' the issue months ago -- Panganiban offers a simple, clear walk-through of the law and jurisprudence governing Cha-cha. Article XVII of the Constitution provides three modes: (1) Con-ass, with Congress acting in constituent-assembly capacity via 3/4 of all members; (2) Con-con, which Congress may call by 2/3 of all members; and (3) People's Initiative under Section 2, requiring at least 12 percent of registered voters nationwide with at least 3 percent in every legislative district -- a double threshold that fails the PI even with 12 percent national if 3 percent is missed in even one district. He flags two constitutional hiatuses and offers his IMHO: first, the Constitution is silent on whether the two chambers vote jointly or separately in Con-ass, and CJ's opinion is they should vote separately because Congress 'meet[s] and vote[s] separately and independently' in ordinary lawmaking and 'no law requires them to meet as one body' for constitutional proposals; second, the Constitution is silent on whether the chambers must even convene jointly, and CJ's opinion is they may convene jointly or separately at their option. He encourages those who sincerely disagree to bring the question to the SC for definitive guidance. The 3/4 and 2/3 requirements are based on ALL members, including absentees -- with 24 Senate incumbents, that means 18 affirmative for 3/4 and 16 for 2/3. Under Lambino v. Comelec (Oct. 25, 2006), 'revision' broadly alters a basic constitutional principle (separation of powers, checks and balances), while 'amendment' adds, reduces, or deletes words without altering principles -- and PI may propose only amendments, not revisions. The 2024 Joint Resolutions adding 'UNLESS OTHERWISE PROVIDED BY LAW' to three economic provisions (public utilities, basic education, ad agencies -- 60-70 percent Filipino-owned) are amendments by Lambino, but the House version's insistence on joint voting will kill the Resolutions because the Senate will not agree. Two logical conclusions follow: solons and Con-con delegates have the exclusive prerogative for revisions and amendments via Con-ass/Con-con; the people have the exclusive prerogative for amendments only via PI; and because the Constitution bars Congress members from holding 'any other office or employment in the Government ... during his term without forfeiting his seat,' they cannot serve as concurrent Con-con delegates. CJ closes with a wider point: our 37-year-old Constitution needs updating because it predates 'internet, mobile phone, bitcoin, AI, Arbitral Award, Unclos, neurotechnology, Facebook, Dingdong Dantes, Taylor Swift' -- but the path should be incremental, proceeding only with the least controversial proviso (public utilities) under SC guidance on the hiatuses; if only for this, 'the noise would have served the nation.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban argues that 'the rule of law is besieged in the South China Sea and the East China Sea' because of aggressive Chinese claims over Taiwan, almost the entire SCS, and ECS islets -- and the challenges posed by riparian states and Western powers. He sketches a historical arc to explain Chinese psychology: a civilizational glory 'rivaling Egypt and its pharaohs, and Greece and its Olympic gods' followed by a 'harrowing decay' from mid-1800s to mid-1900s of shameful one-sided treaties and cruel treatment of nationals -- leaving the Chinese conviction that 'losing face is worse than losing life.' He traces the modern stages: WWII Japanese occupation of Paracels and Spratlys; 1945 Kuomintang acceptance of Japanese surrender; 1950 Mao's takeover; North Vietnam's wartime relinquishment of claims; 1974 China expelling South Vietnamese from Shanhu Island; post-1975 united Vietnam adopting the South's claims -- leaving today's SCS occupation pattern (about 29 features Vietnam, 11 PH, 7 China, 6 Malaysia, 2 Taiwan, 1 Brunei). Despite becoming the second-largest economy and possessing the biggest standing military with a nuclear arsenal, China is 'constricted' by hostile neighbors (its only dependable ones being North Korea, Cambodia, and Mongolia) and can only expand through the ECS and SCS -- to control economic sea lanes, secure its first line of defense against US militarism, and provide passage for nuclear submarines to the Pacific and Indian oceans. To this end it has revived its nine-dash (now ten-dash) line, building 'covertly in the beginning but flagrantly now' fortresses, airstrips, missile silos; it also claims sovereignty over the Diaoyu/Senkaku group disputed with Japan. The PH Arbitral Award (based on Unclos) outlawed the nine-dash line and declared freedom of navigation, but covers only sovereign rights over the maritime domain, not sovereignty over land features -- while China, Vietnam, and others anchor their claims on history, discovery, occupation, control, and cession (Cairo, Potsdam) over sea, air, and land. 'The Philippines is an international pygmy in the rule of force but a giant in the rule of law' -- the Marcos regime, abandoning Duterte's befriending approach, has pivoted to US support, filed hundreds of diplomatic protests, and exposed Chinese 'grey zone tactics' (water cannons, lane cuttings) through open media coverage 'to the international discomfiture of China.' He closes with a symmetric demand: 'While China may have the right to recover its renegade province of Taiwan under the rule of law, will it also observe the rule of law in respecting our maritime rights under the AA and Unclos?'

He first untangles the ICJ from the ICC: both are based in The Hague, but the ICJ (UN organ since Oct. 24, 1945, with 193 member states) tackles state-vs-state litigation, while the ICC (Rome Statute, in force July 1, 2002, with 123 member states) tackles crimes against humanity brought against individuals -- and the US and China are members of the ICJ but not the ICC. The Ukraine-Russia case shows the rule-of-law paradox starkly: Russia accused Ukraine of genocide in Donetsk and Luhansk to justify its February 2022 invasion; the ICJ issued an interim order in March 2022 directing Moscow to stop, which Russia ignored -- yet the order 'emboldened the European Union, the United Kingdom, Australia, the US, and their allies to send military arms, medicine, and food to assist Ukraine,' even as Russia perversely invoked the rule of law to justify its invasion. On Jan. 26, 2024, the ICJ ruled 15-2 that it has jurisdiction over South Africa's accusation that Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza; while declining to order a ceasefire, it issued six commands equivalent to a 'preliminary mandatory injunction': prevent killing/harming Palestinian civilians, ensure military compliance, punish incitement, deliver basic services, prevent destruction of war-crime evidence, and submit a report within 30 days (by Feb. 26). 'Will Israel follow the rule of law and submit its report?' CJ awaits 'with bated breath the Jewish response' -- 'a great challenge to the faith of the free world in the rule of law.' On the Trump cases, the Scotus is taking up the Colorado disqualification appeal (Trump's lawyer 'incredibly argued' on Feb. 8 that the Jan. 6 Capitol assault was 'a riot, not an insurrection'); separately, the Scotus will decide an appeal from a US Court of Appeals ruling rejecting Trump's defense of presidential immunity (the CA held immunity 'adheres only to an INCUMBENT chief executive') -- but the bigger question is whether the courts will decide before November or simply procrastinate, because if they wait and Trump wins, 'all the cases may be dropped due to the presidential immunity of an INCUMBENT president.' If the Scotus disqualifies Trump and he refuses, leading 'a more destructive insurrection or a full-scale rebellion,' the test will be whether Republicans and Trumpsters 'respect the rule of law and obey faithfully, though grudgingly, their highest court.' one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban examines two pending acquittal questions. First -- Maria Ressa's. In Causing v. People (Oct 11, 2023), the SC Third Division (Inting ponente, with Caguioa, Gaerlan, Dimaampao, and Singh) abandoned the 15-year cyberlibel prescriptive period set in the Unsigned Extended Resolution in Tolentino v. People (Aug 6, 2018), holding instead that cyberlibel prescribes in one year -- but counted from discovery of the libelous matter by the offended party, the authorities, or their agents, NOT from the date of posting. Causing himself was not acquitted because he failed to allege or prove the discovery date. Ressa, unlike Causing, went through RTC trial and CA affirmation before the SC. CJ's view: IMHO yes, she is entitled to acquittal -- but subject to two qualifications: she must have proven in the RTC or CA that complainant Wilfredo Keng filed his complaint more than one year after his discovery of the libelous matter on Rappler, AND the case must be ruled on by the SC en banc, not by a Division, because under Article VIII Section 4 Item 3 of the Constitution, '[N]o doctrine or principle of law laid down by the court in a decision rendered en banc or in division may be modified or reversed except by the court sitting en banc.' Second -- Jinggoy Estrada's. The SBN's 360-page per curiam decision acquitted him of plunder (a capital offense) but convicted him of direct and indirect bribery. CJ doubts the SBN will 'just suddenly somersault' on MR. And Estrada's planned SC appeal is very risky because of People v. XXX (June 21, 2021): an appeal throws the entire case wide open, the reviewing tribunal can correct errors or reverse on grounds not raised by the parties, increase penalties, or apply the proper provision of the penal law. This invalidates the immediate finality of the plunder acquittal, reopening the entire case and rendering Estrada vulnerable to a plunder conviction -- though the same appeal could also acquit him completely and absolve him of the accessory penalty of perpetual disqualification from public office. 'Will he take the risk? Abangan.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban surveys the latest Charter-change (Cha-cha) attempts -- a surreptitious people's initiative reportedly led by some representatives, plus a more open constituent-assembly/normal-legislative path led by Senate leaders. He first clarifies that the 'insufficient law' doctrine -- Santiago v. Comelec's 1997 holding (8-5; MR tied 6-6 as 'some justices somersaulted') that RA 6735 was inadequate to implement PI -- is no longer controlling. He personally dissented in 1997 ('I should know. I was already an associate justice'), arguing 'no such thing as an insufficient or inadequate law.' Nine years later, when he was CJ, the Court in Lambino v. Comelec (Oct 25, 2006, 8-7) -- Carpio ponente, Puno leading dissenters -- rejected another PI attempt because the signatories were not shown the full text of the proposed bicameral-to-unicameral shift, a 'grand deception' and 'gigantic fraud,' and because PI can propose only amendments, not revisions (revisions go to con-ass or constitutional convention). On Nov 21, 2006, MR was denied with finality by the same 8-7 vote, BUT the Court -- by a more decisive 10-5 -- clarified that RA 6735 was 'sufficient and adequate' to amend the Constitution via PI, effectively burying Santiago. Today, Senate President Migz Zubiri, Senate President Pro Tempore Loren Legarda, and Senate Finance Chair Sonny Angara have filed Resolution of Both Houses No. 6, proposing three Cha-cha items through normal legislation by adding 'unless otherwise provided by law' to constitutional provisions limiting public utilities (60% Filipino), basic education other than religious-owned (60% Filipino), and advertising agencies (70% Filipino). The nationalistic limits stay in place ipso facto unless Congress legislates change -- neutralizing the self-service charge with reason and logic -- and the proposal has the blessing of both President Marcos and Speaker Romualdez. A similar Belmonte proposal in 2014 failed because PNoy refused to touch what he considered Cory Aquino's great legacy. Filipinos have consistently frowned on Cha-cha as cheap, self-serving schemes to perpetuate the sponsors in power. Today's officials should be more transparent and limit changes to those that do not benefit them in any manner. 'Perhaps, they should no longer dance with the old Cha-cha rhythm but swing with ABBA, or do the TikTok, or better still, craze with Taylor Swift. Perhaps, just perhaps, our people, especially the young, will begin to believe them.'

one_paragraph_summary: In Calleja v. Executive Secretary (Dec 7, 2021), the SC in a 'facial challenge' upheld the constitutionality of the entire Anti-Terrorism Act except for the PROVISO in Section 4 and the 'second mode of designation' in paragraph 2 of Section 25. The 235-page ponencia with 560 footnotes was expertly penned by now-retired Justice Rosmari D. Carandang; together with 11 separate opinions totaling 640 pages -- CJ Gesmundo 199 pages and 762 footnotes (202 more than the ponencia), SAJ Perlas-Bernabe 48, SAJ Leonen 65, Caguioa 130, Lazaro-Javier 41, Inting 21, Zalameda 44, M.V. Lopez 25, Gaerlan 20, J.Y. Lopez 34, Dimaampao 13 -- Calleja is, IMHO, the most intensely deliberated case in the Gesmundo Court. Being a facial determination, the ponencia remains subject to as-applied challenges. Given terrorism's sui generis nature where prevention matters more than punishment, the Court has now promulgated new 'Rules on the Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020 and Related Laws' (effective Jan 15, 2024) that specify 'How' -- how to tiptoe the terror chasm to preserve constitutional rights, ensure privacy, and defend the presumption of innocence. The ATA grants the ATC the power to 'designate' individuals or groups as terrorists and the AMLC the power to issue freeze orders; affected parties may petition the CA to remove their designation on grave-abuse grounds. On SOJ petition, the CA may issue ex-parte within 72 hours, based on probable cause, a Preliminary Order of Proscription to prevent the commission of terrorism, which authorizes AMLC ex-parte preventive freeze orders on terrorism-financing property/funds. After hearing on clear and convincing evidence, the CA may issue a Permanent Order of Proscription effective for three years (shortable/extendable). The CA may also issue ex-parte Surveillance Orders to wiretap with devices and technologies 'now known or subsequently known' and Data Preservation Orders compelling service providers to preserve the surveilled data. The ATA permits warrantless arrest/detention for 14 days, extendable by the proper RTC for 10 more on SOJ verified motion; RTCs may also issue ex-parte Precautionary Hold Departure Orders. These ipso facto powers depart sharply from our normal adversarial system where judges are passive and rely on 'the rapiers of the contending counsels' -- requiring magistrates to be 'activists' in scrutinizing documents minutely and examining witnesses personally. Judicial activism, far from being a politically charged label, is imposed by our Constitution as the solemn duty of our judiciary to strike down grave abuse of discretion -- a unique and indispensable characteristic of the system of checks and balances in our democracy.

one_paragraph_summary: Continuing the sad saga of Dr. Iggy Agbayani -- taken up Nov 13 and followed by CPRA columns Nov 27 and Dec 4 -- Panganiban reports that on Dec 13, 2023, CJ Alexander G. Gesmundo said in a press briefing that the justices will review what happened and may establish new instructions because 'apparently there were some lapses committed by the lawyer.' Agbayani -- a respected orthopedic surgeon convicted by the MeTC of Manila of 'reckless imprudence resulting in serious physical injuries' -- had his appeals denied at the RTC, CA, and SC-Third Division on the same procedural ground: his lawyer's failure to file an appeal memorandum and to append documents required by the Rules of Court. Agbayani died of a heart attack while incarcerated. Under the CPRA, the Court can motu proprio discipline the lawyer -- but, laudable as that is, it falls short of what the family yearns for: a reversal of conviction and a judicial pronouncement of innocence, which cannot be motu proprio because the offended party (Atty. Saul Q. Hofileña Jr.) equally deserves objective justice. CJ recommends the family initiate a petition to reopen the case, with due notice to Hofileña and the OSG. The overarching question is whether a decision that has become final AND executed via incarceration can be reopened. The normal jurisprudential answer is no -- but several 'final and irrevocable' judgments have been revoked. The most glaring example: Justice Manuel Pamaran's Dec 2, 1985 SBN decision acquitting Fabian Ver and other accused of the daring broad-daylight murder of Sen. Ninoy Aquino at the Manila International Airport tarmac on Aug 21, 1983. After Cory Aquino took over in 1986, the SC reopened the verdict, found the trial to be a 'sham,' and authorized a retrial. Justice Regino C. Hermosisima Jr.'s 177-page decision found conspiracy among 16 accused-soldiers including Brig. Gen. Luther Custodio and convicted them of the double murder of Ninoy and Rolando Galman; only Ver escaped conviction by fleeing the country and remaining beyond local jurisdiction. The more common reopenings are convictions later reversed on subsequent proof of impossibility of guilt -- most famously rape convictions overturned by DNA evidence showing the semen belonged to another man. The extraordinary writ of habeas corpus has also been allowed where the ordering court (1) lacked jurisdiction, (2) imposed an excessive penalty, or (3) deprived the accused of constitutional rights. CJ concludes that the Supreme Court is both a court of law and a court of equity. Rules of procedure should never be used as stumbling blocks to common sense, fairness, and equity. The Court cannot be constrained by technicalities and procedural niceties. It is a dispenser of liberating justice, not of suffocating rules. It is neither a machine nor a robot. It is human and humane. Being compassionate and just, it cannot be replaced by the computing power of technology and artificial intelligence.

one_paragraph_summary: Following recent House hearings on whether the present regime should allow the ICC to investigate and prosecute alleged crimes against humanity during the Duterte administration, President Marcos said returning 'under the fold of the ICC' is 'under study... we'll just keep looking at our options.' Panganiban lays out three major options. First, MAINTAINING THE STATUS QUO -- not rejoining but respecting the July 18, 2023 ICC Appeals Chamber 3-2 ruling authorizing Karim Khan to resume his investigation of crimes from Nov 1, 2011 to March 16, 2019. The AC majority of three agreed PH had not shown genuine willingness or ability to investigate especially the 'brains,' but it ignored the more fundamental issue of whether the petition was filed within the two-year reglementary period, claiming PH had waived its right to raise it. The vocal minority of two (and CJ respectfully agrees) insisted the ICC did not acquire jurisdiction because Fatou Bensouda's PTC petition was filed May 24, 2021 and granted Sept 15, 2021 -- both more than two years after PH withdrawal took effect March 17, 2019. Khan's silence on resumption may reflect awareness of this vulnerability. SG Menardo Guevarra has summed up the PH stance: Khan's investigators may enter, roam the countryside, observe and listen, but no government cooperation. Second, REJOINING THE ICC -- since the withdrawal was made solely by the President without Senate concurrence, the President may unilaterally reverse the act by recalling the withdrawal letter; Senate Resolution No. 57 of Aug 23, 2011 ratifying the Rome Statute 'still mightily stands to this day' and needs no new ratification. The SC's Pangilinan v. Cayetano (March 16, 2021), fittingly penned by SAJ Leonen, backed this in an obiter dictum 'with logic, reason, and wisdom.' Third, COOPERATING WITHOUT REJOINING -- without recalling the withdrawal letter, the President can open NBI, PNP, and the DOJ Chief Prosecutor's Office to Khan via cabinet authorization, especially the secretary of justice; this can be justified by 'the comity of nations and our abiding respect for the rule of law.' Either of two seemingly disparate results would follow: the ICC concludes that PH is genuinely willing and able, or investigators rely on their own findings and 'ensnare the alleged perpetrators into the sticky ICC web.' VP Sara Duterte has formally asked the DOJ not to cooperate, supporting Option 1, upholding 'self-respect and dignity of our country' and demonstrating viability of local institutions 'though the heavens may fall.' Which option will the President take? Abangan.

one_paragraph_summary: Continuing his CPRA series, Panganiban summarizes the duties of lawyers under the new 56-page Code, simplifying its six canons into three duty groups: (1) independence and propriety; (2) fidelity; and (3) competence, diligence, equality, and accountability. Under independence (Canon I), lawyers must act with integrity and rely solely on the merits, not allowing the client to dictate procedure while still respecting the client's decision to settle or compromise after explaining consequences. Under propriety (Canon II), lawyers shall not engage in unlawful, dishonest, immoral, or deceitful conduct, nor in physical, sexual, psychological, or economic abuse, and must use dignified, gender-fair, child- and culturally-sensitive language. The law profession is not a business -- PH, unlike other countries, does not allow 'ambulance-chasers' or open hawking; advertising must be dignified, verifiable, factual, and non-self-laudatory, with no payments to media practitioners or award-giving bodies. The primary duty of public prosecutors 'is not to convict but to see that justice is done.' Under fidelity (Canon III), the lawyer-client relationship arises when the client consciously, voluntarily, and in good faith vests the lawyer with confidence -- which explains, in part, why CJ declines to render advice on specific cases referred by readers and always redirects them to a competent lawyer, the PAO, or the IBP. Fidelity prohibits representing conflicting interests except with all concerned parties' written informed consent and prohibits dating/romantic/sexual relations with a client during engagement (unless preexisting). PAO's marginalized-sector access is protected by limiting conflict imputation to the lawyer directly handling and the supervisor only. Under Canon IV, lawyers must observe competence, diligence, commitment, and skill regardless of fee or pro bono status, with lifelong learning required even when engaged in another profession or business. Under Canon V on equality, a lawyer cannot decline a client based on nationality, ethnicity, sexual orientation or gender identity, religion, disability, age, marital or social or economic status, political beliefs, or even the lawyer's or public's opinion on the person's guilt, with narrowly defined exceptions (capacity, conflict, sixth-degree relation to adverse party, fourth-degree to adverse counsel). Canon VI provides for accountability via confidential, summary process at the SC and/or IBP, with the complainant bearing the burden of substantial evidence -- 'the amount of relevant evidence which a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to justify a conclusion' -- not proof beyond reasonable doubt.

one_paragraph_summary: Following his column on the sad saga of Dr. Iggy Agbayani (Nov 13, 2023), which evoked calls to discipline his lawyer, Panganiban begins a two-part series on the new Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability (CPRA) approved by the SC on April 11, 2023 to replace the 1988 Code of Professional Responsibility. Studying the CPRA, he notes, also means looking at the Court's Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovation 2022-2027 (SPJI) unveiled a year ago and detailed in his Sept 25 column -- both turning the judiciary toward hi-tech and AI. The historic turn was expanded by the Court to cover all attorneys-at-law: the old 1988 Code 'reflected the then prevailing trends,' but 'the role of modern-day lawyers has expanded and shifted from advocates to peacemakers, from solicitors to specialists, and from counterparts to collaborators.' The 56-page CPRA is divided into six major Canons, with Canon VI alone containing 53 sections -- over a third of the document -- on the causes and processes by which attorneys are to be held accountable. CJ humbly views the SPJI and CPRA as 'unequivocal endorsements of my own philosophy of liberty and prosperity under the rule of law.' He clarifies that 'attorney-at-law' refers only to bar passers -- including justices, judges, prosecutors, practicing attorneys, notaries public, and lawyers in government, business, academe, or any capacity requiring bar passage -- all bound by the CPRA oath taken before the Court en banc at the Philippine International Convention Center to 'conscientiously and courageously work for justice, as well as safeguard the rights and meaningful freedoms of all persons, identities and communities.' Sections 36-44 of Canon II (Propriety) cover responsible social-media use, beginning with the overarching duty to understand the benefits, risks, and ethical implications of social media and to ensure that posts in any audience-bearing public or restricted setting uphold the dignity of the legal profession. The four prohibited online acts: knowingly or maliciously posting/sharing/uploading false or unverified disinformation; operating hidden-identity accounts to circumvent the law or CPRA; revealing confidential client information; and communicating with court/tribunal/agency officers via social media to influence their official duties. He closes by acknowledging the 15-member sub-committee that finalized the CPRA -- chaired by J Amy C. Lazaro-Javier with vice-chairs Samuel H. Gaerlan and Maria Filomena D. Singh, and 12 members from the CA, SBN, LEB, RTCs, MeTC Makati, the National Bar Discipline office, IBP QC, PALS, PBA, USC, and the OCJ. Next Monday: the duties of lawyers to the country and to their clients, like Doctor Agbayani.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban traces the sad saga of leading orthopedic surgeon Dr. Benigno 'Iggy' Agbayani Jr., convicted of 'reckless imprudence resulting in serious physical injuries' for performing arthroscopy on the left knee of Atty. Saul Q. Hofileña Jr. with an unsterilized arthroscope. Dr. Agbayani died of cardiac arrest on Oct 5, 2023, four and a half months into his confinement, still professing innocence and lamenting what his family, colleagues, and friends consider a 'travesty of justice'; the column quotes at length his wrenching handwritten Filipino poem dated June 15. The procedural history is a cascade of counsel failures: the MTC-Manila convicted him on July 29, 2013; the RTC-Manila dismissed his appeal for counsel's failure to file an appeal memorandum within the 15-day reglementary period despite an extension; the Court of Appeals junked his appeal for failure to append the required documents under the Rules of Court (witnesses' affidavits, prosecution evidence, all prior pleadings); and the SC Third Division, by unsigned extended resolution (UER) on June 23, 2021, denied his petition for review for the same documentary failure -- while shortening his sentence to one month and one day of arresto mayor to one year and one day of prision correccional. The Court explained that the required documents enable the reviewing courts to resolve whether to give due course; though form infirmities may be waived in the interest of substantial justice, counsel's 'heavy workload' excuse 'does not persuade.' The author notes that the petitioner's non-sterilization arguments were barred by the rule that SC petitions for review dwell only on questions of law, not fact, and that the SC majority uses 'the strict or verba legis method of interpretation' (per his Nov 6 column). He places himself in the liberal school of jurisprudence and says he would have voted, if still incumbent, to remand the case to the trial courts to determine whether reckless imprudence occurred and whether it should be attributed to the doctor, the operating-room nurse, the hospital itself, or all of them. He endorses the family's posthumous retention of 'super lawyer Estelito P. Mendoza' to clear Dr. Agbayani's name -- Mendoza's record of resuscitating his celebrated clients' dead cases makes him capable -- but qualifies that the offended party deserves 'justice (not vengeance) in equal measure.' He closes with a doctrinal calming for the medical profession: the UER 'in its present form and language' did not create a precedent on doctor criminal liability for reckless imprudence -- the Court denied the petition pursuant only to existing jurisprudence governing errors or negligence of counsels, and as a rule UERs do not create precedents; only signed decisions and resolutions do.

Gesmundo at 34 -- and reflects on the broader pattern that no CJ has exceeded a 50-percent approval rating in the last fifteen or so years. He argues that unelected CJs should be excluded from such approval/awareness/trust/performance surveys when conducted under the same standards and metrics applied to elected leaders, because such surveys constitute 'embarrassment at least, or even harassment' for the CJs and the Supreme Court. He grounds the argument in constitutional asymmetry: while the President, VP, senators, representatives, and SC justices share three basic qualifications (natural-born citizenship, minimum age, ability to read and write), justices and judges are constitutionally required five additional qualities -- 'proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence,' plus 'Member of the Philippine Bar' -- that are not required of elected officials, who acquire office through popular mandate and political skills (with the Constitution not prohibiting the unschooled, dishonest, dropouts, sycophants, and criminals from running for top executive and legislative posts unless disqualified by a law or a final judicial decision). Of the five additional qualifications, independence is the most prized and is protected by security of tenure, removal only via impeachment ('and arguably, with my respectful dissent, through quo warranto'), and fixed compensation that cannot be reduced by Congress and continues into retirement until death. Jurists must judge cases according to what is just and humane after due process -- not like Pilate who condemned Jesus Christ according to the rule of the mob, or like the Spanish conquistadores who executed Jose Rizal according to the rule of the powerful. Independence may mean working against the popular: a senator or former president cannot be acquitted simply because of popularity or to avoid street rallies, and decisions cannot be influenced through kins, friends, admirers, critical media, investigative journalists, opinion writers, social media practitioners, or even approaches via spouses, children, close relatives, school chums, doctors, or fathers-confessors -- these must be avoided 'like a plague.' Because CJs were not elected by poll respondents and are 'politically unknown,' they will always rank low, so 'let us spare them the embarrassment, nay, the harassment of being badly perceived vis-à-vis our elected officials.' He closes with a warning he will self-quote in subsequent columns: 'I will fret the day if and when CJs would vie for popularity instead of independence, surrender to the mob instead of to the truth based on a fair trial, and judge wickedly to gain fame and favor instead of rendering justice though the heavens may fall.'
