one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with the observation that the judiciary is often likened to the Church and the military -- all three are bastions of conservatism bound by historical respect for traditions, precedents, meritocracy, and seniority. That makes the recent speech of Chief Justice Alexander G. Gesmundo 'pleasantly surprising' yet deserving of acclaim: Gesmundo accepted the challenge of how the judiciary can 'turn tech for good and move from problem to solution' and acknowledged that 'AI has the potential to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of judicial decisions, while at the same time, raise some algorithmic bias.' Panganiban catalogues the new lingo that magistrates need to learn -- algorithmic, tech, AI, Gen AI, ChatGPT (Generative Pretrained Transformer), Bard, Bing, Baidu, neuralink, bitcoin, crypto, metaverse, pod, 5G -- and points to the Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovation 2022-2027 (SPJI) unveiled by the SC a year earlier (deferring detailed exposition to his Nov 14 and 21, 2022 columns). His standard for judging SPJI is generous: even if just one SPJI objective is attained -- speeding up the delivery of quality justice by faithfully observing the Constitution's time limits for final decisions and hastening interlocutory orders -- the Court 'would have achieved a monumental success,' and a 2028-2033 extension with greater hi-tech and AI reliance could compound the gains. He sketches a civilizational-acceleration narrative -- agriculture and industrial revolution took centuries, jets/shinkansen/expressways took decades, then PC 1980s, internet 1990s, smartphone 2000s, cloud computing 2010s, AI 2020s -- and predicts that AI will transform jobs, professions, workplaces, habits, lifestyles, medicine, family relations, longevity, laws, and governance, inducing anxiety and fear of obsolescence; physical ailments may be healed by better medicine but mental disorders 'will become more prevalent and harder to cure.' Yet for every job outmoded, new ones will emerge -- just as tractors and backhoes replaced horses and carabao -- and enduring human values like 'empathy, trust, love, justice, and faith in the Almighty will remain.' His boundary thesis: 'humane justice can be dispensed only by judges, not always by an automated formula' -- because the Penal Code grants a range of penalties to select from and the Civil Code grants the liberality to make 'right and justice' prevail, conferring wide discretion not available to tech bots, to attain a just and humane society where liberty is safeguarded and prosperity is nurtured under the rule of law. On a personal note, he credits his continuing relevance in the hypersonic age to three disciplines: chair roles in international groups (Asean Law Association, Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague) and officer/director/trustee/adviser roles in leading banks, corporations, foundations, and charitable/religious organizations; faithful weekly column-writing for almost 17 years 'without fail despite occasional illness, travel, holidays, disability, death of loved ones'; and access to golf and tennis clubs where he plays several times weekly for physical, mental, and social well-being.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban observes that high-profile criminal cases normally begin in the regional trial courts or in the Sandiganbayan, where the presiding magistrates bear the brunt of public scrutiny -- praised or damned by the peanut gallery -- and where the sub judice rule is relaxed in favor of fair comment and free speech, so that 'trial judges are put on trial in the courts of public opinion.' He uses the three drug-trafficking cases filed against former Senator Leila de Lima (and several others), raffled to three branches of the Regional Trial Courts of Muntinlupa, as his case studies. In one case she was acquitted 'without much ado.' In another, Branch 204 (Presiding Judge Abraham Joseph Alcantara) acquitted her on the ground that -- though the crime may have been committed -- the recantation of former NBI Director Rafael Ragos created doubt on her participation. In the third, Branch 256 (Presiding Judge Romeo Buenaventura) denied her motion for bail because the prosecution's evidence was 'strong.' He cross-references his four earlier columns on the De Lima cases (Jan 30, June 5, June 12, June 26) and pivots here to the judges' tribulations. one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the July 18 ICC Appeals Chamber 3-2 decision authorizing chief prosecutor Karim Khan -- 'a celebrated Queen's Counsel in the United Kingdom' -- to resume his investigation of the alleged 'crime against humanity of murder, committed in the Philippines between Nov. 1, 2011, and March 16, 2019, in the context of the so-called war on drugs.' He walks the reader carefully through the date chronology: Bensouda's Feb. 8, 2018 preliminary 'examination' announcement; PH withdrawal submitted March 17, 2018, effective March 17, 2019; Bensouda's PTC request only on May 24, 2021 (more than two years past effective withdrawal); PTC grant on Sept. 15, 2021; Khan's agreement to suspend at the PH government's request; PTC's Jan. 26, 2023 grant for Khan to continue because the government's inquiry was deemed 'allegedly superficial.' On appeal, the AC took up two issues: complementarity (where the majority agreed with Khan that the PH had not shown genuine willingness/ability under Article 17) and jurisdiction (which the majority skirted, claiming the PH waived the issue by appealing only the Jan. 26, 2023 decision instead of the underlying Sept. 15, 2021 one). The two-judge minority asserted this was error -- jurisdiction will resurface when warrants are sought, so refusing to rule now wastes resources -- and held that the ICC did not acquire jurisdiction because Bensouda's PTC petition was both filed and granted more than two years after effective withdrawal. CJ reads Khan's silence and inaction since the AC ruling as possibly meaning he 'may no longer be minded to pursue the case,' redirecting effort to clearer 'situations' like Russia's war on Ukraine. The PH government's strategic knowledge: two ICC judges are minded to dismiss, and notably no judge has taken an opposing stance on jurisdiction. CJ closes by reducing the whole controversy to one statutory-construction question -- 'Is the Office of the Prosecutor an integral part of the ICC?' -- and answers, 'My short answer is No.'

one_paragraph_summary: Continuing from A102 the prior Monday, Panganiban turns to the second half of statutory construction: how courts read punctuation marks, words, phrases, and qualifiers. The 14 punctuation marks are catalogued in one sentence (period, question mark, exclamation point, comma, semicolon, colon, dash, hyphen, parentheses, brackets, braces, apostrophe, quotation marks, ellipses), with the calibrated rule that they 'are not reliable indicators of intent, but they can buttress interpretations,' illustrated by Agcaoili v. Suguitan (Feb. 13, 1926) -- cited via Prof. Ricardo M. Pilares III's 'Statutory Construction: Concept and Cases' -- which 'in elegant language' distinguished the semicolon (greater separation in thought) from the comma. He then walks through SC constructions of key words: in Romulo v. HDMF (June 19, 2000), 'and/or' takes its ordinary signification 'either and or' with 'and' and 'or' used interchangeably ('butter and/or eggs means butter and eggs, or butter or eggs'); 'shall' is generally mandatory and 'may' is permissive, but Marcelino v. Cruz (March 18, 1983) construed the 18-month (1973 Const.) / 24-month (1987 Const.) case-resolution 'shall' as merely permissive because procedural, invoking the SC's Article VIII Section 5 rule-making power; La Bugal-B'laan v. Ramos (Dec. 14, 2004) held that 'involving' in Article XII Section 2 of the 1987 Constitution should be understood as 'including,' meaning FTAAs with foreign-owned corporations are not limited to mere financial or technical assistance. The restrict-or-modify rule holds that qualifying words apply only to immediately associated words -- 'under two tons' in 'motorbikes, cars, vans, and trucks under two tons' modifies only trucks. And Fortich v. Corona (Aug. 19, 1999) distinguished 'cases' (decided by at least three members of a division) from 'matters' (resolved by a majority): when a division 2-2 vote occurs on an MR, the MR is deemed lost and not referred to en banc. CJ closes with a pedagogical-recruiting invitation: 'To know the many more rules of construction, readers may want to take up law and join the fascinating world of lawyers. Who knows, they may reach the Supreme Court and help frame new rules of interpretation or modify existing ones.'

one_paragraph_summary: Prompted by senators and readers asking how the newly-passed Maharlika Investment Fund (MIF) law should be read -- 'according to the language used or according to the intents of the authors?' -- Panganiban opens with the concession that 'the question seems simple but there is no simple answer,' and endorses Prof. Ricardo M. Pilares III's revised 'Statutory Construction: Concept and Cases' (Ateneo law valedictorian, 2006 bar second placer) as a layman-accessible guide. The basic principle, agreed with Pilares, is to find the meaning intended by the framers and apply it via verba legis (plain meaning) or ratio legis (spirit/reason). Under verba legis, lawmakers are 'presumed to know the meaning of the words, to have used such words advisedly, and to have expressed their intent by the use of such words as are found in the statute,' with interpretation resorted to only when the literal meaning would be 'impossible, absurd or would lead to injustice' -- illustrated by Republic v. Manalo (April 24, 2018), where a Filipino wife whose foreign husband secured a valid divorce was held capacitated to remarry under Article 26(2) Family Code because the statute does not distinguish petitioner from respondent, the Court even noting arguendo that any ambiguity in 'obtained' would be construed against the 'absurd situation' of unequal remarriage. The second rule, ratio legis et anima ('the reason of the law is the soul of the law'), was illustrated in League of Cities v. Comelec (Dec. 21, 2009) -- 'what is within the spirit is within the statute although it is not within its letter' -- and Naval v. Comelec (July 8, 2014) -- 'effect will be given the real intention even though contrary to the letter of the law' -- and dramatized in Salvacion v. Central Bank (Aug. 21, 1997), where the Court ignored RA 6426's letter (which had exempted dollar deposits from attachment to incentivize foreign-currency inflows when the 1983 economy was 'in a shamble') and ordered the release of an escaped American tourist's dollar deposits to a Filipino minor rape victim's family because literal application produced 'outright injustice and inequality.' CJ closes with his own interpretive lodestar -- Civil Code Article 10, 'In case of doubt ... it is presumed that the lawmaking body intended right and justice to prevail' -- which he applied as an incumbent justice 'after prayer and reflection,' and finds both Manalo (verba legis) and Salvacion (ratio legis) correct because each produced right and justice.

one_paragraph_summary: Diagnosing the selective applause / lampoon pattern in PH public reactions to the SC and lower judiciary -- Judge Alcantara's RTC Muntinlupa Branch 204 acquittal of former Senator Leila de Lima drew critics' praise but the same RTC's Branch 256 (Judge Buenaventura) denial of her bail drew condemnation; the SC's disbarment of Larry Gadon was applauded while its earlier habeas corpus release of Jessica 'Gigi' Reyes drew boos; the Sandiganbayan's plunder conviction of Joseph Estrada was thunderously applauded while the SC's later allowance for him to run for Manila mayor after Arroyo's pardon was lampooned -- Panganiban argues that while fair comment is part of free speech, comments should be 'factually true and legally correct,' not knee-jerk reactions and opportunistic media grabs that 'serve transitory glory but injure public trust in the courts.' Members of Congress and Cabinet officials properly respond to current popular sentiment because that is their accountability mechanism, but 'magistrates must live in a world of reason where logic, evidence, and conscience are their only yardsticks,' sourcing legitimacy from the Constitution ratified overwhelmingly by the people rather than ongoing electoral approval. Permanency of tenure and constitutional independence are the 'rare luxuries' that excise jurists from parochial ties and enable consistent objective decision-making free of electoral fear or presidential rebuff. Cases are won or lost by reasoned arguments from legal principles and precedents -- not by votes, palatability, friendship, pecuniary considerations, or 'diplomatic quid pro quo' ('I will vote with you in this case, provided you vote with me in this other case'). The Court depends on public faith because 'it does not command the army, the police, or the raging mob' -- but its dependency is on 'long-term public trust in the institution,' not 'the shifting winds of public opinion.' Quoting the late US Justice Felix Frankfurter that the SC is 'the conscience of society,' CJ stresses that the test of magistrates' mettle is their capacity to stand by their convictions when executive, legislators, and the mob 'rage against them, threaten their families, and chant slogans of hate.' The Court 'does not lust for the brute power of the executive,' nor desire 'the patronage of the legislature' -- it 'prays only for courage, integrity, and sagacity.' He then elevates Frankfurter's formulation: 'the unelected Supreme Court is not merely the conscience of society; it is also the last bastion of democracy and the ultimate defender of the people's rights enshrined in the Constitution.' He closes with the citizen-duty completion: 'Our duty as citizens is to help the Court and the judiciary remain faithful to these high expectations.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains the doctrine of habeas corpus - traditionally, an order directing a person detaining another to produce the physical body and explain the reason, with the single objective of inquiring into the cause of detention; the writ will NOT issue when detention is pursuant to a lawful court order with jurisdiction, especially in capital-offense cases. In Reyes v. Director (January 17, 2023), however, the Supreme Court's First Division issued the writ freeing Jessica Lucila 'Gigi' Reyes from Taguig City Jail despite her detention pursuant to a Sandiganbayan plunder order - as an exception, because her custody had become 'vexatious, capricious, and oppressive, amounting to an infringement on the constitutional right to speedy trial' - releasing her on four conditions (personal hearing attendance, quarterly whereabouts reports to the SBN, SBN-travel authority with 5-day return report, and quarterly SC compliance reports). Panganiban itemizes FIVE distinct doctrinal deviations: no bond required; contrary to settled jurisprudence that release should be unconditional and absolute (accused 'acquitted pronto'); contrary to Section 4 Rule 102 (custody under valid process bars the writ - and the >P172 million plunder charges validated her detention); contrary to the constitutional rule that capital-offense detainees may be released only if prosecution evidence is 'not strong'; and contrary to the rule that habeas corpus is unavailable when bail has already been denied. He also notes that the release order appears to deprive prosecutors of due process - not impleaded, not notified, denied any chance to oppose - yet ruled to have violated speedy trial. Moreover, the order contradicts the IRSC because it was issued as an 'unsigned resolution' signed only by the Division Clerk of Court, lacking required member signatures, Division Chairman attestation, and Chief Justice certification - and under the IRSC, a UR disposing of a case on the merits is 'essentially meaningful only to the parties,' has no doctrinal value, does not constitute precedent, and binds only the parties. Solicitor General Menardo I. Guevarra and team filed on February 3 a 'little-known but... formidable' Omnibus Motion of the UR, which the Court has not acted on. Despite the well-reasoned OM, Panganiban argues that in the spirit of fairness the Gigi exception should be applied (unless reversed or modified) to future cases on all fours and in pari materia - matching the eight-element Gigi pattern (~9-year detention; trial commencing only March 3, 2022; Information filed June 5, 2014; delays from wrong markings of evidence; two confusing SBN pretrial orders; one-witness-per-day limit despite twice-weekly schedule; thousands of exhibits; no prosecution explanation for the long-drawn-out proceedings). He closes with two open questions: how will the Court decide the SolGen's OM, and will Leila de Lima's planned habeas corpus petition succeed despite her bail denial? Abangan!

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban tracks four possible routes by which former Senator Leila de Lima might continue her quest for freedom after the third Muntinlupa RTC's bail denial - having been acquitted in two of the three 2017 illegal-drug-trading cases (the prosecutors' MR on the second acquittal discussed June 5 / A107) and now seeking review of the third (discussed June 12 / A106). Court administrator Raul B. Villanueva had directed Judge Romeo S. Buenaventura to finish the case in nine months, and Buenaventura accordingly rushed the schedule before his inhibition last Friday. Route 1 is De Lima's MR on the bail denial, which argues Buenaventura used wrong legal standards (prima facie / probable cause instead of the constitutional 'strong evidence of guilt'), relied 'absolutely and completely' on direct examination of 'convict-witnesses' without regard to cross-examination, failed to discuss their inherent unreliability as moral-turpitude convicts, and refused to believe Benjamin Magalong (the only credible prosecution witness, who testified De Lima was merely performing her SoJ duties in purging the NBP of drug trading) - and alleges grave abuse of discretion in admitting hearsay, belittling humanitarian issues (hypertension, diabetes, cervical spondylosis with chronic neck pain and severe headaches), dismissing the October 9, 2022 hostage incident as 'isolated' despite it almost killing her, and disbelieving she is not a flight risk given her stature, public record, integrity, advanced age, frail health, and political-persecution context. Route 2 is certiorari to the CA or SC alleging grave abuse - with the MR being a prerequisite. Route 3 is a direct petition for habeas corpus to the SC under the Reyes v. Director (January 17, 2023) exception, where Gigi Reyes was freed via Estelito P. Mendoza's showing that her custody had become 'vexatious, capricious, and oppressive amounting to an infringement of the constitutional right to speedy trial' - a route Panganiban had urged in his January 30 column 'Gigi freed, Leila next?,' but De Lima's lawyers preferred the conventional bail-petition route over the speedy unconventional habeas corpus remedy. Route 4 is relentless pursuit of trial on the merits to secure permanent freedom via acquittal; with two prior acquittals already secured, De Lima's counsels should be able to do it again, though the new presiding magistrate after Buenaventura's inhibition may need more than nine months to study the case, conduct trials, and rule on whether to limit the prosecution's announced 20 additional witnesses. Of the four routes, Panganiban ranks Route 4 most important - because victory there entitles De Lima to permanent and complete freedom via acquittal, while victories in the first three give her merely temporary liberty pending trial. The great challenge to her lawyers is to secure her acquittal 'because of her innocence, not merely because of reasonable doubt on her guilt.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban characterizes Judge Romeo S. Buenaventura's denial of former Senator Leila de Lima's Motion for Bail Ad Cautelam (in RTC Muntinlupa Branch 256, the third drug-trading case) as 'a big, surprising blow' after over six years' detention. The constitutional rule guarantees bail except for those charged with capital offenses 'WHEN THE EVIDENCE OF GUILT IS STRONG' (CJ supplies the caps). De Lima's motion alleged the prosecution failed to show 'proof evident' of conspiracy, that the evidence was incredible/irrelevant/incompetent and actually supported her innocence and SoJ-duty regularity, that she was not a flight risk, and that humanitarian grounds (longing for family, senior-citizen health issues, life-threatening risks shown by the October 9, 2022 hostage-taking incident) supported release. In a 35-page Order, Buenaventura framed the 'sole issue' as whether the prosecution's evidence was strong, and ruled - after careful review of the totality of evidence - that it was indeed strong, showing prima facie crime and conspiracy. He found De Lima as senior citizen had admitted no serious or life-threatening condition (with expeditious medical furloughs granted), distinguished prior SC cases allowing bail for life/health-injurious detention as not 'obtaining in the instant case,' treated the hostage incident as 'merely an isolated occurrence,' and caveated that 'strong evidence' does not equate to 'proof of guilt beyond reasonable doubt' and does not prejudge the eventual outcome. The Supreme Court's 'unprecedented advisory' last Thursday - to allay public apprehension - assured that 'the denial of bail of De Lima is not the final adjudication of the case.' Panganiban was 'frankly surprised' at the denial given the prior Branch 204 acquittal (Judge Alcantara) on the Rafael Ragos recantation, but a recheck of Buenaventura's decision showed Ragos was NOT among Branch 256 witnesses - so the recantation 'has no effect whatsoever' in this case. He further endorses Buenaventura's credibility latitude, citing that 'the credibility of witnesses is best determined - not by the appellate justices - but by the trial judges' who can observe demeanor, body language, voice timbre, facial twitching, eye movement, and finger fidgeting. De Lima has several remedies - an MR already announced by lawyer Boni Tacardon, followed by higher-court appeals if needed - but these will entail further delay and 'oppressive and detestable detention' in case she is found innocent, which is why court administrator Raul B. Villanueva diligently issued the April 28 memorandum directing nine-month resolution. 'Truly, justice delayed is justice denied. Not just for the accused but also for the prosecution and for the rule of law.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban examines the 11-prosecutor Department of Justice panel's 91-page Motion for Reconsideration before Judge Abraham Joseph Alcantara of the RTC Muntinlupa Branch 204, asking him to set aside his decision acquitting former Senator Leila de Lima (and co-accused Ronnie Dayan) in one of two remaining drug cases and to render a new conviction. Though well-written, well-reasoned, and cerebral, the MR is - IMHO - not enough to convince the judge to change his mind, because he had already carefully weighed the prosecution's evidence and ruled that the recantation of former NBI deputy director Rafael Ragos had created 'reasonable doubt' on the guilt of the accused. To secure conviction, the constitutional standard requires evidence showing guilt with 'moral certainty' and/or 'beyond reasonable doubt' - the chain of evidence must be 'so airtight and so strong' to produce in an unprejudiced mind the moral certainty that the crime occurred and the accused committed it; absent that, the court has no choice but to acquit. While drug trafficking in the National Bilibid Prison may have been proven, De Lima and Dayan's participation was not proven with moral certainty - the Ragos recantation broke the chain of circumstances, entitling them to acquittal based on reasonable doubt, NOT necessarily on lack of guilt. 'The recantation created a doubt on culpability, not a certainty of innocence.' Panganiban illustrates with a red-ink-on-white-paper metaphor: imagine an immaculate sheet, then splatter red ink - it is quite difficult to erase. 'Try it. In a similar way, once an unprejudiced mind is splattered with doubt, it is difficult to erase the doubt. The more one thinks of the doubt, the more it lingers.' The prosecutors counter that the SC has ruled in a 'plethora of cases' that recanted testimony is 'exceedingly unreliable' compared with original sworn testimony given in the judge's presence with cross-examination opportunity, and that Ragos failed to answer cross-examination about the alleged coercion, never reported it (despite being NBI deputy director with reporting duty), and was silent for 'more than four years of earsplitting silence' before singing a new 'song of recantation.' De Lima's camp invoked the adage that 'acquittal is final and unappealable,' but the prosecutors are likely betting on the exception that 'an acquittal rendered with grave abuse of discretion is void and legally deemed to be nonexistent.' They 'have everything to gain' by filing the MR - if granted (IMHO unlikely), they win; if denied, certiorari to the CA or SC is available, where the Office of the Solicitor General would replace them as counsel for the 'People,' and Solicitor General Menardo Guevarra was the secretary of justice during De Lima's RTC prosecution - making him a 'formidable ally.' An interesting deferred question: if De Lima's petition for bail in the third drug case is granted, would she be released from detention while the MR and any subsequent certiorari are pending? 'The answer deserves a future column.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban answers the public question why Janet Lim-Napoles (and several others) were freed of criminal responsibility for her alleged 16 separate Section 3-e violations of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act (RA 3019) in the pork-barrel scam exposed by the Inquirer in 2013. He read the 223-page Sandiganbayan decision People v. Revilla (May 22, 2023) penned by Justice Geraldine Faith A. Econg - NOT by Presiding Justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang as erroneously reported by the Inquirer on May 23 and sadly repeated in its May 26 editorial - with Justices Efren N. de la Cruz (Division chair) and Arthur O. Malabaguio concurring. To understand it, he supplies a backgrounder on plunder (RA 7080, approved July 12, 1991) vs graft (RA 3019, effective August 17, 1960) vs Revised Penal Code crimes (effective 'believe it or not' January 1, 1932); plunder is a relatively new crime. Per Jinggoy Estrada v. Sandiganbayan (February 26, 2002), the anti-plunder law was 'crafted to avoid the mischief and folly of filing multiple informations' in the aftermath of the Marcos regime, where the 'multitude and magnitude' of acts produced a 'legal nightmare' - and the law helped unclog dockets while letting prosecutors aggregate predicate acts (malversation, bribery, RA 3019 violations) into a single plunder charge punishable by reclusion perpetua to death. Here, the Office of the Ombudsman prosecutors charged Napoles separately with 16 RA 3019 violations AND filed a separate plunder charge against Sen. Ramon Revilla Jr. and others (including Napoles) using these very same violations as predicates. Since Revilla et al. were earlier acquitted of plunder for the prosecution's failure to prove the predicate crimes beyond reasonable doubt, Napoles could no longer be found guilty of the same unproven predicate acts. Justice Econg's 'masterpiece' patiently narrated the trial testimonies, especially of Benhur Luy, identical to those in the plunder case - and Panganiban suggests she could have shortened her decision by referring to and not reproducing them. He concurs with the Sandiganbayan - though Napoles remains detained on other pending cases. Regardless of whether he agrees with the prior Revilla acquittal, he is bound by such judgment. The OBM prosecutors committed the 'legal nightmare' of multiple prosecutions that the anti-plunder law sought to avoid - and are 'lucky Justice Econg did not chastise them for committing this legal blunder.' He closes with a tribute: Division chairman Justice Efren N. de la Cruz - known as reliable, credible, honest, competent, IMHO 'should have been promoted to the Supreme Court long ago.' The wish is no longer possible because de la Cruz reaches compulsory retirement next year while the next SC vacancy is in June 2025; three of his former Sandiganbayan colleagues (Teresita J. Leonardo-de Castro, Diosdado M. Peralta, and Alexander G. Gesmundo) were promoted and all became Chief Justices - and de la Cruz preceded CJ Gesmundo in the Sandiganbayan.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the six-prong executive-and-legislative effort 'unleashing their superpowers' to bring Negros Oriental Rep. Arnolfo Teves Jr. to justice for the brutal killing of Gov. Roel Degamo of the same province - denounced by Justice Secretary Jesus Crispin Remulla as an alleged mastermind. First, the 292-member House led by Speaker Martin Romualdez unanimously suspended Teves (still abroad) for 60 days for 'defying orders' to return in person; per Alejandrino v. Quezon (September 11, 1924), the Constitution caps representative suspension at 60 days to avoid a hiatus in district representation, 'without ruling out expulsion that may lead to a special election' - Romualdez's warning of more 'disciplinary actions' may signal expulsion. His lawyers led by Ferdinand Topacio claim Teves is willing to come home except for 'serious and credible death threats,' despite President Marcos's safety assurances. Second, Remulla wants Teves tagged as 'terrorist' via the Anti-Terrorism Council and/or Court of Appeals to extricate him from Cambodia (no PH-Cambodia extradition treaty exists), so any UN-member state where Teves is found would be obligated under international law to arrest and return him. But the committee drafting terrorism-case rules headed by retired CJ Reynato S. Puno has not finished its work - and per CJ Puno, even ex-parte proceedings must actively protect respondent constitutional rights. While Panganiban agrees the full might of the state should be used to attain justice, 'I believe laws should not be weaponized' - the Anti-Terrorism Act should not be resorted to merely to bring Teves in; the law should be used only with 'reasonable certainty of conviction shown by the evidence at hand.' 'His return is merely the consequence, not the reason, for prosecuting him under that law. I am not for or against Teves. I am for the rule of law.' Third, with DFA help, Remulla convinced Timor-Leste (where Teves flew from Cambodia) to deny his asylum application - though Teves may ask for reconsideration. Fourth, an Interpol 'Notice' has been issued obligating foreign police forces to report Teves's presence in their jurisdictions, enabling Philippine police tracking. Fifth, Remulla will ask the DFA to cancel Teves's passport - but the right to travel is constitutionally guaranteed, and by law a passport may be cancelled only when the holder (a) is a fugitive, (b) is convicted of a crime, (c) acquired the passport fraudulently, or (d) requests cancellation due to loss or tampering - 'at this point, none of these four causes exists.' Sixth, murder charges against Teves will be filed shortly, and Remulla expects the filing will support declaring Teves a 'fugitive' enabling DFA passport cancellation - but Remulla himself directed prosecutors to file criminal cases only with 'reasonable certainty of conviction' (per CJ's February 20 column 'Don't charge what you can't prove'), and although that directive originally covered first-level courts, 'IMHO' it should apply to Teves's high-profile case and others as well.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban welcomes the 3,992 new lawyers who passed the 2022 Bar examinations (43.47% of 9,183) and took their oath before the Supreme Court on May 2 - comparing the 2022 rate with the 2020-2021 combined cycle (no 2020 exam due to COVID; 8,241 of 11,402 / 72.28% passed, 'the highest in history'), and welcoming the 2022 restoration of the topnotcher announcement that the 2020-2021 results had suspended. 'The ancients in the legal profession, like me, were totally surprised, some even flabbergasted at these gigantic passing percentages' given that the usual prior-year average was about 25%. 'With due respect, I believe the doors to the legal profession should swing on reluctant hinges' - other than the pandemic, Panganiban does not know of any event justifying the doors swinging wide open, and is not aware that law schools have improved enormously enough to justify a tsunami of entrants. Having posted his abbreviated 'Separate Opinion,' he nonetheless yields to and obeys the Court's decision and dutifully welcomes the new 'compañeros and compañeras' with his fervent hope and prayer that they fulfill his Vision-Mission Statement (from his chief-justiceship and up to now): 'competent and ethical lawyers who are responsible, dependable, and morally upright; who courageously uphold truth and justice above everything else; and who safeguard the liberty and nurture the prosperity of our people.' He invites three past 'Numero Uno' to greet the new brethren and advise 2023 aspirants. Joan de Venecia-Fabul (2005, UP; first VP and deputy chief legal counsel, PLDT; 2022 Bar examiner for Civil Law II) reflects on 17 years of lawyering, framing the practice as integrity-first - not subverting justice, not 'taking shortcuts,' not 'arrogantly brandishing the lawyer card to oppress my fellow Filipinos' - and exhorts new lawyers to 'choose to do good and act with justice,' 'wear a badge of incorruptibility,' 'seek and speak for the truth,' and help 'when the law is weaponized against those who have less in life.' Arlene M. Maneja (2002, UST; partner, SyCip Salazar Hernandez and Gatmaitan) welcomes new lawyers with 'Narito na ang exciting part!' and the exhortation to be 'fierce warriors for justice and truth' because 'we may not always win but know that there is honor and meaning in fighting the good fight,' offering 2023 aspirants practical Bar-prep advice (be kind; reasonable study plan; eat well, manage sleep, rest; minimize materials; design to do less near exam dates). Reinier R. Yebra (2009, San Beda; undersecretary, Department of Transportation) closes with the meritocratic-formation line: 'the circumstances in which you were born will eventually become immaterial. What you do with your gifts will define who you are.'

one_paragraph_summary: Continuing from A112's account of the Warren-Court origin of judicial activism, CJ Panganiban argues that the Philippine variant rests on firmer ground than its American template. Article VIII Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution makes activism a duty, not a discretion: it commits 'the courts of justice' both to 'settle actual controversies involving rights which are legally demandable and enforceable' and to 'determine whether or not there has been a grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the government' -- and CJ underlines that 'Power can be relinquished, but a duty cannot under any circumstance be evaded.' Under separation of powers, the three branches remain supreme in their own spheres, so the judiciary may not police internal rules of Congress or confidential internal orders of the Presidency; but where the Constitution imposes 'conditions, limitations, or restrictions' on an otherwise exclusive power, expanded certiorari may police those textual caveats. Francisco v. House of Representatives (Nov. 10, 2003), restraining the House from pursuing a second impeachment complaint against CJ Davide within the once-per-year window, is offered as the worked example -- 'reluctantly, after several days that tested its adherence to the rule of law, the House obeyed.' Comparatively, Philippine libertarianism replicates the famous phrases of US jurisprudence ('separate is not equal,' 'read him his rights,' 'one-man-one-vote,' 'fruit of the poisonous tree') but anchors them to the Constitution rather than to changeable precedent, so 'American magistrates are accorded the luxury of choosing between being passivists or activists' but 'this luxury is denied to all Philippine judges.' The column closes by naming a personal exemplar: recently retired RTC Naga Judge Soliman M. Santos Jr., subject of three earlier CJ columns and author of the forthcoming book 'Judicial Activist' (CJ writing the Foreword), is identified as a 'soulmate' through their shared student-activist past -- CJ as the youngest FEU Central Student Organization president and NUSP cofounder.

one_paragraph_summary: CJ Panganiban traces the origin of judicial activism to the 1950s turn of the US Supreme Court -- a turn that Philippine constitutional thought has inherited because the 1935 and later Philippine Constitutions 'took their bearing from the Constitution of the United States,' especially in the republican presidential system, the tripartite allocation of powers, and the sanctity of human rights. The anchoring anecdote is President Dwight D. Eisenhower's 1961 CBS interview with Fred Friendly: asked whether he had made any great mistakes, Eisenhower snapped 'Yes, two, and they are still sitting in the Supreme Court' -- meaning CJ Earl Warren and J William Brennan, both of whom Eisenhower had appointed expecting deference but who instead teamed with Justices Hugo Black and William Douglas (later joined by Thurgood Marshall and Abe Fortas) to overhaul American jurisprudence via Brown v. Board of Education (May 17, 1954), Miranda v. Arizona (June 13, 1966), Terry v. Ohio (June 10, 1968), Mapp v. Ohio (June 19, 1961), NY Times v. Sullivan (March 9, 1964), Gideon v. Wainwright (March 18, 1963), and Baker v. Carr (March 26, 1962) -- supplying the famous phrases 'separate is not equal,' 'read him his rights,' 'one-man-one-vote,' and 'fruit of the poisonous tree.' The internal opposition came from Felix Frankfurter's Harvard School of judicial restraint and Nuremberg-veteran Robert Jackson, who believed the Court existed 'to establish rules of law, not to provide justice'; the activists countered that 'all heart' had been excised from the law and that abdication, not intervention, was the real threat. CJ then traces the sway-vote era through Sandra Day O'Connor (first woman SCOTUS, retired Jan. 31, 2006) and Anthony Kennedy (CJ's personal 'friend, the brilliant Justice') to the Trump-era transformation: three conservative appointments (Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, Barrett) producing the current 6-3 bulwark, with Dobbs v. Jackson (June 24, 2022) overturning Roe v. Wade (Jan. 22, 1973), and the generational-reversal warning that 'liberals will take generations to reverse Dobbs.' The piece closes with a cliffhanger pointing to A111: while US justices may choose between activist and passivist leanings, their Philippine counterparts cannot -- 'Why? Read the answer next Monday.'

one_paragraph_summary: Even though the media had already reported it, CJ Panganiban gives Ditiangkin v. Lazada (Sept. 21, 2022; uploaded Jan. 19, 2023; Second Division, penned by SAJ Marvic M.V.F. Leonen with JJ Lazaro-Javier, Jhosep Lopez, and Kho Jr. concurring, J Mario Lopez on official business) a lookback because the Supreme Court 'once more demonstrated its activist and libertarian streak' by going beyond two sets of normal rules. The first set concerns appellate procedure: the SC normally dismisses Rule 45 petitions through the unsigned-resolution '1-2-3 rule' when the CA has affirmed the NLRC and the labor arbiter, and it normally refuses to review facts. In Lazada, the Court did the opposite -- waded deep into an exhaustive factual review and overturned the unanimous lower-tribunal finding that the riders were independent contractors. The second set concerns substantive labor classification: under the four-fold test (selection/engagement, wages, dismissal power, control -- with control 'the most significant factor'), Lazada failed to discharge its burden of showing the riders were not regular employees. The Court rejected the independent-contractor framing because the riders neither carried on 'a distinct and independent business' nor possessed the 'unique skills and talents' that distinguish the genuinely independent service class -- canonically the columnist, the basketball referee, and the masiador/sentenciador of cockfighting -- since 'picking up and delivering goods from warehouse to buyers does not call for specific expertise.' The constitutional anchor is the full-protection-to-labor clause and the corollary that 'when a person has no property, his job may possibly be his only possession or means of livelihood' so 'he should be protected against any arbitrary deprivation of his job' -- a closing dictum CJ explicitly recognizes as 'reminiscent of my own philosophy of liberty and prosperity under the rule of law.' The Inquirer editorial called it a 'game-changing ruling for workers'; CJ quotes the label approvingly.

one_paragraph_summary: Opening with the observation that the Gesmundo Court is 'continuing the activist and libertarian streaks of its predecessors,' CJ Panganiban catalogs four signature decisions -- Vhong Navarro v. Deniece Cornejo (Feb. 8, 2023) striking down PI weaponization, Ditiangkin v. Lazada (Sept. 21, 2022) on gig-economy classification, Reyes v. Director (Jan. 17, 2023) freeing Gigi Reyes for constitutional-rights violations, and PCGG v. Ombudsman (Jan. 17, 2023) acquitting the late Roberto Ongpin -- alongside the 'historic Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovation 2022-2027' (SPJI) being pursued 'with unprecedented passion.' The column then drills into Navarro v. Cornejo (Third Division, ponente J Henri Jean Paul B. Inting, with J Caguioa as chairperson and JJ Gaerlan, Dimaampao, and Singh concurring), reconstructing the escalating chronology: Deniece Cornejo filed three increasingly inconsistent complaints against Navarro (Jan. 29, 2014; Feb. 27, 2014; Oct. 16, 2015) covering the same Jan. 17 and Jan. 22, 2014 incidents; Navarro countersued multiple coconspirators (Cedric Lee, Bernice Cua Lee, Ferdinand Guerrero, Raz, Calma, Fernandez) for serious illegal detention, grave coercion, perjury, and extortion; the OCP and DOJ dismissed Cornejo's complaints; the MeTC and RTC of Taguig convicted Cornejo, Cedric Lee, and Fernandez of grave coercion (with Fernandez later acquitted on appeal); but the CA detoured by reversing the DOJ -- without Cornejo's required appeal to the Office of the President -- and ordering Navarro's arrest for rape. The SC's three teachings: (1) PI is executive in nature, judicial intrusion justified only on grave abuse of discretion; (2) PI is a 'crucial sieve' that 'spells the difference between months if not years of agonizing trial... and peace of mind and liberty'; (3) most important, 'the powerful, the rich, and the rogue should never weaponize the law to terrorize the innocent because the long arm of the law will eventually circle back and catch them' -- a thesis CJ shows is already vindicated by the Taguig grave-coercion convictions of Cornejo and Lee.

one_paragraph_summary: Following reader questions on his Feb. 27 column (A116), CJ Panganiban offers the title-thesis answer: the best way to stop the ICC from investigating and prosecuting alleged drug-war crimes -- a scenario the Inquirer's Feb. 28 editorial called 'a nightmare' -- is for the administration to create an independent and credible panel modeled on Ferdinand Marcos Sr.'s 1983 Agrava Board (formed to investigate Ninoy Aquino's assassination). He first lays out the procedural state of play: the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber has granted Prosecutor Karim Khan authority to investigate drug-war killings estimated by PDEA at 6,252 and by critics at 30,000; the OSG had secured a suspension; Khan announced resumption, dissatisfied with slow DOJ action; the OSG appealed to the ICC Appeals Chamber (5 judges including the Court president, different from the PTC, among the 18 total ICC judges serving nine-year staggered terms). The OSG brief was due March 13, with an AC decision expected by August. CJ warns that even an adverse ruling would not require physical entry -- modern technology allows witness testimony and document authentication abroad. Under the Rome Statute's complementarity principle, the ICC defers only if the state is 'investigating or prosecuting' and is not 'unwilling or unable genuinely' -- where 'genuinely' means 'trustworthy, transparent, and thorough.' With due respect, CJ argues, the government has likely lost credibility under this test because PBBM publicly defended Duterte and Sen. Dela Rosa as alleged main perpetrators without first conducting any trustworthy/transparent/thorough investigation -- amounting to presidential prejudgment that, with congressional resolutions defending the former president, taints DOJ and OSG officials despite their personal talent and respectability. Duterte and Dela Rosa, for their part, have said they would face investigation and prosecution 'by Filipinos' but not by ICC foreign judges. The administration's strategic dilemma resolves in the Agrava Board template: a credible, competent, independent body created by executive order to investigate drug-war killings, identify masterminds, and judge with both speed and due process -- sparing 'our one and only Motherland... shame and ignominy before the universe' and the 'grubby company of failed African states.'

one_paragraph_summary: Stepping forward 'as a retired jurist' to comment on 'three crucial legal issues' while leaving political overtones to politicians, CJ Panganiban frames the looming ICC inquiry into alleged crimes against humanity during Rodrigo Duterte's incumbency as Davao mayor (Nov. 1, 2011 - June 30, 2016) and president (July 1, 2016 - March 16, 2019). On sovereignty: while political leaders invoke absolute control, the Philippines partly surrendered sovereignty when the Senate ratified the Rome Statute on Aug. 30, 2011 -- including the binding provision that the ICC retains jurisdiction over crimes committed while the Philippines was a member, which is exactly the date range Khan is investigating. On scope: Rome Statute Article 5 covers genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and the crime of aggression, with Article 7 defining crimes against humanity to include murder 'committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack directed against any civilian population with knowledge of the attack.' The OSG (under Menardo Guevarra) denies the predicate by characterizing the killings as 'legitimate operations against illicit drugs' rather than state-policy attacks on civilians -- a factual dispute CJ defers, noting only that this is exactly what Khan's preliminary investigation (which requires ICC Pre-Trial Chamber authority, unlike Philippine and US PI regimes) is meant to assess. On complementarity -- the 'pivotal' third issue -- Article 17 requires the ICC to defer if the state 'is already being investigated or prosecuted... unless the State is unwilling or unable genuinely to carry out the investigation or prosecution.' CJ decomposes the test into three parts (willingness + ability + genuinely) and identifies DOJ and OSG as the 'immediate targets' who must demonstrate real investigation of the 'lawless killers of drug suspects estimated by our government at 6,117, and by critics at 30,000.' If Khan succeeds, the Philippines will be 'mercilessly debased and numbered among failed African states' -- tainting also the Supreme Court (admired as 'the most powerful in the world' because uniquely empowered to strike down grave abuse of discretion), the network of foreign jurists CJ visited and hosted as CJ (Canada's McLachlin, China's Xiao Yang, Russia's Lebedev, Israel's Beinisch, France's Canivet, US Justices O'Connor and Kennedy who 'became my personal friends'), and revered Filipino jurists at world tribunals (Bengzon at the ICJ, Feliciano at the WTO, Pangalangan recently retired from the ICC itself).

Remulla's Feb. 10, 2023 order requiring prosecutors handling MTC/MTCC/MeTC cases to assess each prosecution for 'reasonable certainty of conviction' (filing motions to withdraw information where that standard is not met), CJ Panganiban identifies the underlying problem as the doctrinal gap between the two operative standards. To file, prosecutors need only show 'probable cause' -- jurisprudentially 'a state of facts... as would lead a person of ordinary caution to believe, or entertain an honest or strong suspicion, that a thing is so,' and explicitly not requiring 'whether there is sufficient evidence to procure a conviction.' To convict, prosecutors must show 'proof beyond reasonable doubt' -- 'moral certainty of the culpability of the accused.' Remulla's order is 'ground-breaking' because it shifts the filing standard upward, but CJ proposes going further: align the filing standard with the conviction standard via Rules of Court revision, and expand the order beyond minor cases to 'ALL CRIMINAL CASES, including those cognizable by the Sandiganbayan and the regional trial courts where capital offenses are prosecuted.' The stakes are made tangible by SC en banc data -- 'as early as Jan. 8, 2013... 80% of the backlog in the first and second level courts involves criminal cases'; on Sept. 4, 2012 'about 40% of criminal cases are dismissed annually'; 'the situation has not improved; it has deteriorated' -- and by the indefinite-detention reality in capital offenses illustrated by two cross-political examples: former senator Leila de Lima 'detained without bail for over six years now due to a charge filed on the basis of probable cause,' and former president Gloria Macapagal Arroyo arrested at NAIA on watch-list orders 'of -- ironically -- then DOJ Secretary De Lima that defied a temporary restraining order of the Supreme Court,' detained for more than four years, then acquitted by the SC for prosecutors' failure to prove beyond reasonable doubt. To implement the reform, CJ proposes a sworn prosecutorial certification covering (a) sufficient allegations, (b) admissible evidence, and (c) sufficient evidence to convict -- designed to deter 'the cyclical weaponization of criminal prosecutions' and the filing of 'frivolous, reckless, malevolent, and politically motivated charges' that 'clog the judicial dockets, harass political opponents, and deprive our people of their constitutional right to life, liberty or property without due process of law.'

one_paragraph_summary: On Valentine's Day eve, Panganiban traces the Supreme Court's progressive liberalization of psychological incapacity (PI) under Article 36 of the Family Code. Imported from Canon Law without prior constitutional, statutory, or jurisprudential precedent, PI was first defined in Santos v. Court of Appeals (Jan. 4, 1995) by gravity, juridical antecedence, and incurability -- and then elaborated in Republic v. Molina (Feb. 13, 1997) into eight guidelines drawn largely from amicus curiae Archbishop Oscar V. Cruz, presiding judge of the Catholic Church's National Appellate Matrimonial Tribunal. The Molina rules proved so strict that very few marriages were nullified, prompting case-by-case relaxations and culminating in Tan-Andal v. Andal (May 11, 2021), which dispensed with the need for expert evidence -- a regime CJ already opined is 'strikingly similar to absolute divorce.' In Macabata v. Macabata (April 6, 2022, reiterated in Republic v. Amata, Nov. 29, 2022), the Court 'refreshingly clarified' that six of the Molina guidelines remain (first, third, fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth), while the second (expert testimony on 'root cause') and the fourth (medical or clinical permanence/incurability) are set aside -- the latter replaced by a 'legal sense' of personality structures so incompatible and antagonistic as to produce 'inevitable and irreparable breakdown.' He then turns to Abines v. Duque (Sept. 20, 2022, uploaded Feb. 6, 2023), which dismissed a continuing-mandamus petition over Dengvaxia on five grounds: continuing mandamus is limited to ecological rights; ordinary mandamus fails because the acts sought involve discretion; the petition violates the hierarchy of courts; it raises factual questions; and the relief had become moot because the executive branch already acted. While admiring the decision's elegant prose and deep research, Panganiban argues it should have been resolved by a short unsigned resolution since no new doctrine was laid down -- and questions whether the Court complied with the constitutional 24-month rule reckoned from the filing of the last memorandum: the Feb. 18, 2020 memorandum order and the Sept. 20, 2022 promulgation point to a deadline missed. 'Were depth and elegance,' he asks, 'worth the risk of violating the 24-month rule?'

Will it be bail, habeas corpus, or dismissal? Abangan!

one_paragraph_summary: As the New Year dawned, CJ Alexander G. Gesmundo announced that the Supreme Court would prioritize public-interest cases in 2023. Panganiban inventories four of them: Romulo Macalintal's constitutional challenge to RA 11935 (which postponed the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections from Dec. 5, 2022 to October 2023); the KAPIT petition against the Metro Manila No Contact Apprehension Policy; CJ Gesmundo's off-the-cuff comment that the P203-billion Marcos Estate Tax could be reopened; and Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen's proposed 'Writ of Kalayaan.' He focuses chiefly on Macalintal, who argues that RA 11935 usurped the Comelec's power to postpone elections, disguised a term-of-office extension as a postponement, and violated the one-subject-one-title rule by embracing three subjects. Comelec chair George Garcia has offered to hold the BSKE in May 2023 if the Court grants the petition before the end of January, and Macalintal has filed two 'extremely urgent' motions for a TRO or SQA directing the Comelec to cease implementing RA 11935 and resume preparations. The OSG, under Solicitor General Menardo I. Guevarra, opposes 'passionately,' arguing the petition failed to allege grave abuse of discretion, that Congress validly exercised police power, that the hold-over is not a term-of-office change, that the three subjects are interrelated, and that COVID and a recent presidential election justified the deferment. Panganiban places his commentary inside the fair-comment doctrine -- truthful, respectful, free of personal attacks, in good faith -- and limits himself to one urging: the Court must resolve the urgent motions within January (even by full decision, given the extensive oral argument and memoranda) to guide the Comelec and the electorate, lest the petition go moot. On the Writ of Kalayaan, he respectfully agrees with a retired colleague's caution that constitutional writs (habeas corpus, habeas data) are designed for self-executory rights; rights requiring legislation (like health care) need enabling laws -- so the Court can issue the writ if Congress first enacts enabling legislation. The other public-interest cases will be taken up later.

one_paragraph_summary: On the day after Christmas, Panganiban turns to the Supreme Court's care for 'the least, the last, and the lost' -- the 'laylayan ng lipunan' -- by featuring Aquino v. Aquino (Dec. 7, 2021), the 47-page ponencia of Senior Associate Justice Marvic M.V.F. Leonen. The decision reverses traditional norms in two ways. First, lexical: the Court refuses to use the 'pejorative and disparaging' label 'illegitimate' for children born of parents not married to each other and coins 'nonmarital' instead -- explaining that, beyond children born to parents with marriage impediments, nonmarital birth covers parents below marriageable age, victims of sexual assault who refused to marry the perpetrator, fathers who died before birth, and parents who chose not to marry though qualified. The Court cannot amend the statute, only interpret it. Second, substantive: it recognizes the right of such children to inherit 'by representation' from their grandparents who died intestate, partly shattering the 'iron curtain' of Article 992 of the Civil Code, which had barred inheritance ab intestato between legitimate and illegitimate lines. Panganiban traces the historical layering of the disability: from the Spanish conquistadores' Civil Code in 'this blessed land of the morning,' through the 1950 Civil Code's trichotomy (natural, natural by legal fiction, spurious), to the 1988 Family Code's legitimate/illegitimate binary that nonetheless preserved many earlier disabilities. He shares his own law-school exchange with Prof. Edgardo L. Paras (later a Supreme Court justice): 'there are no illegitimate children, only illegitimate parents.' The Court -- anchored on 1987 Constitution policies and international treaties -- courageously held that 'we are not duty bound to uncritically parrot archaic prejudices and cruelties' and that 'the best interest of the child should prevail.' He notes in passing SAJ Leonen's parallel Writ of Kalayaan project, worth another column.

one_paragraph_summary: The US Treasury's Dec. 10 (Human Rights Day) sanctions on Apollo C. Quiboloy -- founder and self-proclaimed 'Appointed Son of God' of the Kingdom of Jesus Christ -- for alleged human-rights violations and other offenses freeze his and KJC's US properties and bar US persons from transacting with him. Quiboloy was no longer in the US when the sanctions hit, and he has claimed in local media that the sanctions deprived him of human rights for lack of notice and due process. While no extradition request has been made, Panganiban revisits how one would proceed under the RP-US Extradition Treaty (signed Nov. 13, 1994; Senate-ratified) and the Mark Jimenez precedent. Extradition has two phases: a Phase 1 executive evaluation by the DFA of the requesting state's documentation, and a Phase 2 judicial hearing where the DFA and DOJ file the extradition charge in an RTC, which decides. In Secretary of Justice v. Lantion (Jan. 18, 2000), the Court initially ruled 9-6 -- Justice Melo's ponencia, joined by Bellosillo, Vitug, Kapunan, Quisumbing, Purisima, Buena, Santiago, and De Leon -- that Jimenez was entitled to notice and copies during Phase 1 because under the Treaty the US could request provisional arrest 'in case of urgency,' putting him at risk of deprivation of liberty. Justice (later CJ) Puno and Panganiban dissented, joined by CJ Davide and Justices Mendoza, Pardo, and Reyes, arguing that the DFA only checks documents while the RTC alone issues warrants. On Oct. 17, 2000 -- same 9-6 vote, with Quisumbing, Purisima, and De Leon 'somersaulting' -- the Court reversed itself and adopted the dissents: an extradition case is not criminal in nature; its purpose is merely to determine whether the wanted person should be surrendered to face the charges abroad with all the constitutional rights of the accused. Jimenez eventually faced US criminal proceedings. Though a congressman and close to both Arroyo and Estrada, neither president intervened -- protecting diplomatic relations with America. Quiboloy's alleged offenses (human rights, dollar trafficking, rape of young KJC women) materially exceed Jimenez's (a prohibited foreign donation to Bill Clinton's campaign), so if and when a request comes, the Philippines 'will have no choice but to follow the Extradition Treaty,' just as it did with Jimenez.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban catalogues how the Supreme Court has liberally interpreted Article 26 of the Family Code to recognize foreign divorces obtained by mixed couples -- by judicial or non-judicial bodies, for any cause, and regardless of which spouse initiated -- provided the divorce is valid in the place where it was obtained. The latest decision, Republic v. Bayog-Saito (Aug. 17, 2022, ponente Justice Henri Jean Paul B. Inting), recognizes the divorce granted by the mayor of Minami-ku, Yokohama City, Japan, based merely on a 'divorce notification' filed by Japanese husband Toru Saito with the written acquiescence of his Filipino wife Helen Bayog, and recorded in the Official Family Registry of Minami-ku -- no court appearance required. To obtain Philippine recognition, however, Helen had to submit five DFA-authenticated documents to the Tarlac City RTC: the Certificate of Marriage (Aug. 30, 1999, Pasay City), the Certificate of Acceptance of Divorce Notification by Mayor Takashi Yamaguchi (Oct. 16, 2012), the duly authenticated Family Register of Toru, the Divorce Certificate from Vice Consul Kengo Fukasawa at the Japanese Embassy, and pertinent provisions of the Civil Code of Japan with English translation. He stresses the limit: divorce between Filipino couples remains invalid here -- 'Once married, forever married,' with Muslim Filipinos under a separate law -- and advance-bills a future column on the liberalized PI doctrine. The animating principle of the liberalization is to avoid the 'anomaly that results ... from a Filipino spouse being tied to the marriage while the foreigner spouse is free to remarry.' Republic v. Manalo (April 24, 2018, Justice Peralta) justified the liberal reading on twin canons -- 'Verba legis non est recedendum' (no departure from statutory words) and the purposive principle that laws should be construed to carry out, not defeat, their ends. Republic v. Galapon (Jan. 22, 2020, Justice Caguioa, who had dissented from but had to obey Manalo) extended the rule: the Filipino spouse may remarry where the divorce was obtained (i) by the foreign spouse, (ii) jointly, or (iii) solely by the Filipino spouse.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens on President Bongbong Marcos Jr.'s frustration at China's intransigence in blocking the previous administration's effort to extract oil and gas from the PH exclusive economic zone in the South China Sea -- PBBM warning the government may abandon government-to-government talks and 'find other ways' because what is a 'small matter to China... for us, is something huge.' With PBBM visiting China in January 2023, the new administration has one month to diplomatically secure Chinese cooperation 'within the limits prescribed by our Constitution and without yielding the arbitral gains we already won.' The July 2016 Arbitral Award recognized PH sovereign rights to explore, develop, and utilize (EDU) resources under its EEZ -- ON, BELOW, and ABOVE -- but did not grant sovereignty over LAND areas in the SCS; China rejects the AA, claims almost the entire SCS by historic title, has reclaimed features into 'military fortresses, airfields, and missile silos,' and uses its Coast Guard and militia to swarm 'puny military vessels' and 'fishermen's ancient, motorized cascos.' Nevertheless, China has agreed in principle to 'joint developments' -- requiring first a government-to-government MOU, then private commercial concessionaires for financial, technical, and management implementation. Quietly, Chinese and Philippine diplomats had negotiated for three years; the reported compromise language -- that 'the oil and gas operations shall be subject to the laws of the Philippines' with a non-renunciation clause preserving both parties' SCS claims -- satisfies Article XII of the PH Constitution because EDU stays under 'full control and supervision of the State,' the 60% Filipino-capital rule applies to joint-venture partners, and the President may enter foreign technical/financial assistance agreements for large-scale petroleum EDU. DFA terminated negotiations in February 2022 to give the incoming administration a free hand. CJ argues Chinese cooperation is 'very important, nay, indispensable' because China retains 'effective military control over the SCS' despite US freedom-of-navigation sailings, and 'no private concessionaire will dare invest billions of dollars and operate in the SCS without China's assurance of no interference and no swarming.' The Shell-Malampaya service contract (2001-2022) is the model: $13 billion in cash to government from its 60% gross-earnings share and 3,400 MW of clean electricity (~25% of national requirement). With Malampaya gas exhausting in 2024, Chinese cooperation could enable continued extraction from areas nearby and from new oil fields 'known as SC 72 and 75' in the EEZ.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban returns to the 'ruckus on the gargantuan lump sums' -- especially the P9.3 billion 'confidential and intelligence funds' in the proposed P5.268 trillion 2023 national budget -- that evoke 'a penumbra of PDAF,' as he had argued in his October 17 column. He recalls that Belgica v. Ochoa (November 19, 2013), the 'monumental' decision penned by Justice Estela M. Perlas-Bernabe, unanimously banished the Pork Barrel System / Priority Development Assistance Fund (PDAF) / Countrywide Development Fund (CDF) on six interlocking grounds quoted verbatim -- violating separation of powers (legislators wielding 'non-oversight, post-enactment authority' in budget execution); violating non-delegability of legislative power (personal discretionary funds 'from which they are able to fund specific projects which they themselves determine'); flouting presentment (non-textualized items denying the President item-veto); impairing public accountability (legislator stake in budget execution they oversee); subverting genuine local autonomy (national officers intervening in local affairs); and once more transgressing non-delegability (presidential authority to redirect funds 'intended by law to energy-related purposes only to other purposes he may deem fit'). CJ had closed his October 17 column with the question whether the 2023 lump sums 'could be scuttled using Belgica v. Ochoa' and asked, 'Perhaps, Senator Pimentel can?' He received no answer from Sen. Koko Pimentel -- but did receive an email from the retired Justice Bernabe herself, referring him to her 2022 book 'Perlas-Bernabe On Law and Justice,' which records that less than a year after Belgica v. Ochoa a petition was filed seeking to declare ALL lump-sum appropriations unconstitutional per se. The SC rejected the contention in Belgica v. Executive Secretary (October 8, 2019), clarifying that some lump-sum appropriations remain constitutional 'as long as the lump-sum amount(s) (are) meant as a funding source for multiple programs, projects or activities that may all be clearly classified as falling under one singular appropriation purpose.' Under this 'doctrine of singular correspondence,' the lump sum 'effectively functions as a line-item' compatible with the President's item-veto, regardless of the generality or specificity of the singular purpose. By contrast, the 2013 PDAF's P24.79 billion funded 'multiple unrelated purposes' -- 'scholarships, medical missions, assistance to indigents, preservation of historical materials, construction of roads, flood control, etc.' -- all under 'the vague and amorphous term Priority Development Assistance Fund,' leaving 'no more discernible item' for the President's veto and rendering the appropriation 'constitutionally infirm.' With 'that scholarly clarification by the lady justice,' CJ renews his query to Pimentel: 'will the esteemed Senator Pimentel be able to reply to my query now?'

one_paragraph_summary: Continuing his two-Monday series on the Supreme Court's 'Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovation 2022-2027' (SPJI), Panganiban walks through the present-and-future reforms organized around three desired Outcomes -- Efficiency, Innovation, and Access -- anchored on four guiding principles: Timely and Fair Justice, Transparent and Accountable Justice, Equal and Inclusive Justice, and Technologically Adoptive Management. Outcome 1 (Efficiency) has two objectives. The first streamlines court systems through a top-to-bottom organizational review to 'trim the fat... and purge non-efficient processes,' creation of the SC Management Committee with a Planning and Development Office as its Secretariat, and the cornerstone Caseflow Management Program that converts 'inputs (cases) into outputs (dispositions) to address the problems of delay and congestion.' The second enhances performance excellence via twelve activities including the Judiciary Health and Welfare Program, a socialized health insurance system, Mental Health Units at all court levels, mandatory free/subsidized annual physical and mental health examinations, strengthened child-minding centers, performance-improvement tools, data-driven performance metrics, strengthened judicial education, enhanced legal education for lawyers, greater ethical responsibility for lawyers, the strengthened Judicial Integrity Board, and operationalized Judicial Marshals Office. Outcome 2 (Innovation) has four objectives covering modernized court processes ('Capitalize artificial intelligence' for legal research, AI-enhanced E-library search, online learning platform, eCourt System Version 2.0, revised Rules of Procedure, and collated/published court issuances), strengthened ICT governance (Judiciary Enterprise ICT Governance Framework, a five-year ICT Strategic Plan, four-tier judicial-hierarchy network infrastructure), effective data use (Court Management Office training in management/analytics/warehousing/presentation), and upgraded information sharing for 'seamless delivery of justice.' Outcome 3 (Access) has four objectives: enhanced public access via 'intelligent platforms for self-help services, public assistance, and public access to court-related information and services... including the launch of social media'; strengthened legal aid via six activities (institutionalized clinical legal education, strengthened public-interest legal services, a National Legal Summit on Clinical Legal Education of 2022, a database of free legal aid providers, retooled Enhanced Justice on Wheels Program, and marginalized-access impact evaluation); strengthened Shari'ah Justice via a Committee on Shari'ah, evidence-based expansion of Shari'ah Court mandates, and review of the Shari'ah Rules of Court; and gender fairness and inclusivity via six activities (gender-fair language use, gender-sensitivity workshops, victim-sensitive courts guidelines, a study on gender representation and mobility, the launch of 'Her Story: Gender Award of Distinction,' and a commissioned study on feminism). Though SPJI covers only 2022-2027 in tandem with CJ Gesmundo's term, being 'the collective effort of all the 15 justices,' it will 'remain relevant... until 2036... when the four youngest members hang their black robes.' CJ closes: 'Together with my retired colleagues, I wish the incumbents Godspeed as they embark on their noble journey.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens his two-Monday series on the Supreme Court's 'Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations 2022-2027' (SPJI) by 'reminiscing the past' as CJ Alexander G. Gesmundo himself did at launch. Gesmundo, CJ writes, 'correctly, IMHO, began by recalling the reforms started by CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr.' -- whose 'Action Program for Judicial Reform' (APJR) Gesmundo praised as 'the first structured plan for judicial reform created way back in 2001... a truly impressive plan from which (were) drawn some of (the) present activities in the SPJI.' CJ recounts that in his 536-page 'Judicial Renaissance' (Supreme Court Press, November 2006) -- dedicated to CJ Davide and available in the SC Library -- he traced Davide's 'modest roots from the remote barangay of Colawin in Argao, Cebu' to his career as lawyer, lawmaker, constitution framer, elections chairman, associate justice, and chief justice, and tracked the support the APJR drew from the World Bank, Asian Development Bank, USAID, Canadian International Development Agency, and Japan International Cooperation Agency -- the World Bank including the APJR on its website 'as a model for developing countries to emulate.' Prior to Davide's December 20, 2005 retirement, the SC held the International Conference and Showcase on Judicial Reforms on November 28-30, 2005. CJ thanks Gesmundo for crediting him with 'egalitarian justice' through 'institutionalizing the perspective of law and economics as an essential element of his Liberty and Prosperity Programs,' then 'in all modesty' lays out his own statement of vision-values-goals from incumbency assumption: 'I vow to lead a judiciary characterized by four Ins: integrity, independence, industry and intelligence -- one that is morally courageous to resist influence, interference, indifference, and insolence. I envision a judiciary that is impervious to the plague of ships: kinship, relationship, friendship, and fellowship.' He pledged to strengthen the APJR with focus on the 'four ACID problems that corrode justice in our country: (1) limited access to justice by the poor, (2) corruption, (3) incompetence, and (4) delay in the delivery of quality justice'; sought 'competent and ethical lawyers who are responsible, dependable, and morally upright'; promised to grant maximum benefits to 26,000 judicial employees in exchange for DHL -- 'dedication to duty, honesty in every way, and full loyalty to the judiciary'; with all leading to 'safeguarding the liberty and nurturing the prosperity of our people under the rule of law.' His incumbency capstone was the Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity on October 18-20, 2006; after retirement on December 7, 2006, the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity was formed to continue the philosophy via professional chairs, legal scholarships, dissertation contests, and 'Esmel' fellowships, with ultimate projects of a Center for Liberty and Prosperity housing an interactive Museum in partnership with the SC, and an 'Entrepreneurship Fund.' Gesmundo also hailed CJ Reynato S. Puno as 'father of the great writs of freedom -- the Writ of Amparo, Writ of Habeas Data, and Writ of Kalikasan,' and cited Rules-of-Court amendments by CJ Renato C. Corona (Quezon City Courts and Judicial Affidavit Rule precursor), CJ Teresita Leonardo de Castro (Family Courts and Children in Conflict with the Law), CJ Lucas P. Bersamin (Revised Law Student Practice, Mandatory Clinical Legal Education, 2019 Amendments to Rules of Civil Procedure and on Evidence), and CJ Diosdado M. Peralta (Continuous Trial, 'among others'). CJ closes pointedly: 'Sorry, no mention of Maria Lourdes P. A. Sereno's Four Pillars' -- and acknowledges his epistemic limit, having retired December 7, 2006, referring readers to pio.sc@judiciary.gov.ph for details on post-term reforms now embedded in the Rules of Court.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban surveys the Percival 'Percy Lapid' Mabasa murder case as Justice Secretary Boying Remulla prepares to file (on November 7) separate murder charges against a 'very high person' mastermind and several others in the brutal killing of the radio broadcaster and of NBP inmate Cristito 'Jun Villamor' Palaña -- with the Lapid family lawyers Berteni Causing and Danilo Pelagio already pointing to suspended Bureau of Corrections director general Gerald Bantag as the alleged mastermind of a 'multi-twisted plot reminiscent of Perry Mason mysteries (if the oldies like me will remember).' Days after Lapid was gunned down, Joel Escorial surrendered as the lone motorcycle gunman, fearing elimination by the mastermind he had never personally met; he fingered two 'middlemen' -- Palaña and Christopher Bacoto, both NBP inmates -- who contracted him for P550,000. 'Twist of twists,' a day after Escorial surrendered, Palaña died en route to the NBP Hospital; Bacoto is allegedly safely secured under BJMP custody. 'Disbelieving coincidences' and 'suspecting foul play,' Remulla ordered an NBI autopsy of the already-embalmed Palaña; unnamed NBI medico-legal experts found 'no apparent external injuries,' implying natural causes. Not satisfied, Remulla and the Lapid family asked Dr. Raquel Fortun -- 'the first Filipino woman forensic pathologist in the Philippines and head of the Department of Pathology of the University of the Philippines Manila' -- to conduct a second autopsy six days later. Fortun confirmed no 'significant injury' internal or external, but concluded the death was caused by 'asphyxia or suffocation likely by a plastic bag placed over the victim's head,' and noted 'complications in the lungs (pulmonary congestion, edema, and hemorrhages) and schistosomiasis of the liver, a parasitic disease.' For murder conviction, 'credible testimony of credible witnesses is vital' -- explaining why prospective NBP-inmate witnesses are being readied and why Escorial may be 'included as an accused; later to be discharged from the case and granted immunity as a state witness' (DOJ propose, trial court discretion). The two-autopsy divergence creates a doctrinal tension: under People v. Tuyor (October 12, 2020), the NBI medico-legal report -- by a government doctor -- is admissible without the physician's testimony under the 'entry in official records exception' to hearsay with a 'prima facie presumption of regularity.' Fortun's contradictory finding must overcome that presumption. Critically, 'the news reports did not give any info on what the death certificate said.' Under Lagao v. People (September 15, 2021), the SC acquitted the accused because of variance between the death certificate and the autopsy report -- the variance 'left the evidence in equipoise that warranted the petitioner's acquittal.' A death certificate is a public document, 'the best evidence of its content without need of any testimony,' admissible without proof of execution/genuineness, with entries 'presumed correct unless the party who contests its accuracy can produce positive, contrary evidence.'
