one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban examines Justice Secretary Jesus Crispin 'Boying' Remulla's Department of Justice Opinion No. 21, Series of 2022, which holds that renewable energy (RE) -- 'especially solar, wind, hydro and ocean or tidal energy sources' -- is open to foreign exploration, development, and utilization (EDU). Under Article XII Section 2 of the Constitution, all 'natural resources' and 'all forces of potential energy' are owned by the State, with EDU 'under the full control and supervision of the State' and limited to Filipino citizens or 60%-Filipino-owned entities -- meaning aliens are banned from EDU of such resources and forces. Remulla argues that under the statutory-construction principles noscitur a sociis (interpretation by association) and ejusdem generis (interpretation by class), 'natural resources' covers only resources sharing the characteristic of being 'susceptible to appropriation,' like the enumerated lands, fisheries, forests, and wildlife -- so 'the sun, the wind or the ocean' fall outside because 'they are not subject to appropriation.' Remulla further distinguishes potential energy ('energy at rest,' position-relative -- illustrated by a ball held at head height that loses potential energy and gains kinetic energy as it falls to the floor) from kinetic energy ('energy in motion'), classifying RE sources as kinetic and therefore inexhaustible and 'incapable of ownership by anyone' -- 'All mankind owns them, and their EDU cannot be limited to the nationals of any state.' CJ agrees RE should be open to foreigners but his reasoning is geographic, not physics-based: traditional natural resources like 'petroleum, oil, coal, gold, and other minerals found in the bowels of our land and maritime territory, as well as in our exclusive economic zone' recognized by Unclos and the 2016 Arbitral Award 'belong to the Philippines' and should be reserved solely for Filipinos. But RE sources like sun, wind, and tides 'are not found solely in the Philippines,' so 'our Charter and its framers could not have intended them for the exclusive EDU of our citizens.' Practically, RE EDU 'requires tremendous amounts of capital, technological know-how, and risks-taking that we do not have or are unwilling to undertake'; foreign concessionaires cannot viably export the resulting electric power given PH's distance from other countries -- 'the logistics of bringing them abroad will just be too complicated and unprofitable'; and RE provides 'clean, sustainable, nonpolluting energy that is safe for our planet and healthy for our people,' freeing PH from foreign oil/coal dependence and preserving foreign exchange reserves while assuring 'enough power and energy to turn the wheels of our industries and factories.' The final word: EDU of natural resources, whether renewable or not, whether potential or kinetic, whether open to foreigners or not, remains 'subject to the full control and supervision of the State.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the path forward for multi-awarded Rappler CEO Maria Ressa and former Rappler staffer Reynaldo Santos Jr. after the Court of Appeals' October 10, 2022 denial of their motion for reconsideration of the CA's earlier judgment (penned by Justice Roberto P. Quiroz, concurred in by Justices Ramon M. Bato Jr. and Germano Francisco D. Legaspi) affirming the 37-page Manila RTC decision finding them guilty of cyberlibel. The Department of Justice charged that on or about February 19, 2014, the accused re-published a Rappler article that 'maliciously and publicly branded' Wilfredo Keng -- a private citizen -- 'as a human trafficker, a drug and contraband smuggler, and worst, a murderer.' Libel under the Revised Penal Code requires public and malicious imputation of a crime/vice/defect causing dishonor via printed media; the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012 extended this to 'computer system or any other similar means' and increased the penalty. Keng was never charged with the imputed crimes; because he is a private citizen, malice is presumed by law and the burden to rebut shifted to the accused -- and 'lamentably, the defense miserably failed.' Worse, the lower courts found 'actual,' not just 'presumed,' malice. 'Oddly, both accused did not take the witness stand to contest this point and to explain their defenses.' In past pieces, CJ had opined they should have testified to show that (1) the republished article was fair comment on a matter of public interest, (2) the government weaponized the cybercrime law to 'harass, intimidate and silence' them and Rappler, and (3) Rappler had sufficient reasons for its seven-month refusal to publish Keng's side. Instead they aired their defenses in 'the public fora and the media' -- but 'courts do not base their rulings on media reports and public assemblies.' He had also opined that after the trial court's decision, they should have skipped the CA and appealed directly to the SC to raise their 'truly viable defense' -- that the crime had prescribed because the one-year libel prescriptive period had lapsed when the DOJ filed the charge. The CA was bound by Tolentino v. People (August 6, 2018), an unsigned resolution setting cyberlibel prescription at 15 years; only the Supreme Court en banc can reverse or modify that resolution. Santos was reconciliatory after the MR denial -- 'not surprising but disheartening, nevertheless... we still believe that the rule of law will prevail' -- but Ressa was bitter: 'Philippine legal system is not doing enough to stop it. I am disappointed by today's ruling but sadly not surprised.' Ignoring Ressa's bitterness, CJ hopes the high court justices 'will rise above the emotional outbursts' and 'would -- like me if I were still an incumbent -- veer toward the one-year prescriptive period because, philosophically, I believe that society is better served when cases are filed and prosecuted speedily.' He closes on a rule-of-law principle: by defending themselves with all available legal weapons, both accused 'have shown their trust in our judicial system; thus, they should accept whatever may be the final decision of the highest court. Otherwise, they should have refused to participate in the judicial proceedings from the very beginning like what former senator Benigno Aquino Jr. did when he was tried by a military tribunal that subsequently sentenced him to death.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with the controversy over 'gargantuan' lump sums in the 2023 national budget -- particularly Senate Minority Leader Koko Pimentel's critique of the 'staggering P544 billion lump sum in the 2023 budget of the Department of Public Works and Highways,' which was granted 'blanket authority' to disburse and could become a 'rich source of pork barrel funds for lawmakers' -- describing these as evoking a 'penumbra' of the outlawed Priority Development Assistance Fund. A decade ago, the Inquirer pioneered in exposing the lawmakers' misuse of public funds via ghost projects and overpriced public works undertaken by foundations that allowed huge kickbacks from these pork barrel allotments known as PDAF and its predecessor the Countrywide Development Fund. On November 19, 2013, the Supreme Court en banc -- in Belgica v. Ochoa, 'superbly written by Justice Estela M. Perlas-Bernabe' -- unanimously banished PDAF, CDF, and 'similar pork barrel laws, past and present' on doctrinal grounds: the separation-of-powers principle struck budget provisions granting executive prerogatives to legislators in project selection and fund release, while non-delegability struck provisions giving the President legislative powers over fund use and project funding. The Court 'boldly obliterated' provisions authorizing legislators to 'intervene, assume or participate' in post-enactment budget execution and provisions conferring 'personal lump-sum allocations to legislators from which they are able to fund specific projects which they themselves determine.' Crucially, however, the Court 'did not reverse previous decisions that declared pork barrel constitutional in the cases where the legislators had no power to determine the specific projects, and where their intervention was merely recommendatory and not binding on the executive agencies' -- making the test fact-specific. The Court symmetrically restricted presidential discretion: lump-sum appropriations can be spent only for specific purposes, not 'unlimited choices.' PD 910's Malampaya Fund 'other purposes as may be hereafter directed by the President' clause was invalidated as undue delegation; PD 1869's presidential 'social funds' for 'priority infrastructure development projects' was likewise struck down. The Court directed investigation and prosecution of officials and private individuals for irregular pork-barrel disbursements. 'Fearless Ombudsman' Conchita Carpio Morales dutifully filed plunder cases against three prominent senators in alleged conspiracy with Janet Lim Napoles -- but the Sandiganbayan dismissed 16 cases against one senator on demurrer for 'insufficiency of evidence' without requiring defense presentation, and the two other senators charged with the 'unbailable' crime of plunder were nonetheless granted bail (one by the SC, one by the Sandiganbayan). The question now: do the 2023 lump sums constitute a form of pork barrel scuttle-able by Belgica? CJ closes: 'At this point, not being privy to the penumbral facts surrounding the lump-sum black hole, I cannot answer the question. Perhaps, Senator Pimentel can?'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains the $14.92 billion arbitral award rendered February 28, 2022 by Paris-based sole arbitrator Gonzalo Stampa in favor of the descendants of the Sultanate of Sulu against Malaysia. The heirs bemoaned former press secretary Trixie Cruz-Angeles's brushing off of the victory as 'a private claim' unrelated to PH sovereignty over Sabah (North Borneo), and Solicitor General Menardo I. Guevarra said he was 'carefully studying the legal and constitutional implications' -- leading Amina Rasul, the 'erudite and vigilant' president of the Philippine Center for Islam and Democracy, to lament that the PH government 'would be more supportive of the win.' CJ distinguishes two claims arising from the same historical chain: (A) the Republic of the Philippines's public-sovereignty claim that Sabah is national territory like Sulu and Mindanao, and (B) the private-proprietary claim of the heirs from the 1878 Sulu-Overbeck lease. The chain begins in 1704, when the Sultan of Brunei ceded Sabah to the Sultan of Sulu 'in gratitude for the help extended by the latter in suppressing a revolt'; various European countries (Britain, Spain, the Netherlands) acknowledged the Sultan of Sulu as Sabah's sovereign via treaties, an acknowledgment Malaysia disputes. In 1878, Austrian 'adventurer' Baron de Overbeck persuaded the Sulu Sultan to lease the territory for approximately $1,000; Overbeck sold his rights to British merchant Alfred Dent, who formed the British North Borneo Company and ceded his rights to it; the Company transferred all rights to the British Crown, which on July 10, 1946 -- 'just six days after the Philippines was granted independence by the United States' -- asserted full sovereign rights over North Borneo. In the early 1960s, PH filed its UN sovereignty claim arguing that Overbeck and Dent, not being sovereign states, could not have acquired and transferred sovereign rights to the British Crown, which therefore could not have ceded them to Malaysia at its September 16, 1963 independence -- while Malaysia argued the Sulu Sultan was no longer sovereign. The PH claim was put on the 'back burner' due to intervening events including Malaysia's pivotal role in the Mindanao peace process, and a Sabah referendum allegedly showing the inhabitants' desire to remain Malaysian (PH belittled it because residents lacked 'untrammeled freedom to choose'). The proprietary claim ran separately: the 1878 lease (Malaysia calls it a 'cession' payable in installments) passed through Overbeck → Dent → British North Borneo Company → British Crown → Malaysia, which 'continued to pay faithfully the annual $1,000 fee' until 2013, when it stopped. The heirs filed arbitration under Uncitral 2010 Rules; Stampa ruled on February 28, 2022 -- despite Malaysia's refusal to participate -- that the 1878 agreement was breached and Malaysia must pay $14.92 billion as 'restitution value of the rights over the leased territory' with 10% interest plus all legal and expert costs. CJ fully sympathizes with the heirs but understands Guevarra's need to study constitutional ramifications given PH has not abandoned its sovereignty claim and the proprietary award may affect PH-Malaysia friendly ties; Guevarra is consulting the DFA and the President, may want to understand the $14.92 billion computation, and is studying reports on 'supposed faults of sole arbitrator Stampa' that may affect the award's validity. 'Knowing the skill and patriotism of the SolGen,' CJ expects 'a learned stand in the near future.'

one_paragraph_summary: Following his prior Monday column on PBBM's desire to reopen the P23 billion (allegedly ballooned to P203 billion) Marcos estate tax imposed by the BIR, Panganiban surveys the reactions. The 'most extreme' is from retired RTC Judge Frank Lobrigo, who asserted that the BIR can -- on its own authority under Section 204 NIRC -- 'abate taxes that are excessive or unjust' without needing to reopen Marcos II v. CA (June 5, 2007), which 'merely affirmed' the CA's verdict upholding the BIR's 'summary remedy (levy and sale of the taxpayer's assets)' for assessments that 'had already attained finality.' Lobrigo argued the President has no power to appoint an independent body to review the BIR's findings; 'gallantly,' he disclosed he 'did not vote for (PBBM)' but would accept settlement per the NIRC 'whether the BIR enforces it or abates it' -- after which 'the Marcos estate can file an estate tax return anew and avail itself of the current estate tax amnesty.' 'With due respect,' CJ maintains his three-item position: (1) the BIR should publicly advise on the status of estate-tax collection; (2) the President can and should appoint an independent body to determine the truth and validity of imposed taxes; (3) the SC, on the Marcos heirs' initiative, can review that body's findings. On item 1, he relays Estrella V. Martinez's January 17, 2007 letter to then Finance Secretary Margarito Teves disclosing that 'in partial settlement of the tax liabilities of Ferdinand Marcos and Imelda Romualdez Marcos,' she had forfeited 10 parcels of land originally titled to Imelda -- meaning the original P23 billion (and the 'balloon' figure) may no longer be accurate, other Marcos properties may have been levied and sold, and as reader Jose Oliveros observed, 'All the BIR Commissioners from 1999 to 2022 have remained silent.' On item 2, the President's authority arises from his 'constitutional power of control over the entire executive branch' to create an independent body, analogous to PFM's own creation of the Agrava Board to investigate the Ninoy Aquino murder; former SGV chair Cirilo Noel texted that PH cannot rely 'simply on the BIR's table assessment. This requires a factual determination by an independent body as you proposed.' On item 3, the SC decision became final and executory and affirmed the P23 billion tax liability; abatement or modification 'cannot be done -- as a matter of law or at least of judicial courtesy -- without the SC's imprimatur.' The SC can create its own fact-finding body following the model of Galman v. Sandiganbayan (September 12, 1986), where the commission was composed of retired SC Justice Conrado Vazquez (chair), retired CA Justice Milagros German, and lawyer Eduardo Caguioa; alternatively, per retired SC Justice Adolfo S. Azcuna's text, a 'Special Master' can be appointed. Together these three items determine 'whether there is a miscarriage of justice in the imposition and collection of the Marcos estate taxes.' In a postscript, CJ congratulates retired CJ Lucas P. Bersamin for his 'patriotic and courageous' acceptance of the executive-secretary post -- patriotic for serving under the President at 'a rank lower in the officialdom than his prior post as the chief of a constitutionally coequal branch,' helping minimize poverty/inflation/joblessness/ill-health and uphold constitutional rights; courageous for 'entering the political arena without the protective shields granted by the Constitution to the judiciary,' relying only on continuing presidential trust 'to fend off the intrigues of political warlords and the jealousy of charlatans.' 'May the Lord bless him in his new journey of service to our nation.'

one_paragraph_summary: After PBBM, in a Toni Gonzaga interview, asked for the reopening of the estate taxes imposed on his deceased father's properties, the media noted that the Supreme Court judgment requiring the heirs to pay P23B had become final and executory on March 9, 1999 and had since ballooned to P203B with penalties and surcharges. BIR Commissioner Lilia Guillermo's now-viral reply -- 'P'wede ba maging role model kayo?' -- frames the column. Panganiban revisits Marcos II v. Court of Tax Appeals (June 5, 1997), penned by Justice Justo Torres Jr. and concurred in unanimously by JJ Regalado, Romero, Puno, and Mendoza, which faulted the heirs for never questioning the BIR assessments and described their conduct as 'disregard or even repugnance of the established institutions for governance.' May a final and executory decision still be reviewed? Ordinarily no -- but in CJ's humble opinion, when facts are shown to be grossly erroneous, or law gravely misapplied, producing a glaring miscarriage of justice, review may be entertained. He illustrates with a US DNA-evidence rape exoneration and with the post-EDSA Supreme Court nullification of Justice Pamaran's Sandiganbayan acquittal of Ninoy's killers -- proving that even acquittals, normally immediately final and executory, can be undone in extreme cases. 'Jurists are not mere legal robots,' he writes; they render justice 'to live human beings' and 'give everyone his (or her) due.' His procedural recommendation: before any reopening, the BIR must first publicly answer the unanswered factual questions (how much has been collected, how P23B was computed, how it ballooned to P203B, whether ill-gotten assets were included), and an independent review group modeled on the Agrava Board -- co-led by the IBP and the Philippine Institute of Certified Public Accountants -- should examine the factual bases of the Torres ponencia.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains why most Filipino-Americans need not undertake the tedious renunciation-and-oath process under RA 9225 to retain Philippine citizenship. Article IV, Section 1 of the Constitution provides that children of Filipino parents automatically inherit Filipino citizenship as 'natural-born citizens' -- and David v. SET (Sept 20, 2016) extends this to foundlings. These citizens-from-birth enjoy constitutionally exclusive rights -- only they may run for President, Vice President, senator, or representative, or be appointed Supreme Court (or lower collegiate court) justice -- that naturalized citizens cannot claim. RA 9225's two requirements (renunciation under oath of foreign citizenship and an oath of allegiance to the Philippines) apply only to natural-born Filipinos who lost citizenship through naturalization, not to dual citizens at birth. Walking the reader through a 'simple question' (US-born children of Filipino parents running for senator) and a 'more complicated question' (the hypothetical Maria, born 1991 in the PH to a Filipino father and American mother, listed in the CRBA, US passport for extensive travel), he cites Gana-Carait v. Comelec (Aug 12, 2022, J Ricardo R. Rosario): the CRBA process recognizes US citizenship she already held at birth, not naturalization. The earlier Cordora v. Comelec (Feb 19, 2009, J Antonio T. Carpio) had already held that even an American parent's positive petition for US citizenship was a 'superfluity' because the child was already dual at birth. Roughly one in ten Filipinos lives and works abroad -- most of them, CJ concludes, are recognized by the Philippines (not necessarily by the US) as dual citizens 'without the need to go through the rather tedious process under RA 9225.'

Hernando (First Division), the Court ruled that bigamy is a crime involving moral turpitude and consequently dismissed a Department of Foreign Affairs employee convicted of it -- a decision easy to agree with. Peralta (Third Division), the Court held that Ferdinand Marcos II's failure to file ITRs for 1982-1985 was not moral turpitude -- distinguishing false returns, fraudulent returns with intent to evade, and mere failure to file, and treating only the first two as involving the requisite 'willfulness and fraudulent intent.' This decision, CJ concedes, is harder to agree with -- some may rage against its 'cryptic and strained' explanation -- but it is the prevailing jurisprudence and all are duty-bound to follow it 'while working to reverse or modify or clarify it.' Instead of reversal, however, the en banc in Buenafe v. Comelec (June 28, 2022), penned by 'low profile' Justice Rodil V. Zalameda, affirmed and reiterated it -- clarifying that tax evasion involves fraud through pretenses and forbidden devices while negligent failure to file is 'not of itself immoral.' The Court brushed aside petitioners' request to 'reexamine the totality of circumstances,' which CJ -- with due respect -- believes it should have engaged, if only to explain why a lowly DFA employee is dismissed for bigamy while a presidential candidate who 'gathered 31,629,783 votes, or 58.77%' is treated differently. 'But the Court has spoken' -- and to undo an election requires compelling and unequivocal evidence the COC simply does not bear.

one_paragraph_summary: Defending the Supreme Court's Aug 30, 2022 temporary restraining order on the no-contact apprehension policy (NCAP) -- which halted implementation by the LGUs of Manila, Quezon City, Valenzuela, Parañaque, and Muntinlupa under an MMDA Resolution dated Feb 16, 2016, and barred the LTO from sharing motorist information -- Panganiban explains why the TRO is both legally correct and legally proper. Although issued ex parte, it rests on the petitions' cogent sworn allegations of three constitutional violations: NCAP denies due process by not allowing alleged violators sufficient time to contest before penalty; it oppressively penalizes the registered owner of the vehicle (a non-participant, innocent person) instead of the actual driver; and it crosses the right to privacy because, as petitioner counsel Juman Paa demonstrated, anyone can type a plate number into the LGU website and view the owner's name, address, and violation history -- in violation of the Data Privacy Act. Well-settled jurisprudence grants courts sound discretion to halt such transgressions immediately when sworn allegations appear facially valid. The TRO is also procedurally proper to prevent irreparable injury pending full hearing, and is expressly temporary -- the SC may revoke, modify, or change it moto proprio if the respondents' 10-day non-extendible Comment, or the Jan 24, 2023 Oral Arguments, show fallacy in the petitions or a more overriding public interest. CJ welcomes new SolGen Menardo I. Guevarra -- distinguished nonpartisan DOJ Secretary under Duterte and deputy executive secretary for legal affairs under P-Noy -- to his 'baptism of fire' as the tribune of the people. He acknowledges NCAP's laudable intentions (discipline, anti-corruption, digitalization), but insists that 'there is a right way to do the right thing at the right time by the right person and for the right reasons' -- laudable purposes must be accomplished within the rule of law, because 'autocratic shortcuts done in violation of basic rights are abhorred in democratic societies, for as the adage goes, the road to hell is paved with good intentions.'

one_paragraph_summary: After the Aug 21 commemoration of Ninoy Aquino's martyrdom at the Manila International Airport, readers again asked Panganiban whether President Ferdinand Marcos (PFM), First Lady Imelda Romualdez Marcos (IRM), or Eduardo 'Danding' Cojuangco were complicit in Ninoy's killing. CJ's answer in 2009 was No, and his answer now is still No. He recounts the fact-finding history: three days after the assassination, PFM created a CJ Enrique Fernando committee, soon criticized for bias; replaced on Oct 22, 1983 by the Agrava Board with Corazon Agrava as chair (later joined by Andres Narvasa as general counsel and Bienvenido Tan Jr. as public coordinator), which held 125 sessions, heard 194 witnesses, and consumed 20,377 pages of transcript, concluding that several military officers including Fabian Ver conspired to kill Ninoy. The Pamaran SBN decision (Dec 2, 1985) acquitting all accused was nullified post-EDSA by the reconstituted Supreme Court as a 'sham,' and J Regino Hermosisima Jr.'s 177-page re-trial decision (Sept 28, 1990) convicted 16 soldiers including Brig. Gen. Luther Custodio of double murder. Ver was never convicted because the SBN never acquired jurisdiction -- he fled with PFM to Hawaii on Feb 25, 1986 and died in Bangkok on Nov 21, 1998, never returning home. The SC denied the soldiers' petition for review on July 25, 1991. CJ then asked Tan Jr. directly why the Agrava Board did not name a mastermind; Tan's March 15, 2009 letter -- echoed in his book 'The Public Has the Right to Know' -- replied that 'there was never any evidence linking President Marcos or Imelda or Danding,' and the two Aquino presidents (Cory and P-Noy) never objected to the rulings, the book, or CJ's columns. The remaining controversy is who pulled the trigger: PAO chief Persida Acosta's Aug 2004 motion for a third trial argued for an upward-trajectory bullet allegedly fired by Rolando Galman, not CIC Rogelio Moreno. J Reynato S. Puno's unanimous March 8, 2005 resolution rejected the motion -- the wound of entrance was higher than the wound of exit, and the spongy-bone-deflection theory was 'unthinkable.' 'The Court had spoken unanimously,' and to CJ, that settles the matter -- even though none of the pardoned, freed soldiers has ever admitted responsibility.

one_paragraph_summary: A professor-reader asked Panganiban three questions about the ad interim appointment of George Garcia as Comelec chair: can it withstand constitutional scrutiny; should he have declined given his many clients with pending Comelec matters; and can Saidamen Pangarungan and Aimee Torrefranca-Neri be returned to the Comelec? CJ begins with Article IX-C, Section 1, paragraph 2 of the Constitution: presidential appointment with Commission on Appointments consent for a seven-year term, no reappointment, replacement appointments only for the unexpired predecessor's term, no temporary or acting capacity. Ad interim appointments, per settled jurisprudence, are permanent in nature (term fixed by law until the next adjournment of Congress); in February 2022, Pangarungan was named ad interim chair and Garcia and Neri ad interim commissioners -- all contributing to the peaceful and orderly 2022 elections -- but the CA bypassed them and their appointments lapsed at adjournment. Garcia was then given a second ad interim appointment, this time as chair. Funa v. COA (April 24, 2012) allows a commissioner who resigns with less than seven years served to be promoted to chair for the unexpired portion of the departing chair's term -- provided the vacancy arose from death, resignation, disability, or removal by impeachment -- because a promotional appointment (unlike a same-position reappointment) is not constitutionally barred. Although Garcia did not resign and the vacancy did not arise from one of the four enumerated triggers, CJ argues CA inaction can be considered 'in pari materia' with them, allowing Garcia to validly serve as chair for the unexpired portion, capped at seven aggregate years. Neri cannot be reappointed commissioner (express constitutional bar) and the chair is now occupied; Pangarungan cannot return as chair (no reappointment to the same post) but could be a commissioner if appointed and accepting. As to Garcia's many former clients including the President, senators, representatives, governors, and mayors -- inhibition is neither novel nor unethical; former Solicitors General promoted to the Supreme Court inhibit too. The obligation, however, extends beyond formal inhibition to 'desisting from influencing in any manner the remaining decision-makers.'

one_paragraph_summary: Continuing from his previous Monday column on the three June 2022 Scotus 6-3 decisions (abortion, religious worship, right to bear arms), Panganiban turns to the second and third rulings and contrasts US with Philippine treatment of these rights. He argues that the 1987 Philippine Constitution safeguards religious worship more expansively than the US First Amendment: Article III Section 5 includes both the establishment and free-exercise clauses but goes beyond them by guaranteeing 'free exercise and enjoyment of religious profession and worship, without discrimination or preference' and prohibiting any 'religious test... for the exercise of civil or political rights.' Across three Philippine charters (1987, 1973, 1935), the Preamble has always invoked Almighty God or Divine Providence -- unlike the US Constitution, though the US Congress adopted 'In God We Trust' as currency motto. He recounts the SC's 2001 Centennial Prayer for the Courts (preserved verbatim) recited at every court session and the bolder extension in In Re: Valenzuela (March 7, 2017, SC en banc, one dissent) permitting Catholic Masses and other religious rituals in Halls of Justice -- neither violates separation of church and state because that doctrine requires only 'benevolent neutrality' in the 'competition... amongst different religious denominations,' meaning the government cannot fund a basilica, promote one dogma, pay clergy salaries, or impose a religious work prerequisite. He offers his signature paradox: 'the Philippines is theist, not atheist, not even agnostic. In fact, it is monotheist; it worships one God. At bottom, while there is separation of church and state, there is no separation of the state from God.' On the American right to keep and bear arms -- anchored in the Second Amendment ('A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear arms, shall not be infringed') and born of the 1775-1783 independence struggle -- he diagnoses doctrinal evolution: Scotus conservatives have progressively enlarged its coverage from the 'ancient militia' to all American citizens via the Fourteenth Amendment's due-process and equal-protection clauses, making it 'difficult [for states] to regulate and control gun ownership' despite recent US shootings. The Philippine Constitution grants no similar right, and Congress has passed stringent gun-ownership laws -- a deliberate constitutional-statutory contrast.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the three landmark June 2022 Scotus 6-3 decisions through which the six conservatives ('textualists' or 'originalists') 'flexed their super muscles and asserted their absolute supremacy in construing the US Constitution': Dobbs v. Jackson (June 24, Alito) abolishing the right to abortion; Kennedy v. Bremerton (June 27, Gorsuch) protecting a government employee's personal religious observance from government reprisal; and New York v. Bruen (June 23, Thomas) strengthening the right to keep and bear arms in public for self-defense. He sketches the philosophical map: conservatives believe in originalism (interpret Constitution by framers' original intent) and textualism (interpret laws by the words used, battle cry 'Verba legis'), while liberals/progressives believe in a 'living Constitution' that 'grows with time, solves the vagaries of the present, and anticipates the needs of the future,' relying on intent over words. For about 100 years the Scotus was roughly even; the last two decades saw a fragile 5-4 conservative edge often flipped by Justice Anthony Kennedy or CJ John Roberts. Trump's three appointments (Gorsuch 2017, Kavanaugh 2018, and Amy Coney Barrett 2020 after Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg's September 18, 2020 death -- Barrett was a self-confessed follower and former law clerk of the late conservative leader Antonin Scalia) produced a 'commanding 6-3 majority.' CJ preserves the full lineage: conservatives CJ Roberts (Bush Jr. 2005), Thomas (Bush Sr. 1991), Alito (Bush Jr. 2006), Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, Barrett; liberals Breyer (Clinton 1994), Sotomayor and Kagan (Obama 2009 and 2010). He notes: 'Though much vilified, he was able to name three Scotus justices. In this sense, his legacy is a conservative Scotus that changed, and will continue to change, the constitutional landscape in the US.' He devotes the remaining space to Dobbs, which completely reversed Roe v. Wade (January 22, 1973, 7-2, Harry Blackmun) -- Roe had extracted a right to privacy 'by judicial fiat' from the due-process clause ('nor shall any state deprive any person of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law'), and was narrowed but not overturned by Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992), Gonzales v. Carhart (2007), Whole Woman's Health (2016), and June Medical Services (2020). Dobbs now holds that 'The Constitution does not confer a right to abortion,' though federal or state legislatures may enact such laws; the Scotus 'roared' that 'Roe was egregiously wrong... Without any grounding in the constitutional text, history or precedent, Roe imposed on the entire country a detailed set of rules for pregnancy divided into trimesters.' Philippine doctrine is unambiguous in the opposite direction: Imbong v. Ochoa (April 8, 2014, 14-1) ruled that 'life begins at fertilization, not at implantation' -- and CJ concludes, 'in my humble opinion, abortion can be committed as early as fertilization because life begins at fertilization.'

one_paragraph_summary: When TV journalists pressed incoming BIR Commissioner Lilia Guillermo on how she would address the Marcos estate-tax liability -- allegedly ballooned to over P203 billion from the P23 billion originally assessed -- she 'answered prudently' that she needed to see 'correct data' before committing, and famously said she would ask President-elect BBM, 'P'wede ba maging role model kayo? (Can you be a role model?)' -- going viral on June 23. Panganiban argues the 'correct data' are already publicly knowable from the Supreme Court e-library and the relevant Court of Appeals decision. The undisputed factual record: Marcos died September 29, 1989 in Honolulu; on June 27, 1990, the BIR created a Special Tax Audit Team to investigate the Marcoses and 'family, associates and cronies'; the investigation found the Marcoses failed to file written notice of death, an estate tax return (ETR), and income tax returns (ITRs) for 1982-1986 -- 'all in violation of the National Internal Revenue Code (NIRC).' On July 26, 1991, BIR issued deficiency assessments (over P23B estate tax; smaller ITR deficiencies for the spouses and BBM personally), served at the Marcoses' San Juan address (1991), BBM's House of Representatives office (1992), and via the late Dean Antonio Coronel as estate lawyer (Mrs. Marcos invited to a conference 'to no avail'). The assessments were never administratively protested within the 30-day NIRC window -- and thus lapsed into finality. In 1993, BIR issued notices of levy on Marcos real properties; on July 5, 1993, a public auction was held but 'there being no bidder, the lots were declared forfeited in favor of the government.' BBM sued in the CA on June 25, 1993, lost, and (as administrator of his father's estate, with Mrs. Marcos) elevated to the SC. In Marcos II v. Court of Appeals (June 5, 1997, Second Division, ponente Justo P. Torres Jr., concurred in unanimously by Justices Florenz D. Regalado, Flerida Ruth P. Romero, Reynato S. Puno, and Vicente V. Mendoza), the SC dismissed the appeal, holding that BIR assessments 'are presumed correct and made in good faith,' that 'the taxpayer has the duty of proving otherwise,' and characterizing BBM's course of action as reflecting 'his disregard or even repugnance of the established institutions for governance in the scheme of a well-ordered society.' Notably, the petitioner was named 'Ferdinand R. Marcos II' -- not 'Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr.' -- in the title and textual content of the decision. CJ closes with a catalog of factual questions for the BIR: how much has been collected from the levy and auction? How much remains? How was the P23 billion computed? How did it balloon to P203 billion? What other estate properties remain? What collection actions will BIR undertake? Is BIR open to a compromise on the balloon or the original assessment? 'Let's await BIR's answers.'

one_paragraph_summary: Justice Secretary (and incoming Solicitor General) Menardo I. Guevarra correctly noted that the Philippine National Police has no legal authority to ban rallies and demonstrations planned for President-elect BBM's June 30 swearing-in at the National Museum -- though he added the constitutional caveat that the peaceful-assembly right is 'subject to reasonable regulations to maintain peace and order, including the requirement to obtain a prior permit.' Panganiban affirms the primacy of the right and enumerates the open doctrinal questions (who, where, when, how long, what kind of permit, foreigners, public vs private property), then turns to Bayan Muna v. Executive Secretary Ermita (April 25, 2006) -- penned by 'the erudite Justice Adolfo S. Azcuna' and concurred in unanimously by colleagues including then-CJ Panganiban himself -- as the governing precedent. The decision condemned the Arroyo-era 'Calibrated Preemptive Response' (CPR) policy announced in a Malacañang press release of September 21, 2005 ('CPR will now be enforced, in lieu of maximum tolerance... Unlawful mass actions will be dispersed') and struck it down as having 'no place in our legal firmament... a darkness that shrouds freedom' that 'merely confuses our people and is used by some police agents to justify abuses.' At the same time it upheld Batas Pambansa Blg. 880 (the Public Assembly Act of 1985) as constitutional -- 'it does not curtail or unduly restrict freedoms; it merely regulates the use of public places as to the time, place and manner of assemblies. Far from being insidious, maximum tolerance is for the benefit of rallyists, not the government.' Mayoral permit-issuance authority was valid because subject to the 'clear and present danger' standard. The Court grounded the policy in CJ Panganiban's own prior addresses (which the decision quoted): 'in cases involving liberty, the scales of justice should weigh heavily against the government and in favor of the poor, the oppressed, the marginalized, the dispossessed and the weak. Indeed, laws and actions that restrict fundamental rights come to the courts with a heavy presumption against their validity. These laws and actions are subjected to heightened scrutiny.' The decision 'goes even one step further' by imposing a 30-day deadline on local governments to designate specific freedom parks per BP 880 Section 15 -- and if no such parks are identified within that period, 'all public parks and plazas of the municipality or city concerned shall in effect be deemed freedom parks; no prior permit of whatever kind shall be required to hold an assembly therein. The only requirement will be written notices to the police and the mayor's office to allow proper coordination and orderly activities.'

one_paragraph_summary: Why do all Philippine candidates -- winners and losers -- have to file with the Commission on Elections their Statements of Contributions and Expenses (Soce) within 30 days of Election Day (June 8, 2022 for the May 9 vote)? Panganiban's 'obvious IMHO' four-reason answer: for good governance, to find out whether expenses fell within statutory limits, what they specifically funded, who the donors were and their motives, and whether donors and candidates could truly afford the alleged amounts. RA 7166 Section 13 (passed 1991) sets aggregate expenditure limits at P10 per registered voter for president and VP (about P675 million given 67.5 million 2022 voters), P3 for senators and party-list reps, and P5 for candidates without party support. Three decades later, those limits remain unchanged though expenses 'may have ballooned 10 times,' producing 'faithful (even if sometimes incredible) compliance with the archaic law.' Beyond aggregate caps, OEC (BP Blg. 881) Section 102 itemizes the permissible expense categories -- travel, compensation of campaigners, telegraph/telephone tolls, stationery and printing, watchers, headquarters rent and maintenance, rallies, ads in mainstream media, counsel, voter-list copying, sample-ballot printing -- and creates a trackable-vs-untrackable asymmetry that candidates exploit: 'they simply ignore expenses that could not be easily tracked like cash given to local candidates and to their grassroots leaders, or for political rallies and contributions in kind.' Donors and suppliers (under OEC Section 99) must also file under-oath reports with Comelec -- designed to enable double-checking -- though 'many times, the large donors of the winners use their huge donations as badges to access government largesse.' The Corporation Code, 'unknown to many,' bars ALL corporations from political donations or partisan activity. OEC Section 95 then bars contributions from eight specific categories: (a) financial institutions, (b) public-utility/natural-resource operators, (c) government suppliers/contractors, (d) franchise/incentive holders, (e) borrowers of more than P100,000, (f) educational institutions with public-fund grants, (g) Civil Service and AFP officials/employees, and (h) foreigners. While 'laudable,' these transparency and accountability requirements have 'sadly become useless mountains of paperwork that have not reined in political expenses and corruption of voters.' CJ closes with reform proposals: revise the antiquated laws 'to keep up with the Internet Age,' move backward the 90-day (national) and 45-day (local) reporting windows to capture spending that begins 'a year or two ahead of Election Day,' and impose US-style per-donor caps of around P10,000 'to avoid huge political debts.'

one_paragraph_summary: After the Commission on Appointments bypassed President Duterte's ad-interim appointments to the leadership of the three constitutional commissions -- Comelec (chair Saidamen Pangarungan, commissioners George Garcia and Aimee Torrefranca-Neri), COA (chair Rizalina Justol), CSC (chair Karlo Nograles) -- and 115 AFP officers, with the stated reason 'to give President-elect Ferdinand Bongbong Marcos Jr. a free hand in selecting his own officials,' Panganiban explains the constitutional mechanics and their consequences. Article IX places the three independent commissions under 7-year terms 'without reappointment'; vacancies in their leadership arose from February 2 onward, prompting Duterte's recess ad-interim appointments. Under Article VII Section 16, ad-interim appointments are 'effective only until after disapproval by the [CA] or until the next adjournment of the Congress' -- so all the appointments automatically ended at midnight on June 4 when Congress adjourned (the CA adjourned June 1). The CA is 'a political, not a judicial, body' of 12 senators and 12 representatives with the Senate president as ex-officio chair; its decisions cannot be judicially reviewed except -- 'in my humble opinion' -- 'for grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction.' Importantly, all official acts and opinions rendered during the ad-interim terms remain valid and legal; the appointments themselves are 'deemed by law to be permanent, not temporary' (so they could not have been removed by Duterte during the term, and would have been removable only by impeachment if confirmed); compensations and perks received are legal; retirement benefits possible. The 'orphaned offices' may be filled by remaining commissioners temporarily -- as the four remaining Comelec members did by electing Commissioner Socorro Inting as acting Comelec chair. Duterte cannot re-appoint them ad-interim because Article VII Section 15 bars appointments 'two months immediately before the next presidential election and up to the end of his term, except temporary appointments to executive positions when continued vacancies therein will prejudice public service or endanger public safety' -- and the three independent commissions are NOT 'executive positions.' Brilliantes v. Yorac (December 18, 1990) independently bars 'acting' appointments to the Comelec, with the same reasoning applying to COA and CSC. CJ closes with two appreciations: former commissioner George Garcia's no-regrets disposition -- happily returning to non-partisan election-law practice and teaching (he had been counsel for BBM in his protest vs Robredo and for Sen. Migz Zubiri vs Koko Pimentel) -- and a congratulation to incoming Senate president Sen. Juan Miguel 'Migz' Zubiri as 'a consensus builder, an honest public servant, and a gentleman of the old school,' vindicated by his August 3, 2011 voluntary resignation 'without admitting any fault and with [his] vehement denial of the alleged electoral fraud hurled against (him),' which paved the way for Koko Pimentel and was rewarded by his electoral wins in 2016 and 2022.

one_paragraph_summary: Responding to President Duterte's 'Talk to the People' appeal for his successor 'to abolish the party-list system,' Panganiban diagnoses the party-list system as 'a mongrel without any historical, political, or social anchor in our country' -- borrowed from European parliaments and grafted onto a US-style presidential framework, conceived as an 'experiment' to give 'the marginalized and underrepresented a better chance to be lawmakers.' The Constitution allocates 20% of total representatives to party-list reps and dedicates half of those seats (for three consecutive terms after ratification) to the marginalized, but left the rest to Congress, which passed RA 7941 (the Party-list System Act) imposing a 2% threshold. CJ then traces his own two ponencias: Veterans v. Comelec (October 6, 2000) upheld the 2% threshold and ruled the 20% allocation 'directory, not mandatory'; Ang Bagong Bayani v. Comelec (June 26, 2001) limited eligibility to parties and nominees 'who belong to the marginalized and underrepresented sectors,' with the Court holding that 'The law crafted to address the peculiar disadvantages of the Payatas hovel dwellers cannot be appropriated by the mansion owners of Forbes Park.' These were unanimously reiterated in Partido ng Manggagawa v. Comelec (March 15, 2006) and Cibac v. Comelec (April 13, 2007), and extended to exclude major parties already represented in district polls. The decisions also called on Congress to enact clarifying legislation -- but 'Sadly, Congress did not heed the Court.' Meanwhile, advocates of 'verba legis' and 'dura lex sed lex' accused the Court (and CJ in particular) of 'sacrificing the letter of the law in favor of the intent of the framers.' After CJ's retirement, the Court reversed course: Banat v. Comelec (April 21, 2009) voided the 2% bar, and Atong Paglaum v. Comelec (April 2, 2013) ruled that party-list candidates and nominees need not belong to the marginalized and underrepresented -- 'thereby opening the party-list to everyone.' Consequences: 'the dynasts, the tradpols, the rich, and the powerful invaded the system, misused it to circumvent the three-term constitutional limit, and misrepresented the lowly and the weak'; the House now funds 63 party-list solons (20% of total) with 'pork-barrel-like insertions and reinventions.' CJ proposes three solutions: (1) amend the party-list law -- but the May 17 Inquirer editorial observed that 'party-list representatives [and their allies] who have gamed the system can hardly be expected to initiate any change'; (2) amend the Constitution via a constitutional convention (not a constituent assembly of incumbent Congress) -- but the Inquirer called this 'a cure worse than the disease' because it would let 'the wicked' overhaul better parts of the Charter; (3) have the Supreme Court overturn Banat and Atong Paglaum 'by simply reinstating its first two decisions, via a proper petition filed by the proper parties' -- the path CJ implicitly prefers.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with the Family Code Article 40 puzzle -- whether an accused can be acquitted of bigamy without a prior judicial declaration of the first marriage's nullity -- and reports that the Supreme Court answered YES en banc in Pulido v. People (July 27, 2021), penned by Justice Hernando with three separate concurring opinions, using the chicken-and-egg facts of Luisito (a 16-year-old who married his 22-year-old teacher Nora in 1983, then Rowena in 1995, was convicted of bigamy in 2009, and saw the second marriage independently declared void shortly after). The judicial declaration is now required only 'for purposes of remarriage' and for civil-rights determinations (heirship, legitimacy, estates, property regimes). The column then pivots to Psychological Incapacity, tracing its doctrinal arc from Santos v. CA (1995) -- which adopted the canonical characteristics of gravity, juridical antecedence, and incurability -- through Republic v. Molina (1997), whose guidelines were sourced from amicus Archbishop Oscar V. Cruz of the Church's National Appellate Matrimonial Tribunal, to Tan-Andal v. Andal (May 11, 2021), Justice Leonen's unanimous ponencia (with nine separate concurring opinions) that denounced Santos and Molina as 'restrictive, rigid, and intrusive on our rights to liberty, autonomy, and human dignity' and eliminated the expert-evidence requirement. one_paragraph_summary: In the second installment of his two-part deep dive into Calleja v. Executive Secretary (Dec. 7, 2021, released Feb. 15, 2022), Panganiban turns from Justice Carandang's 235-page ponencia (with 560 footnotes) to Chief Justice Alexander G. Gesmundo's 'masterfully-crafted and delightful to read' 199-page separate opinion (with 762 footnotes, 202 more than the ponencia), which firmly upholds the Anti-Terrorism Act's constitutionality in contrast to the ponencia's libertarian leanings. Gesmundo, advocating that 'we should utilize all possible kinds of legally available measures and approaches -- pre-emptive, preventive, proactive, remedial, and rehabilitative' against terrorism without 'overzealous legalism, imaginative speculation, or very narrow perspectives,' joined six other justices in voting to admit only four of 37 petitions and 'DISMISS OUTRIGHT' the remaining 33, then dismissed the four admitted petitions 'for lack of merit' using strict scrutiny without overbreadth/vagueness. With Justice Marquez, he argued that the ATA penalizes only overt acts including 'speech integral to criminal conduct,' and that as-applied challenges don't foreclose the use of vagueness/overbreadth as tools of scrutiny. Though outvoted in many places, Gesmundo prevailed in two: a 9-6 vote upholding Section 10's last paragraph on membership in proscribed or 'organized for the purpose of engaging in terrorism' organizations (where CJ Panganiban agrees with him against the ponente's vagueness finding), and an 8-7 vote upholding Section 25's 'third mode of designation' empowering the ATC to designate on probable cause and the AMLC to freeze accounts. AT BOTTOM, with only Section 4's PROVISO and Section 25 paragraph 2's 'second mode of designation' struck, 'the government, IMHO, emerged the clear winner' -- 'a little scathed' but intact -- and the petitioners' 71-page Joint Motion for Reconsideration 'pales in comparison' with the exhaustive opinions; their best path forward, with due respect, is to 'wage low-intensity, libertarian as-applied challenges' as the ATA is enforced.

one_paragraph_summary: The Supreme Court issued temporary restraining orders against Comelec -- under chair George Erwin Garcia (GEG) -- stopping the implementation of Resolution No. 11044-A dated Sept 4, 2024, which had disqualified Mandaue City Mayor Jonas C. Cortes, former Albay Governor Noel E. Rosal, and Cebu City Mayor Michael L. Rama from 2025 candidacy based on Ombudsman dismissals carrying perpetual disqualification -- for the very simple reason that those OMB dismissals are still under appeal and therefore not final. GEG himself conceded the TRO was 'timely' ('Sana nga, pero hindi ginawa eh' -- we should have done it but did not) and rightly added that all ~100 such non-final disqualified candidates should be on the May 2025 ballot. The SC's Oct 22, 2024 press release affirming Rosal's disqualification, CJ clarifies via Romulo Macalintal's email, refers to Rosal's 2022 gubernatorial candidacy (won with an overwhelming 230,735-vote majority against then-Gov Al Francis Bichara), while the current TRO is for 2025. After CJ's Oct 14 column expressed hope that GEG would redeem himself, the multiple new TROs have made that hope 'evaporate' -- but CJ refuses to knock him out because GEG faces the more crucial job of assuring HOPE (Honest, Orderly, Peaceful) elections in 2025. Beyond the usual 3Gs (guns, goons, gold), two new challenges loom: artificial intelligence and the untested Miru System. GEG has required all candidates to register their online identities by Dec 13 (only 62 of over 44,000 had complied as of Oct 23) and forcefully threatened disqualification or 1-6 years' imprisonment for endorsements via unregistered social-media outlets -- 'let's see whether the Comelec and GEG have the gravitas and the guts to enforce his big talk.' Comelec's posting of party-list nominees' names for public scrutiny may be challenged, but the SC is likely to uphold Comelec's constitutional authority to assure HOPE. The Nov 5 US presidential election will give the Comelec and the Filipino public an experiential view of how AI can be used, abused, and misused; the Miru System remains untested locally, and CJ leaves its investigation, monitoring, and critique to PPCRV and Namfrel.

one_paragraph_summary: The House quad committee's legislative inquiry on extrajudicial killings, illegal drugs, and POGOs allegedly during Rodrigo Duterte's presidency has become a televised spectacle -- more popular on YouTube and social media than blockbuster telenovelas like GMA's 'Pulang Araw' and ABS-CBN's 'Lavender Fields' (which CJ admits he watches on Netflix every evening except Wednesdays and Thursdays) -- and more lurid and shocking, except that the gruesome murders, police connivance, jarring violence, and kitschy sex are real. Executive Secretary Lucas Bersamin tersely declared 'The Philippines will not return to the ICC,' and quad comm lead co-chair Robert 'Ace' Barbers refused to turn over any records. Solicitor General Menardo I. Guevarra, in a text to CJ, advised the quad comm to refer its findings instead to the DOJ, NBI, or Ombudsman -- and stressed that the government has no legal duty to cooperate with the ICC because Khan was authorized to investigate only in 2021, more than two years after the March 2019 effectivity of the Philippine withdrawal from the Rome Statute, though the ICC prosecutor cannot be stopped from interviewing consenting individuals. Senator Ronald 'Bato' dela Rosa -- stung by what he called unprecedented breaches of interparliamentary courtesy -- announced a parallel Senate inquiry, but Senate President Chiz Escudero limited Senate-break investigations to the blue ribbon committee. Former Senator Leila de Lima is preparing a criminal complaint against Dela Rosa for allegedly coercing quad comm resource person Kerwin Espinosa into linking her to the illegal drug trade, causing her detention for almost seven years before her acquittal. Ironically, ICC supporters 'may be clapping too soon' -- because under Rome Statute Article 17 complementarity, the ICC will act only if the state is unwilling or unable genuinely to prosecute, so the very domestic referrals, prosecutions, and trials may negate ICC jurisdiction. Combined with the two-year-post-withdrawal cap, this means 'ICC has lost its jurisdiction' -- though, in fairness, CJ notes that Bensouda announced her preliminary examination on Feb 8, 2018, and refers readers to his Aug 7, 2023 column for details.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban draws the doctrinal line between two remedies for removing a candidate from an electoral race: disqualification under Section 12 of the Omnibus Election Code and cancellation (denial of due course) of the Certificate of Candidacy under Sections 78 and 74. The pending DQ cases against Bongbong Marcos turn on whether his Court of Appeals conviction for failure to file Income Tax Returns for 1982-1985 is a crime involving moral turpitude under Section 12. He cites Republic v. Marcos II (Aug. 4, 2009, SC Third Division), which distinguished three ITR-related violations -- false return, fraudulent return with intent to evade tax (both involving moral turpitude), and mere failure to file (which does not) -- and held that BBM's offense was not one of moral turpitude. He notes critics may rage against this 'cryptic' ratio but until reversed, modified, or downgraded to obiter by the en banc, it binds the Comelec. The remedies have very different consequences: a cancelled COC is void from the beginning, the votes cast for the erstwhile candidate are stray, and no substitution is allowed; a disqualified candidate, by contrast, can be substituted by another bearing the same surname and political party -- opening the door for a sister such as Imee Marcos to inherit the slot. Panganiban therefore counsels partisans that, if their real goal is to take the Marcoses out of the presidential race, pursuit of COC cancellation (Comelec en banc, then the Supreme Court) is the more potent path than disqualification -- which only rotates the Marcos name on the ballot.

Te. Item 11 of BBM's COC ('I am eligible') and Item 22 ('No' to having been found liable for an offense carrying perpetual disqualification) are, the petitioners say, false material representations. Te counters the Second Division by arguing that the CA need not have expressly imposed the perpetual-disqualification penalty because it is 'deemed written into the conviction' by operation of law; that BBM remained a public officer on March 18, 1986 (the 1985 ITR filing deadline) under the Provisional Constitution, since Castor Raval was sworn in only as 'acting governor' of Ilocos Norte; and that abandonment of office is itself a felony -- 'exceedingly ludicrous' to invoke on the offender's behalf. Te further argues that COC Item 22 asks only whether the offense 'carries with it' the accessory penalty (it does) and that BBM, having appealed his conviction to the CA and SC (later withdrawn) and served as Vice Governor, Governor, Member of Congress, and Senator, is presumed to know the consequences -- 'Ignorantia juris neminem excusat.' Jalosjos v. Comelec (Oct. 9, 2012) authorizes cancellation even when past eligibility had been upheld. Panganiban records his own conviction with the petitioners' core claims, while noting one point ('This is debatable') where reasonable minds may diverge -- leaving the doctrinal-strategic posture pointed sharply at the Comelec en banc and ultimately the Supreme Court.

Kho Jr. concurring via Separate Opinion, and Rey E. Bulay) dismissing the petition to cancel Bongbong Marcos's Certificate of Candidacy. He agrees with the Resolution that false material representation is the exclusive ground for COC cancellation under Section 78 of the OEC, and that adding moral-turpitude and mandatory-imprisonment-over-18-months grounds confuses cancellation with disqualification under Section 12. He concurs that BBM's COC statements were 'material' but parts ways with the Division's rejection of falsity: he disagrees that BBM 'ceased to be a public officer' on March 18, 1986 (the ITR filing deadline for tax year 1985) and flags as 'debatable' the third-element holding that BBM lacked deliberate intent to mislead since the CA Decision did not categorically apprise him of perpetual ineligibility. Marcos (Aug. 4, 2009) for the proposition that failure to file ITR is not a crime of moral turpitude, and its observation that the petitioners 'deliberately misquoted' the original tax law, which gave courts discretion between fine, imprisonment, or both -- mandatory imprisonment only entered with the Jan. 1, 1988 amendment. Out of deference to Theodore O. Te's anticipated motion for reconsideration the next day, Panganiban refrains from full commentary -- modeling the kind of measured doctrinal summary he says lay readers need.

one_paragraph_summary: Picking up from last Sunday's column, Panganiban examines two crucial documents that have surfaced in the Bongbong Marcos COC cancellation case. The petitioners produced a 'Certification' from Rowena Sto. Tomas-Bacud, OIC of Branch 105 of the RTC-QC, stating there is no record on file of compliance with the October 31, 1997 Court of Appeals decision -- purporting to prove BB is still perpetually disqualified. BB's supporters produced a Land Bank 'Official Receipt' dated December 27, 2001 in the name of 'MARCOS JR. FERDINAND' showing P67,137.27 in LEASE RENTAL, INSTALLMENT, INTEREST, and PRINCIPAL -- purporting to trigger the five-year prescriptive period under Section 12 of the Omnibus Election Code. Panganiban's humble opinion: the Bacud Certification is from the wrong officer, because final CA decisions are enforced by the courts of origin and the proper certifier for fines (which become part of the Judiciary Development Fund) is Gregorio C. Tallud, clerk of court of the entire RTC-QC station made up of 57 branches; the petitioners' argument 'could gain cogency' if they secured a similar certification from him. The Land Bank Official Receipt, on the other hand, is facially vague: it makes no reference to the CA disposition, which has two parts -- (a) deficiency income taxes payable to the BIR with legal-rate interest, and (b) fines of P2,000 per charge for 1982-1984 ITRs and P30,000 for 1985 ITR with surcharges -- and BB's supporters must explain how P67,137.27 is to be applied between them, and why the fines were paid to Land Bank rather than to the RTC-QC station clerk of court. He closes by felicitating Justice Jose Midas P. Marquez on his recent SC promotion after a record 13 JBC nominations, noting that this brings to six the number of SC justices from Ateneo de Manila (plus a seventh from Ateneo de Davao), easily besting UP's traditional 'top producer' status with three (San Beda also three; UST and UE one each). Marquez -- 'homegrown' to the Court since 1991 as apprentice, then law clerk to Senior Justice Bellosillo where CJ met him in 1995, then court administrator from January 2010 -- will serve until his 70th birthday on February 16, 2036.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban strips the Bongbong Marcos COC case to its two main issues: did BB commit false material representations in his certificate of candidacy, and did his CA conviction involve moral turpitude? The Petition asserts YES on three grounds -- BB falsely represented eligibility, falsely denied past liability carrying perpetual disqualification, and was convicted of a moral-turpitude crime. Estelito P. Mendoza's Answer counters NO on all three. To strengthen Mendoza's pleading, the Federal Party filed an Answer-in-Intervention alleging that BB has paid the fine and deficiency income taxes from the October 31, 1997 CA decision. Citing OEC Sections 12, 74, and 78 plus Ty-Delgado v. HRET (January 26, 2016) -- which held that a candidate barred by final judgment who declares eligibility in his COC 'clearly makes a false material representation,' and that libel is a moral-turpitude crime -- Panganiban observes that at first sight the law favors the Petition because the CA conviction indirectly imposed perpetual disqualification. However, the accessory penalty under PD 1994 took effect only January 1, 1986 and cannot be retroactively applied to BB's 1982-1984 ITRs; it covers only the 1985 ITR (due April 15, 1986). If the Federal Party's allegation of payment is true, timely, and adequate, BB may be saved because Section 12 says the disqualification 'is deemed removed five years from service of the sentence,' and payment of the fine IS the service of the sentence -- meaning he did not make a false material representation. What remains is the moral-turpitude argument, which Section 12 would disqualify him on independently. In sum: if petitioners can show (i) BB's conviction involves moral turpitude AND the five-year prescription does not embrace moral turpitude, OR (ii) the alleged payment is false, inadequate, or ill-timed, the COC should be cancelled; if not, BB should continue his quest. He urges the Comelec Second Division to resolve this speedily through Memoranda -- reviewable by MR to the en banc and ultimately by the Supreme Court -- and closes by wondering how President Duterte views the case given Prof. Dante Gatmaytan's observation that Duterte is the only post-Edsa president who has never lost in the Court.

one_paragraph_summary: Following up on his November 14 column 'The Bongbong-Sara juggernaut,' Panganiban opens his Bongbong Marcos COC analytical series with a doctrinal map. He summarizes lawyer Theodore O. Te's 52-page petition before the Comelec, which seeks to cancel Bongbong's October 6, 2021 COC on two grounds of false material representation: paragraph 11 declared 'eligible for the office I seek to be elected to' despite the Court of Appeals' final judgment of October 31, 1997 (affirming the RTC judgments of July 27, 1995) convicting BB for failure to file ITRs for 1982-1985, and Item 22 denied past liability for an offense carrying the accessory penalty of perpetual disqualification. The petition argues that PD 1994 (effective January 1, 1986; now Section 253 of the 1997 NIRC) attaches the accessory penalty regardless of the CA's 'inexplicable' omission of the RTC-imposed imprisonment penalty. Bongbong's counter-pleading -- Estelito P. Mendoza's seven-page Answer -- simply posits that the Petition is 'bereft of any specific allegation of a material representation,' asks the Comelec to take judicial notice of BB's prior elective positions and presidential qualifications, denies any CA finding of moral turpitude, and prays for face-to-face argument. Panganiban defers the merits analysis but makes one crucial doctrinal point: if Bongbong's COC is cancelled, 'HE CANNOT BE SUBSTITUTED' because cancellation legally means that the COC never existed -- his votes will not be counted, and the next highest vote-getter would be declared winner. Contrary to media reports and 'analysts,' the petition seeks cancellation under Section 78 (false material representation), NOT disqualification under Section 68 (which is available only for election offenses defined by the OEC and DOES allow substitution by another candidate from the same party bearing the same surname). He closes with two teaser questions for future columns: what would happen if Bongbong's COC were cancelled AFTER Congress declares him president-elect, or AFTER he takes his oath as President?

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban discusses Disini v. Republic (June 15, 2021; full decision released only recently), the 58-page unanimous Supreme Court decision ably penned by Justice Ramon Paul L. Hernando directing Herminio T. Disini to pay the Republic P1 billion in temperate damages plus P1 million in exemplary damages plus 6% legal interest from finality -- recognizing that Disini, a close associate of Ferdinand E. Marcos, acquired ill-gotten wealth via substantial commissions from Westinghouse and Burns & Roe on the 1976 Bataan Nuclear Power Plant project that 'remains inoperable to this day.' However, the Republic's lawyers failed to prove the actual receipt by Disini of the alleged P50.5 billion in commissions because they presented only a photocopy (instead of the original) of a private document listing them, violating the Best Evidence Rule -- prompting CJ's recurring lament: 'Oh, when will our government lawyers learn how to prove their claims via the elementary rules of evidence that ordinary law students know by heart?' Disini's death on June 3, 2014 during the pendency of the case did not foreclose recovery because his heir Herminio Angel E. Disini Jr. was substituted in the suit. Panganiban then turns to the personal history of the case: in PCGG v. Desierto (February 10, 2003) he himself wrote the ponencia directing the Ombudsman to file criminal charges against Disini in the Sandiganbayan, and his March 27, 2011 Inquirer column lamenting that no one had been convicted for the BNPP fiasco triggered a libel complaint against him and then-Inquirer editor in chief Letty Magsanoc -- dismissed by City Prosecutor Feliciano Aspi, reversed without notice by his temporary successor on reconsideration, and ultimately re-dismissed by the Court of Appeals, the DOJ, and Makati's new permanent prosecutor, all holding 'no libel was committed by my citing correctly and quoting verbatim portions of a Supreme Court decision.' While defending himself, CJ vowed to seek 'justice, even revenge' criminally, civilly, administratively, and ethically against the temporary prosecutor, his cohorts, the RTC judge, and Disini himself -- but on reflection and prayer was led to Romans 12:19 ('Beloved, do not look for revenge but leave room for the wrath... Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord') and set aside the vow, enjoying peace of mind in the Lord's promise. 'To God be the glory always!'

Comelec (October 5, 2021), in which the Supreme Court reminded the Commission on Elections that 'election cases must be resolved speedily.' He argues that the Comelec should accordingly deny due course, after summary due process, to the COCs of nuisance candidates whose only purpose is to reserve the position for more 'winnable' substitutes -- because once their COCs are declared null and void for mocking the electoral process, nuisance bets cannot be substituted (their names will no longer appear on the automated ballots and the substitutes cannot be voted into office). He endorses former Comelec commissioner Rene Sarmiento (also a former 1986 ConCom member and former PPCRV chair), whose letter to the Inquirer (October 18) reminded readers that the Comelec may motu proprio cancel a nuisance COC without a verified petition -- historical practice worth restoring. Comelec (October 6, 2000) already pointed to the Constitution's textual ambiguities and pleaded with Congress to revise the Party-list Law to enforce the framers' marginalized-and-underrepresented intent -- but no bill has passed because non-marginalized party-list representatives form a formidable opposing bloc, and Atong Paglaum v. Comelec (April 2, 2013) 'bastardized' the system by opening it to 'the ultra-rich, the overrepresented, the dynasties, and the powerful' (with a 20% House-budget increase and 20% 'pork-like' insertions denounced by Sen. Ping Lacson). one_paragraph_summary: Written as a Q&A column following reader response to his October 3 piece, CJ Panganiban walks through six election-law puzzles around candidate substitution under Section 77 of the Omnibus Election Code and Comelec Resolution No. 10717. He concedes that Romulo Macalintal's proposal to declare 'reservation' filers as nuisance candidates is 'sensible, even patriotic,' but argues the ouster process is itself uncertainty-generating; his own fix is more radical -- abolish substitution for any reason except the death of the candidate. He clarifies that withdrawing presidential or vice-presidential bets can lawfully substitute for senatorial vacancies provided the same political party (or a properly sworn-in member of a new party) makes the nomination, and that this mechanism can produce 'a realignment of political forces.' Post-Nov-15 substitution is permitted only for death or final disqualification and only when the substitute bears the same surname, so the votes flow through to the substitute. The column closes with the most consequential stance: under the 'with due respect' formula CJ openly departs from Quinto v. Comelec (Feb. 22, 2010), arguing that the Court's 'substantial distinctions' rationale for treating elective and appointive officials differently is insufficient, and that all candidates -- elective or appointive -- should be deemed resigned upon filing their COCs to prevent incumbents from leveraging office for campaign advantage. The piece functions as both clarifier of working election law for 2022 aspirants and quiet manifesto for an unrealized electoral reform.

Comelec (Feb. 22, 2010), penned by CJ Puno, which upheld RA 9369 §13 by a 10-5 vote -- but the column's most piercing passage is its forensic explanation of how this came to reverse, less than three months later, the original 8-6 Nachura ruling of Dec. 1, 2009: J Chico-Nazario retired, JJ Brion and Del Castillo flipped sides, and the two new appointees (JJ Perez and Mendoza) voted with CJ Puno. The substitution discussion then walks through the operative mechanics -- withdrawing, disqualified, or deceased candidates of registered political parties or coalitions may be substituted up to Nov. 15 with ballot reprint, while substitution for death or final disqualification under the same-surname rule extends to midday on May 9, 2022. Independent candidates are excluded from the regime entirely. The column closes with politician-specific illustrations -- Pacquiao would be 'jobless after June 30, 2022' if he loses a non-reelection bid; Grace Poe enjoys an unexpired-term safety net; Lacson and Sotto are termed out -- and the title's quiet thesis: in practice, the Oct. 8 deadline is functionally extended to Nov. 15 for candidates of registered political parties.

The doctrinal centerpiece is Republic v. Sandiganbayan (July 15, 2003), penned by then-J Corona and concurred in by CJ Davide, CJ Panganiban himself, and ten others, which forfeited over $658 million in Marcos foundations and -- crucially -- fixed the couple's 'only known lawful income' from 1965 to 1985 at roughly $304,000, the benchmark below which subsequent forfeitures have cascaded. Republic (April 25, 2012, Arelma S.A. $3.37M under a Sereno ponencia, Aquino III presidency), Estate of Marcos v. Republic (Jan. 18, 2017, Malacañang jewelry, Sereno again, Duterte presidency), and the foundational PCGG v. Pena (April 12, 1988, Teehankee CJ, Corazon Aquino presidency) which supplied the recurring language of 'well-entrenched plundering regime' and 'organized pillage.' Albano (Leonen, 2018) dismissed for 'apathetic prosecution,' and the 2019 Benedicto/Tantoco/Gimenez series dismissed for procedural failures -- but pointedly notes that these are prosecutorial collapses, not merits-based exonerations. The piece reads as both anniversary commemoration and pre-election doctrinal reminder: the answer in the case law has been 'a clear and unqualified Yes.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban observes that the Supreme Court has effectively 'decided not to decide' the quo warranto (QW) issue hanging above the heads of its justices -- the 'sword of Damocles' from Republic v. Sereno (May 18, 2018). He recounts that in three earlier columns (April 18, May 16, June 6), he had urged the Court to use the Justice Edgardo L. delos Santos QW occasion to reverse that doctrine, restore the constitutional shroud of judicial independence, and re-establish impeachment as the exclusive removal process. The Court did treat the second certiorari petition as a motion for reconsideration of the dismissed QW petition (which had been thrown out on procedural errors -- wrong remedy, failure to pay docket fees, etc.) -- but then dismissed the MR on the same procedural grounds via 'short shrift,' placing more value on procedural technicalities than on a substantive resolution of judicial-independence. He maps three future pathways through which the issue can return for merits resolution: (1) a fresh, procedurally-correct QW petition against an incumbent SC member; (2) a petition by Maria Lourdes P. A. Sereno to be restored on the ground that Republic v. Sereno was void ab initio for grave abuse of discretion and unconstitutionality; or (3) congressional legislation repealing the QW doctrine on the theory that jurisprudence forms part of the law of the land subject to legislative repeal, followed by judicial review of the new statute. He contrasts QW (majority vote of justices, no trial-type hearing) with the much more careful and rigorous constitutional impeachment process (House Committee on Justice majority for form/substance; House plenary one-third for articles; Senate trial; two-thirds Senate concurrence -- at least 16 of 24 senators -- for conviction), and reminds readers that Sereno was ousted 8-6 (with the CJ inhibited) on grounds the Constitution does not mention as a basis for justice removal. He closes by accepting the Court's verdict in the spirit of internal Court culture: 'we can agree to disagree without being disagreeable, and we can differ without being difficult.'
