one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban argues that the South China Sea and East China Sea have become the playgrounds of a dangerous superpower game of chicken that could ignite a nuclear holocaust. He catalogues US FONOPs (aircraft carriers, warships, submarines, warplanes) -- justified by the Arbitral Award even though the US is neither a party nor a UNCLOS signatory -- and allied deployments (UK's HMS Queen Elizabeth, described by Ambassador Daniel Pruce as 'the largest and most powerful surface vessel in the Royal Navy's history,' plus Australia, Japan, Germany, France). The US sells arms and sends officials to Taiwan in silent disregard of its 'one-China policy' partly because Taiwan hosts the world's biggest and most advanced chip maker whose products feed AI, high-value computing, and military software. China responds with its own armada, jets close enough for pilots to see each other's digital helmets, drones defying Taiwan's ADIZ, periodic sorties near the Senkakus (Diaoyu) -- which the US treats as integral Japanese territory under the US-Japan Mutual Defense Treaty backed by the Seventh Fleet in Tokyo Bay -- and pressure points around the ~30,000 US troops in South Korea. For the Philippines, the operative question is what to do if China builds a Spratly-style military base on Scarborough Shoal, and whether the US will help the way it has helped Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. He recalls the past Scarborough confrontation: the US tried to mediate mutual withdrawal, the Philippines complied, China did not and tightened its grip, and the US did nothing. Yet, despite internal factional dissension narrated in Justice Antonio T. Carpio's last column, former President Noynoy Aquino chose the rule of law and won the Arbitral Award -- which ruled Scarborough a 'high-tide elevation' with a 12-nautical-mile territorial sea boring a hole in the PH 200-NM EEZ -- an award now even the US invokes. He closes that the real question is whether it is in US national interest to defend the shoal and risk nuclear war (it has retreated from chicken before), and that 'in my humble opinion, regardless of what the US (or China) will do to uphold its national interests, we should pursue our own destiny and continue to lean on the rule of law' so the Philippines is not 'just another expendable pawn in the old power game of chess of the international masters.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban demystifies the public reactions to outgoing ICC Chief Prosecutor Fatou Bensouda's last-day (June 14) announcement that she had requested judicial authorization to proceed with an investigation into the Philippine 'war on drugs.' He summarizes the competing framings: Presidential Spokesperson Harry Roque calling it 'legally erroneous... politically motivated... no big deal' based on 'mere hearsay'; the DFA calling it 'deeply regrettable' and 'a blatant violation of the principle of complementarity,' insisting that Justice Secretary Menardo Guevarra's interagency panel be allowed to finish; Edre Olalia of NUPL celebrating 'justice somewhere, somehow'; and Agnes Callamard of Amnesty International calling it 'a moment of hope.' To demystify, he runs a brief on the Rome Statute and the ICC: the RS as the founding treaty (with China, Russia, and the US not signatories); the ICC as the only permanent international court empowered to try and convict individuals, not states, through four organs (Presidency under Piotr Hofmanski; Pre-Trial, Trial, and Appeals Chambers; Office of the Prosecutor; Registry); ICC cases initiated only by the OP via member-state referral, UN Security Council referral, or Pre-Trial Chamber authorization following a preliminary examination; and individual liability requiring a listed crime, a territorial/national-of-member-state nexus, member-state status at the relevant time, and no complementarity. Complementarity means the ICC acts only where the state is 'unwilling or unable to prosecute' through legitimate local investigations. He notes that Bensouda's careful date-selection (July 1, 2016 - March 16, 2019, and even as early as November 1, 2011) was designed to satisfy every requirement except complementarity -- which is exactly why the DFA insists on Guevarra's panel finishing its work. Presidential immunity is a temporary 'unable to prosecute' factor only during the term (the Estrada plunder conviction post-term is the precedent). He concludes that politics aside and legality upfront, Bensouda's bravado is a major leap, but more hurdles abound: progression to charges, arrest, trial, and possible conviction will depend on (1) the PTC's assessment; (2) new Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan's (an eminent Queen's Counsel) follow-through; (3) how the PNP, DoJ, and OMB demonstrate the 'legitimacy' and 'genuineness' of their work; and (4) how the Supreme Court and the entire judiciary uphold their independence and integrity.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban argues that effective adversary analysis requires knowing what drives the other side -- and asks why China is so aggressive in owning almost the entire South China Sea (SCS) and the East China Sea (ECS). He grounds his answer in four drivers. First, civilizational pride: China claims a long history rivaling Egypt's pharaohs and Greece's Olympic gods, set against a 'harrowing decay' from the mid-1800s to mid-1900s of one-sided treaties and cruel treatment of nationals, with the cultural premise that 'to the traditional Chinese, losing face is worse than losing life.' Second, contested historical title: the WWII Japanese occupation of Paracels and Spratlys; the 1945 Cairo and Potsdam Declarations; Kuomintang acceptance of the Japanese surrender; Mao's 1950 takeover of the Paracels and Spratlys after driving the KMT to Taiwan; North Vietnam's wartime relinquishment of claims (later reversed by united Vietnam); the 1974 expulsion of South Vietnam from Shanhu Island; and the current feature-occupation count (Vietnam ~29, Philippines 11, China 7, Malaysia 6, Taiwan 2, Brunei 1). The Arbitral Award gives the Philippines sovereign rights over the maritime domain but not territorial sovereignty over land features and their territorial seas, while China, Vietnam, and others anchor their claims in history, discovery, occupation, control, and treaty-cession. Third, geographic constriction: China is the world's second-largest economy (soon largest), with the biggest standing military and a nuclear arsenal, lunar astronauts and a space station, yet is surrounded by unfriendly neighbors -- Russia on the north, former Soviet republics on the west, India and Vietnam on the south, and Japan, South Korea, and the 'renegade province' of Taiwan (all three with US defense agreements) on the east -- with only North Korea, Cambodia, and Mongolia as dependable neighbors; while the US enjoys friendly neighbors (Canada north, Mexico south) and two ocean buffers plus Caribbean control. China can expand only through the ECS and SCS, which serve as economic lifelines (sea lanes), security buffers (first line of defense against US military adventurism), and offensive corridors (passageway for nuclear submarines to the Pacific and Indian Oceans). Fourth, perceived US-led encirclement: the US Indo-Pacific pivot abetted by the Asia Reassurance Initiative Act of 2018, the Quad alliance with Australia, Japan, and India, and NATO's recent communique (under Biden's prodding) labeling China a 'systemic challenge.' Finally, domestic-political constraint: Chinese leadership has taught its 1.3 billion people that the SCS is cherished inheritance, and any leader who fails to occupy and protect it will surely be 'purged, dethroned, and banished for treason and disloyalty' -- making concession politically impossible for Beijing.

XI Sec. 3-5. The override mechanism in Sec. 3-3 (one-third House vote) is unlikely given (1) the 44-0 unanimity (including Majority Leader Martin Romualdez, a relative of endorser Rep. Angelo Marcos Barba), (2) Speaker Lord Allan Velasco's open backing, and (3) unanimous justices' support, as Leonen himself acknowledged. The second is Justice Edgardo L. Delos Santos's early retirement (approved by the Court 'due to his current state of health,' effective June 30, 2021 -- a year before his 70th birthday) and the new certiorari petition basically alleging the same grounds as the dismissed Feb 18 QW petition (which fell on procedural errors -- wrong remedy, failure to pay docket fees, etc.), now on the en banc agenda. He restates the constitutional case -- impeachment requires one-third House vote, Senate trial, and two-thirds Senate concurrence (at least 16 of 24 senators); the Constitution makes no mention, not even a hint, of QW as a removal method, nor of lack of SALNs as a removal ground; yet the Court ousted CJ Sereno via QW for SALN failure prior to incumbency on a simple 8-of-14 majority (CJ inhibited) and without Senate-style trial. one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban clarifies the legal status of Julian Felipe Reef (English: Whitsun; Chinese: Niu'e Jiao) under UNCLOS, the July 12, 2016 Arbitral Award, and Philippine domestic law. Coastal states are granted sovereign rights -- not sovereignty -- over the marine resources within a 200-NM Exclusive Economic Zone, akin to a lease's right to fruits without Torrens title to the land. Whitsun, a Low-Tide Elevation lying 175 NM west of Bataraza, Palawan, sits within the PH EEZ. However, Whitsun is alleged to be within the 12-NM territorial sea of McKennan Reef, judged a High-Tide Elevation by AA Paragraph 1203-B-3-b -- and under UNCLOS the TS of an HTE is an enclave superior to the overlapping EEZ. China asserts sovereignty over McKennan, Hughes, and most of the South China Sea under its nine-dash line (rejected by the AA), justifying its swarm of vessels and fishing ban; Vietnam asserts sovereignty over Sin Cowe Island (judged an HTE by Paragraph 1203-B-3-f) and claims Whitsun lies within its TS. Manila's claim rests on Marcos's 1978 PD 1596 declaring the Kalayaan Island Group part of Philippine territory -- but the PD predates Manila's 1982 UNCLOS signing and is deemed modified by UNCLOS and the AA, and Manila's victorious use of the AA for the EEZ estops it from denying unfavorable parts. CJ predicts China will not actually invoke the AA because doing so would concede the very authority that overturned its nine-dash claim. The right path, in his humble opinion, is a clear, united, and simultaneous recourse under the rule of law to the ICJ -- the body whose decisions are international law and are invariably implemented by the United Nations.

Sereno (May 18, 2018) QW decision, Panganiban restates his April 8 position: with the Court's new composition (seven of the eight QW majority have retired), it is time to restore the constitutional shroud that justices be removed only by impeachment, and only on the grounds clearly provided. DOTC) by invoking the transcendental-importance exemption from the 'paralysis of procedural niceties' -- the Court's independence is of the highest transcendental importance to the nation. CJ leaves the reversal question to the new Court but poses four 'just, ethical, and wise' questions for reflection: continuing to dangle the 'self-inflicted sword of Damocles' over incoming justices; the participation of justices who had testified at the House impeachment proceedings; the eight's acceptance of posts and benefits their own votes created; and Senior Justice Carpio's honorable decline of the CJ post created despite his dissent. 'Let us pause and reflect. And let history be the judge.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban catalogues the four 'Cs' shaping the administration's West Philippine Sea posture -- spokesperson Harry Roque's three (careful, calculated, calibrated) plus President Duterte's added 'courteous' from his May 3 televised address ('China remains to be our benefactor'). He contrasts these with Foreign Secretary Teddy Locsin's blunt tweet 'GET THE FUCK OUT' addressed to China -- likening Beijing to 'an ugly oaf forcing your attentions on a handsome guy' -- and the next-day apology after Roque's reminder that only the President may use cuss words in diplomacy. Locsin's pique, CJ suggests, came from 78 inadequately answered diplomatic protests since 2016 and the May 3 accusation that Chinese coast-guard vessels were 'shadowing, blocking, [conducting] dangerous maneuvers, and radio challenges' against the PCG. Defense Secretary Delfin Lorenzana was more calibrated ('We will defend what is rightfully ours without going to war') while dispatching the Navy's gray vessels to patrol the WPS, and the PCG shooed away seven Chinese militia vessels. CJ explains that under Senate v. Ermita (2006), the President and Cabinet enjoy executive privilege over state secrets -- making ambiguity sometimes the deliberate cover for long-term strategy: 'No permanent friends or permanent enemies, only permanent national interests.' What the four Cs are fighting for is UNCLOS as applied by the July 12, 2016 Arbitral Award -- but, candidly conceding the doctrinal reality (he chairs the Philippine National Group in the Permanent Court of Arbitration), CJ notes that arbitral awards are not parts of international law and not precedents for future arbitrations; they are binding only on the parties. China's refusal to recognize the AA -- on the ground that WPS issues involve LAND sovereignty falling only under ICJ jurisdiction -- has technical force. He reiterates his April 25 plea: accept China's challenge and let the ICJ decide. ICJ decisions are international law, have precedent value, and are invariably implemented by the UN -- and the great powers (US, Japan, France, Germany) all have sitting ICJ members, with the ICJ president himself an American.

one_paragraph_summary: The Supreme Court sitting as the Presidential Electoral Tribunal dismissed, 15-0, Bongbong Marcos's election protest against VP Leni Robredo 'for lack of merit' in a Feb 16, 2021 decision (released only the week before this column) ably written by Justice Marvic M.V.F. Leonen, with Romulo Macalintal leading Leni's defense and George Garcia leading Bongbong's team. The three causes were dismissed in turn: the first (alleging non-authentic Certificates of Canvass) thrown out at the Pre-Trial Conference of Aug 29, 2017; the second (revision and recount of 36,465 clustered precincts) failing because the recount in the three pilot provinces (Camarines Sur, Iloilo, Negros Oriental) actually grew Leni's lead from 263,473 to 278,566; and the third (annulment of results in Maguindanao, Lanao del Sur, and Basilan for terrorism, intimidation, and pre-shaded ballots in 2,756 precincts) junked because protestant 'utterly failed to allege that protestee instigated' the irregularities. Despite this legal defeat, Bongbong remains a viable, even strong, contender in 2022: Pulse Asia's Feb 22-Mar 3 face-to-face survey -- conducted AFTER public knowledge of the dismissal and for PRESIDENT not VP -- places him at 13%, second only to Sara Duterte (27%) and marginally ahead of Grace Poe, Isko Moreno, and Manny Pacquiao. Leni at 7% places only 6th, having 'apparently failed to take advantage of the political worth of her sweeping legal victory.' CJ predicts Bongbong will file an MR -- not because a 15-0 decision can be reversed but to strengthen his political stock. Five months from COC filing, CJ notes the Pulse Asia field misses Frank Drilon (brilliant, diligent, scandal-free, the most experienced public servant around), Mark Villar (DPWH secretary, Manny-and-Cynthia heir, Build-Build-Build credentials), Gwen Garcia (Cebu and 'One Cebu' regional bloc), and Win Gatchalian (undefeated; 'Kay SARA, WIN tayo'). Tony Carpio leads 1Sambayan's candidate search, not as candidate himself. CJ closes with a six-tandem speculative matrix for ongoing Pulse Asia/SWS testing -- administration, opposition, regional, populist, surprise, and competent-celebrity pairings.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban frames the West Philippine Sea dispute as a contest between two adages -- 'Might is right' (the rule of force) and 'Right is might' (the rule of law). By swarming the WPS with more than 200 militia and coast-guard vessels and prohibiting Philippine fishing in our own EEZ, China is restaging the very rule of force that Britain imposed on it through the Opium Wars, the Treaty of Nanking, and the Unequal Treaties of the mid-1800s -- making a hi-tech, militarily revitalized, and economically dominant China the 'new bully in Asia.' He had hoped the contemporary China would, with lessons learned, instead honor the 501-page July 12, 2016 Arbitral Award, which expressly recognized Manila's exclusive right to fish and develop the WPS under UNCLOS -- a treaty China signed and is therefore legally bound to obey. He notes the 'little ironic' inconsistency that great powers (US, Australia, France, UK) -- none of them parties to the arbitration, and the US not even a signatory to UNCLOS -- selectively invoke AA-favorable provisions for freedom-of-navigation operations; he wishes they would enforce the entire AA to show consistent adherence to 'Right is might.' He fairly states China's position: WPS issues involve land ownership and sovereignty, only the ICJ has jurisdiction; China steadfastly refused to participate in the PCA proceedings. China's discovery-since-time-immemorial claim was rejected by the AA. Au contraire, Justice Antonio T. Carpio and Prof. Jay Batongbacal show that Philippine ownership is documented by the 1734 Murillo-Velarde map, reinforced by the 1898 Treaty of Paris and 1900 Treaty of Washington under which Spain ceded the islands (including the Spratlys and Scarborough) to the US, which in turn ceded them to the Philippines. If the case is strong, Manila can now accept China's challenge and bring it to the ICJ; under the ICJ Charter, only states (not private individuals or organizations) may file. 'Might is right' vs 'Right is might.' Which will prevail?

one_paragraph_summary: Without ubiquitous headlines and TV cameras, CJ Alexander G. Gesmundo quietly took his oath of office on April 5, 2021 and began his 5-year-7-month term as primus inter pares of the SC and leader of the judiciary. Panganiban recalls 'prophesying' Gesmundo's ascent on Jan 6, 2006 -- as then-CJ inducting Gesmundo (whom he didn't yet know) as a Sandiganbayan justice and inviting him to sign his oath in the CJ's chair: 'Please sit down on my chair. One day you will occupy it.' He urges Gesmundo to this early craft a vision/mission statement; of all tasks, speedy justice (starting with the SC backlog) is the most urgent -- and the Court has already adopted a plan in its July 31, 2007 Resolution implementing the recommendations of the Committee on Zero Backlog I (which CJ Panganiban created Jan 26, 2006), needing only resolute implementation. Gesmundo is the third Ateneo Law alumnus (after Claudio Teehankee and Renato Corona) to ascend to the top post, an 'OSG thoroughbred' with SBN, Comelec, and PCGG secondments. Runner-up Ramon Paul L. Hernando, at 54 the youngest and 4th most senior, would have been the first 'homegrown' San Beda CJ (the President's alma mater) and 'I would have faded as the first and only imported chief of the Red Lions.' Senior-most incumbent Estela M. Perlas-Bernabe, 69 on May 14, was named by four presidents to the ascending steps of the judicial ladder (FVR MeTC 1996; Erap RTC 2000; GMA CA 2004; PNoy SC 2011) yet has given none of them any undue favor -- validating her JBC-interview self-description of being 'unpredictable... only when it comes to politically-sensitive cases.' Her catalog shows it: pro-Libingan-Marcos and pro-Mindanao-martial-law on one side; against the Sereno ouster, against the De Lima arrest, and disagreeing with Bersamin's 'main plunderer' doctrine in the GMA plunder ruling on the other. She can take comfort in joining the Honor Roll of revered seniors who did not become CJ -- J.B.L. Reyes, Ameurfina Herrera, Florenz Regalado, Florentino Feliciano, Teodoro Padilla, Antonio Carpio -- 'revered in history more than some chiefs.' CJ closes that Gesmundo is off to an auspicious start, with Hernando and Bernabe (and all his colleagues) gallantly accepting him without rancor and with Bernabe herself administering his oath -- but beyond this felicity, the people expect an independent Court and a judiciary invigorated by speed, integrity, wisdom, and independence.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban responds to reader questions on his previous Sunday's 'Five game-changing SC decisions' column. Q1 -- the Javellana v. Executive Secretary 6-4 majority comprised Makalintal, Castro, Barredo, Makasiar, Antonio, and Esguerra against the dissent of CJ Concepcion (the ponente), Zaldivar, Fernando, and Teehankee, with Concepcion's dispositive: 'there is no further judicial obstacle to the new Constitution being considered in force and effect.' Q2 -- Ocampo v. Enriquez's allowance of the Marcos LNMB interment was based on the Peralta ponencia's four grounds (political question, no locus standi, failure to exhaust administrative remedies, non-observance of the hierarchy of courts) plus a substantive finding of no constitutional/local/international-human-rights contravention; concurring were JJ Velasco, Leonardo-De Castro, Brion, Bersamin, Del Castillo, Perez, Mendoza, Perlas-Bernabe; dissenting were CJ Sereno and JJ Carpio, Leonen, Jardeleza, Caguioa, with J Reyes no part. Q3 -- the Lambino MR was denied with finality on Nov 21, 2006 by the same 8-7 vote, with Carpio as ponente joined by Panganiban himself, Santiago, Gutierrez, Austria-Martinez, Carpio Morales, Callejo, and Azcuna, against the dissent of Puno joined by Quisumbing, Corona, Tinga, Chico-Nazario, Garcia, and Velasco. Q4 -- on party-list abolition, Duterte's wish and Sotto's bill (empowering Comelec to refuse or cancel a party-list's registration) remain unprogressed; Macalintal's reverse-the-decisions proposal was returned by CJ to Macalintal himself ('as a seasoned election lawyer, could initiate the solution'). Q5 -- to CJ's knowledge no petition has been filed to reinstate Sereno or grant her retirement benefits, but former Ombudsman Conchita Carpio Morales texted that Sereno should be considered a 'de facto Justice to be granted the same benefits given to Corona.' Q6 -- many readers asked why only five cases: Simeon Marcelo emailed at length on the December 2001 coco-levy public-funds decision (of which CJ was the ponente; ~P70 billion eventually collected into trust, yet small coconut farmers still not benefiting); retired CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr. inquired about Estrada's constructive-resignation ouster; others asked about the pork-barrel rulings. CJ's short answer: insufficient space to cover them all in one column. 'But, thank you, readers for your questions. In the future, I hope to answer them, directly or indirectly.'

one_paragraph_summary: Following his previous Sunday's catalog of five US cases, Panganiban inventories five Philippine SC decisions that game-changed our constitutional, political, and social landscape -- for better or for worse. First, the 'notorious' Javellana v. Executive Secretary (March 31, 1973, 6-4) upheld the ratification of the 1973 Constitution by raising of hands -- a departure from the paper-ballot plebiscitary tradition designed to protect voters from 'guns, goons and gold' -- and effectively validated Marcos's martial law and PD-issuance powers. Second, Republic v. Sandiganbayan (July 15, 2003, 14-0-1) forfeited $657M+ in Swiss deposits as Marcos ill-gotten wealth on the doctrine that whatever exceeded the Marcos couple's $304K legal income was ill-gotten; followed by Yuchengco (Jan 20, 2006 and Aug 6, 2006), Marcos v. Republic (April 25, 2012), and a cumulative P200B+ PCGG recovery. Yet in Ocampo v. Enriquez (Nov 8, 2016, 9-5-1), the Court allowed the LNMB interment of Marcos 'with ceremonies befitting a national hero' -- a 'strange turnaround' -- and concluded that 'there are certain things that are better left for history--not this Court--to adjudge.' With due respect, CJ disagrees: 'This issue will not rest; the Marcos saga is not over' given the political ascent of the Marcos scions. Third, Lambino v. Comelec (Oct 25, 2006, 8-7) correctly ruled the parliamentary-system people's initiative a 'grand deception' and 'gigantic fraud,' scuttling GMA's possible prime-ministership path -- but it reversed Santiago v. Comelec (March 19, 1997), which had held the implementing law 'insufficient,' and so foreclosed FVR's re-election ('arguably our best president since the 1987 Charter took effect'). Fourth, Bagong Bayani v. Comelec (June 26, 2001, 9-5-1) and Veterans Federation v. Comelec (Oct 6, 2000, 15-0) correctly reserved the Filipino-style party-list system for the marginalized and held the 20% House quota non-mandatory -- until Atong Paglaum (April 2, 2013) and Banat (April 21, 2009) reversed both, letting dynasties invade, veteran politicians circumvent the 3-term limit, the rich own the system, and the powerful misrepresent the lowly. Fifth, Republic v. Sereno (May 18, 2018, 8-6) ousted the chief justice via quo warranto for unfiled SALNs as a UP professor; Justice Leonen's dissent called it a 'legal abomination,' and the unanimous Court turning down a request for Leonen's own SALNs (which could have led to QW against him) hints at sympathetic re-evaluation. 'The betting now is whether the Court would reverse itself and reinstate Sereno, or, at least, grant her retirement benefits similar to what it did recently for CJ Renato C. Corona.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban frames Donald Trump's continuing populist rabble-rousing -- anti-black, anti-Asian, anti-migrant, anti-establishment -- as a jeopardy to two centuries of US libertarian struggle for social, racial, gender, and political equality, and traces that struggle chronologically through five Scotus decisions. First, Dred Scott v. Sandford (March 6, 1857, 7-2) held that black slaves born in the US were not 'citizens' but mere possessions -- a 'hideous decision' that the 13th and 14th Amendments had to overturn, and that 'damned forever' CJ Roger Taney and his six concurring justices. Second, Brown v. Board of Education (May 17, 1954, unanimous) reversed Plessy v. Ferguson (May 18, 1896, 7-1) by holding that the separate-but-equal doctrine in race-segregated schools violated the 14th-Amendment equal-protection guarantee -- separate facilities being inherently unequal. Third, Miranda v. Arizona (June 13, 1966) required police to advise crime suspects of their rights upon arrest -- and 'we did better': the 1987 PH Constitution embedded Miranda rights directly in the Bill of Rights, where violation can lead to acquittal even of the factually guilty. Fourth, Roe v. Wade (Jan 22, 1973, 7-2) read the abortion-privacy right out of the due-process clause; repeated challenges since 1973 narrowed it through Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992), Gonzales v. Carhart (2007), Whole Woman's Health v. Hellerstedt (2016), and June Medical Services v. Russo (2020) but did not overturn it. Fifth, Bush v. Gore (Dec 12, 2000, 5-4) reversed a Florida SC manual-recount order, awarding Florida's 25 electoral votes and the presidency to George W. Bush by a very narrow 271-267 margin though Al Gore won the popular vote. The 5-4 was heavily criticized for partisanship -- Bush's brother Jeb was the Florida governor, Katherine Harris was both election-body head and co-chair of Bush's FL campaign, and the five GOP-appointed justices voted solidly for Bush against the four Democrat-appointed for Gore. In stark contrast to Trump's no-concession stance, Gore conceded -- and when CJ met him in 2006 during his PH visit, Gore explained: 'Mr. Chief Justice, there is something greater than me... The Supreme Court has spoken. Though I disagreed with the decision, I had the duty to respect and obey it...' Pressed by CJ on whether he would have invaded Iraq and Afghanistan, Gore was quick: 'No, never. That was my campaign promise' -- confirming that 'the US would not have spent trillions of dollars in those wars which you could have used to reduce extreme poverty in the world including ours.' Gore chuckled: 'Yes, yes, including the Philippines.' CJ concludes that Trump's populism -- aided by his three conservative Scotus appointees who have tilted the balance to 6-3 -- endangers this libertarian struggle for equality. 'Next Sunday: Five contentious PH cases.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban offers a generic framework for evaluating any Cha-cha proposal -- the four 'Ws': What, Why, When, Who. He recalls the long inventory of failed attempts: Ramos and Arroyo's people's-initiative bids were shot down by the Supreme Court; Estrada's Preparatory Commission on Constitutional Reforms chaired by retired CJ Andres Narvasa produced a report that 'remained unacted upon'; Duterte's Consultative Commission chaired by retired CJ Reynato Puno drafted a sweeping 'Bayanihan Constitution' that 'to this day remains unused.' On What: the present surgical amendments are (1) abolishing or modifying the party-list -- itself 'an experiment' from parliamentary regimes uncomfortably grafted onto a presidential system, with vague text and a Supreme Court that has flipped between restrictive and permissive interpretations -- and (2) lifting the nationalistic provisions, which does not actually remove the restrictions but only authorizes Congress to vary the allowable foreign-equity percentages. On Why: Duterte cites terrorism and rebel misuse of the party-list; Speaker Velasco cites foreign investment, jobs, and poverty alleviation; Finance Secretary Dominguez argues for opening the economy in all areas except land ownership. On When: PCCI's Ambassador Yujuico is right that pandemic-recovery bills should come first, and Congress has very little time before COC filing in October and the May 9, 2022 polls, with the Constitution requiring a 60-to-90-day plebiscite window. On Who: con-ass by sitting legislators -- especially those running for re-election -- raises the trust hazard (term extensions, self-benefiting insertions), and the SC will likely have to resolve the joint-vs-separate-vote question, adding more delay. CJ concludes that Cha-cha's 34-year failure is fundamentally a trust problem, and offers a four-bullet conditional: if lawmakers ride on the President's 91% trust rating, stick to the two proposals only, vote separately, and concurrently pass CREATE and other urgent recovery bills, they could finally overcome the four 'Ws' this time.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban addresses whether presidents can pardon themselves -- categorically 'No' in the Philippines (where pardon requires conviction by final judgment), but unsettled in the United States (where presidents may pardon even before charges are filed, except in impeachment cases). He surveys famous US pardons: Ford's broad September 8, 1974 grant to Nixon covering all federal crimes 'committed or may have been committed' (paired with the US-jurisprudence rule that acceptance of a pardon implies confession of guilt); Carter's January 21, 1977 pardon of Vietnam draft dodgers; Clinton's January 2000 clemency to his actor-brother Roger; and Trump's recent pardons led by Michael Flynn, with reported inclinations to extend clemency to lawyers who tried to overturn Biden's victory. On the self-pardon question proper, a verba legis reading disfavors Trump: the word 'grant' in the US Constitution 'assumes one person giving and another person receiving,' implying giver and receiver cannot be the same. Even if Trump succeeds in self-pardoning (or extracts a Ford-style pardon from Biden), clemency would cover only federal offenses -- state AGs in New York, California, and other states are already preparing post-January 20 suits. CJ raises a possible workaround -- Trump taking leave from office before January 20 to let VP Pence, as acting president, grant absolute pardon -- but asks whether 'his more sedate vice president [will] participate in this caper which could damn them both in history.' In the Philippines, the categorical bar is reinforced by the Anti-Graft Law and Ethical Standards Law prohibiting officials from using office for private benefit; the only imaginable self-pardon scenario (a pre-incumbency conviction) would still run into these statutory barriers. He closes by recalling Risos-Vidal v. Comelec (January 21, 2015), in which the SC held that Arroyo's pardon of Estrada (post-plunder-conviction with reclusion perpetua, disqualification, and asset return) -- 'though hazily worded, was absolute' -- restored his civil-political rights and lifted his disqualification, enabling his successful mayoral run in Manila.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the procedural conundrums embedded in Larry Gadon's impeachment complaint against Justice Marvic M. V. F. Leonen -- filed (with the endorsement of Rep. Angelo Marcos Barba and on behalf of Edwin Cordevilla) after the Supreme Court unanimously rejected the prior SALN requests of Gadon and SolGen Jose C. Calida. (CJ limits himself to the SALN issue because Justice Antonio T. Carpio's December 10 column already debunked Gadon's other allegations on Leonen's alleged failure to decide cases on time.) Gadon intends to ask the House Committee on Justice to subpoena the SC clerk of court and the UP registrar for Leonen's SALNs from his 15 years as UP College of Law faculty before his SC appointment. The doctrinal trap: Republic v. Sereno (May 11, 2018, 8-6) ruled that QW is proper 'only when the subject act or omission was committed prior to or at the same time of the appointment,' while incumbency acts 'cannot be the subject of a quo warranto proceeding but of impeachment.' Since Leonen's alleged SALN omissions occurred before his SC appointment, the proper remedy is QW, not impeachment -- meaning Gadon may not be able to convince the House or Senate to subpoena, and even if a subpoena issues, the Court may halt compliance. A symmetrical conundrum afflicts Leonen: he dissented in Sereno, calling QW for sitting justices 'a legal abomination... [that] should be overturned in the near future.' He must now choose among asking dismissal based on the very Sereno doctrine he attacked, abandoning his dissent, or accepting that despite his dissent all parties remain bound by Sereno. CJ also notes that the SC can halt invalid impeachments: Francisco v. House of Representatives (November 10, 2003) 'barred' the second impeachment complaint against CJ Davide, and the House complied 'even if reluctantly.' Comparative context: Corona was Senate-ousted (2012) based on incumbency-period SALN omissions (impeachment-proper), with the SALNs obtained during trial by Sen. Drilon persuading clerk Enriqueta Vidal to surrender them and Sen. one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban updates readers on the June 29, 2016 election protest filed by former senator Bongbong Marcos against VP Leni Robredo in the Presidential Electoral Tribunal (PET). The protest raised three causes of action: first, that the Certificates of Canvass were 'not authentic' (dismissed August 29, 2017 for 'judicial economy'); second, massive frauds and irregularities in 25 provinces and 5 cities (~39,000 precincts), with three pilot provinces (Camarines Sur, Iloilo, Negros Oriental) selected to 'best exemplify' the anomalies; and third, annulment of all votes in Maguindanao, Lanao del Sur, and Basilan on grounds of terrorism, intimidation, harassment, and pre-shading. The Second Cause was effectively resolved by Justice Caguioa's report after the August 14, 2019 recount: Leni's lead 'even widened from 263,473 to 278,506' (by 15,033 more votes), and he recommended outright dismissal under PET Rule 65. But on October 15, 2019, the PET (11-2) deferred dismissal and required the parties to comment 'consistent with due process of law' -- and a new raffle on October 29 moved the member-in-charge role from Caguioa to Justice Leonen. The Third Cause requires evidence aliunde (not recount), and is subject to the Abayon v. HRET (May 3, 2016) three-condition test: (1) more than 50% of votes cast illegally, (2) impossibility of differentiating lawful from unlawful ballots, and (3) clear, convincing, and strong evidence that the protestee is accountable for the illegal acts -- conditions 'extremely difficult to prove,' with the protest not even alleging Leni's accountability. Bongbong claims that if the three provinces are annulled, the original 477,985-vs-169,160 result there flips to a 306,825 net advantage for him, overcoming Leni's 278,503 lead by 'a very narrow 30,332 votes.' Granting arguendo that the three conditions are proven, Leni's counter-protest involving 18 provinces (8,000 precincts) would still require the same recount route -- making the case academic by May 9, 2022. CJ's preferred pathway: because due process has already been observed (the parties submitted comments per the PET's October 19, 2019 resolution), the PET can apply Rule 65 and dismiss because, 'taking all circumstances into account, the protestant... failed to make out his case.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban responds to the Inquirer's October 29 editorial decrying the 'egregious failure of the justice system that led to the death of baby River Nasino after she was separated from her mother,' detainee Reina Mae Nasino. He sets out a five-step bail framework: (1) Constitution Article III Section 13 -- everyone has a right to bail except those charged with capital offenses when evidence of guilt is strong; (2) Rules of Court Section 7 Rule 114 repeats the rule negatively; (3) the strength-of-evidence question is a factual matter committed to the sound discretion of the trial court, exercised only after a four-step procedure (hearing, prosecution notice, accused's chance to counter, summary determination); (4) the intent is to assure appearance and minimize flight risk; and (5) Enrile v. Sandiganbayan (August 18, 2015) added 'special humanitarian grounds' -- citing advanced age (91), ill health (uncontrolled hypertension, arrhythmia, coronary calcification, ACOS exacerbations), 'social and political standing,' and 'immediate surrender to the authorities.' CJ believes the Supreme Court correctly remanded the matter to the trial court but, 'with due respect, it took too unreasonably long to act' -- the petition was filed in April, the Court acted only on July 28, and announced its action only on September 10. It should have dismissed the facially defective petition outright (per CJ's September 27, 2020 column 'Dismissed on short shrift'). Part of the fault lies with Nasino's lawyers, who went to the SC too soon rather than first insisting on a trial-court bail hearing. Post-remand, the trial court was 'unduly strict' -- it 'mindlessly denied the petition for hospital stay and needlessly separated the baby from her detained mother, to quote again the Inquirer editorial, to tragic results.' Strictly speaking, the Enrile humanitarian grounds do not extend to Nasino because those referred to the accused while Nasino's referred to the baby, not the mother. Nonetheless, CJ endorses the liberal approach proposed by Naga RTC Judge Soliman M. Santos Jr. in an email: bail could have been granted by analogy under Article 3 of the 1989 Convention on the Rights of the Child ('the best interests of the child shall be a primary consideration'), operationalized via the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006's definition of 'best interest of the child' as 'the totality of circumstances and conditions which are most congenial to the survival, protection and feelings of security of the child and most encouraging to the child's physical, psychological and emotional development.' He closes with a hope that 'the Supreme Court and/or Congress will respond to the public outrage by studying and possibly codifying new rules and/or new laws to protect the unborn and the young children of detained mothers.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains why Filipinos are keenly watching the 'rushed, marathon' US Senate hearings to confirm Trump's nomination of US Court of Appeals Judge Amy Coney Barrett, 48, as the ninth Scotus justice. He provides background on the philosophical divide: conservatives hew to 'originalism' (Constitution by framers' original intent) and 'textualism' (laws by words used), while liberals embrace a 'living Constitution' that 'grows with time, solves the vagaries of the present, and anticipates the needs of the future' and relies on intent more than words. US judicial nominations are openly partisan -- Republican presidents pick conservatives, Democrats pick liberals, 'always a campaign issue.' For a century, the Court has been almost evenly divided 5-4; conservatives have held the slim edge for the last two decades, but Justice Anthony Kennedy (now retired) and CJ John Roberts have occasionally swung to enable liberal landmarks. The 5-4 conservative arrangement held until Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, 'a liberal icon,' died on September 18. Trump immediately nominated Barrett -- a 'self-confessed follower and former law clerk' of late conservative leader Justice Antonin Scalia -- to shift the Court to 6-3 conservative. Trump 'feels assured of reelection if not by the ballots, then by his wild claim, without any proof, that the Nov. 3 US presidential election would be fraudulent due to irregularities inherent in mailed ballots,' likely planning to replicate Bush v. Gore (December 12, 2000), in which Scotus 5-4 along the doctrinal divide rejected Florida's manual recount and validated George W. Bush. Scotus is relevant to PH for two reasons. Structurally, our close political, economic, and legal ties to the US matter, and Democrats are 'more sympathetic to us than the America-centric Republicans.' Decisionally, some Scotus rulings directly affect us -- Republic v. Pimentel (June 12, 2008) saw the conservative-dominated Court reject Filipino human-rights victims' bid to attach the $35 million Arelma deposit allegedly owned by the Marcoses at a NYC investment bank -- and others indirectly, like District of Columbia v. Heller (June 26, 2008), in which Scotus 5-4 upheld the American right to bear arms, settling 'a 217-year-old US controversy that reverberated here,' although PH SC in Chavez v. Romulo (June 9, 2004) 'did not find constitutional basis for the right to bear arms.' In a postscript, CJ mourns retired Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio-Herrera, who has 'passed to the Heavenly Kingdom.' Humble and soft-spoken, she was 'a brilliant fortress of competence, integrity, probity, and independence' in the SC and the founding chancellor of the Philippine Judicial Academy (PhilJa). She was CJ's bar examiner in commercial law in 1960; UP class valedictorian and bar topnotcher; could have been CJ had Cory Aquino not reorganized the Court post-EDSA. As CJ, Panganiban secured a P300 million grant from Japan and turned the check over to her on January 26, 2006 from Ambassador Ryuichiro Yamazaki -- funds she 'wisely used to build the PhilJa Center in Tagaytay where continuing education and training for judges are now held. An everlasting monument to honor a brilliant icon!'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reports the 'encouraging' institutional reactions to his prior two columns -- Oct. 4 on prosecutorial reform ('humbly proposed' guidelines to deter 'filing frivolous, reckless, malevolent, and politically-motivated charges') and Sept. 27 on SC short-shrifting facially baseless petitions ('differentiate shysters... from trustworthy lawyers'). On Oct. 4 itself, Compañero Ralph Jerome Salvador, chief of staff of CJ Diosdado M. Peralta, texted that the piece would be included on the agenda of the SC's Committee on the Revision of the Rules on Criminal Procedure, which CJ Peralta chairs. The next day, Justice Secretary Menardo I. Guevarra texted in code-switched Tagalog/English: 'Alam ninyo po, matagal na rin po naming pinag-uusapan ang issue na yan sa National Prosecution Service. You hit the nail right on its head. I intend to do further consultations... with the Supreme Court. Babalitaan ko po kayo.' Sandiganbayan Justice Maryann E. Corpus-Mañalac also texted that the suggested reforms would reduce court congestion and let magistrates focus on pending litigations. Naga RTC Judge Soliman M. Santos Jr. did 'one better' by quoting CJ's Oct. 4 column at length in his October 5, 2020 People v. Orcine decision acquitting an accused 'who had been detained without bail for nearly four years.' CJ hopes 'the huge chasm between probable cause and proof beyond reasonable doubt will soon be bridged and quality justice more speedily rendered.' Pivoting to the Sept. 27 column, he recalls his 'vision for the legal profession' from the back cover of his 2006 'Liberty and Prosperity' book: 'competent and ethical lawyers who are responsible, dependable, morally upright, and who courageously uphold truth and justice above everything else.' Compañero Romulo Macalintal embodies that vision: his guiding principle is 'to handle only meritorious cases,' a maxim he 'passed on to two of (his) children who... are also members of the bar.' In the late 1990s, a Metro Manila mayor who lost his reelection bid handed Macalintal a blank check as professional fee for an election protest; Macalintal honestly told him his case 'would not prosper' and returned the check. As GMA's lawyer he was offered Comelec chair and solicitor general but declined -- 'I did not have the management ability and experience at that time to handle these offices' -- and maintained 'a strict client-attorney relationship... Honesty is always the best policy.' The column closes with Macalintal v. Teh (October 16, 1997): after a judge fined Macalintal P100,000 for filing an inhibition motion alleging bias, Macalintal appealed and the SC ousted the judge and forfeited his retirement benefits for 'gross ignorance of the law.' Finding the penalty too harsh, Macalintal pleaded clemency for the judge over nine years, citing similar cases where respondents were merely suspended or fined; on January 31, 2005, the Court (with CJ already as CJ) granted clemency, allowing accrued leaves (but not full retirement), finding the judge 'sincerely repented for his transgression, reformed his ways, and renewed his life.' Macalintal recalls: 'I thought I would never meet the judge again. But one day, I received an invitation to attend his 75th birthday... We became good friends until his death some years back. I even became a principal wedding sponsor of one of (his) daughters.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban identifies and proposes a fix for the institutional chasm between 'probable cause' -- the abstruse standard prosecutors need to file criminal charges, defined by jurisprudence as 'a state of facts in the mind of the prosecutor as would lead a person of ordinary caution to believe, or entertain an honest or strong suspicion, that a thing is so' (giving 'almost blanket discretion to fiscals') -- and 'proof beyond reasonable doubt,' the much higher standard for conviction defined as the degree of proof producing 'moral certainty of the culpability of the accused.' This huge gap accounts for the poor prosecutor conviction rate, evidenced by SC en banc resolutions: on January 8, 2013, the Court noted '80% of the backlog in the first and second level courts involves criminal cases,' and on September 5, 2012, it cryptically observed 'about 40% of criminal cases are dismissed annually... due to mishandling.' The institutional costs are needless docket clogging, unnecessary detention of the poor who cannot post bail, and 'appalling congestion of our jails.' Worse, in capital offenses the accused is detained indefinitely without bail when evidence of guilt is deemed strong -- the 'internationally reverberating lament' of Sen. Leila De Lima, detained without bail for four years on a prohibited-drugs charge filed by DOJ prosecutors on probable cause, and the 'pitiful lament' of former President GMA, chased and arrested at NAIA 'ironically, and some say, with a dash of karma' under De Lima's own 'watch list orders' that 'defied a temporary restraining order of the Supreme Court,' then by RTC arrest and Ombudsman plunder charge -- all on probable cause -- before SC acquittal 'on the main ground that the prosecutors failed to prove the charges beyond reasonable doubt' after more than four years of detention in a hospital 'near where De Lima is now confined.' This 'revolving door of probable cause and proof beyond reasonable doubt must end,' and CJ believes Justice Secretary Menardo I. Guevarra can end it because he 'possesses sufficient gravitas, integrity, and independence to do it without partisanship, having served the immediate past -- and is still serving the present -- President of the Republic.' The mechanism: new DOJ guidelines with higher probable-cause thresholds barring filings 'dismissible on the plain ground that the information is wantonly insufficient and/or that the evidence is direly wanting' -- 'Why should they sue if they cannot secure the conviction of the accused?' (cross-referencing CJ's Nov. 23, 2014 column). Together with a reader-suggested sworn certification by prosecutors that (1) the allegations in the information are enough to constitute the crime charged, (2) the evidence on hand passes legal admissibility, and (3) the evidence is sufficient to convict despite defenses proffered during preliminary investigation or reasonably expected at trial. This sworn certification 'should deter the filing of frivolous, reckless, malevolent, and politically motivated charges' that clog dockets and deprive citizens of constitutional rights to life, liberty, or property without due process and equal protection of the laws.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban defends the Supreme Court's en banc outright dismissal of Taguiwalo v. Duque (Sept. 1, 2020) -- the petition for mandamus to compel the government to conduct COVID-19 mass testing -- against the 'brickbats' the dismissal provoked. Voting 13-1-1 without asking for respondent comment, the Court ruled that 'courts have no authority to issue writs of mandamus, no matter how dire the emergency, without a showing that an official of the executive branch failed to perform a mandatory, nondiscretionary duty.' CJ articulates the three independent doctrinal grounds: (1) under separation of powers, courts cannot order officials to perform jobs entailing 'discretion or judgment' -- while the judiciary can direct negligent officials to fulfill their duties, it 'cannot tell them HOW to fulfill them'; (2) mandamus is an extraordinary remedy that 'cannot be availed of when a plain and speedy relief is available,' and recourse to Executive Order No. 2, Series of 2016 was the plain, speedy, adequate remedy here; (3) petitioners failed to show exhaustion of administrative remedies. The Court was not discriminatory or biased: it has applied the same short-shrift principle elsewhere -- on Sept. 8 dismissing outright the petition to void the law renaming Manila International Airport as Ninoy Aquino International Airport on 'the same ground of facial inadequacy'; on Sept. 15 summarily denying Atty. Larry Gadon's Sept. 7, 2020 letter and the OSG's Sept. 11, 2020 letter requesting Justice Marvic M.V.F. Leonen's SALNs (1990-2011) 'to look into the possibility of initiating a quo warranto proceeding against Justice Leonen' (CJ promises a future column on the Ombudsman's new SALN-access guidelines). These summary dismissals follow the Court's own dictum in Gio-Samar v. DOTC (March 12, 2018) to reduce backlog by dismissing 'plainly undeserving' pleas or those violating the hierarchy of courts; they align with CJ Peralta's 10-point program (whose first item is 'Elimination of backlog in the Supreme Court'); and they parallel the US Supreme Court's filtering system that decides 'only a very limited number of truly meritorious cases.' Short shrift benefits all stakeholders: the Court (more time for crucial pending cases); the people (the 'justice delayed is justice denied' lament 'would eventually vanish'); the respondents (immediate enjoyment of victory without additional lawyers' fees); the petitioners themselves (timely opportunities for alternative remedies -- Congress, executive officials, ballot, peaceful assemblies -- since 'not all problems can be solved by the judiciary'); and the legal profession, because it 'differentiate[s] shysters who take advantage of the gullibility of their clients from the trustworthy lawyers who elevate only truly worthy petitions, fully aware that patently worthless appeals would cause instant embarrassment for them and for their clients.' CJ closes: 'expect more short shrifts as the Court struggles to solve its backlog.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes a civic primer on how police and military officers should conduct, and how citizens should regard, pandemic-era checkpoints set up to safeguard security, safety, and health. He builds on the prior week's column featuring People v. Sapla (Aug. 19, 2020, ably penned by Justice Alfredo Benjamin S. Caguioa). The constitutional baseline: the right against UNREASONABLE searches and seizures is 'inviolable,' and a search/seizure becomes reasonable as a rule only when ordered by a judge through a written search warrant satisfying six elements -- (1) the judge determines probable cause, (2) via personal examination, (3) of the complainant and witnesses under oath, (4) with the place to be searched and (5) the persons or things to be seized (6) particularly described in the warrant; a judge failing these may be sued and administratively sanctioned. Probable cause has no fixed formula but in general exists when 'facts and circumstances... could lead a reasonably discreet and prudent person to believe (1) that an offense had been committed and (2) that the items, articles or objects sought in connection with the said offense are in the place to be searched.' Jurisprudence has carved seven exceptions to the warrant requirement: (1) incident to lawful arrest, (2) plain view, (3) vehicle, (4) consent, (5) customs ports of entry/exit, (6) stop-and-frisk, (7) exigent and emergency circumstances. He focuses on the third -- vehicle search (boat, car, bus, truck, tricycle) -- which permits as routine only 'visual inspection': (1) drawing aside the curtain of a vacant vehicle, (2) looking without touching, (3) using a flashlight without opening doors, and (4) NOT subjecting occupants to physical or body search. To conduct an 'extensive and intrusive search' beyond visual inspection, the policemen 'must have PROBABLE CAUSE to believe PRIOR TO THE SEARCH that (1) a crime had been committed and (2) the article or object (usually prohibited drugs) pertaining to the crime... can be found in the vehicle.' Critically, the police 'cannot search a vehicle and the occupants thereof on the sole basis of an anonymous tip or a verbal statement by an informant'; the tip must be verified through the officer's own personal knowledge (not hearsay) before the search. 'To repeat, a tip, standing alone, is not sufficient to constitute probable cause.' Citizens have a practical self-help script: bring a hard copy of this and last Sunday's columns to checkpoints; assert rights 'firmly but peacefully (not forcefully).' If they resist forcefully they may be deemed to have waived their rights and consented to the search under Exception 4, after which 'courts will not be able to help them.' Without judge-issued search warrants, police and military officers at checkpoints can conduct only visual inspections; conducting an extensive search or seizure without first determining probable cause exposes them to 'criminal, civil, and administrative' liability -- 'now or in the future.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban salutes the Supreme Court for its 'resolute stand' in favor of the constitutional right against unreasonable searches and seizures by 'striking down with finality' the police practice of conducting warrantless arrests and seizures based solely on unverified tips from anonymous sources. The trial court and Court of Appeals had convicted Jerry Sapla of illegal possession of prohibited drugs and sentenced him to reclusion perpetua plus a P5 million fine. On appeal, the SC in People v. Sapla (June 16, 2020, posted Aug. 17, 2020) acquitted him because the drugs used as evidence were 'illegally obtained' by policemen who arrested and searched him on a jeepney 'on the sole basis of a text message from an anonymous, hearsay source,' and the Bill of Rights bars illegally-obtained evidence 'in any proceeding.' Justice Alfredo Benjamin S. Caguioa wrote 'superbly' for the Court to settle 'once and for all' the question that 'jurisprudence has vacillated over the years' on -- 'whether an accused could be convicted on the basis solely of an unverified tip relayed by an anonymous informant' -- concluding that the prevailing and controlling jurisprudence is that 'exclusive reliance on an unverified, anonymous tip cannot... [justify] a warrantless search of a moving vehicle.' The Court voted 'decisively' 11-3 (one seat was vacant), including its three most senior members -- CJ Peralta and Justices Perlas-Bernabe and Leonen (the last with a concurring opinion) -- 'gutsily supported him.' CJ is 'honored and humbled' that Caguioa cited several of his own decisions safeguarding liberty against unreasonable searches and seizures, and specifically quoted CJ's dissenting separate opinion in People v. Montilla (Jan. 30, 1998) -- 'thereby making it the prevailing jurisprudence now.' The Montilla dissent warned that under a tipped-information regime 'everyone would be practically at the mercy of so-called informants, reminiscent of the Makapilis during the Japanese occupation. Any one whom they point out to a police officer as a possible violator of the law could then be subject to search and possible arrest. This is placing limitless power upon informants who will no longer be required to affirm under oath their accusations, for they can always delay their giving of tips in order to justify warrantless arrests and searches. Even law enforcers can use this as an oppressive tool to conduct searches without warrants, for they can always claim that they received raw intelligence information only on the day or afternoon before. This would clearly be a circumvention of the legal requisites for validly effecting an arrest or conducting a search and seizure.' Caguioa closed 'scintillatingly': 'The Court fully recognizes the necessity of adopting a resolute and aggressive stance against the menace of illegal drugs... Nevertheless, by sacrificing the sacred and indelible right against unreasonable searches and seizures for expediency's sake, the very maintenance of peace and order sought after is rendered wholly nugatory... When the Constitution is disregarded, the battle waged against illegal drugs becomes a self-defeating and self-destructive enterprise. A battle waged against illegal drugs that tramples on the rights of the people is not a war on drugs; it is war against the people. The Bill of Rights should never be sacrificed on the altar of convenience. Otherwise, the malevolent mantle of the rule of men dislodges the rule of law.'

one_paragraph_summary: To the question whether the Philippines should elevate the 2016 South China Sea arbitral ruling upholding its maritime rights to the United Nations General Assembly for enforcement, Panganiban answers 'Yes, but not now, not during this regime.' The UNGA is the best forum: a joint statement by former Foreign Secretary Albert Del Rosario and retired SC Justices Antonio T. Carpio and Conchita Carpio Morales argued that 145 of the 193 UNGA members have ocean and sea borders -- and would 'logically and reasonably' vote to enforce the ruling because doing so reaffirms the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, which extended their territorial sea from 3 to 12 miles, recognized their 200-mile exclusive economic zone, and their continental shelf of up to 350 miles. The US, UK, and other great powers will support the move because the ruling upheld freedom of navigation and overflight in the SCS -- the US (though a non-Unclos signatory) has already begun unilateral enforcement, conducting 'the world's largest maritime military exercises' there a few weeks before the column. But 'not now,' because FS Teodoro Locsin Jr. -- previously PH ambassador to the UN, so qualified to 'do a reality check on how to win in the world body' -- rejected the proposal: 'We won already, why would you want to relitigate something that you already won... Once you throw it to the UN, I'm afraid China has the numbers there and it's about numbers. It's not about law.' CJ unpacks two realities: (1) UNGA members 'do not always vote according to law, reason, or logic' -- they exchange favors via diplomatic quid pro quo ('scratch my back and I will scratch yours'; 'For more vivid samples of quid pro quo, watch Madam Secretary on Netflix'), and Locsin may have 'run out of favors to exchange' or believe PH cannot match China's quid pro quo; and (2) SCS-bordering countries weigh their claims against other dependencies -- 'a huge amount of Brunei's crude oil -- the backbone of its economy -- is imported by China,' so a Chinese cutoff could 'severely imperil' it. These countries may adopt China's counter-arguments: (1) the ruling is void for lack of jurisdiction because the dispute was over land features, not maritime rights; (2) the tribunal didn't rule on Chinese ownership of the land features and the Philippines didn't dispute it; and (3) unlike ICJ decisions, the arbitral ruling 'is not part of international law and has no precedent value.' These can be overcome -- 'Surely' -- but given Locsin's 'unyielding stance,' CJ recommends waiting for a new regime after the 2022 elections that may be 'gung-ho in using all its diplomatic weapons -- reason, logic, law, politics, compromise, back-channeling, and quid pro quo, plus old-fashioned grit and the perseverance to win.' Otherwise, 'to insist now may result in the tragic and irreversible loss of what we already won.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban traces the long-standing SC caseload problem from Francisco v. Permskul (May 12, 1989) -- where the Court already noted 'the tremendous number of cases' filed in restored-democracy PH -- to Gio-Samar v. DOTC (March 12, 2019), where the unanimous Court candidly admitted a 'staggering' 14,491 cases on its docket as of December 31, 2016. With 15 justices, that meant an average of 966 cases each, 'clearly a gargantuan load too heavy to shoulder.' Knowing the Supreme Court of the United States has no backlog and decides all its cases within one year, the Court sent the Gio-Samar writer Justice Francis H. Jardeleza on a US learning visit; Jardeleza (now retired) recently sent CJ his report. The report tracked earlier PH solutions -- minute and unsigned resolutions, routing of NLRC/SEC quasi-judicial decisions and capital-penalty reviews to the Court of Appeals -- but did not track CJ-specific reforms, though it specifically cited the Committee on Zero Backlog CJ Panganiban created on January 26, 2006 (included as Annex A). While awaiting the Committee's report, the Court practiced a judicial 'bayanihan' whereby old cases were surrendered to a pool from which justices with light caseloads voluntarily plucked and decided them; 'After I left, the Court, for reasons unknown to me, abandoned the practice.' On July 31, 2007 (after CJ retired), the Court approved the Committee's recommendations: '(1) ...accept only 500 cases for signed decisions in the next 6.5 years... and (2) ...maintain its output of 1,000 signed decisions until the backlog is cleared. The Court may thereafter decide to accept anywhere from 500 to 1,000 cases per year for signed decisions,' with the rest decided by minute resolutions. Obviously, this was not implemented -- the caseload grew. Jardeleza's report recommends a better method of case selection and docket management via smart technology, including differentiating and tracking separately (1) original-jurisdiction vs appellate-jurisdiction cases and (2) cases (a) denied outright, (b) ordered to file comment, and (c) given due course for full signed decision with strict deadlines. He also suggests shortening filing periods: 'Comments' to 10 days for Division cases and 20 days for En Banc, without extensions and without requiring 'Replies' except in 'extremely meritorious cases,' and 20 days for 'Memoranda' also without extensions. CJ Diosdado M. Peralta began his term with a 'Ten-Point Program,' the first item being the 'Elimination of backlog in the Supreme Court and all other courts' (CJ's January 12, 2020 column). Together with faithful implementation of both the Committee on Zero Backlog and Jardeleza's recommendations, the Court will 'finally solve the perennial problem of justice delayed is justice denied.' CJ Peralta is noted for giving reforms 'transparency and permanency by integrating them in the Rules of Court,' making progress trackable. The column closes with a postscript: an August 24 Zoom roundtable on 'Philippine Foreign Investment Rules' as related to the Asean Comprehensive Investment Agreement, organized by the Asean Law Institute, the Asean Law Association (Philippine Chapter), and the Asian Institute of Management.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban uses the Quezon City Police's homicide filing against MSgt. Daniel Florendo Jr. for the fatal shooting of retired Army Cpl. Winston Ragos to argue that filing a criminal case is only the beginning -- sustained vigilance is the real price of speedy justice. He then catalogues the structural causes of clogged dockets using the Supreme Court's own resolutions -- the March 18, 2014 trial-duration mandate frustrated by Rules-of-Court exceptions, the January 8, 2013 admission that 80 percent of trial-court backlog is criminal and stems from prosecutor and witness absences and PAO lawyer shortages, and the September 4, 2012 admission that roughly 40 percent of criminal cases are dismissed annually because complainants 'simply gave up' after repeated postponements. He closes with the uncomfortable observation that even final-judgment victories often leave civil liability uncollected, renewing his earlier call to the IBP for help -- a call that, he candidly notes, has gone unanswered.

Ermita (Carpio Morales, April 20, 2006, compelling Cabinet attendance at congressional inquiries); Bayan v. Ermita (Azcuna, April 25, 2006, throwing out 'Calibrated Preemptive Response'); and Lambino v. Comelec (Carpio, Oct 25, 2006, striking down the people's-initiative form-of-government change). He notes that Justices Gutierrez and Azcuna prefaced their ponencias with odes to his philosophy of liberty and prosperity and cited those decisions at their retirement as their obra maestra, while Justice Carpio's 'scathing' Lambino language ('deception', 'gigantic fraud on the people') is believed to have cost him the chief justiceship under his former client, Arroyo. He closes by quoting the Salonga-Miranda-Feliciano book 'A Test of Courage' (2007, 231-page Regina Publishing hardcover) -- 'The nation applauded the grit, sharpness and courage of the Panganiban Court... authoritarianism, "creeping" or blatant, has no place in our society' -- and notes that this 231-page tribute felt to him 'equal to, if not better than, the several honorary doctoral degrees' he had received. one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban answers readers querying where the title 'First Female and 24th Chief Justice' for Teresita J. Leonardo-De Castro originated: from the front page of 'Benchmark,' the Supreme Court Public Information Office magazine, Vol. 3 No. 4 Special Issue. He documents De Castro's 42-day CJ tenure (Aug 28 - Oct 9, 2018 midnight) as the shortest in history -- a few days shorter than CJ Pedro L. Yap's 72-day tenure in 1988 -- but anchored in 45 years of government service and 10+ years as an SC Associate Justice (Dec 4, 2007 - Aug 27, 2018), five times Yap's two-year associate stint. She is the only CJ also to have served as Sandiganbayan presiding justice, where she penned the 211-page Sept 12, 2007 decision convicting Joseph Estrada of plunder, sentencing him to reclusion perpetua, forfeiting more than ₱549 million in the Muslim Youth Foundation deposit, ₱180 million in the 'Jose Velarde' deposit, and the 'Boracay Mansion' in New Manila, plus perpetual disqualification -- only for her later, as an SC associate justice, to effectively modify that ruling through Risos-Vidal v. Comelec (Jan 21, 2015), holding that Arroyo's pardon restored Estrada's civil and political rights and allowing him to run and win as Manila mayor. He catalogues her SC vote profile: for distributing Hacienda Luisita to farmers; against Aquino's Truth Commission; against PDAF/DAP; for Marcos's Libingan ng mga Bayani burial; for upholding De Lima's arrest and detention; for the Mindanao martial law and its extension; and for the quo warranto ouster of Sereno. Because she retired by reaching age 70 rather than being removed, De Castro received the full CJ-equivalent retirement entitlement: emoluments for life (lump-sum first five years, monthly thereafter), survivorship benefits for her husband, one month salary and allowances per year of service, leave monetization, and ceremonial Session Hall honors plus a sit-down dinner at a five-star hotel. By contrast, Sereno (ousted by quo warranto, declared ineligible though recognized as a 'de facto officer') and Corona (ousted by Senate impeachment May 29, 2012) received none of these because neither retired -- a doctrinal consequence that CJ closes by noting transferred the title 'First Female and 24th Chief Justice' in law to someone who never expected it even for 42 days, away from someone who had held it in fact for six years and expectedly for a record-breaking 18.

one_paragraph_summary: In this Part 2 column, Panganiban delivers his 'modest answers' to the questions he posed last Sunday on Solicitor General Jose C. Calida's quo warranto petitions against ABS-CBN and ABS-CBN Convergence. Opening with a pedagogical aside that he has never believed in spoon-feeding, he turns to doctrine: under Republic v. Sereno (May 11, 2018), quo warranto applies only when the act or omission was 'prior to or at the time of the appointment or election' rendering the holding invalid from the outset -- acts during incumbency cannot be QW subjects. Sereno was ousted precisely because her pre-appointment failure to file some SALNs negated the constitutional integrity qualification, which is how Teresita J. Leonardo-De Castro became the de jure 'First Female and 24th Chief Justice.' CJ maintains his prior view that impeachment, not QW, is the proper remedy for impeachable officials, but agrees with the pre-existing-invalidity premise. The same logic applies to franchises: the defects must pre-exist the grant. ABS-CBN's alleged KBO operations, PDR issuances, corporate layering, and alleged PSE non-listing all post-date the validly enacted franchises, so under the Sereno dictum, they cannot be QW subjects. He invokes Gio-Samar v. DOTC (March 12, 2019), where the SC held that when factual issues are indispensable to legal issues, the Court will refuse to resolve them regardless of allegations of compelling reasons -- meaning at minimum the petitions should be remanded to the Court of Appeals for factual determination before the SC can act. On the merits of the PDR question, he argues the instruments did not violate the constitutional 100% Filipino ownership/management requirement for mass media: PDRs grant only the right to receive dividends (less administrative expenses) and the right to convert into shares of stock if the converter is Filipino, while a 100% Filipino-owned company unqualifiedly controls and votes the underlying shares. Complaints about alleged violations belong with the NTC and SEC (appealable to the CA and SC), and the penalties under existing law are fines, refunds of fees paid, or halts of the service complained of -- not franchise forfeiture. He closes by allocating institutional responsibility: at bottom, the fate of ABS-CBN and ABS-CBN Convergence rests with Congress (which may approve, veto, or allow the franchise bill to lapse) and the President -- not with the Supreme Court.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban summarizes Solicitor General Jose C. Calida's 67-page (plus 1,000+ pages of annexes) quo warranto petition seeking a Supreme Court judgment 'forfeiting' or 'revoking' the legislative franchises of ABS-CBN Corp. and ABS-CBN Convergence. The petition alleges four classes of violation: (1) operating the Kapamilya Box Office (KBO) pay-per-view channel through free-to-air signals without permit or conditional-access guidelines, allegedly 'illegally exact(ing) money from the Filipino people'; (2) selling Philippine Deposit Receipts (PDRs) -- issued by sister company ABS-CBN Holdings against ABS-CBN shares it owns -- to foreigners, allegedly conveying beneficial ownership in violation of the constitutional 100% Filipino mass-media rule; (3) ABS-CBN Convergence's purchase of controlling shareholdings in Multi-Media Telephony through suspicious 'corporate layering' without the congressional approval required by RA 7908 as amended by RA 8332; and (4) failure to list at least 30% of capital stock on the PSE within five years from the start of operations as required by the same laws. CJ then frames six interesting legal questions: whether Congress's exclusive franchise-grant power implies SC inability (or at least institutional impropriety) to revoke franchises, especially with bills pending; whether QW applies at all against a corporation holding a valid existing franchise allegedly 'abused or misused'; whether 'free-to-air' prohibits 'pay-per-view'; whether a big telco's later post-facto congressional ratification of multiple unconsented transfers and missed listing is precedent here; whether PDRs grant ownership rights or are equivalent merely to bonds; and whether forfeiture is the proportionate penalty for KBO abuse as opposed to refunds, fines, or service halts. He notes that many of the petition's 1,000+ annexes are private documents requiring authentication and that several legal questions presuppose factual answers -- how ABS-CBN actually used free-to-air for KBO, how PDRs actually grant ownership, how 'corporate layering' was actually employed, and why ABS-CBN Convergence actually failed to list -- without which the SC cannot proceed. He withholds his own answers, awaits the respondent's Comment due 'tomorrow,' and closes with the Tagalog cliffhanger 'Abangan ang Part 2: Answers' -- itself a model of judicial-temperance column craft.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the Sandiganbayan's Jan 21, 2020 outright dismissal -- 'without trial and reception of evidence' -- of the two criminal charges against former PNP chief Alan Purisima and former PNP SAF director Getulio Napeñas in connection with the Mamasapano Massacre that killed 44 SAF officers. The 18-page resolution penned by Justice Alex L. Quiroz (concurred in by Justices Reynaldo P. Cruz and Michael Frederick L. Musngi) rests on two grounds: (1) the Anti-Graft Law information under Section 3(a) failed to allege a crime because it did not allege that the accused received or expected 'any material remuneration or consideration' for the prohibited acts; and (2) the usurpation-of-official-functions information lacked probable cause because Purisima -- though suspended by the OMB -- was merely following the direct orders of then-President Benigno Aquino III as CinC, who in turn ordered Purisima to supervise the planning and execution of 'Oplan Exodus' and whose own parallel charges had already been dismissed by the SBN. The SBN held that proceeding to arrest and trial was pointless because even if proven, no conviction was possible, though the dismissal was 'without prejudice to the filing of the appropriate charge/s.' Justice Bayani H. Jacinto dissented on the Anti-Graft Law point, arguing that 'material remuneration or consideration' is required only when the inducement does not involve the commission of a crime -- not when, as here, the inducement involves the commission of acts amounting to a crime. Presiding Justice Amparo M. Cabotaje-Tang agreed with the majority on the Anti-Graft Law dismissal but dissented on the usurpation count, holding that the constitutive elements were sufficiently alleged. CJ frames the strategic question: should the OMB and the SAF 44 ask for reconsideration and ultimately appeal to the SC for clear jurisprudence (with likely remand to the SBN for trial and possible second SC appeal -- adding several more years), or should they accept the SBN ruling and refile 'appropriate charges' per the without-prejudice caveat? Given that the Massacre is already five years past, the informations are two years old, and the long doctrinal path risks witness disappearance, faltering memories, misplaced evidence, and diminished public support, CJ argues it is more prudent to accept the SBN resolution, let the lively legal debate of the SBN justices be resolved in another case, and let speedy justice be done to the SAF 44 now.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens 2020 endorsing CJ Diosdado Peralta's 10-point program and arguing that Peralta would be acclaimed for achieving just the first goal -- elimination of SC and lower-court backlog. He uses 2016 stats from Gio-Samar v. DOTC to indict post-2006 institutional output: 6,526 new cases received but only 1,028 decided (a 6:1 ratio), leaving a 14,491-case docket and giving each of 15 justices an average load of ~966 old cases plus ~400 new ones a year. He revisits his own term's 'Operation Zero Backlog,' a judicial 'bayanihan' in which light-load justices voluntarily picked cases from a shared pool, with a footnote disclosing the pool-pickup to protect the ponente from the laggard charge; by his retirement on Dec 7, 2006, the backlog had fallen to ~200. The successor plan -- the formal July 31, 2007 'Internal Policy to Achieve and Maintain a Zero Backlog' -- was, 'in my humble opinion,' viable in design but failed in implementation: promulgated 'not for release,' it never reached the incoming justices, and retiring justices simply left their backlogs to successors who did not even know the plan existed. By 2016 the docket had ballooned from 8,741 (Jan 2007) to 14,491. Now even super lawyer Estelito P. Mendoza has written CJ Peralta complaining that Republic v. Lucio C. Tan (GR 203592) remains unresolved in violation of the constitutional deadline. Panganiban -- speaking as a former CJ himself -- supports Peralta's effort and prescribes the missing ingredient: a 'doable and transparent' plan that rallies full collegial cooperation, not just procedural design.

The PCGG's memorandum 'did not bother to address' which assets remain outstanding. CJ recommends a motion for reconsideration to clarify the residual -- easy to do, given the PCGG's documented P172B+ recovery since 1986 -- proving the agency is 'not that inutile' as public perception holds, and this monumental case from its 'early hallelujah days' was not dismally and sloppily lost.
