one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with an apparent oxymoron -- 'Honest official convicted by honest judge' -- and spends the column resolving it. Grace Padaca, the Isabela governor (2004-2010), former broadcast journalist, 'Symbol of People Power' and 2008 Ramon Magsaysay Award for Public Service laureate, was convicted by the Sandiganbayan on Nov 15, 2019 of malversation under the Revised Penal Code and of violating Section 3(e) of the Anti-Graft Law (RA 3019). The 57-page ponencia by Presiding Justice Amparo M. Cabotaje-Tang (joined unanimously by Justices Bernelito R. Fernandez and Ronald B. Moreno -- 'who are no pushovers either') traces the chronology: Padaca signed the MOA with the Economic Development for Western Isabela and Northern Luzon Foundation Inc. on Jan 8, 2006 without authority. The Provincial Board's Jan 31, 2006 resolution authorized her prospectively but conditioned the MOA on PB review and ratification -- which she did not seek before the Feb 23, 2006 release of P25 million, of which only P7 million was returned, leaving P18 million unaccounted. By the time the PB ratified the MOA on Jan 31, 2007, malversation had already been consummated; Art. 89 of the Revised Penal Code excludes ratification as a ground for extinguishment of criminal liability. The Anti-Graft Law Section 3(e) conviction stands separately because that provision punishes undue injury 'in addition to acts or omissions... already penalized by existing law' -- and Padaca improperly relied on the legal opinion of Provincial Legal Officer Johnas Lamonera, who was ethically conflicted as a 'registered incorporator' of the Foundation. CJ is careful to clarify: Padaca was neither charged with nor convicted of stealing public money; the SBN found her guilty of allowing others, through her negligence, to malverse public funds. He defers further commentary pending her announced MR -- and closes with symmetric tribute: will the reputedly honest public servant be able to convince the equally honest judge to change her mind on reconsideration?

United States dissent, and the Philippine Supreme Court declared 'the right to privacy' as 'fully deserving of constitutional protection' in Morfe v. Mutuc (1968). The empirical evidence is unmistakable: Akbayan lost its seat for the first time since 1998 and Bayan Muna fell from topnotcher to second place. CJ closes with a shared-blame turnaround: he repeatedly urged Congress to craft a clearer law that could withstand verba legis scrutiny, but the very 'progressives' who benefited from the modifications failed to secure that legislative clarity -- 'three other fingers point back at them. Carpio, failed empirically -- even though the Court itself unanimously admitted in Gio-Samar vs DOTC (March 12, 2019) that its docket had grown from 8,741 cases (January 31, 2007 baseline in the plan's footnote 2) to '14,491 cases in its docket' as of December 31, 2016. He summarizes the plan's design: the Court can promulgate an average of 1,000 signed decisions per year, so accepting more than 1,000 yearly creates structural backlog; routine cases (those not involving novel questions of law, merely reiterating settled doctrines, raising questions of fact in substance, or not showing grave abuse of discretion) must be dismissed by minute resolutions; for 6.5 years, signed-decision acceptances should be capped at 500 total (102 En Banc plus 166 per Division -- CJ notes in brackets that 166 should be 133 to keep the total under 500); and a three-tier monitoring chain (clerk of court, three deputy clerks, judicial staff heads of each justice) tracks acceptances. He discloses he 'did not know this plan until two weeks ago' because it was promulgated 'not for release.' In his 'humble opinion' the plan was 'viable and workable,' but it 'was not implemented properly': the Court accepted more cases than the cap, cases were not disposed in the manner the plan specified, and 'some retiring justices merely left the backlog to their successors who probably did not even know about the plan, considering that it was promulgated not for release in 2007 prior to their assumption of office.' Yet some incumbents -- Justices Carpio, Diosdado M. Peralta, Mariano C. Del Castillo, and Estela M. Perlas-Bernabe -- 'faithfully followed the plan and have no backlog, even if the Court itself carries a hefty caseload,' establishing that compliance is structurally feasible. 'With due respect,' CJ urges the Court to make the resolution public 'instead of being kept in the Court's labyrinths' so new justices can learn and follow it, and to publish per-justice caseloads for closer monitoring.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban responds to the pushback his two prior columns on judicial delays -- 'Confronting SC's mounting backlog' (April 7, 2019) and 'Will judges-at-large solve huge RTC backlog?' (April 14, 2019) -- provoked in the legal community. Leading the pack is 'abogado de campanilla' Estelito P. Mendoza, who complains that he has several SC cases unresolved beyond the 24-month constitutional deadline (Art. VIII Sec. 15) -- particularly Republic v. Lucio C. Tan, et al. (G.R. 203592) -- and asks what consequences attach to the Court's own violation, given that RTC judges 'are penalized at times by separation from service.' CJ answers directly that the SC has not penalized itself or its members. He then explains the definitional complication: the 24 months start from 'date of submission,' meaning receipt of the parties' memoranda -- easy with two parties but unclear with the 27-respondent Republic v. Tan, where Tan, his wife Carmen, and Mendoza-represented controlled companies filed memos 'more than four years ago' while the remaining respondents have not. A February 20, 2018 SC resolution noted that 2017 orders 'could not be served on some respondents' because their lawyers 'moved' and one respondent 'was not residing at given address.' Without commenting on the merits, CJ proposes that the case be deemed submitted on the date the Court ordered memos filed (over four years ago), with non-filing parties waiving their right and their lawyers penalized for failure to comply. He raises a second structural difficulty: new SC appointees 'inherit' cases from retired predecessors and may be 'unloaded' with old cases by incumbents to equalize the per-justice average -- leaving open whether the 24 months begin on assignment date or original memo-receipt date. His view is that 'the Court (and the retired justice) may have violated the 24-month limit, the new justice has not.' Finally, he endorses lawyer Luis M. Ermitano's complementary critique of RTC judges who 'do not start on time,' do not take up calendared cases, and do not fully use stipulations of facts, mediation, or pretrial proceedings -- agreeing that beyond the constitutional requirements of 'proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence,' justices and judges must also be 'industrious and diligent.' He closes by acknowledging the column-space constraint: 'Sorry, I have no more space for other equally important reactions.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban relays the recent UP Diliman lecture of Professor Elizabeth A. Pangalangan -- one of the 15 holders of the Chief Justice Panganiban Professorial Chairs on Liberty and Prosperity -- on human rights, adoption, and surrogacy. Her thesis: adoption and surrogacy are at the outset 'parent-centric' -- contracted by and for adopters and commissioning parents to satisfy their craving for parenthood and family love -- but courts have doctrinally come to lean in favor of 'the best interest and overarching human rights of the children.' Because adoption has been extensively analyzed elsewhere, CJ focuses on surrogacy. He distinguishes two types: traditional (the surrogate is inseminated by the commissioning father's sperm, naturally or via IVF, and is also the egg donor with a genetic link to the child) and gestational (the surrogate carries an embryo created from the commissioning couple's egg and sperm -- illustrated by his March 10, 2019 column 'The delectable twins of Mar and Korina'). Surrogacy generates multi-parent complications absent from adoption: a child can have up to two fathers (biological and commissioning) and up to three mothers (genetic source of egg, commissioning, gestational who bears and gives birth). PH law beyond Family Code Article 164 -- which legitimates artificial-insemination children when both husband and wife authorize the insemination in a pre-birth signed instrument -- does not govern surrogacy. Yet 'surrogacy services are now offered in several local hospitals' and 'many Filipinos have gone abroad to avail of it,' which 'should be enough to impel Congress to legislate.' He presents Pangalangan's four legislative options: (1) prohibit all surrogacy; (2) prohibit commercial but allow altruistic (because 'trading in human flesh is abhorrent') with no payment to the surrogate; (3) allow but regulate commercial; or (4) allow all arrangements. The PH SC has no surrogacy decision yet, but Yamada v. Union of India (September 29, 2008) is instructive: Baby Boy Manji was born to an Indian surrogate from a Japanese husband's sperm; the commissioning couple separated before the birth, the ex-wife refused the child (no genetic link), and the surrogate refused (contract only). Mercifully, the Japanese husband claimed the child, but Japan refused him a passport (doesn't recognize surrogacy) and his adoption petition was denied in India (single-parent bar). On humanitarian grounds, the Supreme Court of India eventually allowed the child to leave with a certification (not passport), and Japan issued him a tourist visa. CJ notes the case 'illustrates the complications that legislation must anticipate to solve similar problems that could involve Filipinos'; the full lecture transcript will be posted on www.libpros.com after Pangalangan finishes editing it.

He argues that the lower-court 50-judge component is unnecessary since MeTC/MTCs are not congested, and proposes instead two complementary reforms: aggressive JBC recruitment to bring the regular RTC vacancy rate from 25% down to 10%, and creating 150 more regular RTC salas in congested areas presided over by regular judges with full institutional dignity rather than the displaced second-class status of judges-at-large.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the constitutional petition asking the Supreme Court to nullify the Philippine Law School Admission Test (PhilSAT) imposed by the Legal Education Board (LEB) under Republic Act No. 7662. He traces the LEB's MO 7-2016 imposing PhilSAT for AY 2016-2017, MO 11-2017 allowing conditional enrollment for those unable to test, and MO 18-2018 barring non-takers, failures, and expired-honor-graduates from enrolling in AY 2018-2019 -- culminating in the SC's March 12, 2019 TRO halting MO 18-2018 enforcement. He describes the jurisdictional clash: petitioners say only the SC may regulate admission to legal practice; the LEB says legal education is an Executive policy prerogative beyond judicial review. CJ refuses to take sides on the live case but endorses the TRO as preventing irreparable injury to current enrollees, and discloses that during his own CJ tenure the Court issued BM 1161 (June 8, 2004) referring four LEB reform proposals including a Mandatory Law School Admission Test -- to which the LEB never responded before unilaterally imposing the PhilSAT. He argues the underlying crisis is the persistent 25% bar passing rate (one in four after eight total years of pre-law and law), which neither side prevailing in court will fix, and calls for the Court, the LEB, and the petitioners (whom he personally knows) to abandon constitutional combat in favor of a common legal-education reform agenda.

He addresses readers asking why he rarely comments quickly on high-profile cases: the Sereno decision alone is 153 single-spaced pages with 334 footnotes, and as a retired CJ he would be 'thoroughly irresponsible' to comment without fully comprehending such treatises -- his preferred role is 'to educate, to edify and to help people study before commenting, to research before committing and to think before shouting.' Nonetheless, to satisfy persistent inquiries, he discloses brief positions 'at the risk of being simplistic': he agrees with Justice Carpio that sufficient grounds existed to indict Sereno in the Senate and that quo warranto was an improper remedy against impeachable officials, would have voted with the minority on Revilla's acquittal, and would have upheld Judge Alameda's Trillanes ruling with some modifications.

Bersamin, as new Chief Justice -- instead of the most senior or second most senior -- and what special qualifications he saw. CJ Panganiban frankly admits he does not know, adding that CJ Bersamin himself disclaimed knowledge, and notes that the Constitution gives the President wide discretion among JBC nominees. Rather than second-guessing the choice, he urges weighing Bersamin when he retires on October 18, 2019. He then summarizes the CJ's role drawing on three of his own ten books: the CJ is primus inter pares of the SC en banc -- presiding, controlling proceedings, shaping the agenda, summarizing deliberations, setting pace -- but with only one vote, relying on moral ascendancy and persuasion, not boss-subordinate relation. The CJ interacts with foreign governments, international bodies, and bar associations; chairs the Judicial and Bar Council ('Quality judgments begin with quality judges'), and is impelled into nonjudicial endeavors for better judicial compensation, security, and facilities; chairs the Philippine Judicial Academy for judicial continuing education; exercises constitutional administrative supervision over all courts and personnel under the Administrative Code, GAA, PD 1949 (JDF), and RA 9227 (SAJ) -- with 'exclusive sole power' to disburse JDF and SAJ funds -- making him a 'visionary administrator, efficient manager and sensible finance wizard all at the same time.' Finally, the CJ must withstand inquisitive-media scrutiny as 'the model of an upright public servant.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban systematically answers the six questions befuddling readers about Imelda Marcos's conviction: why it took 27 years, why she was not jailed, why she was granted bail, why her ill-gotten wealth was not forfeited, why she was convicted only of graft, and why not of plunder. He explains that of the 10 cases lodged against her, five were filed by the Office of the Ombudsman on December 16, 1991, one on December 21, 1993, and four on August 17, 1995 -- alleging the use of Swiss foundations by Imelda and Ferdinand Marcos to hide wealth -- and were raffled to different Sandiganbayan divisions before consolidation in the Fifth Division. Corpus-Mañalac -- appointed to the Sandiganbayan only on December 8, 2017 -- cannot be blamed for the delay; she diligently perused the gargantuan five-foot-thick records and produced a 70-page, single-spaced decision buttressed by 226 footnotes, convicting Imelda in seven of ten offenses and acquitting her in three. Imelda was convicted under the Anti-Graft Law (RA 3019) in relation to the 1973 Constitution; she could not be charged with plunder because the Anti-Plunder Law was enacted only after Marcos was ousted. Forfeiture was not part of the criminal judgment because separate civil suits exist to recover the Swiss-foundation millions, though the judgment perpetually disqualified her from public office. She was granted bail because none of her offenses was a capital one; her original P150,000 bond was forfeited due to her absence at promulgation, an arrest order was issued November 9, 2018, and she posted a new P150,000 bond on November 16, with PJ Rafael R. Lagos ordering her release the same day. Panganiban flags as strange that only Lagos signed the release order (without his Fifth Division co-members Mendoza-Arcega and Mañalac), that her 'Motion for Leave of Court to Avail of Post-Conviction Remedies' had not yet been ruled upon, and that the prosecution did not object to and meekly accepted the bail grant.

one_paragraph_summary: On the 35th anniversary of Ninoy Aquino's August 21, 1983 assassination at the MIA tarmac, Panganiban traces the legal proceedings that identified the soldiers but left the mastermind an enduring enigma. President Marcos first created a fact-finding committee chaired by CJ Enrique Fernando (August 24, 1983), then replaced it on October 22, 1983 with the Agrava Board (chair: Justice Corazon Agrava; assisted by 'Gray Dean' Andres Narvasa as general counsel) -- which held 125 sessions, heard 194 witnesses, and produced 20,377 pages of transcript before concluding 4-1 (Agrava dissented) that Gen. Fabian Ver and several military officers conspired to kill Ninoy. The SBN Pamaran decision of December 2, 1985 acquitted all accused; the newly reconstituted post-EDSA Supreme Court found it 'to be a sham,' nullified it, and ordered a new trial. In the Hermosisima decision of September 28, 1990, the SBN convicted the soldiers and sentenced them to reclusion perpetua, identifying CIC Rogelio Moreno as the triggerman behind Ninoy on the stairway -- though a 2004 PAO motion for a new trial (Persida Acosta) argued forensic evidence pointed instead to Rolando Galman on the tarmac. Ver was charged with murder but never tried: he fled to Hawaii with Marcos on February 25, 1986, died in Bangkok on November 21, 1998, and was never convicted as coconspirator or mastermind. Loose talk linking Marcos, Imelda, and Danding Cojuangco was never substantiated -- the Agrava Board's own public coordinator, former Ambassador Bienvenido Tan Jr., wrote the author on March 15, 2009, that 'there was never any evidence linking President Marcos or Imelda or Danding so that much as we might have wanted... we could not in good conscience come up with that conclusion.' After 35 years and two Aquino presidencies, Panganiban concludes, the identity of the mastermind remains a legal enigma.

He acknowledges the 'foreboding cases' cited by readers (Marcos burial, Mindanao martial law, Sereno ouster) and notes the JBC's political tilt (three Duterte allies among seven, with only the IBP slot held by Fernan-Cayosa appearing outside the President's loop). But he places this in historical context: presidential attempts to dominate the judiciary are not new anywhere in the world, and the Philippines has experienced this before. Under Marcos, Javellana v. Executive Secretary (March 31, 1973) validated a constitution ratified by hand-raising rather than secret ballots -- yet judicial heroes still emerged among Marcos's own appointees: CJ Roberto Concepcion, Justices Teehankee, Muñoz-Palma, and Melencio-Herrera. Under GMA, who had the second-longest incumbency and named a majority and eventually all 15 justices (including three chiefs), the Court still blocked her people's initiative for parliamentary shift and struck down her emergency powers issuance. The ascendancy of the Court ultimately depends on the justices' adherence to the four constitutional standards of 'proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence.' The Court's brinkmanship -- balancing protection of people's rights against the prima facie presumption of regularity of executive actions -- is the ultimate test of independence. Public vigilance insisting on those four standards will protect rights and secure justices' places in history; while not all will be judicial heroes, no one wants to be remembered as a judicial villain.

First, Article I's national territory language unmistakably upholds PH sovereignty over SCS islands and features per the arbitral award, sovereign rights over maritime areas beyond the territorial sea and the extended continental shelf including the Philippine Rise, and -- without naming Sabah -- sovereignty over 'other territories belonging to the Philippines by historic right or legal title.' Second, Article II replaces the AFP provision ('protector of the people and the State') with 'the government is the protector of the people,' removing the text being misused by political adventurers to justify military coups. Third, Article III's Bill of Rights becomes demandable against nonstate actors as well as the state, consistent with international standards -- acknowledging that multinationals, international organizations, and powerful individuals already violate fundamental rights of the poor and weak. Fourth, Social and Economic Rights and Environmental and Ecological Rights are expressly enumerated. Fifth, a double jeopardy exception is provided where the offended party is deprived of due process, there is a mistrial, or the trial court acted with grave abuse of discretion. Sixth, for the first time in Philippine constitutional history, 'political dynasty' is constitutionally defined with self-executing prohibitions -- closing the 'as may be defined by law' gap. Seventh, nationalistic ownership percentages are retained but Congress is empowered to adjust them according to the evolving national interest. Eighth, amendment and revision procedures are simplified with clear separate-voting requirements. The column notes there are more reforms and promises to take them up another time.

Bersamin) that LGUs are entitled to 40% of all national taxes -- not just national internal revenue taxes under the Local Government Code of 1991 -- plus automatic release, pursuant to Article X, Section 6. Per his confidential sources, the Court decided on prospective (not retroactive) implementation, thus allaying Finance Secretary Dominguez's concern that a retroactive computation from 1992 could reach a staggering P1.5 trillion. Economists Villegas and Abola of the University of Asia and the Pacific warned that federalism is expensive, unnecessary, and potentially hyperinflationary (1,000% consumer price surges in some Latin American and European federal states); PIDS researcher Manasan estimated P55 billion in annual additional costs. Sen. Lacson tweeted that simply implementing the LGC could achieve devolution without revising the Constitution. The column closes with two prescriptions: the SC ruling is a 'refreshing pause' for proponents to restudy costs, and the proponents urgently need to unify three divergent and confusing drafts (ConCom, PDP-Laban, House committee) whose incoherence explains why opinion polls show very little support for federalism.

She was not barred from future public office by the QW ouster -- unlike impeachment which carries that disqualification. A third option of continuing public advocacy preserves the CJ claim but exposes her to further punitive action: the show-cause order for violating the Code of Professional Responsibility, the Code of Judicial Conduct, the sub judice rule, and casting aspersions on the Court members; potential criminal and civil cases under the RPC and NIRC; and possible disbarment or contempt. Fading away quietly preserves her from further lashing, but accepting retirement benefits -- substantial, given her combined ~28 years of UP professorship and Court service, entitling her to lifetime incumbent's pay extending to her spouse -- would itself constitute a waiver of any remaining CJ claim. The column closes with the scriptural 'Quo vadis?' -- Peter's apocryphal question to the risen Jesus -- asking Sereno whether she will return to 'Calvary to be crucified again' or simply fade away. The author notes with restrained retrospective judgment that she lost her more powerful pulpit partly by venturing unwisely into the 'murky political thicket' without securing her colleagues' support, thereby incurring the ire of the 'god of the political plains.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban alerts readers to an unintended peril lurking in the Presidential Electoral Tribunal's 50% shading rule in the Bongbong Marcos v. Leni Robredo election protest. The 2016 automated voting machines were calibrated by Comelec to read ballots shaded by at least 25%, but the PET has ruled that only 50%-shaded ballots will count during its manual recount -- thereby disenfranchising voters who shaded between 25% and 50%. The peril is arithmetical: Bongbong identified three pilot provinces where he was most disadvantaged (Camarines Sur, Iloilo excluding Iloilo City, and Negros Oriental), all areas where Leni's margins are enormous. Assuming 5% of ballots fall in the 25-50% gap, Leni would lose approximately 74,675 votes across those three provinces while Bongbong would lose only 10,107 -- a net loss for Leni of 64,568 against her overall canvassed lead of 263,473. That net loss could be significant enough to trigger a full recount of the remaining 22 protested provinces with about nine million votes. The possible overturning of Leni's lead, the column stresses, would not be because of any proven cheating but because of a mechanical shading loophole -- unfair to her and more so to the electorate. The obvious remedy is to revert to the 25% threshold; the better remedy is to rerun the SD cards that contain digital copies of all the ballots -- as was done in Tinga v. Cayetano in Taguig in 2010 -- which is cheaper (avoids paying 50 revisors per party at P1,500 per day), fairer, and faster (pilot precincts alone will take seven months of manual revision; the remaining nine million ballots would take years).

Duterte defended his restraint frankly: 'You're asking me to violate the law. What if I am impeached?' Spokesperson Roque added that the prohibition could only be expanded by legislation. Panganiban uses this as a teachable moment on the legal/illegal divide. On the illegal side: endo/5-5-5 -- hiring for exactly five months to evade the six-month regularization threshold -- is definitively illegal and subversive of public interest; so is labor-only contracting, where the contractor merely supplies workers without substantial capital (below P5 million per DOLE DO 174), without tools or supervision, and the workers perform activities directly related to the principal's main business -- making the contractor a mere agent and the principal solidarily liable for all worker claims (Sasan v. NLRC, October 17, 2008; Valencia v. Classique Vinyl, January 30, 2017). On the legal side: job-contracting is unquestionably valid under the Sasan three-prong test -- (1) independent business under contractor control except for results, (2) substantial capital or investment, (3) agreement ensuring contractual employees' full labor and occupational safety rights. Fixed-term, project, and seasonal employment are also allowed. The President and DOLE may only implement the Labor Code, not modify or repeal it -- Article 239 of the Revised Penal Code penalizes public officers who encroach on legislative power by making rules beyond their authority. The column closes by redirecting organized labor: for the prohibition of all contracting and a mandate of direct-only hiring, look to Congress, not the executive.

Mayor Yap (October 8, 2008), which upheld Proclamation No. 1064 (May 22, 2006) classifying the island into 400 hectares of protected forestland and 628.96 hectares of alienable and disposable agricultural land. Under the Regalian Doctrine -- rooted in Spanish conquest and continued through the 1935, 1973, and 1987 Constitutions -- all land not clearly within private ownership belongs to the state. Only the portions covered by valid Torrens titles, like the 1933 Tirol OCT and its successors-in-interest, are privately owned. Proc 1064 changed the status of 628.96 hectares, opening the path for Filipinos to now apply for judicial confirmation of imperfect titles or other modes of acquisition under CA 141. The column closes with the author's own prescription: President Duterte may repeal or modify Proc 1064 and reconvert Boracay's public lands to protected forest, or better still, designate them a national park that cannot be owned privately -- a stronger and more permanent protection.

one_paragraph_summary: Following a Senate committee hearing chaired by Sen. Grace Poe on fake-news liability for internet intermediaries, Panganiban summarizes the FLP Dissertation Contest second-place treatise (P200,000) by Tess Marie P. Tan of the University of San Carlos, titled 'Liberty and Prosperity in the Digital Age: Determining the Proper Treatment of Online Intermediaries in Light of the United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights.' Tan distinguishes active intermediaries (with editorial control, like Inquirer.net -- liable for both published content and uploaded reader comments and photos) from passive intermediaries (without editorial control, like YouTube, Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, Google, and Yahoo!) and asks whether passive intermediaries should be liable for user content -- including intellectual property infringement and advertiser-fitness determinations. Using the Black Letter Approach, Tan surveys international instruments (UN Guiding Principles, ICCPR, ICESCR, UDHR), ICJ decisions, and the highest courts of the US, EU, France, Hungary, and Estonia, finding that in the US and Europe, passive intermediaries are held liable only if they exercised editorial control -- while more restrictive states like China and Thailand penalize intermediaries for all illegal content, triggering a 'repressive effect' on free speech. The ECHR offers an alternative 'economic interest test' -- liability if the intermediary had a commercial interest in the uploading. Tan's proposal: passive intermediaries should remain neutral platforms; assessing the lawfulness of content is a judicial question best resolved by courts; liability should attach only upon refusal to comply with a valid court order. Full text is at www.libpros.com.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains why the Supreme Court is so protective of its deliberations, beginning with the constitutional anchor: Senate v. Ermita (April 20, 2006, unanimous) held that SC members are exempt from congressional inquiry based on separation of powers, fiscal autonomy, and judicial independence -- even Senate counsel Sen. Joker Arroyo conceded this during oral arguments before CJ Panganiban. He notes analogous confidentiality protections for executive privilege (presidential conversations, cabinet meetings) and congressional executive sessions. The rule is transparency; the exception is deliberation confidentiality. Against the backdrop of the House impeachment proceedings against CJ Sereno, the SC's November 28 en banc resolution permitted administrative officials to testify only on administrative matters, and specifically limited JJ Del Castillo, Jardeleza, Tijam, Reyes Jr., and CA Justice Salazar-Fernando to administrative/non-adjudicatory testimony, with J. Leonardo-De Castro restricted to narrow case-specific subjects (TRO issuance, ponencia merits) but never the deliberations. He describes the deliberation protocol: only the 15 justices (5 in Divisions) are allowed inside the sanctum during deliberations -- no secretaries, clerks, or stenographers -- with sanctity beginning from receipt of the petition to promulgation. In 2009, a justice was fined P500,000 and disqualified from office for leaking an unpromulgated ponencia while it was being routed for signature. Sessions run about three hours covering ~50-page agendas with ~250 items; verbal skirmishes are rare, written arguments preferred. The justification for confidentiality is consequentialist: without it, justices would hesitate to give full vent to their arguments, and leakages would tempt parties to pressure justices through bribery, family appeals, pastoral persuasion, or ugly rumors designed to demonize or inhibit them.

one_paragraph_summary: Noting the House has passed a national ID bill and the Senate will follow after Christmas, Panganiban traces the constitutional controversy through two key rulings. First, Ople v. Torres (July 23, 1998, 8-6) voided President Ramos's AO 308 on two grounds: violation of the right to privacy (J. Puno's ponencia, warning of a 'vast reservoir of personal information' as a 'covert invitation to misuse') and the principle that a national ID can only be instituted by Congress -- though importantly, only three of the eight majority justices gave unqualified concurrence to the ponencia; Panganiban himself wrote a separate opinion (joined by J. Davide) invalidating the AO solely on the congressional-authority ground, not the privacy ground. Six dissented, led by J. Mendoza (data already gathered from existing agencies; identification, not thought control). Second, Kilusang Mayo Uno v. Director General (April 19, 2006) upheld President Arroyo's EO 420 directing executive offices to adopt a unified ID format -- because it was purely administrative, covered only offices under executive control, and did not expand data collection beyond what was routinely required. The Court set three conditions for when legislation is needed: (1) appropriation required, (2) compulsory for all branches and citizens, and (3) data beyond routinary transactional requirements. The author endorses Sen. Lacson's prescription (confine data to basics: name, birthdate, birthplace, age, gender) and Sen. Drilon's prescription (incentive-based, not security-based, to facilitate government transactions rather than screen people) as the constitutional fixes for the pending bill.

one_paragraph_summary: Responding to readers puzzled by the difference between GMA's acquittal (Arroyo v. Sandiganbayan, July 19, 2016, 10-4-1, per J. Bersamin) and Jinggoy Estrada's mere bail grant, Panganiban explains the procedural distinction. The acquittal/bail difference turns on stage of proceedings: GMA was acquitted after the prosecution completed its full presentation of evidence in a trial on the merits, while Jinggoy received bail only after a preliminary bail hearing before the prosecution rested. Both rulings invoked the same new doctrine from Arroyo v. SBN: plunder requires the information to allege and the prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt the identity of the 'main plunderer.' In GMA's case, the information failed to identify one and the prosecution's evidence proved none -- acquittal followed. In Jinggoy's case, the SBN Special Fifth Division (3-2) found that while the information alleged a main plunderer, the prosecution had not strongly established Jinggoy as that person -- hence bail, not acquittal; he can still be convicted. The column turns to a profile of Estelito P. Mendoza -- GMA's SC counsel, Enrile's bail counsel, and newly retained by Revilla. Mendoza rose as Marcos's young solicitor general, winning Javellana v. Executive Secretary (March 31, 1973), earning the grudging moniker 'Champion of the Wrong Side.' His assistants -- Puno, V. Mendoza, and Kapunan -- became SC justices. He chose lifetime private practice over the SC, took lonely causes others shunned, won San Miguel's Cojuangco controlling shares, and at nearly 88, hearing-impaired but mentally agile, still represents both powerful clients (GMA, Enrile, Cojuangco, Lucio Tan) and ordinary Filipinos pro bono.

Second, the vote is more precisely 11-2-1-1 (not 11-3-1): 11 found sufficient factual basis for all of Mindanao; Sereno and Caguioa (2) limited it to three provinces; Carpio (1) limited it to Marawi; Leonen (1) found no factual basis. one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban provides a plain-language explanation of the contractualization debate by walking through two escalating hypotheticals. In the simple version, a homeowner hires a properly capitalized contractor (DO 174: at least P5M paid-up capital or net worth) to build a house; the contractor supplies labor, materials, and equipment, pays workers at least minimum wage, and the homeowner is not the employer -- this is permissible job contracting under Labor Code Art. 106. Labor-only contracting (prohibited) arises if the contractor merely recruits workers while the owner pays salaries, supervises work, or provides equipment. In the complex version, a contractor for a P5-billion multi-building project subcontracts cleaning, security, and medical services to three separately capitalized entities -- each is still legitimate job contracting because the subcontractors control, pay, and equip their own workers. He anchors the analysis in Sasan vs NLRC (October 17, 2008), which sets a three-part test: (a) the contractor carries on an independent business in its own manner and under its own responsibility; (b) has substantial capital or investment; and (c) assures contractual employees full labor and safety standards -- contrasted with the two labor-only contracting elements: no substantial capital, and employees performing activities directly related to the principal's main business. He closes by noting that 'outsourcing is the digital-age synonym of job contracting.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban answers 'Who owns Benham Rise?' by explaining the legal rights the Philippines holds over this underwater plateau 250 km east of Northern Luzon with its 24-million-hectare area and 50-5,000m depth. UNCLOS -- signed December 10, 1982 in Jamaica and in force for the Philippines since November 16, 1994 -- established the four maritime zones measured from baselines defined by RA 9522 (approved by President Arroyo, upheld in Magallona v. Ermita, per J. Carpio, August 11, 2011): (1) 12-NM territorial sea (full sovereignty over air space, bed, and subsoil); (2) 24-NM contiguous zone (customs, immigration, and sanitary enforcement); (3) 200-NM EEZ (sovereign rights to explore and exploit all natural resources); (4) 350-NM continental shelf (exclusive exploitation rights, exclusive even if the Philippines does not yet explore). On April 12, 2012, the UN CLCS recognized the Philippines as an archipelagic state based on RA 9522's baselines -- a Cabinet member's 'We own Benham Rise now!' being 'a little exaggerated and legally inaccurate,' since the Philippines does not 'own' the seabed but holds incontestable exclusive maritime rights over it. China has publicly conceded these rights (even granting innocent passage), unlike its contested claims over the Spratlys and Scarborough. Even innocent passage can be temporarily suspended by the Philippines for security reasons or channeled through designated sea lanes. The column closes with the sidewalk analogy: the Philippines may not 'own' the adjacent sidewalk, but it has rights over it to protect security, health, and wellbeing.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban profiles Justice Samuel R. Martires, Duterte's first SC appointee -- a career jurist at RTC Agoo, La Union (2000-2006) and the Sandiganbayan (2006-2017) who drew curiosity when media reported six points of concern: his acquittal of then Mayor Duterte, a Davao meeting with the President, controversial JBC interview opinions, an admin charge, a short stint (retiring January 2, 2019), and his San Beda alumni status. The author responds to each. All six were known to and vetted by the JBC, which interviewed Martires lengthily on November 16, 2016, and found him worthy. On the Duterte acquittal: the canal-cover case was correctly dismissed for lack of probable cause -- Duterte could not be held liable for demolishing a structure built without permits. On the Davao meeting: it was an out-of-town hearing; the President invited the group but spoke only of student days, the drug war, and respect for the judiciary. On controversial opinions: Martires said the Marcos burial was more political than justiciable, agreed GMA should be acquitted for lack of ill-gotten wealth proof, but dissented from Enrile's bail (advanced age is not a statutory ground) -- a notably mixed, courageous position. On the admin charge: Pangan v. Ganay (December 4, 2004) shows the SC upheld Martires's refusal to issue an arrest warrant as a proper exercise of discretion. On the short stint: he should work extra hard, consistent with his promise of independence ('the Court should not be influenced by any king or president'). On San Beda: de Lima and Saguisag are both Bedan critics of Duterte. The author classifies Martires as belonging to the Analytical School of Jurisprudence -- faithful to statutory text, courageous under JBC grilling -- and endorses welcoming him, noting his three target problems: corruption, government interference, and trial by publicity.

Republic, January 18, 2017). He urges critics to read justices' opinions and track records before condemning them, and to treat the Libingan defeat as a 'wake-up call' -- 'eternal vigilance is the price of liberty.' Executive Secretary (March 31, 1973) -- validating the 1973 Constitution ratified by hand-raising in barangay assemblies rather than nationwide secret ballot -- is the most infamous PH SC decision, creating judicial villains from the majority and heroes from the minority (CJ Roberto Concepcion, Justice Calixto Zaldivar, Justice Claudio Teehankee, who became CJ after EDSA). In comparative perspective, the US paradigm of judicial villainy is Dred Scott v. Sandford (March 6, 1857) -- CJ Taney ruling Black Americans were 'mere possessions,' not citizens -- requiring a constitutional amendment to correct. The US paradigm of judicial heroism is Marbury v. Madison (February 24, 1803) -- CJ John Marshall defining the SC's role and conceiving judicial review, his statue dominating the Court's interior. Every sitting justice, he concludes, knows they too could be hailed as heroes or condemned as villains -- and closes with a call for the PCGG to finally give the public a full account of how much Marcos ill-gotten wealth has been recovered.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban addresses widespread anxiety over Duterte's mixed martial law signals -- including his desire for ML where 'only one person should be in control' without constitutional checks -- by distinguishing constitutional ML from what is truly dangerous. He enumerates the 1987 Constitution's safeguards: ML can only be declared for invasion or rebellion when public safety requires it; it lasts only 60 days; the President must report to Congress within 48 hours; Congress can revoke it by majority vote; the SC can review and nullify it within 30 days; and it does not suspend the Constitution, supplant civil courts, authorize military jurisdiction over civilians, or automatically suspend habeas corpus. If these safeguards are faithfully followed, we need not fear constitutional ML. Moreover, the proposed defanging of Congress and SC still requires a constituent assembly and plebiscite -- a process taking years. What CJ identifies as of immediate concern is not ML under the Constitution but the suspension or abolition of the Constitution itself -- which would instantly eliminate Congress, the SC, and all safeguards, leaving only the President's personal virtue, military loyalty, and popular vigilance as the only restraints. He cites Cory Aquino's 1986 RevGov as a benign historical precedent -- short (one year), leading to the 1987 Constitution -- but, crucially, unlike Duterte, she ascended via a peaceful revolution, not the democratic processes of an existing Charter.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains how Hillary Clinton won the 2016 US popular vote yet lost the presidency to Donald Trump -- and answers friends' how-and-why questions by walking through the Electoral College's quirks. American voters do not directly indicate presidential choices on their ballots; they vote for 'electors' who later vote for the prechosen candidate. Each of the 50 states plus DC allocates electors by local law, supposedly proportional to population -- California with 55, Alaska/Montana/Wyoming/DC with 3 each, totaling 538 with a 270-vote winning threshold under most states' winner-takes-all rule (except Maine and Nebraska). He demonstrates the anomaly with a simplified 9-state, 500,000-voter, 50-elector model: assuming Clinton gets 80% in State 1 (100,000 voters, 10 electors) and 45% in the 8 other states (50,000 each, 5 electors each), and Trump gets the inverse, Clinton totals 260,000 popular votes nationwide but earns only 10 electoral votes (State 1 alone), while Trump's 240,000 popular votes earn him 40 electoral votes from the other 8 -- and wins. He flags the per-elector population disparity (Alaska's 750,000 share 3 electors against California's 39M sharing 55), giving every Alaskan almost thrice the voting power of every Californian, and notes that this same Constitution has been reformed to remove biases against slaves and women but not against this 'constitutional relic' that even Vladimir Putin has mocked: 'And you call your presidential election democratic?'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban examines the Bill of Rights' due-process and search-and-seizure protections -- and how the post-1987 libertarian pendulum has swung too far. He clarifies that the Constitution prohibits not deprivation per se but deprivation 'without due process'; arrest and search warrants require judges to personally determine probable cause under oath with specified place and items, with strict-construction exceptions only for in flagrante delicto and hot pursuit (per his Oct 6 column), Miranda rights to silence and counsel, and exclusion of evidence obtained through torture, force, violence, threat, or intimidation. These iron-clad protections were motivated by fresh memory of martial law abuses, aimed at protecting innocent suspects especially the poor and marginalized. But 'the libertarian pendulum swung too much to the opposite direction,' producing police timidity from admin/criminal liability fears, and 'the net result is the rise in criminality. Grafters, killers, rapists and drug lords misuse the liberality of the Constitution to evade liability.' Even when police strictly observe rights, prosecutorial and judicial failure (ignorance, apathy, laziness, corruption), bribed or missing witnesses, and 'many lawyers thrive in technicalities and delays, rather than in their sworn duty to do justice to everyone' compound the breakdown. The consequence is general revulsion against democratic methods -- overlooking that 'means are as important as ends' -- with due process equated with 'costly suits, tiring delays, inexplicable technicalities, long-winded trials, interminable appeals, unwelcome acquittals and plain injustice'; in frustration, people turn to 'extralegal and extrajudicial shortcuts' (an unmistakable if unnamed reference to the Duterte-era killings). To solve the revulsion to 'overdue process,' police, prosecutors, lawyers, and judges must cooperate, think outside the box, moderate the pendulum swing, and craft innovative ways to provide quality and speedy justice for all -- safeguarding precious constitutional rights without the 'over' in due process.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban traces the dismal drug-case conviction record of past governments to police failure to observe constitutionally-mandated arrest and evidence-gathering procedures, citing two recent Supreme Court decisions both penned by Justice Estela M. Perlas-Bernabe: Sindac v People (Oct 3, 2016) and People v Manago (Aug 17, 2016), both producing acquittals under the fruit-of-the-poisonous-tree doctrine. Typically the drug evidence is shabu or marijuana seized after a search of the suspect's body, effects, vehicle, or home -- but under the Constitution, searches require warrants based on probable cause, with the narrow exception of a search incident to a lawful arrest (arrest MUST precede search; the sequence cannot be reversed, and evidence from an unlawful search cannot justify a post-facto arrest). Warrantless arrests are limited to three Rules-of-Court exceptions: (1) in flagrante delicto -- the suspect's overt act done within the officer's view (officer sees the actual shooting); (2) hot pursuit -- offense just committed plus officer's personal knowledge of facts (officer sees the victim fall and the suspect fleeing with a smoking gun); and (3) escaped prisoner. CJ applies the doctrine through Q&A: in Sindac, an arrest based on reliable surveillance information producing a shabu seizure was held unlawful because 'reliable information alone -- even if it was the product of well-executed surveillance operations -- is not sufficient to justify a warrantless arrest' since the officer lacked personal knowledge; in Manago, an officer who witnessed a robbery but lost the fleeing suspect and traced him next day via investigation could have secured a warrant -- and his pre-arrest vehicle search tainted the shabu evidence. CJ closes with the moral lesson: to improve the conviction rate, the police should study meticulously and follow strictly the constitutional process -- strengthening compliance rather than weakening protections.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban summarizes the Supreme Court's 9-3 ruling (with 3 abstentions) on September 20, 2016, in David v Senate Electoral Tribunal, which held that Grace Poe, a foundling, is a natural-born citizen of the Philippines and therefore qualified for the Senate and any public office requiring natural-born status. The landmark decision, written by Justice Marvic M.V.F. Leonen -- 'the Benjamin of the high court' -- upheld the presumption that 'all foundlings found in the Philippines are born to at least either a Filipino father or a Filipino mother' because this presumption 'arises when the Constitution is read as a whole, so as to effectuate its purpose.' The Court emphatically held that concluding otherwise would create 'an inferior class of citizens who are made to suffer that inferiority through no fault of their own. If that is not discrimination, we do not know what is.' Concurring with Leonen were CJ Sereno and Justices Velasco, Peralta, Bersamin, Perez, Mendoza, Jardeleza, and Caguioa; dissenting were Justices Del Castillo, B. Reyes, and Perlas-Bernabe; taking no part (due to prior SET involvement) were Justices Carpio, Leonardo-De Castro, and Brion. The ponencia also held that Poe validly reacquired her natural-born citizenship under RA 9225 after her US naturalization. This ruling is separate from but consistent with Poe v Comelec (March 8, 2016, 9-6, Justice Perez ponente) which had earlier declared her qualified to run for President -- though that decision was criticized because two majority justices (Peralta and Caguioa) declined to vote on natural-born citizenship and instead invoked Comelec's grave abuse of discretion (since the Constitution vests the power to rule on presidential qualifications solely in the PET), leaving critics to claim natural-born status had only plurality support. David v SET definitively settles this contention with nine justices, including Peralta and Caguioa, voting natural-born. Fortunately the September 20 ruling came 'away from the noise of the 2016 election,' insulating the Court from accusations of political partisanship and reaffirming the well-settled doctrine that election laws should be interpreted liberally with doubts resolved in favor of voter choice -- consistent with CJ's December 6, 2015 column opining that even Rodrigo Duterte's threatened typo-based disqualification should yield to 'substantial justice, not literal interpretation.' CJ closes with a personal coda: some dissenters in these two cases are his close friends, but their honest differences of opinion never affect mutual esteem because their friendship is based on 'mutual respect for the free market of ideas, not on the excessive desire for conformity or on the eerie silence of the cemetery' -- friends can disagree without being disagreeable, and can differ without being difficult.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban argues that since Duterte's federalism proposal is forcing constitutional revision anyway, the Cha-cha 'may as well delve into other basic reforms.' First, Article 1 ('National Territory') needs UNCLOS conformity -- it currently lists 'territorial sea, the sea bed, the subsoil, the insular shelves, and other submarine areas' but is silent on the exclusive economic zone and continental shelf that the Philippines 'so valiantly fought for and won' against China in the July 2016 arbitration. Though the catch-all 'all other territories over which the Philippines has sovereignty or jurisdiction' may arguably cover EEZ/CS, 'in my humble view' it would be better to expressly incorporate them. Second, the Bill of Rights bail clause (Sec 13, Art III) needs clarification of its capital-offense exception ('reclusion perpetua when the evidence of guilt is strong'): Estelito Mendoza's argument in the Arroyo and Enrile bail petitions -- that the strength of evidence can only be determined after prosecution presents its case, meaning the accused should not be detained pre-trial -- was not directly addressed by the SC, which instead released Arroyo via demurrer (acquittal-equivalent, since evidence was not strong) and Enrile on old-age and ill-health grounds. The Office of the Ombudsman countered that Mendoza's argument would create a legal loophole permitting flight; the doctrine remains unresolved and 'needs to be met head-on.' Third, the nationalistic economic provisions are 'long waiting for constitutional review': 60% Filipino ownership for natural-resource exploration, private land transfer, public utilities, and non-religious educational institutions; 100% for mass media (anomalous given CNN/BBC broadcasts and foreign newsstand publications); and 70% for advertising. Former Speaker Feliciano Belmonte's proposed amendment -- letting Congress determine the exact percentage by statute -- would give the country flexibility to adjust to changing economic needs and would spare the Con-ass or Con-con from spending excessive time on hardcoded percentages.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban commends Internal Revenue Commissioner Caesar R. Dulay for issuing Revenue Memorandum Order 44-2016 on July 25, 2016, within his first month in office, clarifying that nonstock-nonprofit educational institutions (NNS) are constitutionally exempt from tax on all revenues used 'actually, directly and exclusively for educational purposes,' and excluding them from the strict conditions of the earlier RMO 20-2013 (July 22, 2013) that had lumped NNS with corporations and associations granted exemption only by the NIRC. Dulay correctly distinguished the two sources: NNS exemption flows directly from the Constitution, requiring only two simple requisites -- (1) nonstock-nonprofit organization, and (2) revenues used actually, directly, and exclusively for educational purposes -- and 'the Bureau of Internal Revenue cannot add, much less vary' these constitutional requirements. Critics complain that the new RMO's documentary requirements (SEC + CHED/DepEd/TESDA certification of operation in good standing; proof that funds are spent for educational purposes only) remain bureaucratic, but they are 'few and reasonable' compared to RMO 20-2013. The Constitution mandates the state to 'establish and maintain a system of free public education in the elementary and high school level,' with elementary compulsory; the state allocates the biggest budget portion to education yet still falls short, and private NNS fill the gap, relieving the state of its constitutional duty. CJ argues the state should not only exempt but financially assist these schools, especially those catering to basic education, since their tuition and donations 'really, directly and ultimately benefit the children, and indirectly, the state.' These NNS are operated by Catholic dioceses and religious orders (Jesuits, Dominicans) and by foundations like the Tan Yan Kee, Metrobank, and Angeles University Foundations. CJ catalogs the institutional reach: the 75-year-old Catholic Educational Association of the Philippines (CEAP, founded 1941) has 1,252 members of which about 700 are mission schools for the poor and marginalized; the Association of Christian Schools, Colleges and Universities (ACSCU, organized 1946) has 118 members (6 universities, 3 seminaries, 40 colleges, 69 basic-education schools); and while there is a global Association of Muslim Schools, CJ is not aware of any local PH affiliate. RMO 44-2016 benefits all religious schools that can document the two constitutional requisites.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban clarifies the institutional nature of the South China Sea arbitral tribunal -- distinguishing it from the International Court of Justice and the Permanent Court of Arbitration -- after China escalated its de-legitimization rhetoric following the July 12, 2016 Award that upheld most Philippine submissions and trashed China's nine-dash line. China, citing the ICJ website, argued the ICJ is 'totally different' from the PCA and that PCA arbitration lacks the sanctity of ICJ adjudication; CJ partially concedes that China is correct on the ICJ distinction (the ICJ is the UN's principal judicial organ; the tribunal is constituted only under UNCLOS Annex VII for this particular dispute) and adds that the PCA itself did not render the decision -- it acted only as the 'Registry.' The decision's own title, 'AN ARBITRAL TRIBUNAL CONSTITUTED UNDER ANNEX VII TO THE 1982 UNITED NATIONS CONVENTION ON THE LAW OF THE SEA' (capitalized in original), neither claims to be the ICJ nor the PCA, despite media and legal-expert mislabeling. After a stylebook digression on UNCLOS→'Unclos' (pronounceable abbreviation rule, contrasting with DOJ/all-caps), CJ explains Art 287(1)'s four dispute-settlement options for signatories: ITLOS (Hamburg), ICJ (The Hague), ad hoc arbitration under Annex VII, and special tribunal under Annex VIII; absent a stated preference, the default is ad hoc arbitration -- so the proper name is 'An Ad Hoc Arbitral Tribunal Constituted Under Annex VII of the 1982 Convention on the Law of the Sea.' Though temporary, its decisions bind UNCLOS signatories like the Philippines and China. The tribunal was constituted June 21, 2013 with five members: Judge Rudiger Wolfrum (German, PH pick); Judge Stanislaw Pawlak (Pole, Itlos-appointed when China declined to name a member); Judge Jean-Pierre Cot (France); Prof. Alfred H. A. Soons (Dutch); and Judge Thomas A. Mensah of Ghana as presiding arbitrator -- a multinational, procedurally proper panel refuting China's 'puppet' characterization. The tribunal's Administrative Directive No. 1 appointed the PCA as Registry, with PCA senior legal counsel Judith Levine serving as registrar (rough equivalent of clerk of court). The PCA has acted as Registry in 11 of 12 Annex VII arbitration cases -- it is not a court but a service institution that transmits communications, archives documents, arranges arbitrator fees, holds arbitration funds, and provides Peace Palace hearing rooms.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban previews the Senate constitutional-amendments committee hearings under Sen. Franklin Drilon on President Duterte's proposal to adopt a federal system requiring Charter change. He distinguishes the textual theory (the President has no formal role in Cha-cha, unlike ordinary legislation requiring his signature) from political reality (the Chief Executive 'dictates every major political twist and turn'), as evidenced by Aquino III's refusal to alter his mother Cory's 1987 Constitution despite Speaker Belmonte's persistent advocacy, contrasted with Duterte's current Cha-cha drumbeat being immediately answered by Speaker Alvarez's marching House. CJ identifies the Senate as the real pivot and enumerates ten questions the hearings will face: (1) Should the Charter be changed at all, or can devolution be achieved through ordinary laws ('Why Cha-cha when we can swing?')? (2) Which mode -- Con-con, Con-ass, or PI? (PI is barred by Lambino v Comelec [Oct 25, 2006] for complicated structural changes.) (3) Since Con-con was rejected by both President and Speaker, will both chambers pass separate resolutions to convene? (4) Convene and vote jointly or separately -- joint voting 'drowns into insignificance' the 24 senators among the 292 House members and eliminates the Senate? (5) Will senators agree to Con-ass without separate-voting assurance, perhaps requiring an SC pre-ruling? (6) Will senators agree to a parliamentary federal system that usually demotes the upper chamber to ceremonial rubber stamp? (7) Which federal system best suits us -- US presidential, France/Germany/Malaysia/Canada parliamentary, or a 'Filipinized' hybrid like the 1973 Marcos Constitution with strong president and weak parliament, possibly with party-list members? (8) Has any country with a centralized government successfully metamorphosed into a federal state, and if not, how can we ensure the new structure survives its proponents? (9) Most governments evolve over time alongside historical experience -- can federalism be imposed from theory alone, or must empirical and historical bases ground a truly Filipino federal system? (10) Given urgent national concerns (budget, traffic, death penalty, freedom of information, tax restructuring, public-private partnerships, agrarian reform, peace process), will the Senate have the time, energy, and competence to also craft a new viable Constitution radically changing government nature and structure? 'We should know soon enough.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the Duterte administration's proposed P3.35 trillion 'budget for real change' for 2017 (11.6% larger than the P3.002 trillion 2016 outlay), with bulk going to infrastructures (airports, seaports, railways, roads) and human capital (education, health, social welfare). DepEd gets the biggest share at P570.4 billion (+31%); the judiciary's share rises from P26.79 billion to P32.54 billion, with CJ Sereno requesting 50 more family courts (added to 48 funded in 2016 -- the courts were created by law in 1997 but funded only starting 2016) and child-friendly equipment. Some lawmakers allege the budget is peppered with the graft-prone Priority Development Assistance Fund (PDAF) and discredited Disbursement Acceleration Program (DAP) -- vehemently denied by Diokno and Alvarez -- stemming from each lawmaker being asked to submit a DBM list of P80M projects. To test the allegation, CJ revisits two SC decisions: Belgica v Ochoa (Nov 19, 2013, J Perlas-Bernabe ponente) struck down PDAF because empowering legislators to specify projects from lump sums AFTER the GAA becomes law violates separation of powers (legislators cannot determine projects, authorize releases, or identify implementing agencies/NGOs post-enactment, except via congressional oversight); the Court enunciated the 'specific appropriation, stated purpose' rule banning lump sums except calamity, contingency, and intelligence funds -- designed to prevent graft. Pre-enactment proposals during DBM drafting and pending congressional consideration remain proper. Araullo v Aquino (July 1, 2014, J Bersamin ponente) declared four DAP acts unconstitutional (not the DAP itself): (1) transferring funds prior to fiscal year end without meeting savings criteria; (2) cross-border transfers from executive to Congress/Comelec/COA; (3) funding PAPs not covered by any GAA appropriation; and (4) using unprogrammed funds absent the national treasurer's revenue-collection certification. The constitutional baseline is strict: 'No public money shall be paid out of the Treasury except in pursuance of an appropriation made by law' and 'No law shall be passed authorizing the transfer of appropriations.' The limited exception is the power of augmentation, allowing only the President, Senate President, House Speaker, Chief Justice, and heads of Constitutional Commissions to augment items in their respective offices from 'actual savings' (defined three ways: PAP completed/discontinued/abandoned; vacant positions or unpaid leaves; targets realized at lesser cost via improved systems and efficiencies) and only within the same branch.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban continues last Sunday's question of whether longstanding PH-US defense relations help or hinder enforcement of the July 2016 SCS arbitration victory. The Duterte administration has laudably chosen diplomacy as its banner SCS strategy, but the geopolitical reality is that 'the best way to assure peace is to be prepared for war' -- and the Philippines alone cannot match China's military might, having historically depended on US assistance. Paradoxically, that dependency has 'lulled us into complacency': even 25 years after the 1991 ouster of US bases, the PH has not developed a strong military apparatus suited to its archipelagic configuration. The 2014 Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (Edca) was meant to bolster the 1951 Mutual Defense Treaty (MDT) and 1999 Visiting Forces Agreement (VFA), allowing US construction of new facilities and prepositioning of defense equipment, supplies, and materiel. The foundational doctrinal split appears in Saguisag v Ochoa (Jan 12, 2016): Justice Antonio T. Carpio's concurring opinion defends the alliance -- 'In modern warfare, the prepositioning of war materials is absolutely necessary and essential to a successful defense against armed aggression, particularly for a coastal state like the Philippines,' arguing that the PH cannot acquire anti-ship/anti-aircraft missiles off the shelf, that anti-ship missile operation requires airborne radar or satellite guidance, that China's air and naval bases will be completed by end-2016, and that 'only one power on earth ... can deter militarily China,' making the MDT 'utterly crucial.' Justice Marvic M.V.F. Leonen's dissent counters that the MDT/VFA were in effect when China invaded features within the PH EEZ and 'the Americans did not come to our aid,' that no 'clear, unequivocal, and binding commitment' was given on MDT applicability to PH WPS claims, that 'the commitment of the United States remains ambiguous,' and that the US 'will not interfere in those types of differences we have with China.' CJ's own answer: national interest is the ultimate motivation of every country on earth -- the PH filed and won arbitration to protect its EEZ, not to enhance American interests or harm China's claims. The US wants SCS navigation freedom for Obama's 'pivot to Asia' and will continue aggressive sail-and-flyover regardless of China; but whether the US will act as decisively to enforce the decision's PH-favorable nitty-gritty depends on US national, regional, and international interests, US-China trade/political/financial relations, and consultation with European and Asian allies plus Russia-balancing. The PH is not America's only friend. US internal issues (budget constraints, intensifying public revulsion of overseas interference) and the November 2016 election (Clinton continuity vs unpredictable Trump's potential radical new direction) make US-policy sustainability uncertain. Bottom line: 'Any premature overdependence on US policy at this point may not be advisable.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reviews PH-US defense relations amid increasing regional tension from US-China SCS military exercises (Russia joining in September) and US Secretary of State John Kerry's recent visit. The relationship was highlighted in CJ Maria Lourdes P. A. Sereno's Saguisag v Ochoa decision (Jan 12, 2016) upholding the Edca's constitutionality. After the 1898 Battle of Manila Bay and the Treaty of Paris (Spain ceded PH to US), the July 4, 1946 'independence' was concurrent with the 1946 Treaty of General Relations -- the 'mother' of PH-US defense relations -- through which the US relinquished sovereignty over the Philippines except in existing military bases. From it descended three defense pacts: the 1947 Military Bases Agreement (MBA, 23 bases, 99 years/2046, subsequently amended to 44 years/1991 with returned bases, recognized PH sovereignty over Clark and Subic, mandatory 5-year reviews, and prior-consultation requirements); the 1947 Military Assistance Agreement (MAA, an executive agreement covering arms, ammunition, supplies, equipment, vessels, services, and training); and the 1951 Mutual Defense Treaty (MDT, Aug 30, 1951) with two features -- mutual assistance in maintaining individual and collective defense capacities, and mutual self-defense against armed attack on either party's territory. On Sept 16, 1991, the Senate's 'Magnificent Twelve' rejected the proposed bases-extension treaty, satisfying Filipino nationalists but minimizing America's Western Pacific power projection -- the resulting vacuum 'gave China the opportunity to replace America as the dominant power in our region.' Joint military exercises continued in the 1990s; large-scale drills were suspended in 1995 and later resumed at reduced level. The alliance was formally revived via the 1999 Visiting Forces Agreement (upheld in Bayan v Zamora, Oct 10, 2000), with VFA II as the counterpart for PH personnel in the US. After the Sept 11, 2001 World Trade Center attacks, US forces arrived in Mindanao in January 2002 for Balikatan exercises combating al-Qaida-linked insurgency, and the 2002 Mutual Logistics Support Agreement (extended twice, expiring 2017) regulated reciprocal logistics. In 2013, the PH filed arbitration after China's Scarborough Shoal occupation -- coinciding with Obama's 'pivot to Asia' -- and after eight rounds of negotiations the two countries signed Edca, expanding rotational US base access, authorizing new facility construction, prepositioning defense equipment, and granting access to 'agreed locations.' CJ closes with a serial-tease: will our defense pacts with the US help or hinder us in addressing our SCS concerns? 'Abangan.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban evaluates the 501-page unanimous Award dated July 12, 2016 as 'exceeding expectations' -- granting 99% of PH submissions -- and analyzes it in three major parts. First, the tribunal ruled China's 'nine-dash line' historic-rights claim contrary to UNCLOS: while Chinese navigators historically roamed SCS waters, 'it is equally true that those of other states did likewise,' and arguendo any preexisting rights were 'extinguished by the entry into force of the Convention' to which China is bound -- making the PH solely entitled to exploit/develop its 200-NM EEZ and opening the SCS to freedom of navigation for the US, Japan, Australia, and other great powers. Second, UNCLOS's four feature categories -- low-tide elevations and submerged banks (no maritime rights), rocks above water at high tide (12 NM territorial sea), and islands sustaining human habitation in natural condition (EEZ + continental shelf) -- yield no 'island' status for any China-claimed Spratly feature, not even Taiwanese-occupied Itu Aba, with the doctrinal anchor 'no amount of reclamation or human work can change the legal status.' Scarborough Shoal and three Spratly features are 'rocks'; the tribunal disagreed with PH on Gaven Reef North and McKennan Reef, ruling them 'rocks' rather than low-tide elevations. Scarborough's surrounding waters do not form part of any EEZ, and traditional fishing rights were not extinguished, so China violated PH fishermen's traditional Scarborough fishing rights -- though Chinese fishermen also enjoy equal traditional rights there. Third, the tribunal catalogued China's PH EEZ violations: (a) Reed Bank petroleum interference, (b) prohibiting PH vessel fishing, (c) protecting Chinese fishermen fishing in PH EEZ, (d) constructing artificial islands -- plus environmental destruction (severe coral-reef harm, harvesting of endangered sea turtles, coral, and giant clams) and Chinese law-enforcement-vessel obstruction at Scarborough. The tribunal denied the PH request that China be 'advised to comply with its duties' as unnecessary; this denial, plus the equal Chinese fishing rights at Scarborough and the Gaven/McKennan ruling, explain CJ's 99% (not 100%) grade. China rejected jurisdiction and won't follow the decision, but instead of 'provocative saber-rattling responses,' the Duterte administration laudably counseled restraint and chose diplomacy. The US used jurisdiction-rejection to refuse the June 27, 1986 ICJ Nicaragua decision (vetoing UNSC call, ignoring UNGA resolution) but eventually settled diplomatically; Mauritius and the UK settled the March 18, 2015 Chagos arbitration through diplomacy. CJ believes 'our dispute with China can be peacefully resolved.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes on the crest of an expected Philippine arbitration victory, agreeing with President Duterte that 'we must not taunt or flaunt our triumph.' The Philippines and China enjoy a long history of friendship and excellent diplomatic, political, and trade relations -- this dispute is only one aspect of that broader relationship -- and humility in victory is the better course for continued friendly engagement; the PH should not, after victory, rule out bilateral negotiation, which China has always wanted. China opted not to participate, and the PH was allowed to present ex parte. Through diplomatic Notes Verbale, position papers, media announcements, and letters to Tribunal members, China repeatedly argued the Tribunal had no jurisdiction. The earlier 151-page Award (Oct 29, 2015) already upheld jurisdiction notwithstanding China's absence -- and the Tribunal announced it would issue its merits decision the impending Tuesday. Despite China's absence, the Tribunal procedurally copied China with all communications, gave notice of all hearings, granted adequate response time, and remained open to China's participation at any stage. The PH's Memorial prayed for 15 submissions, which CJ's earlier column (11/8/15) grouped into three basic claims. First, declarations that the parties' SCS rights and obligations are governed by Unclos and that China's nine-dash-line historic-rights claims are inconsistent with the Convention and invalid; a grant invalidates the nine-dash line and opens freedom of navigation for the US, Australia, Japan, and other big powers. Second, determination of feature characterization (islands generate EEZ + continental shelf up to 200 NM; rocks generate 12-NM territorial sea; low-tide elevations and submerged banks generate nothing; no amount of artificial reclamation alters status); a grant means PH can freely explore/develop/extract/utilize EEZ resources particularly oil and gas, legally barring China -- though the Itu Aba complication (about 0.5 sq km / 46 hectares, ~200 NM off Palawan, Taiwanese-occupied) looms: if ruled an 'island,' it could generate a huge EEZ close to Palawan, and since PH recognizes only one China, the Taiwanese occupation is deemed Chinese, meaning China could exploit that EEZ with naval protection. Third, declarations that China has violated the Convention via interference with PH sovereign rights and through constructions and fishing harming the marine environment; a grant means China can no longer legally chase PH fishermen or ruin EEZ reefs and ecology. The PH did not ask for, and the Tribunal will not grant, any sovereign or ownership rights over any land mass -- the Tribunal's jurisdiction is limited only to maritime rights under Unclos.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban continues his federalism series (after Federalism 101 on June 5 and Federalism 102 on June 12) by discussing how the system can be instituted. Charter change ('Cha-cha') would undoubtedly be needed; the 1987 Constitution provides three methods -- people's initiative (PI), constituent assembly (Con-ass), and constitutional convention (Con-con) -- all requiring electoral ratification via plebiscite. PI cannot be used because Lambino v Comelec (Oct 25, 2006) limits it to minor amendments, not complicated nature/structure changes like federalism. Under Con-ass, Congress (3/4 vote) directly proposes the changes; the big issue is joint vs separate chamber voting, and CJ argues for separate voting via a-fortiori logic: 'If ordinary legislation is separately voted upon, why should the remaking of the most fundamental law be treated any less stringently?' Fortunately, the President per media reports favors Con-con, avoiding the joint-or-separate dilemma and allowing dedicated full-time deliberation of federalism plus other proposed changes (like parliamentary system). Under Con-con mode, Congress convenes the convention by 2/3 vote (or submits to electorate by majority); Duterte's huge mandate makes 2/3 attainable even with separate chamber voting (2/3 = 16 of 24 senators for Con-con call; 3/4 = 18 for Con-ass approval). Incoming Speaker Pantaleon Alvarez took the first step by filing a Con-con bill on June 30, but it can only be taken up when Congress opens session July 25 -- undergoing three readings in both chambers, public hearings, plenary debates on many design questions (all elected or ex-officio, how many, by what method, party-list inclusion, incumbent-kin eligibility, partisan rules); lawmakers will protect their political turf. After bill passage, Comelec needs at least 6 months to prepare (manual or automated), suggesting the Con-con election coincide with October 2016 barangay elections (possibly postponed) or May 2019 congressional elections to save costs (P6.26B was 2016 election cost) and minimize election fatigue for Comelec, public school teachers (Board of Election Inspectors), watchdogs, and voters. The earliest convening is 2018; Con-cons historically take at least a year; a 60-90-day plebiscite window follows approval. The ultimate question: will the new Constitution take effect during or after Duterte's term? Meanwhile, Congress should rush ordinary legislation for non-federalism reforms the President and Cabinet are raring to implement -- tax restructuring, emergency powers for Metro Manila traffic, comprehensive peace agreements with Muslim brethren and the National Democratic Front, wider agrarian reform, and amendment of the Local Autonomy Code to devolve more powers to LGUs.
