one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban argues that the Commission on Elections, voting 4-3, extended the deadline for filing the statement of contributions and expenditures (Soce) from June 8 to June 30 -- thereby 'abetting impunity and virtually granting amnesty, beyond its authority,' to offenders of the election laws it is constitutionally mandated to 'enforce and administer.' Section 14 of RA 7166 clearly requires Soce filing 'within 30 days after the day of the election' (June 8 for the May 9, 2016 election) and 'does not provide for any extension.' Comelec Resolution 9991 (Dec 16, 2015) itself set June 8 as the 'final and non-extendible' deadline, and Comelec repeatedly reminded everyone of this language. No cogent reason was given by the Liberal Party for its inability to file when others did. Cogent reasons would be those that differentiate the LP's situation and make timely filing impossible -- like (a) a fortuitous event (an office fire gutting the records), (b) the party treasurer's sudden serious illness with no capable replacement, or (c) the duly-authorized representative's accident en route to filing. Comelec has equity power to extend only case-by-case for specific applicants with specific cogent reasons, not blanket amnesty for all offenders. Under the law, a candidate failing to file timely is fined (P1,000-P30,000) and/or barred from entering office until filing; a repeat offender faces perpetual disqualification; political parties failing to file are also liable for fines. The harsh additional penalty in Sec 14 -- that 'the same prohibition shall apply if the political party which nominated the winning candidate fails to file' -- does this disqualify VP-elect Leni Robredo and other LP-nominated senatorial, congressional, and other winners even if they filed individually? CJ's answer: No, the harsh proviso infringes due process in relation to the winners' right to hold public office and the voters' right of suffrage; these rights cannot be trashed by the malfeasance or negligence of the LP treasurer whom the winners had nothing to do with; only winners who connived or conspired with the treasurer should be punished. Soces should not 'sleep in the dead files of the Comelec' -- Pilar v Comelec (July 11, 1995) held they should aid in determining whether contributions came from legitimate sources and were spent properly. Donors face parallel obligations: the Corporation Code bars all corporations from political donations; Omnibus Election Code Sec 95 lists eight categories of barred donors -- public/private financial institutions, public utility/natural-resource operators, government contractors/subcontractors, franchise/incentive/exemption recipients, recent (1-year) government loan recipients above P100K, educational institutions with public grants above P100K, civil service officials/employees and AFP members, and foreigners. Sec 99 requires donors to file within 30 days after the election a sworn report stating contribution amount, candidate/agent/party name, and date; violation is an election offense punishable by imprisonment and disqualification. Closing question: 'Will the Comelec also grant donors a virtual amnesty for their violations of these provisions?'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban discusses two intertwined topics. First, the Foundation for Economic Freedom (FEF), an organization of eminent economists, has proposed a national ID system with four advantages: (1) financial inclusion for poor 'unbanked' Filipinos to open bank accounts otherwise impossible without government IDs, (2) welfare beneficiary identification, (3) identity-fraud deterrence online and offline enhancing e-commerce, and (4) preventing criminal identity-faking. The constitutional path is governed by Ople v Torres (July 23, 1998), which voided President Ramos's AO 308 (Dec 12, 1996) establishing a National Computerized Identification Reference System as ultra vires, and KMU v Neda (April 19, 2006), which upheld President Arroyo's EO 420 directing government agencies and GOCCs to adopt a common multipurpose ID. Justice Antonio T. Carpio's KMU ponencia distinguished them: 'EO 420 applies only to government entities that already maintain ID systems and issue ID cards pursuant to their regular functions under existing laws. EO 420 does not grant such government entities any power that they do not already possess under existing laws. In contrast, the assailed executive issuance in Ople v. Torres sought to establish a National Computerized Identification Reference System... a national ID system that did not exist prior to the assailed executive issuance.' EO 420 limited data to 14 specific items: name, home address, sex, picture, signature, DOB, POB, marital status, parents' names, height, weight, two index fingers and two thumbmarks, prominent distinguishing features like moles, and TIN. The Court further explained that three aspects require legislation: (1) special appropriation when no existing one applies, (2) compulsory application to all branches and all citizens whether they use the ID or not, (3) data collection beyond what is routinely required (privacy infringement). Second, Federalism 102 catalogs five debated topics from public discussion: (1) federalism advisability/feasibility given paternalistic/unitary/centralized colonial history -- though Spanish and American colonizers couldn't subdue the Mindanao sultanates and Cordilleras indigenous tribes who still aspire for full autonomy from 'Imperial Manila,' they conquered and united the rest of the country under one central authority; (2) what sovereign powers should be devolved to states vs retained by federal -- the present Constitution already created autonomous regions in Muslim Mindanao and Cordilleras; (3) how many states -- PDP-Laban envisions 12 (Northern Luzon, Central Luzon, Southern Tagalog, Mimaropa, Bicol, Eastern Visayas, Central Visayas, Western Visayas, Northern Mindanao, Southern Mindanao, Bangsamoro, Federal Administrative Region of Metro Manila), Dr. Salvador Araneta proposed 5, Dr. Jose Abueva recommended 11; (4) parliamentary form (Canada, Malaysia, Germany) vs presidential (US); (5) overhaul method (Con-con, Con-ass, PI) or alternative of more generous autonomy law for Muslim Mindanao + Cordilleras coupled with proactive resolute leaders. 'Let the debate continue.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens his federalism series with 'Change is coming!' -- President-elect Rodrigo Duterte's battle cry -- whose cornerstone is his proposed shift to the federal system. Duterte passionately believes only federalism can solve the 'Imperial Manila' lament of Southern brethren and the centuries-old armed conflict in Mindanao, though he has not given details. Basically, federalism is the decentralization of sovereign powers to make government truly 'of the people, by the people and for the people' -- but sovereign power is currently centralized in Metro Manila, with the bicameral Congress enacting laws to which LGU ordinances must conform; theoretically the House of Representatives addresses local plight, but the economy's bounties take time, if ever, to trickle to the countryside. Law enforcement is centralized via the Manila-based president and DILG, leaving 'Imperial Manila' too far removed from the daily needs of the rural folks who constitute the vast majority. The Local Government Code attempted devolution (peace/order, Internal Revenue Allotments) but falls short because the Constitution mandates one national police (to which local police are legally beholden) and the DBM can withhold IRAs. Federalists want the Constitution to separate federal from local powers -- like the US system where the 50 states are constitutionally guaranteed exclusive powers the federal government cannot intrude into, and where much of US Supreme Court lawsuits address federal-state delineation. Federalism is not new to PH: Salvador Araneta proposed it as the 'Bayanikasan Constitution' at the 1971 ConCon, and Jose Abueva (1971 ConCon secretary) has written several papers on his version, though the 1986 Constitutional Commission did not seriously install federalism in the 1987 Constitution despite Davao-consultation discussions. Instituting federalism will be difficult because PH government has been centralized/unitary since Spanish and American colonial periods, with Filipinos looking up to 'a father figure, a strong executive who dispenses governmental powers and largesse.' Duterte's election was predicated largely on personal charisma -- 'the very quality he may need, ironically, to diffuse and devolve authority' -- and his promise to eradicate crime, drugs, and corruption in three to six months 'can hardly happen if he does not have that central authority.' It may not be possible to institute federalism in a 2-3-year timetable; Araneta believed 10-20 years; Abueva proposed two stages within 10 years. The party-list system serves as cautionary tale: 'crafted rather hastily and haphazardly as an experiment, uprooting from the European parliamentary system and planting it in our presidential form,' it is now 'difficult to straighten out the confusion it has wrought.' The forms and structures of governments are 'born out of the experience and history of peoples and nations... not imported from foreign soils and implanted automatically' -- US federalism grew from the 13 colonies and the Civil War between Northern Union and Southern Confederation; the Federation of Malaysia was born from various sultanates' common desire to be independent from British rule. PH federal aspiration 'should be carved from our unique history as a nation' -- examining whether the Mindanao sultanates' independent-historical streaks have parallels in Visayas and Luzon. At bottom, while Duterte deserves leeway to implement his dreams, 'sufficient study, discussion and time are needed to craft a federal system suited to our needs, aspiration and history as a people.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban offers post-election gratitude after the May 9, 2016 polls: 'The queues were kilometric, the heat was searing, and, at times, the voters' receipts were coming out blank and the vote-counting machines (VCMs) were faltering. But the voters came in droves, patiently fell in line, and waited for their turn at the voting centers.' Despite electoral-watchdog complaints (warranting later investigation), the hash code bugaboo, and the failure of elections in 52 clustered precincts (plus added precincts curable via special elections), the Comelec -- from commissioners to career officials to rank-and-file -- deserves the people's gratitude. The national government 'from President Aquino to the last soldier, policeman and barangay tanod, acted with aplomb and integrity to make the Philippines an international showcase of democratic transition.' Public school teachers as 'electoral front-liners' discharged BEI duties tirelessly. Voter turnout was record-breaking -- 81.62% (about 40M of 54.4M registered), better than 77% (2013) and 74.8% (2010); 95% of results were electronically transmitted within 17 hours, easing tensions and enabling quick local proclamations. At the national level, the Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting (PPCRV) posted results from the Comelec transparency server, picked up by media and reported promptly, with credibility validated by early presidential-candidate concessions to presumptive winner Rodrigo Duterte. The computerization, despite glitches ('nothing is 100-percent perfect'), advanced the system to the Information Age -- 'especially marvelous to us seniors who are used to the old manual system which took months to validate' -- and 'the notorious preprocs are virtually as extinct as dinosaurs.' The PPCRV proved its 'mettle as an indispensable electoral watchdog,' with hour-by-hour updates from the Pope Pius XII command center LED screens. More crucial is its role as Comelec's citizen arm: it has assembled 'almost 700,000 volunteers from the different Catholic parishes nationwide, from the urban enclaves in Metro Manila to the distant barangays in Visayas and Mindanao that are reachable only by rugged treks and hourlong banca rides.' These volunteers were trained on VCM operation/repair, flying-voter detection, parallel manual counts, and election-return transport -- resisting bribery by unscrupulous politicians for 'guns, goons and gold' cheating. Unlike public school teachers receiving P4,500 honorarium plus leave/credits, PPCRV volunteers are 'neither paid nor insured,' depending on own resources or charity. Adela Elmida was ambushed and killed delivering returns to a freight company in Pagadian; her 12-year-old daughter survived injured. Another volunteer was struck by a sharp object monitoring General Santos City elections. Many suffered injury, hunger, verbal abuse but 'trudged on, defending freedom and democracy.' Founded in 1991 and headed since then by former Ambassador to the Vatican Henrietta 'Tita' De Villa, PPCRV has 'worked all year round during the last 25 years.' The Church hierarchy's pastoral letters and pulpit pleas for peaceful-election prayers combined with PPCRV lay-faithful action: 'prayer is the life of the hierarchy, but the lay faithful added action to prayer,' bringing about 'credible elections, the crucible of our vibrant democracy.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban provides a Money Laundering 101 primer amid ongoing Senate hearings that have 'glued many to their TV-radio sets and computer monitors' with 'staggering amounts and the audacity of the scheme' morbidly fascinating the public. Money laundering is the crime of transacting cash proceeds of an 'unlawful activity' to make them appear from legitimate sources -- concealing their true nature as illegal-activity proceeds. Example: ransom money deposited in a bank constitutes laundering (separate from the kidnapping); bank officials who 'knew, or could have known' the funds were ransom can also be prosecuted, as can conspirators/aiders/abettors/assistors/counselors and those who fail to report covered or suspicious transactions to the AMLC. Not all laundering is illegal -- only when proceeds come from law-listed unlawful activity: kidnapping for ransom, drug trafficking and related offenses, graft and corruption, plunder, bribery, malversation, car theft, robbery and extortion, jueteng and masiao, piracy, qualified theft, swindling, smuggling, Electronic Commerce Act violations, hijacking, destructive arson, Securities Regulation Code violations, terrorism (RA 9372), terrorism financing (2012 Act), and other special laws. Tax evasion is notably NOT included, though it can be separately prosecuted. Mediums beyond banks include BSP-supervised entities (FX dealers, pawnshops, money changers, remittance companies), Insurance Commission-supervised (insurance, preneed), and SEC-supervised (securities dealers, brokers, investment houses, mutual funds). Notably, casinos are NOT covered mediums -- yet cash from illegal sources can buy chips, and winnings paid in checks deposit as legal money; the same gap exists for real estate and art-piece purchases (cash in, check or legitimate instrument out). Cash transactions above P500,000 are 'covered' and reportable to AMLC within five banking days; smaller amounts can be 'suspicious' under seven enumerated circumstances: (1) no underlying legal/trade obligation/purpose/economic justification, (2) client not properly identified, (3) amount not commensurate to client capacity, (4) structured to avoid the covered threshold, (5) deviation from client profile or past transactions, (6) relation to unlawful activity, or (7) similar circumstances. Money laundering follows a universal three-stage process: (1) Placement -- introducing illegal funds into the financial system, e.g., by breaking large cash into smaller deposits or purchasing checks/money orders with illegal cash; (2) Layering -- disguising the source through multiple-layer transactions, e.g., investment instrument purchase and sale, wire transfers across global bank accounts masked as payments for goods or services; (3) Integration -- criminals openly enjoy the laundered money since its illegal origin is now concealed, integrating funds into the legitimate economy through property, stocks, and other investments.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains the Supreme Court's denial with finality (same 9-6 vote) of the motions for reconsideration on its decision allowing Grace Poe to run for President. The 47-page decision was 'superbly penned by Justice Jose Portugal Perez,' though five concurring and five dissenting opinions plus the decision (excluding separate opinions on MRs) total 688 single-spaced pages. The gut issue: did the Comelec gravely abuse its discretion in holding (1) Poe is not a natural-born citizen, (2) she failed the 10-year residency, and (3) she made false material representations in her COC? Grave abuse of discretion has two forms -- actual lack/excess of jurisdiction, and virtual lack/excess via whimsical, arbitrary, or despotic conduct. The Court held the Comelec rulings 'deadly diseased with grave abuse of discretion from root to fruits' for violating Constitution, OEC, and settled jurisprudence. The OEC grants Comelec authority to cancel COCs 'exclusively' on the ground that a material representation is false and made with deliberate intent to mislead the electorate; veering from this ground to rule on natural-born citizenship and residency, the Comelec usurped a power vested solely in the Court ('The Supreme Court, sitting en banc, shall be the sole judge of all contests relating to the qualifications of the President'). As a newborn foundling found in the Philippines, Poe is presumed a natural-born citizen because 'over 99 percent of babies born here have Filipino parents'; critics carry the burden of proving alien parentage and 'utterly failed to discharge' it. The presumption is strengthened by Poe's 'typical Filipino features: height, flat nasal bridge, straight black hair, almond shaped eyes and an oval face.' The 1935 Constitution's silence on foundlings has 'no restrictive language which would definitely exclude foundlings either,' and framers 'intended foundlings to be covered by the enumeration.' Social justice + equal protection favor foundlings; domestic adoption laws and generally-accepted international law principles obligate PH to grant nationality from birth. The Comelec 'arrogantly' ignored settled jurisprudence that repatriation restores natural-born status. As to residency, Poe's claim of 10 years 11 months on the day before the 2016 elections 'is true': she 'decided to permanently abandon her U.S. residence' and 'actually re-established her residence here on 24 May 2005,' which coupled with her reacquisition application and family's continuous PH stay shows her return 'was for good.' Her COC statements were therefore neither false nor deliberately deceptive. Justice Caguioa, joined by Justice Peralta, concurred on grave abuse but found voting on citizenship/residency unnecessary; Justice Del Castillo dissented but did not vote on citizenship. Critics claim only seven justices upheld natural-born/residency, leaving Poe's qualifications challengeable if she wins; CJ Sereno correctly pointed out that 'seven is a clear majority of the justices who actually voted on these issues.' Anyone can sue anyone in PH's litigious society -- Duterte (Comelec disqualification suit pending), Binay (alleged corruption), Roxas (2010 VP protest precedent against Binay) -- but 'suing is one thing; winning is quite another.' Meanwhile, the losers 'should stop whining. They have put up a good fight and there is honor in defeat. The Court has spoken. Let us respect its final verdict.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban argues that 'the president who will be elected in the May polls can change the composition of the Supreme Court, its legal orientation and, indirectly, its decisions. Thus, choosing a new president is also choosing a new Supreme Court.' At least 10 of the 15 incumbent justices reach the compulsory retirement age of 70 in the next 6 years (2/3 of the full composition), and new appointees could even reach 12. The retirement schedule in chronological order: Perez (Dec 14, 2016), Brion (Dec 29, 2016), Reyes (July 6, 2017), Mendoza (Aug 13, 2017), Velasco (Aug 8, 2018), Leonardo-De Castro (Oct 8, 2018), Del Castillo (July 29, 2019), Jardeleza (Sept 26, 2019), Bersamin (Oct 18, 2019), and Carpio (Oct 26, 2019); two more -- Peralta (March 27, 2022) and Perlas-Bernabe (May 14, 2022) -- retire within the next presidential term ending June 30, 2022. Article VII Section 15 of the Constitution bans presidential appointments two months before the next presidential election through end of term, except temporary executive ones for public service/safety; the SC voted 9-3 in De Castro v JBC (March 17, 2010) that this ban does not apply to the Court because of the 90-day vacancy-filling mandate. This controversial decision enabled then-President Arroyo to name Renato C. Corona CJ after Puno's May 17, 2010 retirement (within the prohibited period). To avoid the controversy, an alternative was found this year when Justice Martin S. Villarama Jr. voluntarily retired early on Jan 16, 2016 (he was scheduled to retire April 14, 2016, within the ban), allowing JBC nomination and Aquino's appointment of Alfredo Benjamin S. Caguioa. If the new president invokes either pathway, he or she could name 12 of 15 justices, leaving only CJ Sereno, Justice Leonen, and Justice Caguioa from the present Court. If the appointees are relatively young (as Arroyo and Aquino did with some appointees), the transformation could leave a lasting jurisprudential impact. Critical too is the JBC, which vets nominees -- though headed by the CJ, it can be swayed by the new president who names 5 of 7 members (SOJ ex officio + 4 regular). The Constitution requires magistrates of 'proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence,' with SC justices natural-born, ≥40 years old, and ≥15 years as lower-court judge or in law practice. CJ adds that justices must be 'industrious and have a sense of urgency' to handle heavy caseload -- assessable from judicial record for career jurists but requiring a craftable method for noncareer ones (private practice, academe). It is also time to weigh legal philosophy -- in the US, Republican presidents appoint 'originalists, textualists or conservatives' and Democrats appoint 'liberals or progressives.' An ongoing controversy is whether Obama should name Antonin Scalia's successor; Obama nominated Merrick B. Garland, but Senate Republicans vowed to 'freeze' the appointment for the next US president to avoid skewing the delicate originalist-liberal balance. 'At bottom, since the metamorphosis of our Supreme Court is at stake in the coming polls, I believe the presidential candidates should disclose how they would appoint new justices.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes Bagumbayan v Comelec (March 8, 2016, written by Justice Marvic M. V. F. Leonen) in which the Supreme Court voting 14-0 ordered the Commission on Elections to implement the Voter-Verified Paper Audit Trail or VVPAT (say 'vivi pat' for easy recall) in the May polls. Comelec immediately filed a motion for reconsideration arguing that the VVPAT was unnecessary, would delay ballot casting, and might force a two-week postponement of elections (May 9 → May 23) for source-code reconfiguration. After oral argument on March 17, the Court speedily denied the motion with finality, again unanimously 13-0. The 2010 and 2013 elections used the now-famous (or 'infamous'?) precinct count optical scan (PCOS) machines; for 2016, Comelec opted for the vote-counting machine (VCM), a 'paper-based automated system' 'seven times faster and more powerful than the PCOS' with updated processor, memory, and security features. The VCM is allegedly capable of producing the VVPAT in two forms -- a printed receipt and a touch screen -- both showing the votes counted, and providing RA 9369's electoral safeguards: (a) voter verified paper audit trail, (b) system auditability with supporting documentation for verifying correctness, and (c) system allowing voter to find out whether the machine has registered his choice. Bagumbayan, led by former Senator Richard Gordon (RA 9369's author), argued that VVPAT lets voters verify their receipt matches actual choices on the ballot, with electronic results auditable and verifiable via paper records. Comelec countered that (a) receipts could be used for vote-buying as proof of vote, (b) voting would be delayed by 5-7 hours, and (c) paper receipt is 'surplusage' since the VCM provides numerous audit trails: paper ballot, ballot image, storage media cards, and on-screen verification; the receipt is required only in a 'direct recording electronic election system' where voters input on a monitor without shading a paper ballot, so with VCM's paper ballot, a printed receipt is unnecessary. The Court held the 'law is clear... The paper ballots cannot substitute for the voter's receipt.' The phrase 'voter verified' modifies 'paper audit trail,' meaning the voter himself or herself must verify the paper trail -- paper ballots are a form of paper audit trail but not voter-verified, and while the paper ballot assists in preventing fraud, 'it does not provide the security to the voter that the machine has correctly recorded his or her vote.' On-screen verification 'is not the VVPAT because it is not paper-based,' and digitized ballot images alone cannot fulfill VVPAT because verification 'at minimum should be paper-based.' To prevent vote-buying, receipts 'should be deposited in a separate ballot box and not taken out of the precinct.' The Court was convinced VCMs can print simple receipts without source-code reconfiguration, with additional security features (precinct/ballot numbers) for future elections; 2016 elections need not be postponed, and 'the poll body has no power to postpone the elections.' Beyond VVPAT, CJ proposes three additional reforms: (1) proclaim winners only after complete, correct, credible COC count -- in 2013 senatorial candidates were proclaimed based on the so-called 'group canvass report' even though only 72 of 304 COCs had been duly canvassed (see CJ columns May 19 + 26, 2013); (2) allow thorough source-code review (it has been deposited in the Bangko Sentral vault, but questions linger because it was not reviewed before deposit); (3) implement random manual audit strictly in accordance with law.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with an elegiac tribute to Senate President Jovito R. Salonga -- his mentor, benefactor, guru, friend, and surrogate father -- recalling Salonga's foremost teaching that one must prioritize values money cannot buy (integrity, honor, dignity, patriotism, love for God) over the things money can buy. He then pivots to commentary on Grace Poe's 9-6 Supreme Court victory of March 8, 2016, contrasting the 'hubris' of critics who denounced the decision before its release as a 'culpable violation of the Constitution and betrayal of public trust' with the 'humility' of Poe's pre-verdict statement that she would accept whatever the Court decided. Using his signature mirror-construction aphorism ('If that is not hubris, I do not know what is' / 'If that is not humility, I do not know what is'), he then offers six 'sidelights' on the case: the Court was not remiss given the Poe case's greater complexity than FPJ's; the original ponente in both Poe and FPJ cases was overruled by the majority; both Poes won by an identical three-vote margin (9-6 vs 8-5); the rumor of a P-Noy 'secret candidate' is refuted by the split among his six appointees (four with the majority, two -- including close friend Justice Reyes -- with the minority); he ascribes the vote pattern to judicial independence, noting justices know they will be 'judged by history, not by baseless knee-jerk reactions'; and asks whether Poe will vindicate her adoptive father by winning the Comelec count and congressional canvass -- 'Abangan!' He closes with a civic-cultural appreciation of three classical music events: the Rotary Club of Makati's 50th-anniversary Vienna Spring Concert (where club president Eddie Yap announced the first air-quality monitoring station in Makati, funded by P50,000 contributions from CJ and 120 members totaling P6 million); the Johann Strauss Society's gala concert; and his own son Dr. Jose Artemio C. Panganiban III's Brahms performances at the CCP and BDO Center. He concludes by urging sponsors to reach not just the mature and privileged but also millennials and the general public, convinced Filipinos appreciate the classics as much as pop music.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban returns to the Grace Poe cases to address reader queries about why the Supreme Court spent five days of combative oral argument on her citizenship and residency when (as he argued the prior week) the gut issue was simply whether the Comelec gravely abused its discretion in cancelling her COC. He answers by laying out the three cumulative requirements for COC cancellation: the misrepresentation must be (1) material, (2) false, and (3) made with deliberate intent to mislead. Poe's statements about citizenship and residency are concededly material, but whether they were false -- and if false, whether made in good faith -- is genuinely contested among the justices. He flags Justice Jardeleza's separate concern that the Comelec may have denied Poe due process, which would ipso facto void the cancellation. Panganiban then offers Tecson vs Comelec (March 3, 2004), the FPJ disqualification case, as the controlling precedent. He recounts how Justice Vitug's 8-justice majority strung together presumptions about Lorenzo Pou's Philippine residence to conclude that mass Filipinization under the Philippine Bill of 1902 extended Filipino citizenship to FPJ's father Allan Poe, and thus to FPJ himself under the 1935 Constitution -- but more importantly, that even if 'the totality of the evidence may not establish conclusively that respondent FPJ is a natural-born citizen,' he could not be held guilty of material misrepresentation since it must be 'deliberate and willful' per Romualdez-Marcos. He extensively quotes Justice Puno's preference to 'let the people decide who will be the next President' on political questions and Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez's warning that disqualifying popular candidates on doubtful claims 'results to violence.' He contrasts these with the strict-interpretation dissent of Justice Carpio, who demanded conclusive proof that Lorenzo Pou was a Philippine inhabitant on April 11, 1899. The closing question: will the Court adopt the FPJ majority's liberal or the minority's strict interpretation in the cases of his adoptive daughter? 'We should know soon enough.'

He answers by reasserting institutional trust: the Court is weighing the issues responsibly and will produce a speedy and fair decision avoiding the dark scenarios he outlined the previous Sunday. He then sharpens the doctrinal architecture: the gut issue in the Comelec appeals is whether the poll body gravely abused its discretion in cancelling Poe's COC under Sec. 78 of the Omnibus Election Code, which 'exclusively' permits cancellation for false material representation made with deliberate intent to deceive -- the three-part test from settled jurisprudence (material, false, deliberately misleading). one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban joins Senate President Drilon, Speaker Belmonte, and the Inquirer's own Feb. 13 editorial 'Of the highest urgency' in urging speedy resolution of the Grace Poe eligibility cases, but redirects part of the critical gaze to the Comelec. He first outlines graduated dark scenarios: if Poe is disqualified BEFORE the election, votes for her will still be counted by the automated machines (programmed to count all printed-ballot names) but boards of canvassers may be barred from canvassing them -- though 'in this age of computers, geeks could still compute the results'; if AFTER the election and canvass but she fails to win, no problem; if AFTER she wins by highest votes, the second-placer would still be proclaimed, spawning political troubles; if AFTER she is proclaimed and AFTER she assumes office, only an election contest at the PET resolves the crisis. The unifying lesson: only NOT disqualifying her avoids dark scenarios. He then defends the SC: CJ Sereno publicly prioritized election cases; oral argument closed with a six-day memo deadline comparable to FPJ's pace. By contrast, he notes the disqualification suits against Rodrigo Duterte remain unresolved at the Comelec en banc -- so dark scenarios persist for him too. He builds two contrasting precedent timelines. Estrada's 2010 case slept in the Comelec for months (Second Division dismissal Jan 10, en banc denial May 4 -- less than a week before election day) and reached the SC only on May 7; the Court dismissed as moot in Pormento vs Comelec (Aug 31, 2010) because Estrada lost. (He notes Vidal vs Comelec, Jan 21, 2015, later held that Estrada's absolute pardon restored his right to seek public office.) FPJ's 2004 case was lightning-fast: petition filed Jan 9, Comelec First Division dismissal Jan 23, en banc affirmance Feb 6, SC Tecson decision March 3 -- Comelec en banc dismissal was 'noteworthy for its deep sleep' in Estrada's case, FPJ's for its 'blinding speed.' In both cases neither candidate was disqualified, the electorate had freedom of choice, votes were counted, and no dark scenarios occurred. The Comelec's asymmetric treatment is striking: it included Estrada on the ballots but cancelled Poe's COC. He closes with confident institutional faith: the Court 'will come up with a speedy and fair decision that will avoid the gruesome constitutional and political crises that critics fear.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban marks the 30th anniversary of Edsa 1 (Feb 22-25, 1986) and the 15th of Edsa 2 (Jan 16-20, 2001, recently passed without fanfare) by drawing both parallels and contrasts. Both revolutions were confluences of unplanned events joined by the middle class and the masses (the 'perfumed' and 'unperfumed' to one pundit, 'bourgeois' and 'proletariat' to an ideologue), happening at the corner of Edsa and Ortigas with the active support of the Church (personified by Cardinal Sin) and the military -- without which neither revolution would have ousted its president or installed Cory and Arroyo respectively. From the legal view, however, the similarity ends there. Edsa 1 was extra-constitutional -- undertaken against the then-prevailing 1973 Constitution under which Marcos had been proclaimed snap-election winner. Cory issued Proclamation 1 announcing she and VP Laurel were taking power, then Proclamation 3 stating that the 'new government was installed through a direct exercise of the power of the Filipino people assisted by units of the New Armed Forces of the Philippines.' She did not ascend via the snap election or the 1973 Constitution. The Cory-era Supreme Court -- composed of her appointees -- summarily concluded in Lawyers League vs Aquino (May 22, 1986) that the legitimacy of her government was not a 'justiciable' controversy; nonetheless, popular acceptance and international recognition made it a de jure government. By contrast, in Estrada vs Desierto (March 2, 2001), an SC with mostly non-Cory appointees affirmed the legitimacy of her ascent -- and rejected Arroyo's lawyers' attempt to invoke the same 'political thicket' defense. The Court held that political questions relate to matters of 'wisdom, not the legality,' delegated by the people to the executive or legislative branch; the 1987 Constitution, unlike its forebears, had trimmed the political thicket by giving the judiciary expanded duties: determining grave abuse of discretion by any branch of government, and reviewing the factual basis of martial law or habeas corpus suspension. The Court distinguished Edsa 1 as 'an exercise of the people power of revolution which overthrew the whole government' from Edsa 2 as 'an exercise of people power of freedom of speech and freedom of assembly to petition the government for redress of grievances which only affected the office of the President' -- Edsa 1 extra-constitutional, Edsa 2 intra-constitutional and subject to judicial review. In other words, Edsa 1 obliterated the 1973 Constitution and all the government institutions under it (including the SC itself), which is why its legitimacy was repeatedly challenged through coup attempts until the people ratified the 1987 Constitution; Edsa 2 preserved the 1987 Charter and its institutions. This is why Estrada vs Desierto explained Edsa 2's constitutionality at length while Lawyers League vs Aquino is notable for its sheer brevity. Sadly for Arroyo, her public satisfaction plunged after her 2004 electoral victory was severely questioned and her governance vilified as corrupt and ineffective. In both revolutions the Church played a pivotal role -- and a 'little-known but serious internal conflict, involving Cardinal Sin and the Vatican, nearly blurred that role,' which Panganiban promises to write about at another time (the column that becomes C89).

one_paragraph_summary: Continuing his post-pardon dialogue with Joseph Estrada -- who asked, 'I appointed six justices, yet none of them voted for me. Why?' -- Panganiban delivers a meditation on judicial independence as the primus inter pares of the four constitutional attributes required of judges (competence, integrity, probity, independence). Independence is most crucial because the judiciary is mandated to check the executive; those who don the black robe undergo a transformation, become different persons, forfeit past activities, relatives, and friends -- 'especially the president who appointed them' -- and devote their full time and attention to the exclusive and reclusive world of decision-making. He explains the doctrinal architecture of Estrada vs Desierto (March 3, 2001): by then the Senate and House had already passed separate resolutions supporting Arroyo's ascent, and those resolutions were beyond judicial review as political questions delegated to the legislative branch; the international community had also recognized her government. He cites the separate opinion of Justice Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez -- Estrada's last appointee, who had taken office just a month before Edsa 2 -- to powerful effect: 'this Court has to declare as a fact what in fact exists. Respondent Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo is the de jure President of the Republic of the Philippines.' He raises the counterfactual: had the Court not affirmed her legitimacy, Arroyo (then controlling the military and police) would have been tempted to set aside the Constitution and establish a revolutionary government, altering Philippine history. Estrada, he notes, is not the first or the last president to lament appointee 'ingratitude' -- even P-Noy has expressed dismay over some of his own appointees. He cites Justice Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa's model JBC reply on how he would decide critical cases involving P-Noy ('my former boss, school buddy and close friend'): 'My impartiality and probity as a judge would not be compromised by utang na loob.' He notes Arroyo herself was probably disappointed by Panganiban Court decisions striking down (1) her EO 464 barring Cabinet from Senate testimony, (2) her calibrated preemptive response against rallies, (3) her declaration of a state of national emergency, and (4) her people's initiative to shift to parliamentary form. The moral lesson: presidents should expect a cutting of umbilical ties when jurists enter the SC's hallowed doors and should be happy, or at least consoled, that their appointees lived up to fiat justitia ruat caelum (do justice though the heavens may fall). When Estrada follows up -- 'If they could not side with me, why did they not just inhibit like you?' -- Panganiban explains the Rules of Court grounds for compulsory disqualification (pecuniary interest, kinship within sixth degree, prior involvement) and voluntary inhibition (sound discretion, including personal bias or prejudice under the Code of Judicial Conduct). None of those applied to the six Estrada appointees; thus they did not inhibit. In his own case, however, Panganiban voluntarily inhibited because counsel Rene A. V. Saguisag filed a formal petition alleging he and CJ Davide may have prejudged the cause. He replied to the Court that 'although petitioner had not proven any legal ground for his request, I was nonetheless voluntarily inhibiting for two reasons: (1) to hold myself above petitioner's reproach and suspicion and (2) to deprive him or anyone else of any excuse to cast any doubt on the integrity of these proceedings and of the decision that this Court may render.' Aside from the totality test ratio decidendi, separate opinions also discussed Estrada's permanent disability and abandonment as alternative justifications for Arroyo's ascent.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with a parish-priest homily about obedience without satisfaction in 23 years of priestly assignments, and an autobiographical recollection of his late father redirecting him from chemical engineering to law just before passing away in his first year of prelaw -- establishing the column's frame: our decisions in life are limited by attendant facts, rules, goals, means, and time. He applies this frame to Jan 20, 2001. Given the choice between actively defending the Constitution and rule of law on one hand, and passively allowing chaos, revolutionary government, dictatorship, or coup d'état on the other, the SC 'courageously chose the first option, to defend the Constitution and the rule of law.' As he put it in a speech, 'The Court descended from its lofty perch on Mt. Olympus to avert a civil strife and to save our constitutional system from collapse.' Though initially incredulous, his colleagues -- after careful weighing -- agreed unanimously to authorize CJ Davide to induct the VP as 'acting president,' with an oath prepared by Justice Bernardo Pardo. This is why, when ambushed by media just before noon of Jan 20, Davide announced he was going to the Edsa Shrine 'to induct the vice president as acting president.' At the shrine, emcee Vicky Garchitorena announced each justice; the crowd chanted 'Da-vi-de, Da-vi-de, Da-vi-de' in awe of his impeachment-trial performance. Arroyo was sworn in at 12:29 pm on Saturday, Jan 20 -- using Pardo's prepared oath but with the word 'acting' orally omitted by both Davide and Arroyo. At the usual Monday breakfast on Jan 22, three justices who had been out of town on the crucial Jan 20 but had given their telephoned consent to the 'acting' oath were livid. Davide arrived at noon (he had been guest speaker elsewhere), acknowledged the consensus to swear in Arroyo as acting president, but explained that taking into account the confluence of events, he had decided on the spot to omit reading the word 'acting' -- ever a gentleman, he humbly took full responsibility for the omission. After heated debate, the 15 justices agreed 'unanimously to CONFIRM the authority given by the twelve (12) members of the Court then present to the Chief Justice on January 20, 2001 to administer the oath of office to Vice President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo as President ... without prejudice to the disposition of any justiciable case which may be filed by a proper party.' That justiciable case came when Estrada sued to stop Ombudsman Desierto from criminal indictment, claiming presidential immunity on the theory that he was president-on-leave and Arroyo was only acting president. The case revolved around Sec. 8, Art. VII: 'In case of death, permanent disability, removal from office, or resignation of the President, the Vice President shall become the President.' Justice Puno's path-breaking ponencia explained that resignation can be oral or written, express or implied, and applied the totality test: 'the totality of prior, contemporaneous and posterior facts and circumstantial evidence bearing a material relevance on the issue' established that Estrada had resigned. The decision traced the 'authoritative window' to his mind: political isolation, Angara's diary indicating intent to give up the presidency, negotiations for graceful and dignified exit and peaceful transfer of power, acknowledgment of Arroyo's oath, leaving Malacañang, expression of gratitude to the people. Panganiban closes with a rebuttal: those interested in the truth should read Estrada vs Desierto carefully before criticizing -- and those who peddle the falsehood that Panganiban concocted 'constructive resignation' could learn a lesson in the responsible use of free speech. True, he proposed the oath-taking and joined the 'acting president' consensus, but having inhibited in Desierto vs Estrada (after Saguisag's petition), he could not have espoused the resignation theory; ascribing it falsely is the actual offense. He ends with a forward-pointer to Estrada's post-pardon question about appointee 'ingratitude.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens the year by marking two milestones: the 30th anniversary of Edsa 1 (Feb 22-25, upcoming) and the 15th of Edsa 2 (Jan 16-20, just passed) -- the SC having characterized them as 'extra' and 'intra' constitutional ways of upholding democracy and the great libertarian and egalitarian principles. He begins with Edsa 2, whose constitutionality was upheld unanimously 13-0 in Estrada vs Desierto (March 2, 2001) -- with Davide and Panganiban inhibiting. As a participant in Edsa 2, Panganiban kept a diary; some passages were highlighted in his Feb 19, 2002 UST Central Seminary speech, later published as Chapter 11 of his book 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- printed by the SC, never sold in any bookstore, and contrary to critics' claims never 'withdrawn'; copies are in archives like the Court library. He recounts: the prosecutors' walkout on Jan 16, 2001 was triggered by the Senate's 11-10 vote refusing to open the so-called second envelope allegedly containing damning evidence of a P3.3 billion secret account under 'Jose Velarde.' Estrada vs Desierto records: 'In disgust, Senator Pimentel resigned as Senate President. The (11-10) ruling made at 10:00 pm was met by a spontaneous outburst of anger that hit the streets of the metropolis. By midnight, thousands had assembled at the Edsa Shrine and speeches full of sulphur were delivered against Estrada and the 11 senators.' On Jan 18, a 10-kilometer human chain of candle-bearers formed from the Ninoy Aquino monument on Ayala Avenue to the Edsa Shrine to symbolize solidarity demanding Estrada's resignation; students and teachers walked out of Metro Manila classrooms; speakers at the rallies, 'all masters of the physics of persuasion,' attracted more and more people. On Jan 19, AFP Chief of Staff Gen. Angelo Reyes defected and announced -- in the presence of all armed-services heads -- that the '130,000-strong members of the armed forces were withdrawing their support to the government.' A little later, PNP head Panfilo Lacson made a similar announcement; several Cabinet and sub-Cabinet officials followed. With AFP, PNP, and Cabinet allegiance shifted to Arroyo, Estrada could no longer govern -- but Arroyo could not yet legally lead either. There was no functioning government. On Jan 20, Panganiban woke at 4 am to a TV panel grimly announcing that Cardinal Sin via Msgr. Villegas was pleading with demonstrators not to march to Malacañang. The demonstrators refused -- they would storm the presidential enclave by 6 am and forcefully oust Estrada. Aghast at the violence and bloodshed that would ensue, with images of past Mendiola massacres haunting him, Panganiban called Davide at 5:30 am: the imminent encounter would be bloody and chaotic; Estrada could no longer govern; Arroyo could only take over by declaring a revolutionary government, which would obliterate the Constitution; the situation was ripe for a coup d'état. To avoid a power vacuum and a coup, he asked Davide to swear in Arroyo by 12 noon -- extraordinary crisis needed an extraordinary solution. When Davide (and later other justices and media) asked for legal justification to swear in the VP while the incumbent was still physically in office, Panganiban replied that while the constitutional text did not expressly cover the critical situation, the CJ could lean on the grand maxim Salus populi est suprema lex -- the welfare of the people is the supreme law -- precisely to save the Constitution and democratic system from destruction. To cut the long story short, Davide agreed and swore in Arroyo at 12:29 pm of that day. The forward-pointer: next Sunday will discuss how this milestone -- started by Panganiban's proposal to Davide and approved by the justices to swear in an 'acting president' -- metamorphosed into an oath for a 'President' (without 'acting'), and how the metamorphosis was unanimously judged constitutional 13-0 (Davide and Panganiban inhibiting).

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with a jurisprudential meditation: most judges apply Austin's Analytical School formula -- law times fact equals decision (LxF=D) -- taught consciously or unconsciously in most law schools, where students master codes, statutes, and precedents and apply them to hypothetical facts under verba legis discipline, with departures denounced as 'judicial legislation' and bad results shrugged off as 'dura lex sed lex.' This formula, he shows, reduces decision-making to an Aristotelian syllogism: 'Anyone who kills shall be jailed; Pedro killed Juan; ergo, Pedro goes to jail.' Like math, the formula is consistent in the abstract -- but math itself fails in reality: one drop of water plus another is not two drops but one bigger drop; one piece of wood divided by four is not one-fourth but four smaller pieces. Two problems plague Austin's formula. First, no science assures discovery of 'the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth' -- witnesses lie, forget, confuse, or fail to observe; documents are incomplete, vague, or fake; scientific and historical evidence is faultily extracted or badly preserved. Second, laws themselves are incomplete, unclear, confusing, contradictory, or obsolete. Textualists default at this point and say what's outside the text is outside legal contemplation -- but justice must be served. The Civil Code itself forecloses this hand-washing: 'No judge or court shall decline to render judgment by reason of the silence, obscurity or insufficiency of the laws,' and 'in case of doubt in the interpretation or application of laws, it is presumed that the lawmaking body intended right and justice to prevail.' When verba legis fails, great jurists rise -- they search 'beyond the text' in six sources: (1) overarching constitutional principles, (2) grand intentions of the framers, (3) great judicial axioms, (4) landmark precedents, (5) international conventions, (6) legal presumptions. He applies this toolkit to Grace Poe's case, which presents 'a rare moment for judicial greatness': the texts of governing laws neither include nor exclude foundlings; her residency facts are torn between her mistaken 2013 COC computation and the truth that she had actually transferred her domicile to the Philippines in 2005. He enumerates six pillars favoring her: (1) as a foundling, she deserves the social-justice principle of giving 'more law to those who have less in life'; (2) the 1935 Constitution framers explicitly stated it was never their intention 'to exclude foundlings from natural-born citizenship'; (3) the grand axiom Salus populi est suprema lex may be invoked extra-constitutionally to render social justice, famously wrote 'the eminent Justice Jose P. Laurel'; (4) Frivaldo vs Comelec teaches that doubt in interpretation favors enabling the electorate's free choice, Bengzon vs HRET affirms that repatriated natural-born Filipinos reacquire their original citizenship, and Marcos vs Comelec instructs that truth (not mistaken COC statements) prevails; (5) the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the covenants on civil and political rights, on the reduction of statelessness, and on the rights of the child all favor foundlings; (6) presumptions of good faith, nondiscrimination, and regularity in performance of duties undoubtedly benefit her. Judging from the 'gutsy Comment' filed by SG Florin Hilbay, Panganiban believes he too has seen the moment for judicial greatness -- and given Hilbay's sterling track record as bar topnotcher and law professor and Panganiban's personal knowledge of his writing ability and excellent reports as a court attorney 15 years ago, if Hilbay were a sitting jurist he could 'rise to the moment and craft a grand historic decision.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban praises the Supreme Court for resolving two crucial electoral roadblocks 'with commendable alacrity and speed' -- both threatening to upset preparations for the 2016 presidential elections. On Dec 8, the Court junked the Kabataan Party-list petition challenging two Comelec resolutions that fixed the voter registration deadline on Oct 31, 2015; on Dec 16, it trashed Kabataan's second petition questioning the 'No Bio-No Boto' policy and lifted its earlier TRO. Whether or not we agree with the decisions, our people should applaud the speed and encourage similar dispatch on all election-related matters. On the first case, petitioners argued the Oct 31 cutoff is more than two months earlier than what the Voters Registration Law (RA 8189) provides, effectively disenfranchising 2.4 million voters who failed to register. After ordering the Comelec to comment on Dec 7, the Court 'Voila' issued its unanimous three-page resolution the very next day dismissing the petition. It held that RA 8189 'merely provides that registration shall no longer be allowed during the period of 120 days before a regular election or, in this case, beyond Jan 8, 2016. It does not, however, mandate the period for registration should be up to such time.' On the second case, 'No Bio-No Boto' is a short, catchy Filipino restatement of the Mandatory Biometrics Registration Law of 2013 (RA 10367) which deactivates voters who fail to have their biometrics validated by the last day for registration. The 18-month Comelec public information campaign (May 2014 - Oct 31, 2015) ran concurrent with continuing voter registrations and gave sufficient notice. Justice Estela Perlas-Bernabe -- and CJ agrees -- explained that a distinction should be made between voters' 'qualifications' and their 'registration': registration is merely a preparatory step toward voting and 'is not one of the elements that make the citizen a qualified voter,' while the biometrics requirement rids the voters' list of 'ghost' and 'flying' voters. CJ acknowledges he initially sympathized with petitioners' disenfranchisement concern but had to consider that extension would imperil the Comelec's meticulously planned preparations and might result in electoral chaos. He enumerates the Comelec's Project of Precincts (POP) logistics: 54.5 million registered voters across 373,786 established precincts and 94,000 clustered precincts in 42,029 barangays, 1,490 municipalities, 144 cities, and 81 provinces; POP data drives boards of election inspectors, forms/supplies allocation, vote-counting machines deployment, and budgets; ballot templates for 18,083 elective positions with at least 45,800 candidates; 1,953 ballot faces to be posted at the Comelec website for candidate counter-checking before final printing. Rather than risk a chaotic poll and to ensure a credible and orderly election on May 9, 2016, he concludes it is much better to abide by and uphold the Comelec's timetable.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban summarizes for nonlawyers the 'praised and pilloried' Morales v. Court of Appeals (Nov 10, 2015) -- the SC decision reversing the 'infamous' condonation doctrine but only prospectively. The facts: on March 10, 2015, Ombudsman Conchita Carpio Morales placed Makati Mayor Jejomar Binay Jr. under six-month preventive suspension over six criminal and six administrative cases arising from alleged anomalies in the Makati Parking Building during his first term (2010-2013). On March 11, Binay Jr. challenged via CA certiorari; on March 16, the CA issued a TRO grounded in condonation -- that his 2013 reelection had condoned the prior-term anomalies. On March 25, Morales filed her SC certiorari, arguing that Sec. 14 of the OMB Law (RA 6770) bars any court from issuing TROs against OMB investigations and reserves OMB appeals exclusively to the SC; she also urged that the condonation doctrine be reversed for contravening the Constitution. The 71-page 'superbly written' Perlas-Bernabe ponencia, concurred in fully by eight magistrates (including CJ Sereno and Senior Justice Carpio), partly by one (Bersamin), with four taking no part and one on leave, is a scholarly dissertation summarized as follows. First, on CA jurisdiction: laws passed by Congress cannot restrict the constitutionally-enshrined duty of the entire judiciary (not just the SC) to determine grave abuse of discretion on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the government; ergo, the OMB Law cannot restrict the CA from hearing Binay Jr.'s certiorari petition alleging grave abuse by the OMB, and TROs are 'mere regulatory processes' ancillary to certiorari. Moreover, the 1987 Constitution grants the SC sole rule-making power and prohibits Congress from increasing SC appellate jurisdiction without its advice and concurrence -- the OMB Law violated both by routing all OMB appeals exclusively to the SC; further, since the OMB is a quasi-judicial agency, not a 'court,' the OMB Law unconstitutionally expanded SC appellate jurisdiction. Second, on condonation: the Court traced the doctrine to Pascual v. Provincial Board (Oct 31, 1959), decided under the 1935 Constitution when graft was not rampant and 'honor, integrity and delicadeza were sacred values practiced universally.' After more than half a century, times have changed for the worse; corruption has become pervasive; the 1987 Constitution mandates transparency, honesty, and accountability. After thorough review, the Court held: 'Election is not a mode of condoning an administrative offense, and there is simply no constitutional or statutory basis ... to support the notion that an official elected for a different term is fully absolved of any administrative liability arising from an offense done during a prior term.' Nonetheless, abandonment is given only prospective effect because under Civil Code Art. 8, judicial decisions form part of the legal system and shall have no retroactive effect unless otherwise provided -- CJ tried researching but found no jurisprudence authorizing retroactivity for abandoned doctrines. In sum: the CA has jurisdiction over OMB administrative rulings, and henceforth condonation by reelection can no longer be used as a defense. Postscript: on Oct 9, 2015, the OMB dismissed Binay Jr. from office, mooting his CA petition.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban uses a nine-question Q&A format to explain the contrasting Comelec 2nd Division and SET rulings on Sen. Grace Poe. Q1 (procedure): Poe will file her MR with the Comelec en banc Monday; David, denied at SET, is poised to go to the SC; all cases -- plus three others pending in Comelec's First Division -- will be consolidated at the SC for a final ruling; meanwhile Poe's name will be printed on the ballots as in Estrada's 2010 case. Q2 (SET justices at SC review): No, having judged below, they can no longer judge above. Q3 (5-4 vote reliability): Not unreliable at all -- many landmark cases have been decided by one vote, including Lambino v. Comelec (8-7, Oct 26, 2006) trashing the parliamentary-system people's initiative and the US Supreme Court's Bush v. Gore (5-4, Dec 12, 2000) halting the Florida recount and ushering in Bush's election. Q4 (Legarda asking electorate to decide legal issues): No -- Legarda quoted Frivaldo v. Comelec (June 26, 1996) at length: 'the question really boils down to a choice of ... how to interpret and apply laws relating to elections: literal or liberal, the letter or the spirit, the naked provision or the ultimate purpose, legal syllogism or substantial justice, in isolation of or in the context of social conditions, harshly against or gently in favor of the voters' choice. In applying election laws, it would be far better to err in favor of popular sovereignty than to be right in complex but little understood legalisms.' She chose the liberal way: in case of doubt involving popular sovereignty, interpret to enable the electorate to elect freely their chosen leader. Q5 (Duterte): If Duterte's alleged DQ rests only on a typographical error, he should be allowed to run under Frivaldo's substantial-justice principle -- this does not mean CJ approves his human rights shortcuts or habitual cussing; legal eligibility is different from electoral acceptability. Q6 (social justice for a non-poor Poe): Social justice equally favors the disabled, sick, abandoned (like foundlings), infirm, mentally retarded, disaster-stricken, and everyone economically, socially, politically, racially, and medically disadvantaged -- not only the impoverished. Q7 (Dura lex sed lex for foundlings?): Dura lex sed lex is a favorite expression of lawyers educated under the Analytical School who interpret verba legis; the better way is to look at the spirit, intent, and substance of the law -- lawyers should be social engineers who help build just societies, not mere automatons or legal technicians applying laws strictly without considering effects on society. Q8 (other natural-born offices): Yes, thousands -- Comelec commissioners, COA, CSC, CHR, ombudsman, most judicial/prosecutorial posts, bureau directorships, board examiners, scholarship grantees, and others too numerous to fit. Foundlings should not be denied entry to all these offices. Q9 (Poe's American period): That is a political, not legal, question better answered by the people via their ballots. Not every question can or should be decided by tribunals. Let Poe explain to the people, and if the majority accepts her explanation and votes her to office, so be it. This is the essence of democracy. Vox populi vox Dei.

Leonardo-De Castro, and Arturo D. Brion, plus Senator-member Nancy Binay. After setting forth the undisputed facts, issues, and arguments, the SET majority held: (1) Poe's being a foundling did not necessarily mean her parents were not citizens; on the contrary, it did not exclude the possibility that they were Filipinos -- a possibility strengthened by her physical features (5'2', brown eyes and dark brown/black hair, low nasal bridge, and oval-shaped face, consistent with the ordinary Filipino) -- giving rise to a 'disputable presumption' her parents are Filipinos, which the petitioner failed to rebut by showing her father was an alien. (2) The 1935 Constitution did not expressly mention foundlings, but Constitutional Convention delegate Manuel Roxas explained that the framers never intended 'to exclude foundlings from natural born citizenship ... and the only reason that there was no specific reference to foundlings ... was that foundlings are few and far in between so that it was not necessary to include a provision on the subject exhaustively,' adding that 'by international law ... children or people born ... of unknown parents are citizens.' Although jus sanguinis is the general rule, the framers created a class of natural-born citizens by 'legal fiction, as an exception.' (3) Various treaties and customary international law, read with the Constitution, affirm Poe's natural-born citizenship. (4) True, Poe lost her natural-born status when naturalized as American, but the SET -- citing Bengzon v. HRET (May 7, 2001) -- held she 'validly reacquired her natural-born citizenship upon taking her Oath of Allegiance to the Philippines'; she never used her US passport from the moment she renounced her American citizenship on 20 October 2010. The dissents: Carpio argued Poe had the burden to prove her biological father was Filipino, which she failed; international law does not 'automatically grant citizenship to foundlings at birth'; Roxas did not cite any international-law principle granting citizenship to foundlings; but a future DNA match to a Filipino parent could still establish her status. De Castro stressed natural-born citizenship is based on blood relationship to a Filipino parent and Poe, admittedly a foundling, does not come within this principle; the 1935 Constitution provided no exception; natural-born citizenship cannot be legislated or conferred by executive acts; the cited international conventions are unratified, and if ratified would grant only naturalized status. Brion argued Poe's citizenship cannot be established, recognized, or presumed under the 1935 Constitution; treaty obligations do not grant outright citizenship; since she was never a Philippine citizen, she had nothing to reacquire; and Bengzon v. HRET is erroneous and should not bind the SET. Senator Legarda summed it up: 'lawyers can argue ad infinitum on legalisms. However, legalisms -- however exalted -- can always be contradicted by other legalisms. But one thing is obvious: In this case, there is no clear violation of our Constitution or our laws. Only by interpretation can anyone really say that Poe is or is not natural-born.' She anchored her vote on the 'unreversed' doctrine in Frivaldo v. Comelec (June 26, 1996) that in case of doubt involving popular sovereignty, interpret to enable the electorate to freely elect their chosen leader. The 'confusing legal gobbledygook' can be simply summed up as a burden-of-proof allocation: the SET majority presumes a foundling natural-born unless rebutted; the dissenters presume the opposite. CJ closes by disclosing he was once a SET member, and that if he were still one he would vote with the majority -- consistent with the Frivaldo decision which he 'had the honor of writing' for the Supreme Court, and with the overarching constitutionally-enshrined social-justice principle of giving more law to those who have less in life.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers a post-victory reality check on the Oct 29, 2015 Arbitral Tribunal jurisdiction award: even if the Philippines wins on the merit, it will still face two grim realities -- enforcement and standoff. Before proceeding, he corrects a 'glaring error' in media coverage: the adjudicating body is neither the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (Itlos, based in Hamburg) nor the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA, based in The Hague), but an ad hoc 'Arbitral Tribunal Constituted Under Annex VII of the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.' When a state signs/ratifies/accedes to Unclos, it must choose one of four tribunals -- Itlos, ICJ, Annex VII ad hoc arbitration, or a special tribunal -- and since the Philippines chose none, it is deemed to have chosen Annex VII. The Tribunal has five members: Judge Rudiger Wolfrum (Germany, PH-nominated); Judge Stanislaw Pawlak (Poland, named by the Itlos president after China opted not to participate); Judge Jean-Pierre Cot (France); Prof. Alfred H. A. Soons (Netherlands); and Judge Thomas A. Mensah of Ghana as presiding arbitrator. The PCA is not a 'court' -- it acts as the Tribunal's 'Registry,' the rough equivalent of the Office of the Clerk of Court of our SC, and has acted as Registry in 11 of 12 Annex VII cases. On enforcement: although the Oct 29 award holds that despite non-participation China 'is bound by any award the Tribunal issues,' the Tribunal has no power to enforce -- no sheriff, policeman, or soldier -- and the Philippines lacks the military, political, and economic muscle to compel China. Filipino international arbitrator Mario E. Valderrama, in several emails, explained the precedent: 'The US, in a dispute with Nicaragua in the International Court of Justice, already did what China is doing -- refuse to participate. And what China is expected to do -- ignore the award -- was already done by the US which even refused to negotiate with the winner, Nicaragua. Being an ICJ case, there were possible mechanisms for enforcement, including recourse to the Security Council. None succeeded.' On standoff: the Philippines essentially asks the Tribunal to invalidate China's nine-dash line as inconsistent with Unclos and to determine whether disputed maritime features are 'islands, rocks, low-tide elevations, or submerged banks,' regardless of who owns or occupies them. Specifically, Scarborough Shoal and eight Spratly features are sought to be declared 'rocks or low-tide elevations or submerged banks' generating no EEZ or continental shelf. A PH victory would allow exploration and development of mineral, oil, and natural resources around these features because they lie within 200 nautical miles of the Zambales and Palawan coasts, unquestionably entitled to EEZ or CS under Unclos. China, on the other hand, maintains these fall inside its nine-dash line and claims 'unquestioned' ownership and sovereignty, justifying its construction of lighthouses, buildings, and airports. The standoff is between the Tribunal's award of maritime entitlements and China's unresolved ownership claim. As the second-largest economy, with a far superior military and a permanent UNSC seat with veto power, China possesses the economic, military, and political clout to back its claims. Given these realities, the Philippines -- even assuming a merit win -- cannot rest on its legal laurels; it must continue diplomacy, negotiation, back-door channeling, and other peaceful settlement modes. CJ closes with the open question whether a merit win will solve the dispute or just incense China and complicate it further, and credits President Aquino, FS del Rosario, SolGen Hilbay (the official 'agent'), international counsel led by Paul Reichler (interestingly Nicaragua's lawyer against the US), and legal-team advisers Justices Carpio and Jardeleza for opting to arbitrate.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains the unanimous Oct 29, 2015 'Award on Jurisdiction and Admissibility' of the 'Arbitral Tribunal constituted under Annex VII to the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea' upholding the Tribunal's jurisdiction over the case filed by the Philippines against China. Our people have every reason to celebrate: had the Tribunal ruled otherwise, the arbitration would have ended immediately as a dismal defeat -- China would have completely won in absentia. Awards are final; unlike in our country, no MR or appeal to any other international tribunal or court is possible. Having assumed jurisdiction, the Tribunal will hold further hearings to decide on the merit. Contrary to some commentators, the Tribunal -- even after assuming jurisdiction -- will not render any decision granting territorial rights to either party; it cannot award ownership over any island or isle claimed or occupied by either side; in fact, the Philippines -- conscious of this limitation -- is not asking for any ruling on 'territorial aspects.' The 151-page Award also explains clearly the respective positions of the parties and how the merits hearing will be conducted. The PH 'Memorial' of June 30, 2014 sets out 15 submissions consolidated into three basic claims. First, the PH 'seeks declarations that the Parties' respective rights and obligations in regard to the waters, seabed, and maritime features of the South China Sea are governed by UNCLOS and that China's claims based on historic rights encompassed within its so-called nine-dash line are inconsistent with Convention and therefore invalid.' (CJ comment: if granted in full, China's omnibus claims over the entire SCS would be illegal under international law; the US sailing a warship within 12 nm of a Chinese-occupied isle signaled conformity to this claim.) Second, the PH 'seeks determination as to whether, under the Convention, certain maritime features claimed by both China and the Philippines are properly characterized as islands, rocks, low tide elevations, or submerged banks.' Islands generate EEZ + CS up to 200 nm; rocks generate territorial sea up to 12 nm; low-tide elevations and submerged banks generate nothing -- and no amount of artificial reclamation can change the status. (CJ comment: if granted in full, all PH-authorized resource explorations and extractions in the WPS would be legally justified.) Third, the PH 'seeks declarations that China has violated the Convention by interfering with the exercise of the Philippines' sovereign rights and freedoms under the Convention and through constructions and fishing activities that have harmed the marine environment.' (CJ comment: if granted in full, the PH would exercise and enjoy maritime, fishing, ecologic, and other similar rights within and beyond its economic zone and continental shelf.) China consistently refused to participate but published a Position Paper dated Dec 7, 2014, wrote many diplomatic Notes Verbales, and sent two letters to Tribunal members, all arguing that the Tribunal has no jurisdiction and that the solution is 'bilateral negotiations and friendly consultations.' China stressed it would not be bound by any decision but did not express any position on the substantive issues. Nonetheless, the Tribunal (a) ensured all communications were promptly delivered to China; (b) granted adequate time to respond; (c) invited comment on procedural steps; (d) provided adequate notice of hearings; (e) promptly provided transcripts of the Hearing on Jurisdiction and all documents submitted; (f) invited comment on anything said during the hearings; (g) made Registry staff available to the Chinese Embassy for any question; (h) reiterated that it remains open to China to participate at any stage. Will our people celebrate again when they receive the Tribunal's decision next year? Abangan! In a postscript clarification re his prior column 'Going for the jugular,' CJ notes that SolGen Hilbay says he would 'really love the chance of crossing swords with' former SolGen Estelito P. Mendoza, but the SBN law requires the OMB's Special Prosecutor (not the SolGen) to defend SBN decisions in the SC.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban summarizes former President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo's plunder appeal to the SC -- asking acquittal on two grounds and 'going for the jugular' by arguing that if she is convicted for approving the release of P366 million to PCSO (from which she did not personally benefit), then President Aquino could be equally guilty of plunder for approving DAP fund releases. Brief background: after the SC granted bail to Sen. Juan Ponce Enrile, CJ wrote 'By the SC, not by the UN' (Oct 18) suggesting Arroyo's lawyers could obtain bail on equal-protection grounds. But her new counsel, Estelito P. Mendoza, did not pursue bail or rely on the controversial 8-4 Enrile decision or the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention's critique; instead he filed a certiorari petition seeking reversal of the SBN's demurrer denial and immediate acquittal. Recall that the SBN Special Division of five voted 3-2 to deny Arroyo's demurrer, ruling that the prosecution had proven her guilt beyond reasonable doubt -- meaning she would be at risk of conviction unless she presented countervailing evidence. Mendoza asked the Court en banc to act on the petition with interim measures: expedite, set for oral argument, suspend further SBN proceedings, and annul the SBN's demurrer denial leading to acquittal. The 116-page petition advanced two major arguments. First, the Information charged Arroyo and nine others with willfully amassing, accumulating, or acquiring ill-gotten wealth 'in the aggregate amount of [P366 million], more or less'; but since the Information did not specify how much each of the 10 accused amassed, the presumption -- under the principle that criminal indictments must be interpreted in favor of the accused -- is that each did so equally, i.e., only P36.6 million each, below the P50M plunder threshold. Second, the gravamen of plunder is that the public officer amasses/accumulates/acquires ill-gotten wealth of at least P50M; yet 'not a single exhibit of the 637 exhibits ... nor a single testimony of the 21 witnesses ... was offered by the prosecution to prove that petitioner amassed, accumulated or acquired even a single peso of the alleged ill-gotten wealth.' Neither was a conspiracy proven. The only act attributed to Arroyo is her scribbled 'Ok' on the requests for the release of PCSO funds -- no PCSO money passed through, was held, or was used by her or for her personal benefit. As a general rule, demurrer-denial certiorari petitions are frowned upon and appealed only after proceedings are completed; but allowing an exception, the SC swiftly acted upon receipt -- stopped the SBN trial scheduled for Nov 3 and directed the SBN to comment. To CJ's mind, these swift actions show the Court was convinced of the prima facie cogency of the petition; but to be fair, it should have also called for oral argument -- cases of lesser public importance have been orally argued for the enlightenment of parties and people at large. Can SolGen Hilbay -- by law the SBN's and prosecution's counsel -- match the clarity, certainty, and creativity of Atty. Mendoza? Nothing less is expected from the 'People's Tribune.' The column closes with a civic-recognition coda: Cheers to the Metrobank Foundation 'Journalists of the Year' -- Inquirer's Nancy Carvajal, GMA Network's Howie Severino, and Rappler's Marites Vitug -- selected by an independent board of judges led by Ombudsman Conchita Carpio Morales, with the Probe Foundation (Che-Che Lazaro) as cosponsor and CJ Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno as guest speaker. MB group chair George S.K. Ty was abroad but ably represented by group vice chair Antonio Abacan Jr., MB president Fabian Dee, MBF president Aniceto Sobrepeña, and MBF senior VP Anjanette Ty-Dy Buncio. As chair of the MBF board of advisers, CJ presided over the ceremonies.
