one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with Liberal Party presidential bet Mar Roxas asking the Comelec to declare Manuel Antonio Roxas a nuisance candidate -- Mar's namesake being one of the 130 who filed COCs for the presidency, alongside 19 for VP and 172 for the 12 Senate seats. These high national posts require only five qualifications: natural-born citizenship, registered voter, ability to read and write, age (40 for President/VP, 35 for Senator), and residence (10 years for President/VP, 2 for Senator). The rationale for these simple qualifications is to give the least of our compatriots an even chance to become our country's leaders, per the constitutional principle that 'the State shall guarantee equal access to opportunities for public service.' While the Constitution theoretically guarantees equal access, it accepts the reality -- per Pamatong v. Comelec (April 13, 2004) -- that 'the State has a compelling interest to ensure that its electoral exercises are rational, objective, and orderly,' since 'the greater the number of candidates, the greater the opportunities for logistical confusion ... a disorderly election is not merely a textbook example of inefficiency, but a rot that erodes faith in our democratic institutions.' Consequently the Comelec has been authorized by the Omnibus Election Code to cancel the COCs of nuisance candidates -- those who (1) put the election process in mockery or disrepute, (2) cause voter confusion by similarity of names, or (3) have no bona fide intention to run. Technically, nuisance candidates are not 'disqualified' because they may in fact possess all five qualifications; their COCs are merely cancelled on the three grounds. CJ agrees with Mar Roxas, but before COCs can be cancelled the Comelec must first ask alleged nuisance candidates to show their bona fides -- usually financial capacity and nationwide-campaign ability -- because 'due process is an indispensable part of our democracy.' The Comelec gave itself an early Dec 10 deadline to weed out nuisance candidates because it must print the automated ballots listing all qualified bets; only printed names can be voted upon and read by PCOS machines. The ballots are 'precinct-specific' -- Manila ballots cannot be used in Makati even where national candidates overlap. Turning to screening other job applicants, while the constitutionally prescribed qualifications for national elective offices are simple, those for appointive ones are difficult: SC Justices need only 2 of the 5 elective qualifications (natural-born, age 40) plus they 'must have been for 15 years or more a judge of a lower court or engaged in the practice of law in the Philippines,' requiring a four-year preparatory law course, a four-year basic law course, and the bar exam (20% average pass rate). Justices must also be 'of proven competence, integrity, probity and independence,' and must pass the JBC -- which acts like the Comelec in screening judicial appointees, but with stricter processes including lengthy interviews, psychological tests, background checks, medical clearances. 88 applicants are vying for the six newly created Sandiganbayan slots, all undergoing JBC screening. In short, elective officials need no scholastic qualities, desirable character traits, or strict screening, while SC Justices must possess at least two academic degrees, pass the bar, and hurdle the JBC. He closes with the reform-by-rhetorical-question: elective officials should have some educational attainment like a college degree and character traits like integrity and honor before they are voted upon -- if appointive officials in lowly rungs are required to possess civil service eligibility including college degrees and moral character, why not the highest officials of our land?

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban examines the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (WGAD) opinion obtained by international celebrity lawyer Amal Alamuddin Clooney, holding that 'the detention of former President [Gloria Macapagal] Arroyo (GMA) was arbitrary and illegal under international law ... with an enforceable right to compensation.' Communications Secretary Coloma responded that GMA 'has been accorded due process and has availed herself of various legal remedies ... in Philippine courts, which have sole jurisdiction to decide on such matters.' CJ adds that the controversy is about a mere opinion of a UN working group lacking the coercive power of a treaty, customary international law, or a decision after trial of an international tribunal like the ICJ, ICC, or Itlos (where the PH WPS claim is being heard). GMA faces two major suits: electoral sabotage (a capital offense) in RTC Pasay for alleged manipulation of the 2007 Maguindanao election results, and plunder (also a capital offense) in the SBN for alleged participation in the illegal use of P366 million in PCSO funds. RTC granted bail on sabotage (affirmed by CA) because the prosecution failed to prove evidence of guilt is strong, but SBN denied bail on plunder. After the prosecution rested in the PCSO case, the defense filed a demurrer arguing the evidence failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; the Special SBN Division voted 3-2 denying the demurrer and ruling the prosecution had proven guilt beyond reasonable doubt -- unless GMA presents countervailing evidence, she would be at risk of conviction. Significantly -- noted in the WGAD opinion -- the demurrer of her four coaccused (former PCSO chair Manuel Morato, former PCSO board members Raymundo Roquero and Jose Taruc, former COA chair Reynaldo Villar) was granted, resulting in their acquittal; former PCSO chair Sergio Valencia was downgraded to malversation (not a capital offense) with P500,000 bail; only GMA and former PCSO executive Benigno Aguas remain neither acquitted nor bailed. Failing in demurrer and bail, GMA filed a motion to transfer confinement from Veterans Memorial Medical Center to her home at 14 Badjao Street, La Vista, Quezon City; in view of the WGAD opinion, she is renewing her plea for bail. CJ believes more compelling than the WGAD opinion -- which, as Coloma pointed out, is not binding on our judiciary -- is the recent SC decision Ponce Enrile v. Sandiganbayan (Aug 18, 2015) granting bail to Sen. Juan Ponce Enrile not because the Ombudsman failed to present 'strong' evidence of guilt but because of (1) Enrile's 'fragile' health (uncontrolled hypertension, arrhythmia, coronary calcifications, exacerbations of asthma-COPD overlap syndrome) and (2) advanced age (over 70 at the time of the alleged offense). Veering from 'strong evidence of guilt' as the sole constitutionally-mandated bail ground in capital offenses, the Court said the SBN 'arbitrarily ignored the objective of bail to ensure the appearance of the accused during the trial.' True, the 8-4 decision was heavily criticized by Justice Marvic Leonen's dissent -- but whether we agree or not, once affirmed final (through denial of the pending MR), it becomes binding precedent. Citing equal protection, GMA's lawyers could obtain bail if they can show that, like Enrile, she is not a flight risk because of fragile health and advanced age. Ineluctably, GMA could secure her longed-for temporary liberty through that SC decision, not the much-publicized WGAD opinion. CJ closes with a postscript congratulating his high school chum Filemon T. Berba Jr. for his book 'Leadership for Extraordinary Results': of the 1,200 Mapa High School Class of 1954 graduates, Berba was indisputably the best in math, whose phenomenal grasp of numbers inspired CJ to aspire to be a chemical engineer -- but his strong-willed father compelled him to be a lawyer. CJ has tried to become not just 'a legal technician who tinkers with and repairs legal imperfections' but a 'social engineer who helps build our nation, with law as my basic tool.' Even in his sunset years he still strives to be the engineer that Jun Berba inspired him to be when they were carving their lives in high school. Acclaimed at the book launching, Berba has rightfully become 'the top honcho -- the chief justice, as it were -- of his engineering-management profession. Cheers!'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban argues for extending the Frivaldo doctrine to Sen. Grace Poe's natural-born citizenship case. He has always believed that doubts on legal issues involving elections and popular sovereignty should be resolved in favor of letting our people decide through the ballot -- whenever possible, election issues (not involving crimes or obvious violations) should be settled by voters, not judges and lawyers. A case in point is Frivaldo v. Comelec (June 28, 1996). Juan Frivaldo was overwhelmingly voted governor of Sorsogon by a wide margin of 27,000 votes in 1988 and 57,000 in 1992, but was twice ousted by the SC for having lost his Philippine citizenship in 1983 when naturalized as American. Undaunted, he ran and won again as governor by 20,000 votes in 1995. Again his victory was challenged by the same candidate he defeated; this time Frivaldo claimed to have reacquired Philippine citizenship under RA 7160 by taking his oath of allegiance at 2 PM on June 30, 1995, the day he assumed office. Raul Lee, his opponent, argued Frivaldo was twice ruled an alien and should have possessed citizenship on the last day for COC filing -- or at the latest on the May 8, 1995 election day -- not on the June 30 assumption date; Lee also attacked the haste in processing the repatriation because Frivaldo filed his application only on the day prior, June 29, 1995. The case was assigned to CJ as a new SC associate justice just after his 1995 assumption -- 'the decision I had the honor of writing for the Court upheld Frivaldo's election.' The Court ruled that 'decisions declaring the acquisition or denial of citizenship cannot govern a person's future status with finality ... because a person may subsequently reacquire, or for that matter lose, his citizenship under any of the modes recognized by law'; the two earlier ousters did not bind Frivaldo's current status. Noting the law did not specify when a candidate must possess citizenship, the Court held it sufficient that Frivaldo became a citizen at assumption of office, not necessarily at COC filing or campaign period. Underlying this liberality is CJ's basic legal philosophy upholding popular sovereignty: 'At balance, the question really boils down to a choice of philosophy and perception of how to interpret and apply laws relating to elections: literal or liberal; the letter or the spirit; the naked provision or its ultimate purpose; legal syllogism or substantial justice; in isolation or in the context of social conditions; harshly against or gently in favor of the voters' obvious choice. In applying election laws, it would be far better to err in favor of popular sovereignty than to be right in complex but little understood legalisms.' Noteworthy too is Justice (later CJ) Reynato S. Puno's concurring opinion: 'I concur in the path-breaking ponencia of Mr. Justice Panganiban which is pro-people and pierces the myopia of legalism ... In cases where the sovereign will of the people is at stake, we must not only be legally right, but also politically correct. We cannot fail by making the people succeed.' The issue in Frivaldo's case was his total lack of citizenship, while in Poe's it is merely her alleged lack of natural-born status -- most critics concede her naturalized citizenship. With far more reasons, therefore, the Constitution and laws governing her case should be more liberally construed by letting the 50 million Filipino voters decide. An even better way of removing doubts is the DNA test. For many years the SC was not convinced of DNA testing's legal viability, but starting with Tijing v. CA (March 8, 2001) and People v. Vallejo (May 9, 2002) the Court changed its mind. In Herrera v. Alba (June 15, 2005), 'the Court moved from the issue of according official recognition to DNA analysis as evidence to the issue of observance of procedures in conducting DNA analysis.' Thereafter, the Court issued on Oct 2, 2007 (to take effect Oct 15, 2007) the Rule on DNA Evidence formally laying down procedural protocols. Poe was reported by her lawyer George Garcia to have undergone a DNA matching test to answer her personal quest of 'Who am I?'; to be legally acceptable, the test must be done pursuant to the Rule's protocols. If her biological father, as shown by the DNA test, was a Filipino at the time of her birth, then she is unquestionably a natural-born citizen.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers a Q&A explainer on Grace Poe's natural-born citizenship in 13 questions, expanding on two prior columns of June 14 and 21, 2015. Q1: Why is natural-born citizenship important? Only natural-born citizens are qualified to be president, VP, senator, congressman, or SC justice -- a contrary final decision would remove Poe as senator, bar her from running, and prohibit her from serving. Q2: What tribunals are authorized? The SET has jurisdiction over senator-qualification cases; the Comelec hears presidential-qualification petitions after COC filing; decisions may be elevated to the SC. Q3: Which Constitution governs? The 1935 Constitution, because it was the basic law in 1968 when Poe was born, listing five citizen sources: (1) those who were citizens at the adoption of the Constitution, (2) those born in the PH of foreign parents who before adoption had been elected to public office, (3) those whose fathers are citizens of the Philippines, (4) those whose mothers are citizens (with election upon majority), (5) those naturalized in accordance with law. The 1935 (and the current) Constitution also adopts 'the generally accepted principles of international law as part of the law of the Nation' -- by this 'doctrine of incorporation,' customary international laws are as binding as statutes. Q4: Which international instruments? Mainly (a) the 1930 Hague Convention on the Conflict of Nationality Laws, (b) the 1948 UDHR, and (c) the 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness -- nationality is synonymous with citizenship in international law. Q5: What 1961-Convention provision applies? Article 2: 'A foundling found in the territory of a Contracting State shall, in the absence of proof to the contrary, be considered to have been born in the territory of parents possessing the nationality of that State.' Q6: PH is not a signatory -- why bound? Because those provisions have become 'generally accepted principles of international law,' as binding as statutes passed by Congress. Q7: Who are natural-born citizens? Under the 1987 Constitution, 'those who are citizens of the Philippines from birth without having to perform any act to acquire or perfect their Philippine citizenship.' Q8: Why is Poe natural-born? Because under Article 2 of the 1961 Convention, she -- a foundling found in Iloilo -- is deemed to have Filipino parents; perforce she is natural-born since her presumed father is accorded Philippine citizenship. Q9: Isn't she naturalized under item 5 -- naturalized in accordance with (international) law? No -- it was her parents who acquired Philippine citizenship pursuant to international law, but she derived her citizenship from her presumed Filipino father; thus she is a citizen from birth without having to do anything. Q10: May her biological father be proven to be an alien? Yes, but the burden of proof belongs to challengers; unless such proof is presented, her parents continue to be presumed Filipinos. Q11: She became a US citizen after marriage -- how did she reacquire natural-born status? By taking an oath of allegiance to the Philippines under the Dual Citizenship Law (RA 9225) and renouncing American citizenship pursuant to American law. Q12: Aside from the doctrine-of-incorporation interaction, can she prove natural-born status by other methods? Yes, by undergoing a DNA test showing her biological father is a Filipino; the SC has issued many decisions affirming the binding force of DNA tests. Q13: How are DNA tests conducted and can they conclusively prove parentage? Yes, if done according to the protocols laid down by the SC. More on this in a future column.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban restates his death-penalty abolition position, occasioned by Mary Jane Veloso's reprieve in Indonesia. Our people are united in sympathizing with and helping Veloso, the poor Filipino female domestic worker convicted of heroin smuggling in Indonesia despite her defense that she was merely duped into carrying the prohibited drug in her suitcase; she was nonetheless sentenced to death in October 2010. Due to a moratorium then in effect, the sentence was not carried out immediately, but newly-elected Indonesian President Joko Widodo lifted the moratorium and she was scheduled for execution by firing squad on the evening of April 29 this year together with eight others. At the last moment, Widodo -- heeding P-Noy's plea -- granted her a reprieve so she could testify at the trial in the Philippines of her alleged recruiters, Maria Cristina Sergio and Sergio's live-in partner Julius Lacanilao. The other eight convicts were executed despite ringing protests of many world leaders. Veloso's heart-wrenching story reminds CJ of 'the grim finality of death as a penalty.' According to Amnesty International, the death penalty has been outlawed in 140 countries as an inhuman and ineffective deterrent. Our 1987 Constitution has also barred the imposition of the death penalty 'unless for compelling reasons involving heinous crimes, the Congress hereafter provides for it,' and the Charter reduced death sentences already imposed to reclusion perpetua. Citing the constitutional exception, Congress enacted RA 7659 prescribing death for certain crimes it defined as 'heinous.' In People v. Echegaray (June 25, 1996 and Feb 7, 1997), the SC upheld the constitutionality of RA 7659, adjudged Echegaray guilty of raping a 10-year-old girl, and meted out the death penalty by lethal injection -- the first under RA 7659. Together with two other justices, CJ dissented from this and all other judgments imposing death on the ground that RA 7659 was unconstitutional because Congress failed (1) to show 'compelling reasons' to revive death and (2) the crimes for which it was prescribed were not 'heinous.' Apart from these legal grounds, CJ also strongly felt the death penalty unfairly targeted the poor, the weak, and the underprivileged; though many decisions were per curiam, he has on many occasions admitted his dissenting opinions and votes. To help Mary Jane and her family escape the agony of firing-squad death, he revisits his arguments. The death penalty militates against 'the poor, the powerless and the marginalized.' The best example: Echegaray's counsel -- like Mary Jane's -- was 'less than competent and enthusiastic' in defending him; the crucial constitutionality issue was not raised in the trial court, not even in the SC, until Echegaray's counsel was replaced by the Free Legal Assistance Group, which belatedly brought it up only in the Supplemental MR. To the poor and unlettered, complex law in strange incomprehensible language and intimidating judicial proceedings engender 'unfounded at times, but unhealthy nevertheless ... a sense of the unequal balance of the scales of justice.' Precisely because the underprivileged are what they are, they require and deserve a greater degree of protection from Constitution, laws, officials, and courts so that, in spite of their situation, they can be empowered to rise above themselves and their poverty. The basic postulate is that ultimately we all want to better ourselves and cannot do so individually to a significant degree if we are unable to advance as an entire people and nation. All the glory provisions of the Constitution aim to help the poor -- yet we were faced with a penalty that effectively inflicted the ultimate punishment on the poor and disadvantaged, so obviously final and irreversibly permanent that it erased all hopes of reform, of change for the better. After a long battle in courts of law and public opinion, Congress finally repealed the Death Penalty Law effective June 30, 2006. Had Congress not abolished it, P-Noy (and others who labored for Mary Jane) would not have had the 'moral ascendancy' to plead for her life. This is one more reason why the death penalty should remain dead -- in deference to and for the sake of our poor, struggling OFWs, many of whom are virtually and unfairly lined up before firing squads in many countries of the world.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban ties Poe's foundling citizenship debate to a broader UN-policy roster, opening: 'The rise to fame of Sen. Grace Poe and the stratospheric viewership ratings of primetime telenovelas on abandoned children (like Niño, Nathaniel, Dream Dad and Munting Heredera) have riveted public attention on foundlings and orphans, to the delight of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).' These children have been discriminated against because they have no known biological parents; they suffer lack of lineage, parental care, family support, inheritance, and succession. Even those legally adopted, cared for, and unconditionally loved by foster parents -- while assured of the civil rights of legitimate children -- are many times restricted in political rights to citizenship and residency, the prerequisites to vote and to be voted to public office. Our constitutions (current or past) and statutes do not expressly grant them these rights -- CJ had to research 'generally-accepted principles of international law' to conclude Poe possesses natural-born citizenship (see prior columns of June 14 and 21, 2015). Natural-born citizenship is a required qualification for the top officials of our country -- president, VP, senators, congressmen, and SC justices. Fortunately, the UN -- since its founding more than half a century ago -- has been fighting for equal treatment of all peoples of the world, regardless of race, color, religion, language, sex, political opinions, ethnic origin, age, and accidents of birth. To alleviate suffering of persons devoid of citizenship, the 1954 Convention Relating to the Status of Stateless Persons mandated the 'Contracting Parties to facilitate the assimilation and naturalization of stateless persons.' More precisely, the 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness, in Article 2, addressed orphans directly: 'A foundling found in the territory of a Contracting State shall, in the absence of proof to the contrary, be considered to have been born within that territory of parents possessing the nationality of that State.' Thus, a foundling found in the Philippines is deemed to have Filipino parents; it follows that under our Constitution that foundling is presumed natural-born and qualified to run for president or VP. CJ's thesis is simple: in our democracy, our 50 million voters should choose our highest officials, not our unelected and politically unaccountable though learned and wise SC justices. For more than 50 years, the UNHCR -- currently represented in the Philippines by Bernard Kerblat -- has been urging PH to accede to the 1961 Convention. True, express accession is not necessary to recognize foundling citizenship because PH has already adopted, acceded, and ratified the UDHR, ICCPR, and CRC. Nonetheless, accession would benefit other disadvantaged individuals like internally-displaced persons. In an aide-mémoire, the UNHCR's PH office said that in February 2015 various agencies convened to develop a national action plan to end statelessness, with accession to the 1961 Convention as a goal by the end of 2016. The Philippines is a country with about 10 million citizens working abroad -- thus it has a keen interest in protecting non-Filipinos within its shores, in reciprocity for its hope that its nationals abroad would in equal measure be treated fairly and justly. It is therefore fitting and proper that it cooperates, as it actually does, with the UNHCR in accommodating and hosting persons of concern to the UNHCR, including: internally-displaced individuals (those forced to flee homes due to armed conflicts, human-rights violations, or natural/man-made disasters -- including the Rohingyas, 'the new boat people' who fled Burma/Bangladesh); refugees (those unable to return on well-grounded fears of persecution for race, religion, or political belief); and stateless persons (those not considered nationals of any state, who suffer travel discrimination for lack of passport). Justice Secretary Leila de Lima has issued Circular No. 58 outlining the procedure for accepting these maltreated persons into the Philippines, announcing PH's willingness to host the Rohingyas. Poe has made it her mission to take care of abandoned children -- she filed Senate Bill No. 2892 to strengthen the system for the birth registration of children needing special protection, including foundlings like her.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the third installment of his series on PNoy's daang matuwid Sona-cited achievements, following his prior columns on the Maguindanao massacre trial (A375) and the PDAF cases of three senators (A374). On a specific point from the prior column, he notes that on August 11 the Supreme Court released a Resolution granting Senator Enrile's petition for a bill of particulars but denied his prayer to annul his arrest and detention -- the more crucial bail petition is still pending. This column takes up the third set of Sona-cited cases: those involving former President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo. Two cases have been filed against her. The first charged her with electoral sabotage for her alleged role in the 2007 Maguindanao election manipulation; her coaccused include former Maguindanao governor Andal Ampatuan Sr. (recently passed away) and Lintang Bedol, the former provincial Comelec supervisor of Maguindanao. Because she was indicted with a capital offense, she was arrested by the Regional Trial Court of Pasay, but on June 12, 2012, the RTC granted her bail on the ground that the prosecution's evidence -- the testimony of a lone witness -- was not strong; the Court of Appeals dismissed the prosecution's appeal. However, she was not released because of the second case: plunder before the Sandiganbayan First Division for the alleged unauthorized disbursement of P366 million in PCSO funds. After the prosecution rested, GMA and her coaccused filed a demurrer. Because the three members of the First Division were divided, a Special Division of five was created per the SBN Internal Rules. On April 6, 2015, a majority of three (Justices Efren Dela Cruz, Napoleon Inoturan, and Rafael Lagos as ponente) denied the demurrer, holding a prima facie case of plunder; unless GMA and her remaining coaccused (former PCSO executive Benigno Aguas) present countervailing evidence, they would be convicted. The minority of two (Justices Rodolfo Ponferrada and Alex Quiroz) opined that the elements of plunder were not proven; charges should be downgraded to malversation, entitling GMA and Aguas to bail. The coaccused outcomes are stark: former PCSO chair Manuel Morato, former board members Raymundo Roquero and Jose Taruc, and former COA chair Reynaldo Villar were all acquitted; former PCSO chair Sergio Valencia was downgraded to malversation with P500,000 bail. Frustrated, GMA filed on April 8, 2015 a motion to transfer her detention from the Veterans Memorial Medical Center to her house at 14 Badjao Street, La Vista, Quezon City, averring she is not a flight risk because she is '68 years old, has undergone three spinal surgeries, remains frail and thin, and to this day enjoys the presumption of innocence... [and] hopes that [her] house arrest can help her recuperate and heal more quickly and fully.' Two precedents support the motion: former President Estrada was allowed to be transferred to his Tanay, Rizal farm during his plunder detention under GMA's own presidency, and during the Marcos regime opposition Senator Jovito Salonga was placed 'under house arrest in the custody of Mrs. Lydia Salonga.' Despite the SBN's MR being pending, hearing on GMA's countervailing evidence is scheduled for August 26. Like the other Sona-cited achievements, GMA's cases will not be decided within PNoy's term ending June 30, 2016 -- CJ promises to answer what happens after he relinquishes the presidency next Sunday.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers the second of a three-column series on PNoy's Sona-cited daang matuwid achievements -- focusing on the PDAF (Priority Development Assistance Fund) cases against Senators Jinggoy Estrada, Bong Revilla, and Juan Ponce Enrile. After DOJ preliminary investigation and OOO probable-cause findings, separate Informations were filed and raffled to three different Sandiganbayan divisions: the First Division for Revilla, the Third for Enrile, the Fifth for Estrada. When charged with capital offenses, accused usually launch three major battles to win their freedom: (1) an initial battle to stop the court from issuing warrants of arrest and detention on the ground that the Information and supporting documents do not show 'probable cause'; (2) an ensuing fight for bail on the ground that the prosecution's evidence is not 'strong'; and (3) a final battle for acquittal on the ground that evidence failed to prove guilt 'beyond reasonable doubt.' Interlocutory orders along the way are often challenged via certiorari petitions in the SC. Estrada: the Fifth Division found probable cause; the SC upheld it; the SBN is now conducting bail hearings every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. Three certiorari petitions are pending -- two by Estrada (to exclude alleged AMLC-reported bank transactions, and to suppress Benhur Luy's cash/check reports and testimony) and one by the OOO (contesting the SBN's refusal to transfer Estrada from the PNP Custodial Center to Camp Bagong Diwa in Taguig). Revilla: probable-cause certiorari dismissed by the SC; SBN fully heard and denied bail Dec 1, 2014; MR denied March 26, 2015; pretrial set Sept 30 -- proceedings in a more advanced stage than Estrada's. Three SC petitions pending: two by Revilla (probable cause and bail denial) and one by the OOO (transfer to Camp Bagong Diwa). Enrile, taking a more proactive stance via counsels Estelito Mendoza and Eleazar Reyes, is challenging the usual procedure with two SC certiorari petitions. First: the Information for plunder filed by the OOO is invalid because it did not allege enough specific facts to enable him to prepare his defense (bill of particulars). Second: the Constitution guarantees bail to the accused at all times -- the only exception being when (1) the evidence of guilt is strong AND (2) the penalty prescribed is reclusion perpetua or life imprisonment. Until the prosecution proves its evidence is 'strong,' the accused cannot be detained; the present procedure of immediately detaining accused prior to that ruling is illogical and unconstitutional. He further argues that even if convicted, reclusion perpetua cannot be imposed because he should be credited with two mitigating circumstances: old age (over 70 years) and voluntary surrender. The SC will resolve these petitions soon; should Enrile win any of them, he may be freed from detention. In sum, given that trial on the merits has not even begun for any of the three senators, these plunder and graft cases cannot be decided during PNoy's term, which ends on June 30, 2016.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens his August 2, 2015 column -- the first in a three-column daang-matuwid series alongside A374 (three-senator PDAF) and A373 (GMA cases) -- with PNoy's Sona excerpt criticizing his predecessor's impunity: 'Every government official takes an oath to do right by our countrymen and to uphold the law. But it was clear: Our predecessor did precisely the opposite. We were all witnesses to the most appalling example, when 58 Filipinos were massacred in November 2009... The worst offense of all: their belief that they could get away with it, because they were in power.' (CJP notes the official English translation did not catch the exact lingual nuance of PNoy's original Filipino.) The opening reopened wounds in the long-winded trial of the November 23, 2009 'gory shooting, mangling and back-hoeing' of 58 defenseless civilians in Maguindanao -- six months before the 2010 presidential election, making the multiple murder a centerpiece of PNoy's search for justice. Many local and foreign benefactors -- like the Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility through Melinda de Jesus -- view this not only as a deadly example of criminal impunity but also as a shameless assault on press freedom, given 32 of the victims were media persons. Yet after five years, the five consolidated murder cases originally filed against 197 accused -- 15 of them surnamed Ampatuan, with Datu Andal 'Unsay' Ampatuan Jr. as main accused -- remain in the trial stage. The cases were given prime attention: venue moved from faraway Maguindanao to RTC Quezon City (better security and media focus, but logistical issues); Judge Jocelyn Solis-Reyes -- competent, with integrity and independence -- was relieved of all other cases and assigned two assisting judges; the SC directed implementation of the Judicial Affidavit Rule (no lengthy direct-examination Q&A; cross-examination retained), authorized partial judgments, and allowed continued trial despite pending interlocutory appeals. To date, of the 197 accused: 1 was dropped, 1 discharged as state's witness, 1 dismissed/virtually acquitted, 4 died (including clan patriarch Andal Ampatuan Sr.). 12 public prosecutors + 7 private prosecutors face 26 defense law firms; transcripts have thickened to 48 volumes and records to 101 'humongous' volumes; the court has heard 174 witnesses (93 prosecution, 23 defense, 58 private complainants) during continuous trials mostly at Camp Bagong Diwa in Taguig. Judge Solis-Reyes and her two assisting judges have disposed of 472 trial 'incidents' with only 22 remaining; they have resolved 59 bail petitions, with only Unsay Ampatuan's bail as the major one left. The court is now hearing the prosecution's evidence-in-chief simultaneously; the prosecution has rested against nine accused (Bong Andal, Saudi Mukamad, Talembo Masukat, Dexton Sapula, Abas Anongan, Kumini Inggo, Warden Legawan, Takpan Dilon, Mohammad Sangki) and expects to fully rest before year-end. But the many defense counsels will still present their sides -- CJP doubts any decision will be rendered before PNoy's term ends June 30, 2016. He closes with the 'Acid test': during his short stint as Chief Justice he focused his judicial reform program on the four 'Acid' problems that corrode justice -- (1) Access to justice by the poor, (2) Corruption, (3) Incompetence of some judges, (4) Delay in delivery of quality justice. From the start of his term up to his last Sona, PNoy has repeatedly alluded to the Maguindanao massacre as the grand example of his predecessor's impunity that he vowed to vindicate and eradicate -- ineluctably making the search for justice in Maguindanao the acid test of the criminal justice system. This system was instituted under the 1987 Constitution to shield the innocent and underprivileged from the strong arm of the state that the Marcos dictatorship wrongly employed to violate civil liberties and perpetuate itself. Ironically, however, these very rights are at times misused and abused to delay and frustrate the dispensation of justice. How to prevent this misuse and abuse is the other litmus challenge -- and in CJ's humble view, the long-term focus of judicial and prosecutorial reforms.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes a jurisprudence-methodology essay triggered by the Catholic Bishops' Conference's plenary conference where he briefed them a few days earlier and was asked: 'Are the Supreme Court justices in the Philippines divided along philosophical lines, like their counterparts in the United States?' The question arose from his prior column on Obergefell v. Hodges, which he had explained was decided 5-4 between four liberal and four conservative justices, with Justice Anthony Kennedy breaking the tie. Unlike their US counterparts, PH SC justices do not vote along philosophical lines -- CJ finds no clear ideological divide. Do they decide based on religious belief? No, not necessarily: some Catholic jurists have voted against Catholic teachings, on legal not religious grounds. Do they decide based on school loyalties? No: 7 of the 15 current justices are UP Law graduates but still voted on opposite sides in many cases; in the US, 5 of 9 SCOTUS magistrates are Harvard alumni but also voted regardless of school affiliation. The sharpest rebuttal: GMA would not be in detention now if 10 of the 15 incumbent justices being her appointees made them loyal to her. Kennedy was appointed by Reagan as an expected conservative but now swings between groups. Obama appointed Sotomayor and Kagan as known liberals; McCain vowed to appoint conservative self-restrained jurists opposing liberal activists. No such pronouncements are heard from Philippine presidential candidates. In general, how do judges decide cases? The analytical school (John Austin) posits F×L=D: a decision is simply the result of applying law to given facts; but this cannot fully explain judgment in complicated cases. The sociological school (Harvard Dean Roscoe Pound) offers S×P=D: stimuli times personality equals decision; the law and facts are the two main stimuli, but there are others -- dire consequences on public interest, illness, and what CJ calls the 'plague of ships': kinship, relationship, friendship, and fellowship. The personality of a judge encompasses education, training, intelligence, legal philosophy, integrity, character, and prior opinions. Pound looked at law as social engineering, not a mathematical tool. Process-wise, every petition or appeal is raffled to a 'member-in-charge' (MIC) who determines whether the case goes to the banc (all 15 justices) or one of three court divisions (5 each). The MIC prepares a facts/issues summary and recommends: dismiss outright for lack of merit, or require a comment from respondents, and whether to grant a TRO. After comment, the Court may dismiss via resolution, require oral argument, or ask for written memoranda. After memoranda, the MIC submits a disposal report; deliberations follow; if the majority agrees, the MIC writes the decision; if the majority disagrees, another justice is assigned to write it and the MIC submits a dissent; other justices may write concurring or dissenting opinions.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes for the CBCP's semestral three-day meeting (July 11-12-13), which will discuss both current events and Pope Francis' recent encyclical Laudato Si. On current events, the bishops will look at the long shadow cast by the US Supreme Court's decision in Obergefell v. Hodges (June 26, 2015) -- passed 5-4 and penned by Justice Anthony Kennedy -- compelling all 50 US states to issue marriage licenses to same-sex couples 'on the same terms and conditions as marriages between persons of the opposite sex.' The majority held that denying marriage licenses to same-sex couples while granting them to opposite-sex couples constitutes a denial of the right to liberty under the due process clause and discrimination based on sex under the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment -- akin to denying school entry to a student because of Black color. The four dissenters employed scathing words. CJ Roberts accused the majority of judicial legislation: 'Five lawyers have closed the debate and enacted their own vision of marriage... Those who founded our country would not recognize the majority's conception of the judicial role.' Scalia charged the majority with 'hubris,' its decision 'couched in a style that is as pretentious as its content is egoistic' with 'profundities [that] are often profoundly incoherent.' Thomas argued that 'liberty has been understood as freedom from government action, not entitlement to government benefits' and warned the decision threatens religious liberty. Alito decried it as usurping 'the constitutional right of the people to decide whether to keep or alter the traditional understanding of marriage.' To fully comprehend these acidic exchanges, the conservative wing -- Roberts/Scalia/Thomas/Alito -- believes the US Constitution should be interpreted in accordance with the original intent of the framers, that the Court should exercise judicial restraint and defer to elected officials, and that state governments should prevail over the federal. The liberal wing -- Breyer/Ginsburg/Sotomayor/Kagan -- believes the Charter should be interpreted to solve current problems, which may require inventing new concepts like Miranda rights, the right to abortion, and the right against racial segregation. Kennedy holds the swing vote; typically, as in Obergefell, he tilts the balance -- this is why the US Supreme Court is often referred to as the 'Kennedy Court' rather than the 'Roberts Court.' The CBCP is watching the long shadow because: (1) PH's 1935, 1973, and 1987 Constitutions carry due process and equal protection clauses in almost identical words; (2) a petition anchored on these clauses had already been filed in our SC on May 18, 2015 -- even before Obergefell -- to nullify portions of the Family Code defining marriage between a man and a woman; (3) after Obergefell, a congressman announced a bill legalizing same-sex marriage. CJ predicts the bishops, Catholic and other religious groups, and concerned citizens will fight this petition and bill as passionately as they did the Reproductive Health Law.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban follows up his 'Grace Poe's residency' column with a Q&A on reader reactions, anchored on one central legal concern: the Maquiling v. Comelec (April 16, 2013) ruling that the use of a US passport after renouncing American citizenship effectively reverses the renunciation and disqualifies one from being elected to public office. He had concluded last Sunday that Poe's domicile of origin was Jaro, Iloilo; that California became her domicile by operation of law after her marriage; and that when she returned for good to the Philippines after the death of Fernando Poe Jr., she acquired a new domicile of choice -- with several acts in 2005 and early 2006 showing her intent to remain -- leading him to conclude she would surpass the 10-year residency requirement by Election Day, May 9, 2016. But a pen-named emailer, Agueda Kahabagan, presented immigration records showing Poe arriving in the Philippines using a US passport on November 9, 2003, December 13, 2004, September 2005, March 11, 2006, July 5, 2006, July 23, 2007, October 5, 2008, May 21, 2009, and August 3, 2009, and departing on July 2, 2006, July 26, 2006, September 11, 2006, November 1, 2006, October 31, 2007, April 20, 2009, July 31, 2009, and December 27, 2009 aboard PAL Flight 112 -- asking: under Maquiling, is Poe disqualified? An anonymous reader replies that Poe renounced her American citizenship in October 2010 -- after her last US-passport use on December 27, 2009 -- and has not used it since. CJ's analysis: if the anonymous reader is factually correct, Maquiling will not affect Poe and her residency still surpasses the 10-year requirement; if he is wrong, all Poe needs to do is renounce again her American citizenship before filing her COC, since Maquiling saw nothing wrong in executing more than one renunciation affidavit. The use of a foreign passport after renouncing foreign citizenship does not divest Filipino citizenship regained by repatriation under the Dual Citizenship Law. Residency is not interrupted by taking a renunciation or allegiance oath -- Japson v. Comelec (Jan 19, 2009); even foreigners may establish Philippine domicile -- Cordora v. Comelec (Feb 19, 2009). Reader Andrew Ramoso asked why the Constitution uses 'resident of' when it means 'domiciliary of' -- CJ replies that the law has its own interchangeable technical words, just as medicine has tongue-twisting terminologies better memorized by physicians scribbling seemingly inscrutable prescriptions. To those who asked whether CJP is campaigning or voting for Poe: that is a 'misleading question' -- it assumes a fact not in existence, since Poe has not decided whether to run or for what position. His columns are objective legal views, not political endorsements. CJ makes his election choices based on: (1) whether there is a candidate, (2) for what position, (3) their platform, and (4) the opposing candidates and their platforms.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers the doctrinal anchor for Grace Poe's presidential eligibility on residency. The Constitution states no person may be elected President (or Vice President) unless he is 'a resident of the Philippines for at least 10 years immediately preceding such election.' In election law, 'residence' is equated with 'domicile,' not necessarily a home address -- a man may have several residences but only one domicile. There are three kinds: domicile of origin (a child follows the parents'), domicile by operation of law, and domicile of choice (freely made by a person of legal age), which 'imports not only the intention to reside in one fixed place but also personal presence in that place, coupled with conduct indicative of such intention.' Three settled rules govern: everyone must always have one domicile; once established, it remains until a new one is acquired; a person can have only one domicile at any given time. Applied to Poe: as a foundling found in Jaro, Iloilo, she acquired the domicile (and citizenship) of her parents who are presumed Filipinos -- so her domicile of origin is Jaro, Iloilo. After she married an American and moved to the US, she lost her domicile of origin and followed her husband's domicile in America. When she and her husband moved back permanently after FPJ's death, she acquired a new domicile of choice. Settled jurisprudence confirms: in Marcos v. Comelec (Sept 18, 1995), the Court held that the fact of residence -- not a COC statement -- is decisive; Imelda's honest mistake of writing 'seven months' for a congressional seat did not foreclose her; similarly, Poe's honest mistake of writing 'six years and six months' in her Senate COC is not binding proof. Cordora v. Comelec (Feb 19, 2009) held that even foreigners may establish Philippine domicile; Japson v. Comelec (Jan 19, 2009) ruled that a former Filipino naturalized abroad may re-establish domicile here even before reacquisition of citizenship; Jalosjos v. Comelec (Oct 19, 2010) held that abandonment of an Australian home, renunciation of Australian citizenship, and settling in Zamboanga Sibugay show 'intent to change domicile for good'; Maquiling v. Comelec (April 16, 2013) clarified that using an American passport after renouncing American citizenship effectively reverses the renunciation. Poe's intent to acquire a new domicile of choice (animus manendi) is proven by her return to the Philippines in the first half of 2005, enrollment of her children here in June 2005, property purchase in late 2005, and construction of her QC family home in early 2006. Her intent to abandon her old domicile (animus non revertendi) is shown by the delisting of her children from their American schools in May 2005 and the sale of her California home in April 2006. Her physical presence is evidenced by passport entries and other authentic documents. Based on these acts, facts, laws and jurisprudence -- unless belied by contravening facts unknown to CJP -- Senator Poe will surpass the 10-year residency requirement come Election Day, May 9, 2016. In a postscript, CJP congratulates Dean Raul Pangalangan for his ICC election, noting he tried for over 10 years to help him land a Supreme Court seat -- 'But the Lord did not will it. Now I know why. Because he was meant for something bigger, loftier and better-suited to his unique specialization.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban follows up his foundational Grace Poe citizenship column with a Q&A on reader reactions. The most exhilarating: an early email from UNHCR's Bernard Kerblat calling CJP's opinion 'a pleasant soothing philharmonic orchestra composition to our ears,' providing badly needed clarification that a foundling in the Philippines is not stateless -- contrary to some uninformed voices -- and declaring 'YES, the UNHCR FULLY supports' CJP's call for PH accession to the 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness. On June 16, Kerblat, deputy Yasser Saad, and legal aide Iya Gallardo visited CJP at home; they explained that during a December 7, 2011 ministerial meeting, the Philippine panel pledged to initiate accession to the 1961 Convention, and that in February 2015 various executive agencies convened to develop a national plan to end statelessness by 2016. Paulino Yusi, a Makati lawyer, objected that Article 2's presumption of Filipino parents does not ipso facto make Poe natural-born -- under the 1935 Constitution, Filipino-mother/foreign-father children need to elect Philippine citizenship upon reaching majority. CJP answers: the 1961 Convention refers to 'parents,' so it is enough that her presumed father is Filipino; Poe derives natural-born citizenship from her presumed Filipino father and need not elect, because her presumed father already conferred that status at birth. Joselito Basilio from Dubai argued Article 2 is based on jus soli while our Constitution is based on jus sanguinis -- incompatible. CJP answers: there is no incompatibility; the 1961 Convention simply says a foundling is presumed to have parents who are nationals of the country where found, and under PH Constitution citizenship follows the father or mother. Ray Lopez from California praised CJP for explaining the issue 'devoid of bias' and criticized critics as 'intellectual prostitutes.' CJP clarifies he met Poe only once at a public forum and has had no other official or personal association. The tougher question, posed by multi-awarded journalist Marites Vitug and Eric Damasing: while Poe may have acquired natural-born citizenship via generally-accepted-principles, she lost it when she married her American husband -- and by taking an oath of allegiance to reacquire it, did she perform 'an act to acquire or perfect her Philippine citizenship,' thereby losing natural-born status? CJP answers no, citing David v. Agbay (March 18, 2015): under RA 9225, natural-born citizens who became citizens of another country before the law's effectivity reacquire Philippine citizenship upon taking the oath, while those who became foreign citizens after the law's effectivity retain their citizenship upon taking the same oath. Since Poe belongs to the first category -- a reacquirer, not a retainer -- she reacquired her original natural-born citizenship. Her taking the oath of allegiance is not 'an act to acquire or perfect'; she had already acquired and perfected her citizenship at birth. Ineluctably, she reacquired the same original natural-born status.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with an ALL-CAPS declaration: 'CRITICS CHALLENGE the citizenship qualifications of Sen. Grace Poe to run for, be elected to and hold a higher public office allegedly because (1) as a foundling, she was stateless, (2) by her marriage, she acquired the American citizenship of her husband, and (3) her adoption by Fernando Poe Jr. and Susan Roces did not confer natural-born citizenship on her. I respectfully disagree.' Under the 1987 Constitution, natural-born citizens are 'those who are citizens of the Philippines from birth without having to perform any act to acquire or perfect their Philippine citizenship.' Since natural-born citizenship requires citizenship 'from birth' and Poe was born in 1968, the governing law is the 1935 Constitution -- which neither expressly conferred citizenship on foundlings, nor did any statute of that era. But the framers explained that an express provision was unnecessary since it could be determined from international law. Both Constitutions adopt 'the generally accepted principles of international law as part of the law of the Nation.' Under Mijares v. Ranada (April 12, 2005), such principles have two elements: (1) established, widespread and consistent state practice; and (2) opinio juris sive necessitates (a belief that the practice is obligatory). Under Article 2 of the 1961 Convention on Statelessness: 'A foundling found in the territory of a Contracting State shall, in the absence of proof to the contrary, be considered to have been born within the territory of parents possessing the nationality of that State.' Applied to Poe -- a foundling found near a church in Jaro, Iloilo, when she was only a few days old -- her parents are presumed to be Filipinos. True, the Philippines is not a signatory. However, the treaty possesses both generally-accepted-principles elements because the grant of nationality to foundlings has been an established, widespread, and consistent practice of many states since 1961. According to Razon v. Taglis (Dec 3, 2009), this international custom could be shown from State practice, legislation, international and national judicial decisions, treaties, patterns of treaties, practice of international organs, and UN General Assembly resolutions. Further, under the 1948 UDHR -- to which the Philippines is a signatory and which the SC has consistently enforced -- 'Everyone has a right to a nationality'; a denial of nationality to Poe would be a plain violation of the UDHR. CJP adds that it is 'high time the Philippines acceded to and joined the 1961 Convention on Statelessness for the benefit of all Filipinos, especially illegitimate children whose parents are unknown, not just of Senator Poe. After all, it is not their fault that their parents have abandoned them.' On American citizenship: Poe acquired it after marrying her American husband but renounced it in accordance with American law; the American Embassy affirmed this renunciation -- and under the 1930 Hague Convention, it is American, not Philippine, law that determines who are American citizens. On adoption: the SC has ruled several times that adoption does not confer citizenship -- but those rulings do not apply to foundlings; they were issued to prevent aliens from short-circuiting strict naturalization rules via adult adoption processes. Poe does not derive natural-born citizenship from adoption but from generally-accepted-principles of international law. Her presumed citizenship can become indisputable if her paternity is established by DNA evidence -- the SC has recognized DNA tests as conclusive proof of filiations since Tijing v. Court of Appeals (March 8, 2001) and People v. Vallejo (May 2, 2002). CJP will take up Poe's residence qualification in another column.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes that the two legislative committees primarily handling the proposed Bangsamoro Basic Law (BBL) both favor peace but use diverse strategies. The House committee headed by Rep. Rufus Rodriguez, voting 50-17, approved the BBL with some amendments but did not revise or delete several provisions that critics claim are unconstitutional because their revision would contravene the government's comprehensive peace agreement with the MILF. The Senate committee headed by Sen. Miriam Defensor Santiago believes that, in addition to passing the BBL, Congress should also amend the Constitution to validate the questionable portions. The congressmen -- swayed no doubt by their meeting with the President a few days ago -- are taking the calculated risk that the bill would survive SC scrutiny, or at least that the Court would not invalidate the entire BBL (but only separable parts), unlike the MOA-AD which was totally scrapped. CJP believes the Senate track is safer and better, for three reasons. First, a constitutional amendment or revision would conclusively solve all the legal objections to the bill -- true, that route takes more time, but as CJP pointed out on Feb 8 ('Saving the peace'), the process can be sped up by Congress tackling its legislative function alongside its constituent function; the whole process can be done within the year if Congress puts its mind to it. Second, constitutional amendments would undergo nationwide debate and plebiscite; the purely legislative route would subject the BBL only to a plebiscite in the Mindanao autonomous region -- but the peace we seek is for the whole country, requiring free and robust national discussion and vote. Third, while BBL would be passed under the present Congress and President, its implementation would be undertaken mostly by the new 2016 president; a purely-legislated BBL would surely be challenged in the SC and given due-process requirements may not be decided within PNoy's tenure; the next president may not be as committed and may not defend it as passionately -- and cases are won or lost because of the prudence and diligence of the parties' presentations. But if the BBL is backed by constitutional changes there would be no challenge to its constitutionality; equally important, the next president would be compelled to implement it in full because it would carry the mandate of the entire electorate, not just of those in the Mindanao autonomous region. POSTSCRIPT -- 'More on arbitration': an internationally-respected arbiter, who requested anonymity (true to their calling), emailed an interesting comment on A383. He explained that Unclos (which created Itlos) has an 'opt out provision' allowing a member like China to 'reject' an arbitration suit; however, China did not expressly invoke this provision in its controversy with the Philippines over the Spratlys -- it 'simply refused to participate.' The question is whether the Itlos panel will construe this refusal as a rejection; if so, PH will probably lose because the tribunal would dismiss for lack of jurisdiction. But if PH hurdles the jurisdictional issue, 'the likelihood is that it will win' because PH is the only one presenting arguments and evidence. The second question: how is the decision enforced against China? The arbiter agreed with CJP that PH would lose moral ascendancy to ask China to honor an unfavorable Itlos decision if PH honors only arbitral decisions it wins (Manila Water) and disobeys those it loses (Maynilad); PH should be consistent in observing the rule of law regardless of outcome. SECOND POSTSCRIPT: the CA's TRO stopping BCDA from evicting CJHDevCo upheld the arbitral decision of the Philippine Dispute Resolution Center Inc. and equally important protected the rights of the innocent bystanders CJP wrote about in A383 -- the locators, condominium owners, and golf-club-share holders who paid CJHDevCo in good faith when the lease was still valid.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the arbitration-decisions doctrinal anchor for the West Philippine Sea case and beyond. Arbitration is becoming a popular mode of settling local and international disputes -- the Supreme Court encourages it because it speedily dispenses justice and helps unclog judicial dockets. Unlike in judicial cases, the arbitral parties select their judges: usually each side nominates one judge, and the arbitral body that conducts the arbitration chooses the third judge who becomes the panel chair. Every arbitral tribunal handles only one case at a time; its decision is final and unappealable. PH has participated in several arbitration cases. It won its arbitration concerning the construction and operation of Naia III against Piatco; the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) in Paris selected the panel chair. It won another Naia III arbitration against Fraport AG, a German company; the International Center for the Settlement of Disputes (ICSID) in Washington appointed the panel chair. PH's most important arbitration involves the Spratlys and other isles in the West Philippine Sea: PH sued China at the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (Itlos) in Hamburg. China is a member of the international group that created Itlos and has a judge sitting on the tribunal -- but it refused to participate, claiming 'indisputable sovereignty.' Itlos continued the proceedings and is poised to issue its decision early next year; PH is confident it will win. The problem: will China, given its superior military clout, respect and obey an Itlos decision dislodging it from those isles? RULE OF LAW: the government, through MWSS, likewise won its arbitration against Manila Water but lost to Maynilad in a separate case; the ICC, like in Naia III, appointed the chair of both panels. MWSS promptly obeyed and enforced its win over Manila Water but refused to obey its loss to Maynilad, arguing it had a duty to set 'just and equitable rates.' In stark contrast, Manila Water laudably accepted its loss while reserving compensation rights under its concession agreement with MWSS. MWSS's double-faced stance is palpably unreasonable: it freely participated in both cases with full knowledge of the finality and binding effect of whatever decisions may be rendered -- it cannot accept and obey only the decision it won. That is the worst kind of selective justice. Just because it exercises indisputable sovereignty and commands the police and military, the government should not impose its will arbitrarily -- it must set the example in following arbitral decisions regardless of outcome and lead in observing the rule of law. Otherwise, how can our government expect China to accept and obey an Itlos decision unfavorable to China if our government refuses to accept arbitral decisions unfavorable to it? PH would be a worse violator of the rule of law than China because it willingly and actively participated while China did not. What is good for the goose should also be good for the gander. INNOCENT BYSTANDERS: the arbitration between BCDA and CJH Development Corp. (CJHDevCo) -- with the Philippine Dispute Resolution Center Inc. as arbitral body -- ended in a draw. The tribunal held that both parties mutually breached their lease agreement over Camp John Hay in Baguio; it rescinded the agreement and directed CJHDevCo to deliver the leased area (with all improvements and constructions) to BCDA, which in turn was ordered to return to CJHDevCo all the rentals paid, almost P1.5 billion. While the arbitral decision settled the BCDA-CJHDevCo dispute, it did not touch on the rights and obligations of the investors, locators, and condominium owners in Camp John Hay who were not parties to the arbitration but had in good faith paid CJHDevCo for their rights over homes, condominiums, golf-club shares, and other improvements built by the developer. Their payments cannot just dissipate into nothingness -- BCDA (which was adjudged to take over) should treat them reasonably, equitably, and fairly. When they contracted with CJHDevCo, the lease was still valid and existing; it became invalid only after February 2015 rescission. As innocent bystanders not party to the arbitration, they should not be penalized and deprived of what they had paid for in good faith.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes that he is glad the Supreme Court is speeding up the legal proceedings involving the suspension of Makati Mayor Jejomar Erwin S. Binay Jr. by Ombudsman Conchita Carpio Morales. Aside from immediately setting oral argument at 2 PM Tuesday in Baguio City, the Court abbreviated the process by requiring the parties to file at noon tomorrow a position paper not exceeding 30 pages backed by a 'table of authorities'; the hearing will begin not with the usual oral presentations but with the justices' interpellation, first of Morales' counsel and then of Binay's. This unprecedented procedure is clearly a reform measure aimed at speeding up proceedings -- justices study position papers in advance and just ask questions to clarify, test, and validate them -- and signals their laudable determination to resolve speedily the rather embarrassing chaos of having two bickering mayors in the nation's financial capital. To be fair and objective in this sub-judice case that will probably split the Court, CJ summarizes the relevant facts, main issues, and arguments. On March 5, 2015, a special panel of investigators submitted a complaint alleging Binay and several others violated the Anti-Graft Law in the construction of the Makati City Hall Parking Building. Morales directed Binay to file his counteraffidavit. On March 10, 2015, without waiting for the counteraffidavit, Morales issued a suspension order placing Binay and 20 others under preventive suspension for not more than six months. This order was implemented by the DILG at 8:30 AM on March 16 by posting it on the wall of the Makati City Hall ('given that all the gates of the Makati City Hall were closed'); at 9:47 AM the same day, Vice Mayor Romulo V. Peña took his oath as acting mayor. Acting on Binay's certiorari petition filed March 11, the Court of Appeals issued a resolution at 'around noon' on March 16 granting a 60-day temporary restraining order. Morales filed a 'manifestation' in the CA arguing that given prior service and implementation of the suspension order 'there is no more act to be restrained by the TRO as it has become moot and academic' and that the TRO was textually vague. Binay then petitioned the CA to hold Morales in contempt for refusing to obey the TRO; the CA directed Morales to comment within three days. On March 25, Morales asked the SC to annul the CA's TRO and stop the CA from adjudicating Binay's contempt petition. Morales argues that the Constitution (Art XI, Sec 13) mandates her 'to investigate any act or omission [that] appears to be illegal, unjust, improper or inefficient,' and that Sec 14 of the Ombudsman Law states 'No writ of injunction shall be issued by any court to delay an investigation being conducted by the Ombudsman.' Binay's suspension is an essential part of her investigation; the CA's TRO illegally delays it. Citing settled jurisprudence, she argues suspension is not a penalty but an 'aid to investigation' to prevent Binay from using the powers and prerogatives of his office to influence potential witnesses -- practically all the documentary evidence is in the city government's custody and potential witnesses are in the city's employ, so there is an imperative need to guard against tampering and intimidation. Morales also contends that as a public officer removable only by impeachment, she cannot be held in contempt because the penalties for contempt are fine and imprisonment, which are criminal in nature, and impeachable officers are criminally liable only after serving their terms. In his comment, Binay avers that Morales' power to investigate and suspend is not absolute; it is subject to the constitutional duty of courts to strike down grave abuse of discretion. Morales gravely abused her discretion because, by merely looking at the complaint, she would have known the irregular acts allegedly against him were done prior to his incumbent term -- invoking the condonation doctrine: 'a public official cannot be removed for administrative misconduct committed during a prior term; his reelection to office operates as a condonation of the officer's previous misconduct to the extent of cutting off the right to remove him therefor.' Payments made during his present term were mere implementations of the building contract entered during his prior term, condoned by the electorate. On the contempt issue, Binay maintains that impeachable officials may be held liable, per Philippine Guardians v. Comelec (March 22, 2011), which ruled that the Comelec -- composed of impeachable officials -- was guilty of contempt for failing to comply with a status-quo order.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the third installment in his BBL doctrinal arc -- following A386 (March 22) and A389 (February 8) -- to offer Congress three vital references it must ingest before enacting the proposed Bangsamoro Basic Law. As CJ explained last Sunday in A386, although the BBL changed the word 'associative' to 'asymmetric,' the MILF's lofty aspiration for self-determination remains unchanged. Notably, the MILF's chief negotiator for both the old MOA-AD and the new Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro (CAB) -- on which the BBL is anchored -- is one and the same person: Mohagher Iqbal. The MILF chair to whom Iqbal reports is also the same: Al Haj Murad Ebrahim. Understandably, their common dream for self-rule remains the same, even though worded differently and the implementing details watered down. The MILF's aspiration for self-rule, by the very terms of the BBL, is exclusive to the Bangsamoro only and distinct from any self-governance given by the Constitution to any local government unit -- going far beyond what has been granted to the ARMM or to any province, city, or town. The Court's decision in North Cotabato v. Government (October 14, 2008) is emphatic in clarity: any law that dilutes, restricts, equivocates, or degrades any power or authority granted by the Charter to any of the three branches (executive, legislative, judicial) or to any independent agency (Comelec, OOO, COA, CSC, CHR), especially those that involve the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the country, would be unconstitutional. Given that only four of the original 15 SC justices who decided North Cotabato are still sitting now -- and given the utter importance of peace -- is there a chance the Court may change its mind and uphold the BBL in its present form? CJ does not think so. The Constitution is the singular deity of the Court. It is the Court's raison d'être. The justices are its high priests and zealous guardians, ever ready to strike down anything that desecrates and defiles it directly or indirectly. Without the Constitution, the Supreme Court is nothing. Despite changes in its composition, the Supreme Court is a continuing entity that rarely reverses or modifies landmark decisions that are protective of the Constitution. Though the decision writer, Justice Conchita Carpio Morales, has retired from the Court, the current most senior justice, Antonio T. Carpio, wrote a concurring opinion that found more constitutional objections than the decision itself. True, three other still-sitting justices -- Presbitero J. Velasco Jr., Teresita J. Leonardo-de Castro, and Arturo D. Brion -- wrote dissenting opinions; however, their dissents were not so much on the substantive issue of constitutionality as on the procedural questions of mootness and prematurity. The three jurists opined the case was mooted after then President Arroyo advised the Court the MOA-AD would no longer be signed and that she had dissolved the negotiating panel. On the other hand, Justice Carpio unflinchingly declared unconstitutional not only the underlying 'associative' concept but, quite significantly, 36 specific provisions of the MOA-AD, the shadows of which can be gleaned in the BBL. Although not a member of the Court when North Cotabato was decided, Chief Justice Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno participated in the controversy as counsel for Sen. (now Senate President) Franklin M. Drilon, who was an intervenor. Her 72-page memorandum was a brilliant defense of the Constitution and a veritable source of her mindset on the conduct of peace negotiations. She detailed the constitutional violations that eroded the sovereignty of the Republic of the Philippines, split its national identity, and created a state within a state -- a concept alien and antithetical to the one sovereign nation embodied in the Constitution. At bottom, CJ believes that before enacting the BBL, Congress would be well-advised to ingest very well three vital documents: (1) the North Cotabato decision; (2) the concurring opinion of Justice Carpio; and (3) the memorandum of then-Attorney Sereno. In past columns, CJ strongly supported the peace process -- and still does. The peace panel worked long and hard to address sensitive issues; together with its MILF counterpart, the panel succeeded in producing the CAB without judicial interference -- unlike the MOA-AD, which did not even see the light of day because its signing was struck down by a TRO. This time around, the Court did not intervene midstream despite the filing of petitions to stop the CAB; this time, the Court did not issue a TRO. How ironic it would be if, despite the lessons taught by the North Cotabato decision, the stirring opinion of Justice Carpio, and the cogent arguments of CJ Sereno, Congress would still enact a constitutionally-defective BBL.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the second installment in his BBL doctrinal arc, taking up the first of two major obstacles besetting the proposed Bangsamoro Basic Law: its constitutionality (the second, political palatability, gets its own column). Much has been said about BBL's constitutionality, but all opinions are mere guesses as to what the Supreme Court would do if the BBL -- in its present form (Senate Bill No. 2408, a 119-page document) -- is brought to it. The Court does not render advisory opinions on the constitutionality of pending bills; its power is limited to actual controversies -- that is, to actual violations of existing constitutional and legal rights, not to academic questions or anticipated laws. Hence, it cannot render an opinion on the constitutionality of pending legislation like SB 2408. CJ thinks the best way to predict what the Court would do is to analyze its decision in North Cotabato v. Government, promulgated October 14, 2008, and compare it with the BBL. This landmark decision, written by Justice (now Ombudsman) Conchita Carpio Morales, invalidated the MOA-AD between government and the MILF -- and fortunately, it also delved deep into the larger issue of the extent of the President's power in pursuing the peace process. The Court explained that while the facts surrounding the controversy center on the armed conflict in Mindanao, the principles and doctrines enunciated should guide future peace talks in all areas of the country. What are the lessons? First: the people have a constitutional right to be informed and the government has a corresponding duty to disclose even if nobody demands the details of peace negotiations -- ours is an open society, with all the acts of the government subject to public scrutiny and available always to public cognizance. Second: since the government's peace negotiators are mere agents of the President, they cannot have more powers than their principal; moreover, they do not represent and do not bind the legislature and the judiciary. Consequently, they cannot guarantee that any peace agreement they entered into will be enacted into law, much less that the law thus enacted will pass judicial review. Third: the associative relation between the Bangsamoro Juridical Entity and the central government, as provided in the MOA-AD, is unconstitutional. The Court solemnly ruled: No province, city, or municipality, not even the ARMM, is recognized under our laws as having an associative relationship with the national government. Indeed, the associative concept implies powers that go beyond anything ever granted by the Constitution to any local or regional government. It also implies the recognition of the associated entity as a state. The Constitution, however, does not contemplate any state in this jurisdiction other than the Philippine State, much less does it provide for a transitory status that aims to prepare any part of the Philippine territory for independence (italics and underscoring in original). The Court explained that the spirit animating the BJE -- which has betrayed itself by its use of the concept of association -- runs counter to the national sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Republic (italics and bold types in original). Consequently, because the defining concept underlying the relationship between the national government and the BJE is itself contrary to the Constitution, it is not surprising that many of the specific provisions of the MOA-AD on the formation and powers of the BJE are in conflict with the Constitution and the laws. Deferring to the Court's invalidation, the BBL abandoned the word associative, instead proposing that the relationship between the Central Government and the Bangsamoro Government shall be asymmetric -- reflective of the recognition of their Bangsamoro identity and their aspiration for self-governance, distinct from other regions and other local governments. Though the descriptive word has changed from associative to asymmetric, the underlying meaning is basically the same. The smoking gun is BBL's own next sentence: The Central Government shall respect the exercise of competencies and exclusive powers of the Bangsamoro Government. Verily, the basic aspiration for self-governance of the MILF has not changed. Like in the old MOA-AD, it still wants self-governance distinct from and not given to other LGUs (not even ARMM) and aspires for powers exclusive to itself -- these distinction and exclusivity are the defining concepts that animated the invalidated MOA-AD. CJ respects this aspiration -- the MILF rebelled because of its inability to obtain its longing for distinct and exclusive powers. The way to peace, as he wrote in 'Saving the peace' (2/8/15, i.e., A389), would be either to amend the BBL to conform to the Constitution, or to amend the Constitution to empower Congress to grant the MILF's asymmetric aspiration.
