one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the first installment of his two-part cybercrime arc, a legalese-to-lay-readers explainer of the just-released CPL decision; the dissents follow next Sunday in A422. The SC's decision (Jesus Disini v. SOJ, Feb 18, 2014) on the Cybercrime Prevention Law (CPL) is a delight for constitutional law scholars. The 50-page, single-space majority ruling penned by Justice Roberto A. Abad as well as the concurring and dissenting opinions of CJ Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno (43 pages) and Justices Antonio T. Carpio (32 pages), Arturo D. Brion (26 pages plus a 9-page annex) and Mario Victor F. Leonen (100 pages) are veritable treatises on the freedom of expression. Old doctrines: they explained the nature and ramifications of the Internet, but Justice Leonen's was the most extensive -- he discussed many details like: 'The allocation of unique identifiers for the internet, such as IP addresses and domain names, is administered not by a public entity but by a nonprofit corporation based in the United States: the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN).' (While reading them, CJ remembered that, unknown to many, a talented and lovely Filipino, Judith Duavit-Vasquez, was elected as the first Asian woman to the ICANN board of trustees in 2011 for a 3-year term.) These treatises indubitably show that the Court understands the complexity of cyberspace -- they were able to correlate and apply the traditional doctrines on freedom of expression to the many complicated aspects of this Information Age marvel. The freedom of expression -- along with its derivatives like the freedom of the press, freedom of peaceful assembly, and, most important, freedom to oppose and to disagree -- is the most basic ingredient of democracy; without free expression, liberty cannot flourish; without the freedom to oppose, elections will be meaningless and democracy will perish. The freedom of expression started with verbal speech, and with the march of science, it encompassed all emerging media, like newspapers, books, placards, leaflets, pulpits, theaters, picket lines, radio, television, billboards, cell phones and now, cyberspace. Majority ruling: the judicial opinions were crafted in legalese and directed mainly to a legal audience -- CJ will try to explain them in simple language for the lay readers to understand them, and to help Congress decriminalize libel without sacrificing the reputation of maligned citizens. Let CJ begin with the majority's ruling which reviewed each of the 21 challenged provisions of the CPL -- this item-by-item review is unusual because the petitions, 'save possibly for one,' failed (as ably pointed out by CJ Sereno and Justice Leonen) to raise an 'actual case or controversy.' Explained Justice Leonen: 'None of the petitioners... have been charged [with] any offense arising from the law being challenged...' -- no one has alleged any actual or imminent violation of any right. In any event, of the 21 challenged provisions, 16 were deemed constitutional and three were declared unconstitutional. First, the provision criminalizing the sending of spam mails -- the Court reasoned: 'To prohibit the transmission of unsolicited ads [under the conditions imposed in the law] would deny a person the right to read his emails... Unsolicited advertisements are legitimate forms of expression.' Second, the provision allowing real-time collection of traffic data, like an email's 'origin, destination, route, time, date, size, duration, or type of underlying data' -- the Court said the real-time bulk (as distinguished from isolated) collection of a person's data violates the right to privacy: 'The power is virtually limitless, enabling law enforcement authorities to engage in fishing expeditions, choosing whatever specified communication they want.' Third, the provision authorizing the DOJ to restrict or block access to computer data that the DOJ suspects violate the CPL -- gives the DOJ, the Court said, the virtual power to search and seize private data without the requisite judicial search warrant, in stark violation of the Constitution. Online libel: to recall, 16 provisions were deemed constitutional, while three were not. On the remaining two, the ruling was mixed. The Court upheld the provision penalizing online libel but only with respect to the original author of the post -- those who simply received the post and reacted to it (say, by resending it via Facebook or Twitter or other social media) are not criminally liable. The Court explained that the CPL copied the provision on cyberlibel from the RPC, which had not been declared unconstitutional during the last 50 years, and the CPL merely extended its application to cyberspace and should thus remain constitutional. The majority also upheld the higher penalty imposed on cyberlibel, reasoning that the determination of penalties is a legislative prerogative; the Court justified the more severe punishment by citing the inherent difficulty of identifying the cyberlibel culprit who 'is able to reach far more victims or cause greater harm.' However, the Court clarified that a prosecution for libel under the RPC bars a prosecution for the same post under the CPL, and vice versa, pursuant to the doctrine of double jeopardy -- a printed article that is also posted online can be the subject of only one libel charge. The majority's refusal to invalidate libel is the most controversial part of the Court's decision; reacting to widespread protests, many legislators filed bills to decriminalize libel altogether. Next Sunday: the dissents, and why CJ agrees with some of them.

The televised testimony of Ruby Tuason before the Senate blue ribbon committee has been hailed as a grand 'slam dunk,' only a 'lay-up,' and a winning 'three-point buzzer-beater' -- these street-smart assessments of how the former Malacañang social queen pinned down her longtime family friend-senator are, of course, familiar to basketball diehards. Purpose of testimony: after the effusive sports lingo, the assessments turned more serious from 'sabotage' and 'worthless' to 'sufficient proof of conspiracy... enough to convict' another senator. CJ thinks all these descriptions should be understood in their proper context. Tuason's testimony was not about basketball or criminal law -- rather, her appearance was about assisting the Senate in crafting or amending legislation to stop graft. For example, the committee could, as a result of its hearing, sponsor a bill on how to prevent suspects from leaving the country, and how to proceed against those who managed to sneak out, without violating their constitutional rights. Or how to make it easier for prosecutors to indict high officials, especially legislators. Or how to find novel ways to prevent and penalize new forms of graft. Tuason did not testify in the Senate to defend herself in the plunder charge thrown at her by the DOJ; neither was it to implicate or protect any of her corespondents; it would be unfair to assess her testimony to show anyone's complicity in any crime -- these are simply not the purposes of the Senate hearing. True, congressional investigation can sometimes engender the belief that a crime had been committed and that certain individuals are possibly guilty thereof -- but Congress cannot indict them in court, much less pass upon their guilt and sentence them to jail; it may, however, recommend their prosecution to the DOJ or the Office of the Ombudsman, but the discretion on whether to indict them belongs solely to these two latter offices. More exacting: criminal procedures are more exacting than congressional investigations. First, the information (or charge sheet) must be filed in the proper court that has jurisdiction over it; and second, the information must be clearly and accurately worded to comply with the constitutional right of the accused 'to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation against him.' Thus, the information must set out (a) the names of the accused, (b) the designation of the offense given by the statute, (c) the specific acts or omissions constituting the crime coached in ordinary and concise language, (d) the approximate date of the offense, and (e) the place where it was committed; as a rule, an information must charge only one offense. In short, the information must contain the 'essential elements' of the crime which must be worded clearly 'to enable a person of common understanding to know what offense is being charged,' to empower him or her to prepare his or her defense. Unless the foregoing safeguards are put in place, guilt or innocence cannot be deduced from the testimony of any witness -- the reason is that the testimony must be received and admitted only when it is both 'relevant' and 'material' to the specific crime charged; furthermore, the questions must be propounded properly and clearly, without misleading or confusing the witness. Finally and most importantly, the adverse party must be given the opportunity to cross-examine the witness -- despite the many scientific advances in crime detection and prosecution, the old-fashioned cross-examination conducted by a skilled lawyer is still the best-known way of testing the truthfulness and credibility of witnesses; unless subjected to cross-examination, testimony is hearsay and cannot be used to convict or prejudice the accused. In congressional investigations, questions are sometimes recklessly asked without sufficient predicate (or basis), thereby eliciting unresponsive, incomplete or wrong answers; moreover, resource persons (they are not called 'witnesses') are not cross-examined by adverse parties, because there are no adverse parties in legislative inquiries. The point is: unless the safeguards in a criminal proceeding are observed, the testimony given in congressional probes cannot be used to indict or incriminate third persons, or for that matter, to free the guilty; this is why the SC has restricted (no longer absolutely banned) live coverage of trials. Context and complications: at bottom, the street-smart assessments of Ruby Tuason's performance should be understood in their congressional context rather than as legal opinions on criminal liability -- let us remember that her testimony was taken without any specific criminal indictment, without any safeguard for the rights of the putative accused, and without the benefit of cross-examination. In the court of public opinion, these open and much-publicized congressional hearings can besmirch reputations, cause sleeplessness and anxiety, and lead to severe consequences to the conscience-stricken or mentally unbalanced -- some politicians may lose their charisma and political clout; others may even go, as some have gone, to the extreme of hara-kiri or suicide. In the courts of law, criminal guilt or innocence is not determined by the passing passion of the political thicket, but by a serene, quiet and rule-based trial speedily conducted by competent, independent and trustworthy judges, assisted by skilled, dedicated and ethical lawyers.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the first installment of his two-part Ruby-Tuason arc (followed by A424 Feb 23), structured as a three-tier role-analysis: DOJ + OOO + SBN. Ruby Tuason, who has been charged with plunder in the OOO by the DOJ, executed an affidavit detailing her participation in the crime, implicating some of her alleged coconspirators, and offering to return her share of the loot, which she admitted to the Senate blue ribbon committee as about P40 million -- is she now free of criminal liability? CJ's short answer: No, not yet. DOJ's role: Justice Sec. Leila de Lima granted her the benefits of the government's WPP on the condition that she would testify and be cross-examined in court to validate her affidavit; the DOJ, with the backing of Malacañang, believes Tuason's affidavit and putative testimony would corroborate, affirm and strengthen the charge against the principal offenders and would result in their conviction in what is expected to be a long and tedious litigation. The WPP Law (RA 6981) authorizes the DOJ to extend several benefits to potential witnesses and their immediate family, including free housing, 24-hour security, financial assistance, traveling expenses, medical treatment, and if needed, 'relocation and/or change of identity at the expense of the Program.' Witnesses who participated in the crime (like Tuason) must 'not appear to be the most guilty'; admission into the program entitles the witnesses 'to immunity from criminal prosecution' provided they comply with their undertakings in the MOA they executed with the DOJ. Ombudsman's role: to repeat, Tuason has been included as a respondent in the plunder complaint filed in the OOO by the DOJ -- thus, the DOJ can no longer exclude her from the complaint because the OOO has assumed jurisdiction over the case; in cases involving public officials and their coconspirators (who may be private people), the OOO 'as a rule conducts the preliminary investigation'; it therefore has the discretion to determine the existence of probable cause and to select who should or should not be charged in the SBN; consequently, it is the OOO that has the prerogative to determine whether to include her in any information; a separate law (RA 6770) authorizes the OOO to grant immunity to coperpetrators -- in short, Tuason's immunity from prosecution depends on the OOO, no longer on the DOJ. Sandiganbayan's role: if the OOO decides to include Tuason in the information, the SBN -- per the Rules of Court -- may still discharge her as an accused, 'provided the court is convinced' that (a) there is absolute necessity for her testimony; (b) there is no other available direct evidence; (c) her testimony can be substantially corroborated; (d) she does not appear to be the most guilty; and (e) she has not been convicted of any offense involving moral turpitude. Once the information that includes her is filed, Tuason, like all the other accused, may be arrested and detained, possibly in the WPP safe house, because plunder is a capital and 'nonbailable' offense; moreover, the SBN can require the OOO to present evidence to 'convince' the court that the five requisites had been complied with; however, once discharged by the court to become a state's witness, she would be released from detention. A discharge made by the court shall amount to an acquittal of the discharged accused and shall be a bar to future litigation for the same offense -- in short, courts grant acquittal to the discharged accused while the DOJ and the OOO give merely 'immunity from prosecution.' More on DAP: CJ wrote last Sunday (A426) that, as a retired jurist, he would not venture an opinion on whether the DAP cases should now be dismissed for having become 'moot and academic' because the SC has not finished hearing the parties -- another oral argument is set on Feb 18. But enterprising readers googled CJ's Separate Opinion in Sanlakas v. Exec. Sec. (Feb 3, 2004) which said that a mooted case 'capable of repetition yet evading review' may still be decided by the Court 'provided the party raising it has been, or continues to be, prejudiced or damaged' -- consequently, venturing an opinion now is premature since the parties have not completed their arguments; CJ needs to see whether the petitioners have been personally prejudiced or injured by the government's mooted actions. Others perceptively opined that the petitioners have not shown any direct personal injury, ergo the DAP cases should now be dismissed for having become moot and academic. For the future guidance of our officials, CJ thinks the Court, while dismissing the mooted petitions, may still tackle two important issues: (1) the nature of the savings that can be realigned, and (2) the validity of cross-border transfer of funds. The Court made this hybrid disposition in Lacson v. Perez (May 10, 2001) when it dismissed the mooted cases but 'enjoined [the government] from arresting the petitioners... without the required judicial warrants...'; both the Sanlakas and the Lacson cases were taken up in CJ's said column. Many now know that CJ's writings are not intended to spoon-feed readers -- CJ expects them to reach their conclusions on the basis of the discussions he presents; he does not wish to mesmerize them into adopting his opinions; rather, he prefers them to analyze, think and make their own conclusions; CJ humbly believes this is the better way of opining and teaching.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the foundational explainer of the moot-and-academic doctrine + capable-of-repetition-yet-evading-review exception, set up to anchor his forthcoming DAP-arc commentary. SolGen Francis Jardeleza, the Harvard-educated and bar-topnotcher counsel of the Republic, argued in the SC that (1) the President 'authorized the disbursements under the DAP,' (2) the 'disbursements [had] an appropriation cover,' and (3) 'the government [had] sufficient savings to support these disbursements.' Moot and academic: in short, he concluded, 'there were actual savings which the President himself authorized to augment existing items in the GAA' -- ergo, the DAP is constitutional. Nonetheless, he added, 'the circumstances that justified the creation of DAP no longer obtain... DAP... lapsed into complete disuse in 2013 and became functus officio... DAP... no longer exists, thereby mooting the present cases.' Should the Court adjudicate the cases by dismissing them without deciding the constitutional issues, because they have become moot and academic? As a rule, Philippine (and US) courts decide issues 'on their merit' only when they present an 'actual case or controversy' that involves a 'conflict of legal rights... susceptible of judicial resolution... not mooted by supervening events.' Unlike judiciaries in Europe, our judges are not authorized to render 'advisory opinions... They do not adjudicate academic or hypothetical or anticipatory questions, no matter how intellectually challenging.' Moreover, 'courts will not pass upon a constitutional question unless it is the lis mota of the case, or if the case can be disposed of on some other grounds,' like its having become moot and academic. Capable of repetition: jurisprudence, however, has carved clear exceptions to this general rule, the most cited being 'when the case is capable of repetition yet evading review.' A good example is David v. Arroyo (May 3, 2006, per Justice Angelina Sandoval Gutierrez): on Feb 24, 2006, then President GMA issued PP 1017 declaring a 'state of national emergency' that resulted in, among others, the warrantless arrest of many, including columnist Randy David and Akbayan president Roland Llamas, as well as in the pillage of the Tribune and the Malaya. A week later, on March 3, 2006, GMA lifted PP 1017; thus, the government asked the Court to dismiss the petitions assailing the constitutionality of PP 1017 on the ground that the lifting had mooted the constitutional issues. The Court, voting 11-3 (with one on leave), refused, reasoning that while the lifting rendered the issues moot and academic, the President's act is capable of repetition while evading judicial review by the expediency of its lifting -- constitutional rights have been violated and private parties suffered as a result. The Gutierrez ponencia rhapsodized: 'The Court has the duty to formulate guiding and controlling constitutional precepts, doctrines and rules; it has the symbolic function of educating the bench and the bar, and in the present petitions, the military and the police on the extent of the protection given by constitutional guarantees.' At other times, the Court followed the general rule. In Lacson v. Perez (May 10, 2001, per Justice Jose A. R. Melo), GMA, 'faced by an angry and violent mob... assaulting and attempting to break into Malacañang' (in what some call 'Edsa 3'), issued Proclamation 38 declaring a 'state of rebellion.' On May 6, 2001, she lifted the proclamation, thus the government asked the Court to dismiss all petitions brought by Panfilo Lacson et al. challenging the constitutionality of the presidential order. Voting 7-4 (with four on leave), the Court threw out the petitions because the lifting rendered them moot and academic, saying that the petitioners, not having been arrested without warrant as they had feared, suffered no damage; further, the mooting changed their nature to one for declaratory relief over which the SC had no original jurisdiction; nevertheless, it 'enjoined [the government] from arresting petitioners... without the required judicial warrants...' Later on, in Sanlakas v. Executive Secretary (Feb 4, 2004, per Justice Dante O. Tinga), President Arroyo issued Proclamation 427 on July 27, 2003, declaring (again) a 'state of rebellion' after some 300 military personnel 'stormed into the Oakwood Premier apartments in Makati City... bewailing corruption...' and 'demanded, among other things, the resignation of the President.' Though the proclamation was lifted on Aug 1, 2003, thereby mooting the petitions, the Tinga ponencia tackled the constitutional issues head-on -- it held that while the Constitution does not expressly grant the President the power to declare a state of rebellion, such prerogative 'springs in the main from her powers as chief executive and... draws strength from her Commander-in-Chief powers.' Three justices joined the ponencia unconditionally; one conditionally via a separate opinion; and three others only 'in the result'; three voted to dismiss the petitions on the sole ground of mootness while two dissented, saying the proclamation was void; one was on leave; one seat was vacant. The foregoing shows that the Court tackled the 'moot and academic' defense in varying ways depending on the peculiarities of each case -- readers may draw their own conclusions; as a retired jurist, CJ would not venture an opinion till after the DAP cases are heard in full; note that the oral argument will continue on Feb 18; Abangan!

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban tests whether the nine senators' 2014 PDAF 'realignments' violate Belgica v. Ochoa (Nov 19 2013, J. Perlas-Bernabe). He reviews the Charter (appropriation bills originate exclusively in the House; the Senate may propose or concur with amendments) and the facts: 15 senators plus VP Binay deleted their P200M PDAF allocations entirely (saving P3.2 billion); nine did not -- five (Alan Peter and Pia Cayetano, Ralph Recto, Miriam Defensor-Santiago, JV Ejercito) shifted theirs to the Calamity Fund; three (Lito Lapid, Ramon Revilla Jr., Antonio Trillanes IV) to specific schools, hospitals, public works, scholarships, charity patients, and soldiers' barracks; and one (Jinggoy Estrada) gave his to Manila (P100M), Caloocan (P50M), and Lla-lo town in Cagayan (P50M). Belgica's doctrine: under separation of powers, Congress enacts and the President implements; legislators cannot participate in implementation; the 'specific appropriation, stated purpose' rule bans lump-sum appropriations and prohibits post-enactment legislator power over lump sums. His four-answer quartet: First, it is erroneous to call these 'realignments' -- legislators have no realignment/augmentation power, which the Charter grants only to the President, Senate President, Speaker, Chief Justice, and constitutional commissions. What actually happened is the senators proposed amendments to the House bill, approved by the bicameral conference committee and by Congress, becoming integral parts of the 2014 GAA. Second, the Calamity Fund amendment is constitutional -- though it is a huge lump sum, the justices exempted it (with contingency and intelligence funds) from the specific-purpose rule because calamities cannot be predicted line-item. Third, the specific schools/hospitals diversion is constitutional because the purposes are specific, executive offices implement without legislator intervention, and provided the items do not increase the President's recommended appropriations. Fourth, Jinggoy Estrada's LGU lump-sums RISK UNCONSTITUTIONALITY -- if the President is banned from lump sums without breakdowns and specific purposes, how can LGUs (parts of the executive branch) exercise MORE power and determine specific projects for the lump sums? He closes with the maxim: unconstitutionality means the allocation is void, even if the goals are laudable -- laudable ends cannot justify unconstitutional means.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reports the Supreme Court's Dec 10 2013 motu proprio resolution instituting five new pro hac vice measures to speed up the Maguindanao massacre trial. He recaps the Nov 23 2009 atrocity -- the most gruesome crime of our time, 58 defenseless civilians (34 media workers) shot, mangled, killed, and back-hoed; 197 accused in 58 separate informations originally filed in RTC Maguindanao but transferred to RTC Quezon City Branch 221 under Judge Jocelyn Solis-Reyes with two assisting judges. Status: 3 accused dead, 194 remaining, 106 detained without bail for capital murder, 88 still at large. The procedural scale is intimidating and unprecedented -- 71 case-record volumes, 38 TSN volumes, 139 witnesses, 560 petitions/motions/manifestations filed (427 resolved), with 64 accused petitioning for bail (8 Ampatuans + 42 police officers + 14 civilians) represented by 39 sets of lawyers. The five SC guidelines: (1) DIRECT implementation of the Judicial Affidavit Rule (promulgated Sept 4 2012 but suspended at the public prosecutors' request -- the Court overrides for Maguindanao); (2) ENJOIN the presiding judge to hold, based on her discretion, separate trials for accused against whom no further prosecution evidence is contemplated; (3) AUTHORIZE separate decisions in any of the 58 cases without waiting for completion of evidence-for-all-accused -- items 2 and 3 are very important because ordinarily a single final judgment would take decades, but under these guidelines judgments can be issued 'in installments' (Ampatuans first, then some policemen, etc.); (4) DESIGNATE a third assisting judge for nontrial incidents like arraignment and pretrials so Judge Solis-Reyes can focus on trials; (5) AUTHORIZE the presiding and assisting judges to resolve motions despite higher-court pendency -- overriding the normal stop-in-deference rule that indefinitely delays trials. Harry Roque, pro bono private prosecutor for 15 media workers and 2 others, hailed the directives and asked the Executive to do its share, also petitioning the AMLC for asset freezes and filing NAPOLCOM administrative-dismissal charges against accused policemen. Panganiban frames the cases as a litmus test of the judicial system and its officials, and the SC directives as raising fresh hopes that the cases will move much faster with partial judgments soon on some accused.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reports good news that the Senate, before its holiday adjournment, started plenary deliberation on the freedom of information (FOI) bill -- buried in the legislative mill for 14 years and resurrected by Sen. Grace Poe's Senate committee approval last September, with SP Drilon expecting chamber passage by end of March. The bad news: the House committee on public information and media has yet to act, giving its technical working group until mid-February to consolidate 19 pending versions. He flags two sticky points -- the 'right of reply' rider insisted on by some legislators (which constitutionalists view as a free-speech violation, compelling media outlets to give criticized officials free print space or broadcast time) and a sneaky effort to exempt House members' SALNs from FOI (when the Ethical Standards Law and Anti-Graft Law already allow public access to SALNs, and even SC justices have released theirs to PCIJ -- so why should legislators be exempted?). He distinguishes the Charter's two information provisions: the Declaration of Principles' full-public-disclosure policy is general state policy needing enabling law; the Bill of Rights' right-to-information is self-executory and enforceable by courts without enabling law. He marshals jurisprudence: Baldoza v. Dimaano (May 1 1976) recognized the right pre-1987 -- 'There can be no realistic perception by the public of the nation's problems, nor a meaningful democratic decision-making, if they are denied information of general interest'; Chavez v. PCGG (July 15 2003) directed government disclosure of Marcoses' ill-gotten-wealth negotiations; Senate v. Ermita (April 20 2006) struck down a presidential order barring Cabinet members from legislative investigations. Permitted restrictions include national security, intelligence, trade secrets, banking transactions (subject to AMLA exception), criminal matters, and other confidential information. He warns Congress with a two-example template: congressional inaction on PDAF impelled the SC's strikedown; legislative failure to revise the Party-list Law impelled Banat v. Comelec (April 21 2009) to strike down the 2-percent threshold, opening floodgates to microscopic-vote winners. The moral lesson: Congress should wisely and proactively use its policy-determining powers instead of waiting for the Court to strike down ill-conceived actions or fill the void left by inaction. He closes with the unusually direct imperative: Pass the FOI bill now!

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the Dec 8 2013 signing of the Annex on Power Sharing of the Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro (FAB) as a significant milestone in the elusive search for lasting peace with the MILF. Prof. Miriam Coronel-Ferrer, the Philippine peace-panel chair, described the 'laborious document' as carried 'in our wombs' for 16 months, with collective relief after the labor pains. He explains the structural difficulty of any negotiation with secessionist undertones: rebels do not recognize the legitimacy of the government or the Constitution overarching it, so their demands are not constrained by the Charter, while government negotiators are duty-bound to it -- on pain of SC strike-down, as in North Cotabato v. Republic (Oct 14 2008), which voided the GMA-administration MOA-AD with the MILF. He observes that the PH negotiators were careful to word the FAB and its annexes to avoid any implication of independence or secession -- they did not include anything similar to the Machakos Agreement (2002), which gave South Sudan the right to self-determination through referendum; nor the Good Friday Agreement (1998), which provided that upon a referendum Northern Ireland may secede from the UK and join Ireland; nor the 1965 Malaysia-Singapore separation. Instead the FAB recognizes the sovereignty of the Philippines, its Constitution, and its legal processes. The annex delineates three governmental power categories: Reserved Powers (retained by the Central Government), Concurrent Powers (shared), and Exclusive Powers (Bangsamoro). The Bangsamoro government will be ministerial in structure, headed by a chief minister elected by a Bangsamoro Assembly of at least 50 members -- a federalized-parliamentary-government structure akin to Malaysia (which is by the way the official facilitator of the MILF peace process). That the basic law must be passed by Congress connotes Constitutional supremacy -- a refreshing departure from the Sudanese and Irish models, the former having resulted in an independent South Sudan that eventually declared war on Sudan, its parent-state -- and means any constitutional challenge to the FAB and its annexes may be premature until the Bangsamoro Basic Law (BBL) is passed by Congress and approved by the President, because it is the BBL that will create and govern the Bangsamoro. He flags the harmonization hurdle: how to fit a ministerial-federalized-parliamentary Bangsamoro government inside the PH's centralized presidential system, both conceptually in the BBL and practically in implementation. Citing Dean Sedfrey Candelaria (CJP Professorial Chair on Liberty and Prosperity), 'a peace agreement, no matter how well crafted, remains vulnerable to the constant test of public scrutiny at every stage of its implementation.' He looks forward to the fourth and last annex on normalization (Ferrer's February forecast) and closes: May our people be gifted with lasting peace as the New Year dawns.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the House committee on suffrage and electoral reforms' approval of an Anti-Political Dynasty Act bill seeking to enforce Art. II Sec. 28 of the Charter -- 'The State shall guarantee equal opportunities for public service and prohibit political dynasties as may be defined by law.' The ban is constitutional policy but neither absolute nor self-executory because it is qualified by the enabling-law clause. The consolidated bill is authored by Teddy Casiño, Neri Colmenares, Antonio Tinio, and Oscar Rodriguez. The big surprise is Sen. JV Ejercito's Senate counterpart bill -- surprise because Ejercito is ringed by political relatives: father Joseph Estrada (Manila mayor, former president), mother Guia Gomez (San Juan City mayor), half-brother Jinggoy (senator), first cousin ER Ejercito (Laguna governor), niece Janella (San Juan councilor). Most politicians support the bill in principle (who is against a constitutional policy?), but the devil is in the details, raised across three question-sets: (1) which relatives -- only direct ascendant-descendants, or siblings/cousins/nephews/nieces; by blood or by marriage; legitimate or illegitimate; full-blood or half-blood/adopted? (2) which offices -- elective and/or appointive; national + LGU; same-office only or across-offices? (3) what geographical limits, what time limitations, same-election or future-elections? Most Congress members are related to other public officials, so they would be hesitant to define the nature, scope, and penalty -- the bill is far from final victory. He surveys live Philippine examples: Cayetano siblings Alan + Pia + Lino, with Lani (Alan's wife) as Taguig mayor; Sen. Bam Aquino as PNoy's first cousin and nephew of Butz and Tessie Aquino-Oreta; Sen. Nancy Binay as VP Jejomar Binay's daughter and sibling of Rep. Abby and Makati Mayor Junjun. The political firmament is littered with well-known clans -- Ampatuans, Angaras, Escuderos, Guingonas, Jalosjoses, Macapagals, Marcoses, Ortegas, Osmeñas, Revillas, Villars -- many of which have produced some of the best leaders, but some the worst. Genes and environment play a great part in politics as in the professions and business; early exposure educates and influences relatives for good or bad. To be fairer, political dynasties are not unique to the Philippines -- the US has the Clintons (Bill, Hillary, Chelsea), Bushes (George Sr., George Jr., Jeb), and Kennedys (John, Robert, Edward, Caroline) though the US Constitution does not ban dynasties; Argentina has the Kirchners (Cristina succeeded husband Nestor); Korea has Park Geun-hye (daughter of Park Cheung-hee); Malaysia has Najib (son of Abdul Razak); Singapore has Lee Hsien Loong (son of Lee Kuan Yew); Burma's Aung San Suu Kyi is the daughter of former PM Aung San. These examples show that a political dynasty is not necessarily evil -- it can be a bane or a boon depending on how it is defined, regulated, and used. Like electricity, mining, NGOs, and guns, political dynasties are not evil per se; they are in themselves neutral. The challenge to Congress is to define and regulate them so they can be used only for good, not for evil.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban observes that the Supreme Court's PDAF strikedown received almost universal acclaim but it calmed the seething anger only by heightening the clamor for prosecution of scammers. The decision is welcomed not as an end in itself but as an auspicious milestone in the long search for honest governance: what practical use is the death of the PDAF if the scammers remain free to frolic on their stolen money? Many readers, lingering doubt over the justice system's ability to catch and penalize malefactors, recall sensational graft exposés that ended with grafters still roaming free. Investigation and prosecution are not the direct responsibility of the judiciary -- case buildup begins with the police, and the principal investigation-prosecution agencies are the DOJ and OOO. Panganiban has no doubt about the ability, sincerity, and probity of Justice Sec Leila de Lima and Ombudsman Conchita Carpio Morales, but they also have the corresponding responsibility to respect the suspects' constitutional right to due process -- railroaded prosecution is as obnoxious as delayed justice. He catalogs the wrongly-accused's suffering (anxiety + besmirched reputation + unnecessary expenses + bail + arrest/detention pending trial, sometimes more devastating to health than physical illness); for capital offenses like plunder, suspects are detained for years or even decades awaiting final judgment, and even if acquitted, the physical suffering, mental agony, lost opportunities, social humiliation, and prohibitive cost of lawyers and litigations can never be adequately compensated. On the other hand, the freeing of the guilty by skewed judgments or prosecutor malfeasance/incompetence appalls both private offended parties and the people at large: an injustice to one person is an injustice to all, the way an injury to an eye is an injury to the whole body. The Constitution, like the sun, shines equally on everyone -- victims and suspects, rich and poor, powerful and powerless. Abhorrent it is when equality is clouded by the misuse and abuse of influence, power, and money, resulting in delayed justice or in the total failure of justice -- the acquittal of the guilty and the conviction of the innocent. More revolting it is when constitutional rights granted to the innocent are misused and abused by the guilty to delay or escape justice. While the Constitution ordains equality under the law, the compelling need is to protect the powerless from the manipulations of the powerful, to shield the lonely from the corruption induced by the vengeful, and to safeguard the guileless from the schemes of the shrewd. He turns to judicial reform: many years ago, CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr. instituted the highly successful Action Program for Judicial Reforms (APJR), adopted as a World Bank model for developing countries; Panganiban continued the APJR during his stint heading the judiciary, but it was discontinued after his term ended in December 2006. The present SC is presumably crafting its own reform program -- CJP has asked the SC's hardworking public information officer Prof. Theodore Te to advise him on these reforms, but to date he still awaits the response. Beyond this monumental PDAF decision, and during these critical times when public approval ratings of political leaders are plunging, the SC can provide stability and trust in democracy by now making public its new reform program to speed up justice -- adding another granite milestone to nation-building.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban answers reader questions about what Supreme Court justices do after retirement, given their reclusive life on Mount Olympus. Quoting the Constitution (justices hold office during good behavior until age 70 or incapacitation), he frames the answer: they just change tires for new journeys; life does not end at 70. Several government offices require retirement from the SC as a qualification -- MCLE chair (incumbent J. Bernardo P. Pardo), Philja chancellor (incumbent J. Adolfo S. Azcuna), and one of the four regular JBC members (vacant since July 2013). Some retired SC members go international -- CJ Cesar Bengzon (ICJ), J. Florentino P. Feliciano (WTO Appellate Tribunal), J. Flerida Ruth P. Romero (ILO). Others land in constitutionally independent offices -- J. Conchita Carpio Morales (Ombudsman; J. Conrado M. Vasquez was first Ombudsman), J. Jose A. R. Melo (Comelec, voluntarily retired after 2010). CJs Hilario G. Davide Jr. and Claudio Teehankee served as UN ambassadors; CJ Reynato S. Puno is a UP Board of Regents member. In the private sector, deanships of law schools -- Bellosillo (CEU), Chico-Nazario (UPHSD), Austria-Martinez (Adamson), Sandoval-Gutierrez (PLM). Some return to law practice -- J. Serafin Cuevas as Estrada and later Corona Senate-impeachment counsel; CJ Andres R. Narvasa as Estrada counsel. Some are choosy -- Feliciano appears only in the SC and in Washington/Paris/Singapore international arbitration tribunals; CJ Puno and retired J. Vicente V. Mendoza serve as counsel for the Chamber of Mines in current SC litigation challenging the 1995 Mining Law. Many become directors of private firms -- Puno (SMC, Union Bank), Davide (Manila Bulletin, Philippine Trust), Bellosillo, Gutierrez (Purefoods, Ginebra), Melo (Fontana, Citystate), Nazario (San Miguel Properties, Ginebra), Ynares-Santiago (San Miguel Global Power), Vitug (Aboitiz Equity Ventures, ABS-CBN). On his own post-retirement journey (after Dec 7 2006): Inquirer Chair Marixi R. Prieto invited him to write a column; former SP Jovito R. Salonga discouraged him with 'No retired chief justice has become a columnist,' but he proceeded -- column writing would force his mind to be agile and let him share humble views on public issues. He serves as independent member/adviser of boards of Philippine Stock Exchange-listed firms, helping them observe good-corporate-governance canons without representing management or any specific shareholder -- work that requires independence, integrity, probity, and competence, the same values he was used to in the SC. He prefers not to practice law (his old law firm dissolved when he joined the SC) and has declined regular teaching jobs and offers to rejoin government, but is involved in several foundations: chair of the board of advisers of Metrobank Foundation (which rewards excellence among teachers, soldiers, policemen, artists, journalists), president of the Manila Cathedral Foundation (overseeing the cathedral's reconstruction), chair of the board of trustees of the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity (which administers 10 professorial chairs in 10 law schools), and chair emeritus of the Philippine Dispute Resolution Center (promoting arbitration and mediation as alternatives to court litigation).

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban prints (in edited form) his Jan 28 2014 remarks at the investiture of Dr. Michael M. Alba as the 11th president of Far Eastern University, asking non-Tamaraw readers to bear with the audience. With characteristic levity-with-grains-of-truth he modifies the conventional framing: 'Many people know me as the first FEU law graduate to reach the highest court of our land' -- but he became a SC justice and the 21st CJ because he is an FEU graduate. What he has been, is, and will be, he owes first to Christ, second to his parents, and third to the education from FEU and the other schools -- noting that only five local schools have produced chief justices (UP, UST, Escuela de Derecho/Manila Law College, Ateneo de Manila, FEU). His Mapa High batch of honor graduates promised one another at the UP Oblation to earn scholarships there, and they did -- but unlike them, CJP could not study at UP because his impoverished parents could not afford the 15-centavo bus fare from their small Sampaloc apartment to UP-Diliman in QC, so they sent him to nearby FEU, which also granted him a scholarship. At FEU he met the important people who molded his young mind: Dean Alejandro R. Roces (later youngest education secretary at 37); the brilliant law Dean Jovito R. Salonga, who took a personal liking to CJP and taught him the FEU model of legal education -- a combination of Salonga's UP basic + Harvard MA + Yale doctorate insights; Fr. Michael Nolan, the erudite FEU chaplain who taught CJP the rudiments of his Catholic faith (in return CJP helped build the FEU Chapel); and Dr. Teodoro Evangelista, the epitome of dignity, prudence and fortitude, FEU president 1952-1971 (19 years overlapping CJP's 1956-1960 six-year stay among 36,000 students), who saw CJP often through student-leadership activities. FEU taught him not only arts and sciences, religious faith, and law, but also gave him the opportunity to excel in student leadership -- youngest and first sophomore president of the FEU Central Student Organization, co-founder and head of the National Union of Students of the Philippines, transforming him from shy introvert (Mapa) to active leader (FEU and the nation), surprising his parents and Mapa batchmates. He knows the FEU presidents who succeeded Evangelista (Nicanor M. Reyes Jr., Josephine C. Reyes, Felixberto C. Sta. Maria, Edilberto C. De Jesus, Lydia B. Echauz). He did not know Dr. Alba until last month when FEU chairman Aurelio R. Montinola III introduced them; in an hour-long conversation Alba impressed CJP as perceptive, knowledgeable, purpose-driven, humble, and possessed of distinct educational ideas designed for the 21st century, blending the legacies of the past with the exigencies of the present and the hopes of the future. CJP marveled five decades ago at black-and-white television and voices through telephone lines; since then have come telex, fax, cell phone, SMS, PC, Internet, email, iPad, smartphones, tablet, Google, GPS, YouTube, Magic Jack, Skype, Facebook, Viber, Twitter, Square. Times have rapidly changed; so have the scope, methods, needs and ends of education. FEU is fortunate to have a varied-interest president: academic (Stanford PhD), economist (DLSU/UP professor, past Philippine Economic Society president), educator (past DLSU dean), internationalist (former WB/ADB/USAid consultant). As a proud alumnus he welcomes Alba's investiture, congratulates the board of trustees for its prudent choice, and believes Alba is the right man for the right job at the right time for the right institution. Cheers!

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban devotes his column to Dean Jose Manuel I. Diokno's lecture as one of the 10 CJ Panganiban Professorial Chair holders on Liberty and Prosperity, asking whether justice is an imported Western concept or whether Filipinos have a native one. Citing his father Sen. Jose W. 'Ka Pepe' Diokno, Diokno argues that Filipinos have katarungan, whose root tarong (Visayan) means 'straight, upright, appropriate, correct' -- making justice for Filipinos a matter of moral rectitude and right action, not mere legality. Karapatan (right) shares the root dapat (fitting, appropriate), tying justice to right; batas (law) merely means command. Unlike Spanish/Italian/French/German, which conflate 'right' and 'law,' Tagalog distinguishes the two, recognizing that what is legal may not always be just. Kapangyarihan (authority) is differentiated from poder and lakas (naked power), and karapatan (native, right) from pribelehiyo (Spanish loanword, privilege) -- with the loanword/native boundary itself read as evidence that privilege and naked power are alien to the Filipino mind. Ka Pepe likened language to the 'bones' and history to the 'flesh': Filipino history's continuous resistance to Spanish, American, Japanese, Marcos and US-bases impositions provides the historical struggle that puts flesh on the linguistic bones. Diokno closes with a five-element definition of Filipino social justice: (1) respect for rights, (2) repair of injustices to the poor, (3) self-sustaining economy distributing benefits, (4) institutional change so that inequalities are not caused by institutions (unless temporarily favoring the least favored at the most-favored's cost -- a Rawlsian difference principle in Filipino voice), and (5) means capable of attaining these objectives. Panganiban closes by previewing the next installment: does our current justice system reflect this concept?

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban hails the SC's unanimous Belgica vs Ochoa decision (penned by Justice Estela M. Perlas-Bernabe) banishing the PDAF as a 'major milestone in nation-building.' Pleasantly surprising, he says, are three qualities: the unanimity of the justices, the emphatic language, and the all-encompassing coverage -- the form-as-substance reading of a landmark ruling. The Court reached not just PDAF but 'all past and present Congressional Pork Barrel Laws, such as the previous PDAF and CDF Articles and the various Congressional insertions,' while preserving the 1994 precedent for cases where legislator intervention was merely recommendatory. He notes the symmetry-of-restriction: the decision also bound the President, ruling that lump-sum appropriations can be spent only for specific purposes, and partly invalidating PD 910 (Malampaya Fund's 'such other purposes as may be hereafter directed by the President') and PD 1869 (Social Funds' 'priority infrastructure development projects') as undue delegation of legislative power. The decision directed return of unspent PDAF to the National Treasury, opening the door to a supplemental budget for earthquake and typhoon survivors -- the very recommendation CJ made in his November 3 column, now being implemented by Senate President Drilon and Speaker Belmonte. The direction to investigate and prosecute scammers 'within the bounds of reasonable dispatch' becomes another milestone; speedy conviction would be a greater one. Responding to doubting readers from last Sunday, he holds that 'we should never lose hope in the rule of law as the basis of reform because the alternatives, like revolution, coup d'état, or military rule, are worse.' He forecasts the milestones still ahead: Anti-Dynasty bill, FOI bill, automated election reforms, voter education, and the election in 2016 of an honest, competent president.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers the second installment of his pork-abolition doctrinal series. On its face, the pork barrel system appears to be a democratic way of apportioning government resources -- inherited from the United States, supposed to allocate funds equally to every congressional district for residents' most urgent needs. The theory: legislators, while their main job is to enact laws not build roads/schoolhouses/clinics/feed orphans/grant scholarships/distribute fertilizers, can on the side serve constituents better by directing government resources to their communities' urgent needs. Over the decades, efforts have been made to deodorize the pork barrel -- renamed Countryside Development Fund, then Priority Development Assistance Fund. Safeguards were instituted (public bidding when implemented by NGOs, staggered releases based on deliveries/performance, posting of bonds for negotiated procurements) -- but in actual implementation all were circumvented or ignored. As Sen. Francis Escudero blurted out after a Senate committee hearing, PDAF was riddled with 'ghost deliveries, fake receipts, NGOs that you can't locate, and nonexistent suppliers'; billions rolled into private pockets. The solution is going back to basic checks and balances -- strip Congress of the prerogative to direct or allocate funds; let executive agencies spend (subject to congressional safeguards); let the judiciary decide conflicts. How to return? Congress should legislate out pork -- not easy because legislators would be acting against their interest. Reader Perry Libre's letter proposes adopting results-based budgeting (CJP will forward to Butch Abad). Alternatively, the Supreme Court can declare pork unconstitutional; petitions have been filed, running counter to a long line of cases (per Sept 7 Inquirer editorial) upholding validity, but the Court can overturn jurisprudence if given cogent reasons -- and has already issued a TRO on PDAF releases for the rest of 2013. Even if pork is abolished, the treasury still needs safeguarding when executive agencies dispense public funds; legislators would be safeguarding via oversight functions and legislative investigations. But the most effective safeguard is public vigilance armed with a pro-people FOI Law. The opposition cites need for confidentiality -- but exceptions are already jurisprudentially handled: Senate v. Ermita (April 20 2006) overturned an EO banning Cabinet secretaries from Senate investigation, while extending executive privilege to military/diplomatic secrets and presidential conversations/correspondences (citing Almonte v. Vasquez, May 23 1995, that 'the President and those who assist him must be free to explore alternatives in the process of shaping policies'); similarly, SC and collegiate-court internal deliberations are privileged. The exceptions should not delay enactment -- the current pork-barrel scandal should be enough reason to hasten passage into law.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban articulates a foundational three-banishment-needs framework for the pork barrel scam: (1) identify, investigate, prosecute, and penalize the scammers; (2) recover as much of the scammed public funds as possible; and (3) avoid a repetition. Today's column addresses item 1 and a bit of 2. Beyond Janet Lim-Napoles, the conniving senators, congressmen, and cohorts must be held accountable -- a job belonging to four gutsy ladies he had dubbed 'P-Noy angels' (Aug 2 2012 earlier column): Ombudsman Conchita Carpio Morales (the constitutional 'protector of the people' with RA 6770 authority to suspend and dismiss elective and appointive officers including Cabinet members, but excluding impeachable officials + Congress + judiciary -- though she can still investigate impeachables for (a) impeachment-charge-filing in the House, (b) civil-recovery-of-ill-gotten-wealth, and (c) criminal-antigraft-indictment, and can investigate/file criminal/civil actions against legislators), COA Chair Grace Pulido-Tan (the 'sentinel of public funds' who revealed the 2007-2009 pork-audit naming lawmakers and will extend the audit to recent years to negate selectivity-impression), Justice Sec Leila de Lima (heading the prosecution arm + NBI, with responsibility for witness-safeguarding and evidence-gathering), and BIR Commissioner Kim Henares (using lifestyle-check + inventory-method 'Al Capone style' to determine criminal and tax liabilities on ill-gotten wealth). Beyond the four angels, the PCGG -- mandated (Cruz v. Sandiganbayan, Feb 26 1991) to investigate non-Marcos graft cases and institute prevention measures when directed by the President -- has extraordinary powers (hold in contempt, take over business enterprises provisionally, enjoin acts impairing functions, request foreign-asset freezing, conduct preliminary investigations) the four angels lack. The AMLC has 5-month Court-of-Appeals authorization to freeze Napoles' bank accounts; it should freeze the public-officials' accounts too. The Senate has its own investigation and may, with 2/3 concurrence, punish Members for 'disorderly behavior' and suspend/expel -- yes, it will take courage and gumption. Too many cooks spoil the broth -- but the Inter-Agency Anti-Graft Coordinating Council (IAAGCC, DOJ + COA + OOO with the latter as head agency) was formed precisely to tackle 'complex fraud-related government transactions with a national impact' covering 'P50 million or higher' and 'high ranking public officials with the position of bureau director or higher' -- contrary to recent news reports limiting it to NGOs. CJP suggests including PCGG + BIR + AMLC. Perhaps the IAAGCC can string together the charges to add up to plunder, a capital offense; penal laws provide jail terms, perpetual disqualification from public office, and forfeiture of unexplained wealth. Speedy and sturdy justice is the cry of our people; the prosecutors know this and will live up to the challenge.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban marks the coming of age of Philippine social media with the Million People March of Aug 26 2013 -- Facebook and Twitter's awesome people-gathering power proven beyond doubt. Traditional media (Inquirer, major radio-TV networks) expanded MPM's span/breadth/depth to reach masses without computers/tablets/smartphones, so that numbers (one million? 400,000? 50,000?) no longer matter -- what matters is that its message penetrated and outraged all sectors. MPM was different from Edsa PP1 (Marcos ouster) and PP2 (Estrada ouster): both had a common major convenor (the late Jaime Cardinal Sin) and led to the instant ouster of top leaders. True, the Catholic Church (World Youth Day), Bro. Mike Velarde, and Iglesia ni Cristo have convened larger Luneta congregations, but these were well-planned religious liturgies; electoral 'miting de avance' and political campaigns have drawn bigger crowds. In contrast, MPM was spontaneously called by an enraged populace to galvanize action against a bedeviling issue of governance -- not to oust a sitting President, renew religious fervor, or propel candidacies. It had no big-name convenor, no institutional organizer, no platform speakers, no grandstanding orators, no pre-planned program, no busses to ferry in the hakot, no financiers, no celebrity singers, no rabble rousers -- yet came the mammoth crowd that vented rage by simply being there, sensed common cause and fervor, and shooed away pretenders and fellow travelers with different agenda. Unlike PP1 and PP2 which ousted chief executives after 4 days of continuous Edsa rallies, MPM gathered only for a day and produced no immediate palpable result. Nonetheless, P-Noy, SP Drilon, Speaker Belmonte, and other leaders heard the cry -- in fact, even before the rally, P-Noy announced PDAF's demise. The 2014 budget still has pork with Budget Sec Butch Abad's safeguards, but given P-Noy's reformist streak, CJP forecasts pork's eventual abolition within the next three years. The people have spoken and P-Noy is not deaf. The abolition will be gradual -- unlike Marcos's and Estrada's ousters -- and MPM is destined to transform not just our leaders but the very culture and mores of our political and social life. That cannot be rushed, lest it disembowels and destroys the very foundations of society that it seeks to strengthen and uphold. Social media are the newest species of the freedom of expression and are entitled to the same Art III Sec 4 constitutional protection -- 'No law shall be passed abridging the freedom of speech, of expression, or of the press, or the right of the people peaceably to assemble and petition the Government for redress of grievances.' Free expression originated in the Middle Ages with people speaking against kings and emperors → followed by the right to peaceful assembly to redress grievances → expanded by the printing press to freedom of the press → joined in the Industrial Age by labor's right to strike and picket → followed by radio, TV, and cinema under constitutional mantle → joined in the last two decades by opinion polls and election surveys. Twitter, Facebook, and other social media are the most recent technological expansion. Originally used for bonding with friends and relatives, they have become new tools of social transformation and reformation. Now that the people have found these novel tools, they will continue to use them -- government may as well adjust to the new vigilance of citizenry. The best way to demonstrate that recognition is greater transparency and accountability, with the FOI bill as the best guarantee. Let's abolish pork, let's investigate and penalize the pork abusers and plunderers -- and let's make sure this mess will never happen again through a new FOI law guaranteeing greater public scrutiny.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the public-private-partnership (PPP) build-operate-transfer (BOT) system through three contrasting Philippine examples. The framework: the country needs modern airports, expressways, railways, water systems, electric power, and other infrastructures, but the government lacks both the funds to build them and the skill to operate them. Under BOT, private concessionaires construct at sole expense (no public funds spent); the government earns without spending and acquires the projects free after 25 years; concessionaires recoup investments plus reasonable profit from user fees adjusted periodically by regulatory agencies under pre-agreed formulas. Failed PPP: NAIA Terminal 3 -- after 20 years of disputes, still unfinished; the government has spent at least P2 billion in litigation/arbitration fees (Jan 6 2011 Inquirer editorial), will spend another P1.9 billion to complete next year, and per the Aug 7 CA decision will have to pay $371 million as just compensation to Piatco; NAIA 3 has become a drag on tourism, unable to serve the millions lured by 'It's more fun in the Philippines.' Successful PPP: Manila Water Company (the eastern half of Metro Manila; the western half is supplied by Maynilad) -- widely hailed as a model PPP by the IMF and World Bank; fully funded by private investors; has religiously paid royalties since 1997; reduced water leakage from 67% to 11% (saving 700 million cubic meters daily -- equivalent to a P25-billion dam); grown from 3 million customers (only 26% with 24/7 supply) to 6.3 million customers (all 24/7, with 1.7 million poor at subsidized rates); invested P75 billion in capital expenditures for potable surging water. Recently attacked for allegedly profiting unreasonably and charging taxes to consumers, Manila Water replied it had faithfully observed 'the agreement that was written, reviewed, approved and guaranteed by the Philippine government.' Probably still pondering the lessons of these two contrasting programs, the present government has been slow on new PPPs -- only two projects bid out in three years (the P2-billion Daang Hari-South Luzon Expressway link and the P15-billion NAIA toll road). Timid PPP: the P60-billion Light Rail Extension to Cavite -- only one pre-qualified bidder filed a 'conditional' bid; the others backed out due to 'unattractive and unbankable' terms. Fares were fixed too low; no realistic fare-adjustment mechanism was allowed (preventing equipment-replacement, proper maintenance, satisfactory service, reasonable profit); the government wanted concessionaires to shoulder real estate taxes (initially about P2 billion a year, escalating) on land they would not own -- why should they pay these taxes? Investors have choices on what projects to invest in and in what country. Consider: in 1988 Forbes Park lots sold at P5,000/sqm; 25 years (the normal PPP concession period) later, P200,000/sqm (40x); Ayala Alabang P1,000 → P45,000/sqm (45x); Jollibee shares P10 → P162 (16x, not counting dividends). It seems the failed NAIA 3 and the belated criticisms of the successful Manila Water PPP have produced over-cautiousness to the point of timidity in the Cavite LRT bidding. While every effort must be made to avoid the NAIA 3 lapses and to secure the best terms for the public, no PPP project will be undertaken if bidding terms are not viable and concessionaires are not allowed reasonable returns. When PPP investors deliver on their contracts and build infrastructures the government cannot provide, they should be commended, not unfairly deprived of contracted returns. The least government should do is honor sovereign commitments and observe the sanctity of contracts -- only then will it truly inspire inclusive growth that creates jobs, alleviates poverty, and promotes prosperity.

Legally: the Court of Appeals' Republic v. Piatco (Aug 7 2013, J. Apolinario D. Brusellas Jr.) fixed just compensation at $371,426,688.24 -- modifying the RTC Pasay's earlier $175,787,245.10 judgment. Both courts used the Republic's $300M 'replacement cost' as of Dec 2002 'when construction ceased,' but the RTC subtracted deterioration/depreciation and Piatco-noncompliance deductions, while the CA did not (ruling these were already factored in) and imposed 6% annual interest under RA 8974 because the Republic should have paid the $300M at its 2004 takeover. Both courts rejected Piatco's $900M-plus-12%-interest claim. Review strategy: before appealing to the SC, the government should first review the arbitration proceedings -- both Singapore and Washington panels dismissed Piatco's claims without award; but at Fraport AG's (the German shareholder of Piatco) initiative, a second ICSID panel annulled the first; a third ICSID panel is now hearing the compensation claim all over again. To prevent possible double payment, retired Justice Florentino P. Feliciano (the Philippine counsel) should be consulted. The overall legal strategy should be reviewed: in 1993, six taipans formed Asia's Emerging Dragon Corporation (AEDC) which submitted an 'unsolicited proposal' under the BOT scheme of RA 6957; both AEDC and Piatco offered to build NAIA 3 for at least $350M at no government cost and pay 5% (escalating to 10%) of gross revenues for 25 years; AEDC guaranteed P135M, but Piatco offered P17.75 BILLION -- Piatco won. But after the 1997 concession contract, the government executed a new agreement and three supplements giving substantial benefits to Piatco; Agan v. Piatco (May 5 2003, J. Reynato S. Puno) invalidated them. Instead of taking over the terminal temporarily 'in the exercise of its police power, not the power of eminent domain' as Puno ruled, the government -- 'for reasons I cannot fathom up to now' -- instituted the long-winded expropriation case in RTC Pasay (and later CA). The more expeditious way was to ask the SC directly (in Agan v. Piatco) to fix compensation for the takeover. As a sitting member of the Court at that time, CJP wrote a separate opinion invalidating the Piatco contracts for 'being riddled with irregularities galore and blatant violations of law and public policy, far too many to ignore'; to avoid unjust enrichment for the government, he opined that Piatco, its subcontractors, investors, and lenders should be reimbursed actual and reasonable construction expenses; and he suggested bidding out the operation under BOT-analogous principles -- with payment to builder/funders/investors/contractors staggered and scheduled into the bids alongside annual guaranteed government payments. The terminal could thus have been completed and operated immediately without expense but with sure income to the government -- however, both the SC's ruling on temporary takeover and CJP's practical suggestion were ignored. NAIA 3 was conceived 20 years ago to fill the aviation needs for the next 25 years -- obviously, the terminal would be almost obsolete as soon as completed. The government should carefully plan the next step: a new international airport for the coming 25 years. And this time, let us do it right.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban identifies the PH-China dispute over the West Philippine Sea (WPS) / South China Sea (SCS) -- over islets and reefs and their underlying resources and overhead airspace -- as the country's most vexing security problem. Origin of dispute: on May 7 2009, China submitted a note-verbale to the UN claiming 'indisputable sovereignty' over all WPS islands and 'adjacent/relevant waters' encompassed by its now-famous 'nine-dash line map,' which covers the entire SCS bordering the shorelines of Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei, Taiwan, and the Philippines -- converting the huge SCS into an internal Chinese waterway, 'similar to a gigantic Laguna de Bay.' For the PH, the dispute mainly involves the Kalayaan/Spratlys (Nansha to China, 700 isles 370 km west of Palawan) and Bajo de Masinloc (Panatag/Scarborough Shoal/Huangyan, 220 km west of Zambales); China created Sansha City (July 24 2012) to 'administer' the whole SCS and sent armed naval vessels 'to safeguard' it. The DFA alleges 'it has become impossible to continue bilateral negotiations' given China's 'rigid' 'hard-line position of indisputable sovereignty.' The PH was thus constrained to initiate arbitral proceedings under the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) -- both PH and China are among 163 ratifiers and bound by it. The PH asks the Arbitral Tribunal to declare: (1) PH and China rights in the SCS were established by UNCLOS; (2) China's SCS maritime claims are contrary-to-UNCLOS-and-invalid; (3) China should desist from violating PH maritime rights. UNCLOS recognizes four maritime zones: territorial waters (12 NM from baselines, sovereignty), contiguous zone (24 NM, customs/fiscal/immigration/sanitation authority), exclusive economic zone (200 NM, exploitation rights to living/nonliving resources), and continental shelf (additional 150 NM subject to conditions). RA 9522 (March 10 2009) defines the PH baselines; the SC's Magallona v. Ermita (July 16 2011, J. Antonio T. Carpio) upheld its constitutionality, complying with the UNCLOS prerequisite. If the PH wins, China's claims will be limited to the four UNCLOS zones; the nine-dash line will be invalidated; the SCS will be opened to international navigation; and the PH can exploit vast oil/gas/mineral deposits -- 'a stirring victory of the rule of law,' per Foreign Sec Albert F. Del Rosario. China refused to participate, arguing UNCLOS does not cover territorial-ownership/maritime-boundary conflicts -- but the PH counters that the dispute is about whether China's map conforms to UNCLOS, and a party's refusal 'shall not constitute a bar to the proceeding.' Assuming arguendo China can prove ownership, the islets are not entitled to maritime zones because they are not independently habitable (only soldiers on ration populate them); even if habitable, China would be entitled only to maritime zones around them, dwarfed by Palawan's and Luzon's longer baselines. Can a PH victory be enforced? World powers like the US will probably continue using SCS as a high sea free from Chinese sovereignty. Since the PH lacks armed clout, we could appeal to the UN Security Council -- failing there (China has veto), world opinion via the General Assembly would be our last enforcement option. Alongside arbitration, we should intensify diplomatic initiatives -- Xi Jinping has been quoted wanting 'to resolve its maritime territorial dispute peacefully and through talks... but will not abandon its legitimate rights and interests, nor will it give up its core national interests'; China has agreed to multilateral talks with Asean, a modification of its earlier bilateral-only stance. CJP truly hopes this vexing security problem can be solved peacefully and amicably without loss of face for the Philippines and China.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban introduces 'Hustisyeah' -- the Supreme Court's recent system-wide but 'rifle-focused' reform project, launched with help from USAID, the American Bar Association, The Asia Foundation, and the Asian Development Bank -- whose immediate aim is to reduce docket congestion and ultimately speed up the dispensation of justice in trial courts. The dockets are congested; the accumulation of prior years' cases aggravated by new filings without corresponding disposition simply produces a huge backlog. Four general causes: (1) delay in adjudication -- protracted/piecemeal trials + dilatory lawyer tactics + lack of investigator-prosecutor coordination in criminal cases (the bulk of congestion) + inefficient case buildup; (2) lack of efficient case management + insufficient management training for judges (addressed separately by eCourt -- see CJP June 23 2013 'Automating the judiciary'); (3) uneven caseload distribution -- some courts have the ideal 300, but most are burdened with thousands. Extreme examples: MeTC Branch 80 Muntinlupa and RTC Branch 19 Cavite each have, 'believe it or not,' over 3,500 cases -- simply impossible to handle. NCR-MeTC branches with over 2,000: Branch 79 Las Piñas, Branch 63 Makati, Branches 32 and 34 Quezon City, Branch 81 Valenzuela; with over 1,500: Branches 68/69/71/72 Pasig and Branches 35/39 Quezon City. Provincial-RTC over 1,500: Branch 16 Bulacan, Branches 89/20/22/23 Cavite, Branches 24/25/93 Laguna, Branches 71/73/74 Antipolo, Branches 66/68 Iloilo, Branches 25/26/53/55/56/60/61 Cebu, Branch 38 Saranggani, MeTC Lapu-Lapu. The rule of thumb: a trial court is congested above 500. (4) Lack of accountability -- no effective monitoring + no judge-incentives. Hustisyeah is not 'one-size-fits-all'; it requires each of the 175 target courts to individually inventory pending cases and identify those easily removable without hearing parties -- 'moto proprio' dismissable: outside-jurisdiction, prescribed/out-of-time, no pretrial brief or appearance, no discovery compliance, or failure-to-prosecute. Criminal cases archive: 6-month unserved arrest warrants, accused of unsound mind, jumped bail before arraignment, un-arrestable despite police due diligence. Civil cases archive: settled out of court, TROed by higher courts, defendant un-servable with summons within 6 months (without plaintiff fault). Other immediate clearance: mediation, arbitration, plea-bargaining agreements not contrary to law or public policy. These mechanics are not easy -- especially for really-congested courts where judges hear cases morning and afternoon and write decisions between trials. Paralegals and law students must be trained and deployed to typologize cases, identify dismissals/archives, prepare case briefs; the SC (through the OCA) needs easy-to-comprehend manuals and modules. Once properly and doggedly implemented, Hustisyeah and eCourt can together decongest the dockets and speed up the delivery of justice in the trial courts.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban replies in column form to President Joseph Ejercito Estrada's two persistent rhetorical questions from their personal encounters: (1) 'The Constitution states that the Vice President may become President only in case of death, permanent disability, removal from office, or resignation of the President. Why then was I ousted, and Gloria Macapagal Arroyo (GMA) installed as President when, clearly, I have not died, have no permanent disability, have not been removed from office, and have not resigned?' and (2) 'During my two and half years in office, I named several justices. Why is it that none of them dissented from the 13-0 decision ousting me? Why did Chief Justice [Hilario] Davide, whom I also appointed, swear in GMA as permanent President, not merely as Acting President?' CJP focuses on his conversations with Estrada. The Supreme Court's role in Edsa II began the early morning of Saturday Jan 20 2001 -- the massive Edsa-Shrine throng was poised to march on Malacañang where Estrada and supporters were entrenched; the AFP and PNP majors had publicly withdrawn support and pledged allegiance to GMA; the majority of Cabinet had resigned. Estrada could no longer govern, but GMA had no legal authority either -- no effectively functioning government. Worried about violence, civil strife, and bloodshed, CJP proposed that Arroyo be sworn in as 'Acting President'; CJ Davide agreed, and in a hurriedly-convened session that morning the justices concurred. But at the historic Edsa Shrine noon oath-taking, Davide swore GMA in 'to act as President,' not as 'Acting President.' The following Monday Jan 22, some justices were furious; Davide accepted full responsibility, saying the words were neutral and could be clarified at the proper time and case. After lengthy deliberation, the Court unanimously passed a resolution confirming the CJ's authority to swear in GMA as 'President of the Philippines.' Then came Estrada v. Desierto (March 2 2001) -- the Court voted 13-0 (Davide and CJP inhibited on motion of Estrada's counsel Rene A.V. Saguisag) upholding the ouster and the legitimacy of GMA's presidency. The decision, written by J. Reynato S. Puno (concurred in by J. Jose A.R. Melo + Leonardo A. Quisumbing + Minerva P. Gonzaga-Reyes + Sabino R. de Leon + Arturo B. Buena 'in the result'), explained that resignation may be express or implied -- though Estrada had written no express resignation, 'the totality of prior, contemporaneous and posterior facts and circumstantial evidence,' put together, could be and were construed as implied resignation: hence 'constructive resignation.' The Edgardo Angara diary (Inquirer serialized) provided 'an authoritative window' on Estrada's 'intent to resign,' confirmed by his leaving Malacañang without disability-claim. The doctrine was strengthened by Congress confirming Teofisto Guingona Jr.'s nomination as VP to replace GMA and by Congress clearly rejecting Estrada's claim of being a mere 'President on leave.' Concurring-opinion variety: J. Bellosillo opined Estrada suffered from permanent 'functional' disability; J. Mendoza clarified that what enabled GMA's assumption was 'the vacuum in executive leadership which made the government rife for seizure by lawless elements'; J. Vitug held that Estrada practically abandoned the presidency, an act equivalent to resignation. Dissenters J. Kapunan + Pardo + Ynares-Santiago + Sandoval-Gutierrez ruled Estrada had not resigned -- but the stark reality was that GMA had actually taken over and was recognized as such by Congress, the international community, and the Filipino people. In J. Gutierrez's words, 'this Court has to declare as a fact what in fact exists.' Pardo, Santiago, and Gutierrez were Estrada appointees -- their 'reality' stance answers Estrada's earlier question. Though Estrada still maintains he did not resign, CJP thinks he has accepted the immutability of his fall; all he now hopes and prays for is to redeem himself in the way he knows best -- by serving the people one last time as mayor of Manila. With full knowledge of his checkered past and heroic effort to resurrect from misfortune, the people have spoken loud and clear -- and in a democracy, the ultimate axiom is: Vox populi, vox Dei.
