one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the second installment of his two-part Estrada arc -- a personal-anecdote follow-up to last week's A454 doctrinal column on the Estrada-Comelec-Jalosjos enigma, now revealing his unprecedented December 2007 first encounter with the ex-president and the conversations that followed. Joseph Ejercito Estrada is a phenomenon. A school dropout (with no college diploma to prop him up), celebrated actor and charismatic politician, he was elected and served as town mayor (1967-1986), senator (1987-1992), vice president (1992-1998), president (1998-2001), and now mayor of Manila (2013-2016). Ousted and convicted: though elected overwhelmingly, his presidency was abbreviated by an aborted Senate impeachment trial, which led to the Edsa II People Power Revolution and, eventually, to his controversial fall on Jan 20, 2001; on March 2, 2001, the SC, voting 13-0, upheld his ouster from the top post (why? well, that question deserves another full column). Thereafter, he was charged with and convicted of plunder on Sept 12, 2007, but was pardoned on Oct 25, 2007 by President GMA; the next day, Oct 26, he walked free. He ran for president in 2010, placed second to Benigno Aquino III, but bested early favorite Manuel Villar and six others; undaunted by his only defeat in his long political career, he ran and won as Manila's mayor last May 13. CJ had a nodding, so-so acquaintance with him since he was a senator, but formally met and conversed with him only on Dec 3, 2007, two months after he was released from detention and a year after CJ retired from the judiciary -- this was during the 75th birthday party at Hotel InterContinental Manila of former Rep. Albertito Lopez, a valued client when CJ was still practicing law prior to his SC stint. Affable encounter: CJ felt rather awkward encountering him at that point when he was just released from detention -- as a retired Chief Justice, CJ had personified the judiciary that sentenced him to reclusion perpetua; but Erap did not seem to mind the surprise encounter -- in fact, he was cordial, polite and deferential. Seated opposite CJ across the rectangular head table, he broke the ice by asking how retired CJ Andres R. Narvasa was; CJ replied that after his wife Jany passed away, Narvasa had been inaccessible and depressed -- to which Erap quipped, 'Yan ang mahirap sa iisa ang minamahal at iisa ang nagmamahal. Di tulad ko, marami ang minamahal at marami rin ang nagmamahal, kaya hindi ako nalulungkot kahit ex-convict.' Embarrassed at the quip made in the presence of his wife seated beside him, CJ apologized, 'Pasensiya na po kayo, Doctora Loi, nagbibiro lang po si Presidente'; to which she gamely retorted, 'Walang problema, sanay na ako diyan' -- that exchange set an affable tone for the rest of the evening. At his request, they met a few times thereafter; he posited pointed questions from which CJ got an insight into his mindset and why he exemplifies and speaks for the masa. One of the most memorable questions he asked was, 'Chief Justice, why was I convicted of plunder and sentenced to a life in jail when I was charged merely with receiving (1) the broker's commissions in the sale of listed shares owned by the Social Security System, and (2) jueteng money? Assuming this is true, how can I be guilty of any crime when I did not steal public funds? Wala po akong ninakaw na pera ng bayan.' CJ replied that the 262-page decision of the Sandiganbayan completely answered his question -- it eloquently spoke for itself; CJ could not add or subtract anything more; in any event, if he disagreed with the verdict, he should have appealed to the SC; by accepting the pardon, he was deemed to have also accepted the judgment and the imposed penalty. People's verdict: Erap explained in his best Tagalog that his trial took more than six years while he was in detention -- had he appealed, he would have had to suffer many more years of detention without any assurance of victory; on the other hand, by accepting the pardon, he became free to seek the people's verdict by running again for public office; he preferred a direct redemption by the people. In his populist mind, all government officials are ultimately judged by the people, not by the courts -- once elected to public office, he would have been exonerated by the people, the real sovereigns of our democracy; this explains his eagerness to run for president in 2010 and for mayor in 2013; even already, the poll victory of his wife Loi and son Jinggoy as senators, and of JV (his son by Guia Gomez) as congressman and later also as senator, are proofs of his popular vindication. Be that as it may, CJ thinks Estrada cannot completely ignore the judgments of our courts and of history -- had he won the presidency in 2010, the SC would have decided his disqualification case, instead of dismissing it for having become moot after his defeat; but now, with his victory as mayor, he can no longer avoid the scrutiny of the SC (see CJ's column last Sunday, A454); indeed, the rule of law and democracy are intertwined and inseparable. They discussed many other interesting topics, which provided CJ a window to see why, despite his ouster from the presidency, his plunder conviction, and his open marital peccadilloes, he continues to be the darling of the masang Pilipino -- CJ does not necessarily agree with his unorthodox views but respects his folksy way of articulating them; 'freedom is not only for the ideas we adore but also for those we may abhor.' At 76, he thinks his 'last hurrah' as Manila mayor will vindicate him in history and will presage his passage from villain to hero in the eyes of both the masa and the intelligencia -- this, CJ will await and see.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the first installment of his two-part Estrada-Manila-mayor arc, the doctrinal half (the personal-encounter follow-up comes next week in A453), filed on the very day of Erap's noon oath-taking. Former president Joseph Ejercito Estrada won the mayoralty race in Manila -- the Comelec proclaimed him the winner, and his opponent, Alfredo Lim, publicly conceded his victory; in fact, he will take his oath and assume office this noon; however, a legal challenge earlier dismissed by the Comelec may have gained some traction due to a very recent en banc jurisprudence, Comelec v. Jalosjos. Brief background: recall that on Sept 12, 2007, the Sandiganbayan -- after a sensational trial from 2001 to 2007 -- found him guilty of plunder and sentenced him 'to suffer the penalty of reclusion perpetua (roughly equivalent to life imprisonment) and the accessory penalties of civil interdiction during the period of sentence and perpetual absolute disqualification.' Moreover, it forfeited in favor of the government (1) P545 million 'with interest and income earned... deposited in the name and account of the Erap Muslim Youth Foundation,' (2) P189 million 'inclusive of interest and income earned, deposited in the Jose Velarde account,' and (3) the so-called 'Boracay Mansion' in Quezon City. The verdict was handed down by a special division of the antigraft court composed of then PJ Teresita J. Leonardo-De Castro (now a member of the SC), who wrote the 262-page decision, Justice Francisco H. Villaruz Jr. (later became presiding justice, now retired), and Justice Diosdado M. Peralta (now also a member of the SC); Estrada denounced the Sandiganbayan as a 'kangaroo court,' and his counsel, Rene A.V. Saguisag, blurted, 'The special division was programmed to convict. We never had a chance.' GMA's pardon: despite these criticisms and initial attempts to appeal his conviction to the SC, the former President ultimately accepted the decision and the penalties imposed on him when he scribbled his agreement to the executive clemency granted him on Oct 25, 2007 by then President GMA; on the next day, Oct 26, he walked free after being detained for six and a half years. For clarity's sake, let CJ copy verbatim the pertinent portion of the 'pardon' signed by President Arroyo and Acting Executive Secretary Ignacio R. Bunye: 'WHEREAS, Joseph Ejercito Estrada has publicly committed to no longer seek any elective position or office, IN VIEW THEREOF and pursuant to the authority conferred upon me by the Constitution, I hereby grant executive clemency to JOSEPH EJERCITO ESTRADA, convicted by the Sandiganbayan of Plunder and imposed a penalty of Reclusion Perpetua. He is hereby restored to his civil and political rights. The forfeitures imposed by the Sandiganbayan remain in force and in full, including all writs and processes issued by the Sandiganbayan in pursuance hereof, except for the bank account(s) he owned before his tenure as President.' In asking the SC to unseat him, petitioner Alicia Risos-Vidal, later joined by Lim two weeks ago, argued that by its clear wording, the presidential pardon was based on Estrada's commitment 'to no longer seek any elective position or office' -- hence, the pardon did not restore his right to run for any elective office; furthermore, the Sandiganbayan's imposition of the accessory penalty of 'perpetual absolute disqualification' from holding public office was not expressly erased by the pardon. Favoring Estrada, on the other hand, is the emphatic provision of the presidential pardon restoring 'his civil and political rights' -- certainly, the right to vote and to be voted is a political right; moreover, by his election to office, the people are deemed to have pardoned him. Warped enigma: convoluting Estrada's legal enigma is Jalosjos v. Comelec, which ruled that 'the accessory penalty of disqualification remains even though one is pardoned as to the principal penalty unless the accessory penalty shall have been so expressly remitted in the pardon.' (This decision, as of CJ's deadline for this column, is not yet posted in the SC website; neither could the Court's spokesman, Prof. Theodore Te, give CJ a copy; CJ took the preceding quotes, as well as those below, from a June 19 Rappler report.) The SC held 'that the penalties of perpetual or temporary absolute disqualification carr(y) with (them) the deprivation of the right to vote in any election for any popular office or to be elected to such office.' It further explained, 'This is based on the presumption that one who is rendered infamous by conviction of a felony or other base offense indicative of moral turpitude, is unfit to hold public office, as the same partakes of the nature of a privilege which the State grants only to such classes of persons (who) are most likely to exercise it for the common good.' The big question is whether the Court will apply this ruling to unseat Estrada, considering (1) that he was convicted of plunder while Romeo Jalosjos was found guilty of two counts of statutory rape (a capital offense for which he, like Estrada, was imposed reclusion perpetua) and six counts of acts of lasciviousness, (2) that he was granted executive clemency while Jalosjos was given only a presidential commutation (or reduction) of sentence, after serving six years of the original penalty, and (3) that he was voted to office while Jalosjos was not because his name was not printed on the ballot by the Comelec -- will these distinctions make a difference? Abangan!

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes an institutional column on judicial computerization following the SC's launch of eCourt at the QC trial courts -- drawing on his own Sandiganbayan-CMIS legacy and CJ Davide's APJR foundation. The SC launched recently in the Regional and Metropolitan Trial Courts of Quezon City a new pilot program, called 'eCourt,' to automate the trial courts -- the aim is to speed up the delivery of justice by reducing case processing time, eliminate sources of graft, and improve public access to performance information in the lower courts. Brief backgrounder: in the 1990s, the SC began computerizing its administrative, personnel and financial processes via stand-alone programs; later, during the term of CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr. (which started Nov 30, 1998), the Court embarked on the computerization of the entire judiciary through its Action Program for Judicial Reform or APJR -- among the many projects of the APJR is the electronic library which was conceived by Justice Antonio T. Carpio. With the support of USAid, the Court under CJ Davide pilot-tested in Pasay City the Case Management System or CAS, a computer program designed to expedite the resolution of cases through the effective monitoring and strict observance of time limits of case events from filing to disposition. A second APJR computerization project, the Court Administrative Management Information System or Camis, supported by the Canadian International Development Agency (Cida), was simultaneously tested in Metro Manila -- it aimed to build and strengthen the capability of the Office of the Court Administrator to evolve a system of tracking the more than 800,000 pending cases in the trial courts. During CJ's term as chief justice, the Court, with the help also of USAid, fully computerized the processes at the Sandiganbayan via an improved version of CAS called Case Management and Information System (CMIS); the antigraft court was then headed by PJ Teresita J. Leonardo-De Castro, now a member of the SC and chair of its committee on computerization. Transparency and good governance: the eCourt was launched by CJ Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno, Justices De Castro and Marvic M.V.F. Leonen, Court Administrator Midas P. Marquez and Executive Judge Fernando Sagun Jr.; it is also supported by USAid and the American Bar Association Rule of Law Initiative or ABA-ROLE headed by Robert C. La Mont; it incorporates the lessons learned in the APJR and improved the past systems in various ways. First, the new program includes the payment of docket fees, which will be collected and accounted for more transparently and systematically, unlike in the manual system which was both slow and susceptible to corruption. Second, new cases were automatically raffled, without the use of the old tambiolos (manually-operated roulettes) which could be manipulated to enable parties to select 'friendly' judges. Third, eCourt flagged detention prisoners to show their places and length of detention -- at present, the accused who are too poor to post bail, or who are charged with capital offenses (and thus not bailable), are detained indefinitely in cramped and overloaded jails simply because there is no system to monitor them; often, they are forgotten and indefinitely detained. Fourth, the new system automatically produced periodic and easy-to-comprehend reports. Indeed, technology is being harnessed to assist the judiciary to declog its dockets, open its processes to public scrutiny, and eliminate occasions for graft -- in the words of CJ Sereno, computerization 'will put the seal of transparency and good governance on the courts.' Suggested improvements: once the pilot in the QC courts is freed of electronic bugs, it will be rolled out 'in major economic centers' nationwide -- this is, of course, most welcome and long overdue. However, beyond these improvements, CJ believes that computerization should not be restricted to stand-alone systems -- it should encompass the whole judiciary including the appellate courts and the SC; CJ knows that under PJ Andres Reyes Jr., the CA successfully installed its own computer program and reduced its backlog to a bare minimum; however, CJ thinks the CA system, as well as that of the Sandiganbayan, the Court of Tax Appeals, and the SC should be electronically standardized and interconnected seamlessly with the eCourt system of the trial courts. Case numbering is an example of an item that needs to be standardized and integrated in judicial automation -- under the present system, the case number in the city and municipal courts (where most cases originate) is not carried through to the regional trial courts; when the case is elevated to the appellate courts, it is assigned a new number, and still another when it reaches the SC; worse, trial courts in the various regions have different ways of numbering their cases -- as a result, it is difficult to identify the origin of appealed cases; this erratic case numbering requires the tedious and time-consuming elevation of the hard copies of lower court records before the appellate courts and the SC can review them, thereby causing long delays. However, once computerization is standardized and interconnected, the appeal process will be simplified because the original case records, often quite voluminous, can be electronically elevated with a click on a computer keyboard; finally, the entire system should be connected to the Internet for easy access by the public.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the fourth installment of his automated-elections quadrilogy (after E100 May 11 + A458 May 18 + B19 May 25 + E99 June 1), this time diving into the underlying doctrinal problem of manual-vs-electronic count discrepancies and his own 1999 dissent in Loong v. Comelec -- with a tribute coda for the June 14-15 servant-leadership conference at SMX. The discrepancies, variances or differences (or whatever the Comelec wants to call them) between the manual count and the electronic count made by the PCOS machines present formidable basic problems which CJ thinks must be solved by definitive legislation. Voters' intent: these counting variances cannot be avoided as long as the rules for manual counting are used in auditing or checking the electronic count; the basic rule in manual counting is to discern and give effect to the voters' intent; thus, anything on the ballot that may show this intent should be respected -- for example, this intent can be shown by a check mark outside the ovals: a ballot with such mark is to be credited during a manual count in favor of the candidate whose name is printed nearest the mark; sometimes, instead of shading the oval, a voter may even write down the name of the preferred candidate on the ballot -- again, in a manual count, this could arguably show the voters' intent in favor of that candidate. On the other hand, machines count ballots according to a program or command uploaded into them -- being machines, they do not think like humans in determining the intent of the voter; they merely count mechanically as programmed. In the above examples in which the oval is not shaded but check-marked or handwritten with the candidates' names, the machines would not count the vote because they are not programmed to do so -- thus a variance or discrepancy would arise, which may not necessarily be fraudulent; the question nonetheless remains: which count -- the manual or the electronic -- should be used in determining the winner? Early jurisprudence: in an early case, Loong v. Comelec (April 14, 1999), our SC said that the manual count should prevail; by way of background, this case arose from the first experiment on automated elections conducted during the May 11, 1998 polls in the ARMM; like the 2010 and 2013 elections, the 1998 ARMM experiment involved the use of preprinted ballots with ovals that were to be shaded by the voters -- however, the counting was not done at the precincts: instead, the ballots were brought by the Board of Election Inspectors (BEI) to the voting centers where machines counted them electronically; the results of the electronic count were preserved in a diskette; later, the entries were consolidated and used to proclaim the winners. One day after the polls, on May 12, 1998, while the automated counting was being conducted at the voting center, three election watchers noted that in the precinct where they voted, their candidate obtained a zero vote, which they protested was impossible; after examining the ballots, technicians determined that the counting problem was caused by the erroneous printing of the ballots -- the ovals had not been properly aligned to the names of the candidates; the local Comelec office stopped the automated counting in the entire province of Sulu, not just in the precinct concerned; all the ballots were thereafter brought to the Comelec head office in Manila where the poll body ordered the simultaneous electronic and manual counting of all the ballots for the entire province of Sulu, not just from the precinct and municipality where the error was found -- nonetheless, only a manual count was actually conducted; no electronic count was in fact made. SC ruling and dissent: upholding the manual count and denying the losing candidate's prayer for a special election, the SC ruled that 'the correctness of the manual count cannot be doubted... the naked eyes could see the check marks opposite the big ovals,' thereby implying that the voters' intent, the basic rule in manual counts, should prevail; CJ dissented on the ground that the rules for manual counting provided by the Omnibus Election Code and by the Comelec assumed that the ballots were to be filled out by the handwritten entries of the candidates' names, not by the mere shading of the preprinted ovals -- the erroneous use of these manual rules necessarily produced results 'not reflective of the automated count.' In short, the ARMM experiment taught us that rules on how to manually read automated ballots should be carefully studied and enacted into law by Congress -- using the rules on manual counting will always show a discrepancy or variance between the manual and machine results; unless these rules are enacted soon, losers in closely contested automated elections will always demand a manual recount. Servant leadership: awesome and spirit-filled was the gathering of the leaders of the various parishes and lay organizations in the Archdiocese of Manila held yesterday and the day before (June 15 and 14) at the huge SMX Convention Center in Pasay City; led by Cardinal Tagle and attended by 1,000 devotees, the conference discussed the 'embodiment of servant leadership with Jesus Christ as role model'; the speakers included Bishop Pablo Virgilio David, Bishop Broderick Pabillo, Msgr. Gerry Santos, Sr. Maria Consolata Manding, and Catholic lay leaders Barbara de los Reyes, Francisco Padilla, Selene Yu and yours truly; congratulations to the Serviam Charismatic Community for sponsoring this meeting, supported by Metrobank Foundation, Megaworld Foundation, Phinma Foundation, BPI, SM, Resorts World, PSBank, Unilab, Inquirer, Inquirer.net, Manila Bulletin, Philippine Star, Veritas, dzRH, dzIQ, etc.; Mabuhay po kayong lahat.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the doctrinal sequel to his B19 column (two weeks earlier on JFC's pained letter), now focusing on the San Roque Power VAT-refund saga as case-study of why retroactive rule-changes destroy investor trust -- anchored on Article 4 of the Civil Code. Applauding the economy's giant 7.8% leap for the first quarter of the year, the World Bank and the MAP (organization of top business executives) called for the conversion of this naked growth to inclusive growth, one that alleviates poverty and creates jobs for our masses. FDIs and hot money: to do that, MAP joined the JFC in urging our government to honor its commitments to regain its credibility and trustworthiness -- in this space two weeks ago (B19), CJ opined that trustworthiness is the reason FDIs have come in trickles to the Philippines but have been poured massively on Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore, Indonesia and other neighbors. FDIs are desired everywhere because, unlike 'hot money,' they are rooted in and stay for many decades in basic industries that spur inclusive growth -- yes, inclusive growth, not just naked economic growth, is the goal of all countries because it promotes the prosperity of both the rich and the poor, both capital and labor, both the entrepreneurs and the masses. Hot money is invested short term, like in the stock market, bonds or bank deposits that can flee as fast as they come in -- FDIs are long-term commitments; once invested, they cannot be withdrawn instantly; hot money is not necessarily bad -- it helps in the expansion of existing businesses and normally precedes the more desirable FDIs. To attract FDIs, the JFC's solution is simple and has been successfully used by other countries: 'Honor commitments. Don't change rules midstream'; MAP added that if rules are changed, the new ones should be applied prospectively so as not to prejudice existing investments. San Roque Power: to help solve the electric power outages in the 1990s, Japanese investors led by Marubeni formed San Roque Power Corp. -- they invested a huge amount of capital in the company, which imported machinery to generate about 400 megawatts of electricity, on the government's promise of exemption from the payment of VAT; at that time, it took $1 million to generate one megawatt -- now the cost has doubled to $2 million per megawatt. The benefits of VAT exemption are enjoyed not just by the investors but also by the power consumers -- without the exemption, the VAT paid to the government would be passed on to the consumers who would thus have to pay higher power rates. Procedurally, San Roque was first required by the government to pay the VAT and then to apply for refund in the BIR -- the devil, as the saying goes, is in the details, and here's where JFC's lament starts; under the law (RA 8424), an application for VAT refund is required to be filed in the BIR; if the BIR rejects the application, or fails to act on it within 120 days, the applicant has 30 days to appeal to the CTA -- otherwise, the VAT refund would be forfeited. San Roque filed its refund application with the BIR on March 28, 2003 -- but even before the lapse of the 120 days, it filed a judicial claim in the CTA on April 10, 2003; this was the accepted practice at that time -- to undergo both the administrative refund process in the BIR and the judicial process in the CTA simultaneously, instead of successively; the simultaneous filing was justified because at that time, the law also required judicial claims for refund to be filed within two years from the submission of the VAT returns; this time-saving practice of simultaneous processing was allowed by both the BIR and the CTA in at least 20 previous refund cases -- but once simultaneous recourse to the CTA was availed of, the BIR suspended its own processing. After appropriate hearings, the CTA granted San Roque the VAT refund -- but unlike in the previous cases in which the BIR simply accepted the CTA decisions, the BIR appealed to the SC, arguing that San Roque filed its judicial claim prematurely because it did not wait for the 120 days to lapse before going to the CTA; on Jan 12, 2011, the First Division of the high court unanimously dismissed the appeal and ordered the BIR to refund the VAT, holding that simultaneous processing was legally justified. Reconsideration: however, the BIR moved for reconsideration -- this time the court en banc, in a split decision last Feb 12, reversed the First Division and held that San Roque was not entitled to the VAT refund because it should have first waited for the lapse of the 120 days in the BIR before filing its judicial claim in the CTA; to this decision, San Roque filed its own motion for reconsideration that is still pending. CJ thinks JFC and MAP are not contesting the wisdom of the new decision -- they are merely asking that it be applied prospectively to new refund applications, but not to San Roque and other similarly situated companies, which followed the old practice of simultaneous processing of refund applications sanctioned earlier by the BIR and the CTA; CJ believes this stance is reasonable, fair and equitable -- new rules in processing applications for VAT exemptions should be applied prospectively; Art. 4 of the Civil Code states: '[L]aws shall have no retroactive effect, unless the contrary is provided' in the law itself; to show good faith, earn the confidence of investors and ultimately spread the fruits of our stunning economic growth with the poor, the government should heed the call of the World Bank, MAP and JFC.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the second installment of his automated-elections quadrilogy -- six days after E100 (Let's all vote Monday) and one week before B19 (Most important investment incentive) -- delivering a sharp three-adjective indictment of the Comelec's installment proclamation of 9 senators on May 16-17 while only 72 of 304 COCs had been canvassed. With due respect to the Comelec, CJ finds no legal and factual basis for the proclamation in installment of six senatorial candidates (Grace Poe, Loren Legarda, Alan Peter Cayetano, Chiz Escudero, Nancy Binay and Sonny Angara) on May 16, and another three (Bam Aquino, Koko Pimentel and Sonny Trillanes) on the next day, May 17. Rule and exception: the Comelec was reported to be trying to finish the official canvass at a late hour on the third day, yesterday May 18 (past CJ's deadline for this column), or today, and to proclaim the last three winners (Cynthia Villar, JV Ejercito and possibly Gringo Honasan) -- this final canvass may moot the prematurity of the two earlier proclamations, but it will not lessen their baselessness and illegality at their inception; it merely raises new questions: no one was chasing the Comelec, why the indecent haste? Why rush to proclaim without legal or factual basis? Why not wait for two days, just two days, and then proclaim all 12 legally and unquestionably? Let us dig deeper. The entrenched legal and commonsensical rule is that winners can be proclaimed only after all ballots have been officially canvassed; the exception to this rule is when the leading candidate(s) posts an insurmountable lead, that is, when the remaining uncanvassed ballots will not adversely affect the results -- the Comelec meticulously and correctly invoked this rule and exception when it instructed the provincial and city boards of canvassers to proclaim the local winners; it should apply the same standard to its own proclamations. To understand the exception, imagine that a total of 50 million ballots were cast in an election, of which 90% (45 million) were canvassed; imagine further that each of the first nine senatorial candidates obtained more than 20 million votes while each of the other candidates had less than 15 million -- here, even if the remaining 10% (5 million) uncanvassed votes were added to each of the other candidates, none of them could overtake the nine; in these imagined facts, the exception applies and the first nine may be proclaimed. Look now at the real facts: when the six candidates were proclaimed on May 16, the official canvass of the Comelec covered only 72 out of the 304 COCs -- these 72 COCs represented just a little more than 13 million of the country's 52 million registered voters; definitely, then, the unreported votes are several times more than the canvassed votes; even if only 70% of the registered voters actually voted, still the uncanvassed ballots will easily swamp the canvassed ones -- hence, the exception cannot apply. Belatedly, the Comelec alleges that its two earlier proclamations are justified by so-called 'group canvass reports' -- in CJ's long years as a lawyer, this is his first time to hear of these electoral instruments; in any event, law and settled jurisprudence require official COCs, not any other documents, as bases of senatorial proclamations; if the Comelec wants to change its rules of proclamation even at the risk of offending jurisprudence, it is required by law to first publish its new rules and wait for the mandatory lapse of seven days after publication before it can use the new rules. Legal enigma: clearly, then, the first two proclamations were premature and illegal -- worse, if the final canvass did not confirm their victory, not even the Comelec or the SC could unseat them; because once proclamation is made, 'the sole judge,' says the Constitution, 'of all contests relating to the election, returns and qualifications' of senators is the SET (composed of 6 senators and 3 SC justices); the SET can act only after the Senate is convened in late July -- by that time, the nine would be sitting in the Senate; on the other hand, not all those who obtained enough votes can sit because the Senate has only 24 members; then, the country would be faced with an undeserved legal enigma. At this point, CJ hopes readers realize that the prematurity and illegality of the two earlier proclamations, unless upheld and cured by the final canvass, could bring unwarranted and unnecessary legal consequences; baseless and premature proclamations should never be repeated, especially during the presidential election in 2016 -- otherwise, they could destabilize and bring unintended consequences on our democracy. Shining moment: if and when the proclamation of the nine is confirmed by the final canvass, CJ believes they should be given new certificates of proclamation, containing the legal justification for their victory -- namely, the correct number of votes and rank they garnered to avoid giving them the dubious distinction of being the only senators in our country's history with premature, imprudent and illegal proclamations. CJ cannot close this piece without applauding the courage and wisdom of Nancy Binay and Koko Pimentel in refusing to participate in the tainted proclamation rites -- Pimentel labeled the proclamation rites as improper, arguing that candidates should not only win the elections fairly but also strictly observe the law; kudos also to Romulo Macalintal for calling public attention to this legal impasse and for asking the proclaimed senators to 'return or surrender their certificates of proclamation... as a shining moment of the democratic process'; CJ dares say that Macalintal's exemplary advocacy is his own shining moment for the rule of law and democracy.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban examines the Sandiganbayan's April 10, 2013 resolution (Justice Martires, ponente) reaffirming the plea bargaining agreement under which AFP Comptroller Maj. Gen. Carlos Garcia pleaded guilty to indirect bribery and facilitating money laundering -- reduced from plunder -- and surrendered P135 million in properties, after the original plunder and anti-money laundering charges against him, his wife, and sons were withdrawn by then Ombudsman Gutierrez. The OSG (under the Aquino administration) and Ombudsman Morales both sought nullification, but the SBN rejected the OSG for lack of standing and ignored Morales's position paper -- which CJ finds 'odd' since Morales complied with the SBN's own written directive. CJ identifies legal grounds for OSG standing in the Constitution, RA 6770, and the Rules of Court requirement that lesser-offense pleas carry the consent of both offended parties (the 'Filipino people' and 'Republic'), arguing that Morales and the OSG effectively withdrew that consent. He closes with a pragmatic dilemma: since the SBN signaled Garcia would likely be acquitted if the PBA were junked (finding prosecution evidence weak and hearsay), the Ombudsman and OSG must either produce stronger evidence or 'swallow the bitter PBA pill to avoid the plague of an acquittal.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban welcomes the Comelec's March 5, 2013 reversal reinstating 238,557 overseas Filipino workers deleted from the National Registry of Overseas Absentee Voters for failing to vote in two consecutive elections (2007 and 2010). He identifies the procedural flaw: the Comelec's notice -- published in only two local newspapers and its website -- was 'miserably inadequate' for people living abroad, producing only 29 filings ('only 29 -- yes, only 29') out of 238,557 delisted voters, effectively denying due process. Applying these, he explains that the Sultan of Sulu holds an ownership claim -- his forebears leased Sabah to the British North Borneo Company, Malaysia inherited the leasehold, and rentals are still paid -- not a sovereignty claim. Malaysia, by contrast, has exercised actual sovereignty since its 1963 incorporation of Sabah following an alleged referendum. The sultan's followers' stealthy armed entry violated Malaysian immigration law, and even a valid perpetual lease does not allow a lessor to forcibly deprive a lessee of possessory rights. one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban continues his Decision-making series (sequel to his October 7 column on the Aristotelian syllogism) by focusing on the fact-finding and decision-writing dimensions of judicial decision-making. He argues that witness credibility is the most crucial element of fact-finding: trial judges have a structural advantage over appellate courts because they observe witnesses on the stand while appellate courts rely only on transcripts -- an advantage he illustrates with everyday analogies (a mother hearing her son describe a sibling's scolding; an irate wife examining lipstick marks). He identifies cross-examination -- testing coherence, consistency, and correctness -- as the historically unmatched credibility tool, especially essential for lawyer-prepared affidavits that are inherently one-sided. For decision structure, he draws on his own Velarde vs Social Justice Society ponencia (April 28, 2004) to articulate the five essential parts: statement of the case, statement of facts, issues/assignment of errors, court ruling (each issue addressed separately), and dispositive portion -- with optional prologue and epilogue for high-profile cases. He specifies the content required for criminal dispositions (guilt/innocence, specific crime, penalty, participation, modifying circumstances, civil liability, costs; plus -- for acquittals -- an immediate release order and a mandatory Bureau of Corrections report within 10 days), civil dispositions (relief granted or denied, costs), and the four-part completeness test: parties know their rights and obligations, know how to execute the decision, no further proceedings are needed, and proper relief is granted.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012 (RA 10175), which the SC enjoined via an ex parte TRO (effective immediately for 120 days) after multiple petitioners -- including the only senator who voted against it, Teofisto Guingona III -- challenged its constitutionality, with oral argument set for January 15, 2013. He sorts the law's three categories: (a) confidentiality/integrity/availability violations (hacking, illegal access, interception, data interference, cyber squatting) and (b) computer-related offenses (forgery, fraud, identity theft) are constitutionally unremarkable -- the 'grain.' But (c) content-related offenses (cybersex, child pornography, unsolicited communications, and online libel) create a 'chilling effect' -- the 'chaff.' He argues that Internet and social media communications are a technological expansion of free expression in the same lineage as the printing press, radio/TV/cinema, and exit polls (ABS-CBN v. Comelec, 2000) -- requiring the same protection from previous restraint and subsequent punishment. A netizen needs no permit to communicate online, just as no one needs a permit to speak at a gathering or publish a book; local-government-style time/place/manner regulations are permissible but content suppression (like a tax on excess email volume) is not. Free expression is not absolute -- lewd, obscene, seditious, and libelous expression remains subject to Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes' clear-and-present-danger test (falsely shouting 'fire' in a crowded theater creates liability; the same words in an open field do not). CJ predicts the SC will separate the chaff from the grain via the crucibles of freedom of expression.

The primary responsibility for economic growth rests with elected leaders and the private sector -- the judiciary's proper role is deferential interpretation: absent a clear constitutional violation or grave abuse of discretion, courts must respect the economic programs of political leaders who are accountable to voters. In human rights cases the rule is reversed: courts strictly construe laws in favor of the people and against the government. He illustrates with two SC cases. Tañada v. Angara (May 2, 1997) unanimously upheld WTO ratification using deferential interpretation -- the Constitution has a bias for Filipino goods but also recognizes globalization, and 'whether such exercise was wise, beneficial or viable is outside the realm of judicial inquiry.' The FDR-New Deal parallel warns against obstruction: the US SC's blocking of New Deal programs prompted court-packing plans, averted only when Justice Owen Roberts joined the liberal bloc ('switch in time that saved nine').

one_paragraph_summary: Using the Hamlet parallel -- 'To disqualify or not to disqualify, that is the question' -- Panganiban explains the legal trap confronting DOJ Secretary De Lima before the JBC. The Corona vacancy of May 29, 2012 must be filled by August 27 (the 90th day, accounting for 31-day months). The JBC's timetable was already delayed by the Chavez petition on the two-Congress-seats issue (temporarily allowing Escudero and Tupas), Escudero's absence from interviews, and a Metro Manila monsoon cancellation. The core problem: the JBC disqualification rule (effective December 1, 2000) bars candidates with pending criminal or regular administrative cases. De Lima, Jardeleza, and Herbosa are covered. The IBP denied De Lima's summary-dismissal request. De Lima asked the JBC to amend or suspend the rule -- citing it as possibly outdated or unconstitutional -- but EO 200 and Tañada v. Tubera (December 29, 1986) require 15 days of publication before any rule amendment affecting public rights takes effect. Any amendment would be effective only after the August 27 constitutional deadline. The column adds an irony: De Lima herself opposed Rep. Tupas's 2011 proposal to allow JBC discretion to exempt deserving candidates, arguing for expedited case resolution instead. The JBC has uniformly applied the rule since 2000 -- former Cabinet members Devanadera and Lotilla were also barred. De Lima can challenge the rule in the SC -- accepting the JBC result or 'taking arms against a sea of troubles' -- but if she can somehow hurdle the disqualification, she would stand more than an even chance of being appointed as the first woman and first outsider CJ (excluding the Yulo Japanese-occupation appointment).

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban surveys the 111-year history of the insider tradition in Philippine Supreme Court chief justice appointments -- every chief since Cayetano Arellano (1901-1920) was an incumbent SC justice at the time of appointment, with a single asterisked exception: Jose Yulo, named by the Japanese occupation military command, not a duly elected Philippine president. The JBC, since its 1987 institutionalization, has also never nominated an outsider in its 25-year history. He details the American-era succession (Mapa, Araullo, Avanceña -- all insiders), the Marcos-era six chiefs (all insiders), and the remarkable Marcos-temptation anecdote: at the height of martial law, Marcos considered UP president Edgardo Angara for CJ but Angara gracefully declined, 'subtly reminding the martial law ruler of the insider tradition.' Even Cory Aquino -- who reorganized the SC after the 1986 EDSA revolution -- preserved the tradition by naming insiders (Teehankee, then Yap, Fernan, Narvasa). Sen. Miriam Santiago failed twice to be included in the JBC short list: the JBC refused to extend the deadline for the Davide vacancy, and she failed to obtain the necessary JBC votes when the author retired in 2006. The tradition's rational basis: career judiciary requires the maturing and seasoning only actual SC experience provides, and limits partisan politicians from using vacancies as bargaining chips. But for the first time, 14 of 20 JBC finalists are outsiders -- and the council is poised to confront whether times have changed enough to break the age-old tradition.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban identifies two urgent constitutional problems facing the JBC in selecting the new chief justice. First, the dual-representation issue: the Constitution says 'a representative of the Congress' -- singular -- yet a senator and a congressman currently sit and each cast a full vote, bloating membership to eight from the constitutional seven, with significant implications for the majority-vote threshold (5 of 8 vs 4 of 7). He traces the history: CJ Teehankee's original practice was one alternating representative; under CJ Davide, Sen. Pimentel persuaded the JBC to grant two full votes on the theory that the unicameral legislature premise became obsolete when the Constitutional Commission adopted bicameralism -- but the Committee on Style failed to update the JBC composition provision. In 2006, CJ Panganiban recounts, Dean Dimayuga formally proposed reverting to one vote but Sen. Pangilinan tabled it, and CJ himself could not opine without prejudging the case. Former SolGen Chavez has now filed a formal SC petition -- CJ agrees Congress should have only one vote given the Constitution's clear text and the structural-equality principle (executive and judicial branches each get one). Second, the presiding-officer issue: CJ finds that Dulay vs JBC (July 3, 2012) definitively resolved that the most senior non-applicant justice presides over JBC proceedings, making JBC members' claim that this is only obiter incorrect -- the issue was specifically raised and decided, making it ratio decidendi, additionally supported by RA 296 which devolves CJ duties to the most senior associate justice during a vacancy.

Under the Constitution, the convicted party remains liable for prosecution -- criminally under RA 3019 (Anti-Graft Law), RA 6713 (Code of Conduct), and the Revised Penal Code; civilly for forfeiture of disproportionate assets under RA 1379 (though the one-year election bar prevents filing in court until after the May 13, 2013 senatorial elections); and administratively for disbarment. The impeachment trial evidence -- including the SALN waivers authorizing the Ombudsman to obtain bank documents -- is usable in subsequent proceedings with due process. BIR Commissioner Henares is also investigating possible tax violations using Corona's bank waiver. CJ identifies the three 'granite-knuckled ladies' -- Ombudsman Morales, Justice Secretary De Lima, and BIR Commissioner Henares -- as the institutional actors now duty-bound to assess the evidence and decide on filings. one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes as the six-week Senate recess ends and the impeachment trial resumes on May 7, 2012. Though the prosecution withdrew five of eight Articles, it established a prima facie case on Article 2: CJ Corona's repeated failure to include properties in his SALNs culpably violates the Constitution and betrays public trust. The Senate's January 27, 2012 order linked non-disclosure to the constitutional duty to completely, truthfully and faithfully declare assets, and held that undisclosed assets disproportionate to known income constitute betrayal of public trust. Prosecution evidence includes undeclared/undervalued houses, condos, and peso deposits appearing manifestly disproportionate to Corona's legal income. On the dollar deposits: PSBank president Garcia admitted five dollar accounts belong to the CJ; the SC issued a TRO; the Ombudsman wrote that the CJ has at least $10M in PSBank and other banks. CJ applies the willfully suppressed evidence rule (Rule 131 Sec. 3): the TRO was addressed to the Senate and prosecution, not to Corona himself -- he can voluntarily give written consent to the bank inquiry without violating it; failure to do so may trigger the adverse presumption. The SWS poll (March 10-13) shows 63% of Filipinos believe Corona has hidden wealth, 12% are unconvinced, 24% undecided -- the Court of Public Opinion has also been persuaded.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes on the eve of the April 30, 2012 SALN filing deadline for all public officials and employees, providing a practical guide to filling out the two-page Civil Service Commission form -- prompted by the Corona impeachment trial's public education effect on SALN requirements. He clarifies the most contested issue: the SALN form requires three real estate values (assessed, current fair market, and acquisition cost), but acquisition cost -- not market or assessed value -- is the legally correct basis for determining whether a public official has amassed ill-gotten wealth, as held by the SC in Republic v. Sandiganbayan (January 30, 2002, CJ Davide). Acquisition cost is the amount in the deed of sale; improvement costs require an honest good-faith estimate; honest errors in approximating market values should not constitute falsification. For personal properties, invoices and receipts provide the data; motor vehicles must be declared (Flores v. Montemayor, 2011 -- dismissal for omitting two cars). Business interests and financial connections must also be declared (Rabe v. Flores, 1997 -- dismissal for failing to disclose a market stall). The SC in Ombudsman v. Valeroso (2007) described the SALN as 'a valid check and balance mechanism to verify undisclosed properties and wealth.' Failure to file complete, accurate, and truthful SALNs may subject the declarant to administrative sanctions (reprimand to dismissal plus forfeiture and permanent ban), criminal liability, and civil forfeiture of properties manifestly disproportionate to legitimate income -- all enforced primarily by the OMB.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban answers readers' question of whether the Corona impeachment trial's two contempt proceedings were 'too much ado about nothing.' Vitaliano Aguirre II was cited for cupping his ears while Sen. Santiago was rebuking the prosecution -- a 'galactic act of epal' in Santiago's words, done in open court (direct contempt, punishable summarily); the Senate resolved to merely admonish him within 2-3 minutes of a caucus, though Aguirre was caught on camera packing his clothes for an expected detention. The entire defense team (except retired Justice Cuevas) was cited for a press conference claiming Malacañang offered senators P100 million each in soft projects -- done outside the court (indirect contempt, requiring formal written charge and hearing); none could name their source; only Jose Roy III was punished, with a reprimand, which he gallantly accepted: 'I thank the impeachment court that [the other defense lawyers] were not included in the penalty.' CJ clarifies that plain admonition is not even a penalty under Rule 140 (Re: Vasquez, 2008) -- making the Aguirre sanction technically nothing. When the source of contempt is protected free expression, courts must be cautious: citing the UP Faculty contempt case (2008, J. de Castro: 'All the Court demands is the same respect and courtesy that one lawyer owes to another') and the 1918 US v. Bustos wisdom that 'a clear conscience, not muzzled critics, is the balm for wounds.' CJ recommends that contempt be invoked judiciously and sparingly, and that courts set an example of dignified restraint.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains the legal framework for using bank deposits as evidence in the Corona impeachment trial. Under RA 1405 (Bank Secrecy Law), deposits are absolutely confidential with six exceptions -- including impeachment cases, making the Senate's subpoenas of PSBank and BPI for Corona's peso deposits legally proper. The defense filed a motion to suppress the peso deposits as the fruit of the poisonous tree (a rule coined by Justice Frankfurter and adopted by the Philippine SC in People v. Alicando, 1995) -- claiming the specimen signature card was illegally leaked to the prosecutors. The Senate rejected the motion on two grounds: bank secrecy laws do not bar admission of illegally obtained bank records, and there is no evidence the government leaked the card. CJ notes the puzzle: Corona himself said the source 'could have come only from the PSBank' -- explaining why he closed three PSBank peso accounts on the day of his impeachment, December 12, 2011 -- yet his lawyers still filed the motion. On the dollar deposits: RA 6426 (Foreign Currency Deposit Act) has only one exception (depositor's written permission); PSBank obtained a SC TRO barring disclosure. But the SC has previously allowed such examination in Salvacion v. Central Bank (1997) and China Banking v. Court of Appeals (2006) to 'prevent the perpetuation of an injustice'; and the Senate argues that 'the statutory rule on absolute confidentiality must yield to CJ Corona's clear constitutional obligation to fully declare and publicly disclose his assets.' PSBank president Pascual Garcia admitted the five dollar accounts belong to the CJ. CJ accepts at face value Corona's TV pledge to explain the accounts and calls on him to demonstrate -- before not just the impeachment court but the nation -- the fitness, integrity, and moral ascendancy worthy of the highest judicial office.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban surveys proof standards across disciplines -- beyond reasonable doubt (criminal), preponderance of evidence (civil), substantial evidence (administrative), laboratory reproducibility (scientific), sensory perception, faith, and hearsay rules of history -- to argue that none of them binds the Senate in an impeachment. Since the Constitution lodged impeachment in the Senate (not a judicial tribunal), and since even non-lawyers serve as senator-judges, insisting on judicial proof standards would be constitutionally inappropriate and disadvantageous. The Senate's sole power to try and decide necessarily includes the ancillary authority to set its own standard of proof -- a point even Corona's own answer concedes by calling impeachment 'admittedly political in character.' The author identifies the ultimate impeachment standard as the national interest: whether the nation will be better served by ousting or retaining the official. This is a policy question driven by political wisdom, not strict legality -- and senators, not lawyers, are its experts.

While the Constitution uses legal language and sets out impeachment parameters in legalese, it lodged initiation in the House and decision in the Senate -- both bodies mostly of non-lawyers chosen by the people as their alter egos. If impeachment were mainly legal, the power would have been given to the SC, limited to lawyers with CIPI qualifications. one_paragraph_summary: Using the Ramgen Bautista murder case -- allegedly masterminded by siblings RJ and Ramona, with money rifts over the ailing Sen. Revilla Sr.'s unequal allowance distribution as the theorized motive -- as his entry point, Panganiban surveys the legal rights of illegitimate children under Philippine law. He opens with his personal moral position: 'there are really no illegitimate children; there are only illegitimate fathers and mothers' who beget offspring outside valid marriage. Under the Civil Code and Family Code, illegitimate children use the mother's surname by default, but the 2004 Revilla Law (RA 9255 -- authored by the senator himself) allows use of the father's surname through express (not implied) recognition in a signed birth certificate, notarized document, or written instrument. Once expressly recognized, illegitimate children gain support rights (sustenance, dwelling, clothing, medical care, education extending beyond majority, transportation -- proportional to the giver's means and the recipient's needs), and siblings of any filiation must support each other under the Family Code. On succession, recognized illegitimate children are compulsory heirs entitled to a legitime equivalent to one-half of what a legitimate child receives -- they cannot be disinherited from their legitime. Adopted and legitimated children (whose parents had no legal impediment to marry at the time of their conception) enjoy the same rights as legitimate children.

Judge Jocelyn Solis-Reyes recently directed the prosecution to prepare 5-6 witnesses per trial day and hear the case three times weekly (from the current twice weekly), but prosecutors balked: witnesses must be transported from Maguindanao, speak only local dialects, need personal reassurance of safety, and require government resources for housing and feeding. CJ argues that time is the prosecution's enemy -- witnesses forget, lose interest, become corruptible, disappear, or die -- and that 'a little more diligence, patience, and gutsiness' is essential. He also flags three structural risks: Judge Reyes's potential promotion would deny the trial the irreplaceable demeanor-observation advantage she has built over two years (the basic rule being that trial courts' credibility findings deserve great weight because they observe witnesses on the stand); the 187 accused each theoretically entitled to a lawyer with different strategies creates unlimited obstruction potential; and any interlocutory ruling could trigger a TRO from a higher court. Under RA 9189 (Overseas Absentee Voting Law), greens may vote for national candidates only if they execute an affidavit declaring they will resume physical residence in the Philippines within three years of registration -- the affidavit overcoming the Macalintal v. Comelec (2003) presumption that permanent foreign residency abandons PH domicile. By contrast, under Nicolas v. Comelec (2006), duals need not establish PH residence or execute the affidavit at all -- the Constitution's implicit authorization of non-resident absentee voting removes the residency requirement. Fil-American lawyer Ted Laguatan argues that greens who remain Filipino citizens (unlike duals who took foreign citizenship) should not be treated worse, and that the affidavit has a 'chilling effect' that negates the constitutional intent to enfranchise all overseas Filipinos. The residency requirement is now an 'anachronistic roadblock' -- overseas Filipinos, the single biggest source of foreign exchange, should vote freely in national elections.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban introduces the unique character of the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity (FLP) law scholarships -- fully funded by the Tan Yan Kee Foundation at P200,000 per scholar per year (tuition, books, monthly stipends) -- which are granted on pure merit rather than financial need, with paucity of funds considered only as a tiebreaker among equally excellent applicants. The scholarship requires recipients to espouse, promote, and fulfill the liberty-and-prosperity philosophy: that legal education has overemphasized political freedoms (due process, equal protection, free speech, free assembly, presumption of innocence) and underemphasized economic and social freedoms (freedom from hunger and want, the right to pursue entrepreneurship and innovation, the right to conquer poverty through the rule of law) plus the corollary responsibility to share prosperity and equitably distribute the fruits of labor and capital. He asserts that 'freedom and food, justice and jobs, ethics and economics, nay, liberty and prosperity are equally important; one is useless without the other,' and that 'the best way to conquer poverty, to create wealth and to share prosperity is to unleash the entrepreneurial genius of people.' He provides the complete alphabetical roster of twenty current scholars (ten third-year and ten fourth-year, drawn from U of Cordilleras, FEU, San Beda, Ateneo de Manila, U of San Carlos, UST, U of Cebu, PUP, and De La Salle), the fifteen past FLP scholars taking the May 2018 bar (results expected May 3), the cash prize structure for bar topnotchers (P200,000 for first place, P100,000 each for second through tenth), and the full TYKF board (Dr. Lucio C. Tan as chair plus 14 trustees including Joaquin Bernas, Amando Tetangco Jr., and Cesar Virata) and FLP board (CJ as chair plus 8 trustees including his late wife Leni).

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban marks the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity's 10th anniversary by reflecting on the FLP's four October themes -- theory versus practice, dreams versus realities, negative versus positive, slogans versus philosophies. He recalls his pre-law political science professor challenging him to refute the Marxist slogan 'From each according to his ability and to each according to his need,' a slogan 'difficult to refute' for a 'dirt-poor student' like him; yet he knew that communism, however appealing in theory, was appalling in practice, leading him later to forge his legal philosophy of 'safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity under the rule of law.' He observes that the Bill of Rights is written mainly in negative language ('No person shall be deprived of life, liberty or property without due process of law...'), as are most of the Ten Commandments ('Thou shall not kill,' 'Thou shall not steal') and electoral mantras (Marcos's 'Alis diyan!' against Macapagal; Cory's 'Tama na! Sobra na! Palitan na!' against Marcos). Constitutional positives -- like 'The goals of the national economy are a more equitable distribution of opportunities, income, and wealth' -- and Jesus's two positive commands ('Love God with all your heart... and love your neighbor as I love you') exist but are outnumbered, and slogans rarely transform into fulfillment without 'sustainable philosophies, implementable programs, and realistic timelines.' He confesses that even his SC decisions were mostly negative in language -- commanding stops, dismissing petitions, enforcing negatively-phrased rights -- with only a few on positive provisions, leaving a yearning that he had not done enough. After retirement, invitations from tycoons to serve as independent director or adviser revealed their own yearnings for philanthropy and CSR, and together with dear friends he organized the FLP on October 13, 2011. Its first decade (2011-2021) achieved sustainability, purchased an office condo HQ in Makati, and sponsored four projects (professorial chairs, legal scholarships, dissertation-writing contests, educational assistance for the poor), funded by over P164 million from family, partners, and friends -- transforming 'the safeguarding of liberty... from a mere dream to a sustainable reality' that will continue 'beyond my lifetime,' with the planned Interactive Museum of Liberty and Prosperity (in partnership with the Supreme Court) as the ultimate first-decade project. During its second decade (2021-2031), the FLP will enlarge its focus to help eliminate extreme poverty, initially by sponsoring scholarships and dissertation contests among MBA students in economics, sustainability, business law, and entrepreneurship -- pivoting from the liberty side to the prosperity side of the overarching philosophy.

He proposes that the authors would constitute a 'Supreme Court for economic matters' and uses the launch to restate his core philosophy: 'Humans need both justice and jobs; freedom and food; ethics and economics; peace and development; liberty and prosperity' -- twin beacons that must always go together because 'one is useless without the other,' achieved by unleashing the entrepreneurial genius of people. He cites Tañada v. Angara (May 2, 1997), which he authored -- affirming Philippine WTO membership and adopting globalization, liberalization, deregulation, and privatization against the then-reigning 'Filipino First' doctrine -- and recalls that he began with only three concurrences but persuaded the other 14 to a unanimous outcome. He recounts CJ Beverley McLachlin of Canada renaming the philosophy 'liberty and prosperity under the rule of law' to stress that 'egalitarian goal should be achieved only via libertarian methods,' and the Global Forum's Manila Declaration. He founded the FLP in 2011 to give equal primacy, sponsoring three projects: 20 Metrobank Foundation professorial chairs on liberty and prosperity, 20 annual Tan Yan Kee Foundation P200,000 scholarships (first batch all passed the bar; two placed first and fifth, with CJ Peralta chairing the board), and Ayala Corporation-funded dissertation contests (~P2 million in prizes, with Senior Justice Perlas-Bernabe as board chair). FLP plans a roving museum in 2020 and a Global Forum reconvening in 2021.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens the first part of his speech at the Asean Law Association's 12th general assembly opening luncheon (February 26, 2015, at Makati Shangri-La) with a famous quotation from Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.: 'If a man does not have a job or an income, he has neither life nor liberty nor the possibility for the pursuit of happiness.' It may seem ironic to begin a speech before the judicial and legal greats of Asean by citing an American civil rights icon -- a foreigner in the 10 member countries -- but CJ quotes MLK not because of his nationality, color, gender, or religion, but because of the truth he said so simply and profoundly: truth is eternal and limitless, not bound by sovereignty, territory, ideology, or legality. And that truth is this -- humans need both justice and jobs; freedom and food; ethics and economics; peace and development; liberty and prosperity; these twin beacons must always go together; one is useless without the other. CJ has always espoused 'Liberty and Prosperity' as the twin anchors of his being as a lawyer and as a jurist. Many of those present attended his valedictory activity as chief justice when on October 18-20, 2006 he convened a 'Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity' at the same Makati Shangri-La. Even in retirement he continues the advocacy: in 2011, when he celebrated his 75th birthday, he organized the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity, which is now honored to cosponsor the general assembly together with the Philippine Supreme Court and the Philippine ALA Chapter. Certain truths transcend sovereignties, territories, ideologies, and legalities. And one of these truths is this: the best way to conquer poverty, to create wealth, and to share prosperity is to unleash the entrepreneurial genius of people by granting them the freedom and the tools to help themselves and society. To prove the thesis, CJ quotes a popular adage from Confucius: 'Give a man a fish and you feed him for a day. Teach him to fish and you feed him for a lifetime.' Indeed, to save a fisherman from destitution, we must help him learn how to fish more effectively, educate him in the skills needed to catch fish more efficiently, assist him in acquiring a boat, allow him the freedom to sail the vast oceans, and teach him how to market his catch. Sometimes, some of us fear that the fisherman may get lost and die in storms, become selfish and want to own the entire ocean and its resources, or become too rich and powerful and metamorphose into a rival, an enemy, or worse, a master. Such fears of possible misjudgments may indeed happen some of the time -- human arrogance, greed, and avarice lurk in all undertakings, but they are the exceptions rather than the rule. We must never stop dreaming for fear that reality may shatter our dreams; that is part of the interesting reality of being human. On the other hand, the goal of governance and of law is to provide guarantees and incentives to help the fisherman prosper, to create the institutions to support him, and to promulgate minimal regulations to prevent him from appropriating all the fishing grounds, from keeping all the earnings to himself, and from forgetting his obligation to pay reasonable taxes -- government must also inspire him to share his consequential wealth with the rest of society. To validate this simple truth, take three countries. The United States, the most powerful country in the world and the great promoter of liberal democracy, attained affluence because of the pioneers who defied monarchical tyrannies and started a new nation that unleashed the inventive, innovative, and entrepreneurial spirit of people like Thomas Edison, Nikola Tesla, Cornelius Vanderbilt, John Rockefeller, Andrew Carnegie, Henry Ford, and J.P. Morgan -- and of great government leaders like Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Dwight Eisenhower who provided them with the encouragement to attain their dreams and the good governance to contain their greed and share their wealth. Then to China, the second most powerful economy in the world and the prime promoter of the communist system: true, Mao Zedong led the masses in a revolt that dislodged the corrupt and inefficient government born of an outdated monarchy, but it was Deng Xiaoping who led this nation to unparalleled economic prosperity by unleashing the entrepreneurial ingenuity of the Chinese under his 'One-Country-Two-Systems' philosophy. Finally, to Korea: as a result of World War II, this country was divided into North and South, which unfortunately could not accept their division and engaged in a terrible war that ruined their economies; rising from the ruins, South Korea relied on the entrepreneurial spirit of the Koreans, built on their private initiative, creativity, freedom, and hard work, and thereby ushered prosperity. In contrast, North Korea -- despite its technological and military bravado -- wallows in abject poverty as a result of its tight grip on creativity and on its inordinate fear of the entrepreneurship, education, and freedom of its people. (Concluded next Sunday in B17.)

II, III, XIII, XIV, XV) and in international instruments including the UDHR and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with the recent Turkish jet shootdown of a Russian warplane, which has raised the specter of nuclear holocaust and prompted readers to ask about the aftermath of his two prior WWIII-hotspot columns (May 31 and June 7, 2015). He recalls Gen. Douglas MacArthur's lament at the Japanese surrender: 'War can no longer be controlled. It can only be abolished' -- provoked by the Hiroshima (Aug 6, 1945) and Nagasaki (Aug 8, 1945) bombs that instantly killed over 100,000 civilians and permanently scarred hundreds of thousands more. Despite this warning, several states have accelerated nuclear weapons production via intercontinental missiles, silos, and submarines, raising the prospect of nuclear annihilation in the Middle East, Ukraine, and South China Sea. He paints the cascade: wiping out most living things, searing earth's foliage, melting polar caps, flooding most countries, shrouding the globe in radioactive clouds, ushering in an ice age. He then proposes a 'new world order' he calls the International Peoples Union (iPU) -- a federation of nonindependent nations modeled on the United States, Russia, or Canada but worldwide, with one central government responsible for peace and order for everyone. Unlike the League of Nations and the United Nations, the iPU will not respect state rights but only human rights; its mandate will come not from victors or losers but from victims -- all becoming citizens of one united world rather than separate independent states. It will have an international police force to enforce its laws. A nuclear holocaust has no victors or losers, only victims with one common aspiration: outlawing war and destroying all weapons of mass destruction. First leaders will be self-anointed, organizing survivors in licking their wounds and healing the earth; nuclear energy will propel machines for peace and prosperity. Eventually leaders will be elected worldwide. The iPU will have absolute dominion over earth's resources for the common welfare of all earthlings. In governance, the individual will be supreme; sovereign rights of states will be severely degraded if not totally eliminated. All earthlings will be governed as equal citizens. International law will radically change into the equivalent of domestic law for the entire world. Concretely, the Unclos maritime entitlements -- 12 nautical miles of territorial sea, 200 nautical miles of EEZ, 150 nautical miles of continental shelf -- will become obsolete because there will be no territorial integrity to protect from inter-state incursion. The International Bill of Human Rights -- UDHR, ICCPR, ICESCR -- is currently unenforced worldwide because many states refuse to recognize it, claiming it contravenes their constitutions under the principle of noninterference in domestic affairs. (The Philippines, by contrast, recognizes and enforces these instruments; its SC has accepted them as 'part of the generally accepted principles of international law that are binding on us.') Under the iPU, the Bill could easily be enforced, possibly with modifications to address criticisms that it contains 'Western biases that contradict some religious beliefs.' All peoples of the earth -- regardless of gender, creed, race, language, religion, or color -- will be entitled to equal protection, dignity, and respect. Loyalty will be primarily to the world, only secondarily to nations and villages. Transparency, responsibility, and accountability will be the hallmarks of governance; meritocracy, integrity, probity, and honor will be the inexorable standards for public servants. He closes with the ironic silver lining: a nuclear holocaust may have the unintended consequence of ushering in a new world order making the individual supreme and the state largely irrelevant.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the companion column to B15 -- last Sunday's three-hotspots survey -- by zooming out to historical arcs and strategic options. Since time immemorial, humankind has been torn by strife and war: beginning among families and tribes, then crossing nations as humans mastered the earth and its resources, with victors enslaving the vanquished, raping their women, plundering their land, and looting their treasury. Weak nations paid tribute to the strong. Pax Romana reigned only while Rome remained absolutely supreme. The recurring cycle continued until the end of World War I when the victors formed the League of Nations as multiparty guarantor of world peace -- which utterly failed within two decades because it had no power to sanction violators, allowing Hitler to rise riding the Nazi rhetoric of condemning the harsh WWI surrender terms that impoverished Germans. After WWII the allied powers learned their lesson: instead of totally impoverishing the vanquished with heavy reparations, the US-led victors assisted them to recover through the Marshall Plan and MacArthur Plan (to rebuild Japan); Germany and Japan now lead Europe and Asia (except China) in economic development and have become America's great allies. The UN was equipped with more teeth, except that sanctions only work if the five victors (US, Russia, UK, France, China) who constitute the permanent SC members are unanimous -- any veto defeats a UN sanction. Consequently, the United States, sometimes by its lonesome or with token aid from its allies, became the sole guarantor of peace: Pax Americana reigned because American arms and men intervened in regional aggressions, as in Korea and Vietnam. But it was not absolutely successful: US-led UN forces protected South Korea's territorial integrity but were not able to sanction the North Korean invaders (assisted by China) who retained their half of the 38th parallel; America was defeated by a defiant North Vietnam (though united Vietnam paradoxically became a US ally in the SCS dispute); the war-on-terror record in Iraq and Afghanistan has been spotty; rising casualties and costs have made America war-weary, to the utter dismay of old allies like Saudi Arabia and Israel. In the face of current threats in the three hotspots (SCS/East China Sea, Ukraine, Middle East) and a fourth suggested by readers (India-Pakistan), the US resolve to maintain Pax Americana is being put to severe test. The crucial question faces the American people who will soon elect a new president: will they continue bearing the high human and economic costs of being the world's policeman? Will they prevent World War III? Will they escape its devastation if it happens? The best way of preventing a nuclear war is to destroy all nuclear weapons -- the US and Russia tried, but other nations did not follow suit and in fact acquired their own atomic arsenals; so the strategy has gone back to aiming for peace but bracing for war. Traditional war-avoidance modes include diplomacy, negotiations, good offices, conciliation, arbitration, boycott, embargo, and blockade. Ironically, however, the real deterrent to a misbehaving nuclear power is the threat of mutual annihilation, as shown by President Kennedy in 1962 when he made clear the US was prepared for Armageddon if Khrushchev did not recall the nuclear-arms-carrying Soviet ships steaming toward Cuba. World War III would mean veritable destruction of all combatants; while America escaped direct devastation in WWI and WWII, it cannot avoid the nuclear fallout of its own ICBMs, not to count the warheads flung by its enemies. Ideally, CJP believes the real guarantee of world peace is the rule of law -- humans conquered the earth not because of brutal muscles of lions and bears or teeth of sharks, but because of their intelligence and reason; only by the same rationality through faithful observance of the rule of law can they assure their survival and prosperity. Until that ideal state is reached, the next best alternative is to work for peace but brace for war.
