one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the first half of a WWIII-hotspots pair -- concluded the following Sunday in B14. WWIII can erupt in three hot spots: (1) the South China Sea (also called West Philippine Sea) and East China Sea, (2) Ukraine, and (3) the Middle East -- in all of which two or more of the seven nuclear powers (US, Russia, China, UK, France, Israel, Iran) are major players. SOUTH AND EAST CHINA SEAS: China is building civilian and military facilities with 'defense and offense capabilities' in the Spratlys and other SCS islets -- also claimed by the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei, and Taiwan -- and is reclaiming huge tracts in eight islets, including an airstrip in an 800-hectare reclamation. In the adjacent East China Sea, China has a bitter confrontation with Japan: it claims 'undisputed sovereignty' and denies Unclos applicability in the Spratlys yet asserts Unclos-recognized EEZ in the East China Sea. It also asserts sovereignty over the Senkaku Islands (Diaoyu in Chinese) -- under Japan's control with oil/gas reserves below -- and on November 23, 2013 declared an Air Defense Identification Zone (Adiz) requiring all aircraft (including over Senkaku) to file flight plans and submit radio/transponder information; Japan said it would not comply. Lately the US has joined the fray, diverting 60 percent (up from 40 percent) of its powerful navy to the SCS/East China Seas; a few days ago it heralded the deployment to Japan of the USS Ronald Reagan, the largest nuclear-powered aircraft carrier in the world, with battleships, cruisers, and destroyers. The Chinese have not yet placed offensive military installations (like missile silos) on reclaimed islets -- but if -- repeat, if -- they send missile-carrying warships, the US may declare a blockade the way Kennedy did in October 1962 when Khrushchev sent missile-carrying vessels to Cuba. Fortunately Khrushchev backed off; will China back off similarly? If not, WWIII could erupt in our backyard. RUSSIA AND UKRAINE: upon the 1991 Soviet collapse, Russia and Ukraine became independent states with uneasy relations as Ukraine veered West, repulsing Russian overtures. About 20% of Ukrainians have Russian roots. Last year, after a controversial referendum, Russia annexed Crimea; separatist forces armed with Russian-made heavy weapons fought the Ukrainian military and occupied Donbass, Donetsk, and Lugansk. President Poroshenko avows the separatists are disguised Russian regulars; Putin denies. Russia stationed about 40,000 troops on the border conducting war games. WWIII risk arises if Russian troops openly cross the border to aid separatists, or if an important military/political leader is slain -- recalling that WWII began with Hitler's blitz of Poland and WWI was ignited after Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie were killed by Serb militants. THE MIDDLE EAST is complicated: in Yemen, Saudi Arabia supports the government while Iran arms rebel Houthis; the US backs the Saudis with logistics and intelligence -- but not much else. Yet the US and Iran are together in assisting the ragtag Iraqi army against the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS). To the chagrin of Saudi Arabia and Israel (America's staunchest ME ally), the US is spearheading a 10-year move to lift trade sanctions against Iran in exchange for Iran's dubious vow to moderate its nuclear ambitions. Hawkish Israeli PM Netanyahu is so enraged that he threatens to unleash a preemptive nuclear strike on Iran -- if he does, the world will be plunged into a holocaust because Iran can retaliate in kind. The Saudis are also inconsolable at US reconciliation overtures and demonstrate their disaffection through the sudden decline of crude-oil prices to discourage US shale extraction and to undercut it at viable commercial prices.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes for Labor Day a foundational FLP economic-philosophy column asking: Will our government ever be able to eradicate poverty? Despite the pessimism of many Filipinos, the World Bank's confident answer is yes -- within one generation, provided the economy sustains its current 6 percent annual growth. The math is striking: at this rate, the Philippines can double per capita income in a decade, raise it five times in two decades, and 11 times in three decades -- average yearly per capita income of $3,300 in 2013 would increase to $35,000 in 2043. Singapore, China, and Malaysia have done it. The usual objection is that they eradicated poverty 'at the cost of freedom.' As Time magazine (April 6, 2015) noted, Lee Kuan Yew -- who died March 23 after serving as PM from 1959 to 1990 and 'mentor' thereafter -- trumped the individual in favor of the community: suppressing dissent, jailing oppositors, curbing press freedom, and micromanaging life to the extent of banning chewing gum (to prevent littering), pushing the educated elite to marry one another (to upgrade the people's genes), limiting childbirth (to control population), and telling everyone to flush toilets (to prevent diseases). To be fair, however, LKY led by example in living modestly, stopped communist insurgency, jailed the corrupt, paid public servants higher than the private sector, and rewarded meritocracy -- making Singapore one of the best places to live, especially now that it has eased speech controls. To eradicate poverty within a generation, must the Philippines ape Singapore or China? Not necessarily, says the WB. What matters per its paper 'Making Growth Work for the Poor' is investing more in health, education, and infrastructure, enhancing competition, simplifying regulations, and protecting property rights -- validated by international aid agencies, think tanks, and credible local economists like Romeo Bernardo and business leaders like Ramon del Rosario. WB president Jim Yong Kim -- whom CJP met personally during his recent PH visit -- boldly announced the Bank's twin goals: ending extreme poverty in the world by 2030 (only half a generation from now) and boosting shared prosperity among the poorest 40 percent in developing countries, without any mention of altering political systems. Authoritarianism, whether Chinese or Singaporean variety, will not work in the Philippines. After the sad experience under Marcos, the people will not allow a return to one-party or one-man rule. True, many cheered the discipline and respite from chaos that martial law brought during its first few years, but later on corruption and cronyism crept in -- unlike Singapore where the leadership was intelligent, single-minded, selfless, and honest. Authoritarian rule has become outmoded -- not just in Asia but in the old Soviet republics, the Middle East, South America, and Africa -- yes, in the whole world. Suppression of individual freedom is no longer possible in the Information Age: the Internet and digital transmission cannot be confined by traditional sovereign and territorial boundaries; despots can no longer hide their crimes; serious offenses can be prosecuted across borders via the ICC; commercial and civil disputes are no longer the monopoly of judicial tribunals because parties can now choose laws and judges through voluntary arbitration. Yes, we Filipinos will just have to work together in freedom to continue the reforms in good governance and the economy. CJ closes with his FLP signature passage from a recent Asean Law Association speech: 'The peoples of the world and of Asean have different histories, traditions, cultures, ideologies and mindsets. But I dare say all of them need liberty and prosperity. Some countries... start with improving their people's economic lives first and restrict temporarily in measured stages their political liberty. Some others begin with political liberty thinking that their economy would flourish as a necessary consequence. Still some others rise with a combination of both liberty and prosperity at the very beginning... But I also firmly believe that eventually and inevitably, all the peoples of the world need and deserve liberty and prosperity in equal measure.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers the second part of his speech at the opening luncheon of the Asean Law Association's 12th general assembly -- companion to B06 (March 1). Asean is the 'darling of the world.' Some members like Singapore have attained First-World status; Malaysia and Thailand are exemplars on how to propel economies; and during the past few years, the 'VIPs of the world' -- Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines -- have exhibited enviable records of GDP growth. Why? Because the peoples' entrepreneurial spirit had been unleashed even if inadequately in some places; because permanent institutions are being strengthened and relied upon instead of upon the apron strings of temporary leaders; because educational standards have been uplifted and have released the spirit of the fisherman; because governments are learning that the best way of governing is to govern the least and to allow people to freely use their innovation and initiative, interfering only to check avarice and to level the playing field. Indeed, the primary role of government is to create just societies -- to focus on improving access to the basic necessities of food, clean water, education, infrastructure, healthcare, decent incomes and jobs; to honor commitments made in good faith; and to protect property rights. The peoples of the world and of Asean have different histories, traditions, cultures, ideologies, and mindsets -- but all of them need liberty and prosperity. Some countries, taking into account their unique backgrounds, start with improving their people's economic lives first and restrict temporarily in measured stages their political liberty; some others begin with political liberty thinking that their economy would flourish as a necessary consequence; still others rise with a combination of both liberty and prosperity at the very beginning. Such differing starts and focus are necessary in the growth of nations -- but eventually and inevitably, all the peoples of the world need and deserve liberty and prosperity in equal measure (the FLP signature passage). World Bank president Jim Yong Kim, an American of Korean descent whom CJ met during a reception hosted by PNoy, grimly said that 'the world's richest 85 people have as much combined wealth as the poorest 3.6 billion.' The 2014 ADB 'Key Indicators' show this glaring disparity is not as grotesque in the Asean region; indeed, Asean as a whole is fortunate to suffer less poverty and enjoy more affluence than many parts of the world -- still, CJ insists we cannot ignore the injustice of wealth inequality and the need to share prosperity. To illustrate: if our next-door neighbor contracts deadly dengue, would we not help him fumigate his house and drain the idle water in his yard -- because the culprit mosquito is capable of flying into our home, without respecting our fence and our legal certificate of home ownership? Of course we will, out of self-protection if not out of love. Similarly, if a bird flu epidemic breaks out in Cambodia, the neighboring countries -- if not the entire Asean community -- would surely come out and help eradicate the disease, remembering that the birds will not respect or care about the sovereignty and territorial limits of states. From simplicity really comes the wisdom of sharing and caring for the less fortunate, for the poor, for the least, lost, and last. The general assembly theme 'Sharing Prosperity at the Crossroads of Asean Integration -- the Legal Challenges' and the desire to solve the legal challenges that impede this altruistic goal should be foremost in mind when tackling, in full session or in separate workshops, the various topics drawn to meet these challenges. Some legal impediments to Asean integration of trade, investments, services, and skilled labor may be formidable -- like constitutional restrictions on ownership of land, media, public utilities, and natural resources -- and may take time to resolve. But some are really simple, like facilitating the opening of new businesses. Karl Kendrick Chua, senior country economist of the World Bank, in a speech on January 29, 2015, said that 'in the Philippines, it takes 34 days and 16 steps to start a business, and it costs 17 percent of per capita income, compared to 6 days, 3 steps, and 7 percent of per capita income in Malaysia.' Certainly, the lawyers of Asean can easily help solve this simple problem by tapping Malaysia as the model -- solving many legal impediments by simply sharing the solutions already formulated by Asean brothers. The simple problems can be resolved immediately during the assembly while the formidable ones can be planned more intensely in future meetings.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with a comparative thesis: unlike its US counterpart, the PH Supreme Court is rarely divided along philosophical or ideological lines. In fact, not many Philippine justices, now or in the past, are known to hold or promote any particular legal philosophy. (See last Sunday's A398 on the legal philosophy of US justices.) Hence, it is difficult to predict how they would vote on specific issues. Why? First, longevity and maturity: compared with the US Court which was born 225 years ago in 1789, the PH SC is much younger, having been born only 113 years ago in 1901; hence it did not have as much longevity to develop jurisprudence along ideological lines. Second, aside from being appointed young (usually in their 50s), US justices serve for life until their death, voluntary retirement, or removal by impeachment; PH justices are usually appointed in their 60s and serve only until they reach 70. In the US Court's 225-year history, only 112 have served as justices (including 17 CJs); in contrast, in its 113-year existence, the PH Court already has had 173 justices (including 24 CJs). On the average, US justices serve for over 15 years, while PH justices average about four. In short, US justices had a long time (26 served for 25 years or more) to perfect their personal philosophies, while their PH counterparts barely had time to warm their seats. Lately, however, some PH justices were appointed young, giving them enough time to mature on the Court -- like Justices Antonio T. Carpio (18 years), Marvic M.V.F. Leonen (21 years), and CJ Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno (20 years). Third, US Court watchers have written tons of books on their Court. In contrast, there is a dearth of literature on PH magistrates, save for a few like Marites Vitug's 'Shadow of Doubt,' 'Hour Before Dawn,' and 'Our Rights Our Victories'; Justice Isagani A. Cruz's 'Res Gestae'; and Justice Jose C. Campos' 'From the Academe to the Supreme Court.' However, these books speak more of the alleged idiosyncrasies, biases, arrogance, or misbehavior of some justices, and less of their legal philosophies or ideologies. CJ too has written one book a year during his over 11-year incumbency (thereby earning, though unworthy, the accolade of being the 'Court's most prolific writer bar none' from the Court itself upon his retirement); but his hard-covered books were really annual reports on his incumbency, as a measure of transparency and accountability, not as an analysis of his colleagues' ideologies. The PH SC publishes selected opinions of retiring justices in separate books; these tomes should make it easy for researchers to read and analyze their favorite jurists. Nonetheless, legal writers have not used them to peer into the judicial minds. Law professors are content writing mostly textbooks. During martial rule, a strong libertarian philosophy was developed by courageous justices like Claudio Teehankee, Ameurfina Melencio-Herrera, and Hugo Gutierrez. After martial law was dismantled, the 1987 Constitution adopted their libertarian advocacy and the 'liberal' decisions of the US SC. Thus, the due-process and 'Miranda' rights of criminal suspects were minutely cobbled into the new Constitution. Too, the Charter required magistrates to be 'activists' in striking down gravely abusive acts. Historically, this duty was instituted to protect the people from oppression and tyranny. Verily, libertarianism ceased to be a mere ideology -- it became a constitutional mandate. Liberty and prosperity: consistent with this mandate, CJ firmly espoused, during his over 11 years on the Court and up to now, an activist stance in safeguarding liberty, but advocated judicial restraint in matters affecting the economy. After all, the 'grave-abuse' duty of the judiciary was instituted to safeguard freedom, not to stifle the economy. Thus, in litigations involving civil liberty and human rights, the scales of justice should weigh heavily against the government and in favor of the people, pursuant to the doctrine of strict scrutiny. But in matters affecting the economy, courts must defer to the executive and legislative branches, in accordance with the principle of deferential interpretation of laws and executive issuances. Grinding poverty is the most odious problem of the country. The most recent SWS poll (conducted Sept. 26-29) affirmed that 55 percent of Filipinos rate themselves 'poor.' Days ago, Sen. Grace Poe described this grim reality in an epic privilege speech: 'This is a country where skinny street kids share one bowl of instant noodles under the foot of neon ads selling liposuction for the obese. This is a country where there is a fried or roasted chicken stand in every corner but the best seller in the slums do not come in buckets but out of garbage cans -- the pagpag double-fried chicken.' (Pagpag is left-over chicken which the poor scavenge from garbage bins, then washed and refried for them to eat or resell.) The responsibility for eradicating poverty and sharing prosperity rests primarily on the political leaders. Should they fail this duty, the people can replace them during periodic elections. Consequently, the unelected judiciary should give the elected leaders maximum leeway in fulfilling their duty. In sum, the unelected should balance activism in safeguarding liberty with restraint in matters affecting the economy, thereby helping the elected eradicate poverty and share prosperity.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the third installment of his automated-elections quadrilogy -- one week after A458 -- and uses the first half to launch his most-important-investment-incentive thesis (trustworthiness), which Sunday A457 will follow up with the full San Roque Power case-study; the second half delivers the 'Proclamations by projection' coda. Now that President Aquino has thumbed down proposals to change the economic provisions of our Constitution, our officials should turn to other ways of attracting long-term FDIs -- these are the kind of investments that spur inclusive growth, alleviate poverty and create jobs; unfortunately, FDIs have, in the past, come in trickles although they have been poured massively on our neighboring countries like Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore and Indonesia. Trustworthiness: why? because, CJ believes, the most important incentive to bring them in -- the trustworthiness of our government -- has been neglected; past regimes are not famous for honoring their word; in contrast, can the present administration be trusted? Is it sensitive and responsive to investors' cry for fairness, honesty and transparency? Testing the PNoy administration's trustworthiness is a recent letter of the JFC lamenting the failure of the government to fulfill its commitments -- this lament cannot be ignored because the JFC represents the largest existing FDIs in the Philippines. For the uninitiated, let CJ explain that large foreign investors have wide options on where to invest their billions; their choices naturally depend on how safe their money would be, how easy or how difficult it is to do business in the country, and how much they would earn for the risks they take; to lure large FDIs, countries compete by showing their advantages as desirable business venues with reasonable rates of return -- they offer various incentives, which always include tax- and duty-free importation of capital equipment that investors need to bring into the country; to understand this competition, let us look at a parallel in the consumer trade -- people choose and buy cars of a specific brand because they trust its engineering, beauty, after-sale service and used-car prices; in the same manner, investors choose countries that offer real and believable value for their money. Pained letter: to attract FDIs to solve the power outages in the 1990s, our government promised many fiscal incentives and benefits, including VAT-free importation of capital equipment; naturally, in making business plans, investors included these fiscal incentives in computing their risks and possible earnings, and compared them with those offered by other countries; in its pained letter to Finance Sec. Cesar Purisima, the JFC wrote that after its members sank in hundreds of millions of dollars in building huge power plants, the government reneged on its promise to exempt them from VAT; procedurally, investors were first required to pay the VAT, and then to apply for refund from the BIR. According to the JFC, 'here is where the system fails: getting the VAT refunded is complicated and overly bureaucratic, with the BIR forcing applicants to go to court, then causing delays in procedures in the Court of Tax Appeals and up to the Supreme Court... How can investors be encouraged to risk their money if they cannot rely on the solemn word of government?' As an example of how our government has over the past many years reneged on its commitments, the JFC cited the case of San Roque Power Corp., which -- after over a decade of grueling litigation -- was denied its promised VAT refund of about P500 million because of alleged midstream change of rules that were retroactively applied; CJ will write on the details of this case at another time (A457). CJ's point now is this: the government must honor its commitments promptly -- for too long, past regimes have resorted to legalistic contortions to avoid honoring commitments; now is the time to right this wrong; to attract long-term FDIs that spur inclusive growth, alleviate poverty, and create jobs, the present administration must show investors that it will honor commitments made by our country, and will refrain from using technicalities to avoid them; let us stop the insidious practice of being centavo-wise and peso-foolish. Proclamations by projection: in response to CJ's column last Sunday (A458), Comelec Chair Sixto Brillantes Jr. said that the poll body used projections from so-called 'grouped canvass reports' in proclaiming the top senatorial winners; CJ does not wish to embarrass Brillantes further by stressing that our election law requires the use only of official COCs, not any other documents or inventions, to proclaim winners -- and that the Comelec has absolutely no power to amend, much less to supersede, this law by passing a self-serving resolution authorizing itself to use mere projections from 'guesstimates' extrapolated from these grouped canvass reports. However, these baseless proclamations by projection must be corrected and banished from our election lingo, preferably by the Comelec itself, by withdrawing them and reproclaiming the senatorial winners with the use of the completed COCs; the poll body should not wait for the SC or Congress to reverse and censure it -- yes, these wayward proclamations should not stay a minute longer in our legal firmament, lest they be used as mischievous precedents to proclaim the alleged winners in the 2016 presidential election; the Comelec would be well advised to correct this mischief now -- otherwise, instead of being hailed for what it trumpets as a generally successful automated election, the present Comelec will be damned in history for inventing these bizarre proclamations by projection.

He cites two sources of joy: complete editorial freedom (equivalent to his freedom in the SC) and the obligation to stay updated, adapt to digital technology (Nokia to iPhone 6-plus, Googling to AI appreciation), and contribute to policy and polity at advanced age with no personal ambition. He announces the recent publication of 'With Due Respect 2' (2011-2016 columns), with a foreword by Dr. Raul Pangalangan (former Inquirer publisher, now ICC judge in The Hague) and a preface by CJ Sereno -- a sequel to 'With Due Respect' (2007-2011 columns, published in 2011 for CJ's 75th birthday).

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers a eulogy at the wake of Jovito R. Salonga, his guru and surrogate father. The 1956-57 school year FEU law students' strike protested the 'unjustified retirement' of their old dean -- and a 'youngish 36-year-old, bespectacled professor walked to center stage, took the microphone, and single-handedly faced the hostile crowd. The new dean, Dr. Salonga, spoke with a forceful tremolo and held the rambunctious crowd spellbound. In 30 minutes flat, the strikers trooped back to their classrooms, convinced of the error in their mass action, and of the wisdom, honesty and sincerity of their new dean.' Active as FEU Central Student Organization president and National Union of Students founder/president, CJ gave secondary importance to academics -- but Salonga's constant recitation-testing during peak student-activity periods produced 'most outstanding student' in third year and Latin honors graduation. Before the 1960 bar exams CJ got sick and faced a flooding rainstorm -- wading 'in knee-deep water from the then FEU Hospital... to the University of the East, the exam venue' -- and after a lackluster first day wanted to quit; but Salonga 'would not hear of it,' and CJ ended up 'copping the sixth highest place.' On Salonga's recommendation, CJ won a Yale Law School scholarship but lacked funds to fly -- the American Embassy denied a travel grant, 'perhaps because of my student activism.' Salonga consoled him: 'Come, join my law office and I will teach you what I learned from the University of the Philippines, Yale and Harvard.' Thus began the surrogate-father tutorship -- CJ's biological father having passed during first-year prelaw -- and Salonga taught the rudiments of law practice and 'the life-defining values of integrity, prudence and fairness. He led by example, not by words. He was a dedicated husband, a caring father, a faithful friend and a devoted man of God. He did not smoke, drink or gamble. Wealth, power, worldly pleasures, titles and honors did not fascinate him.' The religious-faith difference (Salonga devout Protestant, CJ fledgling Catholic) 'did not diminish our over 50 years of surrogate father-son relationship, or my awe, esteem and affection for him. This is probably because we never discussed what separated us, only what truly bound us.' After three years as Salonga's law-office assistant, CJ asked permission to form his own law firm, receiving the blessing 'You now have formidable wings, go and soar the limitless sky!' The greatest honor in CJ's legal career came when Salonga, as Senate president and LP chief, retained CJ as his legal counsel -- 'not by awarding me a plaque of gold or conferring on me an honorary degree, but by retaining me as his legal counsel... Nothing is more fulfilling, more exhilarating, than the honor of being counsel to one's guru and former boss!' Before joining Cory Aquino's 1986 Cabinet, Salonga divested conflicting financial interests and dissolved his prestigious law firm 'not because this was mandated by law but because of his strict personal ethic of being beyond suspicion in serving government' -- and CJ followed his example by dissolving their law firm when joining the Supreme Court. Through multiple JBC screening failures preceding the SC appointment, Salonga 'constantly cheered me up and tirelessly lifted my sagging spirit,' patiently reminding him of Romans 8:28: 'God makes all things work together for the good of those who love Him and are called according to His purpose.' Upon CJ's retirement as Chief Justice, Salonga and Evelyn Miranda-Feliciano published 'A Test of Courage' (late 2007) as a tribute to the Panganiban Court. 'Those who have read my decisions and writings will surely detect the legal philosophy and life values of Dr. Salonga. Indeed, I try to echo, even if unworthily and faintly, his teaching that law cannot be separated from life, that it should be used as a brick in building the social edifice and as a means to fulfill the deepest aspirations of man. The mortal body of Dr. Salonga may have perished but his legacy and memory will live forever. Alleluia!'

one_paragraph_summary: Responding to reader letters following his previous column, Panganiban addresses three issues. First, on Estelito Mendoza's praise for J. Reyes Jr.'s swift GMA right-to-travel decision alongside his lament about an unnamed accused detained for over 1,400 days, he joins the plea for speedier resolution and invokes the constitutional 24-month rule for cases after the last pleading was filed. Second, he definitively corrects repeated misattributions of the constructive-resignation doctrine to himself -- 'I have said it before and will say it again: fake news.' The doctrine belongs to CJ Reynato S. Puno, who wrote the unanimous Estrada-Arroyo decision; Panganiban and CJ Davide took no part in the 13-0 ruling. Third, he responds to two readers who criticized him for hero-worshipping CJ Claudio Teehankee by confirming it unapologetically: Teehankee earned summa cum laude in both BA and LLB from Ateneo and was No. 1 in the 1940 bar -- 'the greatest Ateneo law alumnus of all time.' He extends equal esteem to Jose W. Diokno and Jovito R. Salonga, who tied for No. 1 in the 1944 bar at 95.3% -- Diokno without finishing law school (also the CPA board topnotcher), and Salonga with LL.M. from Harvard and J.S.D. from Yale. Salonga was the author's mentor at FEU and boss at his law firm -- the boss in awe of only Diokno and Teehankee, warning his young assistant to 'prepare our trial brief extra well' whenever either appeared on the opposite side. When Salonga disbanded his firm to chair the PCGG in 1986, the author consciously emulated him by dissolving his own firm (Panganiban, Parlade, Benitez and Africa) upon SC appointment in 1995, living, as he humbly concludes, 'in the penumbra of their great shadows.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban addresses restive congressmen dismayed by alleged Supreme Court 'flip-flopping' -- especially Belgica v. Ochoa (Nov 19 2013) outlawing PDAF and Reyes v. Comelec (June 25 2013) upholding the Comelec's unseating of Regina Ongsiako Reyes -- who are threatening to disobey and impeach justices. He defends both decisions. On PDAF, LAMP v. DBM (April 24 2012) was reversed by Belgica a year later, but this is self-correction, not stare-decisis breach. On Reyes, he rewinds the four-stage chronology: March 27 Comelec First Division cancelled Reyes's COC (she lost Filipino citizenship by marriage to an American and failed to take oath of allegiance and renounce US citizenship); May 14 the en banc affirmed 6-1; May 18 the BOC proclaimed her winner despite the cancellation; May 19 the Comelec ruling became final and executory; June 5 she took her oath and simultaneously sued the SC; June 25 the SC (J. Jose Portugal Perez, 7-4) affirmed the Comelec, citing the HRET-three-element Member threshold (proclamation + oath + June 30 assumption-of-office), and held that the Comelec still had jurisdiction when it decided on May 14 (which became final on May 19, before Reyes met all three HRET-Member elements). The resolution had legal and logical moorings and cited many precedents -- with due respect, he cannot understand why it ignited a congressional conflagration. He delivers the rule-of-law maxim: legislators have the right to disagree but not to disobey. He discloses his own three-stage practice: he disagreed many times as AJ, persuaded colleagues internally as CJ but did not begrudge those who differed, and as retired jurist has critiqued flip-flops but always honored and followed decisions. Congress is not helpless -- it holds the purse, legislates laws, has oversight powers, determines court jurisdictions, can change jurisprudence, and most importantly can impeach justices -- but only for culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, graft and corruption, other high crimes, or betrayal of public trust, NOT for their decisions, opinions, or votes, even if these may later turn out to be erroneous. By the same token, lawmakers can be disciplined only for disorderly behavior, not for bills and votes, even if these may later prove unwise.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes one of his rare biographical-disclosure columns, summarizing his Mapa High School Alumni Association speech delivered the previous Sunday -- Feb 23, 2014, at Metro Tent Pasig before 1,000 alumni. 'Please talk of how you became a sterling example of what a true-blue Mapan should be and how we can give back to society,' was the request of former Cong. Benny Abante Jr., president of the Mapa High School Alumni Association -- CJ's full speech may be accessed at cjpanganiban.com; here's a short version to fit in this space. Mostly poor were the Mapa students of CJ's time; we looked at education and hard work as our keys to success -- CJ had to hawk newspapers, peddle cigarettes and shine shoes to support his study; tired and weary, CJ promised himself he would one day be president of the Manila Times, the largest-circulated daily then. After high school the UP granted CJ a scholarship, but his impoverished parents could not afford the then 15-centavo bus fare to the UP campus in Quezon City. The nearby UST refused CJ a scholarship because he failed to answer the last of three questions of an old Dominican priest: first, 'How many Gods are there?'; second, 'How many persons are there in one God?'; and third, the tough question, 'Name them,' to which CJ sheepishly answered, 'Susmaryosep (Jesus, Mary and Joseph)!' -- yes, CJ was a religious ignoramus. So CJ enrolled at FEU, which gave him a scholarship without any question; CJ wanted to be a chemical engineer but his strict father ordered him to take up law. Inconsolable was CJ's grief at his inability to enroll at UP and to study chemical engineering, but his life turned at FEU -- there CJ met the brilliant law dean Jovito R. Salonga, who taught CJ his insights from the three schools he studied in: UP, Harvard and Yale. After graduating cum laude and placing sixth in the bar exam, CJ was granted a scholarship at Yale; but, like his UP problem, he did not have transport money -- so, he forthwith practiced and taught law, and dabbled in business; CJ organized Baron Travel Corp., which enabled his five children to travel, and finish their graduate degrees at Harvard, Stanford, U. of California, U. of Chicago, and U. of Michigan. CJ also intensified his study of his Catholic faith -- as a result, he was invited to the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines; later, he was named by Pope John Paul II as the only Filipino member for the 1996-2001 term of the Pontifical Council for the Laity in the Vatican; in 1991, he became part-time president of the Inquirer. Supreme Court journey: like his entry into the law profession, CJ did not plan his journey to the SC. On June 17, 1992, then President-elect Fidel V. Ramos offered CJ to be his Secretary of Justice; CJ respectfully declined, saying, 'Thank you, Mr. President, but I am not worthy to join your Cabinet; I did not campaign for you during the last elections.' However, FVR was insistent: 'I know you did not campaign for me; in fact, you did not even vote for me; you voted for Jovy Salonga; but that is all right; I want a nonpartisan Cabinet.' After two weeks, FVR finally relented: 'Ah, sa Supreme Court ka na lang.' A decade later, President GMA named CJ the 21st Chief Justice of the Philippines. As a jurist, CJ espoused his legal philosophy of 'Liberty and Prosperity Under the Rule of Law' -- CJ believes justice and jobs, freedom and food, ethics and economics, democracy and development, and liberty and prosperity must always go together; one is useless without the other. After his retirement in December 2006, he embarked on a new journey as an independent director or adviser of some of the largest firms listed in the PSE, and also writes a column in the Inquirer. Giving back: CJ asks his successful co-alumni to give back to society by sharing their time, talent and treasure -- the sharing of time and talent is just as important as the sharing of treasure; no one is so poor he cannot share something, and no one is so rich he does not need anything. CJ gives back his time and talent by being chair or president of several foundations, like the Manila Cathedral Foundation, Metrobank Foundation, and FLP. The sharing of treasure should really remain anonymous, so CJ will just mention two items already of public knowledge: to celebrate his 75th birthday two years ago, CJ gave half of his retirement pay to FLP and his one-year income as a columnist to the Inquirer Foundation for Newsboys; and today, may CJ contribute eight subsistence scholarships for poor Mapans. To conclude, education, hard work and God transformed CJ from a poor newsboy to being president of the most widely-read newspaper in our country; from an ignorant Catholic to being a member of the highest lay council of the Church in the Vatican; from a frustrated applicant for graduate studies to being father of five wonderful children who each achieved CJ's impossible dream of graduating from a pedigreed US university; from a fumbling shoeshine boy to the boardrooms of the best corporate giants; from an aspiring chemical engineer to a reluctant lawyer; and, finally, to the highest judicial position in our country. As CJ contemplates his life and moves toward its sunset, he knows that God has woven his many pains and gains into a magnificent tapestry showing His mystical presence -- truly, there is one constancy in his life: the presence, care and providence of our Lord Jesus Christ; to Him CJ dedicates all he was, all he is, and all he will ever be.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens the three-part bar-exam-and-legal-education trilogy with this first installment. Conducted annually on the four Sundays of October, the bar examinations determine who will be blessed to carry the exalted title of 'attorney-at-law' and be allowed to practice law in all courts in our country. Bar mystique: the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) supervises the entry to all professions in the Philippines, except the legal profession which is reserved by the Constitution for the Supreme Court. The PRC-administered tests are called 'licensure examinations.' However, the crucible of lawyers is referred to as the 'bar' exam, not because they are more addicted to alcoholic drinks, but because only those who pass it may cross the courtroom railing or bar that separates the lawyers' table and the judges' bench, on one hand, from the seats used by the general public, on the other. Hence, lawyers are collectively referred to as the 'bar' and judges, the 'bench.' The bar exam used to be attended by fanfare galore. Undergraduates held parades and motorcades complete with marching bands and cheering squads that accompanied their school candidates' rides to the exam venue. This gaudy practice had been banned by the Supreme Court during the last several years. But the mystique explodes when the results are released. Traditional and social media herald the passers, complete with the pictures of the topnotchers plastered on the front pages of newspapers and interviewed over radio and television. Law schools take enormous pride in their bar placers and average passing rates. One institution, the University of Cebu, gifts its top 10 with brand-new cars. The most prestigious law firms and best-managed companies offer fantastic opportunities and compensation to the top placers. My personal experience: CJ took the bar exam in 1960 without this opening-day fanfare. In fact, on the first day of the exam, he had to wade alone in rain-induced, knee-deep flood on R. Papa Street, Sampaloc, Manila, which connected the then Far Eastern University Hospital (where he was confined for intestinal flu) and the University of the East, the situs of the exam. Because of his illness, he felt he may have failed the first-day subjects and seriously thought of quitting. But his dean, Dr. Jovito R. Salonga, pepped him up and urged him to go on. Recalling this incident in a speech on Jan 22, 2008, at FEU, Dr. Salonga opined that 'CJ Panganiban could have landed first place (instead of sixth) had he not been sick and hospitalized during the first week of the 1960 bar exam.' CJ mentions this because he believes that placing in the top 10 is not always a reliable measure of achievement. In fact, a classmate and CJ compared their answers after each exam day. CJ was so impressed with his friend's answers that he expected him to fare better than CJ. The point is that the questions during CJ's time called mostly for essay answers and memory work. CJ thought his classmate's citation of authorities was more impressive than his own. But apparently, the examiner's evaluation of their answers was quite subjective and probably veered toward CJ's essayed opinions. Hence, his grades were higher. Exam scope and methodology: the subjective methodology and scope of the bar exam have not improved much since CJ took it. The basic subjects are the same, except that for this year, two subjects -- taxation and labor law -- were added, and the methodology changed to 20 percent multiple choice questions (MCQ) and 80 percent essay. Inquirer publisher Raul C. Pangalangan lamented in his column on Nov 25, 2011, that 'the bar exams have been administered on basically the same template... The model remained unchanged at least for the last 50 years...' To be fair, however, let it be said that during the last decade, the Supreme Court tried to improve the bar exam. Thus, in a resolution issued on June 8, 2004 (Bar Matter 1161), the Court favorably acted on the reforms proposed by retired Justices Vicente V. Mendoza, Ameurfina M. Herrera and Jose C. Vitug (see CJ's April 22, 2007 column for details). Moreover, the Court instituted more reforms in another resolution on Jan 18, 2011, with MCQ at 60 percent of the total exams to measure the 'knowledge and recall of laws, doctrines and jurisprudence' of the candidates plus 40 percent essay-type questions to test their 'skill in writing in English, sorting out the relevant facts in a legal dispute... organizing [their] thoughts, constructing [their] arguments, and persuading readers to [their] point of view.' However, the essays were not 'bar subject specific,' igniting fiery howling from the candidates. In 2012, the Supreme Court reverted to the 'bar subject specific' essays at 40 percent and MCQs at 60 percent. In the 2013 exam, this was changed to 20 percent MCQ and 80 percent essay -- the same format for next month's exam, chaired by Justice Diosdado M. Peralta. Postscript: the Supreme Court unanimously voided the Commission on Elections' edict reducing TV-radio ads during elections to an 'aggregate total' of only 120 minutes for TV and 180 minutes for radio per national candidate. As CJ argued in his Feb 24, 2013 column, this 'draconian reduction suppressed the people's right to know their candidates, and the aspirants' rights to inform the electorate of their qualifications and programs of government.' The good news, however, is that the Comelec accepted its defeat graciously and will not ask for reconsideration. And the better news is that it will, as it should, enforce strictly the legal limits on the candidates' campaign.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens by noting that Christmas and the New Year are grand occasions for family bonding and rejoicing -- last Sunday he featured a sharing by grandson Miguel P. Sandejas (C99); today he presents an essay by another grandson, Rafa P. Yaptangco, a fourth-year student at Southridge School in Alabang submitted to secure college admission at Ateneo de Manila University. Rafa's essay begins: 'Ageless passion is what propelled my grandfather, retired Chief Justice Artemio V. Panganiban, in his rise from rags to riches, not in worldly wealth but in his multi-career fulfillment. His life story is so compelling and so moving that it, deservedly so, was brought to glory in a musicale for his 75th birthday celebration.' The opening message of the musicale comes from one of Lolo's favorite stories -- about a farmer and his 20-year-old son experiencing good fortune, then bad fortune, then good fortune again, back and forth. The whole village would go to the farmer and marvel at his good fortune or show empathy at his bad fortune; and to everything, the farmer simply answered, 'Good news, bad news, who knows? I will just keep on doing my best and let God do the rest.' This has now become Rafa's mantra in life. Thinking back, Rafa never really appreciated who Lolo was until asked to represent the younger version of him in that musicale, titled 'Ageless Passion.' Cringing at fear of singing to a large audience, he politely turned down that opportunity and settled for a minor role; in hindsight he should have taken the challenge. During the experience he saw a different perspective he would not have been able to experience in his immediate society: poverty, both in the storyline and amongst the performers -- most notably the choir, composed of 20 or so boys performing to raise funds for their school. The musicale tells of CJP's transformations: from newsboy from the backstreets of Sampaloc, Manila to the presidency of the Philippine Daily Inquirer; from an ignorant Catholic to an advisor to the Holy Father in the Vatican; from a frustrated applicant for graduate studies to father of five wonderful children who each achieved his impossible dream of graduating from a pedigreed US university; from a shoeshine boy to the boardrooms of the largest blue chips in our part of Planet Earth; and from a frustrated chemical engineer to a reluctant lawyer to the highest magistrate of the land. Rafa was taken aback at the story of Lolo's life -- back then all he really thought of him was a caring father to his Mom who loved (and still does) to take the family out to Sunday dinners. Upon really understanding what Lolo has gone through, it absolutely amazed Rafa. It is incredibly hard to believe that all this was achieved by a single person -- and it was done by Lolo. It was then Rafa realized what character he had and the ageless passion he has radiated; it was then Lolo became his idol, the person he hopes to eventually be like, the person for whom he has infinite respect. He shows that anyone willing to contribute a great deal of hard work for a better future can, indeed, have a better future. Rafa is extremely lucky to have been born into circumstances where finance is not a problem and infinitely grateful to be the grandson of a man so industrious. Following Lolo's life story, Rafa has set out with the general goal: to make Lolo proud. This threw life around, as he did not really have a life goal in mind at that time; to just be successful is not enough. Rafa now sees a light at the end of the tunnel: to employ the ageless passion Lolo has taught him through his life story. Even now, Lolo continues to work hard as he is in the board of numerous big-name companies; most of the things he talks about at the dinner table are about law and business -- this just goes to show how dedicated to his work he is, and Rafa strives to someday achieve that. Rafa has gone on to cofound the Admirals Business Club of Southridge, managing numerous concerts including one to raise awareness for cancer patients in partnership with Moving as One (MAO), money earned given to charity. He has also cofounded Léger de Main, a cardistry, illusions, and deceptions club, teaching people card tricks and other forms of magic -- hoping to instill values of confidence and composure in public performances. As leader he has driven both groups to be more unique organizations in Southridge, setting up a leadership-handoff system to ensure continuity post-graduation. In all this Rafa is thankful for Southridge's philosophy of forming men of integrity, grateful for his parents, older brother, relatives, and good friends -- but most of all knows he must not stray from the valuable lesson of the farmer in Lolo's story. Already he can see himself on the right track to making Lolo proud. Obviously, it will not be a straight path to the goal; there will be highs and lows. 'Good news, bad news, who knows? I will just keep doing my best and let God do the rest' -- circular bookend to the farmer-parable opening.

one_paragraph_summary: On the occasion of the formal launch of 'With Due Respect 3' -- the third Inquirer-published compilation of his Sunday columns from 2016 to 2021 -- Panganiban offers an abridged response of gratitude. He confesses he had 'never written (a column) in (his) life until after (he) retired from the judiciary'; his 'historical romance with newspapers' began as a Sampaloc newsboy helping his impoverished family during grade school and high school, but his late mentor Dr. Jovito R. Salonga had cautioned him that 'Chief Justices make history; they do not write it.' Marixi R. Prieto would not be dissuaded -- 'I do not know of any retired chief justice who had been offered to write a column' -- and a compromise of one column per week became 15 years of unbroken Sunday publication, through illness, travel (five trips a year abroad), and active roles in over 25 companies and foundations. He credits Marixi for the writing career and the acclaim that followed, citing the third-place Amazon bestseller ranking of WDR1 behind only Jeffrey Toobin (CNN) and Antonin Scalia of the US Supreme Court. He thanks incumbent CJ Alexander G. Gesmundo -- who at 65 'could be my son' -- for the formal launch and praises him for embodying the constitutional virtues of competence, integrity, probity, and independence, calling him 'a glutton for work' ready to attack the perennial case backlog and to automate the judiciary. He thanks JV Rufino of the Inquirer Book Company, Sean James Borja (Ateneo law valedictorian 2018 and bar topnotcher of the same year) who arranged WDR3 topically rather than chronologically, and editors Jorge Aruta, Rosario Garcellano (both retired), and Gilbert Cadiz (incumbent opinion editor) -- asking that they 'never tire of teaching this aging jurist the rudiments of the English language and of column-writing.'

one_paragraph_summary: On the closure of the three-day 2024 Bar exam (Sept 8, 11, 15), Panganiban reflects on a profession that must 'swing on reluctant hinges.' His own 1960 batch was 4,178 with 1,667 passers, held over four consecutive Sundays at the University of the East; yearly 1965-1981 cohorts numbered under 2,000; the lowest pass rate was 16.59% in 1999, when an attempt to lower the passing grade from 75 to 74 percent was scuttled by CJ's strong objections -- and the bar-exam chair was reprimanded and his honorarium halved for failing to disclose that a nephew of his was a taker. The most numerous batch was 2021's 11,402 in the first digitized regionalized exam, with a record 8,241 passers at 72.28% and (for the first time) the top 10 unnamed. With due respect, CJ disagrees with this wholesale entry -- the legal profession is the first key to the justice system and lawyers are public officers -- and with the nondisclosure of top 10 placers (since abandoned), because while bar topping is no guarantee of excellence, top 10 placers nonetheless become leading practitioners, professors, corporate counsels, and government officials. Of the 27 Philippine CJs (excluding ousted-via-quo-warranto Sereno, deemed never a de jure CJ), at least 11 are bar placers: Yulo (3rd), Paras (2nd), Bengzon (2nd), Concepcion (1st), Makalintal (7th), R. Aquino (9th), Teehankee (1st), Yap (1st), Narvasa (2nd), Panganiban (6th), and Bersamin (9th). Since student days, CJ has idealized three bar legends: Jose W. Diokno and Jovito R. Salonga, tied at 95.3% in 1944 -- and amazingly Diokno did not finish law school (and also topped the CPA boards); Salonga was CJ's FEU mentor, law-office boss, and lifetime guru, in awe of only Diokno and Teehankee ('Please prepare our trial brief extra well because Pepe Diokno or Dingdong Teehankee is our opponent'); and Claudio Teehankee, Ateneo summa BA and LLB and 1940 bar #1, who remained independent despite his Marcos appointment -- 'in my humble view, the greatest Ateneo law alumnus of all time.' In emulation of Salonga's 1986 PCGG-appointment law-firm dissolution, CJ dissolved his own firm Panganiban, Parlade, Benitez, and Africa on his 1995 SC appointment, orphaning Dean Agustin Benitez (1959 #1), Dean Custodio Parlade (1959 #4), and classmate Leopoldo Africa (1960 #11). 'Please excuse my feeble attempts to imitate these legends of the bar as I humbly try, though undeserving, to live in the penumbra of their great shadows.'

He has 'differed without being difficult with all, repeat all, of my best friends,' and is grateful for their good-faith divergences expressed in gentle though sometimes emphatic language. He distinguishes this sharply from offensive criticisms at imagined defects conceived in malice; those he ignores, refusing to let 'schemers and kibitzers' disrupt his goals, and instead trusting his track record and the judgment of those who truly know him. His scriptural refuge is Romans 12:17-19 -- do not repay evil for evil, live at peace with all, leave vengeance to the Lord. He then cites three close friends as exemplars. First, the late Jovito R. Salonga -- his 'guru, dean and surrogate father,' bar topper, UP LLB plus Harvard LLM plus Yale JSD, three-time senatorial topper, 'the best president our country never had' -- set against CJ's self-deprecation as 'poor newsboy born in squalid Tondo, Manila' with an FEU LLB and bar 6th place. Salonga's foremost teaching was about life, not law: the rare gems money CANNOT buy -- excellence, integrity, honor, dignity, reverential regard for God. At the Jan 22, 2008 launch of Salonga and Miranda-Feliciano's 'A Test of Courage' (with Carpio as guest speaker), Salonga publicly compared CJ to St. Paul on the road to Damascus -- inward journey, blinding light, transformation -- and confessed 'In a deeper sense, Art is my mentor.' Yet they 'agreed to disagree on something very fundamental': Salonga was a revered Cosmopolitan Church pastor, CJ a fledgling Catholic. Second, Archbishop Leonardo Z. Legaspi -- as CBCP president, the presiding officer at PCP II in mid-Feb 1991 -- repeatedly ruled CJ out of order for proposing that priests and nuns be allowed to marry; yet despite CJ's stubbornness, Legaspi (with Ambassador Tita de Villa) recommended him to Pope John Paul II, who named CJ 'though unworthy' as the only Filipino member of the Pontifical Council of the Laity (1996-2001). Third, his wife Leni Panganiban critiques his writing, speech, looks and even dress -- yet remains his closest friend and beloved, because every critical word is uttered with unconditional love. The closing universal principle: 'Friend first before critic, and love first before criticism.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes on Easter Sunday with sad and good news about the Manila Cathedral. The sad news: Archbishop Tagle directed its closure upon the Manila Cathedral-Basilica Foundation's recommendation after a structural engineering team led by Dr. Angel Lazaro III, conducting extensive tests including 30-meter bore holes, determined that soil liquefaction could occur in a major earthquake and endanger the church -- affecting 200 couples scheduled to marry there and ending the annual December pipe organ concerts. Cardinal Rosales had already suspected deterioration, arranging the removal of the cathedral's seven big bells (17 tons) from the belfry and installing computerized Holland carillon bells donated by Alberto and Sylvia Lina -- which also now must be brought down. The good news: at a recent private dinner among Archbishop Tagle, Amb. de Villa, CJ, and San Miguel Corp. president Ramon Ang, Ang 'graciously agreed to contribute P50 million to lead in saving this veritable center of Catholic worship.' The MCBF -- with the Archbishop as ex-officio chair, Amb. de Villa as vice chair, CJ Panganiban as president, and Marixi Prieto as vice president -- is now confident the cathedral can reopen within a year. CJ traces the cathedral's history from its 1581 original construction through World War II devastation and the 1958 reconstruction by Archbishop Rufino J. Santos (the first Filipino cardinal) to its elevation as a basilica by Pope John Paul II, describing it as 'the bulwark of Filipino Catholicism and an enduring witness to the strength and depth of our people's fidelity to our Lord Jesus Christ.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban recounts his speaking engagement at the Third Philippine Conference on New Evangelization (PCNE III) at the UST Quadricentennial Pavilion (July 15-17, 2016), attended by over 5,000 faithful, where Cardinal Tagle invited him to speak on how Catholics can evangelize in governance and public service. He clarifies that the doctrine of separation of church and state does NOT prohibit clergy and laity from advocating pro-Christian tenets -- it merely requires government neutrality in religious 'competition' (no public funds for one group's basilica, no promotion of one's dogma, no salaries for strictly religious duties, no religion as condition for civil/political right). While there is separation of church FROM state, there is no separation of the STATE FROM GOD: the Philippines is theist, monotheist -- not atheist, not even agnostic -- as evidenced by the constitutional preamble 'We, the sovereign Filipino people, imploring the aid of Almighty God,' the prayer-prefacing practices of both Congress chambers and the Cabinet, and the 'Centennial Prayer for the Courts' used by the Supreme Court. Constitution and laws do not bar priests and nuns from public office; only Canon Law sometimes limits clerical political participation. As Catholics, the bearings come from Pope Francis's Evangelii Gaudium No. 182: 'The Church's pastors, taking into account the contributions of the different sciences, have the right to offer opinions on all that affects people's lives, since the task of evangelization implies and demands the integral promotion of each human being. It is no longer possible to claim that religion should be restricted to the private sphere and that it exists only to prepare souls for heaven.' The Catechism and Vatican II urge bringing Gospel values into public and private life. The most crucial temporal matter is federalism, which requires constitutional overhaul (not amendment) -- first challenge is method (Con-ass vs Con-con) and second is making the new Constitution 'as pro-God, pro-faith, pro-life, pro-prayer, pro-family and pro-human rights as possible,' with vigilance from method-decision through delegate-election, deliberations, and plebiscite. The proposed revival of death penalty (by hanging or musketry) and summary execution of alleged criminals without due process must be resisted -- 'we know that the end never justifies the means.' Catholics should support (without violating fundamental rights) the drive against criminality, drugs, and corruption; calamity relief; free education for the poor; job creation with just wages; the peace process; and credible elections. Civil servants may need to use 'freedom of speech to assert, to argue and to denounce' and uphold Christian values 'at the risk of ridicule, censure, or even of losing our jobs.' He closes: 'in all our trials and triumphs, defeats and victories, frustrations and exaltations, pains and gains, crucifixions and resurrections, God will never abandon us. He will always be with us: above us to inspire us, behind us to strengthen us, before us to lead us, and within us to transform us to be another Christ -- humble, loving, and sacrificing.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban gives a fair-minded close reading of Judge Rainelda H. Estacio-Montesa's 37-page decision (fortified by 170 footnotes) convicting Maria Ressa and Reynaldo Santos Jr. of cyberlibel -- finding it 'not baseless or capricious' but appealable to the Supreme Court. He walks through the trial sequence (arraignment, mediation, pretrial, six prosecution witnesses including Wilfredo Keng, two defense witnesses) and identifies the trial court's analytical-school architecture: 'law times facts equals decision,' Austin-style. He explains three crucial doctrinal items. First, the article publicly imputed despicable crimes (human trafficking, drug/contraband smuggling, murder) tending to dishonor Keng, a private citizen; under Article 353/355 and the Cybercrime Law (which extends libel to 'computer system or similar means' with heavier penalty), MALICE IS PRESUMED BY LAW, shifting the burden onto the accused -- and 'lamentably, the defense miserably failed in this regard,' with both accused 'oddly also' opting not to testify on fair-comment-on-public-interest. Second, the retroactivity defense fails: the Information charged the February 19, 2014 republication (post-Cybercrime Law), not the May 2012 original, and every republication is a separate crime. Third, on prescription, Montesa used John Austin's robotic syllogism -- because the Cybercrime Law prescribes 6+ years' imprisonment without setting a new prescriptive period, Act No. 3326's twelve-year rule applies. CJ concludes that the article IS libelous, but the accused can still be acquitted on appeal IF the Supreme Court sidesteps Austin's strict syllogism and embraces Roscoe Pound's more liberal sociological school, which 'regards law merely as a brick -- an important one -- in the building of a just and humane society,' reading the one-year libel prescription back into cyberlibel under the rule that penal laws should favor the accused. He closes with a tribute: 'Tomorrow, June 22, is the 100th birthday of the late Dr. Jovito R. Salonga, my esteemed guru, a respected scholar, low-profile educator, brilliant lawyer, outstanding lawmaker, acclaimed patriot, and statesman par excellence.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes a tribute-eulogy for his balae Linda Manuel Mañalac, who passed to the Eternal Kingdom on March 21 2026 with her 40th day in heaven approaching. Three years ago, CJP's wife Leni passed from this world; since then he has continued living more deliberately while drawing strength from his children and the people around him. Just when none anticipated it, the fragility of life struck again. Tears flowed, yet memories of her generosity have begun to outweigh the grief. Listening to the eulogies, CJP realized her generosity took many forms. To borrow her son Carlos 'Pop' Mañalac's vivid language, Linda 'spent the last days of her life -- as she always lived -- with complete, absolute, unconditional love ... because of her generosity ... we, her children, are at peace -- grief has been turned to gratitude, and pain into peace.' To grandchildren/nephews/nieces -- per common apo Andrea -- she was unfailingly generous with affection and time. Nephew Rico Manuel (Ayala Land top executive) shared, 'We lost our Dad and Mom very early ... but we were never truly alone. Ninang Linda was incredibly generous -- not just with what she had, but even more with her time, her attention, and her sincere care.' Even beyond family, Sonya Garcia recalled how, 30 years ago, looking only at Sonya's 'anxious eyes and salivating mouth' on an undeveloped Alfonso, Cavite estate, Linda pulled out her checkbook and paid the full price for 'penniless me' -- 'and presto, the now famous Sonya's Garden was born and later boomed and bloomed.' Linda hosted Christmas lunch for the Franciscan Missionaries of Mary for over 30 years (25 in Pasay, 5 in Forbes Park) -- per Sister Cho Borromeo, 'they were far more than simple meals; they were sanctuaries of memory that gave us strength during our most trying times'; addressing Linda, Sister Cho added, 'Despite your wealthy background, you moved through the world with a profound heart for the poor ... You were famously stingy with yourself, yet you were incredibly lavish with your generosity towards others.' Fr. Robert Manansala of Santuario de San Antonio Parish said Linda's greatest treasures of the heart were 'God, family, and other relatives, the Southeastern College community, her wide circles of friends, especially the poor and underprivileged.' The one message that kept resounding: she is 'Generosity Personified' -- testified to even by the vendors on the roads to Tagaytay from whom Linda bought boiled corn and camote. CJP had the privilege of personally witnessing her spontaneity, generosity, and magnanimity. At one birthday party, an esteemed visitor met for the first time remarked on how lovely her pearl necklace was; Linda gently removed the necklace and placed it around the stunned visitor's neck, saying 'There, bagay na bagay sa iyo.' Linda and Tong's homes in Makati and Batangas were always open to friends for a day or a week, with household staff and abundance in cupboards and freezers. Fishermen with freshly caught lobsters and crabs near their Punta Fuego home would wait for her, knowing she paid them more than their asking prices to help them provide for their cash-strapped families. Though not too liturgical, she was definitely spiritual in putting to practice the Ignatian teaching of 'giving without counting the cost and of working without asking for reward, save that of knowing and following the Lord's holy will.' She taught by deed not words, by example not trumpets -- without fanfare and drumrolls. To perpetuate her legacy of unconditional love, all of us -- her friends and relatives -- should strive to follow her quiet generosity and pure magnanimity: to paraphrase the Good Book, feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, and visit the prisoners -- keeping her generous spirit alive, magnified through the lives we touch. To Tong Mañalac and all widows and widowers, may we always look back on the past with gratitude and quiet surrender. Tong, Linda, Leni, and CJP were a 'Happy Foursome.' We were not just friends. We were not just relatives. We were soulmates! Together, we laughed, dined, danced, traveled, celebrated. Painful as it is to live now with only their memory, CJP is certain their spouses would want us to move forward -- to carry on, to live life fully, as they did -- until the day God calls us, in His time, to a joyful reunion with them, together with all His angels in His Heavenly Kingdom.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban offers an Easter reflection organized around three capitalized-with-quotation-marks lessons from his 1997 book 'Justice & Faith,' updated with his own journey through passion, death, and resurrection. The great truths of Scripture are not cloistered in the pages of the Bible or the walls of the Church -- they are lived in daily struggles. Lesson 1: 'Sometimes, Adversities and Misfortunes in Life are Preludes to Greater Victories.' Because CJP's father could not afford the then 15-centavo bus fare from Sampaloc, Manila, CJP could not enroll at UP Diliman where he had a scholarship; at Far Eastern University instead, he was blessed to meet and be taught by Dr. Jovito R. Salonga, newly appointed law dean, who became his mentor -- pushing him beyond his limits when CJP wanted to give up on the bar exam after being hospitalized on the first day. There was also a time CJP felt embittered he could not enjoy his Yale masteral scholarship due to inability to pay airfare -- he wallowed in self-pity, but in the end found greater triumph in seeing all his five children travel to and finish their graduate degrees in their chosen US universities. Perhaps providential that he later organized his own company that assured them of travel. In his journey from a poor newspaper boy to Chief Justice, CJP saw how adversity forged character -- 'Court battles lost and won, personal bereavements, the weight of public office: each trial sharpened my sense of purpose and deepened my reliance on prayer.' He has seen the same in countless Filipinos who, after calamity, rise to rebuild with quiet heroism. Lesson 2: 'Whatever Happens, Do Not Lose Heart.' During the 1982 Hong Kong stock market crash, CJP lost everything earned abroad -- heartbroken enough to cause a heart attack; many were reported to have committed suicide. Forlorn and poor again, CJP returned to the Philippines and concentrated on his law practice. In 1983 he joined the Rotary Club of Manila, where he met future President Fidel V. Ramos who later appointed him to the SC in 1995. Working from that high office was never a walk in the park. After his term, he chose to continue creating new meanings in the lives of others through the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity. History too bears witness -- Abraham Lincoln lost businesses, suffered devastating electoral defeats, mourned the death of his beloved, and endured a complete nervous breakdown. But through perseverance and unshakable resolve, he rose. At 60, he became President of the United States -- though tragically assassinated, hailed as one of the greatest leaders in history. Some of us lose heart after only a few disappointments. But remember: no matter what happens, keep working and believing. Trust in your capacity to rise above defeat and in God's unfailing power and providence. Lesson 3: 'Have Faith in God.' During CJP's own season of passion and death, he moved among the high and the lowly, the powerful and the weak, the glitterati and the downtrodden -- outwardly active, yet inwardly hollow. His restless pursuits brought no peace, no fulfillment, no sense of purpose. His turning point came in 1986, when he found Jesus Christ and was baptized in the Holy Spirit. That encounter changed everything. He understood his own resurrection would be incomplete if he kept God's goodness to himself. Since that day -- though feeling inadequate and unworthy as he often does -- CJP has taken up the mission of bringing His Word to every person he meets, quietly and humbly, never noisily and boisterously. We know the story well: Jesus was betrayed, scourged, crowned with thorns, nailed to the cross, and left to die in agony. The suffering was visceral, public, and seemingly final. Hope appeared extinguished. Yet on the third day came the resurrection. This divine pattern mirrors life itself: a pregnant woman endures months of discomfort and exhaustion; labor brings intense pain; yet she embraces it willingly, out of love; and the reward feels eternal at the sound of the first cry. Without pain and love, there is no new life. In the same way, personal trials -- illness, loss, failure -- often become the soil from which our deeper purpose, stronger relationships, and renewed faith spring forth. Today we pray for peace in a world shaken by 'a war none of us wanted, yet one that affects us all.' Though our struggles differ, we collectively bear the weight of these global tensions. The message of Easter is not despair but defiant hope. May we emerge from our suffering not merely as survivors but as victors transformed by our suffering -- more loving, more resilient, more anchored in the God who conquered death itself. That is the ultimate meaning of His passion, death, and resurrection. And that is the eternal lesson our bleeding world desperately needs today.

one_paragraph_summary: Sparked by a Kyodo News item that nearly 30% of Japanese in common-law relationships avoid marriage to preserve their own or a partner's surname (40% among 20-year-olds), Panganiban surveys the names married women may use under the Civil Code of the Philippines. Article 370 offers three options -- maiden name + maiden surname + husband's surname (with a widely tolerated hyphenated form), maiden name + husband's surname, or husband's full name prefixed by 'Mrs.' -- paired with an etymological caveat that 'Mrs.' is the abbreviation of 'Mistress' so strictly 'Mrs. Maria Castillo' is inaccurate, though usage now tolerates it. Married women may also continue using their maiden names, especially where professional licenses, passports, or driver's licenses were earned in the single name; his own youngest daughter, Maria Evelyn Panganiban, still does. Performers may use pen names and aliases (Kyla, Heart Evangelista, Coco Martin, Dingdong Dantes). Widows may continue the married name, revert to the maiden name, or chain mother's-and-father's-and-deceased-husband's surnames (his cousin Evelyn Santos Camus Alcantara illustrates the pattern), and remarried widows may chain first and second husbands' surnames (Boots Anson Roa Rodrigo). Article 371 governs annulled and void marriages: the guilty party reverts to her single name; the innocent party may resume her single name or retain the husband's surname unless the court decrees otherwise or remarriage intervenes. Citing CJ Gesmundo's recent speech, he reports women make up 56% of trial judges, 77% of the CTA, 45% of the CA, and 35% of the Sandiganbayan, but only 13% (2 of 15) of the Supreme Court -- soon to drop further with J. Amy C. Lazaro-Javier's November 16, 2026 retirement. He closes with a 1960 bar-review-class anecdote in which the reviewer dismissed the fewer-than-10 ladies in a 100-student class -- 'guffaw from the men but grit and smirk from the women' -- and his prediction that women soon outnumbering men in the profession will make the men work harder, scrutinize more closely, and prepare for trial more avidly.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes an edited and abridged eulogy for his long-time friend Alberto 'Bert' David Lina, structured around Bert's three loves: family, work, and the Almighty God. Bert loved his wife Sylvia 'endearingly, tenderly, and eternally' -- she was 'the light of his life and the apple and mango of his eyes' -- and even in his 70s he was 'always Sylvia's swain of 20,' singing ballads, composing poems, and crafting love letters. Birthday gifts to Sylvia included a brand-new Jaguar car, a brand-new Bosendorfer piano, and a special pink-gumamela variety bred for her by UP Los Baños in her favorite color; he donated the auditorium at De La Salle Zobel in Alabang and christened it the Sylvia P. Lina Theater. He loved his four daughters (April Rose, Donna May, Sheila, Bertha Ann -- Valentine's roses, but no boyfriends until after college) and his four grandchildren (Andy, Alwyn, Aurelia Joule, Aurora Jane -- the only people who could countermand his orders). His second love was work: he loved to create, innovate, reinvent, and think out of the box, treating problems as opportunities; he loved all his 21 companies (some recently sold to the Ayala Group) across logistics, outsourcing, communications, connectivity, films, creative designs, sports, entertainment, land transportation, solar power, and waste management (the 'polite name of the portalet system he originated'); and he loved his 2,800 employees -- called 'partners and collaborators, not alalays' -- each getting a free daily meal with healthy brown rice, with production bonuses and profit-sharing regardless of rank. He loved the country 'warts and all' and twice took the tough job of customs commissioner against the author's advice -- once under Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, once under Benigno Aquino III. He also loved golf (hosting tournaments at company anniversaries and birthdays) and classical and popular music (indefatigable funder of the Manila Symphony Orchestra; logistics sponsor of the Philippine Philharmonic Orchestra and the Metro Manila Concert Orchestra). His third love was the Almighty: he credited the Lord with everything, framing himself as steward, and at the author's request donated ultramodern computerized Carillons at the Manila Cathedral, St. James Church in Alabang, Naga City, Pila Laguna, and Mandaue Cebu, telling the author that 'they reminded him of his mortality every time they chimed'; he loved the poor through medical-surgical-dental missions, annual company bloodletting, and support for the Red Cross and the little-known Guiding Light Ministries of Aklan. The author has known Bert since 1969 when he was a young L.C. Diaz and Company audit team member, was Bert and Sylvia's wedding sponsor, and considers Donna May his 'daughter by choice' (she calls him 'Dad CJ'). From those peso-and-centavo days, Bert -- 'the poor boy born in Tondo, Manila with roots in Laguna' -- rose to be a Filipino taipan in an authentic rags-to-riches story. The one word that unravels the secret of his gargantuan success was LOVE -- 'his enormous, googolplex love for his family, for his work, and for our Almighty Lord. Truly, to God be the glory!'

one_paragraph_summary: The capstone to CJ Panganiban's four-part stem-cell series summarizes his German clinic observations, reports his own post-LCT healing, and ventures a philosophical bridge between cell science and theology. Operationally, the Block Clinic descends from Dr. Paul Niehans (1931 LCT founder) through Dr. Siegfried Block, daughter Dr. Petra Block (current medical director), and grandson Dr. Daniel Block (administrative director), with a reported 86 percent healing rate; 2,500 cancer-resistant black sheep roam a 25-square-kilometer farm in Landsberg; first-time-mother sheep are selected, 70 initially per patient batch, 20 quarantined a week before treatment, and 2-3 best slaughtered 2-3 days prior with embryo parts emulsified within 40 minutes in an EU-certified laboratory. The empirical-clinical confirmation came at CJ's Oct. 23 evaluation by Dr. Dennis Serrano: prostate cancer cells 'inactive,' PSA at 0.33, hormone treatment canceled, Duodart reduced to twice a week; lumbar pain had not recurred since July; tennis and golf swings 'more robust'; CJ could waltz, tango, and swing nonstop for 30 minutes -- with only modest improvement to carpal tunnel and varicose veins. He commits to an explicit regimen -- intermittent fasting under 70 kilos, gym/tennis Mon-Fri, golf Wed-Sat, Manila Polo oval brisk walks Tue-Thu, Sunday treadmill -- plus a five-point lifelong engagement plan (brain stimulation, 100% board/committee attendance, mediation among corporate and political giants, socializing/traveling/dining/laughing with family, and writing his columns at 100%). Reaching back to his 2003 book 'The Bio-age Dawns on the Judiciary,' written around the April 14, 2003 completion of the human genome sequence, he speculates that stem-cell mystery may share mechanism with Jennifer Doudna's Nobel-winning CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing -- the ability to revitalize weakened tissues by 'natural' analogues to 'cutting out defective parts of a person's genome and inserting new ones.' He closes with a deeper mystery -- the zygote's self-organizing growth from a single cell -- and an Augustinian doxology: 'To God be the glory! My heart had been restless till it rested in Christ Jesus.'
