one_paragraph_summary: Part 3 of the stem-cell series is a procedural walkthrough of CJ Panganiban's July 14-19, 2024 Living Cell Therapy treatment at the Block Clinic in Germany. Nine friends accompanied him; because the Lenggries hotel was under renovation, the LCT was conducted in Bad Tölz at the BSW Isarwinkel Hotel (CJ in Room 220, daughter Len and personal nurse Leonor Ching in Room 219). After arrival on Sunday July 14, male nurse Almer took CJ's ECG and Filipino physician Dr. Andres Morato (Berlin-trained, who joined the Block Clinic in 2023 after Villa Medica was closed by German authorities) took CJ's medical history, documenting six baseline complaints: prostate cancer at stage Pirads 4 (managed with Luprolex hormones and daily Duodart), sharp lumbar pain radiating to feet, knee pain, carpal tunnel syndrome, varicose veins, and general weakness -- with instructions to suspend Pletaal SR 100 mg blood thinner for two days. Monday afternoon, Dr. Petra Block briefed CJ via Morato's English-to-German translation, explaining LCT's organ-specific matching principle (embryo heart parts for heart ailments, lung parts for lung ailments) and the 18,500-euro normal fee inclusive of full board with group discounts available. Tuesday July 16 was injection day: nurse Agie drew blood; Cathy Serrano (Filipino clinic assistant) had CJ gargle and swallow 10 mL of liquid Cortisone -- which CJ promptly expelled with two hours of violent coughing, nose drips, tears, and heavy sweating; then prone face-down, at 10:21 a.m. Dr. Morato administered 10 syringes (about 30 cc each, mostly pink or cloudy white) in rapid succession -- five per buttocks side -- in six minutes timed by nurse Leonor, followed by 30-minute prone immobility. Wednesday July 17 brought room confinement with all meals delivered. Morato shared the practitioner-witness story that converted him to 'alternative medicine': a young Parkinson's-afflicted boy at Villa Medica who walked again 48 hours after LCT injections. Thursday brought a Lake Tegernsee cruise with lunch at Seehotel zur Post; Friday brought 9:30 a.m. checkout, an Augsburg tour, and the Munich Airport return. The Block Clinic lineage (Niehans 1931 founder, Siegfried as Niehans's assistant honored by Pope Paul XII at the Pontifical Scientific Academy alongside Fleming, daughter Petra as current medical director, grandson Daniel as administrative director) and celebrity patient roster (Pope Paul XII, de Gaulle, Eisenhower, Madonna, Picasso) frame the credentials story.

one_paragraph_summary: Part 2 of CJ Panganiban's stem-cell series recounts his autologous stem cell (ASC) infusion experience from Sept. 1, 2013 through Jan. 23, 2014 -- six monthly intravenous infusions at the Medical City, administered by Dr. Denise Lavilles. The first infusion (Sept. 1, 2013) involved an overnight precautionary stay and the IV administration of 20 million of each of four cell types (80 million total): mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) for general wellness, endothelial progenitor cells (EPC) for blood-cell repair, osteoblasts (OS) for bone repair, and chondroblasts (CH) for cartilage repair -- with the only incident a male nurse's failed initial needle insertion producing 'a bubbled and busted vein.' Dr. Bernal explained in CJ's hospital room that after a 'huge debate among local doctors,' Philippine regulators approved only autologous treatment and banned foreign-body injections like 'sheep parts,' and that autologous subgroups (fat, blood) were either ineffective or unsanitary. The remaining five infusions on Sept. 20, Oct. 25, Nov. 23, Dec. 20, 2013, and Jan. 23, 2014 were uneventful, with dosage rising to 100 million cells and ratios shifted (35% EPC, 15% MSC, 25% OS, 25% CH); after the sixth, CJ reported improved physical prowess, more supple hair, and fewer facial lines -- though with the asymmetric outcome that the left face appeared younger than the right. Concurrent ailments (mandibular inflammation under Dr. Nathaniel Yan, elevated PSA of 8.96 with two no-cancer biopsies under Dr. Nikki Magsanoc, age-appropriate knee degeneration under Dr. Antonio Rivera, sleep problems treated by Dr. Deborah Arce Bernardo with Rivotril and melatonin) were handled separately. A planned 2019 repeat ASC was frustrated by COVID-19, Dr. Bernal's subsequent unreachability, possible loss of stored cells, and CJ's cancer doctor's refusal of clearance because he did not believe in stem-cell science. An unnamed retired justice ('RJ') redirected CJ to LCT under Dr. Siegfried Block in Lenggries, Germany; CJ read Block's books 'Miracle Cells' and 'Stay Young and Remain Healthy' on celebrity LCT patients (Pope Pius XII, de Gaulle, Eisenhower, Churchill); prostate doctor Dr. Dennis Serrano consented; and the decision to try LCT was made.

The two types: autologous stem cell (ASC) therapy -- extracting one's own cells (from bone marrow, blood, skin, or other parts), strengthening them in a laboratory, and infusing them back intravenously once a month for six consecutive months -- and living cell therapy (LCT) -- injecting emulsified embryo parts from cancer-resistant black sheep into the patient's buttocks in 10 same-day injections (German law prohibits exporting sheep stem cells). CJ then narrates how he came to ASC under Filipino American Dr. Samuel D. Bernal (MD, PhD, JD, MBA from American universities, clinics in Woodland Hills California and Prague), whose 'miraculous healings' included former Labor Secretary Nieves Confessor's fourth-stage cancer -- still in remission when CJ encountered her at the Feb. 29, 2024 AIM Chapel dedication for his late wife Leni. Romulo auditorium at the RCBC. Asked about his 'diminishing physical and mental agility,' Bernal requested CJ's seven thick medical albums chronicling his condition since 1983; on July 15, 2013, Bernal and Dr. Denise Labilles handed CJ a five-page comprehensive summary and diagnosed 'metabolic syndrome with microvascular complication' -- capillaries failing to deliver blood, inadequate nutrient absorption -- explicitly not Alzheimer's. CJ agreed 'right then and there, without consulting my wife Leni' to bone-marrow extraction under local anesthesia, with four cell types (mesenchymal, endothelial progenitor, osteoblasts, chondroblasts) to be cultured for six monthly intravenous infusions, with some cells frozen for future use. one_paragraph_summary: Ambassador Howard Q. Dee, 94, was proclaimed the sole recipient of the 2024 'RVR Award for Nation Building' on August 20. Moments after delivering his well-applauded acceptance speech and walking back to his seat adjacent to CJ's, he slumped; rushed to St. Luke's Global Medical Center, he died the next day on August 21, Ninoy Aquino Day. As chair of the RVR board of judges, CJ had explained why Dee was unanimously chosen, not realizing his address would become 'a virtual eulogy.' From heaven, the late Ambassador Ramon V. del Rosario Sr. 'must have been smiling' because Dee 'personified to the hilt the twin beacons that he stood for -- matchless excellence in business and extraordinary devotion to the less privileged.' Dee had a brilliant record as Unilab president and CEO, competing favorably with Roche, Pfizer, Johnson & Johnson, Novartis, and Merck. But 'more than being a top business leader, he was God's servant first,' upholding the credo (to which CJ also 'humbly adhere[s]') that though it is important to have what money can buy (food on the table, clothes on our back, a home for the family, and even a car), 'it is far more important to have the things that money cannot buy like integrity, honor, truth, trustworthiness and an enduring love for, and abiding faith in, our God.' Dee pioneered Philippine corporate social responsibility by inviting (with Bienvenido A. Tan) the top 50 tycoons in the early 1970s to form PBSP, with each setting aside 1% of net income before taxes; PBSP today has 230+ corporate members led by Manuel V. Pangilinan. After retiring from Unilab in 1970, Dee founded the Assisi Development Foundation to serve the poor 'just as our Lord Jesus Christ did, without any condition or expectation of reward'; later chaired the government peace panel with CPP-NPA-NDF (1993-1999); Cory Aquino named him ambassador to the Holy See and Malta; in 2018 he received the Ramon Magsaysay Award. What most impressed the board was his founding and chairship of ASA Philippines Foundation (July 1994), lending small sums to the poor: by 2022 it had earned P5.9 billion, served 2M+ clients across 1,683 branches with 11,401 employees, sustaining a 'manageable repayment rate of 93.97 percent' -- defying the banking industry's avoidance of MSMEs. As an aside, CJ announces FLP is launching a 'Prosperity Fund' -- equity investment in and management assistance to MSMEs, 'to help the poor help themselves through private entrepreneurship' -- explicitly non-duplicative of ASA's microlending and (to CJ's knowledge) 'not being undertaken by any organization.' Co-chairs are Amando M. Tetangco Jr. and Estela M. Perlas-Bernabe. For showing 'that the Filipino is trustworthy, credit-worthy, and Christ-worthy,' Dee fully deserves the RVR Award. CJ preserves the full board roster (Bacani, Cuisia, Gosingtian, Kang, Pangilinan, Ramon R. del Rosario Jr., Victor J. del Rosario, Tambunting) and closes: 'Thank you, Ambassador Howard Q. Dee, for your enduring legacy. To God be the glory!'

one_paragraph_summary: CJ surveys the senior-citizen quest for 'lovely longevity' -- 'the art of putting more life to our years under God's providence, not just adding more years to our lives' -- pursued through chat groups including 'Happy Seniors 100,' 'Sousai 100,' 'Retired SC Justices 100+,' and 'Team Lenggries 100 and Beyond.' The fountain-of-youth search is not new: Spanish explorer Juan Ponce de Leon roamed Florida's 'marshes and jungles' in 1513 when average lifespan was 32; Egyptian pharaohs and Chinese emperors directed their minions to find 'magical ways to everlasting life'; Lao-tzu's descendant Tao 'promised immortality to men who could sexually satisfy their partners a dozen times per day'; the Old Testament records Abraham (100) and Sarah (90) with Isaac, while Islamic tradition records that Abraham's firstborn with Hagar (Sarah's handmaiden) was Ishmael. Science and medicine have unquestionably prolonged life: Fleming's 1928 penicillin healed bacterial ailments; anesthesia relieved surgical pain; vaccines and sanitation conquered epidemics; viruses 'can one day be subdued'; biotechnology with AI 'will discover cures for cancer, heart diseases, dementia, and other existing incurables.' Beyond science is Dan Buettner's bestseller 'Blue Zones' (Netflix four-part series), which visited five places with 10x more centenarians per capita than the rest of the US: Okinawa, Ikaria, Loma Linda CA, Sardinia, and Nicoya. Eight commonalities: (1) plant-based diet, mostly fruits and veggies with very little meat; (2) natural body movement -- all-day walking, gardening, chores; (3) social life with relatives, singing/dancing with friends, community mingling; (4) sense of purpose -- 'ikigai' ('a reason for being'); (5) adequate sleep in quality and quantity; (6) reduced stress; (7) stopping eating at 80% full; (8) growing own fruits/vegetables or easy access. The surprise inclusion is Singapore -- lifespan risen to 84 (vs global 73) due to 'policy nudges to eat healthier, an efficient public transport system and park network to encourage people to walk more, imposing an expensive vehicle entry fee to the city center that lessened pollution, and a world-class health care and competitive education systems' -- though very expensive (first-world per-capita income higher than the Americans). CJ is currently in Germany with Team Lenggries 100 in the foothills of the Bavarian Alps (a 'ritzy suburb' ~50km south of Munich) and in nearby Swiss towns around Lake Geneva, where in 1931 Dr. Paul Niehans founded 'living cell therapy,' continued by his 'capable acolyte' Dr. Siegfried Block and later by daughter Dr. Petra Block and grandson Dr. Daniel Block. Germany today has 500+ cell-therapy specialists and ~5,000 occasional prescribers. one_paragraph_summary: At a private family dinner honoring his three grandchildren -- Andrea, Rafa, and Victoria -- for scholarships granted by top US universities (the subject of his previous column), CJ delivered as pater de familia a special message and now publishes an abbreviated version 'easy to remember': 'No pain, no gain. No sacrifice, no victory. No perspiration, no exaltation.' He amplifies the message with four stories. First, his own impoverished youth -- hawking newspapers, shining shoes in grade school and high school, and selling textbooks to classmates in college -- and, during law school, literally building with his brother Nardo, his orphaned half-uncle Frankie Villasenor, and a master carpenter a two-story house in Marulas, Polo, Bulacan (now Valenzuela City). He learned to draft architectural plans, slept in a tent at the site to fend off rain, mosquitoes, and robbers, and acquired the hands-on skills of carpenter, plumber, electrician, cement mixer, concrete-hollow-block maker, and peon. Second, the biography of Jensen Huang, who rose from a Taiwan-immigrant household in the US -- through hard manual labor and seething anti-Chinese prejudice -- to found Nvidia in 1993 and reach a net worth above $100 billion (Forbes, June 4, 2024); Huang told the Stanford graduating class (paraphrased): 'To succeed, you must endure pain and suffering first.' Third, the rise of Lance Gokongwei, a Wharton summa cum laude graduate who began as a management trainee 'selling Jack and Jill snacks to supermarkets, groceries, and sari-sari stores' with no privileges despite being heir apparent, and who inherited a $20-billion conglomerate at his father's 2019 death -- assuming leadership at 52. Fourth, the teaching of Our Lord Jesus, paraphrased: 'He who is worthy of me must take up his cross and follow me.' CJ closes by distinguishing 'pain and suffering' from 'pain and sacrifice' -- for Christians, suffering undergone with love becomes sacrifice, like a mother giving birth or a student burning the midnight oil. To his grandchildren: the scholarship 'is just the beginning' -- be ready to undergo pain and sacrifice 'for your education, for your career, for our family, for our country, and for our God.'

CJ believes -- IMHO -- that the headline-grabbing US student rallies influenced US pressure on Israel to temper its Gaza attacks and to pursue a ceasefire coupled with hostage release. Inevitably and unfortunately, 'outside actors' infiltrated the ranks, shifting the events from free expression to vandalism and violence, and the NYC police responded 'in full force, shields, sticks, and arms.' The Columbia students remind him of his own days as president of the Far Eastern University Central Student Organization (FEUCSO) and of the National Union of Students of the Philippines (NUSP), when he 'led the birth of campus activism here,' battling alongside the UP Student Council under Fernando Lagua, the UP 'Collegian' under editor-in-chief Homobono Adaza, and the UP Student Catholic Action under Emmanuel Soriano. He confesses that, as an impoverished youth who could not study without scholarships and who 'had to hawk newspapers and textbooks,' he was 'enamored by Karl Marx's cry of From each according to his ability, and to each according to his needs.' Two people dissuaded him. First, Fr. Michael Nolan, FEU chaplain and Manila SCA spiritual director, taught him simple catechesis and challenged him to study the actual economic reality of Red China and Russia -- proving communism 'theoretically attractive' but 'not implementable.' Second, Elenita 'Leni' Carpio, editor of the 'Scholastican' and aspiring Benedictine nun, met him as an 'accidental' seatmate on a ten-hour Manila-to-Naga train ride to an NUSP seminar; over three years of conversations she 'converted' him into a 'willing soldier of Christ,' and married him to the 'chagrin of the St. Scho nuns who expected her to join them in blessed singlehood.' Pope John Paul II later named him to the Pontifical Council for the Laity in the Vatican for the 1996-2002 term, succeeding Ambassador Henrietta 'Tita' de Villa. CJ closes with the Philippine arc: student activism here owes its origin to Wenceslao Q. Vinzons (resisting the Japanese invasion in 1941); the late-1950s peacetime activism bloomed into the 1970 First Quarter Storm led by NUSP's Edgar Jopson, UP's Jerry Barican, and Kabataang Makabayan's Jose Ma. Sison and Satur Ocampo -- Jan. 26 to March 17, 1970, against Marcos Sr. While present-day Filipino student leaders are 'not yet' engaged with the Israel-Hamas war, Russia-Ukraine war, or West Philippine Sea tensions, CJ expects they will engage when they realize 'there is no dispute so remote and so misunderstood they would not take a stand on.'

one_paragraph_summary: On March 18, 2024 -- Fidel V. Ramos's 96th birthday -- Panganiban reminisces about the only president to whom he owes his appointment to the Supreme Court. He frames FVR with three superlatives: 'first and only Protestant President of Catholic Philippines,' 'only general to ascend to the constitutional title Commander in Chief of all armed forces of the Philippines,' and 'arguably, the Best President of the Republic, complete with a grand vision of Philippines 2000.' He then narrates the story of how he was 'plucked ... from anonymity' and conscripted 'without passing through the judicial ladder.' On June 16, 1992 -- after the election but before FVR assumed office on June 30 -- CJ, en route to a Manila City Hall court hearing, received a surprise call on his 'huge, extra heavy mobile phone connected to my car': 'Is this Attorney Art Panganiban? This is Eddie.' CJ, irritated, asked, 'Eddie who?' -- and was told 'Eddie Ramos.' The next morning at 7 a.m., CJ knocked at the white door of office '202,' 845 Pasay Road, Makati, where Joe Almonte ushered him to a one-on-one with the President-elect. After an hour of exchanging views, FVR offered him the Secretary of Justice post (also inviting Henrietta 'Tita' De Villa). CJ declined because he had not campaigned for FVR and had voted for his mentor Jovy Salonga; FVR replied, 'I know you did not campaign for me. You did not even vote for me. You voted for your mentor Jovy Salonga. But that's alright. I want to have a nonpartisan Cabinet. I want to be president of all the people, not only of those who voted for me' -- then, 'Munching his unlighted tobacco,' recalled CJ's 1990-1991 Rotary Club of Manila presidency with its 'Love God, Serve Man' vision, 78 printed-manual projects with budget and timeline, and valedictory spreadsheet report, telling him, 'Quite impressive.' CJ ultimately declined Justice secretary but happily accepted associate justice of the Supreme Court -- 'I owe my appointment solely to President Ramos (to him only, as I had no padrinos or sponsors).' FVR respected CJ's independence throughout the 11+ Court years, never voicing or hinting at displeasure even when CJ voted against perceived FVR wishes -- 'Truly, a gentleman of the highest caliber.' At the end of FVR's term on June 30, 1998, the President sent an edifying letter of gratitude, and CJ replied that he had tried to discharge his duties 'with moral courage, integrity, and dedication.' CJ's 1998 book 'Battles in the Supreme Court' was dedicated to FVR as 'Leader, Reformer, Builder, Peacemaker, and Gentleman' -- to which FVR replied, 'I may be off to see the sunset, but don't be too surprised to see me there, with you, at the next sunrise.'

one_paragraph_summary: Continuing Part 2 of his Christmas-season sharing before a Catholic charismatic community, Panganiban completes the five-way reflection on Jesus Christ as leader. Third -- Jesus is a servant-leader who leads by example: 'You know how among the Gentiles who seem to exercise authority lord it over them; their great ones make their importance felt. It cannot be like that with you... The Son of Man has not come to be served but to serve' (Mark 10:42-45). CJ turns the scriptural standard against Filipino politicians who, though elected and calling themselves public servants, 'arrogate unto themselves power and authority over the life and death of our people' -- allocating huge 'pork barrel funds, or whatever it is now called' for patronage, gatekeeping business openings and employment, and inserting themselves into weddings and baptisms as sponsors. Quite the opposite, Jesus washed the apostles' feet (John 13:13-15), modeling that 'as I have done for you, so you must do.' Fourth -- Jesus is a leader of intense prayer and unbending faith: He went up the mountain alone to pray (Matthew 14:23), at Gethsemane prayed so intensely 'his sweat became like drops of blood,' and on the cross prayed aloud 'Father, forgive them for they know not what they do' and 'Father, into Your Hands I commend my spirit'; He Himself taught the Lord's Prayer as the best of all. Fifth and most importantly -- Jesus is a leader of justice AND love. The kingdom of God is not eating or drinking but 'justice, peace, and the joy that is given by the Holy Spirit' (Romans 14:17). He is the ultimate judge (Matthew 25:31-40) testing on food, drink, clothing, and comfort to the imprisoned. But he is also supremely compassionate -- confronted with the adulteress (John 8:1-11) facing Mosaic stoning, He replied 'Let the man among you who is sinless be the first to cast a stone at her,' and the accusers dispersed because Jesus knew their sins. 'To be just is to be wise. But justice is not the most valued virtue in the kingdom of God. It is love.' As St. Paul wrote in 1 Corinthians 13: 'If I speak with human and angelic tongues but not have love, I am a noisy gong, a clanging cymbal... if I have faith great enough to move mountains, but have no love, I gain nothing... If I give everything I have to feed the poor and hand over my body to be burned but have no love, I am nothing... There are in the end three things that last: faith, hope, and love, and the greatest of these is love.'

one_paragraph_summary: Opening his Christmas-week reflection, Panganiban reminds readers that the reason for the season is Jesus Christ, our Lord, King, and Leader -- summarizing across two columns a sharing he delivered before a Catholic charismatic community on why Jesus is relevant today as He was two millennia ago. Jesus is hailed as King of all kings, Ruler of all rulers, Lord of all lords on earth, in the universe, in the heavens, in all of creation -- and yet the gospels present Him as a humble defendant before Pontius Pilate (a Roman procurator, the rough equivalent of a Spanish-era PH governor general), standing alone in a 'kangaroo trial,' abandoned even by His closest disciples. Asked 'Are you the King of the Jews?', Jesus answered with a question -- an answer that 'an alert Filipino lawyer would surely jump to his feet and... move to strike off the record.' Jesus is an unusual King: His throne is a wooden cross, His crown a bouquet of thorns, His scepter a lowly reed, and His ring a rusty nail driven on His wrists. His constituents betrayed Him chanting 'Crucify Him' -- yet He is the only King who resurrected from the dead and thereby conquered sin in all eternity. CJ proposes five leadership traits, with two covered in this Part 1. First, Jesus is a leader with a vision and a mission -- speaking loftily, assertively, and authoritatively to His disciples (the Sermon on the Mount being the greatest teaching of all time), leaning heavily toward the poor, the sorrowing, the simple-hearted, and the peacemakers, and opposing the hypocrite, the arrogant, the proud, and the self-righteous; teaching outsiders through parables intended 'to enable the listener to discover something for himself,' most ending in questions like the good Samaritan (Luke 10:36), the forgiven debtors (Luke 7:42), and the tenants of the vineyard (Luke 20:16). He knew He would suffer and die but also that He would be victorious. Second, Jesus is a leader of enormous courage and unbreakable conviction -- quoting Albert Nolan's 'Jesus Before Christianity': 'a man who has the courage of His convictions... No tradition was too sacred to be questioned. No authority was too great to be contradicted... No assumption was too fundamental to be changed.' He mixed with sinners, tax collectors, a Samaritan woman, a prostitute, and an adulteress, acquiring a 'bad' reputation of being 'a glutton and a drunkard.' He sought no one's approval, denounced sin, called for repentance, and boldly proclaimed a kingdom of God -- opposite to that preached by the Jews and Romans -- 'where the weak is strong; and the strong is just; and the just is compassionate.' His Matthew 23 denunciation -- 'Woe to you scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites!... You are like whitewashed tombs, beautiful to look at on the outside but inside full of filth and dead men's bones' -- exemplifies that courage without mincing words. Next Monday: Jesus as servant leader, as leader of prayer and faith, and as leader of justice and love.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban shares a summary of the speech he delivered on Nov 16 when the Rotary Club of Manila -- joined by several Rotarians from other clubs -- honored him as 'the Only Philippine Rotary President to Become Chief Justice,' at the invitation of district governor-elect Jackie Rodriguez. He situates RCM as the first and oldest Rotary club in Asia (founded June 1, 1919), and recalls that during his 1990-1991 presidency it had 455 members -- the largest in the world outside the United States -- composed of Cabinet members, senators, congressmen, justices, 40 doctors, 50 lawyers, bank presidents, ambassadors, and heads of the country's top 300 companies, meeting at the Manila Hotel, with Presidents Marcos Sr., Cory Aquino, and Fidel V. Ramos using the RCM rostrum for major national messages. Under RCM's unique rule that the board's top vote-getter automatically became president, his name was put forward in 1989; he asked his Bukas Loob sa Diyos (BLD) Catholic charismatic group to discern with him through scripture, and they were led to Isaiah 42:1-8 ('Here is my servant whom I uphold...'). He won by a record margin in December 1989 and used the seven months before his July 1990 induction to plan. Further BLD prayer led to Mark 12:29-32, the Lord's two-commandment summary, from which he distilled the credo 'LOVE GOD SERVE MAN.' He expanded this into a 76-page printed Program of Action -- a 'first' in RCM's history -- with 178 projects, specific timelines, and a P90-million budget (eighteen times the prior P5-million annual outlay). His July 12, 1990 inaugural invoked Matthew 25's 'least of our brothers'; reactions ranged from 'Why is religion now a program of RCM?' to 'Alleluia, what a spirit-filled speech!' The true test came four days after induction, when the July 16, 1990 Baguio killer earthquake (magnitude 7.7, 2,000+ deaths) struck. At the July 19 RCM meeting, he pleaded for assistance and members responded with P7 million cash -- sixteen times his best expectations -- plus medical missions, product donations, clothes and groceries, a 'tent city' for 250 families in Burnham Park, and a 3,300-kilo single airlift from the Rotary Club of Waikiki. He read the response as Providence's answer to the credo. A year later, on June 27, 1991, he delivered his valedictory with a 94-page printed Final Report showing 95 percent of the program accomplished and a roadmap for the remaining 5 percent.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban shares his acceptance speech upon being named the Manila Overseas Press Club (MOPC) 'Journalist of the Year -- Law,' awarded on Oct 25 at the Fairmont Hotel, Makati -- the first such MOPC award in 78 years. The citation called him 'the No. 1 columnist of the Inquirer' with '12 [should be 14] books on law, faith, and the Supreme Court' for 'prolific work and prodigious excellence in writing about law and justice with depth, clarity, and command of language, thereby strengthening the people's faith in the third and often misunderstood branch of government, the judiciary.' Trophy details: bells ordered in Italy ('home to the world's oldest and best bell-manufacturing technology'), 15 inches tall, three kilos, symbolizing freedom, excellence, achievement, glory, perfection of craft. He shares the recognition with three 'Mega Media Movers': MOPC chair Tony Lopez (whose text invitation he initially answered 'I am not worthy... At best, I am just an ACCIDENTAL WRITER; in short, tsamba lang yon' -- and to whom he gave the title-quip 'Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious' to capture how lawyers 'tend to be highfalutin, muddled, and long-worded' while MOPC journalists 'write clearly and simply'); retired Inquirer chair Marixi R. Prieto, whom he first met in the late 1980s when she sold newsprint to the cash-strapped Inquirer and lent it P10 million convertible to common stock, becoming its 'ACCIDENTAL OWNER' when two deadlocked blocs assigned their holdings to her -- and who, on his 2006 retirement, invited him to write a column thrice a week, prompting Salonga's objection ('I do not know of any CJ who became a columnist. Chief justices do not write history; they make it.') and Marixi's retort ('I do not know of any chief justice who had been offered to write a regular column'), which inaugurated the 17-year, once-a-week streak through COVID (Dec 2022), Leni's death (April 9 -- whose eulogy became the most-visited Inquirer.net column as of August 2023), and international travel (e.g., Kuala Lumpur ALA speech), with first compilation volume (2011) ranked 3rd in Amazon's courts category behind Jeffrey Toobin and Antonin Scalia and royalties donated to the Inquirer Newsboy Foundation; and GMA Network chair and CEO Henry Gozon, whom he first knew as opposing counsel in aviation law (Gozon for PAL, author for KLM and Continental) some 50 years ago -- repeatedly invited to join the SC during the author's incumbency but respectfully declining, then visiting on Dec 6, 2006 with GMA president Jimmy Duavit to invite the author to GMA's board, and building GMA into the highest-rated Nielsen network with P7.5B record 2021 net profit under the 'Sa totoo lang tayo' motto. He closes feeling 'like receiving an honorary Ph.D. from the MOPC University of Journalism.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes a humble tribute to Maria Luisa 'Lou' Torres-Morales (June 21, 1944 - Sept 24, 2023), the wife of Dr. Dante Morales -- the brilliant cardiologist and director of Manila Doctors Hospital -- who passed unexpectedly. The news came via a phone call from his balae Linda Manalac ('Pare, our Kumare Lou died yesterday'); the author lost his balance and fell on a nearby chair, the way he had fallen on a chair in the Makati Med emergency room when his wife Leni died suddenly a few months earlier (he recalls embracing her covered body and sobbing 'I am sorry, honey, I failed you'). He reminisces about how Lou and Dan regularly broke bread with him and Leni during Sunday family lunches hosted by Tong and Linda. Lou was a quiet, attentive listener who turned small observations into thoughtful gestures: a gallon of buco-pandan sherbet after he mentioned liking it; dozens of corn cobs delivered after she watched Leni 'heartily munch her favorite corn cobs'; a Japan-trip Viber reminding them to bring winter wear; a perfectly-timed salabat suggestion when Leni had a sore throat; and weekly Viber messages -- many of them about the author's columns ('I can understand it even if I am not a lawyer. It was written in simple, clear, and easy English. I always look forward to reading your opinions') and many simply cheerful ('Have an enjoyable week ahead'; 'Please stay safe and healthy'; 'May your week be filled with fun and joy'). When Leni passed on April 9, Lou immediately wrote: 'Leni was such a wonderful lady. Yes, she was the epitome of a real fine lady in every sense of the word... How I wish I had given her a big tight hug the last time I saw her. We love you, Leni; you will always remain in our hearts.' The author admits that tears well in his eyes as he writes these reminiscences and that he could break into sobs if he continued, so he closes by summing Lou up: 'a true friend who was deeply compassionate, always thoughtful, always cheerful, humble to the point of self-deprecating, and loving to the point of self-sacrificing without expecting any requitement.' She did not burden others with her problems, always listened to friends' difficulties with a patient ear, and offered help across problems both small and big. He ends in prayer-address: 'Adieu dear Lou. Please say "Hi" to my Leni whom I am sure you will meet in heaven, and kindly extend my eternal love to her. And please prayerfully beg our Lord Jesus to bless and guide us here on earth whom you left behind, especially Dan. Until our joyful reunion in the Eternal Kingdom, we shall patiently bear our earthly pains and pines.'

one_paragraph_summary: Marking Toyota Motor Philippines' 35th anniversary, Panganiban begins with a Dec. 19, 2014 private dinner at the home of Dr. George S. K. Ty (Metrobank founder) and his wife Mary, where CJ -- seated to the immediate left of guest of honor Dr. Shoichiro Toyoda -- asked the retired Toyota Motor Corp. chair why his company uniquely yielded majority control of its Philippine subsidiary to the Metrobank Group when Toyota holds majority everywhere else in the world. Toyoda's answer was that Toyota had 'absolute trust' in Doctor Ty because TMP had topped -- and continues to top, for 35 years and counting -- all motor brands in the Philippines, a record 'not even in Japan' equaled or surpassed; the head office repeatedly declined Doctor Ty's offers to surrender control because it knew the company would be 'in the good hands of Metrobank.' Both founders have since passed to the Great Beyond, with heirs Akio Toyoda and Alfred Ty taking the helm. At the Grand Hyatt anniversary celebration, Akio opened with a Jollibee Chickenjoy-and-spaghetti tribute before turning formal and praising President Marcos's 'support, wisdom, and guidance' after a Santa Rosa factory tour; Alfred recounted TMP's 1988 start with 20 employees (4,000 today) and cumulative figures of 1.03 million units produced, 2.24 million delivered, P73.7B invested, P448B in taxes and duties, and $18.76B in auto-parts exports. First Lady Liza Marcos made her signature low-profile appearance to view the prototype of the new Toyota Tamaraw for 2024 production. CJ closes with his 60-year personal Toyota driving history -- from Corolla, Corona, and Crown of old through the Camry that was his CJ official car to his present favorite, the 'senior-friendly Alphard' -- and a benediction on a partnership 'carved in granite' between two companies and two families who 'mutually believe in and practice absolute trust, honor, integrity, hard work, transparency, and accountability. May their tribe increase!'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban publishes the edited and shortened text of his keynote speech at ACCRA Law Office's 50th-anniversary 'Appreciation Dinner' at Shangri-La Grand Ballroom in Taguig City - the 'giant ACCRA (spelled with all caps to differentiate it from the capital of Ghana).' He embraces ACCRA's 'Beyond Legal Excellence' theme of serving the poor through CSR partnerships with NGOs, paralleling his own conviction in 'helping the poor help themselves through private entrepreneurship,' anchored in Confucius's 'teach him how to fish' saying - the conviction that gave rise to the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity. FLP grants 20 yearly law scholarships at P200,000 and 5 yearly fellowships at P450,000 each, with two ultimate SC-partnership projects: an immersive, interactive, AI-powered Museum for Liberty and Prosperity and a multi-billion-peso 'Prosperity Fund' to invest in and help manage MSMEs - and he invites ACCRA to join both. He confesses 'one of the deepest regrets of my humble life': declining the late Edgardo 'Edong' Angara's invitation to join ACCRA at its inception (his own law office, family businesses, and directorships in a commercial bank, insurance company, and mining corporation - all of which became ACCRA clients). He could not decline, however, when Edong founded the ASEAN Law Association in the early 1980s; at the persistent urging of Ave Cruz he became, though unworthy, chairman of ALA Philippines and vice president of the regional ALA since 2015, to be succeeded January 1, 2024 by CJ Alexander G. Gesmundo (the regional presidency lineage runs Ave Cruz, Singaporean CJ Sundaresh Menon, incoming Malaysian CJ Tun Tengku Maimun binti Tuan Mat). Two vignettes from Edong's many-splendored career: as UP president, Edong thanked CJ for arranging Japanese friends' fire-truck donations to UP with a miniature UP Oblation (though CJ was not a UP alumnus); as GOPAC 5th Global Conference chairman at PICC in January-February 2013, Edong named CJ secretary general (though CJ was never a parliamentarian). When current ACCRA MP Trina Prodigalidad quipped 'Maybe, it is best you did not join ACCRA. Otherwise, you would have stayed with us and never became chief justice,' CJ countered: 'If I had joined ACCRA, I would have been the first ACCRA partner to become CJ' - and predicted Trina herself, at 53, more than qualified and young enough to become CJ before retirement, joining ACCRA's existing Senate-president pedigree (SEJA, Drilon, plus senators Sonny Angara and Dick Gordon). He testifies that the named founders and successors - Vinluan, Lazatin, Geraldez, Tan, Herbosa, de Guzman, Puno, Flores, Pantaleon - 'never intruded directly or indirectly in my work in the Supreme Court' because they knew he would be 'fair and objective to all, without fear or favor.' He closes by hoping to be invited to ACCRA's 75th diamond anniversary in 2048, with 'retired chief justice Patricia Ann T. Prodigalidad as the guest of honor and speaker. Cheers!'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers a twin eulogistic tribute opening with the personal-bereavement marker 'Two close friends passed away last week a few days after my Leni had gone' (his wife Leni, distinct from VP Leni Robredo). Oscar M. Lopez ('Oskie,' 93), chair of First Philippine Holdings, was 'a man of honor, dignity, and integrity; he was courageous, patriotic, and - when appropriate - quixotic,' exemplified by his rejection during the FPH-First Pacific consortium's NLEx-concession sale to MPIC of an unsolicited counteroffer P500 million higher: 'No sir, I will not break my word of honor for P500 million, or for any amount.' OML displayed courage and patriotism at annual FPH shareholders' meetings by criticizing sitting Philippine presidents 'without fear of their ire' - yet he never abused his closeness to advance business interests, a pattern Panganiban 'personally witnessed' as an FPH director sitting beside him at monthly board meetings, including throughout OML's close relationship with PNoy Aquino III (2010-2016). In December 2016 just before Christmas, OML, his wife Connie, and his baritone son Piki visited CJ's home and serenaded him and Leni - making up for missing CJ's '80th-birthday musicale, the Ageless Passion of Art Panganiban' at Maybank Theater featuring Ryan Cayabyab and Jeff Agustin. Piki's eulogy invoked the La Mancha Don Quixote figurine OML brought home 14 years before as emblem of OML's quixotic dream-big legacy. Albert F. Del Rosario ('ADR,' 83) had been Panganiban's close friend for over 40 years - 'the triumvirate of business titans Lim-Panganiban-Del Rosario who, as Mr. Chairman, broke bread together every month' until the quartet 'lost' Doming Lim in the 1990s and lost CJ when he joined the Supreme Court; tennis with ADR and his wife Gretchen continued at Manila Polo Club, Wimbledon, and Roland Garros. Per ADR's Ateneo de Manila honorary Doctor of Humanities prologue: 'It is said that a nation has four elements: its people, territory, government, and sovereignty. Albert F. Del Rosario has defended and promoted all of these,' including the protection of OFWs and the West Philippine Sea Arbitral Award. Quixotically, ADR with retired Justice Conchita Carpio Morales filed an ICC complaint against Xi Jinping for crimes against humanity - thrown out for lack of jurisdiction since China was never an ICC member, with the consequence that ADR was banned from Hong Kong. Panganiban closes: 'Adieu, my dear quixotic and patriotic friends. Well done on your earthly sojourn. Till we meet again in the peace and love of our Father in Heaven.'

one_paragraph_summary: A week after publishing his own eulogy for Elenita 'Leni' Carpio-Panganiban (C43, Apr. 17, 2023), CJ Panganiban yields his column space to three of the ten eulogies delivered during her wake -- selecting voices that portray Leni as mother, grandmother, and professor for 37 years at the Asian Institute of Management. Daughter Celine Panganiban-Hannett recalls 'quiet authority' parenting that never yelled, that reasoned at the 'age of reason' (eight), and that turned monthly allowances into a banking lesson -- with siblings either running out and learning installment borrowing, or saving and being rewarded by Leni still buying the pajamas Archie had skipped. Grandson Rafa Panganiban Yaptangco preserves Lola Leni's verbatim greetings at the Dasmariñas house ('Do you want chicheria? Just get, just get, we have plenty!' and 'Do you have a girlfriend na?'), her tutorials in tongue-curling and Uno and Old Maid and Sudoku, and the phone-game hobby (Bounce on her latest device) that Rafa credits as the seed of his tech career. AIM classmate and later co-professor Mari Sison Garcia situates Leni in the male-dominated pioneer batch of 1971 -- 'one of four women' -- who balanced 'the Harvard's case study method' with mothering five children and supporting CJ Art, earning their MBM as 'First Fruits of AIM,' later reuniting as faculty colleagues exchanging encouragement over lunches, and finally serving together in the Bukas Loob Sa Diyos Council of Servant Leaders, where 'CJ Art changed the dynamics of worship and Leni remained his anchor.' The column functions as curated family-and-community memorial in the voices of those who loved her most.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered on the last day of Leni's wake (Saturday, April 15, 2023) at the Santuario de San Antonio Parish Church in Makati and published two days later, this is CJ Panganiban's eulogy for his wife Elenita 'Leni' Carpio Panganiban -- and the most personally exposed piece in his published canon. He opens by naming the 62-year marriage 'idyllic' despite real differences in upbringing, aptitudes, religiosity, and values -- Leni spiritual where he was pedestrian, shy where he was outgoing, private and 'at her best when working alone, painting alone,' against his own appetite for socializing, dancing, public speaking, multitasking, writing, arguing, philosophizing -- and credits God's grace with turning differences into opportunities to grow in the Lord. As memorial framing he recounts their Diamond Wedding Anniversary one year prior in the secluded Carmelite Chapel in Tagaytay, presided over by Cardinal Jose F. Advincula Jr., attended exclusively by 86 incumbent archbishops and bishops, immediate family, Chief Justice Alexander G. Gesmundo (representing the Supreme Court), and Tessie Sy-Coson (whose family hosted the dinner at Tagaytay Highlands). The grief section, signaled by an ALL-CAPS turn ('BUT NOW MY LENI IS GONE'), recounts the sudden Easter Sunday passing -- Leni hospitalized at Makati Medical Center for hypoglycemia already arrested 12 hours earlier by 'two miniature Toblerone chocos,' cold sweat, and general weakness, not heart issues; she had jovially chit-chatted with New York City children and grandchildren the evening before, and 'none of us -- none of us -- expected My Leni to pass so fast.' The consolation hinges on absence of suffering at the end ('she did not wrench. She did not wince. She did not balk') and on the theological promise that the Divine Master will love her 'better than I can ever, ever do.' He declares himself 'drained, exhausted, depressed, shattered. But not defeated,' resolving to 'try to befriend grief for it will never go away,' and closes with the triadic farewell -- 'till we meet again, till we embrace again, till we are joyous again in the Heavenly Kingdom soon.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens the New Year with a celebratory profile of Jollibee Foods Corporation (JFC) and its founder, chair, and self-styled 'chief taste officer' Dr. Tony Tan Caktiong. The recent inaugurations at Times Square in New York and in iconic places in London, Milan, Vancouver, Dubai, Singapore, and across Asia complete JFC's ascent to international QSR status alongside McDonald's, Burger King, Starbucks, and Subway, and place Tan among 'world-class entrepreneurs in the likes of Jack Ma of China and Jeff Bezos of the United States.' From a 1978 mom-and-pop store with wife Grace and the now-celebrated Chickenjoy, JFC has grown to over 6,300 stores with 17 brands sold in 33 countries (Mang Inasal, Chowking, Red Ribbon, Greenwich Pizza, Michelin-starred Tim Ho Wan, China's Yonghe King, America's Smashburger, the world's Coffee Bean and Tea Leaf). Listed in 1993 at P9, JFC peaked at P325 pre-COVID (36x in under 30 years), fell to P100 in the pandemic, and recovered to about P230 -- and aims in eight years to be among the top five global QSRs while doubling store count, sales, and net income. Beyond business, Tan chaired the private-sector counterpart of Apec 2015 in Manila (Nov. 18-19, attended by Obama, Xi Jinping, Medvedev, and Trudeau), and the Jollibee Group Foundation (JGF) -- under his chair-emeritus role -- runs the farmer-supplier program, the FoodAID program (8.4 million meals served from 2020 to June 2022 across 358 cities and 60 provinces), and Busog, Lusog, Talino (BLT) Kitchens (240,000 pupils fed since 2007 with 400+ parent volunteers trained). one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban fills a void in the FVR tributes -- beyond Fidel V. Ramos's legendary workaholism, demand for CSW (completed staff work) and UST (units of time), 'bibingka' approach, passion for democratic reform matched by his abhorrence of autocratic shortcuts, doable legislative agenda, and 'Philippines 2000' vision -- by recounting how FVR greatly respected the Supreme Court and unflinchingly followed the rule of law, through two cases. In Alex David v. Comelec (April 8, 1997), which CJ had the honor of writing, the Court unanimously denied a petition to extend barangay-official terms from three to five years and cancel the May 12, 1997 barangay elections -- despite media buzz that FVR wanted the postponement, and despite the OSG siding with petitioners against its own Comelec client. The ponencia's language was strong: 'The Constitution and the laws do not support them. Extant jurisprudence militates against them. Reason and common sense reject them. Equity and morality abhor them. They are subtle but nonetheless self-serving propositions to lengthen governance without a mandate from the governed.' Yet FVR did not balk or complain -- he asked everyone, including dissenters, to obey, and never hinted regret at CJ's authorship. In the more controversial Defensor-Santiago v. Comelec (March 19, 1997), the Court held 8-5 -- Davide ponencia joined by CJ Narvasa, JJ Regalado, Romero, Bellosillo, Kapunan, Hermosisima, and Torres against dissenters Melo, Puno, Mendoza, Francisco, and CJ himself -- that RA 6735 was inadequate for people's initiative. The dissenters attacked the novel 'insufficient or inadequate law' theory ('a law is either constitutional or unconstitutional but never inadequate or insufficient'). The MR split 6-6, failing the seven votes needed to reverse, and was denied with finality. Crucially, FVR never asked his nine appointees (who outnumbered the six others) to vote one way or the other -- even though a unified bloc could have unlocked his 1998 reelection via people's initiative. 'Indeed, he respected the independence and dignity of the Court and its members to decide freely in accordance with its/their constitutional mandate.'

one_paragraph_summary: On July 19 at the Philippine Embassy in The Hague, the government honored three outstanding Filipino jurists for their exemplary membership in UN-recognized international tribunals: the late CJ Cesar Bengzon (ICJ), former Inquirer publisher Raul C. Pangalangan (ICC), and the late Senior Associate Justice Florentino P. Feliciano (WTO Appellate Body). Keynote speakers were ICJ Vice President Kirill Gevorgian, CJ Alexander G. Gesmundo, and ICJ Judge Iwasawa Yuji (nominated by the Philippine National Group at the Permanent Court of Arbitration, comprising retired CJ Reynato Puno, Justice Jose Vitug, Judge Pangalangan, and CJ as PNG chair, exercising the UN-Charter-granted PCA right to nominate ICJ judges). The Supreme Court additionally published a collection of Feliciano's decisions and resolutions, and CJ was given the honor of writing the Foreword (six times the column's length) -- summarized here. Justice 'Toy' Feliciano was a world-class scholar and jurist: UP BA summa cum laude, UP LLB magna cum laude, Yale LLM and JSD; taught at UP, Yale, and The Hague Academy of International Law; SyCip Salazar managing partner before joining the SC in 1986. When CJ entered the Court in 1995 as 'a Court neophyte in every sense of the word,' Feliciano was already senior associate justice and Third Division chair -- 'our source of enlightenment for difficult issues of law' -- but sympathetic and patient with neophyte colleagues. He retired early to accept membership and chairmanship of the WTO Appellate Body, an honor 'he alone holds in our country.' American colleague James Bacchus called him 'The Aristotelian' for his mastery of reason and logic 'as the torch of wisdom and discoverer of truth,' and described him as 'their great teacher.' Yale's W. Michael Reisman placed him 'in the great tradition of Holmes, Cardozo, and others' -- and because Reisman is 'reputed to be conservative with his language and timid with his praises,' the claim is no braggadocio. CJ's own 'lifelong guru' Dr. Jovito R. Salonga (Harvard LLM, Yale JSD) called him 'one of the finest alumni of Yale not just among Filipinos but amongst all students including Americans.' Had he stayed on the Court, he could have been chief justice -- but he chose the WTO Appellate Body for his remaining 'years of intellectual statesmanship.' Hence CJ's coined epithet: 'The Global Aristotelian Jurist.'

one_paragraph_summary: Repurposing his recent commencement address at the FEU-Nicanor Reyes Medical Foundation as an Easter-season column, Panganiban walks through five life-threatening episodes -- the 1942 dysentery at age six saved by his mother's vigil during WWII, the 1949 jeepney-jump escape under a 6x6 army truck whose road clearance let his lean body slide under its axles, the 1957 ruptured appendix at the FEU Hospital (where Dr. Ricardo Alfonso had him withdraw, in pain, his student-leader opposition to the P6 hospitalization fee), the 1983 diabetes diagnosis under Dr. Augusto Litonjua, and the heart-rhythm anomalies cleared by Dr. Dante Morales's angiogram. Though born Catholic, he had no catechesis until FEU chaplain Fr. Michael Nolan taught him the Our Father, Hail Mary, Glory Be, and the FEU Prayer -- the FEU Prayer becoming a source of the 2001 'Centennial Prayer of the Courts.' From this, his first advice to the medical graduates is to 'pray and trust God always,' asking not for the removal of evils but for the strength to triumph over them 'in His own way, in His own time.' His second advice is to work with 'two Cs -- competence and care,' illustrated by a deceased Filipino multibillionaire's testimony of dehumanizing US hospital care where he was treated as an object rather than a human being needing the companionship, care, and love of Filipino doctors and nurses. The column closes with the Ignatian synthesis: 'Pray as though everything depended on God; work as though everything depended on you.'

First, to those behind the four Rs -- retrofitting, restrengthening, restoration, and renovation -- undertaken from 2012 to 2015, who preferred anonymity per Matthew 6:1 until the Vicar of Christ acclaimed their work: the relocation of the 17-ton belfry bells in 2010 (replaced by 23 lighter computerized Carillon bells from the Netherlands); Cardinal Tagle's 2012 decision upon assuming the Manila archbishopric to close the structurally weakened church lest it topple in an earthquake; and the verbal-trust generosity (without 'as-built' plans, sometimes without written requests) of donor families -- Don Ramon Ang, the late Dr. George S.K. Ty, the brothers Jaime Augusto and Fernando Zobel de Ayala, the Linas, and an anonymous donor -- with DM Consunji's Sid Consunji donating margins. Structural engineer Angel Lazaro and supervisor Salvador Castro reinforced the weakened center columns with carbon fiber and epoxy after chipping off marble covers that were later restored without breakage ('the miracle is that none of the marble covers broke or fragmented'); marble floors were lifted to lay drainage, plumbing, and electrical, with sound and lighting modernized. Second, to those who walked CJ's spiritual journey -- his family, SC brethren, FLP, FLP Scholars Society, the Bukas Loob sa Diyos Covenant Community -- and specifically the late Fr Michael Nolan who as FEU chaplain snatched the impoverished CJ, then youngest president of the FEU Central Student Organization, from Marxist temptation and helped him organize the National Union of Students; the late Leni, who 'set aside her vocation to be a Benedictine nun to marry undeserving me'; former envoy to the Holy See Tita de Villa, who ushered CJ into the inner sanctum of the Church including the Vatican-based Pontifical Council for the Laity; CJ Gesmundo, who foregoing a Bangkok judicial conference to attend; and Tessie Sy Coson, his former Assumption commercial-law student who 'has remained simple, modest, unaffected, and unassuming.' He closed by reciting the 1995 vow he made upon SC entry without prior judicial or public office: 'I hold office by God's grace, and I pledge to serve Him and our people with fortitude, integrity, competence, and prudence. I dedicate all that I am, and all that I will ever be, to Him who is the Source of everything.' To God Be the Glory!

one_paragraph_summary: During the Christmas season of thanksgiving, Panganiban yields the column space to publish (with deletions of about 40%) CJ Alexander G. Gesmundo's speech formally launching 'With Due Respect 3.' Gesmundo recalls being asked at his Judicial and Bar Council interview whether he favored extending Supreme Court Justices' terms beyond 70 toward US-style lifetime tenure, and answering against it on the assumption that productivity wanes with age. 'I may have spoken too soon,' he says -- pointing to Panganiban at 85, 15 years into retirement, 'two decades my senior,' yet 'as incisive and lucid as when he was writing his ponencias for the Court' -- as 'the best argument to lifetime tenure for Justices of the High Court.' He celebrates Panganiban's mastery of what he proposes as the title of CJ's next book, 'The Art of Relevance,' anchored by the Inquirer column 'With Due Respect' which addresses 'the burning legal issues of the day with more freedom than he had when he was sitting in the Court,' articulating views that incumbent justices 'could only wish to say themselves... even mischievously, if I dare say.' The columns are 'incisive and can cut to the quick, but are always insightful' -- staunch advocacy delivered 'with the utmost respect for the Court and its rules.' Gesmundo quotes CJ's own Oct. 31, 2021 column lamenting 'I have not done enough,' observes that 'the work is never finished,' and closes by thanking CJ for service to the judiciary, for paving the road his successors now tread, and for opening 'the gate of our minds to a relevant life after retirement.' He raises his glass to the 'unofficial resident amicus curiae' and to a future 'fourth installment' of 'With Due Respect.' Cheers!

one_paragraph_summary: Writing 10 days after his second Moderna jab from the Cardinal Santos-Meralco Corporate Wellness Center, in the midst of the Delta-variant lockdown that crushed his hopes of 17 months of 'house arrest' ending, CJ Panganiban offers a personal essay structured by the dyad in his title -- age gracefully, learn endlessly. The 'gracefully' half draws on a Couples for Christ lecture by his high-school chum and brilliant psychiatrist Dr. Cornelio Banaag Jr.: aging has a genetic ceiling but is shaped by manageable factors; socialize online via Viber/WhatsApp to release endorphins; the brain's billions of cells are wired by neurotransmitters that grow with use ('use it or lose it,' 'old dogs can still learn new tricks'); telomeres at chromosome ends function as cell-division clocks shortened by toxic stress and leading to dementia. He grounds the framework in his own family longevity data -- father died at 54, mother at 61, but eldest sister at 90, elder brother at 88, another sister still alive at 88, himself 84 and turning 85 in December -- and credits nutrition, sleep, doctors, medicine, and lifestyle for 'overtaking' heredity. The 'endlessly' half is autobiographical: instead of his planned retreat to a Tagaytay farm, tycoons (mostly previously unmet) recruited him as independent director and adviser, philanthropic/legal/economic/religious groups enlisted him, and he is now 'as busy as when I was in the Court.' He carries judicial independence into corporate directorship ('fidelity to the corporations... not to the owners'); enumerates with evident pride the corporate-finance and technology vocabulary he has acquired post-retirement (CCNI, O&M, NIAT, QoQ, EPS, kWh, GLA, PFRS, US GAAP, DU, WESM; 5G, cloud, OLT, AI, sustainability, blockchain, bitcoin, CX centricity, fintech, deep learning, cracks, silos); reports raising P200 million to retrofit the Manila Cathedral and setting up FLP scholarships, professorial chairs, and dissertation prizes; personally types emails/speeches/columns on his desktop and uses MacBook Pro, iPad Pro, and iPhone 12 for online meetings; and plays tennis and golf because 'walloping tennis and golf balls aligns my eyesight with my nervous system and muscles.' The piece closes with the signature line: 'I find retirement to be merely a change of tires to embark on new journeys. I hope to age gracefully, work happily, learn endlessly, and pray unceasingly until the Lord calls me to an even more glorious journey in His Kingdom of Eternity.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the obituary tribute for retired SC Justice Jose A. R. 'Pepe' Melo, who 'passed to the Great Beyond' on October 18, 2020 at age 88. Melo was President Fidel V. Ramos's first SC appointee on August 10, 1992, having previously served as 'much-admired presiding justice' of the Court of Appeals. He was CJ's 'first friend in the Court,' the mentor who patiently taught him 'the little-known processes,' and the principal wedding sponsor of CJ's daughter Marilen on December 20, 1995 -- a friendship anchored in their shared Pampango heritage that they continued to converse in even while traveling abroad for judicial meetings with their spouses. They served on the same SC Division for seven of Melo's ten years (where 85 percent of decisions were deliberated, against 15 percent En Banc), and played golf and tennis on weekends. CJ quotes himself from 'Justice and Faith' (1997, p. 144) on Melo as 'the consensus builder of the Court and living barometer of its leanings and positions on various issues... respected by his colleagues for his objectivity, fairness, lucidity, and openness to new ideas and contrary views,' and from 'Reforming the Judiciary' (2002) with the four-word portrait -- mild-mannered, eloquent, loyal, and open -- each elaborated in turn: mild-mannered meant gentle and fair yet firm in convictions and tolerant of dissent, free of bloated self-opinion ('he felt uncomfortable when praised'); eloquent meant through action, body language, facial expression, gesticulation, grin, and smile rather than 'flowery words or verbal flourishes'; loyal meant to country, Court, his wife Norma, his children Olivia Anne, Jaime Alberto, and Jorge Alfonso, and to friends -- 'especially... when his friend was on the shorter end of an argument' (Melo's aphorism: 'one did not need a friend when one was right. One needed a friend when one was wrong, to be consoled and empathized with while promising to do better next time'); and open meant transparent, 'read like a book,' loathing 'high-powered rhetoric and highfalutin words.' Six years after retiring from the SC, GMA called Melo back to public service on March 25, 2008 at age 76 as Comelec chair -- after the SC had invalidated three poll-agency contracts to automate the 2004 presidential election (causing 2004 and 2007 to be conducted manually). Under his 'gung-ho leadership' Comelec 'courageously automated the 2010 presidential election,' and despite PCOS machines failing test runs, the election installed Benigno Aquino III 'with nary a protest from his opponents.' Melo voluntarily retired from Comelec on January 16, 2011, 'well ahead of his six-year term,' to give his replacement planning time. Given the prior SC defeats and PCOS media criticism, CJ initially thought Justice Pepe 'risked too much in accepting the chairmanship' -- he had retired from the Court with 'an enviable record of performance with no backlog at all.' For 'daring the odds and succeeding,' CJ reiterates his May 26, 2019 designation that Melo should be recognized as the 'Father of Automated Elections in the Philippines.'

one_paragraph_summary: In a Christmas-season column summarizing his talk to retired SC justices at their Christmas party, Panganiban offers a meditation on collegiality, gratitude, nostalgia, and futurism. He opens with his canonical formula for principled disagreement -- 'disagree without being disagreeable... differ without being difficult' -- and explains why lay people are surprised that justices remain the best of colleagues after strongly worded opposing opinions: the disagreement is with views, not with persons. He thanks God for the 'bonus days and years' beyond the Philippine average longevity of 70 (69 men, 71 women), citing a Snoopy-Charlie-Brown cartoon -- 'We only die once. We live every day' -- and exhorts seniors to make each day count: 'Smile, laugh, sing, dance, help the poor, enjoy life... till we reach 100 and beyond.' He indulges generational nostalgia -- 1950s university-belt law schools (UP, Ateneo, USC, UST, San Beda, MLQ, UE, FEU), 15-centavo bus fares on Halili Transit and JD Bus, four pesos to the dollar, dates at Moonlit Terrace and Jai Alai Sky Room, and the singers Sylvia La Torre, Ruben Tagalog, Diomedes Maturan and Pilita Corrales -- and pivots to the futurist arc: 5G smartphone shopping and home CCTV, AI, cryptocurrencies, IoT, and the stem-cell revolution that will let grandchildren live 150 years via grown or traded replacement body parts. 'Death from disease will be optional' in 25 years; aging will be reversed via telomere lengthening, already shown possible in lab experiments. He closes with the trademark Einstein-vs-bar-flunker brain auction joke (Einstein's brain is cheaper because it's already overused) and his signature Filipino valedictory: 'Mabuhay!'

one_paragraph_summary: Responding to reader interest in his October 20 column 'Why Tony Carpio never became chief justice,' Panganiban explores the counterfactual: what would have happened had Carpio been named CJ. He defends the over-110-year SC tradition (broken only during the Japanese occupation) of naming the most or second-most-senior justice as CJ -- even Marcos at his most powerful 'carefully adhered to this tradition,' bypassing Teehankee only to name the second-most-senior -- and grounds it functionally in the Division structure: the Court decides ~85% of cases through three five-member Divisions, with the First Division usually chaired by the CJ, the Second by the most senior, and the Third by the second-most-senior, making the latter two 'little chiefs' grooming the 'big chief.' Of Carpio's five chances, the saddest was after CJ Renato C. Corona's impeachment and ouster on May 29, 2012, when P-Noy reportedly told him he was 'most qualified and most senior' but that 'some Senate allies and three prominent business leaders opposed his elevation' -- CJ Panganiban discloses that he spoke with one of those senators and two of the businessmen, and all denied opposing him, a story 'worth a full column.' Had Carpio been CJ from 2012 to his Oct 26, 2019 retirement, there would have been no CJs Sereno, De Castro, or Bersamin; Sereno could not have been ousted and would have been the most senior AJ today, potentially serving ~20 years (Aug 13, 2010 to July 2, 2030). Because chief justices have 'moral ascendancy' as primus inter pares -- Courts are named after their chiefs, like the Teehankee Court or Warren Court -- Carpio's dissents in this period could have become the decisions: limiting martial law in Mindanao to Marawi City only, rejecting both its extensions, denying the natural-born citizenship of Grace Poe, opposing the Marcos burial at Libingan, refusing to acquit Arroyo of plunder, denying bail to Enrile, and rejecting the validity of De Lima's arrest and detention.

Unlike the Philippine and US Supreme Courts, the ICJ does not assign a single ponente; after oral arguments and written briefs or memorials, the 15 judges deliberate and vote en banc (5-judge panels are possible at the parties' request), elect a committee to draft the decision collegially, then discuss, scrutinize, correct, and vote on the draft part by part, with dissenters writing under their own names. Ad hoc judges of any nationality may be chosen when a litigant lacks an ICJ judge of its nationality -- making 16-judge benches possible. Iwasawa attributed near-universal voluntary compliance with ICJ judgments to the UN Charter's requirement of state-party consent to jurisdiction; the singular exception was the June 27, 1986 Nicaragua v. one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban honors Justice Mariano C. del Castillo, who will be feted by his colleagues on July 26, 2019 -- three days before his 70th birthday on July 29, because the Constitution's 'until they reach the age of seventy' has been interpreted as 'until midnight of the day before' the 70th birthday. He traces Del Castillo's 30-year arc from MTC San Mateo (1989) through RTC Angeles, RTC QC, and the Court of Appeals to the Supreme Court (July 29, 2009), noting that Del Castillo declined his nomination to succeed CJ Leonardo-de Castro in 2018 with the characteristically humble explanation: 'I will be retiring in about eight months, and I don't think I can make a difference as chief justice. I would rather concentrate on my work as an associate justice and as chairman of the 2018 bar exams.' Del Castillo, CJ argues, embodies the constitutional standards of competence, integrity, probity, and independence -- 'friendly yet detached; familiar yet objective; strict yet fair; self-assured yet collegial' -- a gentleman-jurist whose career was modest in honors but rich in substance (his student peak was marrying the 1976 class valedictorian, who later became dean of Ateneo Law). With his retirement, Duterte's appointees rise to 8 of 15; after Jardeleza, Bersamin, and Carpio retire in Sept-Oct 2019, the figure climbs to 11, and by June 30, 2022 to 13 with the chief -- leaving only Leonen and Caguioa from the pre-Duterte court. How this super-majority will affect SC independence deserves a future column, CJ writes, but new justices soon learn 'that the temporaries of the moment are always overtaken by the permanencies of history.'

He sets out his organizing typology: the 'legal technician' interprets law literally to serve commercial causes, while the 'social engineer' interprets law liberally, treating it as 'an instrument in the building of a just society' -- a brick in the social edifice rather than an end in itself. one_paragraph_summary: Marking the Rotary Club of Manila's centennial, Panganiban traces RCM's June 1, 1919 chartering as 'First in Asia' under founding president Leon Lambert and 37 charter members, and its expansion into roughly 800 PH clubs today. Through 100 years of voluntary, self-funded, humanitarian work -- medical and surgical missions, sight and hearing preservation, drug abuse prevention, disaster relief, environment protection, scholarships -- RCM has institutionalized many of its programs into autonomous organizations: Boy Scouts, Community Chest, Philippine Cancer Society, the RCM Eyebank Foundation, the Philippine Rotary Pacemaker Bank Foundation, the RCM Medico-Surgical Missions Foundation, the Safety Organization of the Philippines, the SPCA, Gatches Village, and others -- proving that civic clubs can build durable national institutions. He catalogs the club's storied membership (Henry Sy, Gokongwei, Gotianun, Yuchengco, Del Rosario; Oca, Ople, Laguesma; MacArthur, Romulo, Ramos; Mat Caparas, the only Filipino Rotary International president), and its line of presidents from Arsenio Luz (1933-34) through Bartolome III (1988-89) and on to centennial president Jesus Pineda Jr. He recalls his own 1990-91 RCM presidency -- 'the psychic fulfillment of a job well done more than made up for my loss of professional and business income for one year' -- and frames his post-judiciary turn to the FLP, Manila Cathedral-Basilica, Metrobank, Tan Yan Kee, Teehankee, and ASEAN Law foundations as continuations of the same 'Service Above Self' ethos. He closes by thanking RCM for the June 21, 2019 award honoring him as 'the only Rotary president to be chief justice of our country.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban thanks the Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting (PPCRV) and its half-million volunteers for helping ensure orderly 2019 polls -- a contribution he places on the same plane as Comelec, the Department of Education, and the Philippine National Police. Unlike the paid Election Board chairs (P6,000), members (P5,000), DepEd supervising officers (P4,000), and staff (P2,000), PPCRV volunteers served without compensation, sustained only by 'selfless desire to safeguard our democracy.' He traces PPCRV's origin to 1991, when the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines -- meeting daily for 12-hour sessions from January 20 to February 17 at the San Carlos Lay Formation Center in Makati -- for the first time in the Church's 2,000-year history invited 145 lay leaders to legislate alongside the hierarchy in implementing Vatican II in the Philippines. Led by former PH ambassador to the Vatican Henrietta 'Tita' T. De Villa and encouraged by Jaime Cardinal Sin, the laity organized PPCRV; CJ himself served as PPCRV national vice chair and chief legal counsel until joining the SC in 1995. He traces the succession from De Villa (retired 2016) through former Comelec commissioner Rene Sarmiento (resigned August 2018 for health) to current president Myla C. Villanueva -- 'prodigious and computer-savvy' -- and notes that 'the reward for good work is more work' as the digital age advances. He then welcomes Justice Henri Jean Paul B. Inting, newly elevated to the SC despite junior CA standing because he rose from the lowest rungs (Metropolitan TC, RTC, CA, SC) with longer total bench years than many former colleagues and left his appellate docket with no backlog. one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban replies to readers who challenged the opening sentence of his prior column -- 'Compared with prior exercises, the last elections were generally peaceful and orderly' -- by clarifying that 'Compared with prior exercises' is the operative part: today's vote-buying, automation glitches, and overvoting are real, but the appropriate comparison is to the manual-era cheating that automation replaced. He traces the legislative-judicial chronology: Congress enacted RA 8436 on December 22, 1997, mandating automation; the Comelec entered three contracts for the 2004 polls -- to clean the voters' list, automate counting and canvassing, and hasten vote transmission -- but the Supreme Court invalidated all three in Comelec v. Quijano-Padilla (Sept. 18, 2002), Information Technology Foundation v. Comelec (Jan. 13, 2004), and Brillantes v. Comelec (June 15, 2004), with the middle case (which CJ authored) being most crucial for its finding of 'inexplicable haste, without adequate checking and observing mandatory financial, technical and legal requirements... in violation of law and jurisprudence.' The Court was 'initially hesitant' because invalidation would force reversion to manual elections, but invoked 'Fiat justitia ruat caelum' to fulfill its duty -- and indeed the 2004 and 2007 polls were conducted 'mano-mano.' RA 9369 then updated RA 8436, and retired SC Justice Jose A. R. Melo was named Comelec chair in 2008. Under Melo the ARMM 2009 special polls were first automated, and the 2010 presidential election was 'courageously' automated despite PCOS failures, missing CF cards, late or spoiled ballots, misprinted candidate names, and misaligned ovals -- yet succeeded 'warts and all' because no opponent protested the new president's installation. Melo voluntarily retired early to give his successor planning time. The 2013 and 2016 elections were 'humped with difficulties' (source-code-review refusal, restricted random manual audit, parallel-count aversion); in 2018 the PCOS was modernized and renamed Vote-Counting Machines, and in 2019 the Comelec became 'more transparent, accountable and tolerant of criticisms.' Anchoring the tribute to Melo's 87th birthday on May 30, CJ declares that for 'daring the odds and succeeding,' Melo 'should be recognized as the Father of Automated Elections in the Philippines.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens his Sunday column written in advance from before a Florida Disney World + Royal Caribbean Cruise family trip, thanksgiving-style, for the four new careers he embarked on after ending his SC term on Dec. 7, 2006: column writer, arbitrator/expert witness in international arbitrations, corporate director/adviser, and foundation trustee/officer. Prieto initially asked for three columns per week, which he respectfully declined (citing only his student-era credentials as a fledgling FEU Advocate reporter and FEU Law Review managing editor) before compromising at weekly. He states his editorial philosophy: 'I do not spoon-feed readers. Neither do I stupefy them with grand opinions and holier-than-thou sermons. Rather, I prefer to provide the background, the facts and the law' -- letting readers 'analyze, find their eureka moments and derive their own conclusions' as 'the best way to be independent and responsible citizens.' He notes his biggest writing challenge is the 4,100-character space limit ('I had to work back wearyingly and edit excess verbiage'), his 12-year 100% Sunday-output record, and his system of writing in advance and leaving copies with Inquirer coordinator Christine Ang Buban. On arbitration, he recounts becoming chairman (then chairman emeritus) of the Philippine Dispute Resolution Center -- the only PH private arbitration outfit -- and one of only four Filipino members of the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague, while respectfully declining all offers to rejoin the government.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban summarizes the eulogy he delivered on the evening of November 24, 2018 -- the first night of Dr. George S. K. Ty's wake -- directing readers to cjpanganiban.com for the full text. He acknowledges hesitancy to speak first when the family and Metrobank Group officers had known Dr. Ty far longer, and chooses to share personal stories illustrating Dr. Ty's principles. He recounts meeting Dr. Ty about twenty years earlier when invited to join (and later chair) the board of judges for the Metrobank Foundation's 'Search for the 10 Outstanding Teachers,' during which Dr. Ty -- then active chairman of the conglomerate -- sat patiently on a side chair throughout multi-day interviews without ever intruding. After CJ's retirement from the judiciary, Dr. Ty invited him to become a Senior Adviser of Metrobank and a board member of the Metrobank Foundation, eventually succeeding the late Cory Aquino as board chair after her August 1, 2009 death. When Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala invited CJ to BPI, Dr. Ty told him directly: 'Please accept the offer. I fully trust you. I know you will never reveal any business secret, whether of Metrobank or of BPI or of anyone' -- the column's compact demonstration of trust-based ethos. He recounts Dr. Ty's home visit explaining his commitment to donate 10% of his wealth to philanthropy in thanksgiving for his business success -- an extraordinary commitment given that he was one of the country's richest, and that corporations typically give only a maximum 2% of net income. From this commitment, P1 billion initially established the nonprofit Toyota Motor Philippines School of Technology focused on science and technology to eradicate extreme poverty, with Dr. Shoichiro Toyoda (retired Toyota Japan chair) matching the gift with another P1 billion after CJ informed him. Despite never flaunting his faith, Dr. Ty built the Mary the Queen Catholic Church in Nanjing, China, in thanksgiving for the success of his Chinese Metrobank branches, and became one of the largest donors to the Manila Cathedral renovation. Panganiban closes with the scriptural assurance that 'our Father reserved a dwelling place in heaven for the humble and meek' and that Dr. Ty is now 'a free spirit capable of being with us on earth -- watching us and inspiring us to be the best of what we can be.'
