one_paragraph_summary: In a valedictory tribute to Justice Presbitero J. Velasco Jr., Panganiban opens with the vignette of Velasco still at his desk on the morning of August 7, 2018 -- his retirement day -- fighting to get the Supreme Court to promulgate his Precautionary Departure Order (PDO) rule, filling the gap left by Genuino v. De Lima (April 17, 2018, per J. Reyes Jr.), which had abolished the DOJ's legally unsupported hold-departure and watch-list orders. With help from JJ Perlas-Bernabe and Gesmundo, Velasco succeeded: RTCs may now issue PDOs ex parte upon prosecutor's showing of probable cause for crimes punishable by at least six years and one day of imprisonment. Over a 12-year tenure, Velasco wrote more than 1,000 full-length ponencias plus thousands of minute resolutions, leaving zero backlog for successor Justice Jose C. Reyes Jr. -- described as 'a known exemplar of the constitutional ideal of proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence.' Acting CJ Carpio, in his retirement speech, singled out MMDA v. Concerned Citizens of Manila Bay (December 18, 2008) as probably the most far-reaching -- a unanimous ruling upholding the constitutional right to a balanced ecology and directing government agencies to continuously clean the 1,800-km² bay, introducing the novel 'continuing mandamus' concept (which later spawned the April 10, 2010 Rules of Procedure for Environmental Cases). Hacienda Luisita v. PARC (July 5, 2011) ended 'eons of row' over 4,915 hectares, declaring the 30-year stock distribution plan disadvantageous to 6,296 farmer-beneficiaries and ordering physical land distribution. His political-undertone votes (Marcos burial, Mindanao martial law, Sereno ouster) drew mixed reactions, consistent with the truism that justices cannot please everyone. Velasco paid tribute to his supportive family -- wife Lorna (former congresswoman, now Torrijos mayor), son Lord Allan Jay (Marinduque congressman), daughter Tricia Nicole (party-list rep.) -- and said that retiring at a healthy 70 really means 'changing tires to prepare for a new journey,' a sentiment the author endorses with a forecast of more service from the patriarch of Marinduque.

one_paragraph_summary: Faced with reader and media pressure to comment on the QW ouster of CJ Sereno (May 11, 2018), Panganiban explains his principled silence through Reinhold Niebuhr's serenity prayer: 'Lord, grant me the courage to change the things I can, the serenity to accept those I cannot, and wisdom to know the difference.' He frames himself as a 'family elder' in the SC institution -- and when a beloved family is wracked by internal dissension, excruciating pain, and serious crisis, the right response is to grieve, listen quietly, give private counsel to those who seek it, and pray, not to sermonize, mock, or justify. He cites delicadeza as barring him from disclosing the private conversations with incumbent colleagues, and notes that Cardinal Tagle texted from Bangkok on May 11 when the ouster broke -- the author replying briefly with a plea for a 'more extensive and balanced view' later; Tagle replied, 'Thanks po and we pray po.' He also notes the QW decision is not yet final (MR pending; Senate resolution on QW still to be resolved). He pivots to a tribute for the late Edgardo J. Angara ('EJA, Ed, Edong'), recounting their first meeting in 1979 when Angara was IBP president, his founding of the Asean Law Association in 1980 (of which the author is current Philippine chapter chair), the 1982 UP Oblation miniature from Angara, Angara's facilitation of an honorary UP Phi Kappa Phi membership, the January 2013 Gopac conference in Manila, the June 30, 2012 Baler event celebrating the 113th Siege anniversary and the 200th-Year Cadiz Constitution anniversary, and their Metrobank Foundation association. Against Sen. Zubiri's characterization of Angara as 'one of the best presidents we could have had,' the author chooses to remember him simply as 'a humble, thoughtful and caring friend.'

one_paragraph_summary: With ASEAN marking its 50th anniversary, Panganiban previews the special Governing Council session of the ASEAN Law Association (ALA) that President Duterte -- as ASEAN 2017 chair -- will host and keynote at Malacañang on October 25. About 300 ALA delegates plus the diplomatic corps will attend, followed by a Manila Symphony Orchestra concert. ALA president Avelino V. Cruz and secretary general Regina Geraldez lead the organization; its Governing Council draws from four sectoral groups: magistrates, government lawyers, law professors, and private practitioners. Five of the 10 national chapters are headed by their incumbent chief justices (Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand); the Philippines chapter is headed by ret. CJ Panganiban, while Myanmar, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Lao PDR are headed by an attorney general, practitioners, and a justice respectively. Notable Philippine ALA members include CJ Sereno, SAJ Carpio, Justice Velasco Jr., Executive Secretary Medialdea, SolGen Calida, and UP President Concepcion. ALA is the only non-government law organization recognized by the ASEAN Charter (Annex 3-IV), founded in Jakarta in 1979. Its prime project -- harmonization of laws for trade, investments, banking, and arbitration -- faces the structural challenge that the AEC has no parliament, requiring harmonization to pass through each national legislature under ASEAN's consensus rule. ALA president Cruz has proposed an Institute for Harmonization of Laws. The Philippines concluded mutual recognition agreements for seven professions (engineering, nursing, architecture, land surveying, medicine, dentistry, accounting) between 2005 and 2009 under RA 8981, but law practice remains excluded; ALA is working to allow foreign lawyers to practice foreign law (not PH law) here on a reciprocal basis.

Other than fulfilling my role in the Court, I have no more earth-bound ambition. I live my life with only one consuming passion: on that inevitable day... my Lord and Master will say: Well done on your earthly sojourn.' one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban celebrates the silver jubilee of the Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting (PPCRV) on October 19, 2016, with a Holy Mass officiated by Luis Antonio Cardinal Tagle and the retirement rites of its iconic chair, Ambassador Henrietta 'Tita' T. de Villa. PPCRV was born in 1991 as the laity's response to the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines (PCP II) -- itself a momentous first in the Catholic Church's 2,000-year history: the hierarchy invited the laity to legislate and implement the reforms of Vatican II in the Philippines, with 145 lay leaders led by Tita conducting daily 12-hour sessions at the San Carlos Lay Formation Center in Makati from Jan 20 to Feb 17, 1991. Assisted by the late Jaime Cardinal Sin, the lay faithful organized PPCRV to ensure 'Champ' elections -- clean, honest, accurate, meaningful, peaceful. CJ Panganiban was chosen 'though completely unworthy' as PPCRV's national vice-chair and chief legal counsel pro bono, holding the post until joining the Supreme Court in 1995. PPCRV's initial twofold mission was voter education and poll-watching by an unpaid army of 700,000 Catholic parish volunteers. In 2010, Comelec under retired SC Justice Jose A. R. Melo added a third mission: an unofficial parallel count using one of the eight election-return copies from PCOS/VCM machines. PPCRV media director Ana de Villa Singson explained that PPCRV held 'the purest election data yielded by the machine before the data could be corrupted, intercepted, jammed while [they were] in the netherworld' of transmission to Comelec. Incredibly, PPCRV outdid Comelec in 2013: Comelec received transmissions from only 77.2% of polling precincts and proclaimed senatorial winners on that woefully insufficient count (a proclamation CJ considered illegal in his May 19, 2013 column 'Premature, imprudent and illegal'), while PPCRV -- using its eighth copy -- completed 91.8% of the vote by encoding 12,079 additional precincts. In May 2016, PPCRV's count was faster and more accurate than Comelec's, prompting losing VP candidate Bongbong Marcos to ask PPCRV to shut down due to alleged 'vote trending'; the request was politely turned down since the reason was completely wrong, but PPCRV, 'true to its nonpartisan stance, shared its transparent data with Marcos.' Tita retires confident that PPCRV will be in 'equally good hands' under former Comelec commissioner and constitution maker Rene V. Sarmiento. Cheers!

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban marks taipan John Gokongwei Jr.'s 90th birthday -- the second richest Filipino -- celebrated August 11 at the company-owned Crowne Plaza Galleria in Pasig with a 'family-only' dinner attended by 500 selected representatives of his 35,000-employee conglomerate. The after-dinner program featured anecdote-laden reminiscences by wife Elizabeth, only son Lance (who now co-manages the empire with youngest brother James), modified-lyric tunes sung by the five daughters Robina, Liza, Hope, Faith, and Marcia with baritone Lance, and dance/song numbers led by 21-year-old grandson Jason Pe. Guests received Lance Gokongwei's book 'Lessons from Dad' (with Yvette Fernandez), which CJ then gifted to his grandson Miggy P. Sandejas with the note: 'Not being a lawyer, you cannot be a chief justice. But with this book, you can someday be a tycoon!' CJ extracts three taipan-making tips: (1) Family-first -- Gokongwei is workaholic but always home for dinner; orphaned at 13, he cared for his mother, brothers, and only sister, moving them to China and sending meager remittances from his wares-trading; he hires extended family at fair pay (no more, no less) with no side businesses allowed; he travels with wife and children to museums and shows. CJ notes the same family-first motto in Henry Sy (#1), Lucio Tan (#3), George Ty (#4), and emerging dragons Tony Tan Caktiong and Edgar 'Injap' Sia. (2) Education -- Gokongwei never finished college but is a voracious reader (fiction, biographies, history, business books, three-four newspapers daily, on treadmill, in car, in bathroom, all the way to bed); after six children he enrolled in DLSU's MBA program, taking extra units and graduating in 1977 ('one of the proudest moments of his life'); he ensured all children finished college, with Lance graduating Wharton summa cum laude with double degrees. His birthday-milestone philanthropies: P200M to Ateneo on his 75th (John Gokongwei School of Management), P250M to DLSU on his 85th (Gokongwei College of Engineering), Sacred Heart School donation on his 90th honoring his only sister Lily Ngo, plus earlier gifts to Xavier School and Immaculate Conception Academy. (3) Free competition -- businesses 'weren't rent-seeking, didn't depend on connections' but on the free market, selling 'the best quality at the least price'; he believes in transparency (listing companies publicly), has no boss mentality, leads by example, hires people smarter than himself and pays them well to stay, and disciplines family-business boundaries (the Gokongwei family pays for Cebu Pacific tickets, Go Hotels stays, and Robinsons goods). Lance's closing: 'Those who actually have money don't have to flaunt it. Dad never had to prove he was rich.' CJ's 45-year observation: Gokongwei 'still lives simply, frugally and happily.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban attempts to decode President Duterte through his Bedan (San Beda College) network -- noting that despite Duterte's 25-year political career (mayor, vice mayor, congressman), his circle of friends remains limited to Davao City and San Beda, making the Bedan network the most analytically tractable window into his governance. At a recent SBLAA testimonial reception, CJ (as honorary SBLAA member since 2006) was seated within conversational distance of Duterte at the head table, alongside the only other honorary member, former President Fidel V. Ramos. The informal gathering -- rowdy guffaws, selfies discomforting his security men, monggo soup and fried banana maruya -- revealed a softer Duterte who set aside his prepared speech for heart-to-heart conversation. He generously credited Ramos (with Dureza and Dominguez) for persuading him to run despite his self-description as 'a probinsyano who did not know his way around the corridors of power' with 'no presidential ambition at all.' Self-deprecatingly calling himself 'just an average student in San Beda,' he cited his Bedan Cabinet -- Salvador Medialdea (Executive Office), Vitaliano Aguirre (Justice), Arthur Tugade (Transportation), Rodolfo Salalima (DICT), and Alfredo Lim (Pagcor) -- plus other Bedans not yet in government: Rodolfo Robles (bar topnotcher, his former professor), Sixto Brillantes (former Comelec chair), Avelino V. Cruz (bar topnotcher, former professor, SBLAA chair), and CA Justice Francisco Acosta (SBLAA president); he also praised non-Bedan close associates Carlos Dominguez (his kindergarten-to-HS valedictorian-classmate), Salvador Panelo, Perfecto Yasay Jr. (his YMCA dorm buddy), and Andrea Domingo. Duterte joked about being the first mayor, first Mindanaoan, and first president inaugurated with two first families in attendance; what brought the house down was his ventriloquist-like imitation of CA Justice Arsenio Solidum's stentorian and raspy voice -- his late 'terror-professor,' whom CJ also identifies as his own 'terror-professor' at FEU. CJ notes other Bedan SC Justices Bienvenido L. Reyes (who administered Duterte's oath) and Jose C. Mendoza, plus VP Leni Robredo's San Beda graduate studies. But the column's counterweight is Bedan critics conspicuously absent from the testimonial: Sen. Leila de Lima (Law 1985), the first legislator to lambast the 'daily executions' in the drug war, whose maiden privilege speech mourned 'The day has already come when we can no longer tell who is morally wrong among us: the nine-year-old street child sniffing rugby, or the policeman who shoots the child in the head for sniffing rugby. This is our descent as a nation into the darkness that these men have created for us' and called for a congressional inquiry on extrajudicial killings; and former Senator Rene Saguisag (now frail but acerbically penning): 'The Dutertes may reign forever. Prez, Mayor, Vice Mayor... PD No. 46 punishes giver and recipient who accepts gifts. Whose aircraft is Digong using? The allegedly simple man accepts a Safari and Expedition from Pastor Quiboloy. He does not disclose the family bank account, which, Trillanes alleges, reaches billions. No transparency.' CJ concludes: 'Like it or not, our government is now dominated by Bedans all. But I think the nation is safe in their hands as long as among them are pros and contras, supporters and dissenters, admirers and critics.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reveals a little-known chapter in Edsa 2's history: his role as mediator in a serious internal Vatican dispute over Cardinal Jaime Sin's activism in January 2001. He begins by establishing Sin's indispensable mobilizing capacity -- 300+ parishes and 70 parochial schools under his archbishopric, capable of producing nearly 200,000 warm bodies marching to a single drummer with their own provisions -- and his constant propeace, nonviolent exhortation. But despite this peaceableness, Sin's activism drew Vatican criticism, which surfaced silently during Edsa 2. On Jan 17, 2001, the day after the prosecutors' walkout from the Senate impeachment trial, Msgr. Socrates Villegas phoned Panganiban: Papal Nuncio Antonio Franco, on directive from his Vatican superiors, had asked Cardinal Sin to disperse the demonstrators at the Edsa Shrine. Sin refused -- preferring to resign if the Vatican insisted. To defuse the crisis, both the cardinal and the nuncio asked Panganiban, in his prior capacity as a member of the Pontifical Council for the Laity, to mediate. On Jan 18, Panganiban conferred privately with Franco and Msgr. Robinson Wijesinghe. The Vatican's two concerns were (1) whether Estrada's due process was being violated by demands for resignation without the prosecutors completing their case, and (2) whether church-state separation was being breached by clerical involvement in people power. Panganiban replied on the first point that due process presumes an objective tribunal -- and after the Senate's 11-10 refusal to open the second envelope, the bishops had seen enough to make their own evaluation; pulling the Church back at that point would plunge the nation into chaotic, bloody revolution for which the Vatican (a foreign state) could be blamed, a dismal defeat for peace and for the Church alike, since 'history is written by the victors.' On the second point, he explained that church-state separation in Philippine constitutional doctrine requires state neutrality among religious groups, not state hostility -- the Constitution's preamble itself invokes 'Almighty God,' presidential and vice-presidential oaths end with 'So help me God,' and Congress, the Cabinet, and the SC preface sessions with prayer. The state cannot fund a basilica for one sect or promote one sect's dogmas, but priests as citizens may hold public office. Doctrinally he conceded the Vatican's concern that the hierarchy should prioritize the faith and morals of the flock over secular activities, and prescribed that after Edsa 2 the Church should reexamine its position and strengthen its re-evangelizing and re-pastoring function. Franco said he would report to his superiors. Panganiban was never told what was reported, but at the Jan 20 oath-taking at the Edsa Shrine, Franco was in the front row and whispered upon seeing him: 'We have won!' He closes by noting that by Sin's 2003 retirement, the Archdiocese of Manila had been reduced to about a fourth of its original size, with five new dioceses carved out (Caloocan, Cubao, Novaliches, Parañaque, Pasig), and the low-profile conservative Gaudencio Cardinal Rosales installed in Sin's place.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens his Jan 3, 2016 column with a self-effacing tribute to the late Letty Jimenez-Magsanoc, Inquirer editor-in-chief -- 'fearless, intuitive and spiritual,' and refusing any attention to herself, preferring to ascribe her success to her people and readers. Picking up the second of two pre-holiday columns, he then surveys civilizational change through personal autobiography. Readers can access him via print bought from newsboys (as he once was, racing competitors in Sampaloc and shouting 'Manila Times, Chronicle, Herald' -- the Inquirer was not yet born -- along España Street, peddling leftover copies to jeepney passengers stopped at red lights), or via digital edition on tablets and smartphones, or via Inquirer.net, or via social media. Newspapers retain value beyond breaking news for in-depth opinions and features. Digital cameras killed Kodak; smartphone apps are now killing cameras and will soon replace movie houses, TV, passports, credit cards, keys, even cash. Land lines have been overtaken by mobile; long-distance has been obliterated by Magic Jack, Viber, and Skype; SMS is giving way to iMessaging. In medicine and science, he testifies personally: 2008 cataract laser surgery restored his 20/20 vision (he still wears eyeglasses occasionally because his wife thinks it more becoming a retired chief justice); prostate biopsy and kidney/gall stone surgery have become minimally invasive; IVF enables barren couples to enjoy parenthood; artificial limbs allow the handicapped to walk; biotechnological breakthroughs presage lab-grown body parts. The Paris Agreement is ambitious but a huge milestone, uniting heretofore ideological incompatibles into a single voice to hold the rise of earth's temperature to 1.5°C by 2100. The Hubble telescope reveals our sun as just one grain of sand on the kilometric beaches of the universe; European astroscientists recently piggybacked the Rosetta spacecraft on a comet to investigate how the universe was born. On globalization, the WTO ushered in the era of liberalization, privatization, and deregulation two decades ago -- but many Filipinos still pine for 'Filipino First.' Whether we like it or not, we have to face free trade and open competition; isolationism has no more place. Asean formally integrated three days ago. China embraced capitalism while keeping its communist political system; only North Korea has refused globalization, plunging its people to abject poverty opposite South Korea's prosperity. Engineering, accounting, medicine, and nursing have already accepted reciprocal globalization; it is time for lawyers to allow foreign counterparts to practice here, provided Philippine lawyers are reciprocally allowed to practice abroad. The world is changing fast and so must we, lest we be left behind in ignorance, regression, and destitution. Many businessmen and professionals have proven Filipinos can hold their own against the best of the world. The Filipino can! He closes circularly: 'In facing the new year, let's be like Letty: fearless, intuitive and spiritual.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban marks the Oct 2, 2015 ceremonial contract-signing and groundbreaking for the new SC complex at Fort Bonifacio, Taguig. 'Finally and at last,' the highest court of the land will own its home -- since its founding 114 years ago on June 11, 1901, the SC has been 'squatting' on UP's land and buildings on Padre Faura, Manila. Although actual construction will be undertaken and hopefully finished during the term of his successor, P-Noy -- with Senate President Drilon and Speaker Belmonte -- will be remembered in history for providing the resources. Beaming with noticeable pride, P-Noy graced the ceremony; all incumbent justices were present except Carpio (abroad on official mission) and Brion (indisposed). The three appellate courts were represented by their presiding justices -- Andres Reyes Jr. (CA), Amparo Cabotaje-Tang (SBN), Roman Del Rosario (CTA) -- and the trial courts by Court Administrator Jose Midas Marquez. But only the three lady members -- CJ Sereno, J De Castro, J Perlas-Bernabe -- delivered speeches on behalf of the Court, showing that 'though outnumbered, they are never outgunned.' Even the Court's signatory in the contract-signing was a lady -- clerk of court Felipa B. Anama. 'Women Power at work!' The male justices just sat on the stage silently witnessing the proceedings, and so did CJ. De Castro delivered the welcome remarks; Bernabe detailed the architectural plan and engineering design of the 'modern, green and disaster-resilient' complex. Taking advantage of his captive audience, P-Noy bragged that during his term the judiciary's budget more than doubled from P12.66B (2010, when he took office) to P25.89B (2016, when he will leave). Speaking in his characteristic mixture of English and Filipino, he did not mince words: 'What our bosses expect from us public servants is simple: Instead of just tiis (being patient), let's promote genuine justice. That's why I will take this opportunity to raise some issues with you.' Some serious issues he raised -- zeroing on delays and on the constitutional command that all cases or matters filed must be decided or resolved within 24 months for the SC, 12 months for all lower collegiate courts, and 3 months for all other lower courts. He was particularly distressed at the unusually long litigations involving infrastructure projects, pointing to trial courts' refusal to issue writs of possession even after the government had filed expropriation proceedings -- resulting in delays in the construction of many tollways, the NAIA expressway in particular. 'The complex that will be built will be modern and of high quality ... but for me the most important part of it is the people who will work there ... It's still up to you if you will uphold what is right and just,' he emphasized -- and attacked some decisions as 'judicial legislation.' In her speech preceding the President's, CJ Sereno highlighted five 'innovative' projects to address delays: (1) the e-Subpoena system using email to compel policemen to attend hearings, especially in drug-related cases, citing the cooperation of Secretary De Lima and former interior secretary Mar Roxas; (2) the Enterprise Information System using technology and automation to make processes faster, more efficient, transparent, and predictable; (3) the decongestion project called Hustisyeah, which reduced dockets in 119 target courts by 31.44% as of Oct 1; (4) the Assisting Court System with 47.32% docket reduction in target courts in just five months; (5) the establishment of 48 Family Courts apart from designated RTC family courts. CJ thought these five are really parts of the more extensive 'Four Pillars of Judicial Reform' the SC is undertaking -- not yet known by the public, but quickly: (1) instituting integrity, public trust, and credibility; (2) ensuring predictability, rationality, speed, and responsiveness of judicial actions; (3) improving systems infrastructure; (4) efficient and effective human resources -- promising a future column on them. Only 55, CJ Sereno has 15 more years to steer the judiciary and finish the SC complex -- she will have more time than the next two presidents to permanently reform our judicial system.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers a first-week review of the government's Edsa traffic-decongestion effort: 'moderate at best and spotty at worst,' but good enough for week one -- despite the nightmarish 'carmageddon' Tuesday night due to a massive downpour, and its scary near-repetition Thursday saved this time by the presence of drenched cops and traffic enforcers. The authorities must do better in coming weeks. From Monday, Sept 7, the smartly-uniformed, motorcycle-riding and sufficiently-armed cops fielded by the PNP-HPG, under direct Palace supervision, instilled discipline among drivers and pedestrians, arrested the recalcitrant, and shooed away colorums and provincial buses. The PNP-HPG also cleared the thoroughfare of peddlers and illegally-parked vehicles, ordered walkers to use marked pedestrian lanes, directed buses to stay inside the yellow lanes, and allowed them no more than 30 seconds to load and unload passengers. And 'voila!' -- several choke points were decongested and traffic flowed, even if intermittently. Quite pleased were motorists from the northern end of Edsa going south to Makati: with the clearing of hawkers and towing of illegally-parked vehicles at Balintawak, North Ave, Quezon Ave, and Cubao, coupled with strict enforcement, southbound traffic considerably eased. However, going northward -- especially from Makati to Guadalupe, Shaw Boulevard, Ortigas Avenue, and Cubao intersections -- traffic was still quite heavy and vehicles were still crawling. The downpours on Tuesday and Thursday simply overwhelmed the antique drainage system. These immediate solutions, including the PNP-HPG deployment, were suggested by the Traffic, Transportation and Infrastructure Committee of the MAP, chaired by the energetic Eddie Yap. Two months ago MAP submitted to P-Noy a 'holistic approach' arguing 'the traffic problems besetting our metropolis are behavioral and structural,' to be addressed through 'the three most basic elements, the three Es, of effective traffic management: traffic engineering, education of all stakeholders, and enforcement of traffic rules.' After reading the study, CJ waited to find out what Malacañang would do -- and sure enough, starting last Monday, many of the MAP proposals were implemented and followed through the whole week. Significantly, MAP strongly suggested the appointment of a 'traffic czar' to take full charge and assume responsibility for success or failure: 'Elementary it is in the science of management that someone must always be responsible for the success or failure of any undertaking.' Despite the lack of an official appointment, Cabinet Secretary Rene Almendras is effectively performing the role per Yap: 'Rene talks like a czar, acts like a czar and is a czar except in name' -- though one broadsheet (not the Inquirer) has bannered Almendras' supposedly formal appointment as traffic supremo. With or without a czar, it is now time to implement other MAP recommendations: include all intersecting avenues (Buendia, Shaw, Ortigas, D. Tuazon) and radial roads (C5, Katipunan, Roxas); organize a bus dispatch system; 'channelize' Edsa with more bus-lane delineators; flood-proof low street levels using prefabricated quick-to-assemble steel perforated matting on steel supports similar to those used by the US during WW2 as an emergency measure while awaiting permanent concrete upgrading; install a high-vehicle-occupancy lane for vehicles with at least three passengers; encourage carpools and bus shuttles. Longer-term MAP proposals include new Pasig River bridges, resolving MRT/LRT issues, high-capacity subway systems, educating drivers and pedestrians on traffic rules and road courtesy, and effective flood control. In the past, the government had the wrong focus -- instead of optimizing road usage, it tried to curtail demand by reducing work days, suspending classes, and instituting truck bans, exacting a heavy toll on the economy and the patience of the riding public. As ECOP president Eduardo Lacson lamented, 'The proposal for a four-day workweek is a solution begging for a problem ... It poses risks of accident, low performance, off-spec products due to worker fatigue born of long work hours.' Indeed, we as a people should think more horizontally and avoid what former PM Cesar Virata calls 'short-termism' -- the 'excessive focus on short-term goals at the expense of long-term objectives.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes a tribute to Dr. Raul C. Pangalangan, newly elected judge of the International Criminal Court, opening with his Friday cocktails-reception hosted in Pangalangan's honor -- with Chief Justice Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno and DFA Secretary Albert F. Del Rosario as joint guest speakers, representing the judiciary and the diplomatic corps respectively, both exalted by Pangalangan's elevation. Rare and few are lawyers elevated to eminent international judicial tribunals, CJ notes, because membership is based on both personal qualities and the international political clout of the nominating state. Pangalangan was not even a public official at the time -- he was the publisher of the Inquirer and a professorial lecturer and former dean of the UP College of Law (and other universities here and abroad). The ICC requires nominees to possess the qualifications required in their states for the highest judicial offices, plus expertise in criminal law or international law, especially international humanitarian law and IHRL; the ICC selection panel found Pangalangan eminently qualified. The problem was that the Philippines had exhausted its political quid pro quo clout -- but Secretary Del Rosario led PH diplomats in using Filipino ingenuity, hard work, and battle-tested person-to-person skills to make up for the lack of political and financial resources. Special credit goes to Ambassadors Jaime Victor Ledda (Netherlands), Victoria Bataclan (Belgium), Lourdes Yparraguirre (UN permrep), and Irene Susan Natividad (UN deputy permrep). The result was Pangalangan's stunning victory on June 24, 2015, with assumption to office July 13, 2015 through March 10, 2021. CJ then explains the ICC: organized when 120 member-states signed the Rome Statute on July 17, 1998 (effective July 1, 2002); currently 123 members. The Philippines signed on December 28, 2000 and the Senate ratified on April 23, 2011 by a 17-1 vote (Enrile cast the only negative). Unlike national courts, the ICC disregards heads-of-state immunity, recognizes no prescription of crimes and no amnesty, insists on command and individual responsibility, and serves as court of last resort when national systems are unwilling or unable to prosecute genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and aggression. On other Filipino international jurists: the only Filipino elected to the ICJ was Cesar Bengzon, in November 1966, three months after his retirement as chief justice -- CJ remembers him fondly because Bengzon signed his 1961 bar membership certificate; Asia is assigned only three ICJ memberships, two always taken by China and Japan, the third allocated to the Middle East. On December 13, 1995, SC Justice Florentino P. Feliciano was elected to the nine-member WTO Appellate Tribunal (and later served as chair). Retired Justice Flerida Ruth P. Romero was the first woman and only Filipino named to the ILO Administrative Tribunal. Senator Miriam Defensor-Santiago was elected an ICC judge a few years ago but was overtaken by ill health before she could discharge her duties and had to resign.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes a triple-tribute column in three sections: boxing (Manny), Comelec (Andy and Bing), and Customs (Bert). FULL DISCLOSURE: CJP is not a diehard boxing fan -- he sees boxing as brutal combat reminiscent of the gladiators who duelled to death for the ghoulish entertainment of the Romans; with due respect to Manny Pacquiao's grandiose claim that he boxes 'for the Filipino,' the grim reality in any professional boxing bout is 'money,' as Floyd Mayweather Jr. unabashedly proclaims. CJP expected at least that the promoters and combatants would be fair to fans who paid handsomely (ringside or pay-per-view) and to those who bet hard-earned dollars and pesos. Complete disclosure should be the unbroken rule. Pacquiao and his handlers were unfair for not revealing his injured shoulder on time -- no wonder he faces Nevada sanctions and suits from irate fans and bettors. Fortunately for him, a PH suit may not prosper because gambling is banned here except for those specifically allowed by law (horse racing on specific days in specific tracks, Pagcor outlets including Solaire and City of Dreams, sweepstakes lotteries). Pacquiao's non-disclosure is undisputed; he answered 'No' to the box in the official questionnaire asking about any 'injury to [his] shoulders, elbows or hands.' Speculation: disclosure may have meant postponement or cancellation, meaning no or reduced money. CJP believes Pacquiao should have accepted his defeat graciously -- that would have been most honorable. True, Mayweather just danced his way to victory, a disgusting strategy but allowed by Nevada rules; Pacquiao accepted the rules along with the grand rewards Nevada secures for boxing, gambling, howling, and hype. It is said that no Filipino loses an election -- either he wins or is cheated; must it be the same in boxing? Banter aside, fairness, honor, and transparency should define every public endeavor, including boxing. COMELEC APPOINTEES: Kudos to Dean Andres D. Bautista, new Comelec chair. At only 51, Andy brings freshness, vigor, probity, and integrity to the poll body a year before the May 2016 presidential election. He has pedigreed credentials worthy even of an SC seat -- class valedictorian of Ateneo Law, bar topnotcher, Harvard LLM, FEU law dean, Philippine Judicial Academy lecturer, Philippine Association of Law Schools chair, and among the 10 original holders of the 'Chief Justice Panganiban Professorial Chairs on Liberty and Prosperity.' He practiced law in PH and abroad and, while still a law student, clerked for then-CJ Marcelo B. Fernan. Though his expertise is constitutional and commercial law, he studied election law as a PPCRV trustee. His vast managerial experience -- chief executive of several large firms, PCGG chair -- will help him steer the giant Comelec bureaucracy. The President could not have chosen a better Comelec chief. Congratulations also to new Comelec Commissioner Rowena V. Guanzon. Strong-willed and fiercely independent, Bing has a formidable background: litigation lawyer with a string of landmark victories, book writer, law professor, UP Law dean's lister, Harvard MPA, well-regarded in the legal community (including the SC) for her gender-equality advocacy. Armed with practical experience in rough-and-tumble politics as former Cadiz City mayor, she mirrors the feistiness, bravado, and wit of former Comelec commissioner Heidi Yorac. CJP expects her to team up well with Chairman Andy to assure free, honest, credible 2016 elections. CUSTOMS BOSS: CJP also welcomes the appointment of Customs Commissioner Alberto D. Lina. He has known Bert for over 40 years since he was a lowly clerk at the auditing firm of L.C. Diaz and Associates, and tracked his rise as an innovative, driven, self-made entrepreneur. CJP has no doubt Lina's acceptance was motivated solely by his desire to serve the country. He rejects unverified media reports that Lina took the job to promote the financial interest of his multibillion-peso logistics business -- if all he wanted were a few more billion pesos, he could just list his business on the PSE and presto, the market value of his wealth would multiply several times. His willingness to divest from companies doing business with BoC speaks well of his patriotism. Let's give him a chance to prove his worth and show how his grit, integrity, and skill can transform the most graft-prone office in our government.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the fourth installment of his biographical-naming series, triggered by Mohagher Iqbal -- chief peace negotiator of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front -- using an alias or nom de guerre that has disrupted the peace process unnecessarily in CJP's humble view. Despite being pressed to reveal his real name, Iqbal has remained tightlipped, claiming pseudonyms are normal for revolutionaries; in a GMA News TV 'Balitanghali' interview he said: 'Kahit na si Marcelo del Pilar siyam po ang pangalan, at maging ang tatay ni Presidente na si Ninoy Aquino, in his passport his name was Marcial Bonifacio. So, normal po yan.' Under Republic Act No. 6085, which regulates alias use, no person shall use any name different from (1) the one registered at birth in the local civil registry, (2) baptized for the first time, (3) for an alien -- registered in the bureau of immigration upon entry, or (4) such substitute name as may have been authorized by a competent court -- with exceptions for literary, cinema, TV, radio or other entertainment purposes and in athletic events (Heart Evangelista; Pacman; Pancho Villa). The Civil Code allows a married woman three naming options: (1) maiden first name and surname plus husband's surname, (2) maiden first name plus husband's surname, or (3) husband's full name prefixed with 'Mrs.' -- CJP applies this to his wife: (1) Elenita Carpio Panganiban, (2) Elenita Panganiban, or (3) Mrs. Artemio V. Panganiban. The Civil Code also permits pen names or stage names in good faith without injury to third persons, making 'Doveglion' (Jose Garcia Villa) and 'Quijano de Manila' (Nick Joaquin) perfectly legal. Filipino nicknames -- not expressly allowed by RA 6085 or the Civil Code -- have acquired legal acquiescence: P-Noy, GMA, Erap, FVR, Cory, FM are used without nitpicking. Special laws expressly bar aliases: BSP Circular 251 forbids 'Jose Pidal' or 'Jose Velarde' in bank accounts; fictitious names are not authorized on passports, driver's licenses, and other government-issued IDs precisely because they identify holders. RA 6085 penalizes illegal aliases with imprisonment from 1 to 5 years and a fine of P5,000 to P10,000. Despite these penalties, revolutionaries still use noms de guerre to confuse enemies, avoid capture, and spare their families inconvenience and possible ridicule. Spies and deep-penetration agents like the legendary James Bond employ many names and passports -- stealth and subterfuge are essential to their work -- but this does not make the practice legal; rebels face graver risks of prosecution for rebellion, sedition or murder, so alias prosecution is the least of their worries. Meanwhile, Iqbal and his associates are in no danger of arrest because they have been issued 'safe conduct' passes; should the peace process collapse, the passes would expire; should it succeed, they could be hailed as heroes. Despite the illegal use of a nom de guerre, Iqbal's acts cannot be deemed invalid or illegal -- they were done with the authority of the MILF, whose leadership has expressly affirmed his authority and the binding effect of his acts. Moreover, the government peace panel headed by Miriam Coronel Ferrer (including Sec Teresita Deles) admitted knowledge of Iqbal's nom de guerre and his real name. Once the Bangsamoro Basic Law is approved, it would bind the Republic regardless of the validity of the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro he signed -- assuming it passes judicial scrutiny, the BBL would become part of the law of the land. What's in a name? To many of us, it is our most cherished treasure because it bears our honor and worth as distinct human beings -- especially for members of the judiciary. SC justices always sign their decisions with their complete names including middle initials, as in Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno or Hilario G. Davide Jr. One way of incurring their ire is to misspell their names or to muddle their middle initials.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes an Easter Sunday wellness/lifestyle/longevity reflection -- Easter commemorates the resurrection of Christ and the fulfillment of His promise to rise on the third day, celebrating His gift of eternal and earthly life; for now, however, CJP writes of earthly life. The youngest in a brood of four who are all still alive, he reached his 78th birthday last December; his eldest sibling, now 87, lives in retirement with her husband in Vancouver. He and his siblings are luckier than their parents -- his father died at 54 and his mother at 61 -- and the entire generation can expect to live 20 years longer than the previous one (by which measure CJP would be only 58); per Time magazine (March 2, 2015), American babies born today could live 142 years thanks to science, technology, medicine, and improved lifestyles. He has had brushes with ill health: at 5 during the Japanese occupation he nearly died of dysentery; at 21 while chairing a National Union of Students of the Philippines seminar in Naga City, his ruptured appendix was misdiagnosed as ordinary stomachache in a small clinic in Tabaco, Albay -- given castor oil (!) and injected with morphine which knocked him out for 24 hours -- and two weeks later, the ruptured appendix ached again, was properly diagnosed, and excised surgically by Dr. Ricardo Alfonso. In 1983, Dr. Augusto Litonjua told him 'I am sorry to say you have diabetes. This is incurable but can be controlled by diet, exercise and a little medicine.' He followed the prescription to the letter -- and voila! -- in 1995, prior to his SC entry, Dr. Litonjua formally certified his blood sugar had normalized; his diabetes was gone. He continues to see Litonjua every three months for regular consultation especially on endocrinal secretions. In 1996, Dr. Dante Morales, after three tests (ECG, treadmill, 2D Echo) said he had arrhythmia and may need heart bypass surgery; before the OR, Morales asked Dr. Dy Bun Yok to do an angiogram, with Dr. Jorge Garcia (famous heart surgeon) ready to operate if the angiogram affirmed the three earlier tests. To his complete relief, the final test showed no blocked coronary arteries -- no surgery needed; Dr. Garcia kidded afterwards: 'When you die, it will not be because of a heart problem.' Alleluia! In 2008, while playing golf with Dr. Jack Arroyo, even in bright sunlight he could not see his driven ball 200 yards away on the turf; at the American Eye Center he was advised to undergo cataract surgery. 'I do cataracts, but Dr. Cesar Espiritu is the best cataract surgeon,' Dr. Arroyo humbly said; at his recommendation, Dr. Espiritu replaced his clouded crystalline lenses with artificial implants. Since then his vision has been 20/20 -- if he still sports eyeglasses, it is because his dear wife believes it more becoming for a retired chief justice. He has undergone other medical procedures and conditions: three surgeries for recurrent hemorrhoids in 1958, 1977, and 2005; a biopsy of his prostate by Dr. Nikko Magsanoc which turned out negative; a whole-body MRI in 2012 which showed gallstones and benign liver and kidney cysts; various dental problems; slowed memory retrieval; insomnia; bladder spasms; vertigo; elevated SGPT/SGOT; bone spurs; pulled muscles; stem cell therapy; carpal tunnel syndrome. He is grateful for these medical interventions. Thank God, even in his senior years he can eat almost anything in moderate quantities -- plays golf twice a week and tennis twice a week, exercises in the gym thrice a week, indulges occasionally in ballroom dancing, does not smoke, gamble, or drink anything heavier than a glass of red wine. Retired from the judiciary eight years ago but not from work, his every day is full: board and committee meetings of a dozen publicly listed companies, heading or advising five major foundations and several educational/civic/religious/charitable groups. He enjoys writing this column (encoding it on his own computer to polish typing and keep up with current events), reads printed and digital Inquirer and other publications/books, surfs the Internet, tracks stock markets, watches TV news, science programs (Discovery Science, History Channel), and sports. He maintains a personal website but no social-media account; he likes his new iPhone 6 plus over the iPad and old Nokia. He has an active social life -- diplomatic receptions, concerts, art exhibits, birthdays, weddings, charities -- and prays for the eternal joy and peace of the deceased during wakes. He thanks God for giving him more years than his parents, is grateful to his family and friends who forgive his lapses, laugh at his jokes, and make him feel younger than his age, and is especially thankful to his doctors and priest-counselors. He looks forward to 'more years in my life and more life in my years.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reflects on Pope Francis's six-stop PH visit -- (1) officialdom led by PNoy in Malacañang (where, as a retired chief justice, CJ was invited), (2) priests at Manila Cathedral, (3) families at Mall of Asia, (4) typhoon survivors in Leyte, (5) youth at UST today, and (6) ordinary folks at Luneta -- before the Pope leaves for Rome tomorrow. The Pope is not meeting with tycoons, industrialists, and bankers. Is he anti-rich? Yes, but only against the greedy and the self-centered -- not against the rich who regard themselves as mere stewards of their wealth for the benefit of all, especially 'the naked, the imprisoned, the hungry and the homeless.' In Francis's own words, 'The Gospel does not condemn the wealthy, but the idolatry of wealth, the idolatry that makes people indifferent to the call of the poor.' And CJ adds: our Lord Jesus had rich disciples too, like Joseph of Arimathea who retrieved and buried His body after His crucifixion. In CJ's humble view, to be pro-poor it is not necessary to be anti-rich; in fact, an effective pro-poor program should include and inspire the rich to share their resources -- not by easy doles of crumbs that merely perpetuate the poor's dependence, but by empowering the poor to conquer poverty through education and entrepreneurship. This is precisely what the Jollibee Group Foundation has been doing through two flagship projects: Busog, Lusog, Talino (BLT) and the Farmers Entrepreneurship Program (FEP). During JGF's 10th-anniversary celebration days ago, its president Grace Tan Caktiong noted that although the state provides free elementary and high school education, she was 'horrified to learn' that despite this, the dropout rate was alarming -- and the 'most common and shocking reason' was HUNGER. To reduce dropout drastically, JGF started in 2007 its BLT program of feeding the poorest-of-the-poor pupils every school day. As of end-2014, BLT has reached over 1,000 schools nationwide and fed almost 200,000 pupils -- now the largest private-sector-led systematic school-feeding program in the country, with community participation mobilized by getting parents, teachers, and village elders to prepare and serve the free nutritious meals. To supply its 2,000+ fast-food outlets (Jollibee, Chow King, Mang Inasal, Greenwich, Red Ribbon, Burger King) with high-quality vegetables, potatoes, and calamansi, JFC noticed that small farmers had difficulty producing them. So in 2008, JGF launched FEP -- opening free training centers, providing access to finance, and linking farmers to institutional markets. Today 15 big institutions including JFC source their vegetable requirements directly from FEP-assisted small farmers, guaranteeing year-round profitability; over 900 farmers from 15 provinces have benefited by end-2014. Ms. Tan Caktiong explained that early on, she and her husband Tony (chair of both JFC and JGF) had given millions to charity without knowing exactly how the money was spent -- so they set up JGF to ensure funds are disbursed wisely and accounted for accurately. She resigned from involvement in the business conglomerate to concentrate as JGF president; planning originally to stay only three years, she has been so overwhelmed by the passion to help the poor that she devotes full time, without pay, to alleviating poverty. Even her husband Tony has given up his CEO position to devote more time to philanthropy and overall policymaking. They remind CJ of Bill and Melinda Gates, the world's richest couple, who quit their executive jobs in Microsoft Corp. to focus full-time on multibillion-dollar charity work for the world's poor. The Tan Caktiongs -- who control the giant JFC, ranked 10th-largest in market capitalization among the world's fast-food chains -- may not be as wealthy as the Gateses, but they are driven by the same passion and patience to help the poor. They are exemplars of Pope Francis' call for sharing time, talent and treasure with the least, last and lost. Incidentally, both JGF projects were recognized during the Asian Corporate Social Responsibility Awards Night -- BLT won for education and FEP for poverty alleviation, besting 109 entries from 15 Asian countries; JGF is the first organization to win two awards in the same year. A third project, FoodAID, was established by JGF immediately after Supertyphoon Yolanda hit the country in 2013, setting up mobile kitchens in severely affected communities and providing meals for one month to more than 162,000 survivors as well as to volunteers of various relief organizations.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers a year-in-review of his Christmas-season defining events. For the popular and the show biz, the defining event of the last Christmas season may have been the 'royal wedding' of DongYan -- Dingdong Dantes and Marian Rivera -- at the Immaculate Conception Cathedral in Cubao, Quezon City on December 30, with PNoy as 'witness of honor.' The star-studded nuptial was officiated by 15 men of the cloth (led by Cubao Bishop Honesto Ongtioco with a quotable homily by Bishop Ted Bacani), attended by 40 principal sponsors, 25 secondary sponsors, 18 groomsmen, 18 bridesmaids, 8 bridal showers, 2 marriage proposals and 500 security personnel, and sidelighted by the 'reconciliation' of Kris and Ai Ai. Eight was obviously the couple's favorite number -- evidenced by their 8-second kiss, exact ceremony time (2:38 PM) at the 800-seat Cubao Cathedral, and exact reception time (6:08 PM) at the 18,000-seat Mall of Asia Arena. Lesser mortals had their own momentous season events, perhaps not as grand and as eye-popping but momentous nonetheless. As for CJ, his season events were topped by a quiet dinner for 16 held in honor of Dr. Shoichiro Toyoda, the 89-year-old honorary chair of Toyota Motors of Japan, hosted by Dr. George S.K. Ty, group chair of the Metrobank conglomerate. What made the dinner ultra-significant was not the menu or the VIP attendees, but Dr. Ty's P1-billion donation to the Toyota School of Technology in Sta. Rosa, Laguna. Toyota Philippines is the only Toyota affiliate in the world in which the giant Japanese auto maker holds a minority interest (35 percent) while the local partner (Metrobank group) owns 51 percent (Mitsui and Co. holds the remaining 14 percent); elsewhere Toyota Japan always owns and controls the majority. Toyota has dominated the Philippine motoring industry consistently for all 27 years of partnership with Metrobank -- in no other country has the Japanese automotive giant topped the market continuously for such a long period. Dr. Ty said that, in gratitude, he thought of establishing the TST in honor of Dr. Toyoda, a direct descendant of Toyota founder Sakichi Toyoda. CJ replied that, in so doing, he was really performing a great service to our people because science and technology are essential to propel our country to sustainable prosperity; besides, though established in honor of the Toyota leader, the school will remain in the Philippines. The second major season event was the formal inauguration of the 23 new carillon bells donated by Alberto and Sylvia Lina to the Manila Cathedral. Prior to its recent refitting and renovation, the cathedral received 14 carillon bells from the Linas in 2011; but after CJ (as president of the Manila Cathedral Foundation) requested Bert to add nine more bells, Bert volunteered to order a complete new set of 23 bells from the Netherlands. Explained Bert: 'If I ordered nine new bells, they may not be in tune with the 14 existing. So, I will give a complete set of 23 new ones. After all, to me, bells are the voice of God. When they ring, they call our faithful to worship in His church.' What to do with the 'old' set of 14? 'Well,' Bert said, smiling, 'I can donate them to another church, perhaps in a Yolanda-stricken diocese.' Significant, too, were three books launched during the season of grace. (1) The 'Autobiography' of GMA Network chair and CEO Felipe G. Gozon, written in simple, easy-to-read English, launched at the author's 75th birthday. CJ met Henry, as friends fondly call him, more than three decades ago when both were actively practicing law; fully convinced of his 'proven competence, integrity, probity and independence,' CJ asked him several times in the late 1990s to consider joining SC, but he humbly declined, citing a commitment to develop TV-radio as the prime embodiment of the freedom of expression to transform society. CJ's earlier tribute, quoted on book pages 237-238, says in part: 'It is difficult to define Henry in one word, but I think Gutsy with a capital G as in Gozon comes closest.' (2) 'Stirred, Not Shaken' by Eduardo H. Yap -- CJ's foreword characterizes Eddie's '6Gs': gift of gab (both written and verbal), gift of giving (of himself and his possessions to favorite charities), and gift of genius (manifested in his persona and writings). (3) 'Echoes of God's Love' by Fr. Roberto B. Manansala -- a collection of concise, life-touching, unforgettable homilies for one whole liturgical year (Cycle B). CJ has run out of space for other notable events -- the lovely Christmas musicale at the home of Ave and Helen Cruz, the solemn affiliation of Titoy Pardo to the De La Salle Brotherhood, the 50th wedding anniversary of Louie and Triccie Sison, the 90th birthday of national artist F. Sionil Jose, etc. But let's not ever forget, the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ is the real reason for the joyous season.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains the CBCP invited him to speak during the Asian Conference on the Family -- but CJ thought the audience would be better off hearing the real-life experience of the young like grandson Miguel P. Sandejas. Since Christmas is a season for the family, CJ shares Miguel's talk, slightly shortened to fit the space. Miguel begins: "The word family instantly spurs memories of faces in my head, as I am sure it does yours. Magnificent and kind faces. It spurs memories of feelings so strong that I can almost relive them right now, from where I stand. Because where I stand is where they put me. And I am here today because of them and I will forever be grateful for that." The first memory: "When I was very young, I remember sitting on the lap of Papa pretending to play driver as we entered the gate of my parents love nest in Alabang. They were newly married back then. I remember sitting on his lap and laughing as we honked the horn. The memories of my father abruptly stop there. This is because we lost Papa to a car accident when I was just two years old. From there, my life was populated by one of the most plaguing (and sometimes useless) questions in the English language -- I started to ask: What if? What if I grew up with him by my side, would life be different? What if he were there during fathers day celebrations at school? What if he were there to see me graduate from the University of the Philippines (also his alma mater)? This is where the question what if becomes useless. There is never an answer. It is like talking to a closed door, shouting at it, aimlessly hoping for it to open." The second memory is an eagle-eye view of family -- how, unseemingly, God answered Miguel's questions; how God carried Mom and Miguel through all of these years. Of course He would never abandon us. He would never abandon any of us. Had Papa been around, life would have been different. Mom always said that when God closes doors, He opens new windows. While Miguel was shouting what-if at closed doors, blessings were pouring through the windows God opened for us -- these blessings flooded through and rushed through every nook and cranny they could find, in the form of family. Papa's absence at father's day was filled by Tito Manu, Tito Paco, and Lolo Lito. Miguel's graduation day was celebrated with many people who loved him. Family filled in the empty spaces left by loss -- uplifted us and kept us going even when we thought we could not; rushed to Mom's side when she stood there broken by the death of her husband -- lolos and lolas, aunts and uncles both on the Sandejas and Panganiban sides -- they helped her hold on to the pieces of her broken heart. Mom is Miguel's stronghold -- the strongest root keeping him grounded to what is good and rational. He admires her for keeping herself together through loss, for keeping herself together for him and raising him the way she did. In Miguel's opinion, no one should ever be put through the pain of love and loss; however, the strength of a mother will forever be greater than any superpower anyone can ever have. Mom asked her own what-ifs at that time -- and God answered them too. He gave her Alex, Miguel's stepfather, who helped her put the pieces of her heart back together -- he offered his life and forever support to her in marriage; how many people are lucky enough to find true love twice in their life? He also gave her a second son, Miguel's brother Rafa, who is a Godsend as well. Our family is complete again, even better and stronger than it used to be. The last thing Miguel shares is what he has taken away: in the absence of a father, he realized the presence of many other prominent figures. God gave him parents that raised him to the best of their abilities -- role models in their own trials and triumphs. God gave him three sets of grandparents that serve as models of perfect patriarchs and matriarchs -- pillars of love, support and family. God gave him aunts and uncles to be the older brothers and sisters he never had -- sources of strength and inspiration at any given time. One day Miguel hopes He will give him children with whom to share everything he has learned. There will always be what-ifs. But suddenly, the answers do not seem so important anymore. God already answered them through Miguel's family. There are many times in our lives that we ask why God takes away. God was not selfish when He took Papa to Heaven; Miguel believes that He handpicked Papa from His earthly garden because He needed him a bit earlier than planned. He was taught to accept this unconditionally. He realizes now that life always goes on, even after death. God will always be there -- in the form of Family, in the form of Love, a love that is pure, honest and unfaltering. Family is the ultimate proof that God loves us, and in the end, proof that everything will be okay.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with a recurring reader question: why are Filipino lawyers so fond of citing the American Supreme Court and American jurists to support their cases and causes? His short answer: because PH political, constitutional, international, corporate, and tax laws are American in origin. US precedents in these subjects are cited as authority for local litigations involving the same facts and issues as American counterpart cases. Jurisprudence is authoritarian in the sense that sometimes logic is not enough to understand and interpret a legal provision -- it should be buttressed by accepted usages and precedents from the foreign jurisdiction where the legal provision was sourced. In the not-so-distant past, the PH SC also relied heavily on Spanish decisions and authorities like Manresa and Sanchez Roman in interpreting civil laws (family affairs, marriage, property relations, inheritance, basic commerce) because the Civil Code and the old Code of Commerce were sourced from Spain. This same question of why PH lawyers lean heavily on American authorities was asked when CJP and some SC colleagues visited the Supreme Court of Canada in Ottawa. The Chief Justice of Canada, the Right Honorable Beverley McLachlin, hosted lunch in the inner sanctum of the Canadian Court (known simply as the 'Judges' Dining Room') on Tuesday, June 18, 2002. After breaking bread, they were ushered to an internal conference room for a lively discussion. To start the dialogue, Senior Justice (now retired) Claire L'Heureux-Dubé remarked: 'I notice that your decisions in the Philippines liberally quote from the US Supreme Court, especially from Justices Oliver Wendell Holmes, Hugo Black and Felix Frankfurter. However, I have yet to see one that cites our Supreme Court or our Canadian justices.' For a moment the delegation was stunned into speechlessness; but after a second or two of silence, CJP found his tongue and replied: 'I must admit that Your Honor is correct. In its over 100 years of history, our Supreme Court has not used a Canadian precedent to buttress its judgments. But may I also venture my respectful observation that I, too, have yet to read a Canadian decision citing the Philippine Supreme Court.' That exchange of banter broke the proverbial ice, leading to more in-depth discussions on the role of the judiciary in respective nations' history and development. CJP took the banter to heart. After returning to the Philippines, he penned People v. Genosa (January 15, 2004) adopting for the first time the 'battered woman syndrome' as a form of self-defense, or at least a mitigating circumstance, in a parricide prosecution committed by a wife against her husband. In that landmark case, he expressly cited a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada as authority -- and made sure a copy was sent to the justices in Ottawa. The encounter may have been a minor incident in the great history of the Canadian Court, but it was a major event of CJP's judicial career. He even remembers the menu: onion soup, gingered steak with Napa cabbage salad, vanilla ice cream with fresh fruits, and coffee/tea. It is not every day that the Canadian Supreme Court goes out of its somber ways to host and banter with jurists from a little country halfway across the globe. CJP used the opportunity to invite McLachlin to visit PH, which she did in October 2006 -- attending the Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity, which CJP convened as his valedictory as chief justice. Over 300 chief justices, jurists, and lawyers from all over the world attended, but the brilliant Canadian CJ so loved it here that she extended her stay from her original three days to one week. McLachlin is the first woman and longest-serving chief justice in Canadian history. She started her term on January 2, 2000 and will end it on September 7, 2018 when she turns 75 -- the retirement age in her country (it is 70 here). Ateneo de Manila conferred on her, during her extended stay, an honorary doctoral degree in law. Though appearing stoic and unreachable while presiding on the bench, she is cordial and friendly in informal gatherings among colleagues. She could eloquently deliver scholarly speeches just as she could gracefully pirouette on the stage; she gamely danced the swing and the boogie with CJP during the farewell party. CJP and wife Leni cherish a personal friendship with her and her low-profile husband Frank who accompanied her. At another time, CJP will relate his encounters with other foreign counterparts -- especially the Spanish, Chinese, Russian, Egyptian, and Asean judiciaries -- and will also recall an interesting conversation with then Spanish Prime Minister Jose Zapatero during a luncheon hosted in Madrid. Incidentally, the Asean chief justices, at the invitation of CJ Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno, will be in the Philippines in late February to attend the General Assembly of the Asean Law Association in Makati and Boracay (foreshadowing E95, B06, and B17). The official host is the ALA Philippines Chapter headed by Accra Law's top honcho, Avelino V. Cruz.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with the headline: the Supreme Court topped the latest SWS public satisfaction poll (conducted Sept 26-29) of major government institutions, with 32% net satisfaction rating (54% satisfied minus 22% dissatisfied), followed by the Senate 28%, House 21%, and Cabinet 18%. Although litigations are not decided via public opinion surveys, the poll is significant because the Court, as a democratic institution, must always retain long-term public trust. Especially during tough times, it is the beacon of hope and succor of our people; it cannot perform this role without such enduring trust. Truly, the work of the judiciary is sacrosanct. That is why justices of the SC are referred to as the 'gods of Padre Faura' -- they decide cases involving the life, liberty, honor and property of our people. The Constitution recognizes this unique role by imposing strict requirements for entry to the judiciary. While the Charter requires only citizenship, age, residence, suffrage, and 'read-and-write' qualifications for the top officials of the executive and legislative branches, it commands all magistrates to be of 'proven competence, integrity, probity and independence,' as well as to be members of the Philippine bar and to have practiced law for a fixed number of years. In addition, CJ believes they must also be industrious to cope with the heavy case backlog and render speedy justice, and have a philosophy of law so their decisions can be predictable. The Constitution mandates the Judicial and Bar Council to screen and nominate, based on these qualifications, at least three of the 'best and brightest' lawyers for every judicial vacancy. Only from this limited list may the president choose; no confirmation by the Commission on Appointments is needed. Those finally allowed to enter the restrictive judicial doors are shielded by the Charter from political, financial, and social stresses. They 'hold office during good behavior until they reach the age of 70.' Justices of the SC may be removed only by the tedious process of impeachment; lower court judges can be disciplined, suspended or ousted only for cause and only by the SC. Their compensation cannot be reduced, thereby assuring independence. When much is given, much is required. Those authorized to judge others must pass a higher standard. Otherwise, they lose moral ascendancy, if not their very office. They leave behind all humanity and become gods of law, beholden only to blindfolded justice, and loyal only to the Constitution and the rule of law, not to presidents -- as stressed by CJ Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno. While gratitude and friendships are cherished Filipino values, they end where duty to the Constitution and the people begin. This is why whenever some jurists misbehave, the whole judiciary is diminished, and why disciplinary actions must be meted out speedily and strictly. On the other hand, many litigants cannot accept defeat and spew corruption rumors at the judiciary. Only the untarnished reputation of jurists protects them from these ugly murmurings, as the SWS poll shows. As earlier stated, magistrates should also have a known philosophy of law so their decisions would be predictable, and in turn jurisprudence would be stable and rumor-free. An example is how jurists interpret the Constitution, based on their philosophy of law. The textualists or originalists interpret according to the original intent of the framers, regardless of the dire consequences on current and future events -- they rely on 'dura lex sed lex.' Their self-imposed duty is 'to apply laws faithfully and desist from engaging in socio-economic or political experimentations,' which they denounce as 'judicial legislation.' On the other hand, the liberals or progressives believe in a living Constitution -- one that grows with time, solves the vagaries of the present, and anticipates the needs of the future. CJ belongs to this latter group, which believes that jurists are not mere social technicians and legal automatons; rather, they are social engineers who courageously fix their gaze on the underlying principles and overarching aspirations of the Constitution to nurture a free and prosperous nation. The US SC has been struggling for a long time on these differing interpretation philosophies. As then chief justice, CJP visited US Justice Antonin Scalia, said to be the leader of the originalists in the US Court -- he invited him to speak before the Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity that the SC was sponsoring on Oct 18-20, 2006, just prior to CJP's retirement. Scalia smiled and said: 'Mr. Chief Justice, you do not really want me there. I would be useless in the Forum because I do not believe in international law. When I joined the Court, I swore to defend the US Constitution and nothing else. And I interpret it according to the original intent of our framers, which did not include international law. Please see my friend, Justice Anthony Kennedy. I am sure he will welcome an opportunity to expound on his international ideas.' True enough, when CJP saw Justice Kennedy later, he agreed to speak at the Global Forum even if via teleconferencing only, because he had already committed to be in another venue on those dates. With such known philosophies, one can reasonably predict their positions on specific issues.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban concludes the three-part bar-exam-and-legal-education trilogy with this third installment. The bar exam assesses the students' knowledge of basic laws. Beyond the basics is the responsibility of law schools. By conducting the bar exam, the SC does not and cannot guarantee the applicants' fitness and readiness to take on specialized fields, like law-of-the-sea, patent, or securities cases. Old ways to learn law: the top 10 passers gain enormous advantage because the doors to the top law firms, best corporations, and finest government offices are immediately opened to them; in fact, topnotchers (and honor students with decent bar exam grades) have a choice of which doors to enter, unlike ordinary passers who must fall in line for professional and employment opportunities. CJ was lucky to have been both an honor graduate and a bar placer in 1960 -- Dean Jovito R. Salonga invited him to join his prestigious law firm (which, pursuant to Salonga's high ethical standards, was dissolved much later on when Salonga joined the Cabinet of President Cory Aquino). In Salonga's firm, CJ was immediately assigned over a hundred cases to study and to litigate; in addition, he stayed late evenings researching for big high-profile cases and accompanied Salonga during his litigation combats with the best advocates of his time. Salonga said that the best way to learn how to swim is to be thrown into the water -- he threw CJ not just into the water but into the middle of the ocean where he had to struggle mostly on his own lest he drown. CJ admits that what he picked up from law school did not prepare him for such near-drowning experiences, because he was taught only the basics, and by strict professors who used the old recitation and question-and-answer methods. One professor, a learned judge and textbook author, demanded that the students memorize his opus and graded them according to how they repeated every line of his book to answer his questions. New ways to learn law: fast-forward 50 years, CJ finds that most law schools still teach only the basics and use the old teaching methods (lectures, recitations, Q&A) of his time. However, the leading law colleges, especially Ateneo de Manila and the UP, have introduced new teaching methods and expanded their curricula. They pioneered in the case method developed by Dean Christopher Langdell of Harvard, in which SC decisions are analyzed and debated, thereby enabling students to understand how theoretical principles are applied in real-life cases; they also established legal aid clinics where students, under the guidance of their mentors, rendered assistance to indigents. Since UP has its own charter, it enjoys autonomy in crafting its curricula. This autonomy extended to its College of Law, which thus flexed its curriculum beyond the basics and instituted elective subjects like indigenous law, human rights, law and poverty, and law and population. Ateneo expanded its course even more and conferred the degree of juris doctor (JD), no longer bachelor of laws (LLB). It enriched its curriculum with new subjects like social philosophy, arbitration law, clinical legal education, collective bargaining, environmental law, information technology, securities law, etc. Lately, CJ is glad Dean Sedfrey Candelaria is planning a subject on liberty and prosperity, CJ's legal philosophy. Ateneo students are also required to use their summer breaks to serve as apprentices in law firms, government offices, and courts. Equally important, senior students must prepare and defend a thesis on a novel subject, thereby making them truly deserving of their doctoral degrees. Despite their heavier loads, Ateneo and UP graduates manage to cop the top places in the bar exam, negating the theory that concentrating on the basics prepares best for the bar exam. Many schools, like FEU (CJ's alma mater), De La Salle, and University of Asia and the Pacific, are following the Ateneo lead to expand their curricula and grant JD degrees -- they want to teach not only legal knowledge but also the skills to convert that knowledge into practice. Proposals to upgrade: comes now Justin D.J. Sucgang, a member of the Legal Education Board representing the student sector, raring to upgrade further the standards of legal education. In his 288-page seminal thesis, he envisions an ideal legal education that: (1) ensures that only students with the aptitude for legal studies and practice of law will be accepted (by passing a mandatory national aptitude test for entry to law school); (2) allows law schools to draw their own curriculum, determine their specialization, and have their own unique market; (3) considers law not as an end-all-be-all discipline but rather a tool, a powerful one, that effects social change, and integrates practice-oriented courses such as the Art and Theatrics of Legal Advocacy; (4) allows most law professors to choose their own teaching methods because they will not be bothered by the need to have their students pass the bar exam; (5) respects students not only for their dignity as human beings but also for their unique learning strategies; (6) weeds out the unprepared through other means of screening such as the Mandatory National Screening Program; (7) employs the bar exam only to test knowledge of the fundamental and core subjects of the law, uses only the pass-fail grading system, and abolishes the bar topnotcher system. These proposals are open for discussion.
