one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers the middle column of the three-part bar-exam-and-legal-education trilogy. Let me continue last Sunday's column on the bar examinations which will be held on October 5, 12, 19 and 26. The exams measure the candidates' theoretical knowledge of these basic subjects: Political and International Law; Labor Law and Social Legislation; Civil Law; Taxation; Mercantile Law; Criminal Law; Remedial Law; and Legal and Judicial Ethics. The Supreme Court has issued Bar Bulletin No. 1 describing in detail the scope or syllabus for each of these subjects. Practice of law: they are also the very subjects, broken into several subtopics in the bar exam syllabus, that law schools 'teach' their students. For this reason, the four-year law curriculum is said to be 'bar-oriented' -- that is, designed to help students pass the bar exam, and nothing more. The question frequently asked and debated is one of adequacy: whether hurdling or even topping these subjects both in the bar exams and in the law schools adequately prepares students to practice law in the real world. CJ's answer depends on the meaning given to 'practice of law.' If by practice of law is meant 'litigation,' then the answer is definitely 'no.' Theoretical knowledge alone is not enough to prepare an attorney for court work. In the same manner that passing the medical board exam, by itself, will not magically transform a physician to undertake heart surgery or corneal replacements, hurdling the bar test does not guarantee litigation expertise. Litigation is a specialization in which not all lawyers, not even all bar topnotchers, can succeed. It requires not only legal knowledge but also command of language, intuition, presence of mind, wit, planning, thinking on one's feet, even drama. Moreover, like surgery, litigation has subspecialties -- a heart surgeon would normally not dare operate on the brain, in the same way that a criminal law expert may not be competent to litigate international law-of-the-seas cases. Broad definition: however, if by practice of law is meant the very broad concept set forth by the SC in Cayetano vs Monsod (Sept 3, 1991), then CJ's answer is 'yes.' In this case, the Court defined practice of law as 'any activity, in or out of court, which requires the application of law, legal procedure, knowledge, training and experience... Generally, to practice law is to render any kind of service, which requires the use in any degree of legal knowledge or skill.' The Court explained that practice of law is not 'limited to the conduct of cases in court.' This definition is comprehensive enough to include teaching of law, giving of any advice that requires legal background, preparation of legal documents (like affidavits and contracts), and management of the legal affairs of corporations. In reality, many more lawyers are engaged in non-trial work than in litigation. In fact, some of the highest paid lawyers, both here and abroad, have never seen a courtroom. In the British system, lawyers are classified broadly into solicitors and barristers -- the traditional law offices are staffed by solicitors who listen to clients and advise them on how to solve their legal predicaments, and when necessary, refer them to barristers who represent them in court litigations. Although the solicitor-barrister distinction is not observed here (all bar passers are allowed to appear in court), the big law firms anyway divide functions and responsibilities such that more lawyers get solicitor-type assignments than barrister-associated work. Compared with those working in law firms, far more lawyers are employed in the government and in private corporations. In fact, many take up law to qualify for promotion because a bachelor of laws degree is given the equivalent of a master's degree by the Commission on Higher Education. Expanding legal knowledge: the SC cannot be faulted for requiring only the most basic knowledge of law to pass the bar exams. Those who want to specialize should undertake further study and training either in graduate schools or in actual practice, or in both. It is really difficult to require more than this basic knowledge from bar applicants. During the last three decades, law and jurisprudence have expanded exponentially in the Philippines and in the world, in keeping with the march of knowledge in all disciplines, especially in science, technology and medicine. Apart from the Constitution and the basic codes (Civil Code, Penal Code, Corporation Code, etc.), Congress continues to pass new laws totaling over 10,000 at the end of 2013; and, aside from the Rules of Court (and the perplexing rules and regulations issued by various administrative agencies like the National Labor Relations Commission, Bureau of Internal Revenue, etc.), the SC produces over 1,000 full-length decisions every year. Given the need to keep up with this humongous legal literature, the SC instituted the Mandatory Continuing Legal Education Program (MCLE), which requires all lawyers to take continuing legal education seminars and activities every three years, to 'ensure that throughout their career, they keep abreast with law and jurisprudence, maintain ethics of the profession and enhance the standards of the practice of law.' Next week, as the last part of this series, CJ will take up the valiant effort of the leading law schools to improve legal education and standards, with special mention of the seminal thesis of Justin D.J. Sucgang, a regular member of the Legal Education Board.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes a Manila-Cathedral retrofitting/restoration field-report column in his capacity as president of the Metropolitan Manila Cathedral-Basilica Foundation. After two years of retrofitting, restoration and renovation, the Manila Cathedral-Basilica of the Immaculate Conception (or Manila Cathedral for short) reopened on April 9 with a eucharistic celebration presided over by Luis Antonio Cardinal Tagle, Archbishop of Manila. Cathedral and faithful: PNoy and his sisters Ballsy, Viel and Kris, SP Franklin and Mrs. Mila Drilon, Manila Mayor Joseph and Sen. Loi Estrada, plus 1,800 other faithful from the 92 parishes and different lay organizations of the archdiocese graced the occasion -- most of them came from poor and underprivileged communities; CJ Maria Lourdes Sereno sent her regrets as she was presiding over the SC's summer session in Baguio. The word 'church' in Catholic tradition has two meanings: first, it refers to the material or concrete structure; and second, to the community of the faithful, the churchgoers -- the church building exists to serve the churchgoers who are called by God to love Him and one another in worship, spirit and truth. A cathedral is the ecclesia caput et mater omnium ecclesiarum or the 'head and mother church of all churches' in the archdiocese; it is the home of the entire archdiocese; according to Vatican II, the cathedral-church is the place where Christians, united to their archbishop, live and mature in faith -- thus, believers enter the cathedral for communal devotion of the sacred mysteries and especially for the celebration of the Eucharist. Inside the cathedral is the cathedra or chair of the archbishop, the symbol of apostolic succession in the church -- the cathedra or apostolic chair 'qualifies' or distinguishes a cathedral from a parish church or chapel. Retrofitting and restoration: founded and originally constructed in 1571, the Manila Cathedral was damaged eight times by fire, earthquake, nature and WWII; it has been rebuilt, reconstructed and/or restored eight times also. During the last two years, the church's structure was strengthened by removing the heavy carrara pedestals and marble claddings on all the columns and retrofitting them with carbon fiber wraps, up to 1.5 meters below ground level -- the marble claddings were then restored to their original condition without breakage. The marble flooring had to be lifted piece by piece to construct a huge drainage system to prevent rainwater from seeping in and weakening the foundations; electrical wiring and new plumbing were installed, and the marble flooring was restored to its original position also without any breakage. The decorative capitals and arches near the ceiling were precast and demolished to fiber-wrap the columns to the top and then replaced with the precast ones to look like the originals, including their liturgical symbols; structural steel was installed to strengthen the beams of the roof. New state-of-the-art lighting inside and outside the church, audio-visual systems, and security CCTVs were carefully planned and installed; wall cracks were injected with over 120 gallons of epoxy. Carbon fiber wraps were retrofitted on the weakened columns of the belfry tower; the old heavy bells were earlier brought down and placed at the cathedral's garden side. Not fully complete: the retrofitting and architectural restorations have been finished with the help of kind donors led by Ramon S. Ang of San Miguel Corp., George S. K. Ty of Metrobank, Justa Lee and Antonio Oppen, contractor DM Consunji, and project manager SP Castro; however, the Cathedral's renovations and systems enhancements are not fully complete yet -- the 13-bell carillon donated a few years ago by Bert and Sylvia Lina will be replaced in a few months (also by Bert and Sylvia) with the latest, state-of-the-art 23-bell carillon from the Netherlands; furthermore, the antiquated air-conditioning system will be changed as soon as a generous donor is found. The Metropolitan Manila Cathedral-Basilica Foundation raises the funds for and oversees the retrofitting, restoration and renovation; its officers are Cardinal Tagle (chair), former Ambassador Tita de Villa (vice-chair), Marixi Prieto (treasurer), Msgr. Nestor Cerbo (executive director), Erlito Fider (corporate secretary), and yours truly (president); its board of trustees is composed of Bishop Bernardino Cortez, Fr. Domingo Asuncion, Fr. Alberto Flores, Cecille Alvarez, Mary Ann Chan, Susana Chung, Danny Dolor, Cecille Oppen and Letty Syquia. Cheers to Judith Duavit Vasquez, a director of GMA Network and the first female Asian trustee of the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (Icann), for hosting the 20th anniversary of the Internet at the Crown Plaza Hotel in Pasig City -- over 100 cyber professionals 'conversed' on the present and future of the Internet; among them: legislators (Rep. Susan Yap, coauthor of the Cybercrime Prevention Law), executive officials on cyber (Asst. Justice Sec Guillermo Sy, Supt. Gilberto Sosa), Icann officers (Christopher Mondini, Kuek Yu-Chang, Jia-Rong Low), cyber experts (Drexx Laggui, PLDT's Jovy Hernandez, ABS-CBN's Donald Lim), and plain citizens like CJ; to reach another person on the Internet, one must type an address -- a name or a number -- that must be unique so computers know where to find it; Icann coordinates these unique identifiers in the world; without this coordination, one global Internet is not possible.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reports the Supreme Court's Manila Memorial Park v. DSWD (Dec 3 2013, J. Mariano C. del Castillo ponente) decision affirming the constitutionality and mandatory character of the 20-percent senior-citizen discount on a broad range of purchases (hotels, restaurants, recreation centers, medicine, funeral and burial services, theaters, cinema houses, concert halls, circuses, carnivals, medical and dental services). The 15 justices were unanimous on the discount but divided on cost-bearing. He traces the legislative evolution: under the original RA 7492 (April 23 1992), the government bore the full discount via tax credit; at BIR initiative RA 9257 (Feb 26 2004) treated it as a tax deduction, leaving sellers to bear 68 percent and the government 32 percent (foregone corporate income tax). The majority justified this with police power to regulate liberty/property for public welfare provided not unreasonable, oppressive or confiscatory, noting that nothing prevents sellers from recouping their subsidies by increasing non-senior prices. The 38-page del Castillo ponencia drew lively concurring opinions from Velasco and Bersamin, a novel concurring-and-dissenting opinion from Leonen, and a vigorous dissent from Senior Justice Antonio T. Carpio, who argued the government should shoulder the full cost: the discount is not voluntary but state forcibly taking part of the purchase price from private sellers without just compensation -- under eminent domain, private property cannot be taken without just compensation, so RA 9257 should be declared unconstitutional and the original RA 7492 tax-credit framework should be revived. Panganiban flags that the case is important not only for upholding the discount but for disclosing the justices' philosophical and sociological mindset on the role of law in economics, finance, and business -- deserving another column on those views vis-à-vis his own legal philosophy of liberty and prosperity under the rule of law. He appends a Spirit-of-Christmas postscript agreeing on legal and humanitarian grounds with the Sandiganbayan's order allowing former President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo's family to visit and stay with her at the Veterans Memorial Medical Center on Christmas and New Year's Day. Three justifications: she has not been convicted (constitutional presumption of innocence still applies); her bail petition is still pending (evidence has not been ruled strong); and she suffers from frail health (three life-threatening surgeries, metal brace surgically installed on her spine that could slip at any time causing severe nerve injury or death) plus mental stress, with minimal escape risk and short-duration well-guarded visits. In the spirit of peace and reconciliation commemorating the birth of the Lord of Peace, he believes President Arroyo deserves to enjoy the love and comfort of her family.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban marks the significance of Japanese PM Shinzo Abe's Philippine visit right after the July 24 2013 electoral sweep by his Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) of the upper house (House of Councillors) of the Japanese Parliament (National Diet) -- consolidating the LDP's Dec 16 2012 landslide in the more powerful lower house and Abe's Dec 26 2012 election as PM by 328 of 480 lower-house members. This is a dazzling political grand slam by Abe, who six years ago embarrassingly resigned as PM after losing Diet confidence -- only the second leader in Japan's history (after Shigeru Yoshida in 1948) to come back successfully for a second term. In the past decade, Japan had revolving-door leadership changes (1-year-average PM term), aggravated by a lethargic economy (China overtook Japan as world's second-largest economy two years ago). For Filipinos who elect chief executives for fixed six-year terms, the revolving-door phenomenon could be catastrophic. However, like in mature parliamentary democracies (Britain, Canada, Australia), Japan's competent civil servants (untarnished by partisan politics) kept the country going -- but the disadvantage is civil servants cannot supply vision and direction, which only elected leaders can. The LDP landslide gives Abe a stable term assuring fulfillment of his vision (revitalize economy, defense, international relations). Japanese politicians, unlike Filipino counterparts, do not flip-flop. Abe's visit just after his stunning victory shows keen interest in solidifying friendship with the PH -- Japan may yet be the PH's best ally, rivaling century-old US relations. Per Ambassador Manuel M. Lopez, Japan was already the PH's top trading partner ($16.33B two-way trade in 2012), top ODA source, one of the largest sources of FDI and foreign tourists (412,474 in 2012). Japan has a low-profile representative in the Malaysia-chaired foreign-monitoring-group on the MILF peace agreement and actively supports the PH stance to resolve the WPS maritime dispute peacefully through UNCLOS arbitration (future column). The visit boosted the 'strategic partnership' with Abe's Four Initiatives: (1) foster vibrant economy + Metro Manila transportation-infrastructure improvement + 10-billion-yen ($100M) standby-emergency-credit for disaster recovery; (2) maritime cooperation + 10 patrol vessels for PH Coast Guard via yen loan; (3) strengthen Mindanao Peace Process assistance; (4) people-to-people exchange via relaxed visa rules + more regular flights -- with PH tourists to Japan getting an automatic 30% discount from yen-to-dollar + dollar-to-peso depreciation. Armed with an equally robust popular mandate (May 2013 LP victory ensuring full Congress support, retaining Speaker Belmonte and getting close ally Drilon elected as SP, plus unprecedented 76% SWS / 73% Pulse Asia performance ratings), PNoy has enormous political capital to respond firmly to Abe's initiatives. In Pampango, 'abe' means close friend or bosom buddy -- PNoy hails from that Tarlac part that imbibes and speaks the language. In choosing to hold their summit right after their grand political sweeps, PNoy and Abe may yet turn out to be bosom buddies -- and the Philippines and Japan may yet become BFFs (Filipino colloquial for soul mates or, literally, 'best friends forever'). All for the mutual benefit of both leaders and both nations.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban frames the election of Archbishop Socrates B. Villegas to the presidency of the Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines as the latest chapter in the renewal of the Catholic Church in the Philippines that began with Archbishop Luis Antonio G. Tagle's elevation to the College of Cardinals. Both are young, humble, prayerful, and empowering -- echoing the simplicity and theology of reformist Pope Francis in the universal Church: great communicators in new media, straightforward and uncomplicated, direct from the heart; they unravel the great mysteries of Christianity and the ponderous papal encyclicals via plain everyday language and their simple, austere lifestyle. Newly elevated though they may be and newly minted though their messages may appear, in CJP's humble view they really bring the Church back to its roots -- to the original rock the Lord Jesus Christ founded and anchored it: a Church of the poor, by the poor, and for the poor. He quotes the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines (PCP II, Jan 20-Feb 17 1991, implementing Vatican II 1962-65): 'A Church that embraces and practices the evangelical spirit of poverty which combines detachment from possessions with a profound trust in the Lord as the only source of salvation... A Church that will courageously defend and vindicate the rights of the poor and the oppressed even when doing so will mean alienation or persecution from the rich and powerful... A Church where nobody is so poor as to have nothing to give, and nobody so rich as to have nothing to receive.' The new leaders are steering the Church back to Jesus Christ, who identified Himself with the poor (Mt 25:40,45). By reaching out to the poor and liberating them, they echo Jesus's mission (Lk 4:18). When Pope Francis forsook his gilded seat, CJP was reminded that Jesus's throne was a wooden cross, His crown a bouquet of thorns, His scepter a lowly reed, and His ring a rusty nail driven through His palm. Jesus explained in different ways: to His disciples, loftily and authoritatively (in His Sermon on the Mount favoring the poor, sorrowing, simple-hearted, peacemakers; condemning the hypocrite, arrogant, proud, self-righteous); to nondisciples in parables ending with questions -- Lk 10:36 (the good Samaritan: 'Which of these three, do you think, made himself neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of the robbers?') and Lk 20:16 (the tenants: 'Now, what will the owner of the vineyard do to them?') -- awakening faith and making the nonbeliever discover the truth without being lectured on. Jesus was a leader of enormous courage and unbreakable conviction: 2,000 years ago there was no freedom of speech, dissent, or opposition -- group conformity was the standard of truth and virtue -- but, in Albert Nolan's words ('Jesus Before Christianity'), 'No tradition was too sacred to be questioned. No authority was too great to be contradicted... No assumption was too fundamental to be changed.' Jesus was a servant-leader who led by example (Mk 10:42-45 -- 'whoever would be great among you must be your servant'); to show readiness to perform the humblest service, He washed the feet of His apostles (Jn 13:13-14). And He was a leader of intense prayer and unbending faith -- at Gethsemane, He prayed so intensely that 'great drops of blood formed like sweat and fell to the ground' (Lk 22:44). The renewal of the Church is an ever-continuing process and does not necessarily denigrate the old order -- parents are not diminished when their children surpass them. Congratulations to His Excellency, His Eminence, and His Holiness for renewing the Church and bringing it back to Jesus Christ.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban assesses Cardinal Tagle's real possibility of becoming the first Filipino (and first Asian and first non-European) pope following Pope Benedict XVI's resignation, arguing he has 'more than an even chance.' He grounds the argument in three frameworks: the 1978 historical precedent of the unexpected election of Polish Cardinal Wojtyla (99 of 111 votes on the 8th ballot, defeating two Italian frontrunners); the epochal-transformation analogy of Cory Aquino and Barack Obama making the 'impossible' happen; and the demographic-strategic argument that Asia's combined Catholic and potential population -- China 1.3B, India 1.1B, plus Indonesia, Japan, the Philippines, Vietnam, and others -- makes it the greatest evangelical opportunity for a global institution losing relevance in Europe. He explains conclave mechanics: the 80-year age cap (excluding Cardinals Rosales and Vidal), the Sistine Chapel oath of secrecy, four daily ballots, white/black smoke signals, and the 'Habemus Papam!' proclamation. Appended as a postscript: Filipino WWII veterans' Recinto appeal to the US Supreme Court (the US appellate court dismissed for wrong-court filing, not on the merits), with CJ wishing them luck while noting the US SC's 1% acceptance rate -- and using the comparison to explain why the US SC has no backlog while the PH SC does: the US Charter grants far greater discretionary leeway in case selection.

The San Beda Law Alumni named a moot court in his honor; the PDRCI named its arbitration center (at McKinley Hill, funded by Bert and Sylvia Lina) after him. The Inquirer published 'With Due Respect' -- a five-year column compilation by editor John Nery -- as a 75th-birthday gift. one_paragraph_summary: Writing on Christmas Day, Panganiban recounts the genesis of 'Ageless Passion' -- a Broadway-style musicale celebrating his 75th birthday staged December 20 at the Meralco Theater. What began as a modest home gathering with a string band and 120 guests was transformed when Jeff Agustin, a former PowerPoint preparer now studying at the University of Westminster in London, submitted an unsolicited libretto romanticizing CJ's life at a planning meeting; Eduardo Yap showed it to Ryan Cayabyab who created 7 original compositions in 7 weeks; and producer Donna May Lina Flavier organized the Manila Symphony Orchestra (conducted by Arturo Molina), a cast of six, and multi-awarded director Bart Guingona -- with Alberto and Sylvia Lina as sponsors. The show drew 800+ attendees including VP Binay, former presidents Ramos and Estrada, Archbishop Tagle, SC justices, and business titans (President Aquino was absent tending Mindanao flood victims). The musicale opened with the good-news-bad-news medieval farmer story -- also the late Cardinal Sin's favorite -- whose refrain 'I will just keep on doing my best and God will do the rest' is the column's organizing philosophy, applied to CJ's biographical arc: 'from the poor newsboy in the backstreets of Sampaloc, Manila to the presidency of the Philippine Daily Inquirer; from an ignorant Catholic to an adviser to the Holy Father in the Vatican; from frustrated applicant for graduate studies to father of five wonderful children who each achieved his impossible dream of graduating in a pedigreed US university; from a shoeshine boy to the boardrooms of the largest blue chips; and from a frustrated chemical engineer to a reluctant lawyer to the highest magistrate of the land.' CJ closes by naming all five children and ten grandchildren -- including eldest grandchild Miguel as narrator and two youngest (Joey and Matt Reagan) contributing via video from New York.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban introduces the column as a prelude to the ongoing divorce debate -- before addressing marriage's termination, he first writes about its beginning and its property consequences. The law 'instantly takes over' upon the exchange of vows: the default regime under the Family Code is the absolute community of property, under which all property owned by either spouse before the marriage -- or acquired thereafter -- ipso facto becomes jointly owned, even if titles remain in only one name. Land, condominiums, cars, bank deposits, jewelry and other assets all become communal upon saying 'I do.' The marital evidentiary privilege also kicks in: a spouse cannot testify for or against the other without consent (except in civil or criminal cases filed by one against the other). Exclusions include personal-use property, property acquired by gratuitous title (donations) during marriage, and a widow or widower's property where legitimate children by the prior marriage stand to inherit (subject to a six-month liquidation deadline, failing which complete separation governs any subsequent marriage). Neither spouse may sell, mortgage or donate communal assets without the other's consent; but each may practice their profession, with the income becoming communal. The only escape is a prenuptial agreement -- in writing, signed before the wedding, irrevocable after it (like the marriage vow itself). The most commonly chosen alternative is the conjugal partnership of gains (the regime before the Family Code's August 3, 1988 effectivity): each spouse retains ownership of separate assets, but their income, fruits, and rentals accrue to a common fund.

First, JP II's January 12-16, 1995 pastoral visit to Manila: the author served on the Arrival and Departure Committee under Ambassador Tita de Villa; Archbishop Morelos played the Pope in rehearsals (prophesying the author would be president) while the author played President Ramos (counter-prophesying Morelos would be pope -- neither came true). one_paragraph_summary: On Palm Sunday (May 1, 2011), Panganiban delivers Part 1 of a reflection on Jesus Christ as the eternal leader -- 'the same yesterday, today and tomorrow' -- identifying five leadership qualities of which he covers three. First, vision and mission: Jesus communicated His salvific mission differently to different audiences -- lofty and authoritative to disciples ('the greatest teaching of all time'), parables to non-disciples that ended with questions ('Which of these three was neighbor to the man?'; 'Which of them was more grateful?'; 'What fate do you suppose the owner has in store for them?') -- designed to make the listener discover truth for himself. Second, courage and conviction: in a world with no freedom of speech or dissent, Jesus mixed with sinners, tax collectors, a Samaritan woman, and an adulteress; acquired a reputation as 'a glutton and a drunkard'; and boldly denounced the scribes and Pharisees as 'whitewashed tombs, beautiful on the outside but inside full of filth and dead men's bones.' Third, servant-leadership: Jesus explicitly taught 'The Son of Man has not come to be served but to serve' and demonstrated it by washing the apostles' feet -- contrasting sharply with Philippine political leaders who use pork barrel appropriations for personal patronage, and who make themselves the center of authority 'such that no business can be opened without their blessings and no employment can be secured without their recommendation.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban announces the first batch of LibPros law scholars -- originally planned at 10 but expanded to 11 after the board of judges, led by CJ Maria Lourdes P. A. Sereno, was so impressed it recommended an extra scholar; the FLP happily agreed. The Dec 1, 2016 awarding ceremony at the new UP campus in Fort Bonifacio, Taguig will feature CJ Sereno as guest speaker; each scholar receives full scholarship (tuition + books + monthly stipend up to P200,000), and 10 new scholars will be selected every school year. The distribution across schools: Ateneo, FEU-Makati, San Beda, and UST 2 each; PUP, USC, UP 1 each -- named: Sean James Borja, Kaycelle Anne Castillo, Ervin Frederick Dy, Rexlyn Ann Evora, Ken Kevin Ganchero, Jose Noel Hilario, Violeta Najarro Jr., Dion Ceasar Pascua, Ma Janine Pedernal, Tess Marie Tan, and Vanessa Gloria Vergara. The program is cosponsored by the Tan Yan Kee Foundation (TYKF) in cooperation with the Philippine Association of Law Schools (PALS); the board of judges includes CJ Sereno, FLP president Evelyn T. Dumdum, former education secretary Edilberto C. de Jesus, TYKF legal counsel Ma Cecilia L. Pesayco, and PALS president Ma Soledad D. Mawis, with FLP executive director Martin Angelo L. Esguerra assisting. Qualification requires being a third-year law student in an eligible school, top 10% of class, ≥83% (2.25) average across four prior semesters, full loads with no drops, dean's commendation, an essay on liberty and prosperity, and board screening. The FLP was organized in December 2011 during CJ's 75th birthday to perpetuate the legal philosophy that 'justice and jobs, freedom and food, ethics and economics, democracy and development, nay, liberty and prosperity must always go together; one is useless without the other.' Beyond the scholarships, FLP and the Ayala Group cosponsor a dissertation contest open to all law students nationwide (P300K champion, P200K runner-up, P100K each for 3 honorable mentions, P20K each for 20 qualifying entries); with Metrobank Foundation and MPIC, FLP has created 10 professorial chairs -- 9 already filled by the law deans of Ateneo, FEU, USC, UP, UST, DLSU, Silliman, U Cordilleras, plus the PHILJA chancellor; USC dean Joan Largo will deliver her fourth professorial lecture in Cebu City on Dec 9. FLP acquired its Makati head office with assistance from First Philippine Holdings, Lopez Holdings, Meralco, PLDT, MPIC, and San Miguel's Ramon S. Ang. A postscript clarifies last Sunday's column on US elector selection: each state determines elector election methods by local law -- in some, elector names are on the ballot; in others, presidential candidate names appear but votes still count for the electors, not the candidates directly.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban prefaces today's FLP awards ceremony with a portrait of First Lady Louise Araneta-Marcos -- whose competence as practicing lawyer and law professor he had heard of before her husband's presidency, and whom he met formally on June 28, 2023 (Sistine Chapel reproductions exhibit) and Aug 22, 2023 (Toyota Philippines 35th anniversary), where she acted so spontaneously, occasionally holding his arm, as if they had known each other for years: 'INDEED, A REAL CHARMER.' Invited through compañero Mike Toledo (Chamber of Mines chair and president) for Aug 19, she sent a personalized video citing 'sacred' days and requested a reschedule to today, Sept 2. Three groups of awardees will receive prizes from her, guest speaker Manuel V. Pangilinan (MVP), and CJ as FLP chair: 20 law scholars at P200,000 each (Tan Yan Kee Foundation partnership represented by Lucio Tan III, 'the Stanford summa, president of PAL Holdings and LT Group'), with 10 third-year students (Alberto, Despi, Mirasol, Mutuc, Orajay, Paguia, Sy, Sobreviñas, Te, Viernes) and 10 fourth-year students (Barraquias, Cerillo, David, Gruyal, Laza, Patricio, Aimiel and Allan Reyes, Salcedo, Sanders Jr.) named with their schools; five MBA Esmel fellows at P450,000 each (Metro Pacific Investments Foundation partnership; P350,000 tuition + P100,000 stipend) -- Ballestar, Lucas, Panlilio II, Tuquero, and Villanueva; and 20 dissertation contest winners (Ayala Corp partnership) -- Rachel Gella (USLS) first prize P320,000, Arvin Maceda (FEU) second P220,000, three third placers at P120,000 (De Guia, Loro, Quebrar), and 15 finalists at P20,000 each, with the five winning dissertations accessible at www.libpros.com. The three boards of judges were chaired by CJ Alexander G. Gesmundo (scholars), past BSP governor Amando M. Tetangco Jr. -- 'now chair of the largest conglomerate in our country, SM Investments Corp.' (Esmel fellows) -- and Justice Amy C. Lazaro-Javier (dissertations). UP Law Dean Darlene Marie Berberabe will be inducted into the FLP Professorial Chairs program by Metrobank chair Arthur Ty and Toyota Philippines chair Alfred Ty. The FLP Board of Trustees comprises retired Justice Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez (president), retired Justice Estela M. Perlas-Bernabe, former Education Secretary Edilberto de Jesus, Tetangco, Maria Elena P. Yaptangco, professor Maria Theresa P. Mañalac, lawyers Joel Emerson Gregorio and Arvin Paolo D. Cortez, and CJ as chairperson. In its second decade (2021-2031), FLP aims to set up an immersive, interactive, AI-powered, tech-driven Center for Liberty and Prosperity (in partnership with the Supreme Court) hosting a Museum for Liberty and Prosperity, and a multi-billion-peso Prosperity Fund to help eliminate extreme poverty by investing in MSME equity and helping them through Esmel-fellow management expertise -- unleashing their entrepreneurial ingenuity. 'To our knowledge, while there are firms engaged in microfinancing, FLP is the only entity aspiring to invest in and help manage MSMEs' -- making them 'more credit-worthy and growth-worthy.'

one_paragraph_summary: At the Tañada-Diokno School of Law of De La Salle University, founding dean Jose Manuel 'Chel' Diokno delivered a professorial lecture sponsored by the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity (FLP) and the Metrobank Foundation, exclaiming, 'Let us protect, respect and remedy (PRR) human rights.' Citing the 2011 UN Human Rights Council resolution, he argued that big business -- in addition to the state -- has become a 'duty bearer' articulating the 'global standard for preventing and addressing the risk of adverse impacts on human rights linked to business activity.' He pointed to National Action Plans by the UK (2013), the Dutch bank ABN AMRO (2015), and France (2017), and to the reputational, customer-base, and employee-relations benefits of PRR adoption. The Philippines has yet to develop a NAP but has aligned itself with international human-rights standards by ratifying the UDHR and several covenants, and the Commission on Human Rights and the SEC have urged inclusion of PRR in corporate manuals of publicly listed companies. Diokno argued that engaging business is best done 'in a friendly and nonconfrontational manner,' favoring arbitration, mediation, and good offices over litigation, strikes, and pickets: 'Business, hand in hand with human rights, has the power to transform people's lives and build a nation of liberty and prosperity.' In response, CJ said the FLP supports PRR -- human rights are integral to the broader Bill of Rights -- but FLP is 'more libertarian,' upholding also the constitutional Declaration of Principles and State Policies and 'circumscribed by the rule of law' under which everyone is treated equally: 'Libertarianism cannot coexist with authoritarianism where the authoritarian enacts, enforces, and interprets the law. In a libertarian regime, no one is more equal than others.' He shared his biographical maturation: 'As a student, I was an activist, and as a lawyer, I was trained to litigate. But as I matured, I found that in business, as in every relationship, it is better to be invited than to gatecrash.' FLP goes beyond 'liberty of the mind' into 'liberty of the stomach' -- 'freedom and food, justice and jobs, peace and development -- the two must go together; one is useless without the other' -- operationalized through 20 annual legal scholarships at P200,000 each (Tan Yan Kee), five ESMEL fellowships at P450,000 each (Metro Pacific Investments Foundation), dissertation contests with a top prize of P350,000 plus 20 lesser awards (Ayala), Professorial Chairs at P150,000 per lecture (MBF), and the Panganiban Educational Assistance Program for the poor (Jollibee and Double Dragon). FLP recently announced two 'ultimate projects' -- the Center for Liberty and Prosperity (anchored by an interactive, immersive, AI-powered, tech-driven Museum for Liberty and Prosperity) and the Prosperity Fund (to help the poor help themselves through private entrepreneurship) -- with former BSP Governor Amando M. Tetangco Jr. and retired Senior Associate Justice Estela M. Perlas-Bernabe co-chairing the implementing Task Force.

one_paragraph_summary: On what would have been her 84th birthday -- Feb. 29, 2024 -- the Asian Institute of Management posthumously honored Prof. Leni Panganiban with a trifold tribute: rededicating the Chapel of the Immaculate Conception in her loving memory, naming a ground-floor caseroom after her, and opening the Professor Leni Panganiban Scholarship to be granted starting 2025 to an outstanding iMBA student. Born on a leap year (Feb. 29, 1940) and 'ascended to the Heavenly Kingdom aptly last Easter Sunday, April 9, 2023,' Leni is the first AIM faculty member to be conferred these honors. Presided over by AIM president and dean Dr. Jikyeong Kang, the 'simple but elegant and formal' Dedication Ceremony unveiled two commemorative markers Panganiban reproduces in full: the chapel marker honors Leni's partnership with Fr. James Donelan, SJ (AIM's first chaplain) in 'quietly and anonymously building, adorning, and upgrading this Chapel,' memorializing her 'wisdom, inner strength of character, enduring love for family, and lifelong devotion to our Risen Lord Jesus and to the Immaculate Conception of Our Lady'; the caseroom marker -- signed by CJ and the children Maria Elena, Jose Artemio III, Celine Maria, Maria Theresa, and Maria Evelyn -- recognizes her as the first female professor at AIM (MBM 1971), with over three decades of faithful teaching and service as Associate Dean for the MM Program. In appreciation, CJ and his children gave a modest donation to the AIM Scientific Research Foundation. He then pivots to a related institutional development: a few years ago CJ proposed to AIM a new Master of International Business Law (MIBL) program, inspired by his grandson Jose Miguel 'Mig' Sandejas, who after his Babson College MBA earned a Northwestern University Master of Science in Business Law without a basic law degree, writing CJ that 'knowledge of the law rounded out my business thinking ... The law helps guide the numbers and provides another solution for optimizing income, reducing expenses, and protecting shareholders.' Dr. Kang accepted the proposal and tasked a faculty team headed by professors Olivier Roche and Felipe Calderon to design the two-year-developed curriculum suitable for AIM's local and international milieu. Enrollment for the first batch closes March 15; the MIBL is explicitly a business degree, not a law degree, so graduates 'cannot take the bar exam, much less practice law.' Because the MIBL 'promotes the safeguarding of liberty and the nurturing of prosperity under the rule of law,' the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity, in partnership with the Metro Pacific Investments Foundation, will grant at least two -- perhaps three -- P450,000 fellowships to first-batch enrollees. AIM's own framing positions MIBL as an interdisciplinary program (finance, leadership, risk management, HR, data analytics, information security alongside law) for non-legal-career professionals seeking to 'thrive in the global business environment.'

one_paragraph_summary: At the FLP annual awards ceremony -- 21 Tan Yan Kee Foundation legal scholarships at P200,000 each, 5 MPIF Esmel fellowships at P450,000 each, and 10 Ayala Corporation dissertation writing prizes totaling P1.325M, with CJ Gesmundo as keynote -- Panganiban delivers an abbreviated version of his own address structured around the maxim 'never give up; never say never.' Life is 'a strange interplay of light and shadows,' and 'when a door closes, a much larger and better window opens.' His biography illustrates the principle twice over: a UP scholarship lost over the 15-centavo Diliman jeepney fare his impoverished family could not afford redirected him to nearby FEU, where life-long mentor law dean Jovito R. Salonga and Dr. Alejandro R. Roces shaped him into the youngest FEU Central Student Organization president, the founder of the National Union of Students, a cum laude graduate, and the 6th-placer in the Bar -- and a Yale full scholarship including board and lodging lost when the US Embassy denied his visa over student activism redirected him to PH legal practice and, eventually, the SC, where for over 11 years he buried himself in work 'as a virtual hermit' producing 1,200+ signed decisions, one book a year, and chairing most committees -- earning the unanimous (without his participation) SC resolution naming him 'The Renaissance Jurist of the 21st Century' and 'the Court's most prolific writer, bar none' for 'safeguarding the liberty and nurturing the prosperity of our people.' Five years post-retirement, inspired by Ryan Cayabyab's musical 'Ageless Passion' to convert his philosophy from embedded legal lore into practical reality, he seeded FLP with a P2M personal contribution, then secured P50M from companies and foundations to buy FLP's 700-sqm Makati head office, and another P50M+ for educational projects. The two 'ultimate projects' he outlines are: first, a Center for Liberty and Prosperity in Metro Manila (and later at the new Manila International Airport in Bulacan) with an interactive, immersive, AI-powered Museum for Liberty and Prosperity -- partnered with the SC, allowing visitors to be transported into a virtual SC Session Hall and to converse with AI robots 'mimicking justices' filled with their decisions, speeches, and life-career info -- and second, a multi-billion-peso non-profit-but-sustainable Prosperity Fund to nurture MSMEs and 'help unleash the entrepreneurial ingenuity of our people as the key to eliminating extreme poverty.' To put his money where his mouth is, he has donated to FLP a major family asset -- a Paseo de Magallanes residential lot worth over P100M to be liquified at the appropriate time -- to seed both ultimate projects, the first dedicated to 'the talented' and the second to 'the poor,' because 'whatever you do for the least of my brethren, you do unto me' (Matthew 25:40).

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban summarizes his commencement-style address at the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity (FLP) awarding ceremonies -- honoring bar topnotchers, scholars, valedictorians, and dissertation-writing contest winners -- held via Zoom on June 12, 2020. He builds the address around Lucila Takjerad's Harvard commencement story from a year earlier: in 1994, during the Algerian civil war, Lucila's poor illiterate mother walked through a public market, learned a France emigration list was open, but could not write her own name; an unnamed man chased her and wrote it for her, transporting the family to France where Lucila grew up to graduate from Harvard. Lucila's message -- 'of course, do the most you can do... But also, do the least you can do. Because, the least you can do might turn out to be the most significant' -- leads CJ to his own autobiographical confirmation: peddling newspapers, shining shoes, selling bibles and textbooks; orphaned during law school (his father, a high school graduate and lowly government employee, dying during his pre-law years and his unemployed mother in his senior year); hospitalized on the first Sunday of his bar exams; ready to quit until his FEU law dean Dr. Jovito R. Salonga refused to let him, and until an old friend (now deceased) paid for his bar review on condition of a Top Ten finish -- leading to his sixth-place finish 'with God's grace' and ultimately the highest judicial post. He extends the metaphor to the FLP's own gifts -- financial grants, Supreme Court interviews, judges' tough questions, midnight dissertations, secretariat kindness -- as 'valuable little things' that may twist and turn careers more decisively than the formal honors. He closes with an AI-age credo: contrary to predictions, DiGi Age robots will not eliminate lawyers, because 'lawyers bred in liberty and prosperity... have the heart and the wisdom to dispense compassionate justice especially when the law is inadequate, unclear, or unconscionable.' And with one of his most explicit valedictory passages: in ten or twenty years, when the scholars are DiGi Age leaders, 'my spirit will be hovering above you, behind you, and beside you, smiling and contented, that I have brought you a few little things that made a vital difference in twisting and turning your lives and careers to build a just and humane society under the rule of law in the DiGi Age.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban celebrates 2019 bar exam top scorer Sean James Borja of Ateneo de Manila University, who 'frankly admitted he is gay' while debunking 'the myth that members of the LGBT are meant only for entertainment.' Despite having been 'bullied, discriminated against and deprived of opportunities just because he was thought to be not good enough, just because he was different,' Borja was selected -- along with 20 others -- when the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity's scholarship program launched in 2016, funded by the Tan Yan Kee Foundation at P200,000 per scholar per year. FLP, CJ writes in the institutional first person, 'did not treat him differently' but applied the same two requirements as for all applicants: academic excellence plus leadership, and the ability and willingness to internalize and espouse the philosophy of liberty and prosperity under the rule of law -- 'without any discrimination as to gender, race, color, religious belief, economic status or political affiliation.' Borja topped his class at Ateneo, won moot courts here and abroad, and now aces the bar, earning an additional P200,000 for topping the SC tests and P25,000 for being Ateneo valedictorian. Every member of the first graduating batch (2018) passed the 2019 bar, including Katrina Monica Gaw (AdMU, 5th place, P100,000), Karina Mae Badua, Ervin Fredrick Dy (UP, 17th), Rexlyn Anne Evora (PUP), Summerson Macasarte (St. Thomas More), Nigel Carmelo Reago (La Salle), Jose Angelo Tiglao (La Salle), Althea Vergara (USC), and Vanessa Gloria Vergara (AdMU); class toppers Evora, Reago, Macasarte, and former scholar Jose Noel Hilario (UST, cum laude) each receive P25,000. CJ rosters the ten current fourth-year and ten current third-year scholars by name and university, names the scholarship board of judges chaired by Justice Antonio T. Carpio, and reports the Ayala Corp.-funded Dissertation Writing Contest winners -- Josiah David Quising (FEU, P300,000 first), Diana Lou Boado (Lyceum, P200,000 second), three third-place finishers at P100,000 each (De Belen of San Beda, Lumbera of Lumsa Rome, Sawali of FEU), and five finalists at P20,000 each -- with a dissertation board chaired by Justice Estela M. Perlas-Bernabe. All recipients will be honored at the FLP convocation at AdMU's Rockwell auditorium at 5 p.m. on May 18, 2019. CJ closes with the line that integrates protected-class identity into a merit benediction: Borja is 'excellent, diligent, dignified and gay, and we're mighty proud of him!'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban features the essay of 1st-batch FLP LibPros scholar Sean Borja (Ateneo de Manila) -- abstracted in Borja's own words -- as the column's centerpiece. Borja begins with his vocational certainty since high school's junior year -- sparing him the millennial 'quarterlife crisis' -- but acknowledging that wanting to be a lawyer did not equal understanding what lawyers do. He grounds the answer in Article II Section 9 of the Constitution, which commands the state to 'promote a just and dynamic social order' ensuring prosperity, independence, and freedom from poverty -- making 'Prosperity for all' the goal of social justice. He cites SC jurisprudence: social justice does not champion division of property or equality of economic status but rather 'equality of opportunity, equality of political rights, equality before the law, equality between values given and received, and equitable sharing of the social and material goods on the basis of efforts exerted in their production' -- concluding that justice must be ENABLING, not merely benevolent, and that 'One without the other would simply not do.' He grounds the abstraction in the story of 'Little Prince' Lander Solano, a 9-year-old kesong puti vendor on Filmore Street in Makati who navigates alleys, flyovers, and underpasses daily 'in the company of thieves,' currently out of school but aspiring to engineering; his mother also vends kesong puti behind the Cash & Carry on Osmeña Highway where the family sleeps when goods remain unsold. Borja closes that the rule of law is 'the great equalizer' but 'without lawyers, the law is rendered fictional and out of reach, especially for those at the fringes of society' -- making the lawyer's mission to learn advocacy and 'become the voice that resonates when others go silent,' which gives the column its title.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban announces good news for law schools and law students: the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity (FLP), in cooperation with the Philippine Association of Law Schools (PALS), is sponsoring full scholarships and a dissertation writing contest. The scholarship program, cosponsored by the Tan Yan Kee Foundation, will start with 10 awardees and add 10 more each year, reaching 40 in four years; it covers tuition, a book allowance, a monthly stipend, and bar review expenses, and is open to third-year students from law schools whose 2014 bar passing percentage exceeds the overall -- list at libpros.com. The dissertation contest, cosponsored by the Ayala Group for five consecutive school years, is open to junior and senior law students nationwide; an FLP committee selects up to 20 entries (P20,000 each), a panel of judges prunes to 10, and the 10 shortlisted authors submit new entries from which 5 winners are chosen (1st P300,000; 2nd P200,000; 3 honorable mentions at P100,000 each). FLP was founded in 2011 to promote 'liberty and prosperity under the rule of law'; its ongoing flagship -- the Chief Justice Panganiban Professorial Chairs on Liberty and Prosperity, cosponsored by the Metrobank Foundation -- funds research and propagation of the philosophy at the academic level through 10 chair holders: Chancellor Adolfo S. Azcuna (PHILJA), Dean Sedfrey M. Candelaria (Ateneo), Dean Danilo L. Concepcion (UP), Dean Jose Manuel I. Diokno (DLSU), Dean Andres D. Bautista (FEU, now Comelec chair), Dean Mikhail Lee L. Maxino (Silliman), Dean Joan Sarausos-Largo (USC), Dean Nilo T. Divina (UST), Dean Reynaldo U. Agranzamendez (UC), and new Dean Melencio S. Sta. Maria (FEU). FLP envisions a society that understands and embraces 'the basic interdependence and mutual inclusiveness of the twin concepts of liberty and prosperity,' upholding 'justice and jobs, freedom and food, ethics and economics, democracy and development, liberty and prosperity' -- twin beacons that 'always go together; one is useless without the other.' Its eight philosophical principles articulate the platform: (1) deferential interpretation -- liberty cases favor people, economic cases defer to legislative/executive absent grave abuse; (2) conquer poverty by unleashing entrepreneurial genius via freedom and tools; (3) political leaders + private sector primarily responsible for developing economy, replaceable via elections; (4) private enterprise as engine of growth, government must promote and defend; (5) government must oversee fair/equitable wealth distribution especially to poor; (6) integrity, meritocracy, probity, creativity, and industry as treasured values; education as key to success and fulfillment; (7) transparency, accountability, and responsibility for government and publicly-listed companies; (8) discipline 'is not inconsistent with liberty, prosperity, or the rule of law' but necessary 'to safeguard liberty, nurture prosperity and promote the rule of law.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes a three-section dispatch column -- no overarching thesis, just three distinct topics joined by *** asterisk breaks: UN-WB Fastrac and Bangsamoro risks; Metrobank's Quanzhou-China branch inauguration; and the CJ Teehankee Foundation Rule of Law Awards conferred jointly on retired Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio-Herrera and CJP himself. The Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro forged last year was merely a road map, or a work in progress to attain peace and prosperity in Southern Philippines -- still to be fleshed out are four vital annexes that would lead to the enactment of a Bangsamoro basic law and the eventual creation of a Bangsamoro homeland (for details, see CJ's Oct 21, 2012, column). UN-WB Fastrac: most important, the creation of the homeland must be ratified by the people affected and must conform to the Constitution -- if it does not, the final agreement would be void, or the Constitution should be amended to obviate this dark possibility; yet, despite these still to be crafted essentials, the UN and the WB recently announced the 'Facility for Advisory Support for Transition Capacities (Fastrac),' described as 'a new technical assistance program to support the peace process and the establishment of the Bangsamoro.' In CJ's humble view, Fastrac is both good and bad -- good, because it may help hasten the peace process; it is a financial and technical program, a carrot, so to speak, to speed up the final negotiations, which have been shrouded in mystery during the past few months. It could be bad -- if the final accord fails or the SC for some reason finds it unconstitutional, the Philippines (given the UN-WB Fastrac and the active intervention of Malaysia in the peace negotiations) could be deemed to have recognized the MILF as a 'state of belligerency' which, in international law, grants some rights to the MILF and creates obligations and complications for our country; these legal and political possibilities deserve a future column. Metrobank in China: at Metrobank's invitation, CJ attended last week the inauguration of its branch in Quanzhou, a city in the suburb of (but much bigger and more populous than) Xiamen or Amoy; Quanzhou is the birthplace of Dr George S.K. Ty, Metrobank's founder and patriarch; Metrobank is the only Philippine bank granted a full service banking license in China. Leading the participants were Speaker Feliciano Belmonte Jr., Chinese Ambassador Ma Keqing, and Metrobank top executives Arthur Ty, Mary V. Ty, Alfred Ty, Antonio Abacan, Francis Sebastian and Aniceto Sobrepeña; all the local Chinese officials lauded Metrobank for being the first foreign bank to operate in Quanzhou (and in Nanjing, a city near Shanghai). Filipinos are well regarded in Xiamen -- Henry Sy's SM operates the biggest shopping mall there; John Gokongwei's Robinsons Land and Lucio Tan's Eton Properties are building huge real estate complexes in the city's central district, similar to Ayala Center and Rockwell in Makati; Carlos Chan's Oishi products are sold all over China, especially in Xiamen; Jollibee operates three large Chinese fast-food chains; notably, China built a statue of Jose Rizal in nearby Jinjang, similar to but bigger than the one in Luneta. Rule of Law Awards: may CJ thank the CJ Claudio Teehankee Foundation for conferring on retired Justice Ameurfina A. Melencio-Herrera and CJ the 'Rule of Law Award' during elegant ceremonies held at the Center for the Rule of Law at the Ateneo de Manila. Now 91, Justice Amor, as CJ fondly calls her, was cited '[f]or her dignified obedience to universal concepts of justice, her pioneering spirit as the second woman appointed to the SC, her academic accomplishments commencing from her being valedictorian and cum laude of UP Law Class of 1947 and bar topnotcher, her heading the Philippine Judicial Academy as First Chancellor, and her developing the Academy into the institution it is today that concretely furthers the cause of an independent bench and bar devoted to excellence and legal learning in the service of the greater good, all of which contribute towards a more stable and lasting Rule of Law.' To that citation, may CJ add that had seniority been strictly observed, she could have easily been the first lady chief justice of our country -- she was named associate justice in 1979, but as an aftermath of the 1986 Edsa Revolution, all SC justices resigned; recognizing her integrity and independence, President Cory Aquino reappointed her (along with a few others), but her reappointment was dated a little later than those of new Justices Pedro L. Yap, Marcelo B. Fernan and Andres R. Narvasa who -- appearing to be her seniors based on their appointment papers -- all later became chief justices despite their lesser years of actual service in the Court; Yap served barely two years before being elevated to the top; when Justice Amor retired in 1992, Narvasa was still chief -- despite all these seeming setbacks, she served with gentility and grace, without rancor or recrimination. CJ will just quote without comment the citation given him: 'For his exemplary service in the Philippine SC culminating in his leadership of the whole Philippine Judiciary, for his lifelong commitment and service to a judicial philosophy that is based on Liberty and Prosperity, for his continued advocacy of the need to have a judiciary with independence, integrity, industry and intelligence, a revitalization of the legal profession in the tradition of its noble roots, and a philosophy promoting the twin goals of safeguarding liberty while assuring the prosperity of all citizens, as liberty is an empty vessel without economic equity, all of which contribute towards a more stable and lasting Rule of Law.'

one_paragraph_summary: Following the big-business Integrity Initiative (Makati Business Club, MAP, ECCI, AmCham, AIM Hills Program), Panganiban argues that the culture of integrity must reach the grassroots: SMEs (micro/small/medium enterprises) constitute 99.6% of all businesses, employ 63.2% of the labor force, and account for 35.7% of total sales -- yet are the favorite victims of petty grafters. The column catalogs normalized petty-corruption examples: bribes for sari-sari permits, health clearances, customs releases, tax assessment reductions, fire-extinguisher rackets from 'pre-cleared' suppliers, and traffic violations. The AIM Hills Program on Governance recommends seven practices: (1) prohibit bribery in any form, communicated to all stakeholders; (2) gifts/entertainment policy with nominal-value limits and a central register; (3) conflict-of-interest disclosure form; (4) Code of Conduct with incentives and penalties; (5) periodic anti-corruption training from hire; (6) transparent systems, accurate books, official receipts; and (7) correct tax declarations, using verbal scripts to resist bribe demands ('My company has a very strict policy' / 'It is against my religion to pay bribes'). The column closes with a direct challenge to PCCI president Francis Chua -- who accepted in response to last Sunday's column -- to launch an SME anti-corruption drive at the PCCI national conference.

one_paragraph_summary: Digressing from the trade-and-investment purpose of taipans accompanying Aquino to China, Panganiban surveys their passion for education philanthropy. Gokongwei celebrated his 85th birthday with P250M to DLSU (Gokongwei College of Engineering) and P15M to AGAPP for 18 preschool buildings -- gamely joking that his 80th gift of P200M to Ateneo is roughly equal to the 85th gift when adjusted for inflation. The late Ramon V. del Rosario was honored posthumously by DLSU with a renamed business college; his Phinma Group (now under Hilado and del Rosario Jr.) controls four provincial universities and grants 1,000 teacher scholarships. Washington SyCip received the Order of Lakandula (rank of bayani) at age 90 for the Synergeia Foundation's basic-education work; he co-founded AIM with Ayala Corp and the Eugenio Lopez Foundation. Oscar Lopez (81) donated P25M to refurbish AIM and land for two Ateneo professional schools. School owners include Henry Sy (NU), Lucio Tan (UE), Yuchengco (Mapua), and Emilio Yap (CEU). Tony and Grace Tan Caktiong's Jollibee Foundation runs the Busog Lusog Talino feeding program in 232 schools plus Don Bosco technical training. The centerpiece is George Ty's Metrobank Foundation: the annual Search for Outstanding Teachers, with P350,000 prizes for each of 10 winners (this year conferred at Malacañang by Aquino), P100M total annual grant, and a NOTED network of 306 teacher-awardees since 1997.

one_paragraph_summary: Pivoting from his four-part stem-cell series, CJ Panganiban applies the rejuvenation framework to Baguio City. He opens with the personal memory of 1950s-1960s Baguio -- pine scents, crystal-clear water in Burnham Park, rolling green Mines View mountains 'reminiscent of The Sound of Music' -- and the half-century collapse into 'obfuscating exhaust... crowded, traffic-choked streets, scalded mountains and murky waters.' Three pieces of good news anchor the recovery thesis. First, Mayor Benjamin Magalong wants to remake Baguio on the Singapore model -- the only urban site that has, through law and regulation, replicated the longevity outcomes of the rural Blue Zones (Sardinia, Okinawa, Nicoya, Ikaria, Loma Linda) via congestion fees during peak hours, city-spanning trams cheaper than cars, high car taxes capped at one unit per person, tax incentives for green buildings, and mixed-sector apartment structures. Second, BCDA v. CJH Development (April 3, 2024, en banc, 15-0, J Japar B. Dimaampao) upheld the arbitral order evicting CJH Development from a 247-hectare portion of the John Hay Special Economic Zone, with the Court extensively quoting Adapon v. Medical Doctors (June 14, 2021, J Leonen) that arbitral awards cannot be set aside 'for mere errors of judgment either as to the law or as to the facts' -- affirming arbitration finality as the operative doctrine. Third, the MVP Group, through its subsidiary Landco Pacific Corp., has committed to the interim management of The Manor, Forest Lodge, and the CAMP-John Hay Trade and Cultural Center while BCDA president Joshua M. Bingcang transitions the properties to long-term private partners. CJ closes with the bridging metaphor that ties this piece to the stem-cell series: rejuvenating Baguio is like 'infusing the autologous needles and injecting the living cell therapy into an aging city to rejuvenate, refresh, and reengineer it to a fresh new start. Mabuhay!'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes a tribute-column for retired Senior Associate Justice Antonio T. Carpio, 'one of the most formidable defenders of Philippine sovereignty.' A week ago, at the turnover ceremony of the historic '1875 Carta General del Archipiélago Filipino' map to the National Library, SAJ Tony calmly but firmly urged the government to file a new arbitration case against China -- this time over the blatant denial of PH fishermen's rights at Scarborough Shoal. The clarion call surprises no one familiar with his career. He served with distinction on the SC for 18 years; for almost a decade he was the longest-serving SAJ (a distinct law-granted rank for the sitting Court member serving longest among current colleagues). So respected was he that he was often called the 'Chief Justice we never had' -- time and again, when the CJ was absent or incapacitated, SAJ Tony stepped in as acting chief, guiding the Court with 'quiet authority and unassailable integrity.' Yet it is what he did after retirement that truly elevates him to the heroic rank. Most justices fade gracefully into private life upon mandatory retirement -- not SAJ Tony. He made a different and far more demanding choice: to dedicate the full weight of his remaining years to the defense of our waters. He has remained a vocal, independent figure, emphasizing the rule of law, UNCLOS, and multilateral approaches to the maritime dispute, often positioning the PH case as benefiting the international community. His postretirement work is nonpartisan and advocacy-driven rather than commercial or judicial. During the March 23 2026 Association of Retired Justices of the SC meeting, CJP -- as president -- paid tribute. A few years ago, during a reception for a retiring colleague, one of the 10 wealthiest Filipinos approached Carpio in CJP's presence and offered him a seat as independent director in his conglomerate. He politely declined: 'Thank you, but sorry I cannot accept because I want to devote my full time, energy, and resources to defending Philippine sovereignty in the West Philippine Sea.' The answer stunned the offeror, who could hardly believe his offer -- which included substantial per diems and bonuses -- would be declined. Carpio is the most articulate and relentless champion of the 2016 Arbitral Award -- the landmark victory affirming PH sovereignty and sovereign rights over the West Philippine Sea. He does not do it for power or popularity. He does it because he believes, as every true patriot must, that the international rule of law is the only shield of smaller nations against the world's superpowers. Why does this matter to ordinary Filipinos? Because fishing rights are not abstract legal concepts -- they are the daily bread of thousands of fishermen whose livelihoods depend on rich waters. When blocked, it is not merely a diplomatic tiff but an assault on their right to feed their families. It is about liberty -- freedom to navigate territorial waters without fear and harassment. It is about overflight -- the right of PH aircraft to fly over waters indisputably ours. And it is about prosperity -- the sovereign right to explore and develop oil, gas, and other resources within the exclusive economic zone, including the promising Reed Bank, which SAJ Tony has repeatedly bemoaned has remained untapped due to outside forces. These are the foundations of national dignity and economic survival. In an era when some would rather take the opposite view, SAJ Tony stands as a beacon of principled resistance, reminding us that true friendship among nations is built on mutual respect for the law, not on the surrender of sovereign rights. The government may not have acted yet on his recommendation for a new case. But history will record that when others wavered, one man -- retired from active government service -- never stopped fighting with the same intellectual rigor and patriotic fire that defined his judicial career. Some may oppose his assertions -- that is their right in our democracy. In a similar way, though CJP praises him for his relentlessness and patriotism, CJP did not always agree with him: when both were incumbents, they clashed on his advocacy for the death penalty, while CJP fearlessly opposed it as violative of the Constitution and God's commands. He shows strength not through force, but through the calm and principled exercise of due process, grounded in respect for the rule of law and international covenants. Critics may disagree with him, but his wisdom and unwavering research are more than enough to prevail in any international tribunal. SAJ Tony had left the bench, but he has never left the battlefield for the country. For that, our people owe him a debt of gratitude. He remains a relentless defender of Philippine sovereignty -- a modern-day hero.

one_paragraph_summary: CJP characterizes RA 6713 (Ethical Standards Law) as the 'Bible' of public officials alongside the Constitution + Anti-Graft Law (RA 3019) + Law of Forfeiture of Ill-Gotten Wealth (RA 1379), arguing that the pork-barrel + trillion-peso-legislative-insertion + flood-control scams could have been prevented and the crooks penalized by its strict enforcement, especially by the OMB and Civil Service Commission. Crediting his guru the late Senate President Salonga and the late Sen. Saguisag as co-sponsors (Feb 20 1989 approval), he structures the column in three parts. On norms and duties: (a) public-interest-over-personal + efficient-effective-honest-economic, (b) just-and-sincere especially-for-the-poor, (c) no-undue-favors-to-relatives except strictly-confidential/coterminous staff, (d) no-discrimination-by-party-affiliation -- with the highlighted duty that officials and families 'shall live modest lives appropriate to their positions and income,' plus specific obligations (15-working-day response + three-signature processing + accessible documents). On prohibited acts: financial-interest-in-office-transactions + employment in regulated private enterprises + unauthorized private practice + recommendations to private enterprises with pending official transactions -- continuing for one year post-separation. SALNs must be filed within 30 days of assumption, annually by April 30, and within 30 days of separation, covering officials + spouses + unmarried minor children in household. Penalties graduate from administrative (fine/suspension/removal) to criminal (imprisonment ≤ 5 years + fine ≤ P5,000 + disqualification), with OMB administrative proceedings sufficient for removal even without criminal prosecution and private-individual conspirators tried jointly with public officials.

one_paragraph_summary: Inverting the usual stereotype, Panganiban argues that the Philippine Supreme Court and the Catholic Church -- traditional bulwarks of conservatism -- are moving progressively on a 'rocky road to liberalism,' while the US Supreme Court (Scotus), traditional bastion of liberalism, has turned conservative. The PH SC's liberal trek is illustrated by Republic v Ng (Feb 27, 2024, J Dimaampao, en banc, 13-2), which recognized foreign divorces -- even by administrative process or mutual agreement (as practiced in Japan and Korea) -- by reading Article 26(2) of the Family Code according to its spirit and intent (sparing Filipino spouses from disadvantage when foreign spouses are already free to remarry), and by Pulido v People (July 27, 2021, J Hernando, en banc, 15-0), which acquitted an accused of bigamy even without a judicial declaration of nullity of a void-ab-initio first marriage (though judicial declaration is still needed for remarriage and civil-rights questions like heirship). CJ is surprised that 13 insider-justices trended liberal, with only two outsiders (UP, DOJ) predictably liberal. The Catholic Church has likewise been liberalizing -- Vatican II (1962-1965) made it more humane and ecumenical (vernacular masses, priests facing the faithful), PCP2 implemented this in the Philippines, Pope John Paul II carried it forward, and Pope Francis as the first non-European pontiff is even more determined; his Sept 13 Singapore extemporaneous remarks ('All religions are paths to reach God... God is God for all, then we are all children of God') will 'rock the rafters' and intensify traditionalist opposition. By contrast, Scotus tipped from 5-4 to 6-3 conservative with Trump's three appointees (Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, Barrett), and Dobbs v Jackson (June 24, 2022) reversed Roe v Wade (Jan 22, 1973). Combined with immigration, democracy, jobs, and the economy, abortion has turned the Nov 5 Harris-Trump contest into 'acrimonious combat between liberals and conservatives' whose ramifications will shake the wars in Ukraine, Gaza, and Lebanon, the tensions in the North and South China Sea, and the Israel-Iran standoff. CJ's fervent hope is that liberalism not become 'licentiousness' subverting the rule of law, and that conservatism not become Hitler-style Nazism violating individual liberty -- but he is 'terrified by the rants of Trump that, if elected, he would become a dictator. Heaven forbid!'

The minority of five contended that criminal intent had not been proven and is looking for another similar case to prevail when the Court's composition changes. CJ's simple advice to husbands: infidelity is 'dangerous to life and liberty' -- though RA 9262 punishes only philandering husbands and is sub-silentio on philandering wives. On abortion, hot in the US presidential campaign, CJ notes the battle is passé in the Philippines because abortion is barred by the Constitution and criminalized by law; the only question is when life begins. Imbong v Ochoa (April 9, 2014, J Mendoza, en banc, 11-1-3, 106 pages) ruled that 'a zygote is a human organism' and 'the life of a new human being commences... upon fertilization,' explicitly rejecting Rep. Edcel Lagman's implantation theory; constitutional framers Bernardo M. Villegas and (later CJ) Hilario G. Davide Jr. had stressed protection 'from the moment of conception,' and the right to life is 'grounded on natural law,' inherent and not a creation of statute. Consequently, health professionals cannot be forced to use post-fertilization devices or drugs; some theologians prescribe only the 'rhythm method.' On PCP2, CJ disclaims canon-law expertise but quotes Article 28: lay men and women in responsible positions must help form the civic conscience and promote leaders of true integrity, while bishops, priests, and religious must refrain from partisan politics -- especially from using the pulpit for partisan purposes -- per Canons 287 #2 and 672. Further questions, he says, may be addressed to a canon lawyer or by buying the P308 paperback of the 'Acts and Decrees' from St. Paul's Superstore in San Antonio Village, Makati.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the companion-column to his March 23 2026 'Why not Cecile, Lea, and Lisa,' pivoting from the wonderment-complaint about three super ladies (Cecile Licad, Lea Salonga, Lisa Macuja-Elizalde) not being recognized as National Artists toward a legal-framework survey and a concrete policy proposal. The National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) -- created by RA 7356 on April 3 1992 -- administers the NA conferment. Together with the Cultural Center of the Philippines (CCP), NCCA holds the sole prerogative under that law to recommend to the President the 'Order of National Artists' for Filipino citizens who have contributed to building a Filipino sense of nationhood through their art forms. In Almario v. Executive Secretary (July 16 2013), the SC held the President's discretion is limited to the names submitted by NCCA and CCP -- the President cannot confer the Order on anyone not in the final list. CJP will no longer inquire nor belabor his 'wonderment' why -- despite Cecile's universal excellence in music, Lea's triumphs on the world's most prestigious stages, and Lisa's influence through ballet worldwide -- these ladies have not landed in the final list. Without begrudging any of the NAs or belittling their achievements (in fact lauding them for their much-deserved awards), CJP believes Cecile, Lea, and Lisa merit a separate category recognizing distinction that transcends national recognition. Each has long been part of NA discussions. What becomes evident is the presence of an institutional gap where recognition for globally-distinguished Filipino artists ought to stand. The President can fill this gap by creating the 'Order of Global Filipino Artists' or GFA via executive order, specifically for artists of Philippine ancestry (one or both parents Filipino at the birth of the awardee), with privileges and honors equal to or better than NAs. In time, Congress may institutionalize this category. Marcos Sr. initiated the NA Award via Proclamation No. 1001 (April 27 1972), refined by Proclamation No. 1144 (May 15 1973) and Presidential Decree No. 208 (June 7 1973). Marcos Sr. likewise issued Proclamation No. 1151 (June 7 1973), establishing the 'Award and Decoration for International Artists' for foreign talents contributing to Philippine arts/culture, premised on 'the arts and letters are universal media of expression free of the confines of geography and nationality.' In 1976/1977, pianist Van Cliburn (USA), prima ballerina Margot Fonteyn (UK), and ballet dancer Rudolf Nureyev (USSR/France) were the first proclaimed; in 1982, Russian cellist/conductor Mstislav Rostropovich was recognized following his CCP performance. In this light, the notion of an 'International Artist' must be reimagined -- the current framework does not fully recognize Filipino artists who belong to a distinct class, the Filipino diaspora, whose contributions are acclaimed both within our shores and across the globe: the Global Filipino Artists. After the GFA honor is created by executive fiat and the super ladies selected as the first GFAs, the conferment should be held at Malacañan Palace, the CCP, or PICC -- 'the very institutions that have long stood as the sanctuaries of our artistic heritage.' The President may fittingly invite the three GFAs to perform and transform the conferment into a living testament to Filipino excellence before both the nation and the world. The question is no longer whether they are worthy -- they have long proven that they are. The more compelling inquiry is whether our institutional frameworks can welcome a new dimension of artistic excellence that is global in reach, yet unmistakably, indelibly Filipino in essence.
