one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens his National Women's Month column spotlighting three performing-arts women, back-referencing his Oct 11 2015 'Women power at SC rites' (judiciary) and Jan 26 2026 'Seven empowered women' (private corporate sector) -- explaining he spotlights these women not because they need it (they have long shone brightly), but to share his opinion on why they deserve the highest recognition from the country they have honored. Three women have consistently lifted the Philippine flag higher than most ever dreamed possible. Inexplicably, the Order of National Artist has yet to be conferred on child prodigy Cecile Licad, Broadway icon Lea Salonga, and prima ballerina Lisa Macuja-Elizalde. With due respect to NCCA and CCP, the time has come to right this oversight. These women are living embodiments of Filipino excellence who have earned the respect and admiration of the world; to withhold from them the title of 'National Artist' is to deny ourselves the pride we so richly deserve. Cecile Licad -- at seven formally debuted, at 20 won the prestigious Leventritt Gold Medal in New York (first Filipino) -- has stunned audiences with her interpretations of Chopin, Rachmaninoff, and Tchaikovsky, performing with the Philippine Philharmonic, New York Philharmonic, and London Philharmonic. Critics have called her 'a pianist's pianist.' Per business leader Lin Ilusorio Bildner, 'she inspired young musicians through master classes and benefit concerts.' Her artistry is not loud; it is profound -- reflecting discipline, intellect, and a love for music that transcends borders. Lea Salonga -- from 'The King and I' at a tender age, has grown into a global phenomenon: first Asian to win the Tony Award for Best Actress in a Musical ('Miss Saigon'), first to voice two Disney princesses (Mulan and Jasmine), recipient of an Olivier, a Drama Desk, and countless other honors; sold-out concerts across continents; recently honored with a star in the Hollywood Walk of Fame Class of 2026, on which CJP and his family strolled during the holidays. Lea did not simply 'make it' abroad; she carried the Philippines with her. Every time she sang, she held audiences in breathless silence only to release them into acclamation at the final note. She has opened doors for countless young talents across international and local theaters -- quite simply, a national gem. Lisa Macuja-Elizalde -- the first Filipina to become a prima ballerina in an international classical company and the first foreign soloist ever accepted into Russia's legendary Kirov Ballet. For decades she has danced the great classical roles with unmatched grace and power. Upon returning home, she founded Ballet Manila and brought world-class ballet to ordinary Filipinos. Late Sen. Miriam Defensor-Santiago authored a Senate resolution nominating Lisa for National Artist in recognition of her immense contributions to Philippine culture and arts and for bringing ballet closer to Filipinos' hearts -- 14 years ago. Since then, Lisa has continued to serve with the same passion, now celebrating her 40th homecoming milestone. Why do these three matter so much during Women's Month? Because they prove that Filipino women do not need to wait for permission to conquer the world. They studied, sacrificed, competed against the best, and won the hearts of Filipinos longing for a sense of national pride. They have become role models not only for girls who dream of the stage or the concert hall but for every Filipino who believes excellence has no gender. The Order of National Artists was created precisely to honor such individuals while they are still alive and able to inspire. We have rightly honored the late Lucrecia Kasilag, Andrea Veneracion, and others. But living legends walk among us. The existing selection criteria must be screened with fresh eyes -- allowing layers of judgment to shed the limiting weight of the past. To proclaim Cecile, Lea, and Lisa now would send a powerful message that we value our artists, that we refuse to take their light for granted, and that women who bring glory to the nation deserve the nation's highest artistic accolade. CJP respectfully urges the NCCA, the CCP, and Malacañang to consider this humble opinion. The world already knows their worth. It is time the Philippines officially does too.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban offers a sympathetic but exacting profile of the Independent Commission for Infrastructure under chair ret. SC Justice Andres Reyes Jr., with members former DPWH Secretary Rogelio Singson and SGV country managing partner Rossana Fajardo (Baguio Mayor Benjamin Magalong has resigned as special adviser). Their assignment is to help and facilitate -- not interfere with -- the OMB and DOJ in the flood-control accountability drive, but they confront 24/7 workloads, 16,000 forwarded complaints plus thousands more, no existing organizational backup, suits questioning the ICI's very creation, and contractor cohorts with the financial, political, and physical means to hire the best legal, financial, accounting, tax, banking, and PR experts against them. As public officials sworn before the President, they must disclose financial and business interests, divest from personal investments, resign from outside undertakings, and accept Salary-Standardization compensation; CJ goes further, urging them to publish their SALNs on the ICI website regardless of any agency restrictions and to voluntarily include in those SALNs a waiver of bank-secrecy. He acknowledges that even good-faith disclosure cannot be perfect -- relatives can be scrutinized, weaponized, and used as pressure points -- and that commissioners and their families must be ready to forego their privacy under the microscopes, telescopes, and 'killer apps' of modern tri-media and social media, including long-forgotten indiscretions deployed for political horse-trading. The column closes on the constitutional reminder that public office is a public trust requiring modest lives, and a working-toolkit prescription: always carry the Constitution, Ombudsman Law, Anti-Graft Law, Anti-Plunder Law, Ethical Standards Law, Revised Penal Code, and the Administrative Code.

one_paragraph_summary: Picking up the rhetorical question left open in A62 " why China militarizes the SCS in defiance of UNCLOS and the 2016 Arbitral Award, and why the US (a non-signatory) enforces freedom of navigation in the SCS with allies Australia, France, Germany, and Great Britain -- CJ Panganiban delivers his master answer: national interest. 'All states, including the Philippines, always act to protect and project what is beneficial to them and to their people. National interest is not constant. It shifts according to the present and future political, economic, security, and social aspirations.' He maps the doctrine across three jurisdictions. For China: decades of school-and-media indoctrination that the SCS and its fisheries belong to it have now locked in popular expectation -- 'any Chinese leader who refuses or neglects to protect and project this teaching would be deemed a traitor or a nincompoop to be ousted summarily' -- and a civilizational backdrop of robust history antedating Western powers that 'enslaved' it under long-term leases (Hong Kong, Macau) fuels its 'meteoric rise' to second-largest economy and its ambition to dominate the Pacific via SCS supremacy, in the process crossing the maritime entitlements of Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and the Philippines. For the US: an 80-year arc from neutrality (covertly aiding Europeans before Hitler's Sept. 1, 1939 Polish blitzkrieg) to full entry via Pearl Harbor (Dec. 7, 1941) → German and Japanese (Sept. 2, 1945) surrender → Pax Americana global expansion making American-style democracy, libertarianism, capitalism, and free trade the operative national interest → trillions spent in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan, Iraq 'much of it borrowed domestically and, ironically, from China.' But on Nov. 5, 2024, Americans 'got tired of being the peacekeepers of the world and of gradually losing economic dominance to the surging Chinese': Donald Trump's MAGA victory advances allies-share-the-cost and mass-deportation as the new national-interest formula -- 'Verily, he loves being a disruptor.' For the Philippines: a see-saw -- in 2016, Filipinos tired of compromise-and-free-elections under 'imperial Manila' dynasties welcomed Duterte's autocratic China-pivot abandoning US protection; six-year term limit reset; Marcos Jr.'s 2022 landslide -- 'an absolute majority (well over 50 percent) of the ballots cast' for the first time under the 1987 Constitution -- restored the US alliance for WPS protection. 'With his overwhelming mandate, President Marcos can indeed lead in the protection and projection of our national interest vis-à-vis our Asean neighbors, China, the US, and the world.'

one_paragraph_summary: Reporting on Donald Trump's stunning Nov. 5, 2024 sweep" Pennsylvania (19 electoral votes), Arizona (11), Georgia (16), Nevada (6), North Carolina (16), Michigan (15), Wisconsin (10), the national popular vote by over five million, and both the US Senate and House of Representatives -- CJ Panganiban confesses he 'miserably lost a bet of P50,000 to be donated to a charity' that the winner would designate, having prognosticated 'at least 2.1 days before the winner could be known' based on polls and pundits all of whom Trump's victory shamed. Trump's 'America First' agenda now has full legislative runway, including his vow to chase 'the enemy within' and to call on the national guards and the military 'to neutralize them.' The election raises the comparative question of US readiness for a woman president -- 'the misogynist triumphed over two women democrats, Hillary Clinton in 2016 and Kamala Harris in 2024' (though he lost to Biden in 2020, never conceding), 'a blessing that had rained on the Philippines twice (Cory Aquino and Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo), and in many other democracies like India (Indira Gandhi), Pakistan (Benazir Bhutto), United Kingdom (Margaret Thatcher).' The transition-norm asymmetry is sharp: in 2024 Biden gamely called and welcomed the transition team, whereas in 2020 Trump, as the losing incumbent, refused that tradition and instead called MAGA cohorts to storm the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, damning Mike Pence (the constitutional presiding officer of the Senate) for not stopping the certification of Biden. The 'consuelo de bobo' is that the volatile former president's promised post-election 'mayhem' did not materialize. On the legal front, Scotus justices can now 'rest easy without any risk of being impeached or censured' because Republicans control both chambers -- yet 'none of the justices had the delicadeza (decency) to recuse on the cases affecting Trump, especially on the grant of almost complete immunity for all his public acts as president in 2017-2021,' despite documented enormous gifts, paid vacations (Bali, Monte Rio in California), private clubs, planes, yachts, and one justice's upside-down American flag at two homes signaling Trump sympathy (per CJ's June 16 column 'From awe to dismay at the Scotus'). Jack Smith's pending cases face post-inauguration dismissal as Trump promises to fire him; the 34 NYC convictions for false statements concealing Stormy Daniels payments are scheduled for Nov. 26 sentencing -- 'Will the judge dare punish the convicted felon with multiple imprisonment? Or will he take the cowardly way?' Trump has also pledged to pardon Jan. 6 cohorts and, if convicted, 'he would pardon himself! Incredible. Only in the US of A!' CJ closes: 'I cannot believe these unimaginable judicial malfeasances can happen... in Donald Trump's land of the free and the home of the brave. I am totally discombobulated.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban traces the cascade of government-agency actions against Bamban, Tarlac Mayor Alice Guo arising from the Senate-House Pogo investigations. The Senate committees 'ably chaired' by Sen. Win Gatchalian and Sen. Risa Hontiveros and House counterparts 'started ominously' and 'riveted' on Bamban's Pogos, implicating Guo. President Marcos then delivered 'an inspired off-script finale' in his July 22 SONA announcing an absolute ban on Pogos. Both Houses of Congress may conduct inquiries 'in aid of legislation' and require testimony, with contempt-and-detention power for uncooperative witnesses (as exercised against Guo for repeated subpoena failures), but they 'can merely recommend' criminal prosecutions or civil-liability recoveries. The President may act independently for 'overarching public interest' but -- IMHO -- should issue an executive order detailing the ban; as chief executive, he has power to modify or reverse subaltern licensing actions. The OSG, official legal counsel of the Republic and 'tribune of the people' (free to refuse representing erring agencies), brought quo warranto in RTC Manila to oust Guo and bar her perpetually for lack of Philippine citizenship, with appeals RTC → CA → SC. The OMB, as 'protectors of the people,' issued orders suspending then removing Guo; OMB admin cases appeal to CA, criminal cases filed in Sandiganbayan. The 'amiable' BIR Commissioner Romeo Lumagui Jr. went beyond mere tax assessment to file a criminal complaint for tax evasion in DOJ. Comelec investigates Guo for election-law violations (citizenship misrepresentation in COC, a criminal offense); BI watch-listed her with possible summary deportation; NBI and PAOCC charged her with human trafficking; AMLC convinced the CA to freeze her bank deposits and assets. CJ closes with two comments. one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban catalogues Donald Trump's unique status as the 'MOST SUIT-able PRESIDENTIAL ASPIRANT' -- never in storied US history has any aspirant been as legally and politically vilified, yet he overwhelmingly leads the GOP nomination and edges incumbent Joe Biden in general-election polls. CJ focuses on two sets of legal threats. First, as he expected in his Sept 4, 2023 column 'Prosecuting and disqualifying Trump,' the Supreme Court of Colorado (4-3) and the Maine Secretary of State have banned Trump from their respective GOP nomination processes under Section 3 of the 14th Amendment, which bars from public office any person who 'engaged in insurrection or rebellion against the [US], or given aid or comfort to [its] enemies.' Trump's appeal to Scotus argues five defenses: the prohibition covers 'person' and 'public office' but not 'candidates for president'; the Jan 6, 2021 Capitol attack was not insurrection; Trump had no role in it; his verbal outbursts were First-Amendment-protected; the ban requires a prior criminal conviction; and the amendment is functus officio because its Confederacy-targeting purpose has been accomplished. His 'presidential immunity' defense would put him 'beyond the reach of the rule of law' -- 'Tell that to the marines!' one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban marks May 1 Labor Day by addressing the two perennial demands that 'multiplied and amplified' beyond May 1, 2023 - increase the minimum wage and abolish contractualization. The Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Boards, delegated by Congress under Republic Act No. 6727, fix region-specific minimum wages through tripartite (government-employer-worker) public hearings - currently NCR P570 (nonagricultural), BARMM P341 (lowest), with agricultural workers 'getting even less,' while Senate and House bills propose nationwide increases of P150-P750/day. While agreeing that wages should be maximized as much as possible, Panganiban disagrees that Congress should legislate across-the-board increases - this 'knee-jerk' reaction contravenes the wisdom of depoliticizing wages and ignores varying regional economic and labor conditions, since 'a one-size-fits-all response is never wise or beneficial in the long term.' He concurs with the Foundation for Economic Freedom that the bills 'do not take into consideration the varying local and industry conditions,' and further argues the wage boards have been 'wickedly slow' in adjusting wages - restrictions like once-a-year adjustment make them 'decadent relics.' If Congress must respond, it should amend wage-board authority, duties, and powers rather than 'directly interfering in a framework that has withstood the test of time and only needs to be empowered to meet new and unforeseen expansions in this AI age.' Moreover, the government - especially Congress - 'should also look into its own backyard and maximize the pay of government employees': 'Why should the private sector carry solely the burden of easing the pains of our people?' The government should 'walk its talk' instead of 'muscling with its raw power.' As to the economists' inflationary objection, Inquirer chair Raul J. Palabrica's column (5/2/23) noted that the government's multibillion-yearly subsidy programs (P20.5 billion in 2023) have not triggered unexpected inflation - so reasonable wage increases' inflationary effect 'can be solved by our economists.' Abolition of contractualization, on the other hand, is 'good only for grandstanding' and 'stands no chance of success' because seasonal (harvest farmworkers) and project-oriented (masons, carpenters on a specific house) jobs are legitimate, and 'even past president Rodrigo Duterte, despite his election braggadocio of abolishing contractualization, did not and simply could not fulfill his election promise.' But the abuse via 'endo' or '5-5-5' - services ended after a 5-month probationary period and rehired in 'endless cycles of five months' to evade the 6-month regularization requirement - is 'an abhorrent and illegal circumvention of the law.' Per CJ's prior columns (latest March 27, 2022), the Philippine Constitution, Congress, and Supreme Court have been more protective and promotive of labor than the US Constitution, US Congress, and US Supreme Court. Conclusion: 'while legal contractualization cannot be abolished, it should be minimized only to what is truly legal and constitutional.'

On Cha-cha, CJ Panganiban brands the House's 301-6-1 con-con resolution a 'sneaky attempt to overhaul, not just amend or revise, the Constitution' -- turning on Rep. Rufus B. Rodriguez's TV-interview admission to Karen Davila that, once convened, a con-con cannot be limited to economic provisions and may install a federal-parliamentary system and 'infinite term extensions for lawmakers and other politicians.' Robinhood Padilla's 'laser surgery' metaphor -- and avoiding the multibillion-peso cost of con-con delegate elections, salaries, per diems, allowances, and transportation. Puno's full Consultative Commission recommendations including federalism (even though CJ himself disagrees) rather than disguising the overhaul. On the ICC follow-up to A115, CJ reports support from 'a top judiciary incumbent, a brilliant Cabinet member, and several other readers' for the independent-panel proposal modeled on Ferdinand Marcos Sr.'s 1983 Agrava Board (with Narvasa and Tan Jr. as general-counsel templates), and answers the common objection -- 'are there enough independent and credible citizens?' -- with concrete name-lists: 13 retired jurists fit to head the panel (Abad, Azcuna, Bellosillo, Perlas-Bernabe, Callejo Sr., Carandang, Del Castillo, Gutierrez, Jardeleza, Mendoza, Reyes Jr., Minerva Reyes, Vitug), 31 nominees from business/professions/youth/NGOs, and 7 candidates for the two general-counsel slots (Bautista, Concepcion, Divina, Espinosa, Poblador, Prodigalidad, Villanueva). one_paragraph_summary: Provoked by the Cha-cha hearings, Panganiban turns the dynasty debate from prohibition to formation. He sides with framer Christian Monsod that Congress should first discharge its long-ignored mandate under Article II, Section 26 to define political dynasties -- but answers his own question on why it has never done so: the presidency and Congress have always been dominated by dynasties, placed there knowingly by the electorate. He inventories every Philippine president since 1987 -- all dynastic except Fidel V. Ramos -- naming the Aquino, Estrada, Arroyo, Duterte, and Marcos lineages, and observes that Congress is 'littered with dynasties' (Villars, Cayetanos, Binays, Gatchalians) without calling them 'evil per se.' He widens the lens: Thailand venerates its king under lèse-majesté, Japan its emperor with God-like reverence, Malaysia its sultans and the Yang di-Pertuan Agong. Business conglomerates such as Ayala have succeeded by training their heirs; physicians and lawyers want their children to inherit their practices; ordinary elders want their heirs to absorb 'native ways and folksy wisdom.' He discloses that he dreamed of transmitting his Chief Justice legacy to his heirs but, since none became lawyers, he formed the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity to perpetuate his legacy and philosophy. His thesis: dynasts are here to stay -- 'in the historical genes' of the Filipino people -- so the better course is to transform dynasty into legacy, with forebears leading by example and inculcating in the next generation 'the culture of excellence, integrity, prudence, and humility,' preparing them not only for the here and now but for the hereafter. The civic counterweight is equally important: the populace must demand and expect dynasts to devote 'their full time, talent, and resources to abolish extreme poverty, tame inflation, protect our sovereignty, safeguard liberty, and nurture prosperity under the rule of law.' Transforming dynasty into legacy may seem impossible, he dares say -- but abolishing dynasties is even more so.

one_paragraph_summary: PBBM's laudably simple, traditional, and elegant State of the Nation Address evoked renewed talks of dynastic politics -- centered on the Marcos-Romualdez family (Speaker Martin G. Romualdez as senior deputy majority leader, neophyte Rep. Sandro Marcos as next-gen president-in-waiting, Senator Imee Marcos in the small House) but extending across generations and parties. To be fair, the dynasts preceded the Marcoses: Gloria Macapagal Arroyo (daughter of Diosdado, mother of Mikey); the Aquinos (Benigno III, son of Corazon and Benigno Jr.); Roxas, Osmeña, and Magsaysay aspirants who fell short; and the Dutertes (with Sara possibly succeeding her father). Of post-WWII presidents, only Carlos P. Garcia and Fidel V. Ramos did not sire a presidentiable, while Jovito R. Salonga uniquely banned his own relatives from public service. Other clans with significant clout but no presidency yet -- the Cayetanos, Estradas, Binays, Gatchalians -- litter a political firmament that has produced both 'our brightest leaders' and 'the darkest.' Article II, Section 26 of the Constitution frowns on dynasties as state policy but the ban is neither absolute nor judicially enforceable because Congress has failed to enact the implementing law that would define the ban's scope. The devil is in the details: who counts as relatives (direct ascendant/descendant vs collateral; blood vs affinity; legitimate vs illegitimate; full-blood vs half-blood vs adopted), what offices are covered (elective vs appointive; national vs LGU vs barangay; same office or across), and what geographical and temporal limits apply (same province/city/town; same election or future elections; succession of term-limited officials). Comparing internationally -- the Clintons, Kennedys, and Bushes -- Panganiban notes that the US Constitution does not ban dynasties. He concludes that political dynasties, like electricity, mining, and guns, are 'in themselves neutral' -- neither evil per se nor good per se -- and that to define and regulate them 'so they can be used only for good, and not for evil, is the challenge to Congress.'

one_paragraph_summary: After President Ferdinand 'Bongbong' Marcos Jr. swore in his Cabinet on June 30 -- aligned with his inaugural message of 'unity, hope, and no excuses' -- Panganiban explains the confirmation process. The Commission on Appointments (Article VI Section 18) is a political (not judicial) body of 12 senators and 12 congressmen with the Senate president as ex-officio chairman voting only to break ties, with members elected by each House 'on the basis of proportional representation from the political parties or organizations registered under the party-list system represented therein.' Only heads of executive departments, ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, and AFP officers from colonel/naval captain upward (plus other officers whose appointments are vested by the Constitution) need confirmation; the list is exclusive. Officials with Cabinet rank but not heading portfolios -- like special assistant Anton Lagdameo and Presidential Management Staff head Naida Angping -- are not subject to confirmation, and even higher-ranked officials like the Bangko Sentral governor are excluded. VP Sara Duterte is confirmed automatically as a matter of courtesy; BBM's assumption of the agriculture portfolio requires no confirmation. CJ then turns to the substantive demands of Cabinet service: public scrutiny will surface old indiscretions, dig into income tax payments and private ventures, and pursue horse-trading. Department heads must leave their professions, divest from businesses, disclose assets-liabilities-relatives (by blood and affinity) annually, live simply, and 'be ready to explain how they acquired their mansions and how they can afford to send their children abroad.' They would be 'well advised to carry always an iPad or even an old-fashioned memo book' with the Constitution, anti-graft law, ethical standards law, and relevant Administrative Code portions ready at hand. He offers three named exemplars: the late Dr. Jovito R. Salonga, who dissolved his famous law office upon Cabinet swearing-in to set a high ethical standard though not legally required; former finance secretary Carlos Dominguez III on avoiding conflicts of interest; and former justice secretary (now SolGen) Menardo Guevarra on business divestment. Cabinet members 'will be headlined, columned, broadcasted, texted, Twittered, YouTubed and Facebooked' by what CJ calls 'the freest [media] in the world' on 24/7 call. As 'alter egos' of the President, they 'speak for him and act on his behalf,' must 'instinctively know his mind, his driving force, and his inner self,' must 'subordinate their personal ambitions and march to the beat of a single drummer.' Teamwork, he closes, 'is as essential as brainwork and hard work.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban offers three appreciations of BBM transition figures. First, on the Cabinet: while many appointees came from BBM's political camp (VP Sara Duterte-Carpio at education; Victor Rodriguez as executive secretary; Benhur Abalos at DILG; Jesus Crispin Remulla at justice; Susan Ople at migrant workers; Trixie Cruz-Angeles at press; Anton Lagdameo as special assistant), they 'are qualified and should be given the chance to show their worth.' Remulla has been denounced for 'atrocious track record of shameless apologia for Red-tagging, human rights violations, and attacks on press freedom,' but that was 'his stance as a partisan member of the legislative branch. Now, let us cautiously accord him the opportunity to become a statesman as the dispenser of justice in the executive branch.' BBM's technocrats -- 'the indefatigable' Benjamin Diokno (finance, former Bangko Sentral governor, who has already announced retention of national treasurer Lea de Leon and current finance undersecretaries including 'capable lawyer-CPA' Antonette Tionko), 'economic guru' Arsenio Balisacan (NEDA), former UP president Alfredo Pascual (trade), San Miguel Corp executive Manuel Bonoan (public works), Bienvenido Laguesma (labor), and 'impeccable banker' Felipe Medalla replacing Diokno at Bangko Sentral -- were chosen 'because they are respected professionals, not political wannabees.' Diokno, Balisacan, Pascual, and Medalla are all 'brilliant UP grads -- On their robust shoulders rests our people's hope for better lives.' Second, on Sen. Grace Poe: 'a foundling left in a church in Iloilo,' she 'won decisively in the Supreme Court that definitively upheld, by a vote of 9-3-3, her status as a natural-born citizen of her beloved Philippines' (CJ supported her plea in several 2015-2016 columns), and she did not stop at her own victory -- 'tirelessly labored' to sponsor Republic Act No. 11767 (signed last week) extending the protection to all foundlings 'from the moment of birth.' Third, on Justice Maria Filomena D. Singh (55), 'fittingly elevated' to the seat vacated by Senior AJ Estela M. Perlas-Bernabe: like Perlas-Bernabe before her (who in turn inherited the seat from 'another eminent career lady jurist, Conchita Carpio-Morales'), Singh climbed all four judicial-ladder rungs (QC MeTC → QC RTC → CA → SC). She is 'unpredictable' with 'no backlog since she started her judicial calling,' and has 'more than a fair chance of becoming another SAJ (or even a chief justice)' along with 55-year-old peers Hernando, Marquez, and Kho. Like Perlas-Bernabe, she is an Ateneo de Manila law graduate -- preserving Ateneo dominance on the SC at 6 of 15 (7 with the Ateneo de Davao grad), while UP has only 2 members. CJ's epigram: 'Ateneo dominates the Supreme Court but UP sways the BBM economic team.' Singh is also the first female professorial chair holder in law of the Metrobank Foundation, having delivered her first lecture March 5, 2021 at the SC Session Hall while still an appellate justice. CJ vows to monitor her career and 'her fidelity to the constitutional ideals of proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence as long as the Good Lord would allow me.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban argues that the May 9, 2022 Philippine election 'set some records that will long be remembered' on three axes: speed of digitized result transmission, margins of victory, and 'the resurgence of voluntarism for the vanquished.' Voter turnout reached 83.77% -- 'a truly remarkable feat amid a pandemic' -- and Comelec transparency servers received over 95% of digitized results from vote-counting machines in less than 12 hours after the 7 PM precinct close, 'sealing the massive mandate' of BBM and 'Inday' Sara Duterte. By comparison, the 2020 US election had only ~66% turnout, and Biden's victory was not declared until November 7 at ~11:25 AM EST -- four days after Election Day. For the first time since the 1987 Constitution took effect, both presidential and VP winners each won more than 50% of total votes (prior record: P-Noy at 42.08%); BBM's 31M+ votes were more than double Robredo's <15M, and Sara's 31M+ were more than triple Pangilinan's <10M. The Philippines 'shed its dubious record of being an election slowpoke' and 'may have set a record for being one of the fastest in determining -- unofficially but definitively -- the winners in a nationwide democratic election.' On the volunteerism side, the Robredo-Pangilinan camp's rallies reached 'a crescendo of about one million during its miting de avance in Makati,' marked by volunteers who 'merrily shared their baon, campaigned house-to-house, set up tarps, messaged one another through social media, composed, sang, or played favorite tunes, all at their own initiative and expense.' Leni's hope is that this becomes a permanent 'Angat Buhay' movement. CJ underscores the foundational thesis: 'what differentiates a vibrant democracy from a lifeless autocracy is the freedom to disagree, to oppose. True, the freedoms of speech, of assembly, and of the press are important, too, but without the freedom to oppose, all other libertarian ideals shrink into insignificance.' The majority should 'respect the minority's right to oppose peacefully and loyally under the rule of law.' He locates the volunteerism's lineage in PPCRV, founded by lay leader Henrietta T. de Villa in 1991 with Catholic hierarchy support as the laity's vote-vigilance response, having gathered over 500,000 volunteers to champion 'CHAMP -- Clean, Honest, Accurate, Meaningful, and Peaceful Elections.' Current PPCRV chair Myla Villanueva, 'a techie of the highest caliber,' debunked the alleged '68:32' malevolent pattern with academic experts, and PPCRV's match-rate analysis a week after Election Day reported 98.39% match (with 1.61% to be revalidated or no-match; Comelec stopped transmission at 98.35%); 1Sambayan separately confirmed Comelec System Hash Codes. CJ congratulates the current Comelec for 'a generally peaceful and orderly election' but lists outstanding tasks: replace antiquated VCMs, hold prompt re-polls where 'failure of elections,' speedily decide pre-election cases (disqualifications, COC cancellations), eliminate 'guns, goons, and gold,' and address long-queue complaints.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with the indignation of a former Chief Justice who, checking his own precinct via the Comelec's online 'Precinct Finder' at voterverifier.comelec.gov.ph, was met with 'NO RECORD FOUND' -- a result he photographed on his cellphone and turned over to election lawyer Romulo Macalintal, who used it in a press conference that morning on behalf of hundreds of similarly-affected voters. Macalintal then secured the physical 'List of Voters' confirming CJ and his wife Leni were properly registered in Precinct 0205A, Makati -- proving the registration existed and the tool was the failure. Looking deeper, CJ walks readers through the statutorily-mandated alternatives under RA 8189 (the 90-day posted list at the Office of the Election Registrar and LGU bulletin boards), the Election Day postings at polling places, the PPCRV copy, and most importantly the Election Day Computerized Voters List (EDCVL) which is the prima facie authority on who may vote in a specific precinct. As he wrote, a 'Voter Information Sheet' arrived at his household under RA 7904 with all the correct details -- putting 'to terrible shame' the digital Precinct Finder. He calls on Comelec to 'expurgate' the unreliable tool 'like it unabashedly purges nuisance candidates,' restore it only after thorough testing, and closes with the generalizable principle that hi-tech and digital apps 'should be thoroughly tested before they are inflicted on the public.'

Richard Vercels alongside 'newspaper publications from the internet') were inadmissible -- they had been extracted without counsel of choice and in violation of the right against self-incrimination. one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban takes up the question repeatedly asked by Sara Duterte-Carpio's supporters after she filed her substitute COC for VP under Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo's Lakas-CMD: can Sara still become president before 2028? Sara herself had already said she would be ready for the 2028 election after six years -- but legally, under Article VII Section 8 of the Constitution, she can still become president within 2022-2028 if the elected president dies, becomes permanently disabled, is removed, or resigns, with two modern precedents: Carlos P. Garcia after Magsaysay's plane crash, and GMA after Estrada v. Desierto (March 2, 2001) held that the 'totality of prior, contemporaneous and posterior facts and circumstantial evidence' showed Estrada's constructive resignation. If President Duterte's preferred bet Sen. Bong Go wins the top post, Duterte may urge BG to resign and give way to a Sara presidency, with Sara eligible for a full 2028 reelection if BG's unexpired term is less than four years (Article VII Section 4) -- paralleling GMA's 9-plus consecutive years (second only to Marcos's 21 and ahead of Quezon's 8.7). However, Sara is now officially tandem with Bongbong, not BG, and if Bongbong wins, 'I don't think he will give up the presidency. In fact, he may even frustrate Sara's wish to run in 2028 because, like his father, Bongbong may find ways to enable him to serve for more than six years.' Meanwhile, Duterte is gunning for the Senate (possibly the Senate presidency via Lakas-CMD support) and GMA is running unopposed in Pampanga (possibly returning as Speaker), producing 'dynasties galore, we will in awe implore if they all score as the proud victors.' The opposition's best response is Sen. Ping Lacson's 'winningest-contenders' framework backed by the SWS October 20-23, 2021 poll (Bongbong 47%, Robredo 18%, Moreno 13%, Pacquiao 9%, Lacson and Dela Rosa tied at 5%; VP: Sotto 44%, Sara 25%) -- yielding a likely Bongbong-Sara versus Leni-Tito showdown. But the bets must not wait too long: unity by January 2022 'may be a bit late' because winning candidates may have gained irreversible momentum by then.

Bato dela Rosa as the PDP-Laban / Lakas-CMD presidential bet. Though the 'feisty Inday' has steadfastly refused any national post, CJ would not be surprised if her teeming supporters flood streets, rallies, and social media with 'Run, Sara, Run.' If she relents, she gets ample logistics, slate-selection privileges, and an 'enviable problem' of donation-management; if she refuses, candidates will scramble for administration blessing -- and 'past elections have shown that the administration can shepherd up to 10 percent of the votes,' decisive in tight multiparty contests. Manila Mayor Isko Moreno would probably be the big beneficiary of an Inday cop-out via his 'canny' 'Healing President' positioning -- pandemic critic AND adopter of 'good policies and projects' of Duterte and Marcos, with rejection of dubious ones -- and may even win Solid North blessings by convincing Bongbong Marcos to substitute for Willie Ong as his running mate. Alternatively, Bongbong may join PDP-Laban to actualize Imee Marcos's 'dream team' of Sara-Bongbong (he already chose the little-known Federal Party over 'the tarnished KBL of martial law vintage'). Sen. Ping Lacson, stuck in the Pulse Asia 'cellar,' may have to bite the bullet and save his partner Sen. Tito Sotto a slot elsewhere -- Akyon Demokratiko (Yorme), Promdi (Pacquiao), PDP-Laban, or even the Liberal Party, where VP bet Sen. Kiko Pangilinan has publicly stated willingness (to his wife Sharon's comfort) to withdraw if it enhances Robredo. VP Leni Robredo will remain the opposition's 'hallowed candidate' especially of the anti-Duterte and anti-Marcos crowd, but if Sara runs, Leni loses her 'only lady' distinction -- and her strange choice to run as independent (not as LP nominee, despite chairing the LP) deprives her of the LP's dominant-minority-party legal pluses and 'an army of loyal cadres down to the barangay level' from a 75-year-old party (CJ knows this from his own post-Edsa role as LP chief legal counsel under Senate President Jovito R. Salonga). And 'no independent has ever been elected president.' The pandemic-driven online campaign shift raises crucial questions for Robredo: do her 'kakampinks' have the expertise to match Mocha Uson's 2016 Duterte campaign (4 million likes, 1.2 million engagements per ISEAS-Yusof Ishak's 2020 white paper), and her team should read Damon Centola's 'Change' (January 2021) on 'strength of weak ties' and 'weakness of strong ties' in spreading beliefs to avoid preaching to the converted. In sum, whether she runs or not, 'Sara will be the game changer of the political landscape come Nov. 15.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban summarizes a December 21 note from the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (CDF) -- signed by Cardinal Luis Ladaria and Archbishop Giacomo Morandi, approved by Pope Francis -- that averted a brewing dispute over Catholic acceptance of COVID-19 vaccines developed from cell lines derived from aborted human fetal tissue. Five vaccines use either the HEK-293 line (from a ~1972 kidney abortion) or Janssen's PER.C6 line (from a 1985 retinal abortion of an 18-week-old fetus): CanSino/Beijing Institute, Oxford/AstraZeneca, Janssen R&D USA, University of Pittsburgh, and ImmunityBio/NantKwest. AstraZeneca matters specially to the Philippines because the Concepcion-Sy Coson public-private partnership has ordered 2.6 million doses at $5/dose, the most affordable on offer. The CDF resolves the moral problem by classifying the recipient's cooperation as 'remote' rather than 'formal,' permissible 'in good conscience' given 'a grave danger, in the form of an uncontainable spread of a serious pathological agent' -- and notes that the cell lines are 'immortal,' continuing to divide indefinitely, which minimizes (if not eliminates) demand for new fetal tissues. CJ extends the reasoning by parity: just as later generations have not refused chloroquine (developed from Nazi concentration-camp experiments), slavery-built US railroads, or residence in California (acquired through Polk's unjust Mexican-American war), descendants 'who had nothing to do with' such injustices should not be required to forgo life-saving drugs derived from them. He provocatively localizes the principle: if, fifty years from now, funds plundered from today's poor were used to develop wonder drugs, should the descendants of the plundered refuse them on the same logic? He closes with personal-civic synthesis: 'As for me and my family, we will follow the CDF in full faith. However, as a law-abiding citizen, I will remain vigilant to make sure our government procures only safe, efficacious, and reasonably-priced vaccines for our people.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with a FLASH announcement -- congratulating retired Senior Justice Antonio T. Carpio on the University of the Philippines's conferment (Dec 10) of an honorary Doctor of Laws, with CJ and his wife Leni attending online -- then turns to the question of whether the US election system that elected Trump in 2016 and repudiated him in 2020 is 'undemocratic.' He explains the indirect structure: voters elect 538 members of the Electoral College who in turn elect the president, with state legislatures determining the process by local law (typically supervised by a state secretary of state, a political appointee). The popular-vote-vs-electoral-vote mismatch has occurred five times (1824, 1876, 1888, 2000, 2016 -- including Clinton's three-million-vote popular-vote win lost to Trump 304-227). The structure is locked in by Article V of the US Constitution (1789), which makes amendment 'extremely difficult' -- requiring either two-thirds of both chambers proposing followed by three-fourths-of-states (38 of 50) ratification, or two-thirds of state legislatures requesting a constitutional convention followed by three-fourths ratification. The framers built this difficulty to 'protect state autonomy,' because European immigrants 'zealously guarded their autonomy (or self-rule), ceding only or mostly their defense needs and diplomatic dealings with the outside world (plus relevant taxation) to their federal government.' Autonomy also explains the 100-member Senate (two per state regardless of population) -- counterweighted by population-proportional House representation. CJ argues that this state-equality-with-popular-balance arrangement makes the Union 'democratic in the same way that the sovereign equality of independent states in the United Nations gives every member one vote regardless of population.' Comparative-process examples -- indirect election of British PMs by Parliament, direct election of Philippine presidents by mere plurality -- show 'democracy has many faces depending on a country's history, traditions, and aspirations.' The simplest test, he concludes, is adherence to Lincoln's 'government of the people, by the people and for the people' -- to which he 'respectfully add[s]... under the rule of law.'

one_paragraph_summary: Two days before the November 3, 2020 US election, Panganiban explains 'the race to 270' between Joe Biden (78) and Donald Trump (74). US voters do not elect the president directly -- they elect 'electors' (538 in total, allocated to the 50 states and DC in rough proportion to population: California has 55; Alaska, Montana, Wyoming, and DC have three each), and a candidate needs at least 270 electoral votes to win. Most states (all except Maine and Nebraska) apply a winner-takes-all rule, awarding their full electoral slate to the popular-vote plurality winner. Each state legislature determines its own elector-selection process, but Election Day is fixed (first Tuesday after the first Monday of November) and the winner is sworn in on January 20. Under this complex, indirect system, a candidate may win the nationwide popular vote yet lose the electoral vote -- which has happened in five elections (1824, 1876, 1888, 2000, 2016). In 2016, Hillary Clinton won three million more popular votes than Trump but lost the electoral vote 304-227. The most controversial mismatch was 2000: Al Gore won the popular vote but lost 271-266 to George W. Bush after the US Supreme Court, voting 5-4, rejected a manual recount of 'imperfectly punched automated ballots' in Florida. CJ notes the partisan pattern: Florida's governor was Jeb Bush (George's brother), the state electoral commission was headed by a Bush-appointed Cabinet member, and the five anti-Gore justices were all Republican-appointed while the four pro-Gore were all Democratic-appointed. Yet Gore 'humbly accepted the decision and conceded defeat.' During CJ's CJ-tenure in 2006, Gore visited Manila and in a private conversation answered CJ's question why he had not taken his remedies to America's streets: 'Mr. Chief Justice, there is something greater than me. The survival of our democratic institutions is more important than my personal victory. The Supreme Court had spoken. Though I disagreed with its decision, I had a duty to respect and obey it... Can you imagine a leaderless United States?' -- to which CJ appends, 'Rule of law at its best!' Structurally, the Electoral College's 'theoretical parity among the states' -- reflected also in the 100-member Senate (two per state regardless of population) -- makes the Union 'democratic' in the same way that 'the sovereign equality of independent states in the United Nations gives every member one vote,' so India (>1 billion people) is the sovereign equal of Singapore (<6 million).

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban sorts the good news from the sad. The sad: the 'worrying rise in the ABSOLUTE NUMBER of coronavirus infections,' the 'shocking plunder of PhilHealth funds,' the 'deadly Jolo blasts,' and the President's revelation that his doctors warned his Barrett's esophagus 'may worsen to Stage One cancer.' Against this, he welcomes three 'shiny good news' items. First, Duterte's firm disavowal of RevGov: Defense Secretary Delfin Lorenzana declared it 'illegal and unconstitutional' and Foreign Secretary Teodoro Locsin Jr. condemned it as 'unique in its insanity.' IBP president Domingo Egon Cayosa wants to charge RevGov promoters with 'inciting to sedition'; CJ agrees, 'subject to the caveat that facts must be proven according to the rules of evidence, not necessarily according to media reports.' Historically, 'No RevGov is possible without the military's backing': Cory Aquino's 1986 set-aside of the 1973 Constitution succeeded only 'because our people, backed up by the military, supported it' before the 1987 Constitution took effect a year later -- current RevGov efforts lack that foundational condition. Second, the flattening of the COVID-19 curve per UP OCTA Research Team's Prof. Guido David, with his dispositive caveat: 'flattening does not mean it is over. It means there are still cases but the [TRANSMISSION RATE] is on the decline. Flattening is a long process.' As asymptomatic carriers return to offices, malls, and normal life, 'the chances of contact surge,' requiring continued isolation, physical distancing, face masks and shields, and hand-washing. Third, a more aggressive assertion of WPS maritime rights led by Lorenzana and Locsin: a DFA diplomatic protest over the Chinese Coast Guard's 'illegal confiscation' of Filipino fishermen's equipment near Scarborough Shoal; Lorenzana's debunking of China's 'nine-dash line' as 'fabrication' and accusation of Beijing 'illegally occupying' PH maritime territory; Palace spokesperson Harry Roque's affirmation that military movements in the WPS align with sovereign rights and that supply missions in the Spratlys and overflights in Scarborough will continue. Yet PH refused to join the US Navy's recent 'world's largest maritime military exercises' in the SCS -- Lorenzana citing Duterte's standing order: 'we should not involve ourselves in naval exercises in the [SCS] except in our national waters, the 12-mile distance from our shores.' Meanwhile, the US-China 'war of nerves and tech' escalates: US Health Secretary Alex Azar visited Taiwan; on August 10 China flew fighter planes across the median maritime line separating the mainland from Taiwan; on August 20 the US sold 66 ultra-hi-tech F-16C-D fighter jets to Taiwan; China fired missiles into the SCS showing it could sink US warships; and the US imposed sanctions on 24 Chinese companies that constructed the artificial islands in the SCS. Locsin said he would ask for termination of government contracts with the sanctioned companies -- one of which (with MacroAsia Corp.) was awarded the $10-billion Sangley Point International Airport build. Roque hoped the US and China would resolve their disputes 'amicably and peacefully,' and Malaysian FM Datuk Seri Hishammuddin Hussein was clearer: Asean countries must get together to avoid being 'dragged and trapped' between the two superpowers. CJ closes: 'we should neither be pro-American nor pro-Chinese. Rather, we should always be pro-Filipino and align ourselves with our Asean brethren in dealing with the two giants.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban celebrates the 24-hour transformation of a 6-page Malacañang draft into the 14-page 'Bayanihan to Heal as One' Act (RA 11469), signed by the President in record time and substantially improved by Senate scrutiny. He highlights Executive Secretary Salvador C. Medialdea's quiet decision to drop the feared (though constitutionally permitted under Art. XII, Sec. 17) 'take-over' clause for public utilities and businesses affected with public interest on the rationale that the private sector was fully united with the government in the war on COVID-19. He singles out Senate Minority Leader Franklin M. Drilon -- under voluntary self-quarantine with his wife Mila as a 'super senior' -- who emailed his colleagues a detailed letter justifying amendments anchored in David v. Arroyo (May 3, 2006, four essentials of a valid national-emergency law) and Araullo v. Aquino (July 1, 2014, the doctrinal pathway by which 'unobligated allotments' may be declared 'savings' and legally 'realigned' transparently for emergency purposes). Almost all of Drilon's recommendations were adopted, quieting libertarian anxieties about pork-barrel revival or DAP-style misuse. He notes that Sec. 4 of the enrolled bill enumerates specific presidential powers, replacing the original draft's open-ended 'rules, regulations and directives' grant -- which, 'in my humble opinion,' would have been an undue delegation of legislative power. He summarizes the four power-clusters: (1) WHO-aligned prevention/detection/protection/treatment; (2) cash subsidies of P5,000-P8,000/month for 2 months to 18 million low-income households, special risk allowance plus hazard pay for public health workers, and PhilHealth coverage of COVID-19 medical expenses; (3) P100,000 for severe-infection cases and P1M death benefits for public and private health workers retroactive to Feb 1, 2020; and (4) alternative work arrangements (WFH, reduced hours), health emergency leave, early 13th-month pay release, and increased GSIS and SSS benefits. He closes by pivoting from the enacting story to the implementing challenge: the speedy, fair, and no-nonsense identification of 18 million low-income households (4Ps beneficiaries first, with DOLE Secretary Bello asking employers to submit lists) and 500,000 displaced workers -- and against Duterte's plea for patience, he insists that 'more patience is indeed needed, but even more needed is the speedy, fair, and no-nonsense implementation of the nobly-conceived, bipartisanly-enacted, pro-poor provisions' of the law.

Arroyo) by noting that the enemy here is not state action but unknown microorganisms originating in Wuhan. Acknowledging missteps and the inherent difficulty of feeding the quarantined poor while preventing local transmission, he refuses to fault-find: no country had prepared for a pandemic this terrifying. one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reports the Feb 5, 2020 US Senate acquittal of President Donald Trump as 'an unabashedly partisan vote' -- without trial, without testimonial evidence, and without documentary evidence -- with all 53 Republicans voting to dismiss Article 2 (obstruction of House investigation) 53-47, and all 53 Republicans except Mitt Romney voting to dismiss Article 1 (abuse of power for withholding ~$400M in military aid to Ukraine unless Joe Biden was investigated) 52-48. The preceding 51-49 vote on Jan 31 barring oral and testimonial evidence (with Romney and Susan Collins crossing) made the partisan outcome inevitable. The five ceremonial Senate processes -- oath of 'impartial justice,' oral arguments, written questions read aloud by CJ John Roberts, manager/defense replies, and latitude for Democratic questioners -- formed the carapace of judicial form around a plainly numerical outcome. Republicans argued that 'abuse of power' and 'obstruction' fall outside the US Constitution's enumerated grounds ('treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors') because they are not 'criminal acts' -- a verbal-legis literal interpretation that, in 250 years, has produced no Senate-ousted US president (Andrew Johnson 1868, Clinton 1999, and Trump all acquitted; Nixon resigned). The 1987 Philippine Charter's framers, aware of this literal exclusion, provided 'more encompassing' grounds -- 'culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, graft and corruption, other high crimes and betrayal of public trust' -- so that abuses cannot be textually dumped. The catch-all 'betrayal of public trust' (plus the SALN Law) was partly used in both the Estrada and Corona impeachments. Estrada's trial was truncated by House prosecutors' walkout, precipitating the Edsa II People Power Revolution, but Corona's ran for several months without testimonial blockade -- including testimony from Ombudsman Conchita Carpio Morales and Corona himself -- and ended in a more-than-three-fourths Senate vote 'without any unabashedly partisan alignment.' The Philippine 3/4 threshold (vs the US 2/3) is also structurally higher. CJ concludes that the Philippine impeachment process, though also sui generis, is 'fairer, more democratic and less partisan' than its US counterpart.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with the 'bedeviling question' of whether the ongoing US Senate impeachment trial of President Donald Trump is a judicial or political process -- and how the classification governs Trump's fate. Evidence for the judicial framing: 99 of 100 senators (only Inhofe absent) were sworn before CJ John Roberts to 'do impartial justice,' and the two articles allege discrete misconduct (Article 1: abuse of power by withholding economic and military aid to Ukraine unless Biden's alleged misconduct was investigated; Article 2: obstruction of the House investigation by barring White House assistants from testifying). The Trump-camp legal argument -- led by Alan Dershowitz and Kenneth Starr, the celebrated lawyers against Bill Clinton in 1999 -- is that the articles fail to allege any violation of law and therefore fall short of the constitutional grounds of 'treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors,' while Democrats counter that 'abuse of power' was the principal framers' reason for inventing impeachment. Evidence for the political framing: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell openly announced his support for Trump 'as a matter of party discipline' before the articles were even filed, asked for summary dismissal without trial (retreating after Republican-senator dissuasion), and secured the Senate's rejection of the House's subpoena requests for witnesses and documents Trump had barred -- arguing tit-for-tat that if the Democratic-majority House (228-193 along largely party lines) could impeach, the Republican-majority Senate can acquit. The 67-vote ouster threshold (2/3) means all 45 Democrats + 2 independents + at least 20 Republicans must vote together -- 'Definitely a tough job!' CJ's thesis: impeachment is neither purely judicial nor purely political but sui generis with its own unique genre. If purely judicial, the trial would have been lodged in the Supreme Court or an independent legal body -- but the framers placed it in the House and Senate, composed of individuals from varied education, training, calling, and social status, elected as 'the people's alter egos to enact laws and to discipline those who have become unworthy of their trust.' Beneath the constitutional undertones, legal rituals, and judicial formalities lies a policy question -- will the senators' constituencies be served better by retaining or ousting? -- answered through reason, logic, emotion, and passion, but always justified by senators' sense of what is beneficial for the folks back home. At bottom, impeachment is 'judicial in its search for truth and political in its pursuit of the public weal' -- neither overwhelmingly legalistic as the legalists claim nor blindly partisan as McConnell perceives. It shows 'a veneer of legalism' over 'an imbedded core of public wisdom' -- and the peoples of the world, including the Philippines, are keenly watching this public display of the American brand of democracy and sense of fairness, decency, integrity, and accountability.

one_paragraph_summary: Responding to the post-2019-polls clamor -- from election watchdogs, losing candidates, and millennial voters -- to revert to manual elections, Panganiban catalogues why the 'mano-mano' era was structurally worse than the glitchy present. Under manual voting, ballots depended on voter penmanship and were frequently invalidated for illegibility; the 'guns, goons and gold' could verify coerced votes through identifying marks, peculiar name sequencing, and middle-initial inclusions; the 'lansadera' scheme cycled genuine ballots through safe houses with Board of Election Inspectors complicity; manual counting lasted into the wee hours with ballots misread or untallied, and ballot boxes were stolen or doused with acid; and 'wholesale' cheating altered Election Returns and Statements of Votes -- the classic dagdag-bawas -- with one-digit changes flipping town, district, or provincial outcomes through tedious preproclamation controversies that automation has eliminated. Even Namfrel's proposed hybrid system -- manual writing, manual precinct count, electronic transmission for consolidation -- would gain precinct-level transparency at the cost of reintroducing the entire manual-era vulnerability surface; if transparency is the goal, the answer is a less-opaque automation, not a manual return. With three years before the next elections, Comelec has the runway to reduce glitches and answer 'Namfrel's valid concerns without risking the horrors of manual voting.' No computer system in banking, airlines, or logistics is perfect; the engineering posture is to minimize imperfection, not to demolish the system.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban surveys the three insidious plagues of the 2019 elections -- vote-buying, automation glitches, and overvoting -- while crediting the polls as 'generally peaceful and orderly' compared with past cycles. Pre-election, Comelec Chair Sheriff Abas had already called vote-buying 'rampant,' and PNP Chief Oscar Albayalde observed on Election Day that 'Nakikita natin massive talaga 'yung vote-buying... kaliwa't kanan.' He argues vote-buying has become pervasive precisely because automation and indelible ink eliminated the older cheating channels -- flying voters, multiple-ballot one-hand, delayed-canvass machinations, banned preproclamation controversies -- leaving the remaining evil of bribing citizens to vote a certain way or to refrain altogether. He models the economics: bribing 10,000 voters with P1,000 each totals only P10M, a 'pittance' relative to the hundreds of millions recoverable from 'disguised pork barrel, licensing permits and tax perks' in narrow-margin local and congressional races. 'One glitch is enough to disenfranchise a citizen': former VP Jojo Binay's ballot was rejected eight times until he personally complained at the Comelec office, and many less-standing citizens 'just waited and waited, or worse, left the polling places in sheer exasperation without casting their ballots.' He reserves judgment on whether the glitches converted to fraud pending the June 4 congressional inquiry. On overvoting (shading more than 12 senatorial ovals invalidates a ballot), ABS-CBN's 1.2-million-ballot estimate 'could, just could, have shaken the last two senatorial slots given that... the 11th to the 14th places are separated by about 200,000 to 400,000 votes only.' His prescription is voter education with folk specificity: voters should write a list of choices to bring to the polling place, and the faithful should add 'Huwag kang gunggong' (Thou shall not be stupid) to 'Huwag kang pumatay' (Thou shall not kill) and 'Huwag kang magnakaw' (Thou shall not steal) -- otherwise the dreaded '3Gs' of manual elections will 'metastasize into the new 5Gs of automated voting: guns, goons, gold, glitches and gunggong.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with a paradox from an SWS survey of December 2018: while 'will not be corrupt' topped the qualities Filipino voters seek in senators, the same surveys showed several probable winners not known for honesty. He attributes this stated-preference-vs-revealed-preference gap to voter ignorance about which of the 63 aspirants for 12 slots actually embody incorruptibility, leaving name recall (from Senate incumbency, showbiz, sports, media ads, and entertainment) to dominate choices alongside the '3Gs' (guns, goons, gold), '3Rs' (relationship, kinship, friendship), and 'profligate vote-buying.' He proposes a six-fold framework derived from scattered constitutional provisions on senatorial duties: lawmaking competence with parliamentary skill; substantive oversight-hearing preparation (avoiding 'nauseous grandstanding and intellectual nihilism'); budget literacy detecting disguised pork; quasi-judicial probity in impeachment, electoral tribunals, the Commission on Appointments, and treaty ratification; statesperson serenity on war, amnesty, emergency powers, and martial law/habeas corpus; and constitutional-amendment independence. He closes by asking voters whether their senatorial choices possess any of these qualities -- leaving the diagnostic question rather than naming candidates.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban surveys the state of two simultaneous peace processes. On the MILF front, the Bangsamoro Basic Law has received congressional approval, with the Senate and House versions still disparate; the bicameral conference committee will harmonize them for ratification when Congress resumes on July 23 -- the same day as the SONA. He urges the final version to satisfy the MILF's longing while avoiding the constitutional pitfalls that led the Supreme Court to debunk the MOA-AD in North Cotabato v. Government (October 14, 2008). On the NDFP front, the CPP was founded by Jose Maria Sison on December 26, 1968 in Alaminos, Pangasinan, espousing Marxist-Maoist ideology; its armed wing, the NPA, has sustained the 'longest-running communist insurgency in the world.' Peace negotiations opened with President Cory Aquino on December 10, 1986, continued under Ramos, formally opened in Brussels on June 26, 1995, and produced The Hague Declaration listing four agenda items: (1) human rights and international humanitarian law, (2) socioeconomic reforms, (3) political and constitutional reforms, and (4) end of hostilities. Of these, only the first has been completed -- CARHRIHL, signed March 16, 1998. He clarifies CARHRIHL's legal status: it is not a treaty (no Senate concurrence; Vienna Convention applies only to states) nor a final binding agreement, but an important milestone. The GRP can indirectly enforce it by invoking the Constitution's Articles II, III, and XIII and the ICESCR as generally accepted principles of international law forming part of the law of the land. Formal talks on the second topic -- socioeconomic reforms -- are scheduled to resume June 28, and the column previews the continuation.

First, TRAIN Section 43 already provides an automatic suspension of the 2019-and-beyond excise increases when Dubai crude averages $80/bbl or more in the prior three months -- a ready-made relief mechanism. The BIR's RR 10-2008 imposed a strict-construction, prorated approach: any additional compensation (commissions, allowances, honoraria) stripped MWE status and taxed the entire income. The SC unanimously voided RR 10-2008 in Soriano v. one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with Donald Trump's third-debate refusal to commit to accepting the impending 2016 US election results -- 'I'll tell you at the time. I'll keep you in suspense. Ok?' -- and his pillorying of media for 'rigging' and bewailing 'electoral frauds' reminiscent of Philippine elections, later modified to 'provided I win.' Hillary Clinton was appalled by this attack on 240 years of US democracy in which rigging or fraud had never been raised by losers, raising the question: how is the US president chosen? Unlike Filipinos, American voters do not directly indicate presidential choices on their ballots; they vote for 'electors' pledged to vote later for the chosen candidate, with each of the 50 states plus DC determining the elector selection method by local law. Election Day is fixed as the first Tuesday after the first Monday of November (Nov 8 in 2016); Inauguration Day is January 20. Each state allocates electors in proportion to population -- California 55, Alaska/Montana/Wyoming/DC 3 each -- for 538 total electors with a 270-vote winning threshold under most states' winner-takes-all rule. Normally the popular vote winner also wins the EC, but exceptions occurred in 1824, 1876, 1888, and most strikingly in 2000 when Al Gore won the popular vote but lost the EC 271-266 to George W. Bush after the US Supreme Court 5-4 refused a manual recount of imperfectly punched Florida ballots -- a decision criticized as partisan since Florida's governor was Jeb Bush (George's brother), Florida's election commission was headed by a Cabinet member of the governor, and all 5 anti-Gore justices were appointed by Republican presidents. Despite the widespread howling, Gore humbly accepted the decision and conceded defeat. In 2006, during CJ Panganiban's watch as chief justice, Gore visited the Philippines and during a private conversation explained his reasoning: 'Mr. Chief Justice, there is something greater than me. The survival of our democratic institutions is more important than my personal victory. Had I brought the battle to America's streets, there would have been chaos and political upheaval. The manual recount would have taken many months. Meanwhile, no one would have been sworn in as president that ensuing January. Can you imagine a leaderless United States?' Gore was tall and husky, but in CJ's esteem he 'immediately rose 10 feet taller.' The column closes with the rhetorical challenge: 'Can we expect the same patriotism from Trump?'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban discusses former President and current Pampanga Rep. Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo's bill granting incoming President Duterte emergency powers to solve Metro Manila's traffic mess -- the 'crisis that bastardized our lives' costing P2.4 billion daily per a 2013 JICA study (repeat, daily). Eduardo Yap, MAP traffic czar, asked CJ weeks earlier whether the incoming President is clothed with emergency powers; CJ confirmed: under the Constitution, the President can declare a national emergency and Congress can grant extraordinary powers under reasonable terms for abnormal conditions endangering lives or wellbeing (economic crisis, pestilence, epidemic, typhoon, earthquake) -- but Congress must clearly define the specific powers, which cannot breach due process, just compensation, free expression, or the rule of law as CJ Sereno has stressed. CJ advised Yap to read and reread David v Arroyo (May 3, 2006), the landmark decision by Justice Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez distinguishing three extraordinary presidential powers -- (1) calling-out power vs lawless violence/invasion/rebellion, (2) executive power to ensure faithful law-obedience, and (3) emergency powers -- not to be confused with the more stringent power to declare martial law. The Arroyo bill prudently restricts emergency-powers use to two years (unless sooner withdrawn) and subjects authorized negotiated infrastructure contracts to strict transparency and accountability conditions. Tugade -- a 'de campanilla' lawyer (class salutatorian at San Beda College of Law) -- assured that abuses would be checked by congressional + SC oversight. At the Cabinet's Davao powwow, Tugade admonished top business leaders: 'You expect us not to be corrupt? Can we expect you not to corrupt us?' -- to thunderous delight. The quip reminds CJ of the Integrity Summit (Sept 19, 2014) where he prefaced his anti-corruption-in-judiciary speech with two jokes: (1) a judge summons lawyers and announces 'Compañeros, both of you surreptitiously bribed me. You, counsel for the plaintiff, gave me P250,000 while you, counsel for the defendant, sent me P200,000. As an evenhanded and transparent judge, I will not allow anyone of you to unduly influence me. So, I am returning P50,000 to you counsel for the plaintiff. Now, after I have leveled the playing field, both of you can expect equal treatment from me' -- the wrong way to level the playing field; (2) a lawyer visits the judge offering to sell a brand-new Mercedes-Benz parked on his driveway for P1,000 -- the judge replies 'In that case, I'll buy two, one for me and one for my wife' -- the wrong way to legalize a bribe. These 'devilish games and witchcraft' impelled the Makati Business Club + European Chamber of Commerce 'Integrity Initiative,' and judges 'will not be bribed unless clients inveigle their lawyers to go beyond the outer limits of advocacy and soar to the stratosphere of corruption and malevolence' -- unscrupulous clients telling lawyers 'I do not care whether you know the law. My question is: Do you know the judge?' Closing aphorism: 'there are no bribe-takers, when there are no bribe-givers.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban defends President-elect Rodrigo Duterte's Cabinet selection prerogative -- 'a president chooses his official family according to his personal standards for vetting who can best help transform his thoughts and dreams into reality' -- and argues that incoming President Duterte deserves sufficient leeway because critics have been 'too picky,' undercutting choices before they take seats. Duterte himself is 'unconventional and sui generis,' so it is unsurprising that he selected Cabinet officials who are similarly unconventional and sui generis. Many named appointees -- Carlos 'Sonny' Dominguez, Silvestre Bello II, Perfecto Yasay Jr., Hermogenes Esperon, Vitaliano Aguirre II, Salvador Medialdea, Art Tugade, Alfonso Cusi, and Salvador Panelo -- have served in previous administrations or been involved in high-profile happenings. What matters critically is that Duterte trusts and believes in them; they are his 'alter egos' (extensions of himself), and under the doctrine of qualified political agency their acts are deemed the President's unless he rejects or alters them. 'Their success will be his success. Their failures will be his failures.' Duterte's unpredictable persona and unorthodox utterances catapulted him to landslide victory -- his political party and partisan alliances were less important than his persona, and his slogan 'change is coming' is laden with manifold unspoken but forceful promises. He wants Cabinet members like him: strong-willed, decisive, daring, transparent, unorthodox, and able to deliver on grand promises. CJ then itemizes the high vocational cost: from his earlier column (6/20/10), Cabinet members and families must forego privacy because 'our tri-media, the freest in the world, will use microscopes and telescopes, cameras and recorders to scrutinize the minutest details of their lives and careers. Daily, they will be headlined, columnized, broadcast, texted, Twittered, YouTubed and Facebooked. Twenty-four hours a day, Cabinet members will be on call, not just by the President, but also by radio and TV reporters.' The Commission on Appointments confirmation 'is not a cakewalk either,' with interrogations sometimes used to 'horse-trade political and personal favors' and long-forgotten enemies surfacing slight indiscretions. The Constitution bars Cabinet members from any other office/employment, from practicing any profession or participating in business, and requires strict conflict-of-interest avoidance (Peter Laurel declined the education portfolio for this reason -- his family is deeply involved in education and business); they must live simply, disclose assets and liabilities, and list relatives by blood or affinity at term-start and annually. They should be familiar with the Constitution, Anti-Graft Law, Ethical Standards Law, and Administrative Code -- 'They might as well carry with them copies of these documents or digitize them in their iPads or iPhones for instant reference.' On a more positive note, the credibility created by the peculiarities of the incoming administration's victory + its clarion call for radical change creates the perfect scenario for 'the best and the brightest who have been wary of joining public service' to engage in 'sincere and selfless public service.' The 2016 elections encountered a 'disillusioned electorate' that deeply sought genuine change, willing to gamble on someone believed to be the answer 'even as news about his faults and shortcomings came out' -- making this 'a profoundly hopeful electorate.' CJ welcomes these chosen ones: 'On their shoulders rest the people's trust that they will help him carry out his mandate to effect the meaningful change they long for.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban's election-eve column congratulates nonpolitical winners, since partisan political activities are banned the day before voting. He notes that tomorrow voters should pray for credible polls and that Comelec Chair Andres D. Bautista assured VCM (now-nicknamed, no longer PCOS) results within three days. With Mother's Day falling on Election Day Eve, CJ offers his signature inversion: 'It is said that love flows like a river because it always flows downstream. How true! But today is Mother's Day. Let the river of love flow upstream. Let us all show Nanay that we can love her more than she loves us -- on this one special day.' He congratulates the 1,731 passers out of 6,605 takers in the 2015 bar exams (a 26.21% passing rate), with special felicitations to first-placer Rachel Angeli Miranda of UP (a former Inquirer scholar, 'may she write as succinctly as our staffers and as eruditely as Supreme Court justices') and second-placer Athena Plaza of USC (USC is 'probably the best law school outside Metro Manila'), plus the Bar Exam Committee headed by Justice Teresita J. Leonardo-De Castro. He then pays tribute to RVR Award winners exemplifying the values of the late Ambassador Ramon V. Del Rosario Sr. -- sponsored since 2010 by JCI Manila (Jaycees), the Asian Institute of Management, and the Del Rosario family. The six-year roster: 2010 -- Senen Bacani (founder of La Frutera banana plantation tilled by former Muslim Mindanao rebels) and Jesus Tambunting (founder of MSME-focused Planters Development Bank, now merged with China Bank); 2011 -- 'the principled' Oscar M. Lopez (Lopez Group's 'Power of Good,' green ecosystem); 2012 -- philanthropist Washington SyCip (SGV, largest auditing company in PH and SE Asia); 2013 -- former senator Vicente T. Paterno (now deceased; Philippine Seven Corp, Masicap); 2014 -- 'the visionary' Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala (chair of oldest PH conglomerate spanning real estate, banking, telecom, water, BPO, plus educational/charitable causes); 2015 -- 'the multitalented' Manuel V. Pangilinan (chair of conglomerates in telecom, digital commerce, electric power, water, tollways, railways, hospitals, broadcast/print media, mining; unassuming head of Philippine Business for Social Progress and sports foundations). The RVR Award is unique because it promotes entrepreneurship and nation-building as 'mutually inclusive' rather than exclusive -- together creating 'inclusive progress' that benefits the country: business helping education yields good citizens consuming better food/homes/appliances/clothes/travel/phones, fair employee treatment yields efficient/loyal workers, farmer assistance multiplies resources, vocational training employs out-of-school youth, ex-convict/former-rebel reintegration prevents recidivism, world-class athlete training brings honor. The RVR icons devote 'time, talent and treasures in helping the least, the last and the lost.' CJ hopes the Jaycees themselves emulate these twin values, echoed in their credo: 'That economic justice can best be won by free men through free enterprise; that government should be of laws rather than of men.'
