one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban applies a 'macho power vs woman power' frame to the 2016 PH presidential race -- observing that recent Pulse Asia and SWS surveys show Digong Duterte (DD) and Bongbong Marcos (BM) as the candidates to beat, with Grace Poe (GP) and Leni Robredo (LR) as the closest credible challengers. The two men, especially DD, are 'strong-willed, hyperbolic, magnetic, unorthodox and brash,' while the women are 'polished, compassionate, motherly, loving and humble.' Parenthetically, the same phenomenon appears in the US, where Trump and Clinton 'uncannily... typify the phenomenon of macho power vs woman power.' To demonstrate, CJ uses direct quotations across five policy domains. On peace and order, DD threatens 'it will be bloody because I will order the killing of all criminals... I will recommend to Congress the restoration of the death penalty by hanging in public,' while GP says 'As a mother, I am deeply troubled by the proliferation of crime and drugs. Like every parent, I cannot rest easy until my children are home safe at night.' On corruption, DD bets his life ('if I fail, kill me'); GP commits to hold the corrupt accountable 'whether they be friend or foe' and to push FOI legislation. On poverty alleviation, DD proposes food terminals, Land Bank lending to farmers, DTI-supported credit unions, and continuation/enhancement of 4Ps; GP says (in Tagalog) that alleviating poverty is her priority -- strengthening 4Ps and adding livelihood for additional income. On foreign relations, DD says 'We cannot afford to war with China' but vows to 'ride a jet ski carrying the Philippine flag' to a Chinese-occupied airport (Spratlys), and threatens to sever ties with America and Australia; GP advocates strengthening the military, constructive talks with China, and ASEAN leadership for a code of conduct. On women, DD's mayor-rape comment is preserved verbatim with Tagalog + English translation; GP says (in Tagalog) that more women should be in government because 'we have empathy' and care for family. The Marcos-Robredo VP race exhibits parallel contrasts: Marcos seeks 'leaders that seek to unite, not to divide, leaders that look to the future, not to the past,' aspiring to run DOLE (since employment is the biggest problem); Robredo identifies herself as 'a mother' refusing to abandon children or country, aspiring to streamline anti-poverty programs (not hold a cabinet position).

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban debunks the myth of powerful PH parties by contrasting them with their US counterparts. The US Democratic and Republican parties are 'slugging it out with full media coverage and unlimited spending' -- Clinton vs Sanders, Trump vs Cruz vs Kasich -- and stand for 'opposing principles and projects' with millions of members actively selecting candidates through primaries and caucuses that 'not even incumbent US presidents can dictate.' Pre-EDSA PH party politics, by contrast, was an LP-NP 'duopoly' briefly challenged by Manuel Manahan's Progressive Party (1957) and Raul Manglapus's Party for Philippine Progress (1965). The LP and NP 'did not essentially differ from each other in their political ideology and platform' -- existing 'mostly to perpetuate the political agenda of the party bosses who chose the party's candidates.' The two parties became 'nefarious and notorious' enough that the 1987 Constitution discouraged the two-party system and encouraged multiple parties; unfortunately, it also 'instituted a confused and confusing party-list scheme, borrowed from European parliamentary models and injected into our American-oriented presidential form of government, an experiment which resulted in a political mongrel that, in all humility, I cannot comprehend fully.' Under the 1987 Constitution, parties play a minimal role in PRESIDENTIAL elections. In 1992, the first race under the new Charter, Ramon Mitra (the LDP party-in-power candidate) 'miserably lost to a virtual independent, Fidel V. Ramos who, ironically, was backed by the LDP's titular head, President Cory Aquino.' Ramos formed the Lakas-NUCD to consolidate victory, which then backed Jose de Venecia -- who 'despite the full support of Ramos and the party in power -- also pitifully lost the 1998 presidential race to yet another virtual independent, Joseph Estrada,' who had founded Partido ng Masang Pilipino. Conventional logic says powerful parties propel presidential candidates to victory, 'but history has proven this to be a myth under the present Constitution' -- presidential candidates 'won on their personal charisma, not on the support of powerful political machines.' The only exception was 2004, with Arroyo as incumbent candidate herself. Will history repeat in May 2016 with leading candidates Duterte and Poe not backed by the party in power? 'In three weeks, we should definitely know.' Powerful parties retain some residual advantages: appointment of election watchers, entitlement to election returns and certificates of canvass, allowable additional expenditures by supporting parties, and substitution rights for deceased party-affiliated candidates (independents cannot be substituted). Parties remain crucial for the Senate, where they steer many senatorial bets to victory despite presidential losses. Independents 'do not carry the baggage of discredited parties and need not defend the shortcomings of incumbent presidents.' On the provincial level, locally-organized parties effectively propel candidates, and 'local dynasties thrive better under the present multiparty system. Due to the limited reach of national parties, dynasties are able to distribute local posts to favored members.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with thanks to Tony Tan Caktiong (Apec 2015 CEO Summit conference chair and Jollibee board chair, 9th largest QSR globally by market cap) for the 'ringside seat' on the first row to hear Obama on climate change, Xi Jinping on trade pacts, Medvedev on terrorism, and several other leaders. But by far, in his humble opinion, Alibaba executive chair Jack Ma delivered the most moving speech: the 51-year-old self-made Chinese billionaire and former school teacher (Forbes-rated $23.3 billion, richest in China, 18th in the world) explained with passion and conviction that the Internet is the economic equalizer in our globalized world. Online, impoverished but ingenious manufacturers can reach any buyer in the world -- Laguna wood carvers and embroiderers, Manila tailors selling to New York, London, Beijing -- something nearly impossible in 1989 when Apec was born. Alibaba facilitates delivery and payment via Alipay digital money at the cheapest rates; by 2020 it will account for $650 billion in Chinese trade. Yet Alibaba 'does not own any factory. It is merely an enabler.' In only 15 years it became the biggest Chinese Internet marketplace, founded in a small shack by Ma and 16 friends, half (including Ma) not knowing how to operate a PC. It outsells the older Amazon, largest US online trader, and almost equals Walmart's revenue. Rocket International was formed in Germany two years ago to dominate Internet trading outside the US and China. Apec and WTO both aim to support sustainable economic growth and prosperity by championing free and open trade -- believing in competition through drastically lowering tariffs, quotas, and taxes; privatizing public assets and utilities; deregulating prices and businesses. Unlike WTO, however, Apec is mostly a forum without binding character; the WTO, EU, and Asean require compliance. Upholding membership in both Apec and WTO, Philippine presidents -- especially FVR -- robustly promoted free trade and implemented globalization, deregulation, privatization, and liberalization: telecom, banking, insurance, and airline industries liberated from monopoly; water utilities and tollways privatized; oil business and power generation deregulated. Economist-friend Romeo L. Bernardo's data: GDP growth from 2.9% annual average (1991-2000, first decade of globalization) to 4.8% (2001-2010) to about 5.9% (2011-2014); inflation reduced from 8.3% (1996) to 1.4% present. Critics lament these statistics benefit mostly the rich while the poor wallow in low pay, malnutrition, inadequate shelter, ill health -- they vehemently oppose Apec/WTO globalization. CJ notes the rich-first trajectory is equally evident in the US's 20th-century industrial rise and China's 21st-century digital rise. To hasten the propoor trajectory, Apec leaders now stress inclusive growth -- the call to assist MSMEs (micro, small, medium enterprises) is as loud as advocacies for liberalization and deregulation, hence the concurrent MSME summit. President Obama's 'unorthodox moderating' of a panel composed of Jack Ma and Aisa Mijeno -- the young Filipina who pioneered electricity from salt water -- drew the most applause, showing entrepreneurial ingenuity at its best, an accomplished giant and a very promising startup both buoyed by free enterprise. Ma's rags-to-riches story shows how entrepreneurship and innovation can bridge the gap between poor inventors/producers and unreachable foreign markets, while providing the needed financial, marketing, and logistics muscles. Indeed, the Internet is the globalization equalizer that worked for Ma. It should equally work for Mijeno.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reframes the post-Mamasapano debate. CJ is glad P-Noy, in a televised press conference last Thursday, put to rest the issue of who killed the terrorist Zulkifli bin Hir, alias 'Marwan' -- an issue P-Noy himself reopened during his Inquirer-office visit. But the relevant question that pines for reopening, in his humble opinion, is: 'Who killed the 44 Special Action Force commandos, collectively known as the SAF 44? More pointedly, who are responsible for their massacre?' The President partially answered when he said 90 people from the MILF, BIFF, and private armed groups will be charged for the death of 35 members of the 55th Special Action Company. 'That is a good start but, with due respect, I believe it is far too feeble a response.' Meanwhile, it is pointless to look further into who killed Marwan: Senate, House, and PNP BOI have already investigated 'ad nauseam'; both houses should have gathered enough data to enact remedial laws (congressional inquiries are primarily in aid of legislation). The BOI reports, in what appears to be a first-person account, that the terrorist was killed in a firefight with SAF, with a 'shot in the chest causing his death,' implying he was standing. The MILF counters that 'the trajectory of the bullets indicates that the fatal shot did not come from the shots fired outside the house as the bullet holes are roughly 18 inches above the floor ... In all likelihood, the fatal shot must have been fired at close range and while Marwan was lying on the floor.' At this point it is no longer possible to verify the bullet holes because Marwan's house has been burned to the ground; exhuming the corpse for post-mortem examination is extremely difficult because the grave's location is not known. The SAF 44 families are still grieving and clamoring for justice; their wounds cannot heal until the accountability questions are satisfactorily answered. P-Noy's assurance is too feeble for three reasons. First, his targets -- MILF, BIFF, and others -- are still rebels beyond the reach of law; even serving subpoenas would be extremely difficult. Second, several civilian and military officials were involved directly or indirectly in planning and executing the Mamasapano caper: did some fail in leadership duties? Assume powers beyond their authority? Neglect coordination resulting in or contributing to the SAF 44's death? CJ is not accusing anyone -- that is for the probers to determine. Third, we are in election season; the search for justice should not be tainted with partisan attack -- CJ has great faith in Justice Secretary Leila de Lima, but she will resign soon to run for the Senate, so the public must view the probe as free of any partisan agenda. CJ proposes an independent panel like the Agrava Board that investigated Ninoy Aquino's murder at the Manila International Airport tarmac in 1983 -- composed of retired CA Justice Corazon Agrava (chair), lawyer Luciano Salazar, businessman Dante Santos, labor leader Ernesto Herrera, and educator Amado Dizon, assisted by then-Dean (later Chief Justice) Andres R. Narvasa as general counsel and lawyer Bienvenido A. Tan Jr. (later Ambassador to Germany) as public coordinator. After holding 125 sessions, hearing 194 witnesses, and consuming 20,377 pages of transcript, the Agrava Board concluded that several military officers including then-AFP chief of staff Fabian Ver conspired to kill Ninoy. Despite this, the SBN -- in a Dec 2, 1985 decision penned by Justice Manuel Pamaran -- acquitted all the accused. However, after the 1986 Edsa revolution, the newly-reconstituted SC nullified the Pamaran verdict and returned the case to the SBN for retrial. In a 177-page Sept 28, 1990 decision, the SBN convicted 16 soldiers including Brig. Gen. Luther Custodio of Ninoy's murder. This judgment became final after the SC dismissed the soldiers' petition for review on July 23, 1991; on March 8, 2005, the Court unanimously denied a belated motion for a third trial. 'Without the credible factual findings of the independent Agrava Board, the judiciary may not have been able to decide courageously and with finality the accountability of those responsible for Ninoy's death.' Although the fallen SAF 44 may not be as famous as Ninoy, they deserve equal justice. As we lawyers fondly say, 'Let justice be done though the heavens may fall.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers a strategic outlook on the 'daang matuwid' anticorruption program's future. The cases initiated by Aquino's daang matuwid (straight path) program will not be finally decided when he ends his term on June 30, 2016 -- the inevitable conclusion reached by CJ's last three columns. There is one exception: the ouster of then-CJ Renato Corona was completed on May 29, 2012 when the Senate issued its guilty verdict, instantly final; Corona relinquished office without challenging via SC certiorari. However, his tax-evasion and perjury raps, like all other daang matuwid filings including the PDAF second and third batches, will not be finally resolved by June 30, 2016. What will happen to all these cases? On a broader scale, what is the future of the straight path? Where will it lead? 'Quo vadis daang matuwid?' Daang matuwid's future will rest on the new president to be elected on May 9, 2016 -- though the Ombudsman and SC are deeply involved, investigation, prosecution, and speedy resolution will depend largely on the new president. 'Let me count the reasons.' First, the new president will appoint a new Secretary of Justice and a new Solicitor General. The daang matuwid cases were initiated, investigated, and filed by the DOJ Secretary in the Ombudsman or in the courts; the DOJ Secretary gathered and preserved evidence and granted immunity to key witnesses under the Witness Protection Program. If the new DOJ Secretary will not tend to the cases diligently, they will probably 'wither and die.' The SolGen is counsel of DOJ and Ombudsman when cases reach the appellate courts; a lackadaisical SolGen will also mean death for these cases. Second, Ombudsman Conchita Carpio Morales will end her seven-year term on July 28, 2018; the Constitution bars reappointment. Being solely responsible for filing and prosecuting graft cases against top officials, the new appointee's courage, independence, diligence, and probity will be crucial. By Morales' retirement, the cases she nurtured will probably not yet mature to final judgment -- her successor will need 'big feet to fit into the big shoes she would leave.' Recall that the SBN Special Division took six years of continuous trial before judging Estrada's plunder; had he appealed to the SC instead of accepting a pardon, the case would have dragged a few more years. Third, 11 of the 15 incumbent SC justices will reach compulsory retirement age of 70 during the next president's six-year term -- the next president will therefore name their replacements. Justices are expected to be independent of the appointing authority, but a president always appoints magistrates to propel his/her vision of governance. A new president passionate in pursuing the anticorruption campaign will naturally name magistrates as passionate in ridding society of graft. Justices have wide discretion in determining probable cause, strong evidence, or proof beyond reasonable doubt -- this is why they often disagree. Even in the US, appointment of new justices is dependent on ideological compatibility: Republicans appoint 'conservatives,' Democrats choose 'liberals' (see CJ's July 12 and 19, 2015 columns). The 11 retiring justices: in 2016 -- Martin Villarama Jr. (April 14), Jose Perez (Dec 14), Arturo Brion (Dec 29); in 2017 -- Bienvenido Reyes (July 6), Jose Mendoza (Aug 13); in 2018 -- Presbitero Velasco Jr. (Aug 8), Teresita De Castro (Oct 8); in 2019 -- Mariano del Castillo (July 29), Francis Jardeleza (Sept 26), Lucas Bersamin (Oct 18), Antonio Carpio (Oct 26). Only CJ Sereno, Justices Peralta, Bernabe, and Leonen will not be replaced by the new president. Peralta will retire on March 27, 2022 and Bernabe on May 14, 2022, within the last few months of the new president's term -- but the Constitution bars any appointment 'two months immediately before the next presidential elections up to the end of (the president's) term.' The same bar on 'midnight appointments' precludes P-Noy from naming Villarama's successor (April 14, 2016, within the two-month prohibition) -- though Villarama can retire voluntarily ahead of this period, allowing P-Noy to appoint his successor. Clearly, with prudent use of appointing power, the new president could change the face of the SC, which in turn could effect sweeping reforms in our justice system. It takes both people and system to neutralize the 'ACID' problems that corrode justice: (1) Access to justice by the poor, (2) Corruption, (3) Incompetence of some judges, (4) Delay in the delivery of quality justice. Like the economy, judicial reforms need time and effort to mature, bear fruit, and become truly inclusive.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes that the recent 'exposé' of Sen. Antonio Trillanes IV denouncing an alleged P50-million payoff in the procurement of a TRO and writ of preliminary injunction -- which both stopped the suspension of Makati Mayor Jejomar Binay Jr. -- shook the Court of Appeals like an intensity-7 earthquake. The attack was especially painful to Justice Jose C. Reyes Jr., who enjoys a heretofore unblemished reputation for honesty and probity; CA members and employees look up to him as a model of uprightness and competence. If for this reason alone, Trillanes should back his attack with some proof. True, it is quite difficult to secure documents like receipts or checks because in bribery cases cash is usually passed without paper -- but a credible witness will do. Sometimes the consideration is not cash but a precious object or some unfriendly persuasion: a promised promotion, complimentary airline ticket, paid hospital or medical bill, or compromising photo -- anything that shows the magistrate has been infected by what CJP calls the plague of 'ships': kinship, relationship, friendship and fellowship. The Supreme Court, vested with sole power to discipline members of the judiciary, will welcome some kind of prima facie proof (not necessarily conclusive) to initiate an inquiry. Trillanes may have been well-intentioned, but his mere say-so with nothing more is not enough -- otherwise magistrates would be in constant jeopardy of losing their reputation on unsubstantiated allegations and could lose their moral ascendancy to dispense justice. The SC has investigated and penalized members of the judiciary even without formal charges, provided some proof or leads of wrongdoing, because the quantum of proof in administrative cases is only 'substantial evidence,' not 'proof beyond reasonable doubt.' The case of Sandiganbayan Justice Gregory S. Ong is a good example. Taking a cue from a Senate blue ribbon committee inquiry on the pork barrel scam indicating prima facie violation of the Judicial Code of Conduct, and from an article by investigative writer Aries Rufo published in Rappler showing a photograph of Ong with Sen. Jinggoy Estrada and Janet Lim Napoles, CJ Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno asked the SC to conduct an investigation motu proprio. After receiving Ong's comment, the Court directed retired Justice Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez to look into Ong's link to Napoles; Gutierrez subpoenaed pork-barrel whistleblowers Benhur Luy and Marina Sula, writer Rufo, and Ong himself. Gutierrez found that Napoles was acquitted by the SBN Fourth Division -- chaired by Ong -- in a case involving the questionable purchase of Kevlar helmets by the PH Marine Corps from five companies owned by Napoles. Luy testified that Napoles 'gave various amounts to different people during the pendency of the case which lasted up to ten years. And before the decision in the Kevlar case was released, she also gave money to respondent (Ong) but she did not mention the amount.' Sula corroborated that Ong visited Napoles' office twice sometime in 2012 and that Napoles would tell her staff that Justice Ong would help her in the Kevlar case. Despite Ong's hearsay objection, Gutierrez held Luy and Sula 'testified in a candid, straightforward and categorical manner... carried the ring of truth,' ruling that Ong's act of allowing himself to be Napoles' contact in the SBN, the fixing of the Kevlar case, and accepting money from her constituted gross misconduct; his picture with an accused in his court 'manifests respondent's disregard of the dictum that propriety and the appearance of propriety are essential to promote public confidence in the integrity of the Judiciary.' Upholding her findings, the SC found Ong 'GUILTY of GROSS MISCONDUCT, DISHONESTY and IMPROPRIETY, all in violation of the New Code of Conduct for the Philippine Judiciary' (capital letters in original) -- dismissed from service with forfeiture of all retirement benefits except accrued leave credits, with prejudice to reemployment in government. CJP details the Ong case to show that the SC, even without direct evidence but with a modicum of proof showing only 'substantial evidence,' has shown willingness to penalize erring magistrates -- and by the same passion will not tolerate, and will sanction, reckless imputations of wrongdoing. In sum, fairness demands that Senator Trillanes produce some proof to back his serious charge of graft. If he cannot, the least he can do is admit his lapse promptly and apologize publicly to the CA justices.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with the famous prayer of St. Francis of Assisi -- 'Lord, make me an instrument of your peace...' -- noting that although Catholic in origin, it has been invoked by both Catholics and non-Catholics (former US president Bill Clinton, former British prime minister Margaret Thatcher), immortalized in movies (like 'Rambo') and TV serials (like 'Band of Brothers'), and magnified in countless tunes, dances and dramas. Since the beginning of time, peace has been the elusive quest and eternal aspiration of humankind. It is also the desideratum of the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro and the proposed Bangsamoro Basic Law. However, before real peace can be attained, CJ thinks there must first be justice; and before justice can be reached, there must first be truth. The search for truth is conducted with varied aims and employs varied methods crafted precisely to achieve those aims. First, congressional investigations are held 'in aid of legislation' -- there are no opposing parties, no complainants and respondents, not even witnesses, only 'resource persons' who are invited (or sometimes subpoenaed) to shed light on facts and events to assist Congress in its task of legislation. This is exemplified by the current much-publicized investigations in the Senate and in the House, conducted with the aim of discovering gaps and lapses that attended the killing of 44 Special Action Force officers in Mamasapano, Maguindanao. These inquiries may show the need for laws appropriating more funds for the armory and training of the police, or requiring better coordination among the country's armed units, or providing more stringent safeguards for the BBL. The methodology in congressional inquiries is not 'adversarial' in nature; resource persons are not given the opportunity to cross-examine those who may have linked them to crimes, malfeasance, or irregularities; the questions asked by lawmakers are many times misleading, complex or argumentative -- they will not pass judicial standards. Since the aim is not prosecution or conviction and the methodology is not adversarial, the truth arrived at is limited in its scope; it is not enough to convict anyone of any crime, though it may suffice for impeachment, which is more of a political than a legal process. While Congress can recommend the prosecution of crimes, it cannot by itself prosecute, much less convict. Sometimes legislative investigations, though one-sided, show incontrovertible or admitted incompetence or misfeasance so overwhelming and so damning that the public officials concerned are constrained to resign, like Philippine National Police Chief Alan Purisima. Second, if the purpose of the search for truth is to discover crimes and to indict possible criminals, then it is the Department of Justice or the Office of the Ombudsman -- not Congress -- that conducts the investigation. Here the methodology is different: the respondents are given the opportunity to defend themselves before they are criminally indicted. Third, should 'probable cause' be found, the DOJ or OOO shall file the proper charges in our courts of law, where the methods of searching for the truth are more stringent: the accused are given the chance to defend themselves, to cross-examine the witnesses against them, and to avail themselves of the constitutional guarantee that 'no person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law, nor shall any person be denied the equal protection of the laws.' Fourth, the search for truth is also conducted by the Board of Inquiry of the Philippine National Police; since its goal is not legislation or prosecution or conviction of a crime but the improvement of the police service, its methodology is simpler. From these searches for truth comes justice in terms of resignation for the conscience-stricken, remedial legislation, streamlining of military processes, and administrative and judicial sanctions for the guilty. These verities of truth and justice are not inconsistent with the peace goals of the BBL -- in fact, CJ dares say that a BBL that prudently takes them into account will lead to more lasting peace for all. In a postscript that foreshadows B06 and B17, CJ announces that the Asean Law Association will hold its general assembly at the Makati Shangri-La hotel on February 26-28, with over 300 jurists, academics, and practicing lawyers from the 10 Asean countries (Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Myanmar, Malaysia, Philippines, Thailand, Singapore, and Vietnam) attending. With the theme 'Sharing Prosperity at the Crossroads of Asean Integration -- the Legal Challenges,' the assembly will be keynoted by Chief Justice Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno, who will later host a 'Summit of Chief Justices' on March 1-3 in Boracay. CJP has been invited to address the opening luncheon on February 26. Based on the rotational system, this year marks the turn of the Philippines to assume the ALA leadership: the ALA Philippine Chapter has nominated Accra Law's founding partner Avelino V. Cruz to succeed Indonesian Chief Justice Hatta Ali as ALA's president for 2015-2017. The ALA conferences are sponsored by the Supreme Court, the ALA Philippine Chapter, and the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers the foundational ACID-mnemonic column in the corpus -- chronologically the earliest ACID-mnemonic attestation, predating A375 (Aug 2 2015) by ~10 months. Together with Sen. Grace Poe and Rep. Leni Robredo, CJ addressed the 'Integrity Summit' last week at the Dusit Thani Hotel in Makati. He was invited to speak on how to stop corruption and reform the judiciary, and began his address with two anecdotes. Tale of two judges (1): Before the trial in a case began, the judge summoned the lawyers of the parties to his chambers. He told them: 'Compañeros, both of you surreptitiously bribed me. You, counsel for the plaintiff, gave me P250,000, while you, counsel for the defendant, sent me P200,000. I will not allow anyone of you to unduly influence me. So, I am returning P50,000 to you, counsel for the plaintiff. Now, after I have leveled the playing field, both of you can expect equal treatment from me.' Tale of two judges (2): Another judge was visited at his home by a practicing lawyer. 'Compañero,' the magistrate boomed, 'why are you here? Don't you know it is unethical for a lawyer to speak with a judge outside the courtroom?' Meekly the lawyer explained: 'Your Honor, I did not come here to speak with you about my pending case. I came here to sell you a brand-new Mercedes Benz that is now parked on your driveway.' After peeping out the window to view the car, the judge retorted, 'Ah, you came as a car salesman, not as a lawyer. How much is the car?' The enterprising lawyer whispered, 'The price is P1,000, Your Honor.' The judge smiled and said, 'In that case, I'll buy two, one for me and one for my wife.' These stories are anecdotal and meant to be jokes -- but they demonstrate some of the witchcraft that may have impelled the Makati Business Club (MBC) and the European Chamber of Commerce of the Philippines (ECCP) to sponsor this Integrity Summit. The first joke shows the wrong way to level the playing field; the second shows the no-way to justify a bribe. How to stop corruption: judges will not be bribed unless clients inveigle their lawyers to go beyond the outer limits of advocacy and soar to the stratosphere of corruption and malevolence. At times, lawyers are told by unscrupulous clients: 'I do not care whether you know the law. My question is: Do you know the judge?' CJ could really end his address now -- he has already explained how the business community can stop corruption. Remember, there are no bribe-takers when there are no bribe-givers. However, CJ has been tasked by MBC president Ramon del Rosario Jr. to bore the audience with a long peroration on how to properly level the playing field and how to properly solve corruption, and help the nation prosper through judicial reforms. Whenever judicial reform is the topic, CJ is always reminded of the comprehensive 'Action Program for Judicial Reform' (APJR) started by his esteemed predecessor, CJ Hilario G. Davide Jr., in 1998. The APJR was supported not only by the PH government but also by international aid institutions; it was so successful that the World Bank uploaded it on its website as a model for all developing countries applying for WB assistance. ACID problems: during CJ's term as chief justice, he continued the APJR with emphasis on what he calls the ACID problems that corrode justice. During his incumbency, he announced his 'Vision and Mission' as follows: 'I vow to lead a judiciary characterized by four Ins: Integrity, Independence, Industry and Intelligence -- one that is morally courageous to resist influence, interference, indifference and insolence. I envision a judiciary that is impervious to the plague of ships -- kinship, relationship, friendship and fellowship. I pledge to continue and strengthen the Supreme Court's ongoing Action Program for Judicial Reforms with special focus on what I call the ACID problems that corrode justice in our country; namely, (1) limited Access to justice by the poor; (2) Corruption; (3) Incompetence, and (4) Delay in the delivery of quality justice. I look for competent and ethical lawyers who are responsible, dependable, and morally upright, and who courageously uphold truth and justice above everything else. I shall grant maximum financial and fringe benefits to our 26,000 employees nationwide from whom, in turn, I ask for three things: (1) Dedication to duty, (2) Honesty in every way, and (3) full Loyalty to the judiciary, or DHL. All the foregoing visions and objectives must lead to the loftier goals of safeguarding the liberty and nurturing the prosperity of our people. The twin beacons of LIBERTY and PROSPERITY constitute my core judicial philosophy.' To propel this philosophy, CJ convened the 'Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity' in Makati on October 18-20, 2006, as his valedictory project prior to retirement. Led by the chief justices of Canada, Russia, France, and several others, over 300 jurists, lawyers, and law professors from all over the world attended this conference. Unfortunately, CJ's successors in office did not continue both CJ Davide's and his judicial reform initiatives. Consequently, the aid agencies discontinued their assistance; the World Bank deleted the APJR from its website. Fortunately, the current Court saw the need for judicial reforms along the lines of APJR and ACID, but with its own modifications and updates -- already, the World Bank, Asian Development Bank, and other aid agencies have shown renewed interest in helping. For lack of space, CJ has to end here -- but for those interested, his complete speech may be accessed at cjpanganiban.com, then click 'Speeches.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the second half of his two-part jails series -- a deeply personal field-report-as-pastoral-reflection following E98 (Aug 3) which had described the subhuman conditions of Philippine jails. A gathering of convicts: the most surprising reaction to CJ's column last Sunday came from an ex-convict who had served his 20-year sentence -- he reminded CJ of a handwritten note he gave him during CJ's visit as a sitting member of the Supreme Court at the New Bilibid Prison (NBP) in Muntinlupa City over a decade ago. The SC's security team had advised CJ to decline the invitation to visit the NBP. However, CJ decided to accept it after attending a Mass in which the Gospel reading was Matthew 25:31-46 -- about the Final Judgment, about our Lord asking whether His disciples visited Him when He was in prison. CJ told himself, 'better to risk the ire of the inmates than to risk the ire of the Lord!' And so, one sunny afternoon, CJ motored to Muntinlupa -- the first and, as far as he knows, the only incumbent member of the highest court of the land to set foot on this notorious home of criminals. CJ was pleasantly surprised at the sheer size of the penitentiary. Imposing, high-walled and barbed-wired was the building housing the maximum-security inmates; around this concrete behemoth was a vast tract of land planted with fruit trees and shrubs. CJ was ushered to a makeshift 'auditorium' on the greenery outside the forbidding building where some 500 inmates were seated; they broke into thunderous applause while gawking at their visitor. Their prison band played 'Mabuhay' as CJ entered, and the Philippine National Anthem to begin the convocation; a solemn invocation soon followed. CJ was genuinely entertained by the talent show -- especially a comedy skit about life in jail -- and some 20 inmates enlivened the program with folk dances and hip-hop. At the end, they asked CJ to speak. He began by asking how many of them he had personally judged. About 30 sheepishly raised their hands, to the whistles of the rest. Then he cautiously asked how many of them felt they had been wrongly sentenced. To CJ's great relief, he saw no raised hand. CJ spoke boldly of hope. He said that iron bars may restrict their movements and may subject them to ostracism and ridicule, and that nonetheless, they should not hate the world and lose their faith. He explained in Filipino: 'Iba't iba po ang mga kulungan. Dito po sa Muntinlupa, rehas na bakal ang kulungan. Ang mas mahirap na kulungan ay ang kulungan ng kaisipan tulad ng mga luko-luko at kulang-kulang; kulungan ng katawan tulad ng mga lumpo; at kulungan ng tiyak na kamatayan tulad ng mga may terminal cancer. Ang mga kapansanang ito ay higit mahirap harapin. Walang gamut para sa kulang-kulang at sa cancer. Samantalang ang mga nasa loob ng rehas na bakal ay mayroon laging pag-asa, sapagka't may taning ang kanilang kulungan. At maaari pang mabawasan ang sentencia sa pagpapakita ng mabuting asal at pagreporma.' Those imprisoned behind bars, he said, have real hope because one day after serving their sentences, they would be freed; in fact, with good behavior, their penalties could be commuted, or they could even be pardoned -- but those imprisoned by greed, by feeble minds, by incurable illness, or by lame bodies could be condemned to pain and suffering all their lives. Difficult questions: as CJ ended his speech, the inmates gave him a standing ovation; some of them handed him handwritten letters. One of them gave CJ a note in Filipino which he now translates to English: 'Isn't it true that all the commandments of the Lord can be summed up in one sentence, Love God and love your fellow beings? Why then did you have to consign me to prison? Contrast this with the way our Church treats sinners. After confessing my sins, the priest merely counseled me, then asked me to pray the rosary and forgave me. Why didn't you just follow my confessor's example? Why did you have to jail me?' It was late already, and CJ didn't have the time to read his note. But his letter now begs CJ to answer his decade-old questions. CJ will begin with Matthew 25, the Gospel reading that inspired him to visit the NBP. Here, the Lord was judging His people, separating the sheep from the goats, placing 'the sheep on His right' and 'the goats on His left'; those who refused to give food to the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, visit the sick and the imprisoned, He condemned to 'eternal punishment,' and those who did, He promised 'eternal life.' CJ believes that just as there are human and physical laws, there are also spiritual laws -- just as there are consequences for the violation of human and physical laws, there are penalties for the violation of God's laws. For example, civil laws protect the sanctity of contracts, and a party who breaks them can be held liable for damages; one who injures another violates criminal laws and is jailed as a consequence; so too, a violation of the laws of physics impels consequences -- hence, when one jumps out of a window, one falls to the ground in accordance with the law of gravity. Similarly, spiritual laws operate on our spirit whether we like it or not -- when we transgress the Lord's commandments, our spirit suffers the consequences by being damned in eternity; just as there are reparations for violation of human and physical laws, there is also salvation from our sins, by repentance, restitution and reformation -- the three Rs of salvation.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens his two-part jails series with a field-report-style indictment of Philippine detention conditions, triggered by the Napoles-Reyes BJMP-Bicutan transfer brouhaha. The brouhaha over the transfer of Janet Lim Napoles and Jessica 'Gigi' Reyes (accused of plunder related to the PDAF scam) to the detention facilities of the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) in Bicutan, Taguig brought to public focus the decrepit, congested and subhuman condition of our jails. Jails for the high-profile: since Sept 1, 2013, Napoles had been confined at the tolerable facilities of Fort Santo Domingo in Sta Rosa, Laguna, upon orders of the Makati RTC where she is facing trial for the serious illegal detention (kidnapping) of Benhur Luy, the principal whistle-blower in the multibillion-peso PDAF mess. However, the Sandiganbayan (a higher court) ordered her confinement at the BJMP jail because Fort Santo Domingo 'is not a detention facility for those facing trial.' Napoles is charged with serious illegal detention and plunder, both 'nonbailable.' Reyes was originally detained at the basement of the Sandiganbayan building in Quezon City, in a 23-square-meter cell equipped with a single bed, a small kitchen sink, a toilet and an electric fan; she was the first occupant of this new facility built in December 2013. A few hours after her transfer to the congested BJMP female dormitory, Reyes suffered a 'panic attack,' hypertension and neurocirculatory asthenia, prompting her jailers to rush her to the Taguig-Pateros District Hospital and later to the Philippine Heart Center in Quezon City; allegedly, she abhorred the prospect of being cooped up with suspected female members of the New People's Army. Reyes wanted to be moved to the much more comfortable PNP Custodial Center where Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Ramon Revilla, also charged with plunder, are confined; their coaccused, Sen. Juan Ponce Enrile, is detained at the PNP General Hospital due to his advanced age (90 years) and frail health. Government prosecutors have lately asked the SBN to transfer both Estrada and Revilla to a regular jail; the two lawmakers objected, arguing they 'are not hardened criminals' and that, being 'high-profile' inmates who need more security, they are allegedly entitled to the PNP Custodial Center. Jails for the no-profile: on the other hand, ordinary accused are detained in decrepit city and provincial jails overcrowded by an average of 400 percent. Specifically, jail warden Elena Rocamora told the Sandiganbayan that the female dormitory in the Quezon City Jail, where prosecutors originally wanted Reyes to be detained, is crammed with 504 detainees yet its rated capacity is only for 56 -- it is 800 percent overcrowded. Elsewhere, the overcrowding is the same -- the Manila City Jail, built to hold 1,000 inmates, actually houses over 5,000; it is so congested that inmates stand up most of the time and take turns to lie down to sleep. Minors, who should be under the care of the DSWD, are mixed with murder suspects. Detainees sleep on the cement floor, wear uniforms of yellow T-shirts and brown pants, make do with a daily meal allowance (for breakfast, lunch and dinner) of P50, and line up for hours in communal toilet/baths. CJ stresses that detainees in city and provincial jails are not convicted felons -- they are put behind bars either because they are charged with capital offenses or, more often, even though charged with bailable crimes, they are unable to produce the needed bail bond due to sheer poverty or plain ignorance of their right to bail. The BJMP, under the DILG, manages the detention facilities while the Bureau of Corrections (BuCor), under the DOJ, runs the National Penitentiary and other correctional institutions where convicts by final judgments are held. Reforms needed: needless to say, reforms are urgently needed to alleviate these subhuman conditions. Convicts are 'luckier' than the presumed innocents because a year ago, on May 24, 2013, PNoy signed into law Republic Act No. 10575 that upgraded the BuCor's prison facilities, increased the number and pay of prison guards, and established the Philippine Prisons Academy to educate prisoners and guards. To decongest the BJMP's jails, the SC issued a resolution last May 18 limiting trials to only 180 days (see CJ's July 13 column / A406 for details); in addition to the speedy implementation of this time limit, trial judges should prioritize the cases of detainees, especially of minors, who cannot post bail -- many times they are detained longer than the prescribed penalty for the offenses they are charged with. Of course, jail wardens should turn over minors to the DSWD and should not mix them with recidivists; they should not forget that detention prisoners are not convicts -- they are detained only to ensure their presence in court (for those charged with capital offenses) or, to repeat, only for their inability to post bail bonds (for those charged with bailable crimes) due to poverty or ignorance of their right to bail. Compelling and urgent is the need to build more and better detention facilities worthy of human dignity, remembering always that the average conviction rate of prosecutors is only about 20 percent -- thus, a vast majority of detention prisoners have a more-than-even chance of being acquitted, yet they are unjustly deprived of their liberty.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the fourth installment of his automated-elections quadrilogy -- three weeks after E100 (the vote-now column), two weeks after A458 (the installment-proclamation indictment), and one week after B19 (the FDI-trustworthiness column) -- turning to the human beneficiaries of PCOS automation and acknowledging the poll watchdogs who critiqued it. Public school teachers, whom the Comelec always deputizes to administer the polls at the precinct level, are the big winners of the PCOS (precinct count optical scan) automated system -- no longer required to tally manually the election results, they were spared from harrowing physical work, nighttime terror threats and tedious legal hassles. No manual tallying: under the old manual system, the teachers remained at the polling places after the voting had closed, often into the wee hours of the following morning, to count manually the handwritten entries on each ballot and to enter them in 'taras' on tally boards and score sheets; sometimes, these written entries were illegible, or appear to have been prepared by two different hands, making the ballot invalid; at other times, the candidates' names were written on the wrong spaces, as when aspirants for mayor surfaced on the spaces for vice mayor; and many times, some extraneous writings or strange drawings were scribbled on the ballots, making them suspects as 'marked ballots' -- these markings were used by bribers to verify the votes of their 'victims'; of course, the ensuing legalistic 'objections' from lawyers confounded the teachers and interminably delayed the count. All these tedious difficulties were eliminated by automation because the machines tallied the ballots instantly and transmitted the results electronically to the municipal or city boards of canvassers, sparing the teachers not only from the long horrifying process, but also from physically carrying the election documents and the ballot boxes from remote polling places to the town centers in the dead of night. (CJ is not unmindful of the fact that due to transmission glitches in many -- as many as 18,000 of the 78,000 -- PCOS machines, several teachers unfortunately had to bring the compact flash cards and/or the machines themselves to the election centers.) No legal hassles: because the PCOS count at the precinct level happened faster than the speed of knowledge, the old technical delays became obsolete -- teachers no longer needed to pass upon befuddling verbal skirmishes while tallying the ballots at the polling places; under the automated system, the election returns were no longer manually prepared by the teachers who were thus spared from signing, sealing, packing and locking them inside the ballot boxes; consequently, they could no longer be blamed and sued by nosy lawyers and desperate candidates looking for scapegoats for their defeat -- they no longer need to defend themselves from false or malicious charges of bias or complicity in election frauds. Because of the speedy electronic preparation of the election returns, there is no more time to question their genuineness, or the authenticity of the entries therein; thus, under the automated system, there are no more preproclamation controversies, which were the scourge of teachers because they were often bribed or threatened or forced to falsify election returns, which were to be used as evidence in these preproclamation suits -- testifying during these contests is harrowing, and at the very least, very demanding on the teachers' time. Other winners: also big winners are the PPCRV led by Ambassador Tita de Villa and the other poll watchdogs, notably the AES Watch, Kontra Daya, and Namfrel; PPCRV conducted two parallel counts: (1) electronic and (2) manual -- the manual count was based on the paper election returns printed by the PCOS machines at the precincts prior to their electronic transmission; PPCRV collected these printed returns and used them to validate and verify the electronically transmitted ones; the manual count will be the final check on the accuracy of the automated canvass, which by the way, PPCRV was not allowed to complete when the Comelec started its own canvass of the senatorial and party-list candidates; it has a volunteer army of 350,000 who staffed the precincts all over the country, guarding not just the automation process but also the traditional 'guns, goons and gold' irregularities that automation could not eliminate. AES Watch, Kontra Daya and Namfrel kept the Comelec and Smartmatic on their toes, monitoring closely the entire automation process; special credit should be accorded them for bringing to public attention the PCOS malfunctions, particularly the transmission glitches in 18,000 out of the 78,000 machines; despite the ballistic tantrums, dismissive attitude and threats of suits of Comelec Chair Sixto Brillantes Jr., these watchdogs gallantly stood their ground and kept the public updated on the election hitches -- the nation owes them an everlasting debt of gratitude. It is CJ's hope, as it is the hope of everyone concerned with the viability of our democracy, that the watchdogs continue critiquing and reviewing the automation -- the PCOS system had been given two electoral chances to show its worth, but it has not been flawless; it has not delivered its promised 99.99% efficiency; many of the present election commissioners, including Brillantes, will no longer be on the saddle come the 2016 elections -- but CJ trusts Gus Lagman, Joe Dizon and their fellow reformers will pursue the same patriotic zeal to dissect the PCOS system, and in the alternative, to help the new Comelec replace it with a better and more reliable one in light of lessons learned in the 2010 and 2013 elections.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the first installment of his automated-elections quadrilogy -- published the day before May 13 Election Day -- opening the entire arc with a pragmatic 'let us all go out and vote' civic-duty call, balancing his acknowledgment of PCOS criticisms against his historical-precedent confidence. Despite scathing criticisms damning the PCOS system, the automated elections will be held tomorrow (Monday) as scheduled -- let us all go out and vote. Major criticism: the critics' main complaint is that the PCOS system lacks transparency, making it very vulnerable to fraud and manipulation -- from the time the ballot is inserted into the machine until the winners are known, the counting, transmission and canvass are done faster than the speed of knowledge in total secrecy without human intervention, thereby preempting any lawyerly 'Objection!'; compounding the secrecy is the failure of the Comelec to open the source code for review at least six months prior to the casting of ballots, as mandated by law; that the source code was made available a few days ago gives critics little comfort because it can no longer be tested and scrutinized before Election Day; and if corrupted, it can no longer be exposed and corrected on time. Critics also lament the use of rewritable compact flash (CF) cards, thereby allowing the embedded program to be altered; they aver that the fraud-proof WORM (write-once-read-many) CF types should have been procured; inserted into each of the 82,000 PCOS machines, the CF cards are programmed to read the names of the local candidates printed on the ballots in specific towns and cities -- once corrupted, they would not be able to read the 'precinct-specific' ballots. The adamant refusal of Comelec Chair Sixto Brillantes Jr. to conduct a parallel manual count to countercheck the secretive electronic count, and his sequestration of the random manual audit (RMA) to only one per legislative district, aggravate the critics no end -- worse, the Comelec chief's justification for his aversion to a parallel count (that a manual count will not match the electronic count) boggles them into concluding that the PCOS system is unreliable and should not have been adopted in the first place. These criticisms are not really new -- they were aired during the 2010 presidential election; nonetheless, CJ agrees that, ideally, they should have been addressed, settled and cured by the Comelec during the last three years; that would have quieted down the criticisms and ensured more credible 2013 elections. Orderly and peaceful: having said that, CJ nonetheless believes that, barring unforeseen circumstances beyond the Comelec's control, the elections tomorrow will be generally peaceful, orderly and credible -- why? Definitely and most assuredly, the preparations for this year's elections are better than the previous one in 2010 when the CF cards had to be hurriedly replaced 10 days prior to Election Day, and when logistical nightmares (like the hodgepodge delivery of 'precinct-specific' ballots) threatened the viability of the election; during the 2010 polls, there were genuine fears that, should automation fail, no new president would be elected (no-el) and proclaimed (no-proc), thereby enabling GMA to hold over indefinitely, or military adventurers to take over amid the electoral vacuum; this time, these dire scenarios are nowhere -- the presidency is not at stake, and even if automation fails, the government can continue functioning. Despite all these criticisms and the Comelec's sloppy preparation, the 2010 exercise turned out well and the overall results were accepted by the people and by most defeated candidates -- to his eternal credit, second-placer Joseph Ejercito Estrada acknowledged the People Power tsunami and promptly conceded the presidency to Benigno Aquino III, a tribute to him and to the much-maligned PCOS automation system; notably, none of the election protests filed in the Comelec and the House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal belied the PCOS counts -- true, there were minor glitches here and there, but no electoral protest succeeded in discrediting the automated count. Parallel manual count: the delay in the review of the source code is not a legal ground to stop or annul the elections; Brillantes repeatedly assured our people that the binary code, the machine-readable equivalent of the human-readable source code, is already embedded in the CF cards that will run the PCOS system -- CJ thinks Smartmatic and Dominion, the hardware and software suppliers of the system, will not risk their worldwide automation businesses by delivering a defective source code; Brillantes's reluctance to conduct a parallel manual count is understandable -- a parallel count is not only expensive and tedious but also confusing and troublesome; the manual count will not always match the electronic count simply because different rules of appreciation govern the two counting systems -- for example, the PCOS machines are programmed to read shaded ovals and will not count 'checked' ones; on the other hand, a checked oval shows the voter's intention to vote; hence, a manual count will include it; machines will always count as programmed, but humans are not 'programmable' and will not count like automatons. Automation hastens the counting and canvassing, and lessens the opportunity for human machinations -- but it is not completely fraud-proof or error-free; neither will it eliminate 'guns, goons and gold' and vote-buying; but all these risks should not deter us from casting our ballots tomorrow -- CJ invites the proponents and critics of the PCOS system to lay aside their verbal wars temporarily, go to the polls early, queue up patiently, shade their ballots carefully, and choose our leaders wisely and peacefully.

He reproduces SCA's two signature prayers: the opening Prayer of Generosity by St. Ignatius ('to give without counting the cost; to fight without counting the wounds') and the closing Radiating Christ by Cardinal Newman ('let me preach You without preaching -- not by my words but by example'). Founded in 1936 by Fr. Edward McCarthy and reaching its Golden Age under Fr. Michael Nolan (archdiocesan spiritual director until his death at age 40 in 1964) with Columban and Jesuit guidance, SCA became CJ's formative institution: recruited by Fr. Nolan, the 'rebellious young man' had his 'personal rebellion expertly canalized into constructive endeavors' -- most notably organizing the National Union of Students. CJ acknowledges growing up a 'Catholic ignoramus' with parents who also did not know their faith, titling his contribution to the book 'SCA Introduced Me to Christ.' The organization was suppressed by martial law in 1972 and never fully recovered its luster, though it still operates in about 32 dioceses under National Chaplain Bishop Rolando Tria Tirona (himself an SCAn from San Beda).

one_paragraph_summary: Responding to two readers who challenged him to demonstrate his judicial self-restraint thesis, Panganiban mounts a two-ground rebuttal of the Gamboa v. Teves (June 28, 2011) majority's 'beneficial ownership' conclusion. First, it is not legal: the Constitution does not speak of dividends or how much each type of share should earn -- it speaks only of control of public utility corporations, not 'beneficial ownership.' Second, it is not logical: the majority noted PLDT preferred shares earn P1 while common shares earn P70 -- but failed to compute actual rates of return. By CJ's calculation, a preferred shareholder earns ~9% per peso invested (P1 on ~P11 market price); a common shareholder earns only ~3% (P70 on P2,328 market price). Preferred shares earn three times more than common shares. Par values are not determinative of real worth; investors buy based on risk appetite -- conservatives prefer preferred (fixed, like bank deposits); the adventurous choose common (potentially exponential growth, as with Microsoft/Gates, or PLDT under Pangilinan -- net income from P3.4B in 2001 to P34B in 2005 and P40B in 2010 while the common share price rose from P417 to P2,554). Common shares can also collapse, as in 1997 and 2008. Business is about taking and managing risks -- not for jurists to intrude into unnecessarily. CJ closes with a tribute to Justice Morales's appointment as Ombudsman -- the longest and most thunderous ovation at P-Noy's SONA -- saying that despite their few differences on economic issues, he has never doubted her probity, integrity, independence and love of country.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reports that 8.5 million OFWs across 194 countries remitted $18.7 billion in 2010 (BSP data), keeping the Philippine economy afloat more than anyone else. Yet despite four decades of overseas employment experience and two landmark laws (RA 8042 and RA 10022), OFWs remain 'almost always shabbily treated' -- good laws with bad results. While he can understand the government's difficulty responding to crises caused by wars in Egypt, Tunisia, Libya, and Japan's earthquake/tsunami, he cannot fathom its neglect of problems arising from Philippine shores: as illustrated by the Stella Gonzales exit-permit ordeal (former Inquirer staffer and current Financial Times of London editor subjected to useless forms and desk-to-desk shuttling for a dubious exit permit that immigration officers at the airport did not even look at -- of doubtful constitutionality). There is no systematic coordinated mechanism for dispatch response before issues become crises; labor attaches are not selected by qualification and lack proper orientation for rigorous 24/7 OFW welfare work. By contrast, Migrante International -- operating a website with an online complaint form -- is typically the first to know and publicly raise OFW problems (e.g., Saudization/Nitaqat work restrictions in Saudi Arabia), responding without diplomatic red tape. CJ noted he wrote extensively on OFW laments in early 2008 -- but to this day, the problems remain. DOLE must reinvent itself and implement permanent solutions rather than repeat skin-deep Bagong Bayani acclamations.

Roxas's personal clout remains intact -- his friendship with P-Noy was 'forged in platinum'; Roxas set aside his own presidential ambitions and VP campaign after Cory Aquino's death to concentrate on P-Noy's victory. CJ closes: given Roxas's demonstrated political, diplomatic, and technocratic skills, he will come out the clean hero -- 'If he cannot solve the problems, I wonder who can.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban maps the six 'essential generals' of P-Noy's war on corruption: the DoJ and OSG (executive-controlled) and the OMB, COA, SBN, and SC (constitutionally independent). He notes that while Justice Secretary de Lima is 'the spark plug' of the anti-graft engine, the DoJ cannot prosecute -- only the OMB can. He highlights the OMB's unique power: it decides alone (vs SC's collegial action) and can suspend or fire officials alone -- making it more powerful than a single SC justice. After Merceditas Gutierrez's sudden resignation, P-Noy has the opportunity to name a new ombudsman. He can also name a new SBN presiding justice when Justice Sandoval retires June 20. On the SC, P-Noy faces a mathematical constraint: he can appoint only four justices in the normal course (one already done -- Justice Sereno; two more as Justices Nachura and Carpio Morales retire; a fourth when Justice Abad turns 70 in May 2014). He cannot appoint a new SC chief because CJ Corona turns 70 only on October 15, 2018 -- way beyond his June 30, 2016 term end. June 2011 is thus a turning point: P-Noy can complete his generals roster with OMB and SBN heads, in addition to DoJ, OSG, and COA (newly headed by Ma. Gracia Pulido-Tan and joined by Commissioner Heidi Mendoza) -- but must 'adjust his battle plans' to the reality that he cannot dominate the SC. CJ rates Solicitor General Cadiz very good and recalls his 2003 IBP inaugural with a 'psychedelic choice of heroes' (Kennedy, Ho Chi Minh, Mandela, Jose Abad Santos), but notes a checkered record thus far -- recommending the OSG be added to the Anti-Corruption Cabinet Cluster for better coordination.

He notes VP Binay's magnanimous 'I am a team player' statement despite not heading any cluster. Responding to lawyer Alentajan's letter arguing that the OMB can bind the Republic as offended party in the Garcia plea bargain like regular fiscals, the author rebuts: fiscals are subalterns of the DOJ Secretary who is the President's alter ego -- they can represent the President; but the OMB is a constitutionally independent office, not under the President's control and supervision, and therefore cannot represent him. In the second section, he recounts First Pacific Company Limited's 30-year rise -- from HK$7 million with six employees in a 50-square-meter Hong Kong office in 1981 (co-founded by Manuel Pangilinan and Anthoni Salim) to US$44.57 billion aggregate market cap with 104,000 employees across multiple industries -- celebrated with a dinner-musicale featuring exclusively Filipino performers. The column closes with a tribute to Alejandro Roces -- National Artist for Literature, the author's student-leadership adviser, and Secretary of Education 1961-65 who retained him as legal counsel right after he passed the bar -- who passed away on May 23, 2011 at 86.
